books.title: The Elements of Style
books.author: William Strunk
books.subject: writing
books.licence_note: The 1918 first edition. Author died 1946. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Strunk held that a short set of firm essentials, learned well, serves a writer better than a long list of rules. He believed that most people get the most from individual guidance based on their own work.

Strunk advised that a learner should follow the standard rules of writing until they can write plain, clear English well. Only after that should they study the great writers for the finer secrets of style.
Strunk noted that skilled writers sometimes break the rules, but usually they gain something in return. Unless you are sure you can do as well, it is safer to keep to the rules.

Strunk's rule is to put a comma after each term in a series of three or more, except the last, so that each item stands clearly apart. He also holds that a parenthetic expression needs commas on both sides, never just one.

Strunk's rule is that a restrictive clause, which identifies the thing it describes, takes no commas, while a non-restrictive clause, which only adds a side remark, is set off by commas. Ask whether the sentence still works if the clause is removed.

Strunk warns that a writer who makes every sentence tight and formal wears out the reader, so an occasional loose sentence gives relief. He also advises replacing a casual so with as or since to make the link between clauses clear.
Strunk holds that two closely related independent clauses may be joined by a semicolon, or split into two sentences, rather than run together with only a comma.
Strunk holds that a semicolon joins two closely related statements, even when a connecting adverb like thus or therefore follows, and that this device is one of the most useful in writing.
Strunk warns that an opening phrase must describe the subject of the sentence, so the writer should check who or what is actually doing the action before writing.
Strunk's rule is to give each topic its own paragraph, since a new paragraph signals to the reader that the subject has moved on to a new step.

Strunk's rule is that a good paragraph opens with a topic sentence, builds on it with explanation or proof, and closes by reinforcing the main point or stating its consequence. Ending on a digression or a trivial detail should be avoided.

Strunk holds that a paragraph should be written so the reader knows its purpose from the first line and keeps that purpose in mind to the end. Transitions like 'therefore' or 'again' can link it to what came before.

Stevenson held that a walking tour is best taken alone, so that you can set your own pace, change direction on a whim, and stay open to whatever you see. Company turns it into something closer to a picnic.

Lecky held that historians in the eighteenth century shifted from simply painting a picture of the past to trying to explain it, tracing chains of causes and effects in the life of whole peoples rather than only their kings.

Strunk suggests that a paragraph often opens with a clear topic sentence that holds the details together. Narrative can drop this and let a short, separate paragraph act as a pause that highlights one detail.
Strunk says to avoid the passive voice when it hides the actor or when one passive depends on another. Pick the subject that fits what the paragraph is about, then choose the voice that suits it.
Strunk's rule is to replace limp phrases like there was or could be heard with a strong active verb. Vivid, direct sentences make ordinary description and explanation far more lively.

Strunk holds that a negative is weaker than a positive: tell readers what something is rather than what it is not. Say it was dishonest rather than not honest, and say it was forgotten rather than not remembered.
Strunk says vivid writing comes from definite, concrete details, so the reader can picture the scene. Even general principles need particular examples to land.

Herbert Spencer held that specific words are easier to take in than abstract ones, because the reader does not have to work out a picture from a general term. Choosing the concrete word saves effort and gives a stronger impression.
Strunk's rule is to cut needless words, such as stock phrases like 'the fact that' that can usually be replaced by a single plain word. Write the direct version, since it is shorter and clearer.
Strunk warns against a string of loose sentences joined by 'and' and 'but', which becomes monotonous. Combine related ideas into one well-built sentence instead.

William Strunk held that a run of sentences built on the same mechanical pattern becomes monotonous, so the writer should vary them with simple, compound, or periodic sentences that match the real shape of the thought.
William Strunk held that parallel ideas should be written in matching form, so the reader can see at once that they are alike, and that a writer who keeps switching forms looks undecided.
William Strunk held that the words of a sentence should be placed so that related words stay together, since word order is the main way a reader tells how the parts of a sentence connect.
William Strunk advised placing a modifier next to the word it modifies, such as 'only' before the word it limits, so that no wrong meaning is suggested to the reader.

Strunk's rule is to keep one tense throughout a summary, since switching between present and past makes the writer seem uncertain and irresolute. Say once at the outset that what follows is a summary, rather than repeating 'he said' along the way.
Strunk warns that in criticism the writer should not slide into retelling the work; a good discussion makes general conclusions supported by evidence, not a summary with occasional comment.

Strunk's rule is to place the emphatic words at the end of a sentence, since the end is the most prominent position. The same principle applies to the sentences of a paragraph and the paragraphs of a composition.
Strunk's rule is to write dates and serial numbers in figures or Roman numerals, never spelled out. Put an aside in parentheses without changing the punctuation the sentence would have on its own.
Strunk advised that familiar phrases and proverbs need no quotation marks, and the same goes for colloquialisms and slang. Quoting them only signals that the writer is not comfortable with the words.

Strunk held that when a writer finds a worn-out expression in a sentence, the fix is to rebuild the sentence around what he means, not to swap one word for another. Ready-made formulas save thinking, so refuse them.
Strunk warned against stacking one contrast on another with repeated but, which leaves the reader confused. Rearranging the sentence so the ideas sit in clear order usually fixes it.
Strunk noticed that filler words such as case and character often add nothing and come from habit. Cutting them, as in Hostile acts instead of Acts of a hostile character, makes writing tighter.
Strunk's rule is that the writer with a definite meaning to express will not hide behind vague words like effect used loosely. Be concrete about what you actually mean.
Strunk's rule is to avoid hackneyed words like factor and feature, since they usually add nothing and can be replaced by something more direct. Say what you mean in plain, specific words.
Strunk's rule is to skip the perfunctory preamble such as calling something interesting. Make the point interesting by telling it directly, without announcing it first.
Strunk's rule is to use less for quantity and fewer for number, and to use as rather than like before a phrase or clause. Small distinctions like these make writing precise.
William Strunk warned that a writer seeking freshness should drop worn-out phrases such as along these lines, which have been so overused they have lost their force. Say the plain thing instead.

William Strunk noted that literal and most are often stretched beyond their meaning for exaggeration, so writers should use almost or plain words when they mean that. Precision beats inflated emphasis.
William Strunk held that a sentence should be recast whenever a clumsy construction stands in for something simpler. Choose the plainer wording, such as an if clause, over a tangled phrase.
William Strunk advised cutting needless words like respectively, and replacing padded phrases such as student body with the simple word. Short, direct wording is almost always stronger.
Strunk advises replacing a weak word like 'very' with words that are strong in themselves when emphasis is needed. Use sparingly, since overuse dulls the effect.
Strunk says a distributive word such as 'each' or 'everybody' takes a singular pronoun, even though it implies more than one person. Plural pronouns with these words are a common mistake.
Strunk's test for a sentence built on 'while' is to rewrite it as two separate statements joined by 'at the same time'. If the rewrite makes sense, the use is fine; if not, a semicolon is better.
Strunk holds that for habitual action the plain past tense is briefer and more emphatic than adding 'would'. Brevity usually makes a sentence stronger.

Strunk's passage on the 1788 French crisis shows how a leader who misjudges the gravity of a situation can drive people to act in ways he never intended. Byron's account of Childe Harold shows that a writer's strongest work often lies in concrete description rather than in the invented persona.

Strunk's examples teach that a sentence should make clear what it is about, so modifiers and participial phrases must attach to the word they describe. A stated principle of law, that a person is innocent until proved guilty, is a good model of a clear, balanced idea.

preview.text:
This book aims to give in brief space the principal requirements of
plain English style. It aims to lighten the task of instructor and
student by concentrating attention (in Chapters II and III) on a few
essentials, the rules of usage and principles of composition most
commonly violated. In accordance with this plan it lays down three rules
for the use of the comma, instead of a score or more, and one for the
use of the semicolon, in the belief that these four rules provide for
all the internal punctuation that is required by nineteen sentences out
of twenty. Similarly, it gives in Chapter III only those principles of
the paragraph and the sentence which are of the widest application. The
book thus covers only a small portion of the field of English style. The
experience of its writer has been that once past the essentials,
students profit most by individual instruction based on the problems of
their own work, and that each instructor has his own body of theory,
which he may prefer to that offered by any textbook.

The numbers of the sections may be used as references in correcting
manuscript.

The writer's colleagues in the Department of English in Cornell
University have greatly helped him in the preparation of his manuscript.
Mr. George McLane Wood has kindly consented to the inclusion under
Rule 10 of some material from his _Suggestions to Authors_.

books.title: The Notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci
books.author: Leonardo da Vinci
books.subject: art
books.licence_note: Author died 1519, translator died 1937. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Richter observed that a hard task can still be mastered with practice and patience, even when the method looks awkward or backwards at first.
Leonardo da Vinci worked as an enquirer, testing things one by one through detailed research. He never gathered his findings into order, which left his notes in confusion.

Leonardo da Vinci held that each observation should be finished on the page where it began. Richter notes that a clear final arrangement can still be built from scattered material if each part is well defined.

Leonardo's notebooks can be put in order by their dates and page layout, and a numbered index lets a reader trace each passage back to its place in the original. Checking where a note came from keeps the record trustworthy.

Copies made from copies drift away from the original, and a compiler who leaves the order unsettled hands the mess on to every later editor. Go back to the source where you can, and do not adopt someone else's arrangement without checking it.

The editor gained access to the original manuscripts by asking owners and institutions directly and thanking them for their help. Careful research depends on patient requests and on being open about who helped you.

Leonardo's genius is judged to lie in his restless curiosity across many fields, not in a squandering of effort. The editor argues that his studies needed centuries of work just to begin to explain them.
Leonardo's principles often agreed more with later science than with his own contemporaries. Good thinking can be ahead of its time and be recognised only when others catch up.
Leonardo meant to arrange his scattered notes by subject before publishing them. The notes were a working collection, and the job of sorting them was a discipline in its own right.
Leonardo held that a painter needs theoretical knowledge of how the eye works, not just skill with the brush. Understanding the reasons behind what you see makes the craft sounder.
Leonardo da Vinci treated careful observation as the basis of skill, testing how distance, light and shade change the way things look before drawing them.
Leonardo da Vinci studied nature closely, noting how light, shade and wind change a tree, so that his work rested on watching the real thing.
Leonardo da Vinci held that an artist must work with industry and thoroughness, and that a painter should learn anatomy and study widely rather than only one narrow skill.
Leonardo da Vinci advised a student to choose his company carefully and to plan his time for study, so that daily habits support the craft.
Leonardo da Vinci held that a useful science should always include its application and use, so that the knowledge does not end up useless.
Leonardo da Vinci admitted that his notes were a disordered collection, and he meant to sort them later by subject, so a messy first draft is fine if you plan to tidy it.
Leonardo da Vinci separated theory from practice when arranging his work, so each proven principle came first and its practical uses followed, keeping the whole coherent.
Leonardo da Vinci ordered his teaching from simple cases to complex ones, starting with simple beams before moving to supported and suspended ones.
Leonardo da Vinci held that a man of wisdom values the food of the mind above material riches, and that the soul's possessions outrank those of the body.
Leonardo da Vinci held that experience, rather than borrowed words, is the true mistress of those who write well, so he would rely on observed evidence over quotation.

Leonardo da Vinci held that inventors and interpreters of nature deserve more esteem than those who only repeat the works of others, and that trusting pure experience beats deferring to reputed authority.
Leonardo da Vinci held that the certainty of mathematical demonstration lifts the mind, and he planned to set out his ideas in short, ordered steps that move from causes to effects and back again.
Leonardo da Vinci held that a picture needs both convincing depth and varied, purposeful action in its figures, so that the people shown do not all look alike.
Leonardo da Vinci held that practice must be founded on sound theory, since a painter who works by eye alone without reasons is like a sailor with no rudder or compass.
Leonardo da Vinci held that knowing your own mistakes lets you correct them and avoid repeating them, and that sound judgment grows from clear understanding built on tested experience.
Leonardo da Vinci held that we should not accept old authorities on matters that can be checked, and should test claims against our own careful observation and experience.

Leonardo da Vinci held that painting rests on the attributes of sight, such as light, shade, colour, form, position, distance and motion, and that a painter must master these to imitate nature. Looking at a thing closely and carefully is the basis of good work.

Leonardo da Vinci noticed that a flat picture seen with one eye can look like real relief, while seen with both eyes it does not. The lesson is that how you look at something changes what you perceive.

Leonardo da Vinci observed that a shadowed place looks darker when you step in from bright light, because the eye adjusts to the light it has just been in. Judge a thing by what you see after your eyes have adjusted, not by the glare you came from.
Leonardo da Vinci noticed that the eye takes time to adjust when moving between bright and shaded places, so it cannot see well right away. He learnt this from a painting he had made of an eye.

Leonardo da Vinci suggested a simple test: hold a candle near a star and lower it slowly, and the star seems to fade as the light grows. The point is that what we see depends on the light around us as well as the thing itself.

Leonardo da Vinci held that perspective is the best guide to painting, and that it makes flat things look raised and raised things look flat. Good work starts with understanding how the eye actually sees.
Leonardo da Vinci used the camera obscura to explain how the eye forms images, which gave painters a way to build a true picture of depth from observation rather than guesswork.

Leonardo built his account of perspective on the basic terms of geometry: point, line, angle, surface and solid. He insisted that a point is not part of a line, so the simplest parts must be clear before the harder problems can be solved.

Leonardo held that a line has no substance and is closer to an imagined idea than a physical thing. Study the outline of every object closely, noting whether its curves are arched convexities or angular concavities.

Leonardo advised painters not to surround bodies with hard lines, since outlines blur at a distance and the parts of small objects vanish. Show edges through light and shade rather than drawn borders.

Leonardo described perspective as a reasoned way of showing that every object sends its image to the eye through a pyramid of lines converging at one point. Bodies of equal size look smaller as they recede because their pyramids shrink.
Leonardo da Vinci held that the eye takes in an object clearly only when its image lies along the central line of sight, so we must turn the eye from letter to letter to read a row of them.

Leonardo da Vinci argued that every visible object sends its lines to the eye in a pyramid meeting at one indivisible point, so a tiny object seen from afar keeps its size rather than shrinking into a speck.
Leonardo da Vinci observed that the eye is a poor judge of distance between objects of equal size, and that a vertical plane, the standard of perspective, is needed to judge them correctly.
Leonardo da Vinci taught that the nearer a cut is made across the pyramid of sight, the smaller the image of the object appears, which is the basis for drawing true size on a flat surface.

Leonardo da Vinci held that the eye judges both how far away an object is and in which direction it lies, and both must be read together, kept on the same level. Objects on a flat ground seem to rise toward the eye with distance but never rise above the eye's own level.

Leonardo da Vinci suggested a simple test of perspective: walk beside a ploughed field and watch the straight furrows seem to draw together toward a point in the distance. That meeting point is the vanishing point that moves as you move.

Leonardo da Vinci showed that you can measure distance by sliding a rod back and forth until its ends line up with a tower's ends, then noting how the image shrinks as the rod is brought nearer the eye. Judging size by comparison with a known object works without any instruments.
Leonardo da Vinci held that every body fills the surrounding air with images of itself, so each small part of the air carries the whole form of the object it comes from.
Leonardo da Vinci's method was to test a claim against a concrete example, such as a light between two mirrors, before trusting it.
Leonardo da Vinci observed that two facing mirrors reflect each other endlessly, a small example of how many images can share the same space without mixing or blocking one another.
Leonardo da Vinci reasoned that the eye sends its own image out to the objects in front of it while taking in their images, which is why seeing is a two-way exchange through the air.

Leonardo da Vinci observed that images of objects spread through the air in every direction, so that every point of a scene is present in every part of the air. He tested this with pinholes in a dark chamber.

Leonardo da Vinci argued that the eye does not send out a visible ray to reach the sun, since such a ray would take time to travel and would be bent by the wind. Seeing happens instantly and undisturbed, so the eye must receive images rather than project them.

Leonardo da Vinci reasoned that if objects sent their images to the eye, they would shrink as they lost material. He proposed instead that the air itself draws in the images of things, like a loadstone, and so the nature of the medium matters as much as the object.

Leonardo observed that a small hole in a wall lets light from a sunlit scene project an upside-down image onto the opposite wall. Every point of the scene reaches every part of that wall, so the picture is complete in each small piece.

Leonardo held that the eye works like a darkened chamber with a small opening, where images cross and arrive upside down. He tested this by letting sunlit objects pass through a pinhole onto white paper inside a dark room.

Leonardo noted that light bends when it passes from thinner air into denser water or glass, so objects seen through water appear out of their true place. He used this to explain why the eye's judgment of position can mislead.

Leonardo da Vinci reasoned from experiment: if you shift one edge of a small hole in a dark room, the image moves, because light travels in straight lines and each edge decides which rays get through. Careful observation of how a simple setup behaves can reveal how light works.

Leonardo da Vinci held that every point of a line can be treated as a point, so a whole circle's image can meet at one point without the rays getting in each other's way. Working through a problem by breaking it into its simplest parts can make a hard idea clear.

Leonardo da Vinci argued from first principles that a line has no thickness, so two sides of it cannot cross each other. Testing an idea by moving the parts in your head and checking what must follow is a sound way to think.

Leonardo da Vinci observed that the narrower the opening, the closer to the opening the light rays cross each other. Small changes to the size of an opening change the whole pattern, so look closely at how each part of a system shapes the result.

Leonardo da Vinci observed that an image cannot be seen between the object and the opening that admits its light, since the air there is not visibly lit. He also noted that where images overlap they look darker.

Leonardo da Vinci described perspective as seeing objects through a flat transparent plane, such as glass, and drawing what the eye sees on it. Each object is traced along lines running to a single point in the eye.

preview.text:
That, notwithstanding this eagerness to possess the Manuscripts,
their contents remained a mystery, can only be accounted for by the
many and great difficulties attending the task of deciphering them.
The handwriting is so peculiar that it requires considerable
practice to read even a few detached phrases, much more to solve
with any certainty the numerous difficulties of alternative
readings, and to master the sense as a connected whole. Vasari
observes with reference to Leonardos writing: "he wrote backwards,
in rude characters, and with the left hand, so that any one who is
not practised in reading them, cannot understand them". The aid of a
mirror in reading reversed handwriting appears to me available only
for a first experimental reading. Speaking from my own experience,
the persistent use of it is too fatiguing and inconvenient to be
practically advisable, considering the enormous mass of Manuscripts
to be deciphered. And as, after all, Leonardo's handwriting runs
backwards just as all Oriental character runs backwards--that is
to say from right to left--the difficulty of reading direct from the
writing is not insuperable. This obvious peculiarity in the writing
is not, however, by any means the only obstacle in the way of
mastering the text. Leonardo made use of an orthography peculiar to
himself; he had a fashion of amalgamating several short words into
one long one, or, again, he would quite arbitrarily divide a long
word into two separate halves; added to this there is no punctuation
whatever to regulate the division and construction of the sentences,
nor are there any accents--and the reader may imagine that such
difficulties were almost sufficient to make the task seem a
desperate one to a beginner. It is therefore not surprising that the
good intentions of some of Leonardo s most reverent admirers should
have failed.

books.title: Talks to Teachers on Psychology
books.author: William James
books.subject: learning
books.licence_note: Author died 1910. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: William James held that a learner's mind is a living whole, not a set of separate compartments, so teaching should help people see ideas as they flow rather than chopping them into neat boxes.
William James held that no single mind can grasp the whole truth, so many people must look at life from their own view, and we should tolerate whatever is not itself intolerant.
William James held that teaching methods must agree with what psychology shows, but cannot be drawn straight from it, so teachers still need judgement in the classroom.
William James held that a teacher's job is to train pupils in behaviour, since conduct is what education ultimately produces.

William James held that habits are made by repeated exercise, so the aim of education is to make useful habits automatic. Start a new habit with strong initiative, act on it without exception, and seize the first chance to act.
William James held that we cannot recall anything without a cue, so memory depends on connecting ideas. To remember something, one must think about it and link it to what one already knows.
William James held that effort of will is largely effort of attention. Holding your attention on the right course of action is the core of building good character.

William James saw teachers as the reflective leaders who shape a nation's future, since a nation's renewal starts among its thoughtful people and spreads outward. Teachers who keep examining the highest aims of their work are a sign of real progress.
William James warned that a hyped 'new psychology' can mystify teachers, and that disciples should stay independent and critical rather than simply accept whatever is handed down from above.
William James held that psychology is a science while teaching is an art, so psychology cannot produce classroom methods directly; an inventive mind has to make the application.
William James held that knowing a science like logic or ethics does not make a person reason or behave well; it only helps us catch and check our own mistakes.
William James held that good teaching depends on tact and ingenuity in meeting the actual pupil in front of you, and no body of theory can supply that.

William James held that teaching is like strategy: the principles are simple, but the real difficulty is that the pupil's mind is an active opponent that the teacher must read through tact and intuition.
William James held that knowing the principles of how minds work is useful mainly for ruling out methods that will fail, and for giving a teacher confidence and a fuller view of each pupil.
William James held that most teachers need only a general, sound grasp of how the mind works, enough to fit on the palm of a hand, rather than deep technical study.
William James held that teachers should not be forced to become researchers, since the caring, concrete attitude toward a child can clash with the detached attitude of an observer.
William James held that a teacher who feels like a failure at psychology should not carry a bad conscience about it. The best teacher and the best contributor of research are often different people.

William James held that the most basic fact of the mind is that some stream of awareness is always running, whether we are awake or asleep. Describing and sorting that stream is a sound starting point, even before asking why it works as it does.

William James admitted that we do not really know where our thoughts come from or how the brain produces them. He thought it wiser to admit that gap plainly than to dress up a vague explanation as if it were knowledge.

William James observed that our experience is always mixed, with a clear centre of attention surrounded by a fringe of feeling and thought. When the mind wanders, the thing in front of us fades to the edge, which explains why we can miss what is said right in front of us.

William James held that our awareness has a focal object and a marginal one, and that these can shift, swap places or change together. Vague descriptions of this stream are safer than neat, over-sharpened ones.

William James warned against building the mind out of tiny fixed mental bricks, a theory he called 'ideas', because it is only conjecture. A looser picture of the stream of thought, always changing, is enough for practical work such as teaching.

Wundt admitted that after decades of laboratory self-observation, psychology still had no universally accepted body of doctrine. Honest reflection on one's own inner experience can be useful, even when its results remain uncertain.

Wundt came to see mental life as one indivisible, fleeting process, where thinking, feeling and willing are closely joined rather than separate parts. He concluded that the neat labels we give mental functions are often self-deceptions.
William James notes an old split: popular belief judges the mind by its practical effects, while philosophers have prized pure contemplation as the higher life.
William James argues that evolution has shifted psychology toward the practical side, since consciousness is best understood as a tool for guiding useful conduct.
William James suggests that when learning a hard subject, you first grasp one deep, basic aspect firmly, then gradually add the neglected features that complete the picture.
William James reasons that since the brain's signals run back out into action, and even lofty thought depends on practical capacity, practical purpose is the more basic result of the mind.

William James held that no truth, however abstract, is ever taken in without some day shaping our action. Even theoretical thinking has practical effects, because it changes what we answer, read and do later.

William James held that a teacher's main job is training the pupil in behaviour, meaning every fitting reaction to life's circumstances. Holding back from speaking or acting is also a deliberate reaction that takes real effort.

William James described education as the organising of acquired habits of conduct and tendencies to behaviour. A truly educated person can work through situations they have never met before, using memory and general ideas.

William James observed that even quiet listening is a active form of conduct, with the body and attention set in a particular way. Every impression we make on others tends to build their capacity to act, so it is worth keeping that in mind.
William James held that every impression a teacher gives should be met by some reaction from the learner, since no reception without reaction is the rule to keep in the classroom.

William James held that ideas stick best when they lead to some action by the learner, because doing something with a thing is what clinches it in memory. Passive reading or hearing alone leaves little behind.

William James held that hands-on work such as experiments, drawings and measuring trains precision, honesty and self-reliance. Making things shows plainly whether you really understand, which words alone can hide.
William James held that learning is incomplete until the learner gets news of what they did and what came of it. Feedback about our actions is part of the whole experience, not an extra.
James argued that a learner's wish to know how well they are doing is natural and should rarely be blocked. Unless there is a specific practical reason, people should be told where they stand.

William James held that most learning builds on what a person already does by instinct, either adding to that reaction or replacing it. A good teacher starts from the learner's existing tendencies, since nothing can be taught without some first response to build on.

William James showed that memory is what turns a single experience into learning: the learner recalls the earlier result and changes course before repeating the mistake. An easily taught learner may need only one lesson to set a new habit.

William James held that a new habit works by substitution: a learner keeps the native impulse but turns it toward a new object or response, so the teacher's first task is to understand the child's natural reactive tendencies.

William James held that people keep their instincts even when reasoning overlays them, so the life of instinct is disguised rather than lost. Fear and love remain powerful levers for a teacher, and being liked gets results a forbidding manner cannot.
William James held that curiosity is strongest in childhood and youth and fades in middle life, when routine absorbs attention and new, demanding ideas feel out of reach.

William James held that young learners are first drawn by material objects, movement, living things and human action, so teaching should begin with things shown or done, and abstract reasons can wait until adolescence.

William James held that we become who we are mainly by imitating others, and that each generation passes on its language, arts and sciences by imitating the last. Invention and imitation are the two legs humanity has walked on.

William James observed that a teacher's own visible effort is more persuasive than exhortation, so a teacher should never ask pupils to do what she cannot do herself. Showing beats telling: 'Come and let me show you how' works better than 'Go and do it as the book directs.'

William James noted that the tone of any school or workplace is a tradition passed on by imitation, and it shifts slowly, mostly when a strong new personality sets a fresh pattern. Good culture depends on the character and tact of the leader who sets the example.
Rousseau argued that children should be spurred by measuring their own progress over time rather than by rivalry with others. Comparing someone with their former self builds drive without jealousy.
William James held that rivalry is rooted in human nature and can be channelled into fairness and generosity. Banning all competition may throw away a useful ally in learning.
William James observed that people are moved most by seeing others act, so the spectacle of effort wakes and sustains our own. A runner pushes harder when rivals are at his heels.

William James argued that a stubborn unwillingness to be beaten by difficulty, and the pride that goes with it, can be a healthy spur. Interest cannot be found in every step, so some hard work must be met head on.

William James saw a strong urge to own things as part of human nature from early childhood. Any plan to remove private property would have to reckon with this deep need for something that is one's own.
William James held that the collecting impulse can be turned into school work, so that neatness, order and method are picked up along the way rather than forced on the child.
William James observed that children learn the world by handling things, and that real, hands-on acquaintance with objects gives a firmer grasp of reality than books alone.
William James described a law of transitoriness: an instinct that is not met with the right object at its ripe moment may fade, and a habit that should have formed may then be hard to teach later.
William James held that a child's interests ripen in a set order, and that a teacher should press a skill when the native impulse is strongest, since that window may be short.
William James advised teachers to start from a pupil's existing impulses, even unhelpful ones, because those natural reactions are the best place to begin shaping new behaviour.
William James argued that our virtues are habits just as much as our vices, and that habit forms because the living nervous system is plastic and grows to the way it is exercised.
William James observed that most of our daily activity runs on automatic habit, so the most useful thing to build early is a set of habits that will serve us for life.
William James held that the great aim of education is to make our nervous system our ally, by making useful actions automatic early on, so our higher powers are free for their proper work.

James's first maxim is to launch a new habit with as strong an initiative as possible, surrounding yourself with reinforcements, incompatible commitments and even a public pledge. His second is to never allow an exception until the habit is firmly rooted.

preview.text:
Teachers, of course, will miss the minute divisions, subdivisions, and
definitions, the lettered and numbered headings, the variations of type,
and all the other mechanical artifices on which they are accustomed to
prop their minds. But my main desire has been to make them conceive,
and, if possible, reproduce sympathetically in their imagination, the
mental life of their pupil as the sort of active unity which he himself
feels it to be. _He_ doesn't chop himself into distinct processes and
compartments; and it would have frustrated this deeper purpose of my
book to make it look, when printed, like a Baedeker's handbook of travel
or a text-book of arithmetic. So far as books printed like this book
force the fluidity of the facts upon the young teacher's attention, so
far I am sure they tend to do his intellect a service, even though they
may leave unsatisfied a craving (not altogether without its legitimate
grounds) for more nomenclature, head-lines, and subdivisions.

Readers acquainted with my larger books on Psychology will meet much
familiar phraseology. In the chapters on habit and memory I have even
copied several pages verbatim, but I do not know that apology is needed
for such plagiarism as this.

The talks to students, which conclude the volume, were written in
response to invitations to deliver 'addresses' to students at women's
colleges. The first one was to the graduating class of the Boston Normal
School of Gymnastics. Properly, it continues the series of talks to
teachers. The second and the third address belong together, and continue
another line of thought.

books.title: The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals
books.author: Charles Darwin
books.subject: emotions
books.licence_note: Author died 1882. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Charles Darwin held that many expressions come from habits that once served a purpose, such as the three chief principles he sets out in the first chapter. Expressions can outlast the reason they first existed.

Charles Darwin's principle of antithesis suggests that opposite moods often show up as opposite postures. A relaxed, friendly stance is often the reverse of a hostile one, and people read these signals without being taught.
Charles Darwin noticed that the body reacts to strong feelings without waiting for the will. Blushing, trembling and changes in the skin show what someone feels even when they try to hide it.

Charles Darwin observed that people of very different backgrounds show many of the same expressions. Recognising a face or gesture is largely instinctive, so most of us can read a stranger's mood without a shared language.

Charles Darwin noted that Sir Charles Bell's real service was showing how the movements of expression are tied to breathing. He also showed that the muscles round the eyes tighten during hard breathing out, to protect the eyes.

Charles Darwin held that a list of how a face looks is not enough; a good account must also explain why each muscle moves as it does under each feeling. Flowery descriptions that never explain the cause add little understanding.

Charles Darwin warned that confident explanations which are really just fancy can be worse than none. He quoted Le Brun's theory of fright as an example of nonsense dressed up as science, so claims should be tested, not admired.

Darwin praised Duchenne for studying each facial muscle closely and for showing which muscles are hardest to control by the will. He also noted that a careful researcher can be right even when some of his claims are overstated.

Darwin held that many gestures, like a billiards player nudging a wayward ball, come from long habit: we repeat the body movements that once worked, even when they no longer do anything. Habit can explain behaviour that looks purposeless.

Darwin suggested that a dog's pricked ears and fixed gaze are linked because the two actions were repeated together for many generations. A simpler habit-based explanation is often better than a mystical idea of sympathy between body parts.
Charles Darwin noted that Bain saw expression as part of feeling itself, a general spreading of excitement through the body. Darwin judged this too broad to explain any particular expression.

Charles Darwin held that many expressions grow out of the actions that feeling would naturally bring on, such as the cries, tremblings and tensed muscles of fear. Spencer's law is that strong feeling spills over into bodily action along the most habitual nerve routes.

Charles Darwin argued that a feature shared with other species, such as the facial muscles we have in common with apes, is unlikely to exist only for display. Before assuming a single purpose, look for the other jobs a thing might do.

Darwin argued that animals, like the dog greeting its master, show real emotional expression, so claiming it is only instinct or will is too narrow a view. Careful observation should replace a quick assumption that the matter is settled.

Darwin held that if each species is seen as a separate creation, the question of why we show emotions is closed off and nothing is really explained. Viewing all creatures as gradually changing from common ancestors opens up useful investigation.

Darwin warned that sympathy during a strong emotion and our own expectations both make careful observation harder, since we easily see what we expect to see. He recommended watching infants first, because they show feelings more plainly than adults.

Darwin held that the best way to learn about extreme emotion was to study people who give their feelings uncontrolled vent, and he gained much from an expert who shared notes freely. Learning from a generous specialist can speed up your own understanding.

Darwin found that viewers who saw photographs without any explanation disagreed widely about what the faces showed. He also saw that once he read the intended meaning, he judged the pictures far more truthful, showing how easily our imagination misleads us.

Darwin reasoned that if the same expression appears across very different peoples, it is probably natural rather than learned, since learned gestures would vary like languages do. Look for patterns that hold across different groups before trusting a conclusion.

Darwin asked his questions in a way that favoured actual observation over memory, and he admitted later that his queries could have been much better written. When gathering evidence, ask for what people have directly seen, and be willing to say your method could be improved.
Charles Darwin held that answers resting on a written record of the circumstances and the expression itself deserve more trust than bare yes or no replies. Vague general remarks count for less.

Charles Darwin held that watching animals is a safer guide than watching people, since animals are less shaped by imagination or convention. Their expressions give a firmer basis for working out where behaviours come from.

Charles Darwin held that observing expressions is hard, because fleeting changes, distraction, imagination and long familiarity all bias what we think we see. He stressed checking what we believe against careful evidence.

Charles Darwin held that a theory is best tested by checking whether the same principle also explains related cases, including animals as well as people. A good idea should hold up across the wider evidence.

Charles Darwin held that a question should be approached with a fresh view once a working belief forms, so he reframed each expression as something needing its own rational explanation rather than accepting a fixed answer.
Darwin's approach was to test an idea by gathering many careful observations from people across different places, not by relying on a single authority's account.
Darwin noted that people often hide their feelings around strangers, so observers must be patient and trusted before they can read what is really going on.
Darwin valued a habit of careful, detailed observation, showing that a skill built in one field, such as botany, can sharpen judgement in another.

Charles Darwin noted that the facial muscles vary a great deal from one person to another, in both their structure and what they can do. So any single textbook picture only describes the typical case.

Charles Darwin held that useful actions tied to a state of mind become habits, so they keep happening under that state even when they no longer serve any purpose. Muscles least under the will are the most likely to slip out.
Charles Darwin held that when a directly opposite state of mind arises, we tend to make movements that are the opposite of the earlier ones, even though those movements do no good.
Darwin held that habit makes complex movements easy over time, and that repeated use can even be passed on to offspring, as with trained gaits in horses and pointing in young dogs.

Darwin noted that an inherited tendency often needs some practice in the individual before it works well, since young dogs may point at the wrong scent. Good results depend on both inheritance and experience.

Darwin quoted Bain's principle that actions and feelings occurring together tend to become linked, so that one later brings the other to mind. Many everyday habits, like putting on gloves without thinking, come from this.

Darwin observed that people often scratch their heads, rub their eyes or cough when perplexed or embarrassed, as if relieving a small discomfort. Many of our habits are small ways of responding to our own inner states.

Darwin noted that we often shut our eyes or turn away from things we reject, and raise our eyebrows when trying to remember something, even when there is nothing to see. Our bodies tend to act out our thinking in ways we rarely notice.

Darwin observed that we often copy or mirror the movements of people around us, such as clearing our throats when a singer is hoarse. Much of what we do in company is driven by imitation and sympathy rather than deliberate choice.

Darwin explained that many actions, such as coughing and sneezing, happen without thought, and even a decapitated frog can wipe off acid with a leg. Some behaviour that looks intelligent runs on automatic nerve responses.

Darwin observed that acts we perform by will are often weaker and slower than the same acts done by reflex, because the conscious mind takes time and effort to act. Deliberate effort can get in the way of what the body does best.
Darwin's wager showed that a strong wish to succeed can stop a natural reflex from working. Trying too hard at a simple, automatic act can make it harder to do well.

Darwin found that resolving calmly not to flinch failed the moment a threat seemed real, because reason alone cannot override what the imagination believes is danger. Fear is often stronger than logic, so plan for that rather than trusting willpower alone.
Darwin observed that his infants started at sudden sounds but did not blink, and he reasoned that a reflex learned by experience over many generations could be passed on before it is needed.
Darwin suggested that some actions first done on purpose, such as expelling an irritant by sneezing or coughing, can become automatic reflexes over long habit and inheritance.
Darwin argued that some reflexes, such as the iris narrowing in bright light, cannot have been learned by the will and fixed by habit, so they need a different explanation.
Darwin held that reflexes, like other bodily traits, vary slightly, and useful variations tend to be kept and passed on, so a reflex built for one purpose can later be adapted to another.

Charles Darwin held that many habits are inherited movements that once served a purpose, such as a dog turning round to flatten grass. Such habits are often repeated long after they have stopped being useful.

Darwin observed that a habit can be triggered by circumstances where it no longer fits, such as a dog crouching when it sees a distant stranger on an open road. Actions can outlast the situations that first gave them a point.

Darwin noticed that the dog's habit of scratching backwards after going to the toilet is a leftover from an ancestor that covered its waste, even though dogs no longer do this. Some habits are kept for a very long time without any clear use.

Darwin observed that a terrier will toss, roll on and worry a biscuit as if it were prey, which suggests that a habit can supply a feeling of value that the situation lacks. Habits can run on their own logic rather than on what the mind knows to be true.

Darwin noticed that a horse rubbed on the neck will move its jaws as if nibbling another horse, since it could never reach its own neck. Expressions can be stirred by a stimulus that the animal cannot actually act on.

Darwin observed that a habit can be set off by the wrong cue, as when a kitten scraped ashes over spilt water, or shook its feet at a sound of pouring. Routines fire on signals that look like the real trigger, not only on the real thing.

Darwin saw that a movement which began as a feeding action, kneading the mother for milk, can later become a sign of comfort, as with cats pounding a soft shawl while purring. Over time, an old action can turn into a way of showing a feeling.

Darwin noted that some useful actions, such as a chick pecking at food, can be triggered by a simple cue like a tapping sound, not by sight or smell. Many skilled habits run on a single signal, so the cue matters as much as the skill.

Charles Darwin held that a movement which once served a feeling becomes habit, and can still appear faintly when that feeling returns, even when it does no good. Under strain, the will gives way first on the muscles it controls most.

Charles Darwin held that the principle of antithesis means a strongly opposite state of mind tends to produce movements opposite to those of the first state, even when those movements serve no purpose.

Charles Darwin observed that a dog's friendly greeting is the reverse of its hostile stance: a relaxed body, lowered tail and smooth hair, where the threatening dog stands stiff and upright. Such signs are easier to read once you know the opposing state.

Charles Darwin noted that a cat's anger and its readiness to fight show in a crouch, lashing tail and flattened ears, and that a leaping predator shows much the same signs. Reading body language means comparing a creature's posture against its likely intention.
Charles Darwin noticed that a dog's gloomy look at being turned away from a walk was the opposite of its joyful bearing, showing how a small disappointment can change a whole posture at once.
Charles Darwin observed that social animals depend on being understood by one another, so gestures and expressions matter greatly to their survival and to getting along together.
Charles Darwin held that a gesture can be inherited even if it began as a deliberate act, since habits repeated over many generations may eventually become innate.

and they are in consequence somewhat indistinct. Nevertheless they are

however carefully executed.

DETAILED CONTENTS.

INTRODUCTION

CHAP. I—GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF EXPRESSION.
The three chief principles stated—The first principle—Serviceable
actions become habitual in association with certain states of the mind,
and are performed whether or not of service in each particular case—The
force of habit—Inheritance—Associated habitual movements in man—Reflex
actions—Passage of habits into reflex actions—Associated habitual
movements in the lower animals—Concluding remarks

CHAP. II—GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF EXPRESSION.—_continued_.
The Principle of Antithesis—Instances in the dog and cat—Origin of the
principle—Conventional signs—The principle of antithesis has not arisen
