impulses

CHAP. III—GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF EXPRESSION.—_concluded_.
The principle of the direct action of the excited nervous system on the
body, independently of the will and in part of habit—Change of colour
in the hair—Trembling of the muscles—Modified
secretions—Perspiration—Expression of extreme pain—Of rage, great joy,
and terror—Contrast between the emotions which cause and do not cause
expressive movements—Exciting and depressing states of the mind—Summary

books.title: The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
books.author: Benjamin Franklin
books.subject: habits
books.licence_note: Author died 1790, editor died 1926. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Franklin rose from a poorly schooled runaway apprentice to a respected printer by steadily building his own trade, using his newspaper and almanac to reach ordinary readers.
Franklin pursued science and public work in the spare time left over from earning a living, and he sold his business once he had enough to free himself for study.
Franklin wrote his life story for his son so that his descendants could copy the practical habits that had lifted him out of poverty. He believed a record of what worked was worth passing on.
Franklin says that if he could live his life again he would still accept, and that writing down one's past is the next best thing. Looking back carefully is a way to learn from experience.
Franklin admits his vanity and argues it can do good for the person and those around them. Owning up to your own motives honestly is better than pretending to have none.
Franklin credits his past success to providence, while admitting he cannot know the future. Staying humble about what you cannot control is a sound way to approach both good and bad fortune.

Franklin's family history shows that a person's life can be shaped by encouragement, such as a patron who backed a bright young man's learning. Support for a capable person can change the course of a whole family.

Benjamin Franklin described an uncle who kept a large private collection of pamphlets and notes on public affairs, and who was thoughtful and steady in his interests. Keeping careful records and a habit of study can outlast any single job or station in life.

Benjamin Franklin noted that his father's friend Peter Folger wrote openly under his own name, favouring liberty of conscience, so that his criticism would be known to come from good will. Speaking up honestly and owning your words is a principle worth keeping.
Benjamin Franklin learnt that nothing is truly useful if it is not honest, after his boyhood wharf built from stolen stones taught him the lesson.
Benjamin Franklin admired his father's sound understanding and solid judgment in practical matters, the kind of prudent sense that made neighbours seek his advice and settle disputes.
Benjamin Franklin's father steered dinner talk toward sensible and useful subjects, so the children learnt to value what was good, just and prudent over fuss about food and comfort.

Benjamin Franklin noted that his parents, with no estate and no steady income, raised a large family comfortably through constant labor and industry. Diligence in one's calling, and not distrusting that things will work out, are his lessons.

Benjamin Franklin's father took him to watch joiners, bricklayers and other craftsmen so he could see where his interest lay. Watching good workers closely before choosing a trade is a sensible way to find the work you will actually stick at.

Benjamin Franklin spent his small earnings on books and sold cheap ones to buy better ones, so his reading grew as his means did. Reading widely, even in small amounts, can shape how a person thinks for the rest of their life.

Benjamin Franklin borrowed books from booksellers' apprentices, returned them promptly and in clean condition, and read through much of the night. Keeping your word and treating lent items with care earns the trust that opens doors to more.

Franklin held that a habit of contradicting others for sport sours conversation and can create enmities where you later need friendship. Winning every argument is rarely worth the cost to relationships.

Franklin learned that his father's quiet feedback on his writing, about elegance, method and clarity, mattered more than simply winning the point. Ask for honest critique of how you say things, not only whether you were right.

Franklin improved his writing by reading a good essay, noting its main ideas, and rebuilding it from those notes before comparing it with the original. Deliberate practice with a model beats reading alone.
He also rewrote his notes after a few weeks had passed so he could practise arranging thoughts in a clear order. Clear structure is a skill you can train on purpose.
Benjamin Franklin found that a light, simple diet kept his mind clear and quick, so he had more energy left for study. He also saved money from his board to buy books.
Benjamin Franklin tackled a subject he had failed at as a schoolboy by working through a textbook alone and at his own pace. Being ashamed of a gap in his knowledge was enough to make him act.

Benjamin Franklin held that a modest, tentative way of speaking, such as saying 'I conceive it to be so', persuades better than a positive, assuming manner that provokes opposition. He learned this after giving up winning arguments by trapping people with questions.

Benjamin Franklin submitted an anonymous piece to his brother's paper so that his work would be judged on its merits rather than on his name. The praise he heard from its readers gave him confidence to keep writing.

Franklin noticed that a brother who was also his boss expected more from him than a stranger would, and he felt that a family relationship should bring more patience, not less. Clear expectations between people who work together matter.

Franklin admitted that taking advantage of a loophole to win an argument was unfair, and he counted it among the first mistakes of his life. Being honest about our own wrongs, even when the other side was also at fault, is worth doing.

Franklin found that his older brother had quietly blocked him from work with every other printer in town. A person who leaves a business or a job can be hurt by a former employer who turns others against them.

Benjamin Franklin noticed that Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress had spread across most of Europe's languages, and that Bunyan was among the first to mix narration with dialogue so the reader feels present in the scene.
Franklin's story of Dr. Brown shows that a chance conversation with a stranger can become a lasting friendship. Being willing to talk with people you meet on the road often pays off.

Benjamin Franklin observed that a man is sometimes more generous when he has little money than when he has plenty, perhaps from fear of being thought poor. Small gifts given freely can matter more than large ones.
Franklin noticed that he had not known the local names and prices of bread, so he paid for something he did not expect. Learn the local terms and prices before you buy or sell in a new place.
Franklin found that a plain, honest stranger could still be helped by a kind word from a stranger. Being open and courteous with people you do not know can open doors that money alone cannot.

Franklin saw that Bradford, by asking artful questions and raising little doubts, drew Keimer into explaining all his plans. Listening quietly while others talk can reveal far more than talking yourself.
Franklin fixed the broken press and got the shop ready before doing the job asked of him. Taking care of the basic tools of your trade first makes everything you do afterwards possible.

Franklin judged the two printers by their real skills, noting that one was untrained and the other knew composing but not presswork. Be honest about where your own skills stop, and find people who fill those gaps.
Franklin kept his own counsel while building a new life, sharing his whereabouts only with a trusted friend. Discretion about your plans can protect them until they are ready.
Franklin's reasoning, as he tells it, shows that a clear, fair letter can change how others see you. Explaining your reasons calmly and fully can win over someone who first thought you were mistaken.

Franklin's account suggests that people with influence often open doors for capable young workers who show promise. Being willing to be seen and to accept an invitation can turn a quiet skill into real opportunity.
Franklin met a rough return with composure, arriving well presented and with savings in hand, which spoke for him more than words could. Steady progress often answers doubters better than argument.

Franklin's father judged that a youth should not be set up in business before he is mature enough to manage it, since a business needs careful handling and preparation. Showing off one's possessions to others can also build resentment, as his brother's anger shows.

Franklin's father advised that steady industry and prudent saving, rather than borrowing or help from others, would build a young man's start in business. He also urged him to earn general esteem and avoid mocking or slandering others.

Franklin took the advice of an older, experienced stranger who warned him about company that seemed pleasant but was dangerous. Heeding a sensible warning about people, even when they seem friendly, saved him from theft and worse.
Benjamin Franklin saw that a friend who was gifted and promising could still be undone by one habit, drink, which turned his talents to waste. Watch for the slow decline in people you care about.

Franklin learned that lending money to a friend who keeps promising to repay, while having no income to show for it, can leave you exposed. Be careful about how much you let someone borrow from you when their prospects are unclear.
Franklin held that anger and a sour mood cloud judgment, so a small quarrel can grow into a bigger one than it needs to be. Notice when your own feelings are steering your decisions.

Franklin found that an offer of help can look generous and sincere while hiding a habit of making promises that are never kept. Check a person's reputation with others before you rely on their word, especially when you are depending on it.

Benjamin Franklin saw that going to the source in person, choosing your own stock and meeting the people in your trade, can pay off in useful contacts and better goods. Being on the spot often beats ordering from afar.
Benjamin Franklin noticed how easily a reasonable mind can find a reason for whatever it already wants to do. Be wary of building arguments to suit your appetite.
Benjamin Franklin used a Socratic method of patient questions that led an opponent step by step into contradictions. It works best when you ask, not when you lecture, and it wins people over.
Benjamin Franklin observed that a sudden change of habit often sits easier than a slow, gradual one. He also warned that a plan you have lost interest in is easily abandoned when temptation arrives.

Benjamin Franklin noticed that Osborne's advice to Ralph was sound: steady diligence and punctuality can earn a start in business, even without capital. Ralph, by contrast, was chasing a dream that was unlikely to pay.

Franklin passed off Ralph's poem as his own and let his friends judge it on its merits. Praise for work that is unsigned or unclaimed shows what people really think of it, and it humbled Osborne's habit of criticising too freely.

Franklin's tale of the governor shows how a promise of help that keeps being postponed can leave a person stranded. Ask for a firm date and written commitments before you plan around someone else's word.

Benjamin Franklin learned to check claims before relying on them: he compared the letters he was given with what he knew of the sender. Trust should follow evidence about a person's character, not just a polite manner.

Benjamin Franklin took his setback to a trusted, experienced friend, who advised him to improve his skills in his own trade while in London. A setback can become a chance to build the skills you will need later.
Benjamin Franklin observed that a man who wishes to please everybody, and has little to give, ends up giving only expectations. Promises that cannot be kept do lasting damage to trust.

Benjamin Franklin passed on information to Hamilton, who was in a position to use it, even though it was not in his own interest to make a fuss. Telling a person what affects them is a fair and useful thing to do.

Franklin saw that his friend Ralph kept chasing jobs that were beneath his pride, and so kept failing. Being willing to take honest, modest work while looking for something better is a sound way to get by.

Franklin called his own choices like neglecting a far-off obligation and printing a provocative pamphlet his 'errata', and wished he could correct them. Owning past mistakes plainly, without excuse, is a useful habit.
Franklin got ahead by making himself useful to people and by showing a curious, willing mind, so new acquaintances opened doors. Good work and an open manner tend to bring useful contacts.

preview.text:
Benjamin Franklin was born in Milk Street, Boston, on January 6, 1706.
His father, Josiah Franklin, was a tallow chandler who married twice,
and of his seventeen children Benjamin was the youngest son. His
schooling ended at ten, and at twelve he was bound apprentice to his
brother James, a printer, who published the "New England Courant." To
this journal he became a contributor, and later was for a time its
nominal editor. But the brothers quarreled, and Benjamin ran away, going
first to New York, and thence to Philadelphia, where he arrived in
October, 1723. He soon obtained work as a printer, but after a few
months he was induced by Governor Keith to go to London, where, finding
Keith's promises empty, he again worked as a compositor till he was
brought back to Philadelphia by a merchant named Denman, who gave him a
position in his business. On Denman's death he returned to his former
trade, and shortly set up a printing house of his own from which he
published "The Pennsylvania Gazette," to which he contributed many
essays, and which he made a medium for agitating a variety of local
reforms. In 1732 he began to issue his famous "Poor Richard's Almanac"
for the enrichment of which he borrowed or composed those pithy
utterances of worldly wisdom which are the basis of a large part of his
popular reputation. In 1758, the year in which he ceased writing for the
Almanac, he printed in it "Father Abraham's Sermon," now regarded as the
most famous piece of literature produced in Colonial America.

books.title: On the Origin of Species
books.author: Charles Darwin
books.subject: big ideas
books.licence_note: Author died 1882. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Charles Darwin's opening quotes hold that events come about through general laws rather than separate interventions of divine power, and that a person should keep studying both the book of God's word and the book of God's works. Keep learning widely and never stop.

Darwin observed that every species can increase far faster than its food and space allow, so competition is universal. The fiercest struggle is usually between individuals and varieties of the same species, not between different kinds of creatures.

Darwin noted that traits that are used grow stronger and those left unused tend to fade, and that changes in one part of a body often bring changes in another. Competition among small differences is what shapes which forms survive.

Darwin spent years gathering and reflecting on facts before he trusted his conclusions, and he said so openly to show he had not been hasty. Careful, patient evidence-gathering comes before a firm decision.

Darwin held back his work for years, but he chose to publish a shorter version once another researcher had reached much the same ideas. Sharing your work in time matters more than waiting for it to be perfect.
Darwin held that a conclusion about descent is unsatisfying until you can show how the modifications arose. Explaining fine adaptation by a vague outside cause is not enough.
Darwin held that the best way to understand how living things change is to study domesticated animals and cultivated plants, which show variation openly. He thought this was neglected but valuable.
Darwin held that more individuals are born than can survive, so any slight variation that helps an individual has a better chance and is passed on. Small advantages accumulate over generations.

Darwin held that our knowledge of how living things depend on one another is so limited that much about the origin of species will stay unexplained for a long time. He still saw that these relations shape the future of every living thing.

Darwin argued that species are not fixed but descend from earlier, often extinct, species, much as varieties descend from their parent species. He saw natural selection as the main, though not the only, means of change.

Darwin observed that cultivated plants and animals vary more among themselves than wild species do, likely because they are raised under less uniform conditions. A change in conditions has to last several generations before it produces noticeable variation.

Darwin suspected that most variation starts in the reproductive elements before conception, since confinement and cultivation disturb breeding far more than other bodily functions. Changes in conditions can quietly stop an organism from reproducing.

Darwin noted that 'sporting' buds, which suddenly differ from the rest of a plant, are rare in nature but common under cultivation. He took this as support for the idea that variation comes from the parent's treatment before reproduction.

Darwin observed that seedlings and young from the same parents can differ noticeably even under identical conditions. So the direct effect of food, light and climate is usually small compared with the laws of reproduction and inheritance.

Darwin held that use and disuse shape a body over generations, so a domestic duck with less flying and more walking ends up with lighter wings and heavier legs. Habit can therefore leave a lasting mark that is passed on.
Charles Darwin noted that changing one part of an animal often changes other, distinct parts too, so a breeder who selects for one trait will likely alter others without meaning to.
Charles Darwin argued that inheritance should be treated as the normal rule and non-inheritance as the exception, since rare traits that reappear in a family are unlikely to be coincidence.
Charles Darwin observed that a trait tends to show up in offspring at the same stage of life it first appeared in the parent, a rule he thought central to understanding embryology.

Darwin argued that the claim that domestic varieties always revert to wild ancestors is unproven. Reversion is possible, but the outcome depends on changed conditions, and natural selection decides which new traits survive.

Darwin held that domestic races of one species differ from each other much as closely related species do in nature, only usually to a lesser degree. Experts often disagree whether a given form is a variety or a distinct species.

Darwin noted that it is hard to measure how different domestic races are when we do not know whether they came from one parent species or several. Settling that question would bear on whether closely allied wild species are truly fixed.

Darwin doubted the idea that people chose animals and plants for domestication because they were unusually variable or hardy. Early humans could not have known such traits in advance, and any species given time under breeding would vary much as domesticated ones have.

Darwin admitted that the origin of most ancient domestic animals and plants cannot be settled, since old records show diversity that may have arisen long before those records. Ancient evidence can only show when a breed was already known, not how it began.

Darwin warned that it is absurd to assume a separate wild ancestor for every slight, true-breeding variety. Inherited variation within a species can explain much of what looks like many separate origins.

Darwin held that crossing two very different breeds rarely gives a stable new one, since the mongrels of later generations differ widely. Producing a lasting new form takes careful, long-continued selection of the best individuals.

Charles Darwin held that choosing one special group to study closely, such as domestic pigeons, is the best way to learn general truths. He kept every breed he could obtain and talked with expert fanciers.

Charles Darwin noticed that many separate features of a body, from bones to feathers to eggs, can each vary independently. Careful study means looking at all of these traits, not just the most obvious one.

Charles Darwin reasoned by testing each rival explanation against the evidence. He asked whether the supposed original stocks could still exist unnoticed, or could have vanished, and found the second story hard to believe.

Darwin held that when many unlikely coincidences must all be true for a claim to work, the claim becomes improbable in the highest degree. He weighed how many strange chances a theory needed, not just whether it could be true.

Darwin held that when a trait keeps reappearing after crossbreeding, the simplest explanation is that the birds share a common ancestor, since the trait is hidden in their family history. Competing explanations often need several improbable assumptions to hold at once.

Darwin held that when several separate pieces of evidence each point the same way, taken together they can justify a conclusion that no single piece could. He also warned against stretching a hypothesis, such as easy fertility between distinct kinds, without any direct test.

Darwin held that a claim gains strength when it is backed by many independent lines of evidence, such as a smooth series of forms, traits that vary widely within a group, and long human records. He treated careful watching and patient breeding over time as a real source of knowledge.

Darwin noticed that breeders are firmly sure their breeds came from separate species, yet they accept slight differences as they win prizes by them. He urged caution before dismissing an idea just because its steps are too small to see.

Darwin held that the great variety of useful domestic breeds comes from accumulative selection: nature supplies small variations, and people add them up in the directions they find useful, one generation at a time.

Darwin pointed out that skilled breeders treat a living form as something they can shape steadily over the years. Patient, repeated selection, judged again and again, can change a flock far more than most people expect.

Darwin observed that the real gains came from small differences, too fine for an untrained eye, piled up over many generations. Mastery needs a sharp eye, years of study and sustained perseverance, and most people will not reach it.

Darwin noted that different varieties of one plant species often differ sharply in one valued part, such as leaves, flowers or fruit, while looking nearly alike in others. Choosing one trait over generations can reshape that part alone.

Darwin argued that the principle of selection was not a modern discovery, since ancient writers and early breeders already valued it. Careful attention to what gets passed on is an old and common practice.

Darwin held that unconscious selection works quietly: each person who keeps and breeds from their best individuals slowly changes a line over time, even without meaning to. Small steady choices add up to large change.

Charles Darwin observed that small, steady choices over generations can make animals and plants very different from their origins, and that breeders following the same method can end up with two quite different strains.
Charles Darwin held that people often keep the most useful animal alive in hard times, so the best individuals leave more offspring and a quiet selection happens even without anyone intending it.
Charles Darwin argued that gardeners improved fruit and flowers by always growing and saving seed from the best plant they had, so that progress came slowly and almost unconsciously.
Charles Darwin noted that improvement built up over centuries is why the wild ancestors of many garden plants are now hard to recognise at all.

Charles Darwin held that breeders can only select from variations nature first provides, and that the breeder rarely sets out to build a final form, since the first small deviation is what catches the eye.
Charles Darwin observed that people notice very small differences and value any novelty they own, so a slight change can matter far more to a keen eye than it would to an outsider.
Charles Darwin noted that improvements usually build up slowly and unrecorded, like a dialect, so the true history of a gradual change is often lost even when its results are plain to see.
Charles Darwin argued that improvement comes from keeping many individuals and paying close attention to small differences, since useful variations appear only now and then and are easily neglected.

Darwin noted that breeders succeed more easily when they can keep different lines apart and mate animals reliably, since pigeons pair for life and can be bred quickly in numbers. Breeds only form where someone actually chooses which animals to keep and breed.

Darwin held that the accumulated effect of selection, whether done deliberately and quickly or unconsciously and slowly, is the strongest force shaping change. Many other causes add to this, but they are harder to predict and matter less.

Darwin admitted that no one has yet given a definition of a species that satisfies every naturalist, yet people still use the word with a rough shared understanding. Good working terms can stay useful even when their exact edges are disputed.

Darwin noted that individual differences within one species are common, and that even important-looking parts vary. He warned that people who assume important features never vary are arguing in a circle.

Darwin observed that experts often dislike finding variation in what they consider key traits, so they seldom examine internal organs across many specimens. Careful, patient checking often shows more variety than expected.

Darwin observed that when two forms are linked by intermediate examples, scientists usually class one as a variety of the other. He warned that assumptions about missing links open a wide door to doubt and guesswork.

Darwin held that when judging whether a form is a species or a variety, the opinion of experienced, sound-judging experts is the best guide. Where they disagree, a majority view is often the practical answer.

Darwin noticed that experts often disagree on whether a form is a species or a mere variety, so the line between them is vague and arbitrary. Ask two careful judges and you may get two different answers.
Darwin held that arguing over whether a doubtful form is a species or a variety is pointless until the terms are clearly defined. Settle what you mean by the words before you argue about the answer.

Darwin weighed a case from many angles, such as appearance, habitat, range and crossing, and found the evidence pointing in different directions. Judge a hard question by gathering several kinds of evidence, not by one striking feature.

Darwin observed that the things people care most about get studied most, and so they collect the most disputed labels. Close, patient investigation usually brings careful people to agreement in the end.

Darwin observed that a beginner tends to make too many species, because they are impressed by small differences and lack wider knowledge. Only by studying widely does one learn to tell varieties from species, and even then at the cost of admitting more variation.

Darwin held that there is no clear dividing line between species, sub-species, varieties and individual differences, which blend into one another in an unbroken series. Each slight difference can be seen as a first step towards a more marked one.

books.title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.subject: detective
books.licence_note: Author died 1930. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In A Scandal in Bohemia, Doyle has Watson describe Holmes as a reasoner whose cold mind refuses strong feeling, because emotion can cloud the judgement that good thinking depends on.
In A Scandal in Bohemia, Holmes separates seeing from observing. Watson has climbed the stairs hundreds of times without noticing how many there are.
In A Scandal in Bohemia, Holmes warns that it is a capital mistake to theorise before you have data, because the mind starts bending facts to suit a theory rather than the reverse.

In A Scandal in Bohemia, Holmes reads small details of a letter, such as how a sentence is built, to work out where its writer comes from. Close attention to the small things narrows a question quickly.
In A Scandal in Bohemia, Holmes keeps a docketed index of people and things, so he can furnish information on almost any subject at once. Good records make hard questions quicker to answer.

In A Scandal in Bohemia, Holmes gets his best information from stable hands and cabmen, people at the edge of the household who see everything and are seldom asked. Look for the quiet people who watch the daily routine.
In A Scandal in Bohemia, Holmes lists the open questions in his case and notes what each answer would change. Knowing which unknown matters most tells you where to spend your effort next.
In A Scandal in Bohemia, Holmes reasons that a valued thing is usually kept where its owner can reach it quickly. He then chooses to ask rather than to search blindly.

In A Scandal in Bohemia, Watson feels ashamed of deceiving a kind woman, yet keeps his word to his friend. He weighs the harm his actions do against the harm they prevent, and that is a test of conscience worth remembering.

In A Scandal in Bohemia, Holmes waits rather than grabbing the photograph while the coachman is watching, because a little over-haste may ruin everything. Patience at the right moment is part of good work.

In A Scandal in Bohemia, Irene Adler only sees through Holmes's disguise after the alarm, and she keeps the photograph as protection rather than revenge. Even the sharpest reasoner can be outwitted, and a clever opponent is worth respecting.
In The Red-Headed League, Holmes argues that life itself is more daring than anything the imagination can invent, so real events can be stranger than fiction.
In The Red-Headed League, Holmes notes that the strangest cases often lie in small matters. A careful listener lets the client tell the whole story before judging what it means.
In The Red-Headed League, Holmes admits his deductions look like magic only because people do not know the method behind them. Explaining the reasoning turns wonder into understanding.
In The Red-Headed League, Jabez Wilson argues himself out of a too-good offer, then decides to check it with his own eyes rather than dismiss it on reasoning alone.
In The Red-Headed League, Holmes observes that the more bizarre a matter looks, the less mysterious it often proves. Plain, featureless facts are the harder ones to read.
In The Red-Headed League, Holmes sits still for a long while to let a problem settle, then moves with purpose once his mind is made up. Thinking before acting is part of good work.
In The Red-Headed League, Watson notes that Holmes's sharpest work came after days of idle rest, when his mind had been allowed to wander. Rest can prepare a mind for a hard job.
In The Red-Headed League, Watson feels dull beside Holmes, who sees what is about to happen where Watson sees only confusion. Watching a sharper mind at work can teach you to look more closely.
In The Red-Headed League, Holmes works out that a strange plan stops looking strange once you ask what it is for. Find the purpose behind an odd action and the rest often follows.
In The Red-Headed League, Holmes follows one small clue, the worn knees of a trouser, to a hidden tunnel. A single well-noticed detail can open up a whole plan.
In The Red-Headed League, Holmes describes his solution as a long chain in which every link must ring true. A good argument holds at every step, not just at the end.
In A Case of Identity, Holmes says the ordinary matters often leave the most room for observation, since the motive behind a large crime is usually obvious and the small ones need a sharper eye.

In A Case of Identity, Holmes holds that the little things are infinitely the most important. A small habit, like a man preferring typed letters less than handwritten ones, can reveal more than a grand statement.
In A Case of Identity, Holmes tells Watson never to trust general impressions and to concentrate on details instead. Careful attention to particulars is where good judgement starts.
In A Case of Identity, Holmes shows that a typewriter, like a handwriting, carries its own quirks, so even a disguised writer can be traced by the marks left on the page.
In A Case of Identity, Holmes asks who actually profits from a strange event. Then he checks each suspicious fact against the others, and the separate facts all point the same way.
In The Boscombe Valley Mystery, Holmes warns that there is nothing more deceptive than an obvious fact. Evidence that seems to point one way can point another if you shift your point of view.

In The Boscombe Valley Mystery, Holmes judges a suspect's reaction by whether it fits his position. A calm, frank response can mark an innocent man as easily as a careful one, so no single sign settles the question.

In The Boscombe Valley Mystery, Holmes points out that the critics pick only the strongest points against a suspect. He suggests taking the other version seriously and following where it leads, which is fairer than a verdict built on the worst reading.
In The Boscombe Valley Mystery, Watson weighs each fact by how far it really goes. A blow from behind helps the accused only a little, since the older man may have turned away before it fell.

In The Boscombe Valley Mystery, Holmes waits until he is rested before doing careful work, because a tired mind is a poor tool for fine judgement. Know when you are at your best and save the hard tasks for then.
In The Boscombe Valley Mystery, Holmes says a case often turns on two or three crucial points, and the rest can wait until those are settled. Find the few facts the whole matter depends on.
In The Boscombe Valley Mystery, Holmes asks why a man would press so hard for a match the other party opposed. Ask why a fact is odd, because the oddity is often the clue.

In The Boscombe Valley Mystery, Holmes narrows a whole district to one kind of man, using a dying word, a map and a few small facts. Patient inference from trifles can shrink a vague problem to a clear one.

In The Boscombe Valley Mystery, Holmes says that anyone could have fallen as the killer did, and that only good fortune keeps most of us clear of it. Judging others with that humility keeps a detective fair.
In The Five Orange Pips, Watson recalls how Holmes settled a poisoning case by reading a dead man's watch, showing that an ordinary object, checked carefully, can fix the time of events.
In The Five Orange Pips, Holmes admits he has been beaten four times, three by men and once by a woman. A good reasoner owns his losses plainly and does not pretend to a perfect record.

In The Five Orange Pips, a father refuses to take a real warning seriously and forbids the police, because he would rather not look foolish. Pride can keep a person from the help that would protect them.
In The Five Orange Pips, Holmes tells a frightened client that safety comes first, then understanding the mystery, and that revenge can wait. Put the most urgent need at the front of the queue.
In The Five Orange Pips, Holmes says a skilled observer who understands one link in a chain of events can work out the others. A single well-understood fact can reveal the whole sequence.

In The Five Orange Pips, Holmes says a person should keep in the mind what they are likely to use and store the rest where it can be fetched when needed. Know what you use daily and where to find the rest.
In The Five Orange Pips, Holmes reads the delay between each threat and its deed as a clue to how far the sender had to travel. The time between events can itself be evidence.
In The Five Orange Pips, Holmes admits that a client's death hurts his pride and makes the case personal. Admitting what drives you is more honest than pretending to be a neutral observer.
In The Man with the Twisted Lip, Watson notes that people in grief came to his wife like birds to a lighthouse. Being a steady, kind presence draws others to you when they need help.
In The Man with the Twisted Lip, Holmes values Watson's silence because it lets him think aloud. A quiet listener who does not interrupt can help a thinker as much as any advice.

In The Man with the Twisted Lip, Holmes takes a theory as a working hypothesis when nothing better is available, while admitting the questions are still open. A useful theory is held loosely enough to drop when the facts disagree.

In The Man with the Twisted Lip, Holmes shows that a sign which looks like a cry for help may have an ordinary explanation. Test the obvious reading against the other possibilities before you act on it.

In The Man with the Twisted Lip, Holmes turns a hard problem over for days, rearranging the facts and looking at it from every side, until he either solves it or knows his data is not enough. Patient turning-over is how hard problems give way.
In The Man with the Twisted Lip, Holmes admits he has been as blind as a mole, and says it is better to learn wisdom late than never. Owning an error and correcting course is part of thinking well.
In The Man with the Twisted Lip, Holmes tells a man who hid his secret that he would have done better to trust his wife. Concealment often costs more in the end than the truth would have.
In The Blue Carbuncle, Holmes notes that a crowded city produces many odd events that are strange without being criminal. Not every puzzle is a crime, and it helps to tell them apart.

In The Blue Carbuncle, Holmes tells Watson that he sees everything but fails to reason from it, and is too timid in drawing inferences. Good observation needs the nerve to draw a conclusion and hold it with suitable care.
In The Blue Carbuncle, Arthur Conan Doyle shows Holmes reading a man's habits from small marks, like five tallow stains, and reasoning from evidence rather than guesswork.
In The Blue Carbuncle, Holmes says to try the simplest means first, such as a plain advertisement, and only then turn to harder methods.
In The Blue Carbuncle, Holmes notes that a man drawn into a wager gives away far more than he would if simply asked, because he forgets to guard what he says.
In The Blue Carbuncle, Doyle shows how the temptation of sudden, easily gained wealth can overwhelm a man who has never gone wrong before, and how quickly the temptation turns to ruin.
In The Blue Carbuncle, Ryder's guilt makes every passer-by look like a policeman, so Doyle shows that a frightened conscience can be its own worst watchman.
In The Blue Carbuncle, Holmes lets a frightened thief go, reasoning that a man already shaken into repentance may be saved, while a prison sentence could make him a criminal for life.
In The Adventure of the Speckled Band, Doyle traces the Roylott family's ruin to generations of waste, and shows the son rebuilding his life by adapting to new conditions and applying his own skill.

I could not help laughing at the ease with which he explained his
process of deduction. “When I hear you give your reasons,” I remarked,
“the thing always appears to me to be so ridiculously simple that I
could easily do it myself, though at each successive instance of your
reasoning I am baffled until you explain your process. And yet I
believe that my eyes are as good as yours.”

“Quite so,” he answered, lighting a cigarette, and throwing himself
down into an armchair. “You see, but you do not observe. The
distinction is clear. For example, you have frequently seen the steps
which lead up from the hall to this room.”

“Frequently.”

“How often?”

“Well, some hundreds of times.”

“Then how many are there?”

“How many? I don’t know.”

“Quite so! You have not observed. And yet you have seen. That is just
my point. Now, I know that there are seventeen steps, because I have
both seen and observed. By the way, since you are interested in these
little problems, and since you are good enough to chronicle one or two
of my trifling experiences, you may be interested in this.” He threw
over a sheet of thick, pink-tinted notepaper which had been lying open
upon the table. “It came by the last post,” said he. “Read it aloud.”

The note was undated, and without either signature or address.

“There will call upon you to-night, at a quarter to eight o’clock,” it
said, “a gentleman who desires to consult you upon a matter of the very
deepest moment. Your recent services to one of the royal houses of
Europe have shown that you are one who may safely be trusted with
matters which are of an importance which can hardly be exaggerated.
This account of you we have from all quarters received. Be in your
chamber then at that hour, and do not take it amiss if your visitor
wear a mask.”

books.title: Grimms' Fairy Tales
books.author: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Authors died 1863 and 1859. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Golden Bird, the two elder sons lose their quest to a warm, lively inn and forget both their task and their home, which shows how easily pleasure can pull us off course.
In The Golden Bird, the youngest son succeeds because he takes the fox's advice and is thankful for it, where his brothers had brushed it aside.
In The Golden Bird, the fox helps the youngest son again after he ignored its advice, showing that good counsel can still be offered to someone who failed to heed it.
In Hans in Luck, the Grimms show a man who trades each prize for something smaller and still calls himself lucky, a reminder that how we value what we have shapes how fortunate we feel.
In Hans in Luck, the hero trades for a cow without checking whether it gives any milk, a quiet reminder to find out what a deal actually delivers before counting on it.
In Jorinda and Jorindel, the young shepherd does not give up after his first failure, and he searches for the magic flower for eight days before finding it on the ninth.
In The Travelling Musicians, four old animals cast aside by their owners gather on the road and find each other's company, so rejection becomes the start of a new life together.
In Old Sultan, the old dog is offered a bribe by the wolf to look the other way, and he refuses, choosing to stay true to the master who has kept faith with him.
In The Straw, the Coal, and the Bean, the coal loses her nerve halfway across the bridge, and the whole plan falls apart, a reminder that bold starts need steady follow-through.

In Briar Rose, the twelfth fairy cannot undo the thirteenth fairy's curse, but she softens it, so the princess sleeps rather than dies, showing how a kind word can limit harm that cannot be fully reversed.
In The Dog and the Sparrow, the cruel carter loses his horses, his wine and his corn, and finally his life, because his cruelty keeps feeding his own ruin.

In The Twelve Dancing Princesses, the youngest sister keeps sensing that something is wrong while the eldest brushes her fears aside, a reminder that a persistent unease is sometimes worth taking seriously.
In The Fisherman and His Wife, Ilsabill is granted each wish and still wants more, showing how endless wanting can outrun any gain and leave a person less content than before.
In The Willow-Wren and the Bear, a tiny gnat overhears the enemy's plan and carries it back, showing that the small and overlooked can decide a contest that looks hopeless for them.
In The Frog-Prince, the king reminds his daughter that a given word must be kept, and she honours a promise she had made only to get rid of the frog.
In Cat and Mouse in Partnership, the cat lies again and again to steal the shared store, showing how a partner who deceives a trusting friend will eventually empty the larder they built together.
In The Goose-Girl, the princess meets her servant's rudeness with patience and says nothing, a quiet gentleness that the story later vindicates when the truth comes out.
In The Goose-Girl, the old king tricks the false bride into passing sentence on herself, showing how a person's own words can expose them when the truth is told plainly.

In Chanticleer and Partlet, Partlet hides the biggest nut for herself instead of sharing as agreed, and it chokes her, a small warning about what keeping things back from the people we share with can cost.
In Rapunzel, a husband steals herbs out of love for his wife and so promises away the child they have not yet met, showing how one desperate act can commit us to a heavy price later.
In Rapunzel, the prince is blinded after his fall, and Rapunzel's tears restore his sight, showing how faithful love can heal what despair has broken.
In Fundevogel, Lina and her foster brother keep their promise to stay together, and their steady loyalty outwits every pursuer sent after them.
In The Valiant Little Tailor, the small tailor beats a giant by quick wits and calm nerve rather than strength, though his boasting shows that a reputation built on a bluff needs constant upkeep.
In The Valiant Little Tailor, the giants end up fighting each other after the tailor stirs up their suspicions, a reminder that rivals who distrust one another often defeat themselves.
In Hansel and Gretel, Hansel quietly gathers pebbles and then crumbs to mark the way, showing how a small, careful preparation made in the dark can carry a frightened family through.
In Hansel and Gretel, Gretel keeps her wits when the witch sets a trap and turns the oven back on its keeper, showing how calm thinking can reverse a danger that looks certain to end badly.

In The Mouse, the Bird, and the Sausage, the friends grow restless in their comfort and begin to resent one another's share of the work, showing how envy can spoil a partnership that was working well.
In Mother Holle, the diligent stepdaughter stops to help the bread and the apple tree before anything else, and the story shows that willing kindness and steady work are repaid in the end.
In Mother Holle, the lazy sister gets only a shower of pitch because she grows idle and careless, a plain reminder that a reward for effort can be lost through neglect.

In Little Red-Cap, the girl leaves the path to pick flowers because the wolf's sweet talk draws her away from the duty she was given, showing how a flattering distraction can pull us off the road we meant to keep.
In Little Red-Cap, the grandmother outwits the wolf by thinking ahead about what will draw him in, showing that a little foresight can beat brute force.

In The Robber Bridegroom, the bride tells her terrible night as a dream in front of the wedding guests, letting them judge the danger for themselves, a clever way to expose a threat that would never be believed if told plainly.
In Tom Thumb, the little man makes the best of each setback, from a mouse-hole to the inside of a cow, and keeps his wits about him instead of giving in to misfortune.
In Tom Thumb, the little traveller who has seen mouse-holes, snail-shells and a wolf's belly ends by agreeing that there is no place like home, a plain point about where a person's real riches lie.
In Rumpelstiltskin, the queen undoes a desperate bargain by sending messengers far and wide and listening for the one thing she needs, showing how patient searching can answer what fear could not.
In The Old Man and His Grandson, a father sees his cruelty to a frail grandfather reflected in a small child's play and changes his ways, showing how children quietly teach us how we treat the old.
In Frederick and Catherine, the wife does each foolish thing because nobody told her not to, a comic reminder that people cannot follow expectations that were never spelled out for them.
In Sweetheart Roland, the faithful maiden keeps her loyalty to a man who has forgotten her, and it is her song that finally brings his memory back to him.
In Snowdrop, the queen cannot bear to be outshone and keeps asking her mirror for reassurance, a sharp picture of how vanity makes a person miserable when someone else flourishes.
In Snowdrop, the servant sent to destroy the girl cannot bring himself to do it, and he spares her, showing how a moment of mercy can outweigh an order given in anger.
In Snowdrop, the girl who has refused every warning finally eats the apple when a kind-seeming stranger urges her, showing how even the most careful person can be worn down by a persuasive voice.
In The Pink, the servant girl refuses to kill the innocent boy in her care even under threat, showing how conscience can hold firm against someone who has power over you.
In the Grimms' tale of the wronged queen, she keeps her faith and calm while she is shut away and mistreated, and her steadiness outlasts the cruelty around her.
In Clever Elsie, the Grimms show a household that weeps over a misfortune that has not happened yet, and the worry spreads from one person to the next.
In Clever Elsie, the heroine keeps putting off the work in front of her, eating first and then sleeping first, until the whole day is lost. The story makes the lesson about getting on with the job.
In The Miser in the Bush, the Grimms show a stingy farmer paying three years of faithful work with a small sum, and a servant who sees clearly that he has been cheated.
In The Miser in the Bush, a countryman who has saved three years of wages gives it all to a poor stranger out of pity, and the story treats that generosity as the true richness.
In The Miser in the Bush, the Grimms show a greedy man who grew rich by cheating poor people, and his own greed is turned against him.
In The Miser in the Bush, the miser is finally forced to admit that his gold was stolen, and the story shows that a cheat's gains do not stay with him once the truth is pressed.
In Ashputtel, a dying mother asks her daughter to stay good and kind, and the girl keeps that promise through years of harsh treatment from her stepmother and stepsisters.
In Ashputtel, the girl asks her father for nothing grand, only a twig, and she plants and tends it on her mother's grave until it grows into a tree that gives her what she needs.
In Ashputtel, the birds come to help the girl sort the peas, and the story shows that a person who has been gentle and good often finds help arriving when it is needed.
In Ashputtel, the girl keeps returning to the hazel-tree she planted, and the story shows that steady, faithful return to what you have tended brings help when you need it.
In Ashputtel, the eldest stepsister cuts off her own toe to fit the golden slipper, and the story shows how far vanity and ambition can push people to hurt themselves.
In The White Snake, the servant stops to rescue three fish and to spare an ant-king's people, and the story shows that small kindnesses come back to a person when they are most needed.
In The White Snake, the young man gives up his own horse to feed starving young ravens, and the Grimms show generosity that costs something real.
In The White Snake, the creatures the youth helped repay him in a way he could not have managed alone, so help freely given can return at the moment it counts.

In The Wolf and the Seven Little Kids, the kids refuse to open the door to a voice they know is wrong, and the Grimms show that checking the evidence protects you from a tempter who is good at disguise.
In The Wolf and the Seven Little Kids, the youngest kid hides in the clock-case and is the one who escapes, so the smallest and quietest person in the room can still be the one who survives.

In The Wolf and the Seven Little Kids, the mother and her children rescue their siblings by working together, first with scissors and then with stones, and the story shows that patient teamwork can undo a greedy bully.

preview.text:
Then the gardener’s eldest son set out and thought to find the golden
bird very easily; and when he had gone but a little way, he came to a
wood, and by the side of the wood he saw a fox sitting; so he took his
bow and made ready to shoot at it. Then the fox said, ‘Do not shoot me,
for I will give you good counsel; I know what your business is, and
that you want to find the golden bird. You will reach a village in the
evening; and when you get there, you will see two inns opposite to each
other, one of which is very pleasant and beautiful to look at: go not in
there, but rest for the night in the other, though it may appear to you
to be very poor and mean.’ But the son thought to himself, ‘What can
such a beast as this know about the matter?’ So he shot his arrow at
the fox; but he missed it, and it set up its tail above its back and
ran into the wood. Then he went his way, and in the evening came to
the village where the two inns were; and in one of these were people
singing, and dancing, and feasting; but the other looked very dirty,
and poor. ‘I should be very silly,’ said he, ‘if I went to that shabby
house, and left this charming place’; so he went into the smart house,
and ate and drank at his ease, and forgot the bird, and his country too.

Time passed on; and as the eldest son did not come back, and no tidings
were heard of him, the second son set out, and the same thing happened
to him. He met the fox, who gave him the good advice: but when he came
to the two inns, his eldest brother was standing at the window where
the merrymaking was, and called to him to come in; and he could not
withstand the temptation, but went in, and forgot the golden bird and
his country in the same manner.

books.title: The Enchiridion
books.author: Epictetus
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died about 135, translator died 1911. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Epictetus held that philosophy practised as a way of life is what makes a person free, even when the outside world is restrictive.
Epictetus taught Stoicism as both a doctrine and a way of life, aiming to turn the study of ideas into daily conduct.
Arrian's record of Epictetus shows a teacher who applied philosophy to each student's real situation, so ideas were practised rather than finished.
Epictetus held that we are free when we separate what is in our power, such as our judgements, intentions and choices, from what is not, such as reputation, wealth and death.
Epictetus taught that if we claim only what is truly ours and see other people's affairs as they are, no one can compel or restrict us.
Epictetus advised us to direct our aversion at what we can control, and to hold back our desire for things beyond our reach.
Epictetus held that people are disturbed by their own views of events, not by the events themselves.
Epictetus taught that when something is taken from us, we should see it as returned, holding what we have as something on loan.
Epictetus advised that whoever wants to be free should want nothing, and refuse nothing, that depends on other people.
Epictetus advised that when someone grieves, we can sit with them and share their sorrow in conversation, while keeping our own inner judgement clear.
Epictetus judged success by what we keep of our honour and integrity, not by money, office or the praise of others.
Epictetus noted that we accept other people's losses calmly but are overwhelmed by our own, and urged us to judge our losses as we judge theirs.
Epictetus advised weighing the costs and consequences of a venture before starting, so that enthusiasm alone does not lead us to quit when the hard parts arrive.
Epictetus taught that our duties follow from our relationships, as parent, citizen or neighbour, and that we keep our own conduct right whatever others do.
Epictetus advised keeping conversation to what is needful and away from gossip and complaints about others.
Epictetus suggested imagining how Socrates or Zeno would act before meeting someone important, so we face hard moments with composure.
Epictetus held that when we act from clear judgement that something is right, we should not shrink from being seen doing it, even if others misunderstand.
Epictetus said everything has two handles, and that we should take hold of a wrong by the side we can bear, such as a brother's shared upbringing.
Epictetus advised showing our principles through action rather than talk, and staying quiet about them among people who do not share them.
Epictetus warned that being able to explain a wise teacher's words is worth nothing unless we act on them.
Epictetus urged us to stop postponing self-improvement, since putting it off day after day means we accomplish nothing at all.
Epictetus said the most important part of philosophy is putting principles into practice, yet we often spend more effort arguing about why they hold.

preview.text:
That there was a rebirth of Stoicism in the centuries of rebirth which
marked the emergence of the modern age was not mere chance.
Philosophical, moral, and social conditions of the time united to cause
it. Roman Stoicism had been developed in times of despotism as a
philosophy of lonely and courageous souls who had recognized the
redeeming power of philosophical reason in all the moral and social
purposes of life. Philosophy as a way of life makes men free. It is the
last ditch stand of liberty in a world of servitude. Many elements in the
new age led to thought which had structural affinity with Roman Stoicism.
Modern times had created the independent thinker, the free intellectual
in a secular civilization. Modern times had destroyed medieval liberties
and had established the new despotism of the absolute state supported by
ecclesiastical authority. Modern philosophies continued the basic trend
in Stoicism in making the subjective consciousness the foundation of
philosophy. The Stoic emphasis on moral problems was also appealing in an
era of rapid transition when all the values which had previously been
taken for granted were questioned and reconsidered.

books.title: The Secret Garden
books.author: Frances Hodgson Burnett
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1924. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Secret Garden, Frances Hodgson Burnett shows how a child who is never loved or attended to can grow sour and selfish, and how much attention can change her.
In The Secret Garden, Burnett observes that people in a crisis tend to think only of themselves, so a child nobody loves is easily forgotten.
In The Secret Garden, Burnett shows a child who sees unpleasantness in everyone else but not in herself, a blind spot most people share at some point.
In The Secret Garden, Mary's pity for her gloomy uncle turns to disdain the moment she decides he deserves his troubles, which shows how quickly we harden against people we have not met.
In The Secret Garden, Martha loves the moor that Mary finds bare, which shows that a place looks empty or full depending on how well you have come to know it.
In The Secret Garden, Martha insists that doing things for yourself does you good, and that a child waited on hand and foot never learns to look after herself.
In The Secret Garden, Mary's first interest in someone other than herself is the start of a better nature, and Burnett calls it a healthy sentiment, which is how real change tends to begin.
In The Secret Garden, Mary only recognises that loneliness makes her sour when she says it aloud to the robin, which shows that naming a feeling can be the first step to changing it.
In The Secret Garden, Ben Weatherstaff gives Mary the plain truth about her temper, and it unsettles her because nobody has been that frank with her before.
In The Secret Garden, Mary counts feeling sorry for someone among her good things, which shows how compassion can grow quietly out of ordinary days.
In The Secret Garden, Dickon goes out in the rain because he says wet days show things that fair weather hides, a reminder that the dull or difficult days can teach you the most.
In The Secret Garden, Mary wants to take a nest of mice home because they are frightened, a small early sign of the tenderness she has not yet shown to people.
In The Secret Garden, Mary decides she will find out what the crying was, and Burnett uses that stubborn curiosity to carry the story forward.
In The Secret Garden, Martha's mother asks her daughter how she likes herself, a question that brings a person to their senses faster than any scolding would.
In The Secret Garden, Ben Weatherstaff says that real growth comes a little at a time, so you have to watch closely and be patient, since things do not grow up in a night.
In The Secret Garden, Martha's mother asks her to picture how she would feel alone in a big place, a simple route to empathy that anyone can practise.
In The Secret Garden, Mary admits she is not used to thanking people, and her stiff thank you is the first small sign that she is starting to notice what others do for her.
In The Secret Garden, Mary hopes the roses that look dead might still put out leaves, and that quiet hope about something that seems lost is what drives the story forward.
In The Secret Garden, Mary decides the garden is not dead because other things are alive, a useful habit when a whole project looks lost: look for what is still growing.
In The Secret Garden, Mary forgets the time while she weeds, which shows how absorbing work can bring a happiness that idleness never does.
In The Secret Garden, Martha says bulbs help themselves and spread for years when left alone, a reminder that some growth needs patience more than meddling.
In The Secret Garden, Ben Weatherstaff warms to Mary once she becomes more civil, which shows that the way we speak to people shapes how they answer us.

In The Secret Garden, Ben Weatherstaff says you cannot judge a rose by its bare grey twigs, and you must wait for spring to see whether it lives, a reminder not to write off what looks dead too early.
In The Secret Garden, Mary finds the world seems to get nicer once she has something to care about, which shows how a purpose can lift a low spirit.
In The Secret Garden, Mary finally tells Dickon her secret and bursts into tears, showing how carrying something alone can wear a person down until sharing it brings relief.
In The Secret Garden, Dickon praises Mary for clearing space around the little plants without knowing much about gardening, a reminder that close attention often does more than expertise.

In The Secret Garden, Dickon suggests there is little need to be contrary when there are flowers and friendly creatures about, a gentle reminder that good work and fine surroundings soften a sour mood.
In The Secret Garden, the grieving Mr Craven gives Mary leave to make neglected ground come alive, showing that real kindness can come from someone who is himself badly hurt.
In The Secret Garden, Dickon keeps Mary's secret by sending her a silent picture, showing that a promise of trust can be kept without a single word being spoken.
In The Secret Garden, Colin has been obeyed all his life and never asked to do anything he dislikes, and Burnett shows that a child never expected to do for others grows sad rather than strong.
In The Secret Garden, Colin tells Mary that if you stay in a room you never really see things, a reminder that a narrow life misses what going out into the world shows.
In The Secret Garden, Colin blames his mother for dying and turns away from her portrait, showing how grief can harden into blame when it has nowhere else to go.
In The Secret Garden, Mary sings a frightened boy to sleep simply because she is sorry for him, showing that kindness often starts with noticing that someone else is unhappy.
In The Secret Garden, Mary turns a gloomy talk about dying into talk about living and loved things, and the change of subject lifts them both.
In The Secret Garden, Colin says Mary makes him forget his troubles, which is why he wants her near, showing that good company can lighten a heavy mind more than constant fussing.
In The Secret Garden, Mary decides to find out whether Colin can keep a secret before trusting him with one, a sensible way to extend trust gradually rather than all at once.
In The Secret Garden, Colin screams and bites at the stares and whispers of people who pity him as a dying child. Burnett shows how being constantly looked at can make a person close up.
In The Secret Garden, Dickon teaches that shy wild things only come close when you stop watching them so hard and keep still. Patience lets the robin come to trust you.
In The Secret Garden, Dickon warns that you can lose a friend by being too curious and meddling with their ways. Respecting how another person works is part of caring for them.
In The Secret Garden, Dickon's mother lets her son keep his own secrets and trusts him to know what is right. Trust given freely helps a young person grow steady.
In The Secret Garden, Dickon sees that a worried mind fixes on the wrong things, and that turning attention to growing things lifts a person. Where we put our attention shapes how we feel.
In The Secret Garden, Mary realises that people who have been ill and nervous can learn to master their tempers, rather than pass their misery on to everyone around them.
In The Secret Garden, Mary's blunt honesty stings Colin, but it gives him a real argument for the first time. Burnett shows that a frank friend can do more good than soft pity.
In The Secret Garden, Colin's fears grow larger because he lies alone for years thinking only about himself. Burnett shows how isolation and self-focus can feed a person's worries.
In The Secret Garden, Colin and Mary make up after their quarrel by each reaching half way. Burnett shows that making peace often takes just one small gesture from each side.
In The Secret Garden, Mary calms Colin not by ordering him to sleep but by describing a hopeful place for him to imagine. A gentle picture of something good can settle a frightened mind.
In The Secret Garden, Mary admits she disliked people until she met the robin and Dickon. Burnett suggests that kind company and living things can soften even a sour temper.
In The Secret Garden, Dr Craven privately fears that a healthy Colin would cost him an inheritance. Burnett shows how self-interest can quietly shape a person's choices, even when they are not cruel.
In The Secret Garden, Susan Sowerby says nobody owns the whole orange, and that grabbing at all of it leaves only the bitter pips. Burnett's point is that greed defeats itself.

In The Secret Garden, Dickon goes round and round the moor until he finds a lost lamb that is crying for its mother. Burnett shows that patient searching for something small and helpless is a form of care.
In The Secret Garden, Dr Craven says he would trust Dickon with a new-born child, because of how Dickon treats animals. Burnett suggests you can judge a person by how gently they handle the helpless.
In The Secret Garden, Burnett says that wonder at a sunrise or in the stillness of a wood can make a person feel, for a moment, that life is endless. Such moments are worth noticing.
In The Secret Garden, Colin resolves to watch everything grow and to grow alongside it. Burnett shows that a person comes alive again by taking an active part in something that is growing.

In The Secret Garden, Dickon tells Colin that the magic he feels is the same magic that brings crocuses up out of the earth. Burnett suggests that wonder is found in the ordinary work of things growing.
In The Secret Garden, old Ben keeps tending a dead woman's roses for years out of loyalty to her. Burnett shows that love can carry on through small, faithful acts long after the person is gone.
In The Secret Garden, Mary notices that Colin is rude because nobody has ever dared to contradict him. Burnett shows how people who are always deferred to lose sight of how they treat others.

In The Secret Garden, Colin finds that if you watch long enough you can see buds open and insects going about their work. Burnett shows that patient attention turns an ordinary day into a wide world of small wonders.
In The Secret Garden, Colin says that scientific people are simply curious, asking "what is it?" about things they do not yet understand. Burnett presents curiosity as the real start of learning.

In The Secret Garden, Colin believes that words repeated every day, like a soldier's drill, will sink in until they become part of you. Burnett shows the power of steady practice, even when the reasons are mistaken.

In The Secret Garden, Dickon says the way to make plants thrive is to be their friend and give them what they need, because they want to live as we do. Burnett shows that patient, caring attention is the real secret of good gardening.

preview.text:
When Mary Lennox was sent to Misselthwaite Manor to live with her uncle
everybody said she was the most disagreeable-looking child ever seen.
It was true, too. She had a little thin face and a little thin body,
thin light hair and a sour expression. Her hair was yellow, and her
face was yellow because she had been born in India and had always been
ill in one way or another. Her father had held a position under the
English Government and had always been busy and ill himself, and her
mother had been a great beauty who cared only to go to parties and
amuse herself with gay people. She had not wanted a little girl at all,
and when Mary was born she handed her over to the care of an Ayah, who
was made to understand that if she wished to please the Mem Sahib she
must keep the child out of sight as much as possible. So when she was a
sickly, fretful, ugly little baby she was kept out of the way, and when
she became a sickly, fretful, toddling thing she was kept out of the
way also. She never remembered seeing familiarly anything but the dark
faces of her Ayah and the other native servants, and as they always
obeyed her and gave her her own way in everything, because the Mem
Sahib would be angry if she was disturbed by her crying, by the time
she was six years old she was as tyrannical and selfish a little pig as
ever lived. The young English governess who came to teach her to read
and write disliked her so much that she gave up her place in three
months, and when other governesses came to try to fill it they always
went away in a shorter time than the first one. So if Mary had not
chosen to really want to know how to read books she would never have
learned her letters at all.

books.title: Treasure Island
books.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
books.subject: adventure
books.licence_note: Author died 1894. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Treasure Island, Stevenson shows that a man who lives in fear of his past cannot rest, even when he is the loudest and most feared person in the room.
In Treasure Island, Dr. Livesey shows courage as calm steadiness. He keeps talking plainly while a dangerous man threatens him with a knife.
Stevenson shows that a firm, calm warning from someone with real standing can stop a bully better than shouting. Dr. Livesey names the consequence and then acts on it.
In Treasure Island, Jim turns down a golden guinea for a favour and gives only what he owes. He shows that integrity is a choice you make when someone offers you a shortcut.
In Treasure Island, Jim's mother refuses to let fear decide for the village. She says she will go back herself, and that is enough to show that courage often starts with one person stepping forward.
In Treasure Island, Jim's curiosity is stronger than his fear, so he creeps back to watch the attack. Stevenson shows that a steady nerve often comes from wanting to know the truth.
In Treasure Island, Pew's greed and rage turn his gang against itself. Stevenson shows that a crew held together only by fear and shared greed falls apart once its leader loses control.
In Treasure Island, Jim chooses whom to trust with the valuable packet. He picks a man he already knows over the first helpful stranger who offers, which is good judgment under pressure.

In Treasure Island, Dr. Livesey names the risk he fears most, which is his enthusiastic friend's loose tongue. He then sets a plan to protect the venture, showing that a candid warning to a friend is a form of loyalty.
In Treasure Island, the squire hires a cook out of pure pity and does not check him closely. Stevenson shows how kindness that skips judgment can open the door to danger.

In Treasure Island, Jim sets aside his old fear of the one-legged sailor once he meets the real man in front of him. Stevenson shows that fears built from rumour should give way to what you can see yourself.
In Treasure Island, Silver's easy charm and quick excuses disarm even a suspicious boy. Stevenson shows that a warm, confident manner can hide what a person is really doing.

In Treasure Island, Captain Smollett speaks plainly about his doubts, even at the risk of giving offence. He asks why things are being kept secret, which is how an honest leader tests a plan before sailing.

In Treasure Island, Captain Smollett refuses to be talked out of his caution. He says a leader who answers for every life aboard has the right to ask for precautions, even when others call him fearful.

In Treasure Island, Silver shows how a man can have a comfortable life for years and still lose everything. Stevenson suggests that steady saving and self-control protect a person far better than spending freely on whatever is in front of them.

In Treasure Island, Jim overhears Silver win over one honest sailor after another with flattery. Stevenson shows how people are often corrupted slowly, by being praised and made to feel special, rather than by a single bad choice.
In Treasure Island, the squire admits he was wrong about the captain and hands over the plan. Stevenson shows that owning a mistake openly is what lets a group change course in a crisis.

In Treasure Island, Captain Smollett defuses a mutinous mood by giving the crew an afternoon ashore instead of forcing a showdown. Stevenson shows that a leader can often ease tension by offering a way out, while still staying ready for trouble.

In Treasure Island, the honest sailor Tom refuses to go along with Silver and turns his back on his old shipmate, knowing it may cost him his life. Stevenson shows that doing right is often a choice made alone, when no one else is standing with you.

In Treasure Island, Jim's courage returns once he remembers he is not defenceless, and the wild stranger turns out to be as frightened as he is. Stevenson shows that a steady mind often sees the other person's fear too.

In Treasure Island, Dr. Livesey makes up his mind at once while the others are shaken, and acts without wasting time. Stevenson shows that a calm decision, made quickly under pressure, can save more lives than long debate.

In Treasure Island, Captain Smollett gives a wavering sailor a clear chance to change sides, with a short deadline and no shaming. Stevenson shows that a firm, fair offer can bring a frightened person back to the right side.
In Treasure Island, old Tom Redruth serves without complaint from start to finish, and the squire is left kneeling by him at the end. Stevenson honours quiet loyalty that asks for nothing in return.
In Treasure Island, Stevenson shows Captain Smollett counting his stores honestly, allowing for good luck without planning on it. That is how a sensible leader plans when resources run short.
In Treasure Island, Stevenson shows Captain Smollett refusing to lower the flag under fire. A steady refusal to look beaten steadies the people around you and unsettles the enemy.
In Treasure Island, Ben Gunn will deal only with a gentleman who gives his word, showing that a careful person can insist on trust before offering any of their own.
In Treasure Island, Stevenson shows Captain Smollett keeping his crew from brooding by giving everyone a task and working alongside them. Busy people stay steadier than idle ones.
In Treasure Island, Smollett tells the mutineer Silver that his present position is his own doing. A person's situation usually follows from the choices they made earlier.
In Treasure Island, Smollett answers a rival's demands by listing plainly what the other side cannot do. Knowing exactly where your opponent is weak is worth more than bluster.

In Treasure Island, Smollett admits his men are outnumbered, then names the shelter they hold and their discipline. Naming your real advantages steadies a team better than pretending the odds are fine.

In Treasure Island, Smollett steadies his men by measuring the odds against where they actually started, not against the worst number they first feared. The honest comparison is usually the kinder one.
In Treasure Island, Jim lets envy and disgust grow until he takes the first step toward a reckless act. A small resentment left alone can slowly steer a sensible person toward a foolish choice.
In Treasure Island, Jim admits that sneaking out made a sound plan wrong. The way you carry out an idea can spoil the idea itself.

In Treasure Island, Jim stops when he remembers that a taut rope cut suddenly could knock him into the sea, and waits for the wind to change. Pausing to check a risk you have forgotten is often the wisest move.
In Treasure Island, Jim is pulled by curiosity into real danger when he grips a trailing cord to peer through a window. Curiosity makes a fine teacher, but it needs a limit set before you start.
In Treasure Island, Jim judges a dangerous shore against a gentler one and saves his strength for the better option. Choosing where to spend your effort is a skill of its own.

In Treasure Island, Jim keeps his head while frightened by first doing a small, safe task, bailing out the boat, and then studying how it behaves. Calm attention to what is in front of you beats panic.
In Treasure Island, Jim helps the wounded Hands but keeps his own supplies out of reach. Kindness and prudence can go together, and a sensible person does not have to choose one.
In Treasure Island, Jim takes command of the ship by speaking as if it is already his to run. Plain, steady confidence can carry a moment that noise and force could not.
In Treasure Island, Jim decides he can trust Hands only on the one point where their interests line up. Trust a person where your aims truly match, and nowhere else.
In Treasure Island, Jim's pistol misfires because he never reloaded and checked his weapons earlier. Preparation done in calm moments is what saves you when the crisis arrives.
In Treasure Island, Jim, pinned and terrified, slowly calms his breathing and finds his nerve again. Steadying the body often steadies the mind enough to act.
In Treasure Island, Jim slows down and approaches his own camp with care, knowing a hurried return can end in a mistake. Caution is owed to friends as well as to enemies.
In Treasure Island, Silver woos Jim by flattering him as a picture of his own younger self. Flattery offered to recruit you deserves a second look.
In Treasure Island, cornered Jim lays out the plain facts of what he has done and shows the men that sparing him serves their own interests. Clear, honest reasoning can turn a threat into a bargain.
