In Treasure Island, Silver answers each accusation in turn, calmly and in order. Taking charges apart one at a time is more persuasive than shouting over them.
In Treasure Island, Jim pities Silver even though Silver is wicked, because he sees a man straining to save his own life. Compassion does not require approving of someone's conduct.
In Treasure Island, Doctor Livesey keeps treating the mutineers' sick with plain professional care while they hold him captive. Keeping your own standards when others drop theirs is a real strength.
In Treasure Island, Jim turns down a chance to escape because he has given his word. A promise kept when it costs you something is what gives your word its worth.
In Treasure Island, the men are spooked by a dead captain's old tricks more than by any living danger. A frightening story can grip a group harder than a real threat in front of them.
In Treasure Island, a plain question about why a ghost would have an echo loosens the crew's fear. A small, concrete question can calm people better than a grand reassurance.
In Treasure Island, once the gold is close, Silver forgets the promises he made when it was far off. Greed within reach makes people drop the commitments they once cared about.
In Treasure Island, Silver loses his fortune in an instant, yet keeps his head and changes his plan before anyone else has caught up. Quick recovery from a setback is its own kind of strength.

In Treasure Island, Ben Gunn gives up his stores and his chart to protect the treasure he has hidden and to guard it for the people who stood by their duty. Loyalty to those who stood by you can outweigh any single prize.
In Treasure Island, Stevenson pauses over the gold in the cave to count the lives, sorrow and cruelty it cost. A fortune's real price is often hidden from the people who hold it.
In Treasure Island, Gray uses his share of the treasure to study his trade and rise in his profession. A sudden windfall is worth most when it turns into a lasting change in what you do.

preview.text:
He was a very silent man by custom. All day he hung round the cove or
upon the cliffs with a brass telescope; all evening he sat in a corner
of the parlour next the fire and drank rum and water very strong. Mostly
he would not speak when spoken to, only look up sudden and fierce and
blow through his nose like a fog-horn; and we and the people who came
about our house soon learned to let him be. Every day when he came back
from his stroll he would ask if any seafaring men had gone by along the
road. At first we thought it was the want of company of his own kind
that made him ask this question, but at last we began to see he was
desirous to avoid them. When a seaman did put up at the Admiral Benbow
(as now and then some did, making by the coast road for Bristol) he
would look in at him through the curtained door before he entered the
parlour; and he was always sure to be as silent as a mouse when any such
was present. For me, at least, there was no secret about the matter, for
I was, in a way, a sharer in his alarms. He had taken me aside one day
and promised me a silver fourpenny on the first of every month if I
would only keep my “weather-eye open for a seafaring man with one leg”
 and let him know the moment he appeared. Often enough when the first
of the month came round and I applied to him for my wage, he would only
blow through his nose at me and stare me down, but before the week was
out he was sure to think better of it, bring me my four-penny piece, and
repeat his orders to look out for “the seafaring man with one leg.”

books.title: The Importance of Being Earnest
books.author: Oscar Wilde
books.subject: plays
books.licence_note: Author died 1900. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Importance of Being Earnest, Jack keeps one name in town and another in the country, and Algernon's teasing shows how a small pretence can be found out by anyone paying attention.
In The Importance of Being Earnest, Algernon suggests honesty is seldom neat, and that people often bend the facts to make their lives run more smoothly.
In The Importance of Being Earnest, Lady Bracknell judges suitors by surface marks such as address and family background, a satire of people who weigh status above character.
In The Importance of Being Earnest, Miss Prism says memory is the diary we all carry about with us, a reminder that people keep their own edited version of events.
In The Importance of Being Earnest, Cecily insists there is some good in everyone and pushes her stiffer elders toward generosity, while the grown-ups hold back their judgment.
In The Importance of Being Earnest, Cecily admits that talk about Algernon made him attractive before she had met him, a sharp look at how reputation can stand in for real acquaintance.
In The Importance of Being Earnest, both young women claim to be perfectly candid, and their quarrel shows that plain speaking is often a cover for spite.
In The Importance of Being Earnest, Jack tells the truth only once he is cornered, and the story shows how a web of small lies stays up only until someone asks the right question.
In The Importance of Being Earnest, Lady Bracknell complains that people now value surfaces over the solid qualities that last and improve with time, a complaint that still lands today.

In The Importance of Being Earnest, Miss Prism owns that one moment of distraction changed two lives, and she has never forgiven herself for it, a reminder that small lapses of attention can cost a great deal.
In The Importance of Being Earnest, Jack challenges the double standard of his day, asking why men and women should be judged by different laws, and whether repentance can wipe out folly.
In The Importance of Being Earnest, Jack finds that the name he had been using all along was his real one, a comic reminder that people often know more about themselves than they admit.

preview.text:
ALGERNON.
[Retreating to back of sofa.] But why does she call herself little
Cecily if she is your aunt and lives at Tunbridge Wells? [Reading.]
‘From little Cecily with her fondest love.’

JACK.
[Moving to sofa and kneeling upon it.] My dear fellow, what on earth is
there in that? Some aunts are tall, some aunts are not tall. That is a
matter that surely an aunt may be allowed to decide for herself. You
seem to think that every aunt should be exactly like your aunt! That is
absurd! For Heaven’s sake give me back my cigarette case. [Follows
Algernon round the room.]

ALGERNON.
Yes. But why does your aunt call you her uncle? ‘From little Cecily,
with her fondest love to her dear Uncle Jack.’ There is no objection, I
admit, to an aunt being a small aunt, but why an aunt, no matter what
her size may be, should call her own nephew her uncle, I can’t quite
make out. Besides, your name isn’t Jack at all; it is Ernest.

JACK.
It isn’t Ernest; it’s Jack.

ALGERNON.
You have always told me it was Ernest. I have introduced you to every
one as Ernest. You answer to the name of Ernest. You look as if your
name was Ernest. You are the most earnest-looking person I ever saw in
my life. It is perfectly absurd your saying that your name isn’t
Ernest. It’s on your cards. Here is one of them. [Taking it from case.]
‘Mr. Ernest Worthing, B. 4, The Albany.’ I’ll keep this as a proof that
your name is Ernest if ever you attempt to deny it to me, or to
Gwendolen, or to any one else. [Puts the card in his pocket.]

JACK.
Well, my name is Ernest in town and Jack in the country, and the
cigarette case was given to me in the country.

books.title: The Man from Snowy River
books.author: Banjo Paterson
books.subject: Australian
books.licence_note: Author died 1941. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Man from Snowy River, Paterson shows that a slight, underestimated rider can have more courage and judgement than the crowd expects, so appearances can mislead.
In Old Pardon, Paterson shows a horse written off by everyone who then came on strong at the end, a reminder that persistence often counts for more than early form.
In Clancy of the Overflow, Paterson sets a clerk's hurried city life against open country and asks what a life of routine and anxious haste costs a person.
In Conroy's Gap, Paterson shows Jim Carew riding a hundred miles through the night to reach his wife, a picture of devotion that keeps its nerve under pressure.
In Our New Horse, the mates try to pass off a horse they know is unreliable, and the scheme comes back on them. Paterson makes the point that dishonest dealing tends to bite the one who starts it.

In Saltbush Bill, Paterson shows drovers and squatters fighting over shared grass on the stock routes until both sides settle on rules they can live with, a reminder that shared resources need fair terms.
In On Kiley's Run, Paterson shows what is lost when an absent owner cuts every cost he can: the loyal men and good neighbours leave, and the place loses its heart.
Paterson's poem In the Droving Days has a narrator buy back an old grey horse the market had written off, a reminder that loyalty from a faithful companion is worth far more than its sale value.
In Over the Range, Paterson lets a bush child's simple trust stand against the wisest adult's view, and admits that our own sight is bounded like a range.
In Black Swans, Paterson writes to an old mate who keeps facing a hard drought with a stout heart, and admits the old days cannot be recovered, only carried forward in the mind.
In How Gilbert Died, Paterson tells of an outlaw who stays behind to hold off the troopers so his mate can get away, a story that shows loyalty under pressure, even when the cause is a poor one.
In Johnson's Antidote, Paterson mocks a man who sells a cure he never tested, and sets him against a careful scientist. The lesson is to test a claim before you stake your name on it.
In Ambition and Art, Paterson warns that ambition can cost honour and friendship, and sets against it the steadier reward of loving one's craft for its own sake.
In Defence of the Bush, Paterson argues that a visitor who judges the country on one hot, dry trip misses its seasons, and that people who really know a place stay loyal to it through all its moods.
In Come-by-Chance, Paterson imagines a town nobody can find and concludes it is only where dreamers drift. It is a playful reminder that waiting for good luck is not a plan.

preview.text:
Come-by-Chance
        As I pondered very weary o'er a volume long and dreary --

Under the Shadow of Kiley's Hill
        This is the place where they all were bred;

Jim Carew
        Born of a thoroughbred English race,

The Swagman's Rest
        We buried old Bob where the bloodwoods wave

THE MAN FROM SNOWY RIVER AND OTHER VERSES

The Man from Snowy River

There was movement at the station, for the word had passed around
    That the colt from old Regret had got away,
   And had joined the wild bush horses -- he was worth a thousand pound,
    So all the cracks had gathered to the fray.
   All the tried and noted riders from the stations near and far
    Had mustered at the homestead overnight,
   For the bushmen love hard riding where the wild bush horses are,
    And the stock-horse snuffs the battle with delight.

There was Harrison, who made his pile when Pardon won the cup,
    The old man with his hair as white as snow;
   But few could ride beside him when his blood was fairly up --
    He would go wherever horse and man could go.
   And Clancy of the Overflow came down to lend a hand,
    No better horseman ever held the reins;
   For never horse could throw him while the saddle-girths would stand,
    He learnt to ride while droving on the plains.

And one was there, a stripling on a small and weedy beast,
    He was something like a racehorse undersized,
   With a touch of Timor pony -- three parts thoroughbred at least --
    And such as are by mountain horsemen prized.
   He was hard and tough and wiry -- just the sort that won't say die --
    There was courage in his quick impatient tread;
   And he bore the badge of gameness in his bright and fiery eye,
    And the proud and lofty carriage of his head.

books.title: The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.subject: detective
books.licence_note: Author died 1930. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Memoirs of Sherlock Holmes, Conan Doyle shows Holmes separating the framework of established fact from the guesses of theorists and reporters before he draws any inference.
In Silver Blaze, Holmes finds that talking a case through with someone else clears his own thinking, so he lays out the facts aloud before he asks for help.
In Silver Blaze, Conan Doyle has Holmes describe Inspector Gregory as thorough and competent but without imagination, a reminder that diligence alone can stop short of the answer.
In Silver Blaze, Holmes tests a case against a suspect by listing the questions it cannot yet answer, such as why the horse was taken from the stable and where it could be hidden.
In Silver Blaze, Holmes sets a working hypothesis about where the horse must be, then follows it across the moor to see what it leads to, rather than waiting for more facts.
In Silver Blaze, Holmes argues that imagination is what lets an investigator act on a reasoned guess, test it on the ground, and find it holds.
In Silver Blaze, Holmes treats the watchdog that did nothing in the night as the key clue, showing that an absence can tell you as much as an event.
In Silver Blaze, Holmes says that one true inference invariably suggests others, so each solid conclusion opens the next question to test.
In The Adventure of the Cardboard Box, Holmes rebuilds Watson's wandering thoughts from small shifts in his eyes and face, showing how close attention to people reveals more than they say.
In The Adventure of the Cardboard Box, Holmes reads the wrapping, the string and the handwriting in turn, and each small clue narrows down who sent the parcel and what kind of person they were.
In The Adventure of the Cardboard Box, Holmes assumes his reasoning is right, then asks what each answer would require of the sender, until the tangle of the case comes loose.

In The Adventure of the Cardboard Box, Holmes says he and Watson began with an open mind, observed first and drew inferences only afterwards, which is the same discipline a business owner needs before picking a fix.
In The Adventure of the Cardboard Box, Holmes tests a second, unlikely explanation anyway, because a plausible-looking answer should be checked before the case is closed.
In The Adventure of the Cardboard Box, Browner's confession shows how unspoken suspicion and quarrels about nothing can slowly widen the gap between two people who once trusted each other.
In The Yellow Face, Holmes reads a stranger's habits from an old patched pipe, showing how ordinary objects hold honest evidence about the people who use them.
In The Yellow Face, Munro's suspicions grow wilder with each sleepless hour, showing how a mind short of facts will keep inventing theories that are less and less likely.
In The Yellow Face, Holmes holds his theory only as a provisional one, to be reconsidered as soon as new facts arrive that it cannot cover.
At the end of The Yellow Face, Holmes asks Watson to warn him if he grows over-confident or gives a case less care than it deserves, a habit that keeps a craftsman honest.
In The Yellow Face, Grant Munro answers a painful secret with generosity, admitting he is no saint but hoping he is better than his wife has given him credit for.
In The Stockbroker's Clerk, Holmes notes that a piece of reasoning looks simple once it is explained, so good work often seems obvious only in hindsight.
In The Stockbroker's Clerk, Pycroft gets a chill of doubt when a too-good offer comes from people he knows little about, a warning that suits anyone weighing a deal today.
In The Stockbroker's Clerk, Pycroft notices the empty offices with no company name on the wall and feels uneasy, but he ignores the warning signs a shrewd businessman would check first.
In The Stockbroker's Clerk, Holmes finds that a tangled affair often hinges on two points, then asks what the other side wanted that it could only get one way.
In The Gloria Scott, young Holmes reads a host's past from a loaded stick, boxer's ears and a half-erased tattoo, and the reasoning is only as good as the evidence it starts from.
In The Gloria Scott, Holmes says a praise from an older man first made him feel that a hobby could become a profession, a reminder that an honest encouragement can change the course of a life.

In The Gloria Scott, Holmes cracks a coded note by trying one pattern after another, backwards, then alternate words, until the key finally shows itself. Persistence with a method beats a single lucky guess.
In The Gloria Scott, Holmes reasons that the words a person reaches for without thinking, such as sporting terms, reveal their real interests more honestly than a planned answer does.
In The Gloria Scott, a handful of men refuse to join in cold-blooded killing even when the group pressures them, a reminder that conscience can hold firm inside a bad crowd.

In The Musgrave Ritual, Holmes says his name grew slowly, through a few early cases that came by introduction from old friends, a reminder that a reputation for good work is built one referral at a time.

In The Musgrave Ritual, Holmes tries to find the one starting point that links a butler's disappearance, a maid's breakdown and a lake full of junk, because a tangled run of events usually hangs on a single first cause.

In The Musgrave Ritual, Holmes's careful calculation fails until his client checks the written instructions and points out a two-word phrase he had skipped. A forgotten detail in the source can undo a sound plan.
In The Musgrave Ritual, Holmes works out a plan by putting himself in the place of the man he is studying and asking how he would have acted with the same skill and the same obstacles.
In The Reigate Squires, Doyle shows that even Holmes's iron constitution broke after two months of fifteen-hour days, and that a sharp mind needs real rest before the next problem.
In The Reigate Squires, Holmes reasons that the missing part of the note must have been taken because it incriminated someone, so asking who wanted it gone points the way to the culprit.

In The Reigate Squires, Holmes asks the simple question everyone had skipped: what if the thing taken for granted, that the burglar never got in, was not true? Testing the assumption changes the whole case.
In The Reigate Squires, Holmes says the art of detection is sorting which facts are incidental and which are vital, so that attention is concentrated rather than scattered.
In The Reigate Squires, Holmes says he holds no prejudices and follows the facts wherever they lead, even when they point at someone everyone else has ruled out.
In The Crooked Man, Holmes explains that a clever deduction looks remarkable only because the listener missed the one small point it rests on, which makes it seem elementary once shown.
In The Crooked Man, Holmes reasons by elimination: since the couple could not have taken the missing key, a third person must have, which turns the search to whoever could have come in by the window.

In The Crooked Man, Holmes first tries a tidy explanation, then drops it when the facts that do not fit, such as the word David, refuse to go away. Good detectives test their guesses against the awkward evidence.

In The Resident Patient, Holmes will not advise a man who keeps back the facts, because no adviser can help when the person asking hides what is really going on. His answer is simply to speak the truth.

In The Greek Interpreter, Holmes holds that to underrate yourself is as much a departure from the truth as to overrate yourself, so an honest assessment of your own powers counts as much as any other fact.

In The Greek Interpreter, Holmes says his brother Mycroft reasons brilliantly from an armchair but will not check his own answers, and that a good idea still has to be proved in practice before it counts.

In The Greek Interpreter, Holmes reads a stranger's history from small visible things, such as posture, the way a hat sits and the state of his boots, showing that careful observation of ordinary details can reveal a great deal.
In The Naval Treaty, Holmes asks what small trace the intruder might have left, a stray hair or a scent, because a trifle that looks unimportant can be worth more than a grand theory.
In The Naval Treaty, Holmes says the hardest problem is the one with no obvious purpose, so he asks first who profits from it. Asking who gains is a sound way to start any unclear question.

In The Naval Treaty, Holmes says the main difficulty was too much evidence, with what was vital hidden under what was irrelevant. The skill is picking out the few facts that are essential and putting them in order.
In The Final Problem, Holmes warns Watson not to think meanly of a rival. A clever opponent should be measured as an equal, because assuming he is slow is how a careful plan gets caught out.

In The Final Problem, Holmes looks back on his work and finds comfort that, across a thousand cases, he cannot recall using his abilities on the wrong side. It is a fair test to set against any working life.

preview.text:
“It is one of those cases where the art of the reasoner should be
      used rather for the sifting of details than for the acquiring of
      fresh evidence. The tragedy has been so uncommon, so complete and
      of such personal importance to so many people, that we are
      suffering from a plethora of surmise, conjecture, and hypothesis.
      The difficulty is to detach the framework of fact—of absolute
      undeniable fact—from the embellishments of theorists and
      reporters. Then, having established ourselves upon this sound
      basis, it is our duty to see what inferences may be drawn and
      what are the special points upon which the whole mystery turns.
      On Tuesday evening I received telegrams from both Colonel Ross,
      the owner of the horse, and from Inspector Gregory, who is
      looking after the case, inviting my co-operation.”

“Tuesday evening!” I exclaimed. “And this is Thursday morning.
      Why didn’t you go down yesterday?”

“Because I made a blunder, my dear Watson—which is, I am afraid,
      a more common occurrence than any one would think who only knew
      me through your memoirs. The fact is that I could not believe it
      possible that the most remarkable horse in England could long
      remain concealed, especially in so sparsely inhabited a place as
      the north of Dartmoor. From hour to hour yesterday I expected to
      hear that he had been found, and that his abductor was the
      murderer of John Straker. When, however, another morning had
      come, and I found that beyond the arrest of young Fitzroy Simpson
      nothing had been done, I felt that it was time for me to take
      action. Yet in some ways I feel that yesterday has not been
      wasted.”

“You have formed a theory, then?”

books.title: Andersen's Fairy Tales
books.author: Hans Christian Andersen
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Author died 1875. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Emperor's New Clothes, Andersen shows how a whole court will praise what it cannot see, because each person fears being the only one who looks foolish.
In The Swineherd, Andersen has the Prince leave a princess who would trade a real rose and nightingale for a cheap plaything, so she cannot tell true worth from a trinket.
In The Shoes of Fortune, Care doubts that getting every wish fulfilled would make anyone happy, which is a useful check on what we chase.
In The Shoes of Fortune, the Councillor longs for an older, grander age, then finds he is miserable in it and is glad of his own time, faults and all.
In The Shoes of Fortune, the watchman swaps places with the lieutenant, finds the officer's life heavier than his own, and wants his old life back. We tend to envy lives we have not lived.

In The Shoes of Fortune, a man stuck in a railing is too proud to call for help and forgets the one wish that would free him. We often miss the simple way out because we are busy protecting our pride.
In The Shoes of Fortune, a young man who wants to see into other people's hearts finds the sight of a sick mother's quiet faith makes him feel humbler and better than before.
In The Shoes of Fortune, a flower credits the light for its beauty, and a poet answers that the air is what keeps it alive. The things that quietly sustain us are often the ones we overlook.
In The Shoes of Fortune, a clever parrot mocks everyone for sport, while the canary is the one who quietly opens a cage door. Andersen shows that wit without kindness is poor company.

In The Shoes of Fortune, the young man crosses the Alps and then wishes himself across again, unable to enjoy the view while fretting over his papers. A restless mind carries its worries wherever it goes.

In The Fir Tree, the little tree wants to be grown up and far away, so the sun, the birds and the children who admire him give him no pleasure. Wanting always to be somewhere else can hide the good we already have.
In The Fir Tree, the tree only sees how happy it was when its good days are over. Andersen suggests we often do not notice the happy times while we are living them.

In The Snow Queen, a single splinter of a spiteful mirror carries the power of the whole thing, so people see only what is ugly. Andersen suggests a small habit of cynicism can colour how we see everything.
In The Snow Queen, Kay copies the faults of everyone around him and the crowd calls him clever. Andersen shows how easily mockery gets mistaken for wit.
In The Snow Queen, Gerda offers her red shoes, her most precious thing, to the river for Kay. Andersen shows love that is willing to give up what it treasures most.
In The Snow Queen, the old woman's comforts slowly make Gerda forget Kay. Andersen shows that a soft, easy life can quietly cost us the people we most need to remember.

In The Snow Queen, suitors who chatter freely in the street fall silent before the throne, and the hungry ones will not share their bread. Andersen shows how grandeur can silence people and make them unkind.
In The Snow Queen, a wild robber girl decides to protect Gerda after hearing why she is travelling so far. Andersen shows that a sincere story told plainly can soften even a hard heart.

In The Snow Queen, the Finland woman tells Gerda that her power already lies in her own heart, and that she must reach Kay herself. Andersen suggests that sincere love is a strength that needs no borrowed magic.
In The Snow Queen, Gerda's warm tears thaw the ice in Kay's heart. Andersen suggests that patient, honest love can reach someone who has grown cold.
The Snow Queen ends with Kay and Gerda grown up yet still children at heart. Andersen suggests that growing older need not mean losing the warmth and wonder of childhood.
In The Elderbush, an old couple forget the date of their anniversary but remember every moment of their youth. Andersen suggests a shared life lives on in memory long after the dates are lost.
In The Elderbush, old Nanny says the most wonderful stories grow out of ordinary reality. Andersen suggests everyday life, looked at closely, holds all the wonder a story needs.
In The Elderbush, Andersen names the tree's spirit Remembrance. A kept flower stays fresh long after the moment has passed, so the things we hold in memory keep their colour.
In The Bell, most of the crowd stop at the first willows and still claim they have found the bell. Andersen shows how easily people settle for the nearest thing and call it the destination.
In The Bell, the King's Son goes on alone when others turn back, because he hears a call he cannot ignore. Andersen admires the resolute person who keeps going past the easy stopping points.

In The Old House, a small boy who has never spoken to the lonely old man across the street sends him a pewter soldier. Andersen shows that a small, unasked kindness can open a door to someone who has been left alone.
In The Old House, when a young wife hears about the lonely old man, she promises to remember him. Andersen suggests that remembering people who were forgotten is a kindness in itself.

In The Story of a Mother, the grieving mother warms a freezing thorn-bush against her breast to learn the way, and the bush blooms. Andersen shows that a loving search asks us to give something of ourselves along the road.

In The Story of a Mother, Death shows the mother both flowers and their futures, and she gives up her bargaining, asking that God's will be done. Andersen shows love learning to accept what it cannot control.
In The False Collar, a collar boasts about the boot-jack and comb of its master as if they were its own. Andersen mocks people who borrow importance from others and then talk as if it were theirs.
In The Shadow, a scholar sends his shadow off to spy on a neighbour and it never comes back. Andersen warns what can happen to the parts of ourselves we let run off without us.
In The Shadow, the shadow rises to wealth and honour by exposing other people's secrets, and people both fear him and fawn on him. Andersen shows how gossip can buy a false standing.

In The Shadow, the learned man who tries to tell the truth is threatened with prison, and the princess believes the confident shadow over him. Andersen shows how a bold liar with power can be trusted over an honest man.

In The Little Match Girl, each small match gives the girl a moment of warmth and a glimpse of comfort. Andersen shows how small comforts can carry someone through a hard night, and how much suffering goes unseen.
In The Dream of Little Tuk, a boy who helps an old washerwoman finds help come back to him in a dream. Andersen suggests kindness given freely tends to return in ways we do not expect.

In The Naughty Boy, a kind old poet lets a cold, drenched child into his warm room without asking who he is. Andersen treats taking in the cold and wet as the simplest kindness, one that needs no cleverness to offer.
In The Red Shoes, Karen goes to her confirmation thinking only of her shoes and forgets to pray. Andersen shows how vanity can crowd out the things that matter most while we are standing in them.

In The Red Shoes, Karen finds peace only after she gives up wanting to be admired and takes humble work in a clergyman's house. Andersen suggests that service and quiet devotion can repair what vanity has broken.

preview.text:
“Is not the work absolutely magnificent?” said the two officers of the
crown, already mentioned. “If your Majesty will only be pleased to look
at it! What a splendid design! What glorious colors!” and at the same
time they pointed to the empty frames; for they imagined that everyone
else could see this exquisite piece of workmanship.

“How is this?” said the Emperor to himself. “I can see nothing! This
is indeed a terrible affair! Am I a simpleton, or am I unfit to be an
Emperor? That would be the worst thing that could happen--Oh! the cloth
is charming,” said he, aloud. “It has my complete approbation.” And he
smiled most graciously, and looked closely at the empty looms; for on no
account would he say that he could not see what two of the officers of
his court had praised so much. All his retinue now strained their eyes,
hoping to discover something on the looms, but they could see no more
than the others; nevertheless, they all exclaimed, “Oh, how beautiful!”
 and advised his majesty to have some new clothes made from this splendid
material, for the approaching procession. “Magnificent! Charming!
Excellent!” resounded on all sides; and everyone was uncommonly gay. The
Emperor shared in the general satisfaction; and presented the impostors
with the riband of an order of knighthood, to be worn in their
button-holes, and the title of “Gentlemen Weavers.”

The rogues sat up the whole of the night before the day on which the
procession was to take place, and had sixteen lights burning, so that
everyone might see how anxious they were to finish the Emperor's new
suit. They pretended to roll the cloth off the looms; cut the air with
their scissors; and sewed with needles without any thread in them.
“See!” cried they, at last. “The Emperor's new clothes are ready!”

books.title: Selected Discourses of Epictetus
books.author: Epictetus
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died about 135, translator died 1879. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Epictetus held that the rational faculty is the one power we have that can examine itself and every other faculty, judging what each is for and when to use it.
Epictetus tells of Agrippinus, who heard he was condemned and asked only whether his property was safe, then went to dine. A calm mind is not undone by bad news it cannot change.
Epictetus held that we are pained most by what our reason judges irrational, and that a hardship we accept as reasonable becomes bearable. Our opinion of a hardship shapes how it feels.
Epictetus said we each carry a share of reason that we have from the gods, and that remembering this stops us thinking meanly of ourselves.
Epictetus taught that real progress means letting go of desire for things outside our control and using aversion only on what depends on our own will.
Epictetus judged progress by how a person handles desire, aversion and judgment day to day, not by how many philosophy books they have read.
Epictetus said real progress is learning to be free of lament, fear of death, exile and loss, and that reading books about this is worth little unless it changes how a person lives.
Epictetus observed that people guard their bodies from pain but care little for the soul's shame, and that a deadened sense of shame is wrongly taken for strength.
Epictetus taught that we share basic needs with animals, but our power to understand what things are for is what asks more of us, so living well means acting in an orderly way that fits our nature.
Epictetus asked why people travel far to see wonders when the works of nature are already around them, and reminded them they have greatness of soul to bear the discomforts of any trip.
Epictetus said we are given the means to bear whatever happens, and that blaming the gods for hardship shows a meanness of spirit rather than strength.
Epictetus taught that true freedom is not getting everything we wish for, but learning to wish that things happen as they do, the way a student learns to write a name as it should be written.
Epictetus suggested we call time alone tranquillity and freedom, and call a busy gathering a festival rather than a trouble, so that we accept our circumstances with contentment.
Epictetus argued that a person is only truly imprisoned when they are where they are against their will, as Socrates was not, because he stayed by choice.
Epictetus told anyone given authority over others to remember they are kin by nature, and not to become a tyrant just because they hold the higher place.
Epictetus said the art of living is each person's own life, so philosophy cannot secure outside things like health or reputation, only keep our own governing part in line with nature.
Epictetus held that a wrongdoer is mistaken about what matters and deserves pity rather than anger, and that we only lose what we already have, so clinging to possessions is what makes loss hurt.
Epictetus said a tyrant can chain the leg and take the neck, but cannot touch the will, and that steadiness should be practised first in small things like a headache.
Epictetus asked a tyrant what real power he had, since no one can guarantee their own desires or avoid every error, and noted that respect for a position is not the same as respect for a person.
Epictetus said that our own opinions disturb us more than any threat, since a person who values their own will cannot be enslaved by threats to the body.
Epictetus noticed that people give thanks to the gods for public honours but rarely for good desires or acting in line with nature, and warned that titles and names fade quickly.
Epictetus said a person should be content to desire and act in line with their own nature, and that chasing the applause of people one considers mad is pointless.
Epictetus held that people share basic ideas of what is good and right, and that most disagreements arise from applying those ideas to particular cases.

Epictetus defined education as learning to apply our natural ideas to particular things, and to tell apart what is in our power, our will and our actions, from what is not, such as the body, possessions and family.
Epictetus warned that if we place our good in property, health and reputation, we will end up fighting others for them and resenting the gods when we lose.
Epictetus said hard circumstances show what people are, and that a difficulty can be useful training, as a wrestler is matched with a rough young opponent to grow stronger.
Epictetus praised Diogenes as a good scout who showed by his own calm and courage that poverty and pain were nothing to fear.
Epictetus said what is truly ours is our integrity and our sense of shame, which no one can take unless we give them away by chasing what belongs to others.
Epictetus said we squeeze ourselves with our own opinions, and that an insult gains its sting only from the weakness of the person insulted.
Epictetus taught that to break a bad habit we should practise the opposite habit, and meet deceptive appearances with reason and steady practice.
Epictetus said death cannot be escaped, so the sensible course is to face it bravely, since the real trouble is wanting things to be other than they are.
Epictetus argued that we assent only to what appears true to us, so those who do wrong are usually mistaken rather than wicked, and anger at them is misplaced.
Epictetus held that people act on what seems good to them, so a person who does harm is deceived and deserves pity, and understanding this takes away the urge to anger.
Epictetus said the real ruin of a person comes when they lose modesty, fidelity and right judgment, not when they lose possessions or power.
Epictetus taught that a good life is drawn from our own will and judgment, since a tyrant can threaten only the body, and nothing else can overcome the will itself.
Epictetus pointed to Socrates, who said his accusers could kill him but could not harm him, and accepted his death calmly as the will of God.
Epictetus said that whatever happens outside our will is nothing to us, and that we should seek advantage only in what is truly within our control.
Epictetus said the world needs fewer clever arguments and more people who live out what they have learned, so that their own conduct becomes the example.
Epictetus said the things that frighten us are the real masters we serve, and that once we stop fearing them we are no longer bound.
Epictetus taught that we should be patient with people who are ignorant, excusing them as acting on what they think is good for themselves, as Socrates was kind to his jailer.
Epictetus said courage and caution belong together: be confident about what lies outside our will, and careful only about what we control.
Epictetus observed that we fear things outside our control and act recklessly about things within it, and that the fear of pain or death is harder to bear than pain or death itself.
Epictetus said we should meet death with courage rather than flight, since its terror comes from inexperience, like a child frightened by a mask that does not bite once turned over.
Epictetus held that real freedom is the power to live as we choose, without fear, sorrow or error, and that the educated are the ones who truly possess it.
Epictetus said that if we keep to what is in our own power, such as being modest and faithful, no judge or tyrant can take that away from us.
Epictetus compared a trained writer to a person prepared for any event: skill and good habits let us respond to what is needed, rather than waiting to be told.
Epictetus compared life to a sea voyage: do your own part well, then leave the storm to the master of the ship, and neither panic nor blame God when the ship is in danger.
Epictetus said a foot is only a foot while it belongs to the body, so we should see ourselves as parts of a wider whole and accept illness and loss as part of that larger life.
Epictetus advised that where we lack training we should yield to those who have practised, and stay content with firmness of mind rather than envy them.
Epictetus said that when we do not get what we wanted, we should ask whether the outcome was ever ours to control, and stop claiming what belongs to someone else.
Epictetus said we need not lean on fortune-tellers for what is good, since reason within us can show our duty, and that fear is what makes us flatter them.
Epictetus taught that each person carries a share of the divine reason within, so impure thoughts and deeds dishonour what we carry, and should be avoided.
Epictetus compared us to a statue made by a master: we were trusted to keep ourselves modest, faithful and free from disturbance, and should honour that trust.
Epictetus said a philosopher's real strength shows in steady desire, careful choice and considered assent, not in an outward show of dignity.
Epictetus said we keep our humanity by acting as a reasoning being should, since rash, gluttonous or angry acts diminish us while modest and faithful acts strengthen our character.
Epictetus warned that learning alone is not enough: unless we put right opinions into practice, we are only repeating other people's ideas, like bread stored away and never eaten.
Epictetus said that as a citizen of the world with the reason to see how things fit together, we should act for the whole community and not only for ourselves.
Epictetus said our duties follow from the roles we hold, such as son or brother, and that giving way in small matters brings a better temper and a larger share of what truly matters.
Epictetus said each role we hold, such as senator, youth or old man, marks out our proper duties, and that losing modesty or gentleness is a far greater loss than losing money.
Epictetus argued that the real harm we risk is to our own will, since wronging another damages our character far more than it damages the person wronged.

preview.text:
OF THE THINGS WHICH ARE IN OUR POWER AND NOT IN OUR POWER.—Of all the
faculties (except that which I shall soon mention), you will find not
one which is capable of contemplating itself, and, consequently, not
capable either of approving or disapproving. How far does the grammatic
art possess the contemplating power? As far as forming a judgment about
what is written and spoken. And how far music? As far as judging about
melody. Does either of them then contemplate itself? By no means. But
when you must write something to your friend, grammar will tell you
what words you should write; but whether you should write or not,
grammar will not tell you. And so it is with music as to musical
sounds; but whether you should sing at the present time and play on the
lute, or do neither, music will not tell you. What faculty then will
tell you? That which contemplates both itself and all other things. And
what is this faculty? The rational faculty; for this is the only
faculty that we have received which examines itself, what it is, and
what power it has, and what is the value of this gift, and examines all
other faculties: for what else is there which tells us that golden
things are beautiful, for they do not say so themselves? Evidently it
is the faculty which is capable of judging of appearances. What else
judges of music, grammar, and the other faculties, proves their uses,
and points out the occasions for using them? Nothing else.

books.title: Pride and Prejudice
books.author: Jane Austen
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1817. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: George Saintsbury argues that in Pride and Prejudice every scene earns its place, since hardly a character or incident could be cut without loss to the story.
George Saintsbury holds that living characters and sharp dialogue matter more than a neat plot, because a badly built novel with real people beats a faultless plot acted by puppets.
George Saintsbury says that seeing mixed motives and noticing that seeming is not being is not cynicism, but the ordinary sense of a person who knows the world.
George Saintsbury praises Austen for joining humanity to art, where small, unforced true strokes build a whole picture and nothing in it is false or superfluous.
George Saintsbury finds Darcy believable because his pride was spoilt rather than damaged at heart, so an honest shock like Elizabeth's refusal could truly change him.
George Saintsbury notes that Elizabeth Bennet is clever and quick-tongued but never ill-natured: she answers an attack well but never starts one.
In Pride and Prejudice, Austen shows a marriage where one partner's wit is never understood by the other, a reminder that people can share a home for decades and still miss each other.
In Pride and Prejudice, Austen shows how a first impression formed in one evening, on a single slight, hardens into a verdict the whole room repeats without checking it.
In Pride and Prejudice, Austen sets Jane's generous charity against Elizabeth's sharper eye, two kinds of good judgement that each need the other to see a person whole.
In Pride and Prejudice, Mary separates pride, which concerns what we think of ourselves, from vanity, which concerns what we want others to think of us.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth insists that a few evenings of acquaintance cannot reveal a person's real character, a useful caution against judging too quickly.
In Pride and Prejudice, Darcy's contempt softens once he watches Elizabeth closely, showing how careful attention can change what we see in someone we had dismissed.
In Pride and Prejudice, Mary argues that feeling should be guided by reason and effort matched to what is needed, a sensible reminder that good intentions still need judgement.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth walks three muddy miles alone to nurse her sick sister, showing that loyalty to family is worth a little discomfort and a lot of effort.
In Pride and Prejudice, Bingley sees Elizabeth's muddy walk as love for her sister, while his sisters see only the mud, showing how generous eyes find the good in what spiteful eyes ignore.
In Pride and Prejudice, Bingley says a family's connections would not make its members less agreeable, a plain reminder to judge people by their character rather than their relations.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth tells Bingley that a plain, easily read character is no less estimable than a deep and intricate one, a fair reminder that honest simplicity has its own worth.
In Pride and Prejudice, Darcy warns that the appearance of humility is often carelessness or an indirect boast, a sharp reminder to look past how someone presents themselves.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth argues that agreeing to a friend's request can come from affection rather than weakness, while Darcy holds that agreement should rest on conviction.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth is not hurt by Darcy's scrutiny because she cares too little for his good opinion to be wounded by it, a quiet kind of self-possession.
In Pride and Prejudice, Darcy names his own faults plainly, a stubborn temper and slow forgiveness, and that honest self-knowledge is worth more than pretending to have none.
In Pride and Prejudice, Mr Collins is a mix of pride and servility, with self-importance resting on a borrowed position, a sharp study of how status can make a person both grand and small.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth takes Wickham's charming account of Darcy without hearing the other side, a warning that a likeable storyteller can mislead us most when we already want to agree.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth tells Darcy that those who never change their opinion must be sure to judge properly at the start, a fair point that firm people carry the burden of getting first judgements right.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth rejects Miss Bingley's sneer that a man's descent proves his guilt, a clear stand against judging people by birth rather than by their conduct.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth will not be swayed by a friend's defence of a man, since that friend has learnt the story from one side only, a habit worth keeping when we hear someone's account second hand.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth refuses Mr Collins plainly and does not let him reinterpret her no as encouragement, a clear and honest answer that spares both of them false hope.
In Pride and Prejudice, Mr Bennet, pressed by his wife, asks only for the free use of his own understanding, a good reminder to keep your own judgement when others push you to decide.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth tells Jane that she must decide for herself, weighing what she values against other people's disapproval, a good reminder that the wishes of others should not make your choice for you.
In Pride and Prejudice, Jane Austen shows Charlotte Lucas choosing security over romance with her eyes open, knowing the happiness she hopes for is uncertain.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth fears for her sister's happiness and cannot stop the worry from returning, even though she knows it will not help Jane.
In Pride and Prejudice, Jane refuses to think ill of those who hurt her and takes her disappointment with grace, showing that generosity can be a quiet kind of strength.
In Pride and Prejudice, Mrs. Gardiner's loose talk of being "violently in love" hides how little anyone actually knows, and Austen shows how a vague word can stand in for real evidence.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth admits her attraction to Wickham rather than pretending otherwise, and promises only to be careful. Honest self-knowledge is the first step to sound judgement.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth checks her own heart honestly and finds she was never truly in love, which lets her wish Wickham well without bitterness. Looking closely at your own feelings keeps you free of resentment.

In Pride and Prejudice, Charlotte Lucas makes a comfortable home within an imperfect marriage by choosing what to hear and what to notice. Contentment is often a matter of where you put your attention.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth judges Lady Catherine by her manner rather than her rank, and finds that grand titles and wealth look less frightening once you see them clearly.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth plainly argues that the youngest sister has as much right to enjoyment as the eldest, and says so to a formidable woman. Speaking up for fairness takes courage.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth finds peace on a quiet path that nobody else values, out of reach of someone else's curiosity. A small private place to think can make a hard season bearable.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth refuses to be cowed by a grand household, and answers the attempt to intimidate her with wit. Not being frightened by others' airs is its own kind of courage.

In Pride and Prejudice, Darcy admits he is ill at ease with strangers, and Elizabeth notes that he could have tried harder. Austen shows how a reserved manner can look like pride to people who do not yet know the person.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth says that whether a distance is near or far depends on the circumstances, such as money and the cost of travel. Judge what is close or far by the actual conditions, not by a fixed rule.

In Pride and Prejudice, Colonel Fitzwilliam passes on a story he has only half guessed at, and Elizabeth's view of Darcy hardens around it. Austen shows how a secondhand half-truth can shape how we judge a person.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth checks her own anger by admitting she does not know all the particulars, and says it is not fair to condemn someone on partial facts. Being fair before you judge is a discipline worth keeping.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth's dislike of Darcy began with small everyday manners, not one grand offence. Austen shows that character tends to reveal itself in how someone treats people in ordinary moments.
In Pride and Prejudice, Darcy says he did not judge Jane's feelings by what he wished, but by what he honestly observed. Checking whether your hopes are bending your judgement is a useful habit.
In Pride and Prejudice, Darcy's letter owns one of his actions as beneath him and does not try to excuse it. Naming a specific mistake plainly is more believable than a general apology.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth reads Darcy's letter with a strong prejudice and tries to reject its facts at once. Austen shows how anger and a settled opinion can make us refuse evidence we would rather not hear.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth trusted a charming stranger's story because of his manner, and only later sees how little evidence she had. Charm is not the same as proof.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth realises that her pride in her own judgement had hidden her vanity and her prejudice. Being willing to see your own mistake, even when it humbles you, is where wisdom starts.

In Pride and Prejudice, once Elizabeth sees she judged Darcy unfairly, her anger turns on herself and she can feel compassion for him, even though that does not change her answer. Being fair to someone is not the same as agreeing with them.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth is shocked to hear in Lydia's talk an attitude she once half-believed herself. Noticing your own old habits in other people is a useful way to keep growing.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth sees that speaking with bitterness grows out of the prejudices she let herself feed. Harsh words often come from a judgement that was never checked.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth chooses not to spread what she has learned about Wickham, knowing that public verdicts can ruin people and that she cannot prove everything. Restraint is sometimes the fairer course.
In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth comes to see that the gentleness which first delighted her was partly a performance. Time and honest attention can show us what a first impression hid.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth finds that an event she had longed for does not bring the satisfaction she expected, so she looks ahead to something new. Anticipation keeps hope alive, but it can also keep the present from being enjoyed.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth notes that a plan where every part promises delight rarely works out, and that some small expected vexation can keep big disappointment away. Expect a few ordinary frictions and do not build your hopes on perfection.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth decides that it is her business to be satisfied, and her temper to be happy, and turns a disappointed plan into a good trip. Choosing your attitude is part of the job.

In Pride and Prejudice, Elizabeth hears the housekeeper speak warmly of Darcy and begins to doubt her firm opinion. The people who work closely with someone can show you a side your own experience missed.

In Pride and Prejudice, Darcy meets Elizabeth's relations with courtesy even though he has just discovered who they are. Real good manners do not depend on who is watching or what someone can do for you.

preview.text:
_In the first place, the book (it may be barely necessary to remind the
reader) was in its first shape written very early, somewhere about 1796,
when Miss Austen was barely twenty-one; though it was revised and
finished at Chawton some fifteen years later, and was not published till
1813, only four years before her death. I do not know whether, in this
combination of the fresh and vigorous projection of youth, and the
critical revision of middle life, there may be traced the distinct
superiority in point of construction, which, as it seems to me, it
possesses over all the others. The plot, though not elaborate, is almost
regular enough for Fielding; hardly a character, hardly an incident
could be retrenched without loss to the story. The elopement of Lydia
and Wickham is not, like that of Crawford and Mrs. Rushworth, a_ coup de
théâtre; _it connects itself in the strictest way with the course of the
story earlier, and brings about the denouement with complete propriety.
All the minor passages--the loves of Jane and Bingley, the advent of Mr.
Collins, the visit to Hunsford, the Derbyshire tour--fit in after the
same unostentatious, but masterly fashion. There is no attempt at the
hide-and-seek, in-and-out business, which in the transactions between
Frank Churchill and Jane Fairfax contributes no doubt a good deal to the
intrigue of_ Emma, _but contributes it in a fashion which I do not think
the best feature of that otherwise admirable book. Although Miss Austen
always liked something of the misunderstanding kind, which afforded her
opportunities for the display of the peculiar and incomparable talent to
be noticed presently, she has been satisfied here with the perfectly
natural occasions provided by the false account of Darcy’s conduct given
by Wickham, and by the awkwardness (arising with equal naturalness) from
the gradual transformation of Elizabeth’s own feelings from positive
aversion to actual love. I do not know whether the all-grasping hand of
the playwright has ever been laid upon_ Pride and Prejudice; _and I dare
say that, if it were, the situations would prove not startling or
garish enough for the footlights, the character-scheme too subtle and
delicate for pit and gallery. But if the attempt were made, it would
certainly not be hampered by any of those loosenesses of construction,
which, sometimes disguised by the conveniences of which the novelist can
avail himself, appear at once on the stage._

books.title: The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde
books.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
books.subject: adventure
books.licence_note: Author died 1894. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Stevenson shows Mr Utterson as a steady friend to men going downhill. He is inclined to help rather than reprove, and says he lets his brother go to the devil in his own way.

In The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Enfield lives by a rule: the more a thing looks like trouble, the less he asks. Stevenson shows that restraint can be wisdom, and also a way of looking away.

In The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Utterson cannot pin his distrust of Hyde to any one fact. Stevenson shows a sound instinct that feels the whole of a person before the reasons can be named.

In The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Utterson promises his friend to help a man he admits he will never like. Stevenson shows that fairness can be kept for people we do not care for, and that a promise can outlast our own feelings.

In The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Jekyll admits that his narrow escape taught him a lesson he will not forget. Stevenson shows that a shock can open a person's eyes, though often only after the harm is done.

In The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Stevenson notes that it is one thing to hold back curiosity and another to conquer it. Utterson restrains himself outwardly while the wish to know keeps working inside him.

In The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Utterson first reaches for a comfortable explanation. When Poole's account becomes serious, he decides it is his duty to check the facts rather than explain them away.

In The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Jekyll confesses that he hid his pleasures behind a grave public face. Stevenson shows how a secret double life can grow out of high standards, and how shame can then take hold of a person.

In The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Jekyll realises that his experiment had no moral direction of its own. It only released what was already inside him, so the spirit a person brings to a choice shapes what comes out.

In The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Jekyll shows how blaming a second self for his conduct let his conscience slumber. Stevenson makes the point that disowning our own actions is a slow way of losing our grip on them.

In The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Jekyll keeps his resolve for two months, then the fear behind it fades and temptation wins. Stevenson shows how a good promise to ourselves can wear away once the alarm that made it has gone quiet.

In The Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, Jekyll excuses his lapse by comparing himself with his neighbours, who he thinks are no better. Stevenson shows how measuring ourselves against others can quietly lower the bar we set for ourselves.

preview.text:
“Tut-tut!” said Mr. Utterson.

“I see you feel as I do,” said Mr. Enfield. “Yes, it’s a bad story. For
my man was a fellow that nobody could have to do with, a really
damnable man; and the person that drew the cheque is the very pink of
the proprieties, celebrated too, and (what makes it worse) one of your
fellows who do what they call good. Blackmail, I suppose; an honest man
paying through the nose for some of the capers of his youth. Black Mail
House is what I call the place with the door, in consequence. Though
even that, you know, is far from explaining all,” he added, and with
the words fell into a vein of musing.

From this he was recalled by Mr. Utterson asking rather suddenly: “And
you don’t know if the drawer of the cheque lives there?”

“A likely place, isn’t it?” returned Mr. Enfield. “But I happen to have
noticed his address; he lives in some square or other.”

“And you never asked about the—place with the door?” said Mr. Utterson.

“No, sir; I had a delicacy,” was the reply. “I feel very strongly about
putting questions; it partakes too much of the style of the day of
judgment. You start a question, and it’s like starting a stone. You sit
quietly on the top of a hill; and away the stone goes, starting others;
and presently some bland old bird (the last you would have thought of)
is knocked on the head in his own back garden and the family have to
change their name. No sir, I make it a rule of mine: the more it looks
like Queer Street, the less I ask.”

“A very good rule, too,” said the lawyer.

books.title: Hamlet
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.subject: plays
books.licence_note: Author died 1616. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Hamlet, Shakespeare has Horatio propose taking what the watchmen saw straight to Hamlet, the one person it concerns, rather than keeping it among themselves.
In Hamlet, the prince says mourning clothes and sighs can be put on like a costume, and that his real grief lies within, past what anyone can show.
In Hamlet, Polonius sends his son off with advice to listen to many people but speak to few, judge carefully, and above all stay true to himself.
In Hamlet, the prince notes how one flaw can cast a shadow over a person's many good qualities in other people's eyes.
In Hamlet, the prince resolves to clear his mind of trivial records and keep only the one thing that matters most to him.
In Hamlet, the prince tells his friend that the world holds more than any one school of thinking has dreamt of, so keep some humility about what you think you know.
In Hamlet, Polonius is so sure he has found the cause of the prince's trouble that he offers to give up his post if he is wrong, and that certainty stops him testing other explanations.
In Hamlet, the prince tells his old schoolfellows that nothing is good or bad except that our thinking makes it so, which shows how the frame we choose shapes how a situation feels.
In Hamlet, the prince doubts a ghost's word, so he stages a play that mirrors the crime and watches the king's reaction. He tests a suspicion before he acts on it.
In Hamlet, the prince's famous soliloquy warns that too much deliberation can drain away resolve, so that bold plans never turn into action.
In Hamlet, the prince tells the players that the point of their craft is to hold a mirror up to nature, and that overdoing it is a fault the thoughtful will always notice.
In Hamlet, the prince praises Horatio for taking fortune's highs and lows with the same even thanks, and says that steady judgement is what he most wants in a friend.
In Hamlet, the play within the play has a king observe that resolutions made in the heat of strong feeling often fade once the feeling passes.
In Hamlet, the prince refuses to be played like a pipe by the men sent to read his moods, and insists that he cannot be made to sound a tune he does not choose.
In Hamlet, Claudius finds he cannot pray his guilt away while he still keeps what the crime won him, so sincere repair means giving up what was taken.
In Hamlet, the prince refuses to strike his uncle while he prays, judging that a deed done for a cheap advantage at the wrong moment is not true justice.
In Hamlet, the prince tells his mother that covering a rotten problem with a surface fix only lets the rot spread unseen, so real repair means owning the fault and stopping what feeds it.
In Hamlet, the prince advises his mother to break a bad habit one night at a time, because each refusal makes the next one easier, and habit can in the end reshape a person's nature.
In Hamlet, the prince shames himself for delaying, saying that overthinking the outcome is part wisdom and mostly cowardice, and that real greatness acts when the stakes are truly at hand.
In Hamlet, the prince jokes over a skull that a lawyer's endless deals and land purchases all end in the same dirt, a reminder that every fortune is levelled in the end.
In Hamlet, the prince holds Yorick's skull and remembers the jester by his jokes and warmth, not by his death. Shakespeare shows how we keep people alive by who they were.
In Hamlet, the prince finds that a rash move he made without a plan saved him when his careful plots fell apart, and concludes that we can plan, but we cannot fully shape where things end.
In Hamlet, the prince accepts that the hour of any event is beyond our control, so being ready matters far more than trying to pick the moment.
In Hamlet, the dying prince asks his friend to tell his story truly to those who have not yet understood it, so that a good name is not left to rumour.
In Hamlet, the schemes of the plotters fall back on their own heads, a reminder that cunning used against others often returns to the one who devised it.

preview.text:
HORATIO.
And then it started, like a guilty thing
Upon a fearful summons. I have heard
The cock, that is the trumpet to the morn,
Doth with his lofty and shrill-sounding throat
Awake the god of day; and at his warning,
Whether in sea or fire, in earth or air,
Th’extravagant and erring spirit hies
To his confine. And of the truth herein
This present object made probation.

MARCELLUS.
It faded on the crowing of the cock.
Some say that ever ’gainst that season comes
Wherein our Saviour’s birth is celebrated,
The bird of dawning singeth all night long;
And then, they say, no spirit dare stir abroad,
The nights are wholesome, then no planets strike,
No fairy takes, nor witch hath power to charm;
So hallow’d and so gracious is the time.

HORATIO.
So have I heard, and do in part believe it.
But look, the morn in russet mantle clad,
Walks o’er the dew of yon high eastward hill.
Break we our watch up, and by my advice,
Let us impart what we have seen tonight
Unto young Hamlet; for upon my life,
This spirit, dumb to us, will speak to him.
Do you consent we shall acquaint him with it,
As needful in our loves, fitting our duty?

MARCELLUS.
Let’s do’t, I pray, and I this morning know
Where we shall find him most conveniently.

[_Exeunt._]

SCENE II. Elsinore. A room of state in the Castle.

Enter Claudius King of Denmark, Gertrude the Queen, Hamlet, Polonius,
Laertes, Voltemand,
Cornelius, Lords and Attendant.

books.title: While the Billy Boils
books.author: Henry Lawson
books.subject: Australian
books.licence_note: Author died 1922. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In An Old Mate of Your Father's, Henry Lawson shows children meeting a rough, half-forgotten friend of their father with easy warmth, and how kindness can outlast the years.
In An Old Mate of Your Father's, Henry Lawson asks whether the old mates were kinder to each other than his own generation is to its fathers, and fears the honest answer is no.
In Settling on the Land, Lawson follows Tom through one setback after another, and the comedy of his stubbornness is also a portrait of courage.
In Settling on the Land, Jacob sits with a ruined Tom through the hailstorm, then brings wine and a tune. Lawson shows that kindness in hard times often needs no speeches.
In Enter Mitchell, a swagman will not be ashamed of his worn swag or his old dog for anyone's sneer, and Lawson shows that an honest life carried for years deserves respect.
In Stiffner and Jim, Lawson shows how a man who decides honesty only makes a fool of him can talk himself into every petty dodge, and how easily that belief spreads to his mates.

In When the Sun Went Down, Lawson shows Tom torn over a quarrel with his brother until the wrath he has been nursing turns into fear for him. Old advice about not letting the sun go down on anger still holds.
In The Man Who Forgot, Lawson shows Tom taking under his wing a man others mock. Tom's loyalty to the vulnerable, even when it makes him unpopular, is a quiet kind of decency.
In Hungerford, Lawson watches a storekeeper hand a broke swagman rations for the road, and suggests such unrecorded kindnesses are written down somewhere else.
In His Country-After All, Lawson lets a quiet coach driver stand by his own view of Australia against a loud, bitter stranger, and the silence he leaves does the arguing.
In His Country-After All, a man who swore never to go back is undone by the smell of gum leaves, and Lawson shows how much of home stays in a person long after they have left it.

In A Day on a Selection, Lawson shows a farmer who spends hours at a fence calling a row of sticks an orchard. Activity that only looks like progress is an old trap, and it is one small business owners still fall into.
In That There Dog o' Mine, a battered shearer refuses to be admitted to hospital unless his loyal old dog is taken in too. Lawson shows that a true mate is measured by who stood by whom.
In Going Blind, Lawson shows that real care is often quiet and practical, such as a brother handling a blind man's boots, tie and collar without any fuss.

In Arvie Aspinall's Alarm Clock, Lawson mocks a newspaper that turns a poor child's hardship into a tidy sentimental story. Charity done for the giver's credit tends to help the giver more than the child.

In Arvie Aspinall's Alarm Clock, a boy starts to doubt a verse engraved on his clock. The story is a reminder to test the sayings we repeat without thinking, and to ask whether they hold for real people.
In Stragglers, Lawson looks at a ragged swagman and admits he might be a very different man under kinder conditions. Hard circumstances can make people look worse than they are.

In The Union Buries Its Dead, Lawson shows a drunk shearer pulling himself together to show respect for a stranger's funeral. Lawson suggests respect is often shown in small, honest acts rather than in the grand show of a funeral.

In The Union Buries Its Dead, Lawson notes that a drowned stranger was buried under a name that was not even his, and that the mourners already cannot recall it. Every stranger, he suggests, was once somebody's son.

In In a Dry Season, Lawson notes that stranded workers are helped by a publican and a coachman, while the wider system leaves them to fend for themselves. He treats that gap as a fact worth remembering.
In He'd Come Back, a teller turns a desertion into a tale of repentance and his mates lap it up. Lawson shows how a good story can quietly excuse a man from what he did.
In Drifted Back, a man returns to his old town after fifteen years and finds that the people he came to see have gone. Lawson shows how hard it is to go back to a place that has moved on without you.
In While the Billy Boils, Henry Lawson shows two old mates keeping in touch through small gestures, like a newspaper sent along with a few marked crosses.
Henry Lawson shows that old friends can stay close through good-humoured teasing, even when they still argue over everything.
Henry Lawson admits that a small piece printed in a local paper, marked up by an old mate, can mean more to a writer than praise from far-off critics.
In While the Billy Boils, the landlord shows that a plain, honest request would have served the two travellers better than sneaking off in the night.
Henry Lawson shows a boy who takes pride in doing his share beside his father, while Long Bob quietly looks out for him by pretending he is only passing the time.
In While the Billy Boils, Henry Lawson shows a father who keeps his hands busy with steady work while he carries a grief he cannot speak about.
Henry Lawson shows a man who keeps going after great loss, because a child still needs him and that duty holds him up.
In While the Billy Boils, poor fossickers pool what little they have, a table and a shirt, to give a dead child a decent farewell.
Henry Lawson shows a stranger offering a grieving man the simple gift of a mate, asking gently whether he wants another mate.
In While the Billy Boils, a cook's quiet complaint about endless work shows how the men who lean on someone hardest often never notice the load.
Henry Lawson argues that a poor man keeps his dignity only when he can rest and wash in some privacy, and that city poverty strips that away and leaves him feeling like a criminal.
Henry Lawson tells of a poor office man who quietly leaves food out each night for a hungry stranger, asking nothing in return, and shows kindness that goes unseen.
Henry Lawson observes that customers chase the cheapest option until the weaker rival is gone, and then pay far more for worse service.
After losing a coin on a rough crossing, Henry Lawson's narrator shares a drink with a stranger and decides to let the loss go and enjoy the company.
In 'Some Day', Lawson shows a man who keeps promising to go back to the girl he loved, until years of drifting have made the choice for him.
In the Billy Nowlett yarns, Lawson shows how one unchecked letter can change what a family believes about a person, so it pays to check news before you act on it.
In 'Brummy Usen', Lawson shows a crowd so set in its view that it ignored the one woman who knew the truth, and it kept arguing the point until she died.
In The Drover's Wife, Lawson shows a woman who is frightened but not a coward. Her courage is quiet and practical: she keeps going through the night, alone and worried, because her children need her.
In The Drover's Wife, Lawson shows that a person can fight hard against a flood or a fire and still lose, and that getting back to the work anyway is its own kind of courage.
Lawson gives his bushwoman a keen sense of the ridiculous, so that she can laugh at her own tears and her handkerchief full of holes. A dry sense of humour can carry a person through a bad hour.
At the end of The Drover's Wife, Lawson shows a boy who sees his mother's tears and throws his arms around her. It is a small act of tenderness, and it shows what children notice.
In An Unfinished Love Story, Lawson has Brook look back on his hard childhood with contempt rather than pity. It is a quiet warning about how easily a person forgets where they came from.

In An Unfinished Love Story, Lawson shows Brook pressing a hesitant young woman for promises she is not sure of. The story shows that pressure is not the same as care, and that a person's doubts deserve to be heard.
In His Colonial Oath, Lawson notices that living in the city can leave a man out of touch with his old mates, and then wonders whether the change was in his old friend or in himself.
In A Visit of Condolence, Lawson shows a rough, cheeky boy who turns gentle at a dead friend's side and speaks plainly and kindly to a grieving mother. Decency can show up in unlikely places.
In A Visit of Condolence, Lawson shows a boy who never told his mother he was being bullied at work. Some of the hardest troubles go unspoken, and the people closest to us may never know.

In A Visit of Condolence, Bill is a rough boy with little of his own, yet he offers to mend the broken step and to send his mother round. Lawson shows that help often comes from the people who have least to give.

In Rats, Lawson shows the shearers play along with an old swagman's pretend fight so he can keep his pride, and Sunlight quietly gives him tucker and kind advice. Kindness can be done without making someone feel small.
In The Bush Undertaker, Lawson's old shepherd scolds his dead mate for drinking away everything he earned, then still lays him out with care. Loyalty can outlast a friend's faults.
In The Bush Undertaker, Lawson's old shepherd buries his mate with care, even though no parson will come. Grief often arrives all at once in a flood of memories, when the work is finally done.
In Our Pipes, Lawson's tired swagmen grumble about society, then feel better after a feed, a rest and a smoke. A hard day often eases once you sit down and talk honestly with a mate.

In Our Pipes, Mitchell remembers how his father, when he was caught out, asked for a fill, and how they shared many solemn smokes together afterwards. Ordinary moments with a parent are often the ones we keep.
Lawson ends a passage about shedding a tear with a note on craft: it is best to be exact when you write from experience. Plain, honest description is more believable than polished feeling.
In Coming Across, Lawson notices men hurrying to hide their shabby underwear, and reminds us that we cannot see deep into one another. Kindness starts with not judging what people keep hidden.

In Coming Across, the men feel doubtful and mean about taking oranges, then a clever argument makes them feel better. Lawson shows how easily we reach for an excuse, and why it is worth listening to the doubt first.

In The Story of Malachi, the station hands tease a shy, awkward man for years, and only learn at his deathbed that he had a mother and a brother he had worked hard for. Lawson shows how little we know about the people we mock.

In Two Dogs and a Fence, Mitchell notes that a quarrel is often kept going by the person who claims they never started it. Lawson's point is that two dogs who meet on the other side of the fence might be the best of friends.

In Jones's Alley, Lawson shows each person in a chain of rent and repairs as right by their own lights, so the widow who is worst off ends up paying for everyone else's comfort. It is worth asking who pays for a decision.

preview.text:
You remember when we hurried home from the old bush school how we were
sometimes startled by a bearded apparition, who smiled kindly down on
us, and whom our mother introduced, as we raked off our hats, as “An
old mate of your father's on the diggings, Johnny.” And he would pat
our heads and say we were fine boys, or girls--as the case may have
been--and that we had our father's nose but our mother's eyes, or the
other way about; and say that the baby was the dead spit of its mother,
and then added, for father's benefit: “But yet he's like you, Tom.” It
did seem strange to the children to hear him address the old man by his
Christian name---considering that the mother always referred to him as
