“Father.” She called the old mate Mr So-and-so, and father called him
Bill, or something to that effect.

Occasionally the old mate would come dressed in the latest city fashion,
and at other times in a new suit of reach-me-downs, and yet again he
would turn up in clean white moleskins, washed tweed coat, Crimean
shirt, blucher boots, soft felt hat, with a fresh-looking speckled
handkerchief round his neck. But his face was mostly round and brown
and jolly, his hands were always horny, and his beard grey. Sometimes
he might have seemed strange and uncouth to us at first, but the old
man never appeared the least surprised at anything he said or did--they
understood each other so well--and we would soon take to this relic of
our father's past, who would have fruit or lollies for us--strange that
he always remembered them--and would surreptitiously slip “shilluns”
 into our dirty little hands, and tell us stories about the old days,
“when me an' yer father was on the diggin's, an' you wasn't thought of,
my boy.”

books.title: The Hound of the Baskervilles
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.subject: detective
books.licence_note: Author died 1930. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes says some people, though not geniuses, have a rare power to bring out the best thinking in others. Good company sharpens good work.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes builds his picture of a stranger one step at a time from a dated stick and a checkable career, asking at each step what the evidence actually allows.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, the old family manuscript argues that no burden is so heavy it cannot be lifted by repentance. The wise response to the past is to learn from it, not to be ruled by fear of it.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, the captive woman escapes by her own nerve, climbing down the ivy in her fear. Courage often shows up when someone has no good options left.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, the old manuscript notes that what is clearly known carries less terror than what is only hinted at and guessed. Plain facts calm people more than rumour does.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, the one detail nobody can explain is the change in the footprints past the gate. The loose end that refuses to fit is often where the truth is hiding.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Dr. Mortimer shows how a family legend, taken too much to heart, can wear a sensible man down until fear shapes every choice he makes.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes works out how long a man stood still from a small, checkable fact: ash dropped twice from a cigar. Small details often carry more weight than the big picture.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes says he works only within this world, yet insists a footprint is material evidence that must be explained. Stay with what can be examined, and do not wave away the awkward fact.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes points out that the world is full of obvious things that nobody ever actually notices. Attention, not cleverness, is most of the detective's craft.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes insists that every ordinary explanation must be exhausted before anyone reaches for the strange one. Ask first whether a crime happened at all, and then how it was done.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes tests a theory by asking whether the behaviour makes sense: a frightened man should run toward help, not away from it. A story is coherent only when every fact fits.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes shows that expertise is seeing differences others walk past. Each specialist finds the obvious in their own field, and that trained eye is what makes the work look like magic.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes says the detective balances probabilities and picks the most likely explanation, using the imagination but always starting from some material fact.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Sir Henry answers a warning by asking whether the danger comes from a legend or from people, then refuses to be scared off his own home. Courage that asks the right question is worth having.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes owns his own mistake plainly, going through what he should have done instead. Naming where you went wrong, without excuses, is how you get better at the work.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes can switch his mind off a hard problem for hours at a time and lose himself in art. Stepping fully away from a puzzle is often how the next clear idea arrives.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes says a hard case is worked by following several threads, knowing some will waste time, until one leads to the truth. Keep following the threads.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes cannot go himself, so he recommends the friend he trusts most to stand beside a person in danger. Knowing your own limits and asking a steady friend to help is good judgement.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Conan Doyle has Holmes refuse to treat a run of strange, apparently pointless incidents as separate accidents. He sets himself to find the scheme that joins them.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes admits plainly that he is uneasy about sending Watson into danger, and says he wants his friend back safe. Honest worry is a kind of care.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes refuses to drop suspects early. Clearing the innocent is an injustice, and dismissing the guilty loses the chance to prove it, so he keeps everyone on the list until the evidence settles it.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson reads Sir Henry's eagerness and bearing and judges him a companion who would bravely share a risk. Character often shows in how a person meets the world.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Sir Henry will not drop a household that has served his family for generations just because he is new. He values long loyalties and does not treat people as disposable.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson notices that a small detail, the butler's denial against the woman's red eyes, does not add up. He follows the mismatch instead of brushing it aside.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson tests each explanation against the whole pattern. A simple motive does not fit a web of schemes, and he admits he has not reached a conclusion yet.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson sets aside his wish to stay by his friend's side, because the papers there are not his to help with. He takes up the task that was actually asked of him.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson presses Miss Stapleton to be frank with him. When everything feels full of shadows, he says, a plain answer is worth more than a polite one, and he asks for it directly.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson reads Stapleton by his looks and by how he keeps his sister and the baronet apart, not by his polite words. Actions and small signs often tell more than speeches.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Frankland fights lawsuits for the pleasure of fighting and takes either side. Watson shows how a quarrel pursued for its own sake can cost a man his whole fortune.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson keeps what he saw apart from what he suspects. He reports the watching figure at the window and admits he cannot yet say what it means.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson admits his first suspicion was a love affair and reports it anyway, though it proved unfounded. He would rather show his reasoning and be wrong than keep it to himself.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson's conscience will not let him excuse himself after letting Sir Henry go out alone. He sets off at once to put it right rather than make his failing sound reasonable.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Doyle shows that a plain, honest admission can disarm anger. Watson owns up to following Sir Henry, and the baronet's temper gives way to a rueful laugh.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Stapleton's apology shows how fear of losing someone can drive a person to say things they later see as selfish, especially when that person has been their only company.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Doyle shows two men keeping a long, dull watch through two nights. Patient interest, the kind a hunter brings to a trap, is what keeps them going when nothing happens.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Mrs Barrymore explains how her family indulged her brother until he thought the world existed for his pleasure. Indulgence, she shows, can grow into a harm nobody meant to cause.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Sir Henry admits his fright and asks Watson for the plain truth. Naming a fear openly, Doyle suggests, makes it easier to face.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson insists on common sense, yet admits that facts he cannot explain still deserve a fair hearing. He weighs both explanations honestly instead of picking the one he prefers.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Sir Henry separates a truth given freely from one forced out of someone. Doyle shows that the way a confession comes out can change how it is judged.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson pities the escaped convict out on the cold moor. He concedes that whatever the man's crimes, he has suffered something to atone for them.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Mortimer judges a woman's ruin fairly, saying the fault may not have been entirely on one side. Several neighbours then quietly helped her earn an honest living.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson reasons that a formal visit would yield less, so he goes alone and keeps things low-key. Doyle shows that the way you approach people shapes what they will tell you.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson tests a witness's story against what could practically have happened. He reasons that a secret trip that hard to hide was unlikely, so part of her account is probably true.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Frankland wins every quarrel with his neighbours and still calls it a red-letter day. Doyle shows how a passion for being in the right can crowd out any real peace.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson finds that a meek admission he has spoken without all the facts pleases the old man and loosens his tongue. Doyle shows that humility can open a door that argument keeps shut.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson swears that he will not miss his chance through lack of energy or perseverance. Doyle makes the point that a lead is worth little unless someone is willing to follow it through.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes keeps Watson in the dark because a friend who knows too much can give the game away without meaning to. Doyle shows that discretion can be a kind of care.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes traces Stapleton through a true story he once told about his own past. Doyle shows how a person often gives themselves away through an honest remark made without thinking.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes takes his share of the blame for a client's death instead of hiding behind the facts. Owning a failure plainly is part of being trustworthy.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes will not act on suspicion alone. He insists the case must be proven, because one false move can let a clever villain escape.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes keeps pressing on the detail that does not fit, such as how the convict knew the hound was after him. Anomalies are worth chasing.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Barrymore's wife grieves for a man the world sees only as violent, because to her he is still the boy she once knew. The people closest to us often see more than strangers do.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes says his eyes are trained to look past a face's trimmings, such as dress and disguise. Looking past surface details is a basic skill of good judgement.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes lays out his evidence openly and invites the witness to check him for error. A fair test of a case is whether the other person can find a mistake in it.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes keeps his plans to himself until the moment they unfold, and his helpers find this trying. Caution can be sound, but a leader who hides the plan from the team wears them out.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Watson's terror breaks once he sees the monster can be wounded. Fear often shrinks when you find out what the thing is actually made of.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Mrs Stapleton, long controlled and abused, chooses to tell the investigators the truth and help them. Breaking free of a manipulative person can take real courage.

In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes sees that Stapleton could hide his hound but could not hush its voice. Every scheme has a weak point that gives it away, and finding that point is often how a case is solved.
In The Hound of the Baskervilles, Holmes keeps an indexed list of his cases because new work crowds out memory. Written records are how a busy mind holds on to what it has learned.

preview.text:
“Really, Watson, you excel yourself,” said Holmes, pushing back
      his chair and lighting a cigarette. “I am bound to say that in
      all the accounts which you have been so good as to give of my own
      small achievements you have habitually underrated your own
      abilities. It may be that you are not yourself luminous, but you
      are a conductor of light. Some people without possessing genius
      have a remarkable power of stimulating it. I confess, my dear
      fellow, that I am very much in your debt.”

He had never said as much before, and I must admit that his words
      gave me keen pleasure, for I had often been piqued by his
      indifference to my admiration and to the attempts which I had
      made to give publicity to his methods. I was proud, too, to think
      that I had so far mastered his system as to apply it in a way
      which earned his approval. He now took the stick from my hands
      and examined it for a few minutes with his naked eyes. Then with
      an expression of interest he laid down his cigarette, and
      carrying the cane to the window, he looked over it again with a
      convex lens.

“Interesting, though elementary,” said he as he returned to his
      favourite corner of the settee. “There are certainly one or two
      indications upon the stick. It gives us the basis for several
      deductions.”

“Has anything escaped me?” I asked with some self-importance. “I
      trust that there is nothing of consequence which I have
      overlooked?”

books.title: Aesop's Fables
books.author: Aesop
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Ancient author, 1912 edition. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Aesop's life, his fables were a tool for persuasion. He used them to win over the people of Corinth and Athens, a reminder that a good story can carry a point further than a lecture.
In The Stag at the Pool, Aesop shows a stag so proud of his antlers that he despises the legs that would have saved him. What is truly valuable is often underrated.
In The Wolf and the Lamb, Aesop shows that a tyrant will always find a pretext, so the innocent cannot reason their way out of an unjust oppressor.
In The Bear and the Fox, Aesop reminds us to show people respect while they are alive, not only once they are gone.
In The One-Eyed Doe, Aesop shows that danger often comes from the direction we least suspect, so we should not guard only the side we fear.
In The Mouse, the Frog, and the Hawk, Aesop shows that whoever plots harm for others is often caught by their own scheme.
In The Lion and the Boar, Aesop shows that rivals who keep fighting are watched by others who will profit from their defeat, so making peace can be the wiser choice.
In The Mischievous Dog, Aesop shows that people who win notoriety often mistake it for fame, when the bell and clog they wear mark them out as a nuisance.
In The Wolf and the Sheep, Aesop shows that a hypocrite's fine words are easily seen through, since the wolf asks for help while planning to eat the helper.
In The Widow and her Little Maidens, Aesop shows that an unlawful act taken to escape trouble only brings more trouble.
In The Fox and the Lion, Aesop shows that familiarity softens fear, since the fox grew bolder with each meeting.
In The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse, Aesop shows that a modest meal in safety is better than a rich feast surrounded by danger.
In The Monkey and the Dolphin, Aesop shows that a falsehood needs more lies to hold it up, and sooner or later it will get the teller into trouble.
In The Boy and the Nettle, Aesop shows that a timid touch invites a sting, while a firm grip makes a hard task easier.
In The Trumpeter taken Prisoner, Aesop shows that the one who stirs others to fight carries as much blame as those who fight.
In The Lion and the Mouse, Aesop shows that ambition can push us to reach for more than we can hold, and alliances built on that pride often end in ruin.
In The Milkmaid and her Pot of Milk, Aesop shows how quickly plans built on imagined profits can collapse, so it pays to wait for real gains before spending them in your head.
In The Man and the Satyr, Aesop shows that someone who blows hot and cold with the same breath cannot be trusted by anyone.
In The Mother and the Wolf, Aesop shows that words spoken in anger or thoughtlessness are not always meant, so it pays to wait before believing them.
In The Old Man and the Three Young Men, Aesop shows that planting for those who come after us is a duty, and that none of us can be sure of tomorrow.
In The Horse and the Stag, Aesop shows that whoever seeks to injure others often injures only himself, since the horse handed himself over to man to punish a stag.
In The Lion and the Dolphin, Aesop shows that each of us does best in our own element, and blaming others for what nature denied us helps no one.
In The Fighting Cocks and the Eagle, Aesop shows that pride goes before destruction, because the cock that crowed loudest from the high wall was the one the eagle spotted and carried off.
In a story of a shepherd who left his flock in a wolf's care, Aesop shows that an evil mind will show itself in evil action, sooner or later.
In The Frog and the Ox, Aesop shows the folly of puffing ourselves up to match something far bigger than us, because the frog could never swell to the size of the ox.
In The Lion and the Mouse, Aesop shows that no one is too weak to do good, since the mouse who was spared later freed the lion from the hunters' ropes.
In The Crow and the Pitcher, Aesop shows that when we are stuck, patient effort and clever thinking can solve what brute strength cannot. Necessity is the mother of invention.
In The Old Hound, Aesop shows that an old dog should be judged for what he was in his strength and not blamed for infirmities that age brings.
In The Ass Eating Thistles, Aesop shows that what one person rejects another may value highly, so we should not judge others by our own tastes.
In The Trees and the Axe, Aesop shows that giving up the rights of others can put our own at risk, because the first concession starts a loss that spreads.
In The King's Son and the Painted Lion, Aesop shows that hiding from a dreaded fate can bring about the very harm we fear.
In a story of travellers who waited for a ship that turned out to be a bundle of sticks, Aesop shows how our expectations can run ahead of what life delivers.
In The Rat and the Elephant, Aesop shows that sharing one trait with the great does not make us their equal in everything.
In The Eagle and the Kite, Aesop shows that a smooth promise made to win something is worth little, since the kite promised an ostrich and brought back a mouse.
In The Fisherman and the Little Fish, Aesop shows that a sure gain in hand is worth more than a bigger profit that is only promised for later.
In The Fox and the Crow, Aesop shows that flattery serves the one who gives it, so a wise listener is wary of praise that seems to want something in return.
In The Mountain in Labor, Aesop shows that a great deal of noise can end in a very small result, so judge the outcome rather than the commotion.
In a story of two travellers and a bear, Aesop shows that misfortune is what tests the sincerity of friends.
In The Two Soldiers and the Robber, Aesop shows that a boast from someone who ran at the first sign of danger earns no trust. A record of action counts for more than words.
In The Two Frogs, Aesop shows the value of thinking through consequences before acting, since the frog who asked how they would climb back out asked the wiser question.
In The Mouse and the Boasting Rat, Aesop shows that a loud boast of courage is no defence, and a plan built on bluster can leave others in the lurch.
In The Thief and the House-Dog, Aesop shows that sudden kindness from someone with hidden aims should make us more watchful, not less.
In The Fowler and the Ringdove, Aesop shows that people often fall into the very trap they set for others, as the hunter was stung by the adder while aiming at a bird.
In The North Wind and the Sun, Aesop shows that gentle warmth persuades where force fails, because the traveller shed his cloak only when the sun shone on him.
In The Snake and the Cottager, Aesop shows that it is hard to forget an injury while the one who caused it stands in front of us every day.
In The Boasting Traveler, Aesop shows that the best cure for a boaster is to put his claims to the test, and let the facts speak for themselves.
In The Stag and the Fawn, Aesop shows that the loudest braggarts are often the most fearful when real danger arrives.
In The Hare and the Hound, Aesop shows that a runner fighting for its life will often outlast one running only for a meal, because the stakes shape how hard we push.
In The Dog in the Manger, Aesop shows that we should not deny others a blessing just because we cannot enjoy it ourselves.
In The Cat and the Fox, Aesop shows that a little common sense is often worth more than a great deal of cunning.
In The Frogs Asking for a King, Aesop shows that before we try to change our condition, we should be sure the change will leave us better off.
In The Dog and his Master's Dinner, Aesop shows that someone who stops to argue with temptation is very likely to give in to it.
In The Buffoon and the Countryman, Aesop shows that critics are not always to be relied on, since the crowd cheered the fake performance and missed the real one.
In The Fox and the Goat, Aesop shows that we should look before we leap, since the fox had never checked the way out before he went down the well.
In The Oxen and the Butchers, Aesop shows that we should not rush to replace one evil with another, because the old butcher knew the known harm was better than the unknown one.
In The Lark and her Young Ones, Aesop shows that when the field owner stops relying on friends and does the work himself, it is time to act. Self-help is the best help.
In The Boy and the Filberts, Aesop shows that grabbing too much at once leaves us stuck, and taking half is the way to get anything out.
In The Woman and her Hen, Aesop shows that greed defeats itself, since the woman who overfed her hen for two eggs a day ended with no eggs at all.
In The Hawk and the Nightingale, Aesop shows that a sure gain in hand beats chasing bigger prizes that are not yet even in sight.
In The Hen and the Swallow, Aesop shows that nourishing something harmful brings it to life, and sooner or later it turns on the one who fed it.

preview.text:
On the invitation of Croesus he fixed his residence at Sardis, and was
employed by that monarch in various difficult and delicate affairs of
state. In his discharge of these commissions he visited the different
petty republics of Greece. At one time he is found in Corinth, and at
another in Athens, endeavoring, by the narration of some of his wise
fables, to reconcile the inhabitants of those cities to the
administration of their respective rulers, Pariander and Pisistratus.
One of these ambassadorial missions, undertaken at the command of
Croesus, was the occasion of his death. Having been sent to Delphi
with a large sum of gold for distribution among the citizens, he was so
provoked at their covetousness that he refused to divide the money, and
sent it back to his master. The Delphians, enraged at this treatment,
accused him of impiety, and, in spite of his sacred character as
ambassador, executed him as a public criminal. This cruel death of Æsop
was not unavenged. The citizens of Delphi were visited with a series of
calamities, until they made a public reparation of their crime; and "The
blood of Æsop" became a well-known adage, bearing witness to the truth
that deeds of wrong would not pass unpunished. Neither did the great
fabulist lack posthumous honors; for a statue was erected to his memory
at Athens, the work of Lysippus, one of the most famous of Greek
sculptors. Phædrus thus immortalizes the event:--

Æsopo ingentem statuam posuere Attici,
  Servumque collocarunt æterna in basi:
  Patere honoris scirent ut cuncti viam;
  Nec generi tribui sed virtuti gloriam.

books.title: On Benefits
books.author: Seneca
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 65, translator died 1918. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Seneca warns that we make people ungrateful ourselves, by demanding repayment harshly, regretting what we gave and finding fault over trifles.
Seneca says a benefit is received in the same spirit it is given, so gifts handed over grudgingly, late or with insults are rarely thanked.
Seneca holds that we should give benefits rather than lend them out at interest, since expecting a return turns a gift into a loan.
Seneca says giving is simple bookkeeping: a return is clear gain, and a good giver who gets nothing back has lost nothing, because he gave for the sake of giving.
Seneca wants people taught to give, to receive and to repay, and to aim at outdoing one another in kindness, the giver by forgetting and the receiver by remembering.
Seneca says a benefit is not the gift itself but the goodwill behind it, so a kindness lasts even after the thing given is lost.
Seneca says a benefit lies in the mind of the giver, since the thing given is neither good nor bad in itself and the spirit behind it decides its worth.
Seneca says we prize what comes from a willing hand more than what comes from a full one, so a small gift given gladly can mean more than a large one given grudgingly.
Seneca says ingratitude is the root of most great wickedness, so guard against it in yourself and forgive it in others.
Seneca advises giving what is necessary first, then what is useful, then what is pleasant and lasting, and always with thought for the receiver's own life.
Seneca warns that a gift can insult when it reminds someone of their failings, or when it is useless to them, so the receiver's needs must guide the choice.
Seneca prefers gifts that last, and things people have long wanted but could not find, since a rare gift is valued more than a costly one.
Seneca says a gift handed to everyone earns little thanks, so generosity should be steady and still give each person some sign that they are singled out.
Seneca insists generosity needs discretion, since a careless gift pleases no one and a benefit is worth most when we are proud to say who gave it.
Seneca says the best gift anticipates a friend's wish, sparing him the shame of asking, because a benefit that comes unasked is remembered.
Seneca says a yes given with a sour face spoils the gift, so join kind words to kind actions and let the giver's warmth show.
Seneca warns that a promised kindness delayed or passed through many hands loses its gratitude, so deliver what you promise promptly and in full.
Seneca says long delay is bitter, and that some people drag out their promises to feel important, being swift to do harm but slow to do good.
Seneca says a gift handed over while reproaching the receiver turns into an insult, so save the criticism for another time.
Seneca says help given only to humiliate someone is reproach rather than a benefit, and the person who needed it will remember the shame.
Seneca says help that raises a person's standing can be given openly, but help for someone in want or disgrace should be given quietly, so they are spared the shame.
Seneca says a giver should judge a kindness by how it serves the receiver and be content with his own conscience, not by being seen to do good.
Seneca says a giver who keeps reminding others of his favours turns the gift into a debt they can never escape, so let the receiver tell the story.
Seneca says a benefit needs tending after it is given, as a seed does, and that giving is not enough without caring for the person you helped.
Seneca says pride turns every benefit into an insult, and that gifts given humbly, on the receiver's level and at the time of need, are welcomed.
Seneca says a giver should refuse what would harm the receiver even when begged, since the person will later hate the one who helped ruin them.
Seneca says a gift should be weighed against the giver's means and the receiver's character, neither too burdensome for the giver nor too small or too large for the receiver.
Seneca compares giving to a game of ball: a benefit must be thrown to suit the one who catches it, so a gift must fit both the giver and the receiver.
Seneca says the best giver gives readily, asks for nothing back, and is glad when a return comes because he has truly forgotten what he gave.
Seneca says we should be more careful about whom we owe than whom we give to, since being indebted to someone we dislike is a great misery.
Seneca says a kindness creates a lasting bond that feeds friendship, unlike money which is simply repaid and forgotten, so owe your debts of kindness to people worthy of them.
Seneca says no one is obliged for a gift they could not refuse, and that help given without goodwill does not make the helper a true benefactor.
Seneca says a kindness done by accident, like a lion sparing its old keeper, is not a true benefit, because real benefit needs good intent behind it.
Seneca says a worthy person should not be made to suffer for our sake, and that we should be ready to take the risk ourselves rather than cost a friend his safety.
Seneca admires a man who refused money from someone of bad character, reasoning that he would not take from a man what he would not share a drink with.
Seneca says gratitude should be spoken openly, since thanking someone in public repays the first instalment, while thanking them in a whisper is a quiet way of denying the debt.
Seneca says thanks should match the size of the kindness, neither disdainful nor grovelling, and that keeping a kindness in memory is itself a way of showing gratitude.
Seneca says true gratitude is feeling you can never fully repay a kindness, and that a grateful person should watch for the first chance to return it.
Seneca says self-regard makes us think we have earned whatever we receive, so we judge every gift as too little and too late.
Seneca says greed never lets anyone feel grateful, since the more we get the more we want, and an ambitious man looks only ahead and never back at how far he has come.
Seneca says jealousy makes us count what others were given, and the cure is to make the most of what we have and be content with it.
Seneca says we should stop fixating on what we lack and count the blessings we already have, since nearly everything is given to us except what could not be granted.
Seneca says a person who receives a kindness with goodwill has already begun to repay it, because gratitude is measured by the spirit of receiving.
Seneca says the first reward of a kindness is the satisfaction of having given it well, like a sculptor who is pleased with his work before he sells it.
Seneca says a kindness received warmly is already repaid in goodwill, though a material gift still asks for something material in return, so accept gracefully and owe with a quieter conscience.
Seneca says forgetting a kindness is worse than ungratefulness, since the one who still feels the debt can be shamed into repaying, while the one who has forgotten it can never become grateful.
Seneca says gratitude costs no money, time or luck, since remembering a kindness is itself thanks, and what we keep in view never grows rusty.
Seneca says we forget kindnesses because we fix on what we want next, and no one can be both jealous and grateful, since the jealous are sad and the grateful are glad.
Seneca notes that people begging for favours promise eternal gratitude, then forget once they have what they wanted, so a promise of thanks is worth little.
Seneca thinks ingratitude should be hated rather than punished by law, since no penalty could be measured fairly for a fault that varies so much.
Seneca argues gratitude loses its virtue once it is forced by law, since a benefit becomes a loan when it can be sued for, and the finest part of a gift is that it was never conditional.
Seneca says a gift's worth depends on its timing and the spirit behind it, so the same sum is little to the rich and everything to the man who had to beg for it.
Seneca says some of the greatest help goes unseen, such as warning someone of danger, holding them back from crime, or simply sitting with the sick at the right moment.
Seneca points out that no day is set for repaying a kindness, so a debt of gratitude can be paid later, and the greatest benefits often rest only in the silent knowledge of two people.
Seneca says we do not choose every benefit we receive, and a favour we would have refused does not bind us in the same way as one we accepted freely.
Seneca argues that a law against ingratitude would make people less willing to give, since giving loses its beauty when the giver is protected from loss.
Seneca says no law can make full repayment for a benefit, so we must rely on the honour of the receiver, and turning kindness into a commercial deal dishonours it.
Seneca says the one who gives should act like a god and not like a moneylender, so do not ask for surety when you help someone.
Seneca says the ungrateful are punished by losing the joy of receiving, while the grateful enjoy a steady happiness that comes from the giver's intention rather than the gift itself.
Seneca argues that a person's station does not decide whether they can give a benefit, since virtue is open to all, free or enslaved, and what matters is intention.

preview.text:
Among the numerous faults of those who pass their lives recklessly and
without due reflexion, my good friend Liberalis, I should say that there
is hardly any one so hurtful to society as this, that we neither know
how to bestow or how to receive a benefit. It follows from this that
benefits are badly invested, and become bad debts: in these cases it is
too late to complain of their not being returned, for they were thrown
away when we bestowed them. Nor need we wonder that while the greatest
vices are common, none is more common than ingratitude: for this I see
is brought about by various causes. The first of these is, that we do
not choose worthy persons upon whom to bestow our bounty, but although
when we are about to lend money we first make a careful enquiry into
the means and habits of life of our debtor, and avoid sowing seed in a
worn-out or unfruitful soil, yet without any discrimination we scatter
our benefits at random rather than bestow them. It is hard to say
whether it is more dishonourable for the receiver to disown a benefit,
or for the giver to demand a return of it: for a benefit is a loan, the
repayment of which depends merely upon the good feeling of the debtor.
To misuse a benefit like a spendthrift is most shameful, because we
do not need our wealth but only our intention to set us free from the
obligation of it; for a benefit is repaid by being acknowledged. Yet
while they are to blame who do not even show so much gratitude as to
acknowledge their debt, we ourselves are to blame no less. We find many
men ungrateful, yet we make more men so, because at one time we harshly
and reproachfully demand some return for our bounty, at another we are
fickle and regret what we have given, at another we are peevish and
