books.title: Sense and Sensibility
books.author: Jane Austen
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1817. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Sense and Sensibility, Austen shows how a generous promise feels easy to make while it costs nothing to imagine, and how much harder it is to keep once the cost is real.
In Sense and Sensibility, Austen shows Elinor with a warm heart and the judgement to govern it. Feeling deeply and acting sensibly can go together.
In Sense and Sensibility, Austen shows grief being nursed and even sought out. Elinor feels the same loss just as keenly, yet still does what the people around her need.
In Sense and Sensibility, Mrs John Dashwood reasons her way out of a generous promise one plausible step at a time. Austen shows how easily self-interest can pass itself off as good sense.
In Sense and Sensibility, Mrs Dashwood judges a suitor by his character rather than his fortune. She holds that people alike in disposition should not be kept apart by money.
In Sense and Sensibility, Austen values Edward for his open, affectionate heart rather than for looks or ambition. His family wants him distinguished in some vague way that he does not care for.
In Sense and Sensibility, Marianne sets a standard for a husband so high that she is sure no one will meet it. Austen lets the reader see how demanding perfection can leave a person alone.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor says a person's worth only shows to those who take the trouble to know them past shyness and a first impression.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor will not let wishes pass for hopes, or hopes for certainties. She tries to see the real state of things before she acts on her feelings.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor will not claim more certainty about Edward than she has. Her sister's imagination has already run well ahead of the facts.

In Sense and Sensibility, one friendly letter changes Mrs Dashwood's whole view of where she should live. Austen shows how a kindness at the right moment can reorder what once seemed out of the question.

In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor sets aside her own reluctance and does not oppose her mother's plan, because it is sensible on its merits. She judges a plan by its sense, not by how she feels about it.
In Sense and Sensibility, the Dashwoods agree to appear happy for one another's sake. That shared choice does much of the work of making a new place feel like home.
In Sense and Sensibility, the Dashwoods learn to be content with a modest house as it is. They make it a home by arranging their own belongings around them.
In Sense and Sensibility, Sir John Middleton shows his welcome in practical deeds, such as garden produce and carrying their post, rather than in fine words. Austen measures kindness by what it does.
In Sense and Sensibility, Austen shows the Middletons filling their lives with company and sport, a busyness that covers a lack of inner resources. She is gentle about it, but clear-eyed.
In Sense and Sensibility, Sir John takes real pleasure in welcoming newcomers and helping those whose fortunes have fallen. Austen suggests a good heart finds its satisfaction in kindness itself.
In Sense and Sensibility, Marianne softens her harsh judgements and comes to respect Colonel Brandon for his quiet attention, making allowance for his years. Her sensibility grows into fairness.
In Sense and Sensibility, Mrs Jennings is quick to see romance everywhere. Her eagerness to spot attachments makes her certain of things that are only guesses.
In Sense and Sensibility, Marianne reads every small sign as proof of a secret, while Elinor keeps her self-command. Austen shows how over-reading can be its own kind of blindness.
In Sense and Sensibility, Austen shows Marianne turning a stranger into the hero of a favourite story. She warns how quickly a lively fancy supplies what it has not yet seen.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor asks the sensible questions about a stranger: where he comes from and what he has. Marianne is taken with his manner. Austen contrasts the two ways of judging.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor points out that a friendship built in a hurry on shared tastes has little left to discover. Austen shows how frankness can be mistaken for intimacy.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor sees Willoughby's fault clearly: he says what he thinks without regard for people or circumstances. Austen shows that charm can hide a want of caution.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor respects Colonel Brandon for his gravity and reserve and pities the hurts she guesses at. Austen shows her seeing worth that the lively young people overlook.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor takes pains to talk with people others overlook. She tells Willoughby and Marianne that dismissing a man for being quiet is an injustice.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor warns that judging a person's faults in the mass, from one's own imagination, makes fair praise sound cold. Austen shows the cost of judging from fancy.

In Sense and Sensibility, Marianne and Willoughby are so open with their feelings that ridicule cannot shame them. Elinor's quiet advice about self-command goes unheeded. Austen weighs candour against prudence.
In Sense and Sensibility, Colonel Brandon warns that when romantic ideals give way, they can harden into something more dangerous. Austen lets his own old hurt show through his caution.

In Sense and Sensibility, Marianne accepts a costly gift with delight before weighing what it will cost. Elinor is the one who thinks of the consequences. Austen shows how generosity can be imprudent.
In Sense and Sensibility, Marianne holds that intimacy depends on disposition, not on time. Austen lets the reader test that claim against how the story unfolds.
In Sense and Sensibility, Colonel Brandon is mindful of other people's feelings on every occasion, and quietly steers a company away from a painful subject. Austen shows tact as a form of kindness.
In Sense and Sensibility, Willoughby assumes the worst of a man's motives with no evidence, and Marianne agrees at once. Austen shows how easily a group can settle on an unkind story.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor reminds her sister that how pleasant an outing is does not prove it was proper. Austen shows how a good time can blind a person to what others see.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor is puzzled by a secrecy that hides nothing, yet she chooses to wait rather than press her sister. Austen shows patience as a kind of respect.
In Sense and Sensibility, Willoughby's warm words run well ahead of his actions. Austen shows that feelings expressed beautifully are not the same as promises kept.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor resolves to judge everyone candidly and allows that a person may have good reasons they cannot yet share. Austen gives her honesty and generosity together.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor separates wanting proof of affection from wanting proof of an engagement. Austen shows how wishful reading can pass itself off as evidence.
In Sense and Sensibility, Austen shows Marianne feeding her grief on purpose, choosing the songs and books that hurt most. She takes the intensity of a feeling for proof of its worth.
In Sense and Sensibility, Mrs Dashwood's tender delicacy shuts out the plain questions that common care and prudence would ask. Austen shows that kindness also needs honesty.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor chooses to treat Edward by their past kindness and family ties rather than by his present coldness. Austen shows steady conduct as a form of fairness.
In Sense and Sensibility, Edward says he wants to be happy in his own way, not in the way his family would choose for him. Austen lets him make a quiet case for modest contentment.

In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor admits she often misjudges people, fancying them gayer or graver than they are, and guided by what others say instead of by taking time to judge. Austen models self-correction.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor notices that a person can drop one affectation only to pick up another. Austen is always alert to the pose behind a pretence.
In Sense and Sensibility, Marianne blurts out a hurtful remark, and her regret is as sharp as the pain she caused. Austen shows how thoughtlessness can wound even a warm heart.

In Sense and Sensibility, Mrs Dashwood argues that a real calling gives a person interest and direction, so they know where to go. Austen makes the case that purpose is a kindness a person owes themselves.
In Sense and Sensibility, Edward admits he drifted into idleness because nobody helped him find work that suited him. Austen shows how a life without purpose can be shaped by other people's choices.

In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor keeps busy and neither seeks nor avoids Edward's name, so her grief does not grow. Austen contrasts her quiet self-command with Marianne's deliberate sorrow, and shows both as ways of acting on feeling.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor reasons that when company feels tedious, the change may lie with the listener rather than the hosts. Austen models fair-minded self-examination.

In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor sees that Mr Palmer's contempt for others comes from a wish to seem superior, and that rudeness wins no one's affection. Austen shows scorn as often a costume for insecurity.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor knows that glowing praise for newcomers tells you little, since good people are found everywhere. Austen trusts the reader to tell praise apart from proof.

In Sense and Sensibility, Austen notes that flattery wins over people who crave praise for their children, and that the most eager flatterers are often the most calculating. Her eye for social performance is sharp.
In Sense and Sensibility, Marianne cannot say what she does not feel, while Elinor is kind without pretending. Austen shows politeness and honesty sitting side by side.
In Sense and Sensibility, Sir John thinks that being in the same room is the same as being close. Austen lets the gap between proximity and real friendship show plainly.

In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor pities Lucy's lack of education but judges her lack of sincerity more harshly. Austen separates sympathy for a person's circumstances from judgement of their character.
In Sense and Sensibility, Austen shows Elinor keeping her self-command after a painful shock. Composure under strain is a choice a person can make, even when they feel it sink.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor weighs Edward's fault against his affection and judges him fairly even while she is hurt. Austen shows that fairness can survive a painful wound.
Austen shows Elinor bearing a private sorrow alone so her mother and sister are spared it. Carrying a hurt quietly can be a kindness to the people you love.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor gets her way through a little tact that pleases everyone at the table. Austen contrasts it with Marianne, who scorns that kind of address and loses something by it.
In Sense and Sensibility, Elinor stops reopening a painful subject once it only hurts her. Austen shows that knowing when to end a conversation that wounds you is a form of self-respect.

preview.text:
When he gave his promise to his father, he meditated within himself to
increase the fortunes of his sisters by the present of a thousand
pounds a-piece. He then really thought himself equal to it. The
prospect of four thousand a-year, in addition to his present income,
besides the remaining half of his own mother’s fortune, warmed his
heart, and made him feel capable of generosity. “Yes, he would give
them three thousand pounds: it would be liberal and handsome! It would
be enough to make them completely easy. Three thousand pounds! he could
spare so considerable a sum with little inconvenience.” He thought of
it all day long, and for many days successively, and he did not repent.

No sooner was his father’s funeral over, than Mrs. John Dashwood,
without sending any notice of her intention to her mother-in-law,
arrived with her child and their attendants. No one could dispute her
right to come; the house was her husband’s from the moment of his
father’s decease; but the indelicacy of her conduct was so much the
greater, and to a woman in Mrs. Dashwood’s situation, with only common
feelings, must have been highly unpleasing;—but in _her_ mind there was
a sense of honor so keen, a generosity so romantic, that any offence of
the kind, by whomsoever given or received, was to her a source of
immovable disgust. Mrs. John Dashwood had never been a favourite with
any of her husband’s family; but she had had no opportunity, till the
present, of showing them with how little attention to the comfort of
other people she could act when occasion required it.

books.title: Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea
books.author: Jules Verne
books.subject: adventure
books.licence_note: Author died 1905, nineteenth century translation. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Jules Verne shows that the facts of a sighting matter more than the guesses built around it, and that people lean toward the marvellous. Weigh the evidence before deciding what is real.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Verne shows a public quarrel over a sea monster sliding into mockery while the evidence sits unexamined. Ridicule is not the same as proof.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, the narrator admits that when he cannot form an opinion he swings from one extreme to the other. Being unable to judge is a reason to slow down.
Verne has his narrator test each theory against what could be checked in many countries, and drop the ones that cannot survive the inquiry. Test an idea by asking who would have to know.
Verne's narrator reasons that if our knowledge of the sea is incomplete, we should leave room for what we have not yet seen. Admit the limits of what you know before ruling things out.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax admits his hedged newspaper article was cowardly, written to protect his dignity. Being honest about your own motives is part of good judgment.
Verne makes Conseil steady, loyal and willing to follow wherever science leads, never complaining of a long journey. Devotion of that quiet, reliable kind is worth more than showy loyalty.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Verne says Captain Farragut believes in the monster by faith rather than reason, and will not let anyone dispute it. Certainty that cannot hear doubt tends to steer a crew wrong.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Ned Land will not accept a claim until he sees proof, and says so plainly. Asking for proof before belief is a sound habit on any subject.

Aronnax argues backwards from what a creature would need to survive the deep, and lets the numbers do the persuading. Start from the constraints any claim must satisfy, and test the idea against them.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, the crew's warmest supporters become its loudest critics once the search drags on. Captain Farragut steadies them with a clear three-day limit, which is a useful habit for any long pursuit.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Farragut refuses to risk his ship in the dark against a thing he does not understand, and waits for daylight. Gather more light before acting on a fright.
Aronnax measures the creature for himself and trims the exaggerated reports down to what he can see. Check second-hand claims against what you can observe directly.
When brute speed fails to close the gap, Captain Farragut switches to a different method and fires the forecastle gun. Pushing the same effort harder is not a plan.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Conseil answers a disaster with "we have still several hours, and one can do a good deal in some hours." Calm attention to the time you still have is often the best help.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, the two men take turns towing each other so neither exhausts himself at once. Sharing a long strain in turns is how a hard struggle gets survived.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Conseil calms the angry Ned Land with "Do not cry out before you are hurt." Find out where you stand before you let anger decide your next move.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax asks his angry companions to wait before forming an opinion of their captors, since they have not yet learned enough to judge. Judge people on what you have actually seen.
Aronnax works out how the boat must be getting its air by choosing the simplest explanation, a surfacing breath like a whale's. Prefer the explanation that needs the fewest extra assumptions.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, the commander says he delayed his answer so he could learn who his prisoners were and reflect first. Hear the whole story before deciding what to do with the people in it.
Verne's commander cuts himself off from society and answers only to his own conscience. Verne shows that a life no one can hold to account is a warning, not a kind of freedom.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Nemo tells Aronnax that his careful book stopped where land-based science could see. Even thorough expertise has limits, and the wise expert knows where they lie.
Captain Nemo says that masters have no age, because great work is always contemporary and outlasts the fashions of its own time. Judge a craft by what lasts, not by what is newest.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax lists the questions that matter for any machine: how it steers, how it goes deep, how it comes back up, and what keeps it there. Ask those before you trust any plan.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Nemo says he trusts his vessel because he is its captain, builder and engineer all at once. Knowing every part of the thing you depend on is a kind of safety.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax tells a restless companion to set aside the wish to escape for now and watch what passes around them. Waiting while you learn is not the same as giving up.
While the captain stays out of sight, Aronnax starts a daily journal so he can recount events with more exactitude. Writing things down as they happen keeps your memory honest.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Nemo tells Aronnax that he should never judge any man lightly, and asks him to hear the explanation before calling it folly. Give people the chance to explain before you decide they are mad.
Aronnax feels real grief at crushing the shells under his feet as he walks, even though he has no choice but to go on. Notice what your progress costs others, even when you cannot avoid it.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax admits he had never thought of the dangers below until a monstrous creature appeared. Before you go deeper into anything new, ask what you have not yet considered.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Nemo answers a claim about new land by saying the earth needs new people more than new continents. Progress depends on people more than on the ground they claim.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Verne has the narrator marvel at huge reef walls built by creatures too small to notice, growing about an eighth of an inch a century. Slow, steady work repeated over ages can add up to something enormous.

Verne shows Dillon and Dumont d'Urville chasing the lost La Perouse expedition for years, following every scrap of evidence and every rumour until the wreck was found. Persistence on a faint lead can pay off.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Conseil says a happy year would be one in which they could see everything. Verne makes curiosity itself the source of happiness, even for someone trapped.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Nemo meets a grounding calmly and calls it an incident, not a disaster. Staying composed lets a person see what can actually be done.
Faced with a choice between a known captivity and unknown dangers ashore, Aronnax judges that staying aboard is safer. Weighing the risks honestly beats acting on a hunch.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax grieves over a broken rare shell, then tells Conseil that no shell is worth a man's life. Keeping a sense of proportion matters most when a loss stings.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Nemo speaks of the explorer D'Urville with real respect and says what he has done under the sea matches it. A good person can honour the work of someone whose path was different from their own.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Nemo does not trust indirect readings from clumsy instruments and goes down to test the sea's temperature himself. Sometimes the surest way to know something is to check it at first hand.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Nemo, who seems unmoved by most things, has tears in his eyes as a crew member dies. Grief can show through even the hardest outer shell.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax is never bored on the long voyage because he fills his days with walks, reading and writing his memoirs. Real interest in one's surroundings and steady absorbing work keep restlessness away.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax notices that an invitation sounds like fun when it is about a bear or a lion, and only pauses when the hunt is a shark in its own element. Take a moment to weigh what an invitation really asks of you before saying yes.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax sees an enormous bed of oysters that could seem endless, yet he notices that the sea keeps producing far more than people take. Verne reminds readers that a living resource is only safe when it is harvested with restraint.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Nemo leaves a great pearl in its shell so it can keep growing in layers, year after year. Some good things need to be left alone for a long time to become what they can be.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Nemo risks his own life to save a stranger, and Aronnax concludes that his heart has not been entirely crushed. Compassion can survive even a deep bitterness toward the world.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Nemo points out that the ancient sailors feared the Red Sea with good reason, given their planks and guesswork, and that progress takes ages. Dangers shrink as people build better tools and better knowledge.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Nemo credits Lesseps with succeeding where ancient rulers had failed, after many rebuffs, through sheer determination. Steady will can carry a long project through years of discouragement.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Nemo proves a hunch about a hidden passage by tagging fish with copper rings and finding the same ones again months later. Testing an idea against evidence turns a guess into knowledge.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax tells Ned that a bid for freedom must be serious and must succeed the first time, because a failed attempt may never be followed by another. Weigh a single chance carefully before you take it.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Nemo hurries through the Mediterranean because its waters bring back too many memories and regrets. Beautiful surroundings can still weigh on a person who carries the past with them.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax weighs his gratitude toward a generous host against his wish to escape. He decides that thankfulness does not oblige him to give up his own freedom, but the conflict still weighs on him.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Captain Nemo bristles when Aronnax assumes his wealth is wasted, insisting he means to help the suffering. A person can be judged harshly and still have a heart that beats for others.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax says he must know where he is at any cost, and Verne shows how a sharp question can drive a person to keep looking.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Nemo shows a habit of planning ahead: he stores sodium and mines his own coal, so the Nautilus never has to rely on the shore.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Ned Land turns a chance find of wild bees into food for the whole group, showing how practical resourcefulness makes the most of what is at hand.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax reasons that what cannot be won by force might be won by persuasion, and weighs carefully when a request could help or hurt his cause.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Conseil reminds the others that Ned is homesick and his restlessness deserves understanding, not just judgment.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Nemo kills only for food and argues that destroying animals for sport is wasteful and wrong.
In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Nemo answers a blocked route by asking whether the way can go under the obstacle instead, a useful habit when the usual path is closed.

In Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea, Aronnax lists his doubts about the plan, then argues for it so hard that Nemo points out he has switched sides, a reminder that a good critic can become a strong ally.

preview.text:
The facts relating to this apparition (entered in various log-books)
agreed in most respects as to the shape of the object or creature in
question, the untiring rapidity of its movements, its surprising power
of locomotion, and the peculiar life with which it seemed endowed. If
it was a cetacean, it surpassed in size all those hitherto classified
in science. Taking into consideration the mean of observations made at
divers times,—rejecting the timid estimate of those who assigned to
this object a length of two hundred feet, equally with the exaggerated
opinions which set it down as a mile in width and three in length,—we
might fairly conclude that this mysterious being surpassed greatly all
dimensions admitted by the ichthyologists of the day, if it existed at
all. And that it _did_ exist was an undeniable fact; and, with that
tendency which disposes the human mind in favour of the marvellous, we
can understand the excitement produced in the entire world by this
supernatural apparition. As to classing it in the list of fables, the
idea was out of the question.

On the 20th of July, 1866, the steamer _Governor Higginson_, of the
Calcutta and Burnach Steam Navigation Company, had met this moving mass
five miles off the east coast of Australia. Captain Baker thought at
first that he was in the presence of an unknown sandbank; he even
prepared to determine its exact position, when two columns of water,
projected by the inexplicable object, shot with a hissing noise a
hundred and fifty feet up into the air. Now, unless the sandbank had
been submitted to the intermittent eruption of a geyser, the _Governor
Higginson_ had to do neither more nor less than with an aquatic mammal,
unknown till then, which threw up from its blow-holes columns of water
mixed with air and vapour.

books.title: Macbeth
books.author: William Shakespeare
books.subject: plays
books.licence_note: Author died 1616. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Macbeth, Shakespeare first shows Macbeth as a brave soldier that the king praises for his courage, so his later fall comes from ambition and choice rather than from lack of worth.
In Macbeth, Banquo tells the strange women that he neither begs nor fears their favours or their hate, and he weighs their prophecies with a cool head.
In Macbeth, Banquo warns that the powers of darkness often tell the truth in small things so that they can lead us into greater harm.
In Macbeth, the hero finds that a secret thought of murder already shakes him, so he sees that temptation is strongest in the imagining, before any deed is done.
In Macbeth, Malcolm says the traitor Cawdor died well, owning his treasons and repenting, which shows that how a person faces the end can outweigh a whole life.
In Macbeth, Lady Macbeth urges her husband to look like the innocent flower but be the serpent beneath, showing how ambition learns to hide behind a friendly face.
In Macbeth, the hero sees that cruel lessons taught to others come back to plague the one who teaches them, so harm returns to its maker.
In Macbeth, the hero realises that the good opinions he has earned are fragile, and that one bad act can undo the reputation it was built on.
In Macbeth, Banquo wants to grow in honour without losing his loyalty or his clear conscience, showing that a person can seek advancement and still keep their integrity.
In Macbeth, guilt takes away the sleep that restores the mind, so the hero hears a voice cry that he will sleep no more.
In Macbeth, the hero argues that no one can stay wise, calm and loyal in a sudden rush of feeling, which shows how strong emotion can outrun reason.
In Macbeth, Ross says ambition is thriftless because it devours the very means of a person's own life, so greed destroys what it needs to survive.
In Macbeth, the hero admits that power means little unless it is kept safe, so his prosperity is always shadowed by fear.
In Macbeth, the king tries to win two desperate men to murder by flattering their pride, showing how a manipulator uses other people's anger and grief against them.
In Macbeth, the hero realises that harming an enemy without ending the threat only leaves the danger alive, so half-finished harm brings no real peace.
In Macbeth, the hero argues that once he has waded deep into wrongdoing, going back is as hard as going on, so one wrong act traps a person into the next.
In Macbeth, Hecate warns that overconfidence is mortals' chiefest enemy, because a person who feels secure stops guarding against danger.
In Macbeth, the hero notes that a passing purpose is only carried out if the deed follows at once, so a wise person acts before a resolve cools.
In Macbeth, Ross observes that fear turns decent people into suspects, as they chase rumours without knowing what they are really afraid of.
In Macbeth, Malcolm says that even when evil wears the face of goodness, goodness must still look like goodness, so true virtue does not need to disguise itself.
In Macbeth, Malcolm falsely confesses vices worse than Macbeth's to test whether Macduff is loyal, showing how a false confession can reveal a friend's true character.
In Macbeth, Ross describes a land so worn down by fear that its people are almost afraid to know themselves, showing how tyranny wears away a whole nation's spirit.
In Macbeth, Malcolm urges a grieving man to give sorrow words, because grief kept silent whispers in the heart until it breaks.
In Macbeth, Lady Macbeth sleepwalks, rubbing her hands and unable to wash the guilt away, showing that a conscience cannot be cleaned by simply tidying up after a wrong.
In Macbeth, Angus says the tyrant's borrowed title hangs loose on him like a giant's robe on a thief, showing that a title taken by wrong never fits well.
In Macbeth, the hero sees that a life built on wrongs lacks the honour, love and friends that should come with age, so the reward for a bad choice arrives as loneliness.
In Macbeth, the hero's despair reduces life to a poor player's brief hour on the stage, showing how someone who has lost their moral footing can feel that nothing means anything.
In Macbeth, the hero realises too late that the prophecies he trusted were tricky half-truths, a warning that words which sound certain can hide a trap.
In Macbeth, Siward hears that his son died bravely and says he would wish his sons no fairer death, showing how a parent can grieve deeply and still honour a worthy end.

preview.text:
MALCOLM.
This is the sergeant
Who, like a good and hardy soldier, fought
’Gainst my captivity.—Hail, brave friend!
Say to the King the knowledge of the broil
As thou didst leave it.

SOLDIER.
Doubtful it stood;
As two spent swimmers that do cling together
And choke their art. The merciless Macdonwald
(Worthy to be a rebel, for to that
The multiplying villainies of nature
Do swarm upon him) from the Western Isles
Of kerns and gallowglasses is supplied;
And Fortune, on his damned quarrel smiling,
Show’d like a rebel’s whore. But all’s too weak;
For brave Macbeth (well he deserves that name),
Disdaining Fortune, with his brandish’d steel,
Which smok’d with bloody execution,
Like Valour’s minion, carv’d out his passage,
Till he fac’d the slave;
Which ne’er shook hands, nor bade farewell to him,
Till he unseam’d him from the nave to the chops,
And fix’d his head upon our battlements.

DUNCAN.
O valiant cousin! worthy gentleman!

SOLDIER.
As whence the sun ’gins his reflection
Shipwracking storms and direful thunders break,
So from that spring, whence comfort seem’d to come
Discomfort swells. Mark, King of Scotland, mark:
No sooner justice had, with valour arm’d,
Compell’d these skipping kerns to trust their heels,
But the Norweyan lord, surveying vantage,
With furbish’d arms and new supplies of men,
Began a fresh assault.

DUNCAN.
Dismay’d not this
Our captains, Macbeth and Banquo?

SOLDIER.
Yes;
As sparrows eagles, or the hare the lion.
If I say sooth, I must report they were
As cannons overcharg’d with double cracks;
So they
Doubly redoubled strokes upon the foe:
Except they meant to bathe in reeking wounds,
Or memorize another Golgotha,
I cannot tell—
But I am faint, my gashes cry for help.

books.title: A Study in Scarlet
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.subject: detective
books.licence_note: Author died 1930. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In A Study in Scarlet, Doyle lets a friend warn that a passion for exact knowledge can be pushed too far, a useful check for anyone who loves their craft enough to lose sight of its limits.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes and Watson list their faults before agreeing to share rooms, so that each knows the worst of the other before they live together.
In A Study in Scarlet, Watson has little to do while his health keeps him in, so he turns his idle hours to the puzzle of his housemate. Curiosity gives a quiet life a purpose.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes compares the mind to a small attic with limited room, so a careful person stocks it only with the tools they need and keeps those tools in good order.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes says that practising on small things, such as a man's cuffs or boots, sharpens observation and teaches a person where to look and what to look for.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes reaches conclusions so quickly they seem like instinct, yet each one rests on steps he could lay out and check. Trained judgement is still reasoning.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes warns that theorising before you have all the evidence biases your judgement, so it is wiser to wait for the facts before deciding what they mean.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes admits that much of his skill is patient, thorough care, and that every small action serves a clear, practical end. Hard problems are solved by diligence.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes says he is only applying careful observation to ordinary life. A small detail, like the length of a stride, can reveal a great deal when someone looks closely.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes spots that a clue left at the scene was a ruse to send the police the wrong way. It pays to ask who gains from a sign that looks too neat.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes scolds a constable who had the key witness in his hands and let him walk off. Noticing something is worth little unless you act on what you saw.

In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes works out his trap by putting himself in the criminal's shoes, asking what a worried man would think and do next. Good thinking often starts with the other person's view.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes laughs off a failed night's work, saying he can afford to because he will get even in the long run. A setback is easier to bear when you keep your sense of humour.

In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes admits he was fooled by a disguise, then draws a useful lesson from it: the man he hunts has friends willing to take risks for him. Being outwitted still teaches you something.

In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes notes that people speak freely in front of ordinary street lads, while an official-looking person shuts mouths. Good sources of information are often the ones nobody watches.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes says that to a great mind nothing is little. A detail that looks trivial, such as the size of a hat, can open up the whole case.
In A Study in Scarlet, Alice Charpentier tells her mother that no good comes of falsehood. The detective agrees that a half-told story does more harm than silence.

In A Study in Scarlet, Lestrade admits his favourite theory was wrong once new facts arrived, then reasons from where a separated man would most likely go. Changing your mind on the evidence is a strength.

In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes is shaken when one fact seems to break his reasoning, then admits he should have trusted the chain more. An apparent contradiction usually has another explanation, so check before you abandon the reasoning.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes says strangeness is not the same as mystery. Odd details give a careful thinker more to work with than a plain case does.
In A Study in Scarlet, Doyle shows a hardened man kneeling to pray beside a frightened child, and suggests it is never too late to return to what you once knew to be right.
In A Study in Scarlet, John Ferrier claims the frightened child as his own because he saved her, showing that real care is built by standing by someone when it counts.
In A Study in Scarlet, Ferrier builds his standing through steady work, improving and tilling his land morning and evening until the effort compounds over years.
In A Study in Scarlet, Doyle shows how a climate of fear silences honest doubt, until people grow so wary of their neighbours that nobody speaks about what matters most to them.
In A Study in Scarlet, Ferrier decides to plan his escape while still reassuring his daughter, showing that a sensible person prepares quietly before the danger arrives.
In A Study in Scarlet, Ferrier finds new heart when a loyal friend arrives to share his danger, showing how the right ally can change how a hard situation feels.
In A Study in Scarlet, Ferrier leaves behind the fields he built, judging his daughter's honour and happiness to be worth more than anything he owns.
In A Study in Scarlet, Hope's grief hardens into one fixed purpose that takes over his whole life, a warning about how loss can narrow a person's world until nothing else fits.
In A Study in Scarlet, Hope sees that wearing himself out would only hand his enemy the win, so he rests and rebuilds his strength instead of burning out.
In A Study in Scarlet, Hope decides he will be judge, jury and executioner once the courts fail him, showing how a fair wish for justice can slide into a crime of its own.
In A Study in Scarlet, Holmes says most people reason forwards from causes, but the more useful skill is reasoning backwards from a result to work out the steps that led to it.

preview.text:
“Very right too.”

“Yes, but it may be pushed to excess. When it comes to beating the
subjects in the dissecting-rooms with a stick, it is certainly taking
rather a bizarre shape.”

“Beating the subjects!”

“Yes, to verify how far bruises may be produced after death. I saw him
at it with my own eyes.”

“And yet you say he is not a medical student?”

“No. Heaven knows what the objects of his studies are. But here we are,
and you must form your own impressions about him.” As he spoke, we
turned down a narrow lane and passed through a small side-door, which
opened into a wing of the great hospital. It was familiar ground to me,
and I needed no guiding as we ascended the bleak stone staircase and
made our way down the long corridor with its vista of whitewashed wall
and dun-coloured doors. Near the further end a low arched passage
branched away from it and led to the chemical laboratory.

This was a lofty chamber, lined and littered with countless bottles.
Broad, low tables were scattered about, which bristled with retorts,
test-tubes, and little Bunsen lamps, with their blue flickering flames.
There was only one student in the room, who was bending over a distant
table absorbed in his work. At the sound of our steps he glanced round
and sprang to his feet with a cry of pleasure. “I’ve found it! I’ve
found it,” he shouted to my companion, running towards us with a
test-tube in his hand. “I have found a re-agent which is precipitated
by hæmoglobin, and by nothing else.” Had he discovered a gold mine,
greater delight could not have shone upon his features.

“Dr. Watson, Mr. Sherlock Holmes,” said Stamford, introducing us.

books.title: The Arabian Nights Entertainments
books.author: Andrew Lang (editor)
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Editor died 1912. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Andrew Lang notes that old stories outlive their tellers, passed from grandmothers to children in every country and changed only in small customs.
In The Arabian Nights, the tales are framed as a wife telling stories to a cruel Sultan, so the storyteller's craft becomes a way of staying alive.
In The Arabian Nights, the Sultan's grief at one betrayal hardens into a rule that punishes innocent people, and a whole town pays for it.
In The Arabian Nights, Scheherazade chooses a deadly risk on purpose, with a plan, to end a cruelty that everyone else has simply accepted.
In The Arabian Nights, Scheherazade brings her sister into her plan before she acts, turning a private fear into a shared task with someone she trusts.
In The Arabian Nights, a merchant asks for a year to settle his affairs and gives his word to return, and the genius trusts that word.
Before facing his fate, the merchant in The Arabian Nights pays his debts and provides for his family, so he leaves his affairs in order.
In The Arabian Nights, an old man's pity for an animal's tears leads him to refuse a cruel order, and his wife's scorn cannot change his mind.
In The Arabian Nights, a merchant who has recovered his fortune shares half of it with his ruined brother and tells him to forget his losses.
In The Arabian Nights, a merchant shares his savings with brothers who squandered their own, and does not reproach them, a generosity that outlasts their folly.
In The Arabian Nights, the merchant is spared because three storytellers take the trouble to speak up for him, which shows how much a kind word can do.
In The Arabian Nights, the fisherman outwits a boastful genius by asking him to prove his claim, showing that a calm question can turn a threat around.
In The Arabian Nights, a husband kills his parrot for lying, then finds it told the truth, a reminder not to act in haste on a doubtful word.
In The Arabian Nights, a jealous vizir dresses up his envy as concern for the king, and the weak king listens. Good advisers are worth testing.
In The Arabian Nights, a cruel king who has an innocent man killed is undone by his own greed for a trick, and the dying man's last words name the lesson: cruelty comes back on the cruel.
In The Arabian Nights, the Sultan goes alone to solve a mystery himself rather than sending others, and his court waits in the tent, a picture of a leader who checks the facts first-hand.
In The Arabian Nights, the Sultan is moved by a stranger's suffering and sets out to put it right, so his power is shown to be used well.
In The Arabian Nights, a house warns over its door that whoever meddles in other people's affairs will hear truths they do not like, a rule any host or team could still use.
In The Arabian Nights, the porter tells a rude guest that not everyone has to live the same way, a plain reminder that other people's choices are not ours to judge.
In The Arabian Nights, the porter begs not to be punished for other people's faults, a plea for fairness that even the angry hostess finds hard to refuse.
In The Arabian Nights, a prince breaks a secret oath because keeping it would cost his uncle his son, showing that some promises must give way to a greater duty.
In The Arabian Nights, a prince who has lost everything takes up honest work cutting wood, so he can provide for himself until better times come.
In The Arabian Nights, a prince refuses to kill an innocent stranger even with his own life at stake, saying he would not deserve to live if he were that kind of coward.
In The Arabian Nights, an envious man plots to ruin the neighbour he resents, and his plan fails, showing how envy wastes the person who carries it.
In The Arabian Nights, a dervish who was once nearly killed by an envious neighbour answers him with honour and reward rather than revenge, a picture of forgiveness that goes beyond mere pardon.
In The Arabian Nights, the Sultan judges writing by its quality and sets aside the reputations of the famous writers, a fair way to weigh any work.
In The Arabian Nights, the clever princess says there are many out-of-the-way things it is good to know, but one should never boast of them. Skill is quieter when it is not shown off.
In The Arabian Nights, the freed prince says he would rather have stayed a monkey than see the princess who saved him die, showing loyalty that counts for more than his own comfort.
In The Arabian Nights, Agib forgets the warning he was given the moment relief sweeps over him, and the warning is what undoes him. Relief is when we are most likely to slip.
In The Arabian Nights, Agib gives up his plan to harm the frightened youth and offers him friendship instead, turning a feared enemy into a companion.
In The Arabian Nights, ten young men blame their own idleness for their ruin, showing how a person can look honestly at the cost of a wasted life.
In The Arabian Nights, Agib talks himself into opening a forbidden door by telling himself that looking is not really entering. The story shows how curiosity can argue down a clear conscience.
In The Arabian Nights, the rich Sindbad tells the envious porter that his wealth came from years of toil and danger, which no one sees from the street where the envy starts.
In The Arabian Nights, Sindbad admits he squandered his inheritance on pleasure, and that money managed badly flies away, so he turned to honest work at sea.
In The Arabian Nights, the captain who kept a lost man's goods refuses any reward for his honesty, a plain picture of integrity that asks nothing back.
In The Arabian Nights, Sindbad grows restless with an idle life, sails again, and is stranded, regretting that he did not stay content. Restlessness can cost us the safety we had.
In Sindbad's second voyage, the narrator shares his diamonds with the men who had been cheated of their trade, and they warm to him. Generosity can turn rivals into friends.
In Sindbad's second voyage, a merchant takes only one stone from the great heap, saying that one is enough to end his toil. The story is a lesson in knowing when you have enough.
In Sindbad's third voyage, the stranded sailors turn despair into action: Sindbad lays out a plan to escape and a fallback with rafts if it fails. A backup plan steadies people when all seems lost.
In Sindbad's third voyage, a stranded man who wants to live builds a shelter piece by piece through the day, and it holds through the night. Steady effort is what gets people through.
In The Arabian Nights, Sindbad's companions eat the food of their captors until they lose their wits, while Sindbad tastes only a little and stays clear-headed. Restraint keeps a person safe.
In The Arabian Nights, Sindbad earns respect in a strange land by noticing a real need and making something useful for it, here a saddle for the king's riders.
In The Arabian Nights, Sindbad speaks up against a cruel custom that is not his own, and the king's easy acceptance of it shows how habit can hide cruelty from those who live by it.
In The Arabian Nights, Sindbad is saved in a dark pit by a small animal that shows him a way out he could never have found alone, so help can come from unexpected places.
In The Arabian Nights, Sindbad admits that being alone in a strange land makes him wish he had stayed home, and that morning restores his courage. Fear often feels larger in the dark.
In the Sindbad story, a clinging old tyrant is beaten not by force but by a simple trick that turns his own greed against him. Cleverness can outlast strength.
In the Sindbad story, the captain shares out the last of the food equally before anything else. When supplies run short, a fair split keeps a group together.

In The Arabian Nights, Sindbad, with little left and no way forward, notices a river running underground and reasons that trying costs him nothing he does not already lose. Hope often starts with a careful look at what is left.
In The Arabian Nights, the Caliph judges the king of Serendib to be wise from his letter alone, reasoning that a good ruler and a worthy people reflect one another.
In The Arabian Nights, the master who has profited from Sindbad's work sets him free and rewards him. Fair dealing is often paid back, even by people who once held power over you.
In The Arabian Nights, Sindbad bears a long, dull caravan journey with patience, reflecting on the dangers he has already escaped. Gratitude makes a tedious stretch easier to carry.
In The Little Hunchback, one accident leads to a chain of lies and cover-ups, each worse than the last. A single concealment can drag innocent people into trouble.

In The Little Hunchback, the purveyor steps forward in public to confess, even though it costs him, because he cannot bear for an innocent man to die for his fault. Owning up to a wrong can stop an injustice.

In the story of Alnaschar, a glassware seller plans his whole fortune in his head before he has sold a single bottle. Dreaming ahead is not the same as doing the work, and the plan has no foundations.
In the Alnaschar story, pride makes a man careless, and only the wreck of his basket brings him back to his senses. Vanity can cost more than the thing it was meant to gain.
In the Alnaschar story, a man is so eager to believe in an easy fortune that he follows a stranger into a trap. A promise that seems too good to be true usually deserves a second look.

In the Barmecide's feast, a hungry beggar plays along with an imaginary banquet, and his host rewards his good humour with a real welcome. Going along gracefully with someone's game can earn lasting goodwill.
In the Barber's tale, a man who looks closely at the evidence before accepting a verdict reveals the truth. Careful examination can overturn a hasty judgment.

In the Camaralzaman tale, a wise vizir advises that a young heir learn to rule by sharing in counsel first, rather than being handed power all at once. Responsibility grows when it is given step by step.
In the Camaralzaman tale, the vizir reminds the king that much is gained by patience, and that harsh force is often regretted. Waiting can get a better result than pushing harder.

preview.text:
The stories in the Fairy Books have generally been such as old women in
country places tell to their grandchildren.  Nobody knows how old they
are, or who told them first.  The children of Ham, Shem and Japhet may
have listened to them in the Ark, on wet days.  Hector's little boy may
have heard them in Troy Town, for it is certain that Homer knew them,
and that some of them were written down in Egypt about the time of
Moses.

People in different countries tell them differently, but they are
always the same stories, really, whether among little Zulus, at the
Cape, or little Eskimo, near the North Pole.  The changes are only in
matters of manners and customs; such as wearing clothes or not, meeting
lions who talk in the warm countries, or talking bears in the cold
countries.  There are plenty of kings and queens in the fairy tales,
just because long ago there were plenty of kings in the country.  A
gentleman who would be a squire now was a kind of king in Scotland in
very old times, and the same in other places.  These old stories, never
forgotten, were taken down in writing in different ages, but mostly in
this century, in all sorts of languages.  These ancient stories are the
contents of the Fairy books.

books.title: The Republic
books.author: Plato
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died about 348 BCE, translator died 1893. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Plato's Republic tries to connect everyday life with deep speculation, linking politics with philosophy in a way few other books of his do.
Plato holds that justice is hard to see in one person, so he searches for it first in the larger picture of an ideal city.
In The Republic, Plato treats justice and the ideal state as two faces of one truth: justice is the order of the state, and the state is its visible form.
Plato's ideal city is best read as a vision. Whether it could ever be built has nothing to do with whether its ideas are true.
Plato's Cephalus is an old man at peace with a well-spent life, and he admits that wealth helps a person stay clear of dishonesty.
Plato's Polemarchus lives by rules of thumb rather than principles, and is left bewildered once Socrates starts to test them.
Plato's Thrasymachus shows how bluster and insolence can cover confusion, and how someone who cannot defend a claim often falls silent.
Plato shows morality as a climb: from inherited rules of thumb, to clever generalising, to young thinkers who want to understand the nature of things more deeply.
In the Republic, Plato turns simple examples into allegory, such as the cave, so that an idea already argued in the abstract can be seen in concrete form.
Plato's Socrates meets people in error with patience rather than anger, treating them with pity or a wry kind of affection.
Plato's Socrates tests a simple rule, to tell the truth and pay your debts, by asking whether it has exceptions, such as returning a borrowed sword to a madman.
Plato's Socrates tests the rule of helping friends and harming enemies until it breaks, which shows why careful definitions matter.
Plato's Socrates argues that returning evil for evil only makes people more evil, so a just person should not do it.
Plato's Thrasymachus says justice is the interest of the stronger, then escapes a quick defeat by quietly changing interest to what the ruler thinks is his interest.
Plato's Socrates argues that every craft serves the good of those it works on rather than the private gain of the craftsman, and that justice is best judged the same way.
Plato suggests most rulers take office for reward or out of fear of being ruled by someone worse, not for love of the work itself.
Plato's Socrates compares justice to skill: the skilled work to a standard and do not seek more than is right, while the unskilled make random excess.
Plato's Socrates argues that a house divided against itself cannot stand, so even wrongdoers need a remnant of good to act together.
Plato's Glaucon asks whether justice is valued for itself or only for its rewards, a question that still separates integrity from reputation.
In The Republic, Glaucon imagines a ring of invisibility to test whether a person would stay just if no one could ever see them.
Plato's Glaucon says a truly just person may be mistaken for the worst, so the real test is whether we value being just over seeming just.
Plato's Adeimantus points out that people are often taught to be good for rewards and reputation, which leaves virtue resting on the wrong foundation.
Plato's Adeimantus warns that people who sell quick fixes for wrongdoing can win over whole cities, so easy promises deserve a second look.
Plato's Adeimantus says people taught early that justice lives in the soul would guard themselves, rather than need outside guardians to keep them honest.
In The Republic, a little experience may make a person cynical, but more experience tends to bring them back to a kinder view of the mixed nature of people.
In The Republic, the ideal of justice always looks like a paradox beside ordinary life, yet it still serves as a basis for education and an ennobling influence.
In The Republic, Socrates holds that a person should do their duty first, without asking whether it will bring happiness, since happiness tends to follow as an accident.
In The Republic, goodness is shaped more by education from within than by laws imposed from without, because a good person and a good citizen only fully match in a well-ordered city.
Plato's Socrates shows a city growing from simple wants, with people dividing labour because one person does one thing better than many.
Plato's Socrates shows how luxury multiplies wants, and how those wants can push a city to take its neighbours' land and go to war.
In The Republic, Plato treats a falsehood believed inside the soul as worse than a lie told to others, because the person deceived cannot easily free themselves.
Plato warns that the mask an actor wears can become his face, so what we keep pretending to be can slowly shape what we become.
Plato compares learning virtue to learning to read: first the letters, then the words, and only later the patterns in real life.
Plato argues that too much of one thing hardens the spirit and too much of another softens it, so the aim is balance between reason and passion.
Plato says people trusted with power must be tested again and again over time, since pleasure, pressure and persuasion can each lead a person off course.
Plato warns that luxury and greed can turn protectors into wolves, so people who guard others should not be tempted to profit from their office.
Plato's rule that style should suit the subject still helps today. A writer is often the worst judge of whether others can follow their meaning.
The Republic proposes that a person's place should rest on their qualities rather than the family they were born into, a bold idea for Plato's age.
Plato treats reason and desire as a higher and a lower part of us that often pull apart, and the work of a good life is to bring them into harmony.
Plato's Socrates argues that a well-ordered city should be judged as a whole, not by whether each part is as comfortable as it could be.
Plato holds that education is the great matter, since small changes in what people learn at play can spread over time into customs, trade and laws.
Plato suggests that what people call expediency is really right limited by the conditions of human society, so ideals still matter even when they cannot be enforced.
Plato's Socrates defines wisdom as the skill of advising about the interests of the whole, not the skill of any single trade.
Plato says courage is steady belief about what to fear, laid down by good upbringing, so that the pressures of pleasure or pain cannot wash it out.
Plato points out that being master of yourself sounds absurd, since the master is also the servant, and means the better part of a person ruling the worse.
Plato's Socrates finds justice in each person doing their own work, since trouble starts when someone leaves their trade to meddle in what is not theirs.
Plato's story of Leontius, who wanted to look at corpses and was disgusted by them, suggests a third force in us, spirit, that can side with reason against desire.
Plato says good actions form good habits in the soul, so virtue is the health of the soul and vice is its disease.
Plato holds that injustice is like a mortal disease that makes life not worth having, so asking whether wrongdoing pays is a ridiculous question.
Plato describes spirit as the lion heart with which reason makes a treaty, the source of courage to endure pain and face hard thinking.
In The Republic, Socrates says that whoever kills the truth is a murderer, so he insists on speaking honestly even when his friends would rather he did not.
Plato's Socrates observes that much of custom is simply habit, so what once seemed shocking and later became ordinary is not always worth laughing at.
Plato argues that a difference in one respect does not settle what a person may do, just as a bald man may still be a cobbler and a hairy one may not.
Plato says a quarrel between people of one family should aim at reconciliation rather than ruin, since fighting among kin is unnatural.
Plato argues that an ideal is not worse for being impractical, just as a picture of a perfectly beautiful man is not diminished because no such man has lived.
Plato holds that opinion is shaky ground, because things look different from different points of view, while knowledge rests on what is steady and true.
Plato has Adeimantus argue that people who devote their lives to philosophy usually end up rogues if bad and fools if good, so a fine ideal can be hard to trust in practice.
In Plato's parable of the ship, a skilled pilot is ignored by a crew who think navigation cannot be learned, so the fault lies with those who refuse expert help.
Plato argues that the strongest natures need the right soil, and that public opinion shapes young people more than any single teacher does.
Plato criticises a patchy education, where someone dabbles in learning in youth and never masters its hardest part, and urges steady training from the start.

preview.text:
The Republic of Plato is the longest of his works with the exception of
the Laws, and is certainly the greatest of them. There are nearer
approaches to modern metaphysics in the Philebus and in the Sophist;
the Politicus or Statesman is more ideal; the form and institutions of
the State are more clearly drawn out in the Laws; as works of art, the
Symposium and the Protagoras are of higher excellence. But no other
Dialogue of Plato has the same largeness of view and the same
perfection of style; no other shows an equal knowledge of the world, or
contains more of those thoughts which are new as well as old, and not
of one age only but of all. Nowhere in Plato is there a deeper irony or
a greater wealth of humour or imagery, or more dramatic power. Nor in
any other of his writings is the attempt made to interweave life and
speculation, or to connect politics with philosophy. The Republic is
the centre around which the other Dialogues may be grouped; here
philosophy reaches the highest point (cp, especially in Books V, VI,
VII) to which ancient thinkers ever attained. Plato among the Greeks,
like Bacon among the moderns, was the first who conceived a method of
knowledge, although neither of them always distinguished the bare
outline or form from the substance of truth; and both of them had to be
content with an abstraction of science which was not yet realized. He
was the greatest metaphysical genius whom the world has seen; and in
him, more than in any other ancient thinker, the germs of future
knowledge are contained. The sciences of logic and psychology, which
have supplied so many instruments of thought to after-ages, are based
upon the analyses of Socrates and Plato. The principles of definition,
the law of contradiction, the fallacy of arguing in a circle, the
distinction between the essence and accidents of a thing or notion,
between means and ends, between causes and conditions; also the
division of the mind into the rational, concupiscent, and irascible
elements, or of pleasures and desires into necessary and
unnecessary—these and other great forms of thought are all of them to
be found in the Republic, and were probably first invented by Plato.
The greatest of all logical truths, and the one of which writers on
philosophy are most apt to lose sight, the difference between words and
things, has been most strenuously insisted on by him (cp. Rep.; Polit.;
Cratyl. 435, 436 ff), although he has not always avoided the confusion
of them in his own writings (e.g. Rep.). But he does not bind up truth
in logical formulae,—logic is still veiled in metaphysics; and the
science which he imagines to ‘contemplate all truth and all existence’
is very unlike the doctrine of the syllogism which Aristotle claims to
have discovered (Soph. Elenchi, 33. 18).

books.title: A Christmas Carol
books.author: Charles Dickens
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1870. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In A Christmas Carol, Dickens shows how a man who shuts out every warm connection grows so cold that even strangers and dogs keep their distance from him.
In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge's nephew answers his uncle's sneers with good humour rather than anger, and the warmth holds its ground.
In A Christmas Carol, the nephew argues that kindness is worth keeping even when it brings no money, because it lets people open their shut-up hearts to others.
In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge's nephew keeps offering friendship without anger, showing that steady kindness can outlast a long refusal.
In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge hands the poor off to prisons and workhouses and says it is not his business, a way of passing on responsibility that Dickens exposes as cold.
In A Christmas Carol, Dickens shows Scrooge docking a day's pay for a holiday and calling it fair, showing how a hard employer can persuade himself his stinginess is principle.
In A Christmas Carol, Dickens describes Scrooge's gloomy rooms as a place that has forgotten the way out, showing how a life closed to others becomes its own dark prison.
In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge spends the day refusing to think of his dead partner, yet the thought returns in the knocker, showing that avoided worries do not stay buried.
In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge keeps calling the ghost humbug even as it passes through his door, showing how a mind will cling to denial long after the senses have given way.
In A Christmas Carol, Dickens makes Marley's chain out of the cash-boxes, ledgers and purses he hoarded in life, showing that the things we grasp for ourselves can become the chains we drag.
In A Christmas Carol, Marley's ghost says the spirit within a person must go out among others in life, or it is doomed to wander after death, seeing what it could have shared.
In A Christmas Carol, Marley's ghost says his real business was mankind and the common welfare, and his trade was only a drop of water in that ocean. Dickens offers this as a test for any owner.
In A Christmas Carol, Dickens shows phantoms who want to help people but have lost the power to act, suggesting that good intentions left unpractised become a hollow regret.
In A Christmas Carol, Dickens notes that the more Scrooge tries not to think about the ghost, the more he thinks, showing how pushing away an unsettling question only keeps it turning.
In A Christmas Carol, the Ghost of Christmas Past tells Scrooge he needs reclamation and must take heed. Dickens treats honest looking at one's own past as the first step towards change.
In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge recognises every gate and tree on the road of his boyhood, showing that the people we once were are still close, even after we have forgotten the way back to them.
In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge is moved to tears by a neglected child left alone at school, showing how a hard heart can still be opened by seeing a lonely child.
In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge weeps at the sight of his lonely boyhood self, showing that the softest pity often starts with seeing our own forgotten self clearly.
In A Christmas Carol, Scrooge regrets that he did not give the carol singer something. The Ghost lets him see it, showing that regret for a small unkindness can be the start of a better habit.
In A Christmas Carol, the Ghost calls Fan, though delicate, a woman with a large heart, showing Dickens' view that a person is measured by love rather than by strength.
In A Christmas Carol, old Fezziwig ends work early on Christmas Eve so his staff can celebrate. Dickens uses him to show that a good employer's generosity earns loyalty.

Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grind-stone,
Scrooge! a squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping,
clutching, covetous, old sinner! Hard and sharp as flint,
from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire;
secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster. The
cold within him froze his old features, nipped his pointed
nose, shrivelled his cheek, stiffened his gait; made his
eyes red, his thin lips blue; and spoke out shrewdly in his
grating voice. A frosty rime was on his head, and on his
eyebrows, and his wiry chin. He carried his own low
temperature always about with him; he iced his office in
the dog-days; and didn't thaw it one degree at Christmas.

External heat and cold had little influence on
Scrooge. No warmth could warm, no wintry weather
chill him. No wind that blew was bitterer than he,
no falling snow was more intent upon its purpose, no
pelting rain less open to entreaty. Foul weather didn't
know where to have him. The heaviest rain, and
snow, and hail, and sleet, could boast of the advantage
over him in only one respect. They often "came down"
handsomely, and Scrooge never did.

Nobody ever stopped him in the street to say, with
gladsome looks, "My dear Scrooge, how are you?
When will you come to see me?" No beggars implored
him to bestow a trifle, no children asked him
what it was o'clock, no man or woman ever once in all
his life inquired the way to such and such a place, of
Scrooge. Even the blind men's dogs appeared to
know him; and when they saw him coming on, would
tug their owners into doorways and up courts; and
then would wag their tails as though they said, "No
eye at all is better than an evil eye, dark master!"

He was recommended by the Barings, with whom he had an open credit. His
cheques were regularly paid at sight from his account current, which
was always flush.

Was Phileas Fogg rich? Undoubtedly. But those who knew him best could
not imagine how he had made his fortune, and Mr. Fogg was the last
person to whom to apply for the information. He was not lavish, nor, on
the contrary, avaricious; for, whenever he knew that money was needed
for a noble, useful, or benevolent purpose, he supplied it quietly and
sometimes anonymously. He was, in short, the least communicative of
men. He talked very little, and seemed all the more mysterious for his
taciturn manner. His daily habits were quite open to observation; but
whatever he did was so exactly the same thing that he had always done
before, that the wits of the curious were fairly puzzled.

Had he travelled? It was likely, for no one seemed to know the world
more familiarly; there was no spot so secluded that he did not appear
to have an intimate acquaintance with it. He often corrected, with a
few clear words, the thousand conjectures advanced by members of the
club as to lost and unheard-of travellers, pointing out the true
probabilities, and seeming as if gifted with a sort of second sight, so
often did events justify his predictions. He must have travelled
everywhere, at least in the spirit.

In The Sign of the Four, Holmes warns that personal charm or dislike can bias judgement, since the most winning person may be guilty and the most repellent may be kind.

“The only unofficial consulting detective,” he answered. “I am the last
and highest court of appeal in detection. When Gregson or Lestrade or
Athelney Jones are out of their depths—which, by the way, is their
normal state—the matter is laid before me. I examine the data, as an
expert, and pronounce a specialist’s opinion. I claim no credit in such
cases. My name figures in no newspaper. The work itself, the pleasure
of finding a field for my peculiar powers, is my highest reward. But
you have yourself had some experience of my methods of work in the
Jefferson Hope case.”

“Yes, indeed,” said I, cordially. “I was never so struck by anything in
my life. I even embodied it in a small brochure with the somewhat
fantastic title of ‘A Study in Scarlet.’”

He shook his head sadly. “I glanced over it,” said he. “Honestly, I
cannot congratulate you upon it. Detection is, or ought to be, an exact
science, and should be treated in the same cold and unemotional manner.
You have attempted to tinge it with romanticism, which produces much
the same effect as if you worked a love-story or an elopement into the
fifth proposition of Euclid.”

“But the romance was there,” I remonstrated. “I could not tamper with
the facts.”

“Some facts should be suppressed, or at least a just sense of
proportion should be observed in treating them. The only point in the
case which deserved mention was the curious analytical reasoning from
effects to causes by which I succeeded in unraveling it.”

In The Cat That Walked by Himself, the Woman wins a wild dog over with a good meal and fair work in return, a generous way of building loyalty that still holds today.
In The Cat That Walked by Himself, the Cat refuses to be anyone's friend or servant, and his stubborn pride is what leaves him waiting outside the warm cave.
In The Cat That Walked by Himself, the Cat wins his place by patiently playing with a crying baby, a kind act of care that does more than any clever bargain.

In The Butterfly That Stamped, Solomon realises that power used out of pride would have shamed him, and that the same power used for a small kindness and a joke does good.
