So the Whale swam and swam and swam, with both flippers and his tail,
as hard as he could for the hiccoughs; and at last he saw the Mariner’s
natal-shore and the white-cliffs-of-Albion, and he rushed half-way
up the beach, and opened his mouth wide and wide and wide, and said,
‘Change here for Winchester, Ashuelot, Nashua, Keene, and stations on
the _Fitch_burg Road;’ and just as he said ‘Fitch’ the Mariner walked
out of his mouth. But while the Whale had been swimming, the Mariner,
who was indeed a person of infinite-resource-and-sagacity, had taken his
jack-knife and cut up the raft into a little square grating all running
criss-cross, and he had tied it firm with his suspenders (_now_, you
know why you were not to forget the suspenders!), and he dragged that
grating good and tight into the Whale’s throat, and there it stuck! Then
he recited the following _Sloka_, which, as you have not heard it, I
will now proceed to relate--

By means of a grating
  I have stopped your ating.

For the Mariner he was also an Hi-ber-ni-an. And he stepped out on the
shingle, and went home to his mother, who had given him leave to trail
his toes in the water; and he married and lived happily ever afterward.
So did the Whale. But from that day on, the grating in his throat,
which he could neither cough up nor swallow down, prevented him eating
anything except very, very small fish; and that is the reason why whales
nowadays never eat men or boys or little girls.

The small ‘Stute Fish went and hid himself in the mud under the
Door-sills of the Equator. He was afraid that the Whale might be angry
with him.

books.title: Apology
books.author: Plato
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died about 348 BCE, translator died 1893. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Plato shows Socrates naming public opinion as his oldest accuser, a reputation built from years of talk that no formal charge can fully answer.
Plato's Apology has Socrates test a claim of wisdom by questioning politicians, poets and craftsmen, and finds that people who think they know everything are the ones who learn least.

Plato's Apology has Socrates reason that since he cannot know whether death is good, he will not abandon the post he believes he was given, because leaving a duty he knows to be right is the real harm.
Plato's Apology shows Socrates, once condemned, refusing to beg for his life or offer a bargaining penalty, preferring to die on his own terms than to live on his accusers' terms.
Plato's Apology has Socrates keep his usual manner in court, refusing to say anything that might bend the course of justice, even though a more agreeable defence might have won him acquittal.
Plato's Apology has Socrates admit he does not know what lies beyond death, and refuse to dress that ignorance up in confident myth.
Plato's Apology has Socrates say that if eloquence means the force of truth, then he is eloquent, so he speaks plainly in his own words and trusts the truth to do the work.
Plato's Apology has Socrates notice that skilled craftsmen were often sure they knew everything, and that excellence in one trade made them overconfident about matters outside it.
Plato's Apology observes that people exposed as not knowing what they claim often blame the questioner rather than themselves, and repeat stock charges against him.
Plato's Apology has Socrates test an accuser with plain follow-up questions, asking who improves the young, and when the answer is that everyone does, the claim falls apart.
Plato's Apology argues that no sensible person would deliberately corrupt the people they live among, since they would be the first to suffer for it.
Plato's Apology argues that a good person should weigh whether an action is right or wrong, not calculate their chances of living or dying.
Plato's Apology has Socrates say that virtue does not come from money, but that from good character comes money and every other good thing.
Plato's Apology has Socrates say that a bad person cannot really harm someone better than themselves, and that the greater harm falls on the one who does the wrong.
Plato's Apology has Socrates liken himself to a gadfly stinging a large, sluggish horse, a reminder that a useful critic is often unwelcome but still needed.
Plato's Apology recounts Socrates refusing to join an unlawful trial, and refusing to help arrest an innocent man, even when powerful people threatened him for it.
Plato's Apology has Socrates say that a life never examined is not worth living, and that daily talk about virtue and self-examination is the greatest good a person can have.
Plato's Apology has Socrates say the hard task is not avoiding death but avoiding wrongdoing, because wrongdoing runs faster than death.
Plato's Apology has Socrates say the easiest and noblest way to deal with criticism is not to silence the critics but to improve yourself.
Plato's Apology has Socrates read the silence of his inner sign as proof he was not doing wrong, so he trusts his own conscience as the guide to his choices.
Plato's Apology has Socrates forgive his judges, saying they did him no real harm even though they never meant him any good, and that he would rather gently blame them than hate them.

preview.text:
The first part commences with an apology for his colloquial style; he
is, as he has always been, the enemy of rhetoric, and knows of no
rhetoric but truth; he will not falsify his character by making a
speech. Then he proceeds to divide his accusers into two classes;
first, there is the nameless accuser—public opinion. All the world from
their earliest years had heard that he was a corrupter of youth, and
had seen him caricatured in the “Clouds” of Aristophanes. Secondly,
there are the professed accusers, who are but the mouth-piece of the
others. The accusations of both might be summed up in a formula. The
first say, “Socrates is an evil-doer and a curious person, searching
into things under the earth and above the heaven; and making the worse
appear the better cause, and teaching all this to others.” The second,
“Socrates is an evil-doer and corrupter of the youth, who does not
receive the gods whom the state receives, but introduces other new
divinities.” These last words appear to have been the actual indictment
(compare Xen. Mem.); and the previous formula, which is a summary of
public opinion, assumes the same legal style.

books.title: Great Expectations
books.author: Charles Dickens
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1870. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Great Expectations, Pip builds a whole picture of his unseen parents from their gravestones. It reminds us how readily we fill gaps in what we know with guesses that feel like facts.
In Great Expectations, a terrified Pip still asks, politely and sensibly, to be kept upright so he can think and attend better. Fear makes thinking harder, and small calm requests can help.
In Great Expectations, Joe Gargery is gentle and good-natured, strong in body but soft in manner. Quiet decency often counts for more than force.
In Great Expectations, Pip's guilt over one small secret wears him down long before anyone finds out. Dickens shows how a hidden wrong weighs on a person from day to day.
In Great Expectations, Pip reflects that terror can push a frightened child into promises and deeds it would never choose in calm. Fear bends people away from their own nature.
In Great Expectations, Pip answers a hungry, frightened man with plain kindness, and his simple courtesy matters to someone treated as less than human.
In Great Expectations, Dickens notes that a virtue can be applied so harshly it makes everyone miserable. Some people keep the rules of cleanliness or religion in a way that defeats their purpose.
In Great Expectations, the Christmas guests use a child's faults as a platform for their own moral lectures. Dickens shows how self-righteous company can make a child feel small.

In Great Expectations, the villagers enjoy the hunt for two fugitives as entertainment, while Pip feels pity for the hunted. Dickens shows how easily a crowd's pleasure rests on someone else's misfortune.
In Great Expectations, Joe forgives the thief who ate the stolen pie and says no one should be starved for it. His mercy comes without any show of virtue, and it is more moving for that.
In Great Expectations, Pip admits he stayed silent about his wrong because he feared losing Joe's good opinion. Dickens shows how cowardice can pass itself off as prudence.

In Great Expectations, Joe tells Pip there is room for him at the forge, a welcome given freely and without conditions. Dickens shows that a plain, open welcome can mean more to a lonely child than any gift.

In Great Expectations, Joe says he would rather risk being a little inconvenienced himself than fail the people who carry the heaviest load. Dickens shows a quiet kind of moral courage in choosing to err on the side of care.
In Great Expectations, the house once named Satis, or Enough, was meant to show that its owner could want nothing else. The name hints that knowing when you have enough is a kind of wealth.
In Great Expectations, Pip starts to feel ashamed of his hands after Estella scorns them. Dickens shows how easily we catch the contempt of others and begin to believe it about ourselves.

In Great Expectations, Pip observes that children feel injustice keenly, even small injustice, because their world is so small. Dickens reminds adults that a child's hurt is never trivial to the child.
In Great Expectations, Pip admits his silence came from fearing he would not be understood. Dickens suggests that much of people's reticence rests on exactly that dread.
In Great Expectations, Pip confesses his invented tale to Joe, the person whose good opinion he most wants. Dickens shows that honesty is hardest, and most needed, with those we love.
In Great Expectations, Joe tells Pip that even a king had to begin with the alphabet, and that you cannot become uncommon by going crooked. Every mastery starts with plain, honest first steps.
In Great Expectations, Pip sees a room of people who all pretend not to notice that they are flattering one another. Dickens shows how a shared pretence can keep a whole company polite and false.
In Great Expectations, Cousin Raymond asks whether a man who is not his own neighbour can be anyone's. Dickens shows how easily people preach kindness to others and forget to extend it to themselves.
In Great Expectations, Miss Havisham stops every clock at the hour of her wound and refuses to let anyone speak of it. Dickens shows how refusing to let time move on can turn grief into a prison.

In Great Expectations, Pip respects the pale young gentleman who keeps getting up after every fall. Dickens shows that courage is most plain in someone who loses again and again and still will not stay down.

In Great Expectations, Pip confides in Biddy, the humble friend who is honest with him, rather than the grand people who flatter or use him. Dickens suggests the steadiest friends are often the least grand.

In Great Expectations, Joe is awkward and ashamed in fine company, yet he is honest and dignified where it counts. Dickens shows that a plain, decent man can hold more dignity than the grand people looking down on him.
In Great Expectations, Pip finds it miserable to feel ashamed of the home and people who raised him. Dickens shows how shame about where we come from can poison our own gratitude.

In Great Expectations, Pip admits that his good conduct came from the steady example of Joe rather than from his own restless ambition. Dickens honours the faithful, contented man whose influence reaches further than he knows.

In Great Expectations, Pip notices that his sister deliberately works herself up into rage, and says passion is no excuse when it is cultivated on purpose. Anger that is chosen and fed is a habit we can refuse.
In Great Expectations, Pip observes that feelings which look serious in a man can seem comical in a boy, though they are just as real. Dickens asks the reader to take young hearts seriously.

In Great Expectations, Pip keeps an old secret for years until it grows into part of himself and is hard to tear away. He keeps postponing the confession, reopening the question each morning and settling it in the negative.
In Great Expectations, the police fit the facts to the ideas they already hold, instead of letting the facts shape the ideas. Testing your own theories against the evidence avoids the same trap.
In Great Expectations, Biddy solves a puzzle that Pip could not by asking who the clue points to, not just what the object is. Looking at the people involved can unlock what the facts alone will not.

In Great Expectations, Pip feels that the stopped clocks have stopped time in Miss Havisham's house, while the world outside keeps growing older. Refusing to let time move on leaves a person stuck and out of step with life.
In Great Expectations, Pip realises he has not thanked Biddy, who taught him first and asked for nothing back. Thank the people who helped you early on while you still can.
In Great Expectations, Biddy hears Pip call himself coarse and common and asks who said it. Before you accept a harsh judgement about yourself, ask where it came from and whether it is actually true.

In Great Expectations, Biddy asks Pip whether he wants to become a gentleman to spite Estella or to win her over. The reason behind a goal matters, so ask what is really driving it before you chase it.
In Great Expectations, Pip admits that Estella would make him miserable, while the steady and kind Biddy would not. The person who thrills us is not always the one who is good for us.

In Great Expectations, Pip finds that one stray hope can scatter his good sense again, undoing a clear plan to settle into honest work. Notice when one distracting thought keeps knocking your steady plans off course.

In Great Expectations, a stranger reminds a pub full of men that a person is presumed innocent until proven guilty, and that they had judged too quickly. Be slow to pass judgement on what you have only heard second-hand.
In Great Expectations, Jaggers catches a man repeating a story from memory when the printed paper says otherwise. Before you pass a claim on, check the source rather than trusting what you remember.

In Great Expectations, Joe refuses to want anything in return for letting Pip go, and the lawyer is surprised. Some of the most valuable people ask for nothing back, and their integrity is worth more than any payment.

In Great Expectations, Pip looks back on Joe's gentle, faithful love and sees how ungrateful he was while he was getting ahead. Value the people who stand by you, and tell them so before the chance to do it has gone.

In Great Expectations, Pip asks plainly whether he may say goodbye to people before he leaves, so he keeps to the conditions he was given. Ask clear questions about what is expected of you, so you can keep your word properly.

In Great Expectations, Pip takes the kind looks of Joe and Biddy as mistrust, because his unease is really with himself. When kindness from people who wish you well stings, check whether the sting is about you.

In Great Expectations, newly fortunate Pip is ashamed of his humble roots and hides from the people who knew him, and Joe gently points out the cost. Success that makes you ashamed of where you came from costs more than it gains.
In Great Expectations, Pip sees Joe's pipe smoke drifting from the door and feels it as a blessing, a quiet kindness never announced. Some of the most loving acts are never spoken about.
In Great Expectations, Pip plans a village feast and then sees that it would carry a good deal of condescension. Generosity that looks down on people is not really generosity.

In Great Expectations, Joe is content with who he is, and Pip is disappointed that Joe does not seem more moved by his rise. Contentment that asks for nothing is a kind of wisdom that snobbery tends to miss.

In Great Expectations, Biddy gently asks whether Joe might be proud, and Pip answers by accusing her of envy instead of considering it. When someone says something uncomfortable, think about it before you decide they are the problem.

In Great Expectations, Mr. Trabb becomes fawning as soon as he hears of Pip's fortune, showing how quickly people change their manner towards money. Notice whether you treat people differently once they seem to matter more.

In Great Expectations, Pip finds that shopkeepers give him their full attention once they hear he is rich, and that much of their respect depends on what he has. Notice how much of the regard you get depends on what you have rather than who you are.

In Great Expectations, Pumblechook's flattery over wine leaves Pip feeling he has misjudged the man, even though he knows the praise is false. Be wary of lavish praise that arrives just before a request.

In Great Expectations, Pip admits he wanted to leave alone to avoid the contrast with Joe, and then regrets it. Notice when a choice is really made to avoid embarrassment, and be honest with yourself about it.

In Great Expectations, Pip weeps as he leaves his village and finds he is better for it, more sorry for his ingratitude and gentler. Letting yourself feel the loss of what you leave behind can make you kinder.

In Great Expectations, Jaggers turns away a witness who will swear to anything, because testimony that bends to any side is worth nothing. Your word only means something when it does not bend to convenience.
In Great Expectations, Herbert Pocket openly admits his rooms are modest and that he must earn his own bread. Being plain about your means makes it easier for others to trust you.
In Great Expectations, Pip asks his new friend Herbert to point out whenever he goes wrong, a humble request many people avoid. Asking for honest feedback early saves a lot of embarrassment later.
In Great Expectations, Matthew Pocket holds that polish cannot disguise the grain of real character, and the more you varnish it, the more it shows through. Manner cannot fake character for long.

In Great Expectations, Herbert says the grand thing is to look about you while you work, then move when you see your opening. Watching closely from a modest post is a practical way to find your chance.

In Great Expectations, Herbert bears his poverty with the same good humour he showed after a defeat, and does not puff himself up even though he expects to succeed. Quiet modesty in hard times is worth noticing and copying.

preview.text:
I give Pirrip as my father’s family name, on the authority of his
tombstone and my sister,—Mrs. Joe Gargery, who married the blacksmith.
As I never saw my father or my mother, and never saw any likeness of
either of them (for their days were long before the days of
photographs), my first fancies regarding what they were like were
unreasonably derived from their tombstones. The shape of the letters on
my father’s, gave me an odd idea that he was a square, stout, dark man,
with curly black hair. From the character and turn of the inscription,
“_Also Georgiana Wife of the Above_,” I drew a childish conclusion that
my mother was freckled and sickly. To five little stone lozenges, each
about a foot and a half long, which were arranged in a neat row beside
their grave, and were sacred to the memory of five little brothers of
mine,—who gave up trying to get a living, exceedingly early in that
universal struggle,—I am indebted for a belief I religiously
entertained that they had all been born on their backs with their hands
in their trousers-pockets, and had never taken them out in this state
of existence.

books.title: The Time Machine
books.author: H. G. Wells
books.subject: adventure
books.licence_note: Author died 1946. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Time Machine, Wells has the Time Traveller ask whether we are as free as we assume. We move easily in two directions, but gravity limits us, and balloons changed what had seemed fixed.
In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller answers Filby's refusal to be persuaded by asking him plainly what reason he has. Asking someone to name the objection gets further than arguing past it.
In The Time Machine, Wells has the Time Traveller answer doubt with a demonstration rather than more talk. For a business, showing the result often persuades better than explaining it.

In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller asks his guests to inspect the table and the model for trickery before he starts it. Inviting people to check your work for themselves is a fair way to earn trust.
In The Time Machine, the Medical Man says to wait for the common sense of the morning before believing a bold claim made late at night. Sleeping on a striking idea is a sound test of it.
Wells observes that people trust a man whose motives they can see, and distrust one who makes hard things look too easy. Being too smooth can cost a person credibility.
In The Time Machine, the Editor and the Journalist mock the story before they have heard it. Wells shows how quickly ridicule can take the place of listening.
Before telling his story, the Time Traveller asks his listeners not to interrupt, admitting that most of it will sound like lying. Asking for a full hearing before judgement is a fair request.

In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller accepts a risk calmly in the workshop, then in the moment his nerves get the better of him and he hurries the lever. Wells shows how a choice made under strain can undo careful planning.

In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller pockets the machine's levers while he is still learning whom he can trust. Keeping hold of what you cannot afford to lose, while you find out about people, is a sound instinct.
Wells has the Time Traveller judge a whole people from one odd exchange, then catch himself. A first impression can mislead, so it is worth testing it before deciding.

In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller learns a strange language by pointing at concrete things, starting with a single fruit, then a handful of nouns. Starting from what you can point to is a practical way to learn anyone.
In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller calls his explanation simple and plausible, then admits that most wrong theories are too. A neat story that fits what you see is not the same as a true one.

After a night of panic, the Time Traveller looks at his situation in plain daylight and asks himself what he will do if the worst is true. He then resolves to be calm, learn the local ways and plan from there.

In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller grabs a frightened man in anger, then lets go when he sees the horror on the man's face. A flash of temper can cost more than it gains, and another person's fear can stop you.
Telling himself to be patient, the Time Traveller resolves to watch the world and learn its ways before making guesses about it. He also laughs at the trap of his own making.
The Time Traveller's first explanation for the air shafts is obvious, and he later says it was absolutely wrong. An obvious answer deserves a test before you trust it.

In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller drops his tidy theory of a comfortable, decaying future once it fails to explain what he sees. He admits he has no other, which is an honest way to stay with the evidence.
The Time Traveller had expected no gratitude from the child he pulled from the river, and he was wrong. Expecting the worst of people can blind you to what they will give back.
Absorbed in his large problems, the Time Traveller only slowly realises what Weena's friendship means to him. Important things can arrive quietly while your attention is somewhere else.
The Time Traveller sees that the people dread the dark, yet still ignores what that fear is telling him. Noticing a clue and then failing to act on it is a common way to go wrong.

In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller feels fear rise, then reminds himself of what he knows about the world and steps forward to speak. His voice comes out harsh, but he goes on. Courage often looks like that.

When the Time Traveller presses Weena with questions and she bursts into tears, he drops the subject at once to comfort her. Noticing someone's distress and easing off is a decent instinct, even when you want an answer.
In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller admits his urge to explore a new palace was really a way of putting off the descent he dreaded. Noticing your own excuses for delay is an honest habit.
The Time Traveller admits he set out assuming the people of the future would be far ahead of him in everything, so he came unprepared. An untested assumption can leave you without the basics.
The Time Traveller burns through most of his matches without thinking to save them, and only notices when he is in the dark. Resources you take for granted are the ones to plan for.
Before facing the strange world, the Time Traveller decides he must first secure a place where he can sleep. Making your base safe gives you the confidence to meet what lies outside it.

The Time Traveller guessed the walk at seven or eight miles and it was nearly eighteen. He had judged it on a misty afternoon, when distances seem shorter. Plan for the harder conditions, not the ones you judged in good weather.
Under the night stars, the Time Traveller's troubles seem to shrink. Stepping back to look at the wide view can put a private worry back in proportion.

The Time Traveller tries to hold scorn for a decaying people, but cannot keep it up, because they still share enough of his humanity to claim his sympathy. Contempt is hard to sustain once you look closely at people.

In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller lingers over fascinating machines while the afternoon runs out and his urgent needs go unmet. Pleasant curiosity can crowd out the work that matters most right now.

In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller nearly wrecks his own plan. Carried away by excitement, he strikes a case that might have blown up everything he hoped to gain. Eagerness that is not checked can destroy the very thing you want.
Worn out and irritable, the Time Traveller ignores a feeling of warning and pushes on through the wood. Pressing ahead when you are depleted is often where poor judgement creeps in.

In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller keeps striking at his attackers until he sees they are helpless in the firelight, and then he stops. Knowing when a threat has passed is part of keeping your own humanity.
In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller plans a clean escape, then overlooks one small thing: his matches only light on the box. Check the ordinary details before you count on the plan.

Having once fallen headlong, the Time Traveller slows right down when he tries to return, moving cautiously and bringing his pace under control. Letting a painful lesson change how you approach the next attempt is sound.
In The Time Machine, the Time Traveller admits he hardly believes his own story. Saying plainly where your doubts lie can earn more trust than insisting you are certain.

The narrator cannot dismiss the wild story because the teller is so calm and sober about it, and he goes to see the evidence for himself. A plain, measured account can earn more belief than a dramatic one.

In the epilogue of The Time Machine, Wells's narrator says that even if the future looks bleak, we must live as though it were not so. A grim outlook is no excuse for giving up on the work in front of you.

preview.text:
“Well, I do not mind telling you I have been at work upon this geometry
of Four Dimensions for some time. Some of my results are curious. For
instance, here is a portrait of a man at eight years old, another at
fifteen, another at seventeen, another at twenty-three, and so on. All
these are evidently sections, as it were, Three-Dimensional
representations of his Four-Dimensioned being, which is a fixed and
unalterable thing.”

“Scientific people,” proceeded the Time Traveller, after the pause
required for the proper assimilation of this, “know very well that Time
is only a kind of Space. Here is a popular scientific diagram, a
weather record. This line I trace with my finger shows the movement of
the barometer. Yesterday it was so high, yesterday night it fell, then
this morning it rose again, and so gently upward to here. Surely the
mercury did not trace this line in any of the dimensions of Space
generally recognised? But certainly it traced such a line, and that
line, therefore, we must conclude, was along the Time-Dimension.”

“But,” said the Medical Man, staring hard at a coal in the fire, “if
Time is really only a fourth dimension of Space, why is it, and why has
it always been, regarded as something different? And why cannot we move
about in Time as we move about in the other dimensions of Space?”

The Time Traveller smiled. “Are you so sure we can move freely in
Space? Right and left we can go, backward and forward freely enough,
and men always have done so. I admit we move freely in two dimensions.
But how about up and down? Gravitation limits us there.”

“Not exactly,” said the Medical Man. “There are balloons.”

“But before the balloons, save for spasmodic jumping and the
inequalities of the surface, man had no freedom of vertical movement.”

books.title: The Return of Sherlock Holmes
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.subject: detective
books.licence_note: Author died 1930. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Empty House, Watson admits his own attempts at Holmes's methods met with only indifferent success, a reminder that careful reasoning is a skill built slowly through practice.
In The Empty House, Watson recalls Holmes's advice that every investigation begins at the line of least resistance, the simplest and most testable path to try first.
In The Empty House, Holmes turns his apparent death into a trap, letting his enemies grow careless while he waits. It is a lesson in patience and in seeing a setback as an opening.
In The Empty House, Holmes tells Watson that work is the best antidote to sorrow, a steadying idea for anyone getting back on their feet after a loss.
In The Empty House, Holmes turns the watchers into the watched, showing that whoever keeps observing a situation calmly and closely often holds the advantage.
In The Empty House, Holmes hands the credit for the arrest to Lestrade, showing that a good leader can let others take the glory and still be respected for the work.
In The Empty House, Holmes cannot act on suspicion alone, so he watches and waits until he can prove the crime. It is a reminder that patience and proof often beat hasty action.
In The Empty House, Holmes admits that even a logical mind can be wrong when it moves beyond the evidence into conjecture, so a sensible theory should be held loosely.
In The Norwood Builder, Holmes says that even the faintest trace can reveal a larger pattern to someone who knows what to look for, so small details deserve attention.
In The Norwood Builder, a young solicitor is so flattered and grateful for a sudden windfall that he drops his guard, a useful story about how a generous offer can hide a trap.

In The Norwood Builder, Holmes tests Lestrade's neat theory by asking whether a sensible person would really act that way. Stepping into the other person's shoes can expose a story that is too obvious.
In The Norwood Builder, Holmes argues that the logical place to start is the earlier, odd event, since understanding it may simplify what followed. Begin with the piece you least understand.
In The Norwood Builder, Holmes warns that a mild and respectable appearance proves nothing about a person's guilt or innocence, so judge by evidence rather than manner.

In The Norwood Builder, Holmes points out that new evidence is a two-edged thing that may cut in a different direction from the one it first appears to. Check what a fresh fact really supports before acting on it.
In The Norwood Builder, Holmes rejects a seemingly final proof because it contradicts what he personally saw earlier. A conclusion, however neat, has to fit the facts you directly observed.
In The Norwood Builder, Holmes says the villain's scheme was ruined by his failure to know when to stop. He kept tightening a plan that was already working, and overreach undid him.
In The Dancing Men, Holmes explains that a deduction looks absurdly simple once each link is laid out. Great reasoning is a chain of small, careful observations.
In The Dancing Men, Hilton Cubitt is sure his wife would do better to trust him, since a frightened silence can cut a couple off from the one person who could help.
In The Dancing Men, Holmes says a sample too short to test gives no real basis for an investigation, so he asks for more evidence before he acts. Wait for enough facts to judge.
In The Dancing Men, Holmes works for two hours alternating between progress and bafflement until the pattern finally gives way. Hard problems yield to sustained, patient effort.
In The Dancing Men, Holmes warns that the absence of a telltale sign proves little, though its presence can be decisive. Be careful about what a missing clue really means.
In The Dancing Men, Holmes finds a bullet hole in the window because he looked for it. Good observation comes from actively searching for what ought to be there, not waiting for it to appear.
In The Dancing Men, Holmes cracks the cipher by taking the most common letter as a working hypothesis, then testing it against the next clue. A provisional guess is useful when it can be checked.

In The Dancing Men, Holmes reasons about who would be writing and what they would likely say, and that context unlocks what letter counts alone could not. Knowing the people involved is part of solving the puzzle.
In The Dancing Men, Holmes holds that whatever one person can invent, another can discover. A clever scheme is only as safe as the patience of the people trying to understand it.
In The Dancing Men, Holmes turns a code used to lure a man into a trap into a message of rescue. Knowledge and skill can serve either side, and the choice of use is what matters.
In The Solitary Cyclist, Holmes narrows a puzzle by exclusion, ruling out each route that cannot be right until only one remains. Eliminating the impossible is often the quickest path to the likely.
In The Solitary Cyclist, Holmes sends Watson to observe the facts for himself and act on his own judgment. Trusting a capable colleague to see for themselves is a fair way to share the work.

In The Solitary Cyclist, Holmes tells Watson that a distant, poorly placed watch learns little, and that real knowledge comes from getting close and asking where local people talk. Go to where the information lives.

In The Solitary Cyclist, Holmes admits plainly that he failed to allow for an earlier train, then turns straight to repairing the damage. Owning a mistake openly and acting at once is a habit worth keeping.

In The Solitary Cyclist, Watson tells Carruthers that his secret watching and his silence, though meant as devotion, look more like selfishness. Caring for someone while hiding the truth from them is a test of honest love.

In The Adventure of the Priory School, Holmes tests a theory by asking what a clever deceiver would really have done. When the answer is absurd, he drops the theory but keeps the clue as a starting point.
In The Adventure of the Priory School, Holmes keeps asking how a person could know a thing, not just what they believe. Every claim gets traced back to its source.
In The Adventure of the Priory School, Holmes narrows a puzzle by closing off possible routes one at a time on a map, using what reliable witnesses saw at each point.
In The Adventure of the Priory School, Holmes tells two tyre tracks apart because he has studied so many of them. Deep familiarity with the small details of one's field is what makes a clue readable.
In The Adventure of the Priory School, Holmes sets aside a possibility he cannot disprove yet and goes back to the evidence he can check. Leaving a question open is better than forcing an answer.
In The Adventure of the Priory School, Holmes stops to separate what is known from what is incidental before pursuing a new lead. Writing down the facts you can trust keeps you from chasing noise.

In The Adventure of the Priory School, Holmes treats a missing action as evidence: the master never ran after the boy, so the boy must have had a faster way to escape. What did not happen can tell you as much as what did.
In The Adventure of the Priory School, Watson calls the innkeeper a villain on sight, and Holmes reminds him that a sinister manner is not evidence. First impressions are a poor substitute for facts.
In The Adventure of the Priory School, Holmes holds that a man who starts a crime is responsible for the other crimes that follow from it. You answer for the consequences of what you set in motion.

In The Adventure of the Priory School, the Duke's secret grows out of one kind act after another, until each concealment demands the next. Shows how a single hidden truth can spread into a family's whole life.
In The Adventure of the Priory School, the Duke keeps yielding to pleas for delay, and each small concession gives the guilty man more time to run. Putting off a hard choice often makes it worse.
In The Adventure of the Priory School, Holmes says that to shield a guilty son the Duke has put an innocent son in danger. Protecting the wrong person often costs someone who did nothing.

In The Adventure of Black Peter, Watson notes that Holmes turned away rich clients whose problems bored him and gave weeks to humble cases that stirred his imagination. He chose work by what engaged him.

In The Adventure of Black Peter, Holmes tests a theory by trying the act himself and finds his own strength cannot do what the theory needs. Test an assumption with your own hands before you believe it.

In The Adventure of Black Peter, Holmes holds that anyone who moves through a room leaves some trace, so a careful searcher should always find something. Evidence is usually there if you look for the disturbance.
In The Adventure of Black Peter, Holmes admits that a newly found notebook overturns the theory he had built. When a new fact does not fit, the theory has to give way.

In The Adventure of Black Peter, Holmes reasons that an intruder who failed with a small blade will come back with a better tool. Asking what someone will try next, based on how they failed, lets you prepare for them.

In The Adventure of Black Peter, Holmes says a good investigator always looks for an alternative explanation and prepares for it, even when the first theory seems to be holding. Keep a second line of inquiry open.
In The Adventure of Black Peter, Holmes shows that when a few clues agree, each step narrows the field until only a handful of people fit. He then goes and finds those people directly.

In The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton, the blackmailer admits that making an example of one victim keeps all his other debtors paying. His reputation for ruthlessness is what he actually sells.

In The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton, Watson refuses to be left behind and tells his friend he will act alone if he must. Loyalty that stands its ground can change the choice of a stubborn friend.
In The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton, Holmes grows uneasy when a door is unlocked that should not be. An easier path than expected is a reason to slow down and look again.

In The Adventure of Charles Augustus Milverton, Holmes stops Watson from stepping into a fight that is not theirs to join. He then makes sure the letters that could ruin the innocent are destroyed. Know which duties are yours.

In The Adventure of the Six Napoleons, Holmes refuses to call any small oddity trivial, because some of his most famous cases began with the least promising detail. Take the small strange thing seriously enough to look at it.

In The Adventure of the Six Napoleons, Holmes says an odd fact should be remembered and filed away, since a later discovery may give it meaning. Keep a log of puzzling details, not only the ones that fit today.

In The Adventure of the Six Napoleons, Holmes tells Lestrade to pursue his own line of inquiry while he follows his, then compare notes so each can fill the other's gaps. Two different approaches often cover more ground than one.
In The Adventure of the Six Napoleons, Watson sees that even the coldest reasoner is moved by a friend's honest praise. Behind a sharp mind there is still a person who wants to be appreciated.
In The Adventure of the Six Napoleons, Holmes rebuilds a whole chain of events by working backwards from the known result. Reading the sequence in reverse can show how the pieces connect.
In The Adventure of the Three Students, a key left in a door for a few minutes leads to a serious scandal. Small lapses in routine can cost far more than they seem to at the time.

preview.text:
It can be imagined that my close intimacy with Sherlock Holmes
      had interested me deeply in crime, and that after his
      disappearance I never failed to read with care the various
      problems which came before the public. And I even attempted, more
      than once, for my own private satisfaction, to employ his methods
      in their solution, though with indifferent success. There was
      none, however, which appealed to me like this tragedy of Ronald
      Adair. As I read the evidence at the inquest, which led up to a
      verdict of willful murder against some person or persons unknown,
      I realized more clearly than I had ever done the loss which the
      community had sustained by the death of Sherlock Holmes. There
      were points about this strange business which would, I was sure,
      have specially appealed to him, and the efforts of the police
      would have been supplemented, or more probably anticipated, by
      the trained observation and the alert mind of the first criminal
      agent in Europe. All day, as I drove upon my round, I turned over
      the case in my mind and found no explanation which appeared to me
      to be adequate. At the risk of telling a twice-told tale, I will
      recapitulate the facts as they were known to the public at the
      conclusion of the inquest.

books.title: The Blue Fairy Book
books.author: Andrew Lang (editor)
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Editor died 1912. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Bronze Ring, the gardener's son shares his purse and his lame horse with a starving old woman, while the rich minister's son turns her away. The story shows that kindness to a stranger, given at some cost, is what sets a person up for good fortune.

In The Bronze Ring, three mice quarrel over which of them deserves the credit for recovering the ring, and in the argument the ring falls into the sea. The story shows how fighting over credit can undo a success the group already had.

In Prince Hyacinth and the Dear Little Princess, the Prince is taught from childhood that his own flaw is a beauty, and everyone agrees. A person shielded from honest feedback can grow sure of something untrue.

In Prince Hyacinth and the Dear Little Princess, the Fairy says that self-love keeps us from seeing our own faults, and that reason only shows us a fault once it gets in the way of what we want. The lesson is to look for flaws before they cost us something.

In East of the Sun and West of the Moon, the girl lights the candle against her promise and loses the bear-prince, who says one more year of patience would have freed him. Patience can be the most valuable thing a person gives.

In East of the Sun and West of the Moon, the girl says she has no fear and keeps going, even when the North Wind is spent and sinks low over the sea. Her steady resolve carries her further than any magic does.

In The Yellow Dwarf, a mother who never corrects her daughter's faults and fills her with flattery leaves the girl proud and scornful of everyone. Love that only praises can do real harm, and a child who is never told no grows up poorly served.

In The Yellow Dwarf, Bellissima becomes much less proud after her frightening meeting with the dwarf. The story shows that a humbling scare can change a vain person for the better, though the change is partly driven by a wish to escape.

In The Yellow Dwarf, the captive King notices the fairy's griffin feet and hides that he knows, waiting with patience and cunning rather than reacting in anger. Staying calm and keeping your real knowledge to yourself can be a stronger move than a quick reply.
In The Yellow Dwarf, the mermaid helps the King escape by stating plainly why she is helping and asking only for his trust. Being open about your motives makes it easier for others to act with you.

In Little Red Riding-Hood, the girl cheerfully tells a stranger in the wood where she is going and why, and the wolf uses that information against her. The story is a plain warning that a friendly voice can still want something from you.

In The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood, the youngest fairy cannot undo the old fairy's curse of death, but she softens it to a hundred years of sleep. When you cannot fix a harm outright, you can still reduce it.

In The Sleeping Beauty in the Wood, the kitchen clerk ordered to kill a child hides her and serves a lamb instead, risking his own life. The story shows a quiet conscience finding a way around a cruel order.

In Cinderella, the young stepdaughter bears her harsh treatment patiently and never turns cruel back, and it is her goodness that the fairy godmother later rewards. The story shows that quiet kindness under unfairness is a strength, not a weakness.
In Cinderella, once she is raised up, Cinderella forgives the sisters who treated her badly and finds them good matches at court. The story shows that generosity after winning is a virtue of its own.

In Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp, the false uncle plays the warm relative to win the boy's trust, all while planning to take the lamp and kill him. The story shows that warm manners do not prove good intentions.

In Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp, Aladdin wins the people's hearts and wins battles for the Sultan, yet stays modest and courteous as his success grows. Rising in standing without losing decency is one of the more useful things the story shows.

In The Tale of a Youth Who Set Out to Learn What Fear Was, the youngest son, written off by everyone as stupid, sets out to learn what shuddering means and says plainly what he wants. The story shows that an early dismissal is not a final verdict on a person.

In The Tale of a Youth Who Set Out to Learn What Fear Was, the youth meets each strange terror in the castle with a plain, practical act, and stays steady enough to sleep. The story suggests that calm courage often comes from dealing with the next problem in front of you.

In Rumpelstiltzkin, the miller's daughter, desperate to escape the King's demands, promises her first child to a little man, and the promise comes back to haunt her. The story is a warning about pledges made under pressure.

In Beauty and the Beast, the youngest daughter keeps her spirits up and sets to work to make the best of a ruined family's new life, while her sisters sulk over what they have lost. The story values steady good humour in hard times, and the practical effort that comes with it.

In Beauty and the Beast, Beauty accepts the blame her sisters heap on her, even though she did nothing wrong on purpose, and offers to go in her father's place. The story shows responsibility taken with grace, without bitterness.

In Beauty and the Beast, Beauty finds after an hour's talk that the Beast is far less terrible than she feared, and she gives him an honest answer even though it might anger him. The story suggests that a first impression of a frightening person can change with patient acquaintance.
In Beauty and the Beast, Beauty's father reasons that the Beast's gentleness deserves a loving return, whatever his appearance. The story ties love to character rather than to looks.

In The Master-Maid, the prince struggles with a huge job until the princess shows him to turn the pitchfork round and work with the handle, and the task suddenly becomes easy. The story is a plain case for finding the better method before working harder.

In The Master-Maid, the prince promises to take only the horses and not to taste anything at home, then forgets his bride after one bite of an apple offered by a bride's sister. The story shows how a small temptation can undo a commitment made in earnest.

In The Master-Maid, the sheriff comes courting only after learning the maiden has money to be had, and his greed leads straight to his humiliation. The story mocks suitors who come for a person's wealth rather than for the person.

In the tale of the Master-maid, she lends the court her calf, shovel-handle and porch-door without grudge, even after they have mocked her. Generosity to those who have not earned it can still carry the day.
In the tale of the Master-maid, she refuses to be summoned like a servant, and the King comes to her instead. Holding your dignity without rudeness can change how others treat you.
In Why the Sea Is Salt, a wise old man at the gate gives the poor brother practical advice before he goes in. Good counsel from a stranger is worth more than a bargain made in haste.
In Why the Sea Is Salt, the skipper buys the magic mill without first learning how to stop it, and the sea is salted for ever. Learn how to control a powerful tool before you rush to use it.

In The Master Cat, or Puss in Boots, the youngest son is left with nothing but a cat, yet the cat's cleverness turns that poor inheritance into a fortune. What you are given matters less than what you make of it.

In The Master Cat, or Puss in Boots, the cat wins the king's trust with small, steady gifts over several months before asking for the big favour. Trust is built by showing up consistently, one small gift at a time.

In Felicia and the Pot of Pinks, a gentle girl is left the smallest share of her father's goods by a selfish brother, yet she keeps caring for what she has. Kindness under unfair treatment is still a kind of strength.
In Felicia and the Pot of Pinks, the Queen is won over by Felicia's modest, honest answers rather than by any show of wealth. Plain truth, told with grace, opens doors that pretence cannot.
In Felicia and the Pot of Pinks, Felicia gives the Queen her last silver ring in thanks and says that friendship is enough for her to do well. Gratitude offered from very little is remembered.
In Felicia and the Pot of Pinks, Felicia refuses to have her cruel brother punished, and the Queen admires her for it. Letting go of the wish for revenge is its own kind of strength.

In Felicia and the Pot of Pinks, Felicia asks the Queen to forgive her brother because her own happiness makes her want everyone else to be happy too. Joy that is not hoarded turns a person generous rather than vengeful.

In The White Cat, three princes promise to share their good fortune and never let envy divide them, and the story then tests whether that promise holds. Pledges of friendship are easy to make and only show their worth under strain.

In The White Cat, a magic draught makes the Prince forget his father's errand, and only the White Cat's gentle reminder brings him back to it. Comfort can quietly cost us what we came to do, and a true friend tells us when it is time to leave.

In The White Cat, the Prince offers to give up his ambitions to stay with the White Cat, and she sends him back to his duties instead. Caring for someone sometimes means encouraging them to go and do what they must.

In The White Cat, the Prince takes a small sharp scratch from the cat as encouragement and keeps going until he finds what was hidden in the smallest seed. A small sign of support from someone who cares can carry us through a hard task.

In The White Cat, the Prince pleads to be given any other proof of his devotion, then steels himself to do the painful thing the Cat asks. Love sometimes means doing what hurts because trust requires it.

In The White Cat, the Queen trades her newborn daughter for fairy fruit, and the desperate bargain brings grief and ruin on her kingdom. A rash promise made in a moment of want can cost far more than the thing it was meant to win.
In The White Cat, the Princess already has six kingdoms and asks the King only for his friendship and his son's hand. Someone secure in what they have does not need to grab for more.
In The Water-Lily, The Gold-Spinners, the maiden forgets her old caution in the joy of a new conversation, and she pays for it. Pleasant company can make us neglect warnings we already know.

In The Water-Lily, The Gold-Spinners, the maiden does not sit in despair but sends a raven with a message, and help comes by a roundabout path. Reaching out for help, even by an unlikely route, is a sensible thing to do.
In The Water-Lily, The Gold-Spinners, the Prince hesitates for a long time before he acts, until a crow urges him on. Set fear against a lasting sorrow, and the choice to act often becomes clear.

In The Water-Lily, The Gold-Spinners, the Prince forgets the maidens who helped him once his own troubles end, and is shamed back into keeping his word. Gratitude slips easily when our own sorrows lift, so keep the promises made to those who helped us.
In The Terrible Head, a king is so frightened of a prophecy that he locks away his daughter and then casts her out to sea. Fear of what might happen can do far more harm than the thing feared.
In The Terrible Head, the boy regrets his hasty oath but resolves to keep it anyway. A word given in pride still binds us, and keeping it is a matter of character.

In The Terrible Head, the young man takes off his own shoes and lends them to a stranger he has just met, asking only that they be returned. Generosity offered without fuss is a quiet kind of courage.

In The Terrible Head, the boy frees a girl chained to a rock for a sea monster, and then uses the very weapon he has been given to save her. Courage matters most when it is spent on someone else's need.

In The Story of Pretty Goldilocks, Charming makes a rash remark at Court and is shut in a tower, and his freedom comes only when the King listens to him properly. Careless words can cost dearly, and a fair hearing can undo a hasty judgement.
In The Story of Pretty Goldilocks, Charming spares a gasping golden carp that he could have eaten for dinner, and the fish later promises to repay him. Small mercies are rarely wasted.

In The Story of Pretty Goldilocks, Charming sinks into despair and brushes aside his little dog's encouragement, yet a morning walk to the river brings the answer he needed. Hope often needs only one more small act of trying.

In The Story of Pretty Goldilocks, the Princess remembers the faithful man she had let be locked away, and she frees him and makes him her king. Gratitude that is acted on, even late, can change a life.

In The History of Whittington, the narrator points out that people quick to call the poor idle often do nothing to find them work, and that this is not real charity. Helping someone into work is worth more than judging them for being without it.

In The History of Whittington, a poor boy carefully weighs how to spend his only coin on a cat, and that choice becomes the start of his fortune. A small thing chosen with care can be the beginning of something larger.

In The History of Whittington, the boy sets out to run away but turns back when he hears the bells promise a better future. Persistence often looks like going back to the hard work you had almost given up on.

“Good-day to you, young traveler,” said the beggar-woman.

“Good-day, good woman,” answered he.

“Young traveler, have pity upon me.”

“Take my purse, good woman,” said he, “and mount behind me, for your
legs can’t be very strong.”

The old woman didn’t wait to be asked twice, but mounted behind him,
and in this style they reached the chief city of a powerful kingdom. The
minister’s son was lodged in a grand inn, the gardener’s son and the old
woman dismounted at the inn for beggars.

The next day the gardener’s son heard a great noise in the street, and
the King’s heralds passed, blowing all kinds of instruments, and crying:

“The King, our master, is old and infirm. He will give a great reward to
whoever will cure him and give him back the strength of his youth.”

Then the old beggar-woman said to her benefactor:

books.title: The Nicomachean Ethics
books.author: Aristotle
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 322 BCE, nineteenth century translation. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Aristotle held that good character is the indispensable condition of happiness, which he saw as the goal of all human action.
Aristotle paired wide ideas about human nature with close attention to how people actually behave, and that mix is what keeps his ethics useful.
Aristotle held that the point of studying ethics is practical: knowing what is best for people and how to bring it about.
Aristotle held that rules for living are general guides that admit exceptions, and that real understanding of them comes from experience of good character.
Aristotle argued that happiness is not pleasure, power, honour or wealth, but a life of activity guided by reason that suits human nature.
Aristotle held that character is formed by habit: repeating good acts gradually makes them easy and, over time, a second nature.
Aristotle taught that right action means doing just the amount a situation calls for, with excess and deficiency both going wrong.
Aristotle held that a virtue is a steady disposition to act well in recurring situations, and that rules must be applied with judgement to each case.
Aristotle held that the acts we choose after deliberating are the most telling evidence of what we are, because the whole person enters into them.
Aristotle saw justice first as the fair-minded habit every citizen needs in order to take part in public life, as a judge, official or juror.
Aristotle held that practical wisdom lets a person produce the right rule from within, because they understand the end they are aiming at and can justify the choice.
Aristotle held that practical wisdom and good character depend on each other: neither is fully possible without the other.
Aristotle observed that people can know what is good and still fail to act on it, and he saw the desire behind that failure as not wholly unreasonable.
Aristotle gave friendship two full books, treating it as a necessary part of a good life rather than an extra.
Aristotle held that pleasure naturally comes with activity done well, so the highest pleasures accompany the highest activity.
Aristotle said anyone who wants to make themselves or others better must become a small legislator, studying the principles of law, morality and education.
Aristotle opens the Ethics by observing that every art, inquiry and choice aims at some good, and that the highest good is what all things aim at.
Aristotle reasoned that the highest good is the end we want for its own sake, since otherwise our wanting would go on without limit.
Aristotle likened the search for the right course to an archer aiming at a mark, since a clear target makes it more likely we hit it.
Aristotle held that we should seek only as much precision as a subject allows, because demanding proof where persuasion is the right tool is a mistake.
Aristotle said a young person is not ready for moral philosophy, because it needs experience of real actions and a mind not ruled by passing desires.
Aristotle noted that people agree on the word happiness but disagree about its nature, and that one person may call health or wealth happiness depending on their mood.
Aristotle argued that honour is too superficial to be the good, because it depends on those who give it and can be taken away.
Aristotle observed that wealth is wanted for the sake of something further, so it cannot be the good we are finally seeking.
Aristotle argued that a physician studies the health of this particular patient, not health in the abstract, so practical knowledge belongs to concrete cases.
Aristotle held that we choose honour, pleasure and virtue partly for the sake of happiness, but we never choose happiness for the sake of anything else.
Aristotle held that the good life lacks nothing, yet people are made for social life, so it includes family, friends and fellow citizens.
Aristotle concluded that a person's good lies in activity of the soul guided by reason and done well, just as a harp player's good is playing the harp well.
Aristotle said one fine day does not make a spring, and one good stretch does not make a person happy: happiness is judged across a whole life.
Aristotle held that virtue is something we do, not just something we have, since a person asleep may have good character yet do no good at all.
Aristotle held that a good person takes real pleasure in acting well, so virtuous action is pleasant in itself and not only a duty.
Aristotle held that happiness comes through learning and steady effort, so most people who are not crippled in their capacity for virtue can reach it.
Aristotle argued that a person's steadiness comes from acting in line with virtue rather than from fortune, because good and bad luck keep moving around the same people.
Aristotle said a good person bears misfortune with dignity and does the noblest thing the circumstances allow, as a good general makes the most of the troops he has.
Aristotle observed that we are born with a capacity for virtue but become just, brave or self-controlled by doing just, brave or self-controlled acts, as builders learn by building.
Aristotle insisted that the point of studying ethics is to become good, not merely to know what goodness is.
Aristotle offered a test of real virtue: a brave person faces danger with little or no pain, and a self-controlled person is glad to abstain, not merely able to.
Aristotle held that good education trains people to feel pleasure and pain in the right things, since pleasure often leads us to do wrong.
Aristotle held that knowing the right thing is not enough for virtue: we must choose it for its own sake and act from a settled character.
Aristotle warned that talking about virtue does not make anyone good, any more than a patient who listens closely to the doctor and then ignores the advice gets well.
Aristotle held that the right amount depends on the person: ten is too much food for a beginner and too little for a champion wrestler, so the mean is set relative to us.
Aristotle noted that there are many ways to go wrong but only one way to go right, which is why doing right is hard and going astray is easy.
Aristotle held that some acts, such as theft, are wrong in themselves, so they have no right amount to aim at and cannot be done well at all.
Aristotle paired each virtue with two faults, one of too much and one of too little, such as courage lying between rashness and cowardice.
Aristotle noted that we often judge a person by the extreme they are nearest, so the brave look rash to a coward and cowardly to a rash person.
Aristotle observed that our own natural bias makes one extreme feel further from the mean, and since people lean toward pleasure, self-indulgence seems the worse fault.
Aristotle advised pushing against our own bent, as one straightens warped timber, and keeping well clear of the extreme most opposed to the mean.
Aristotle advised guarding most carefully against pleasure, because we are not impartial judges of what pleases us.
Aristotle judged that a hard choice made under pressure, such as throwing cargo overboard in a storm, is voluntary at the moment, because the person weighs the lesser loss.
Aristotle distinguished wishing from choosing: we wish for ends such as health, but we choose the means, and choice applies only to what lies within our power.
Aristotle held that we deliberate only about what is within our power and still uncertain, and that for great matters a wise person seeks the counsel of others.
Aristotle observed that we deliberate about the means to a goal already set, working backwards step by step and dropping any plan that proves impossible.
Aristotle noted that most people are misled by pleasure, which looks like good without being good, so they choose what pleases and avoid what hurts.
Aristotle observed that once bad habits have set, a person cannot simply wish them away, though they were free to shape those habits at the start.
Aristotle pointed out that we blame illnesses brought on by our own excess or neglect, but pity those we did not cause, and held that character works the same way.
Aristotle held that a brave person fears the right things in the right way: disgrace is worth fearing, while poverty or illness not caused by one's own fault need not be feared.
Aristotle held that courage is shown by facing what is feared for the sake of what is honourable, at the right time and in the right measure.
Aristotle observed that the rash often put on a show of courage they do not have, so they run when real danger arrives.
Aristotle held that the brave person faces danger because it is honourable, while fleeing hardship is only softness, not courage.
Aristotle held that doing right out of fear of punishment ranks below doing it from a sense of honour, since fear is not the motive of a good person.

preview.text:
We must, however, remember that the production of good character is not
the end of either individual or state action: that is the aim of the
one and the other because good character is the indispensable condition
and chief determinant of happiness, itself the goal of all human doing.
The end of all action, individual or collective, is the greatest
happiness of the greatest number. There is, Aristotle insists, no
difference of kind between the good of one and the good of many or all.
The sole difference is one of amount or scale. This does not mean
simply that the State exists to secure in larger measure the objects of
degree which the isolated individual attempts, but is too feeble, to
secure without it. On the contrary, it rather insists that whatever
goods society alone enables a man to secure have always had to the
individual—whether he realised it or not—the value which, when so
secured, he recognises them to possess. The best and happiest life for
the individual is that which the State renders possible, and this it
does mainly by revealing to him the value of new objects of desire and
educating him to appreciate them. To Aristotle or to Plato the State
is, above all, a large and powerful educative agency which gives the
individual increased opportunities of self-development and greater
capacities for the enjoyment of life.

books.title: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer
books.author: Mark Twain
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1910. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In the preface to The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Mark Twain says his hero is a blend of three boys he knew, and that adults may enjoy the book too because it reminds them of who they once were.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Aunt Polly knows her soft heart stops her from guiding Tom properly, and she feels that failure every time she lets him off.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Aunt Polly thinks she is a master of hidden cunning, yet her traps are transparent, and Twain shows how people often overrate their own cleverness.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Twain notes that a new absorbing interest can push troubles out of mind, and that diligence and attention are what bring the knack of any new skill.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Tom turns a dull chore into something his friend wants to do, showing how the way a task is presented can change how people feel about it.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Twain observes that making a thing hard to get makes people want it more, and that a task turns into work the moment we are obliged to do it.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Twain shows Tom nursing his hurt feelings and enjoying imagined regret, a reminder that self-pity can feel sweet while it keeps us from making things right.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Mary earns her Bibles through two years of patient work while most pupils give up, and Twain suggests the few who persist are the ones who truly gain.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Twain notes that the grown-up officials at the Sunday school are showing off too, a reminder that vanity does not end when childhood does.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, the boys who traded their tickets to Tom realise too late that they helped him, and they despise themselves for being dupes of a clever trick.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Twain observes that the less a traditional custom has to justify itself, the harder it is to get rid of.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Huck seems free to every boy who feels hemmed in by rules, and Twain shows how envy sees the freedom of an outcast but not the cost of it.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Tom wins Becky's notice by quietly returning a peach again and again rather than pushing, a small picture of patience winning over resistance.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Tom breaks an agreed rule the moment the temptation grows too strong, and his friend who trusted him is quick to call it out.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Tom's pride walks him out of the room, and Twain shows that going back to say sorry takes more nerve than leaving in a huff.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Twain notes that the elastic heart of youth cannot stay in one shape for long, so a hurt boy's gloomy wish to disappear soon gives way to new plans.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, when Tom's marble charm fails, he blames a witch rather than doubt the charm, a clear picture of how people protect a belief from the evidence.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Tom's waiting mind turns the ordinary creaks and ticks of the night into spirits, a reminder of how fear feeds on imagination.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Injun Joe nurses a grudge for years and then turns it into violence, showing how an old resentment can grow into a terrible act.

In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Tom and Huck bind themselves to silence to protect their own skins while an innocent man faces hanging, showing how fear of consequences can drown out a sense of justice.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Tom admits that he might have been good like Sid if he had tried, an honest moment of self-judgement that only fear seems to bring out.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Tom finds that his aunt's quiet grief hurts more than any whipping, showing that the disappointment of someone who loves us can be the heaviest lesson.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, a village rushes to a verdict on Muff Potter before any evidence is weighed, a warning about how a crowd can be certain long before it is fair.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Aunt Polly feels remorse when Tom turns her own method back on her, and sees that cruelty to a creature can be cruelty to a child too.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, the boys excuse their small thefts by pointing to others, but their conscience will not accept the excuse, because the same reasoning fails for bigger wrongs.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, a boy lying still at dawn notices the worms, ants and birds, and Twain shows how quiet attention can find wonder in the ordinary.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, the boys hide their homesickness because each is ashamed to speak first, a familiar way that unspoken fears spread through a group.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Joe's doubts are crushed by Tom's mockery, and the group quickly silences the one who wants to go home, a picture of how peer pressure ends honest doubt.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Tom hears his aunt's grief and learns how much she loves him, showing that people often discover what they had only when they fear losing it.
In The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Tom quietly kisses his sleeping aunt and slips away unseen, a small act of tenderness that shows a good heart beneath the mischief.
After a storm ruins their camp, Twain's boys patiently coax the fire back to life from the dry wood under a log. Setbacks can be recovered from with steady, practical effort.
In Tom Sawyer, Tom lifts his gloomy friends by inventing a new game. A good leader often lifts a discouraged group by changing the activity rather than arguing with their mood.
In Tom Sawyer, the congregation realises too late that they had only seen faults in the boys. Many of us judge people harshly until we see them whole.
In Tom Sawyer, Tom refuses to let Huck slip away unwelcomed, saying somebody has to be glad to see him. Twain shows loyalty as standing up for the outsider everyone else has shunned.
In Tom Sawyer, Aunt Polly tells Tom that caring shows in the small effort of thinking of someone. Thoughtlessness often hurts people more than unkindness does.
In Tom Sawyer, Tom's vanity makes him refuse to make up with Becky, and then his jealousy leaves him miserable. Pride can cost us the very thing we want most.
In Tom Sawyer, Alfred ruins Tom's spelling book out of spite, and Becky lets Tom take the blame. Twain shows how spite pulls people into harm they would never choose in a calmer moment.
In Tom Sawyer, Aunt Polly chooses not to test whether Tom's words were true, because the comfort they gave her mattered more. Sometimes gentleness is the wiser choice than certainty.
In Tom Sawyer, Tom takes the blame for Becky's torn picture and takes the punishment without complaint. Real courage often means accepting a cost so that someone else is spared.
In Tom Sawyer, the boys' revenge on the schoolmaster keeps failing because each retaliation brings a harsher answer. Twain shows that revenge tends to escalate rather than settle a wrong.
Twain mocks school compositions stuffed with borrowed fine words and forced sermons, which win prizes without saying much. Plain, sincere writing that says what it means is worth more than ornament.
Twain notes that promising not to do something tends to make people want to do it. Tom's first vow is tested by the very temptation it forbids, which shows how strict rules can backfire.
In Tom Sawyer, Tom resolves to reform after a storm, but then decides to wait in case there are no more storms. Good resolutions fade quickly once the fear that prompted them has passed.
In Tom Sawyer, Tom and Huck pity Muff Potter, a man everyone has condemned, and remember his small kindnesses. Twain shows that a person's failings do not erase the good they have done.
In Tom Sawyer, Muff Potter remembers the small kindnesses the boys showed him, even from his cell. Kindness given without reward is often remembered long after it was offered.

In Tom Sawyer, Tom's voice shakes as he testifies in front of the man who threatens him. Once he starts telling the truth, the words come more easily. Courage often starts with a small, unsteady voice.
In Tom Sawyer, Tom and Huck keep digging in the wrong places because they only guessed at the time. When a plan keeps failing, it is worth checking the assumption underneath it before digging harder.

In Tom Sawyer, the boys let talk of blue lights and ghosts steer their plans, and Twain's humour shows how fear can dress itself up as reasoning. Ask what the real risk is before letting a story decide.

In Tom Sawyer, the boys forget every fear the moment they glimpse gold. Twain shows how quickly the promise of a windfall can drown out caution, which is worth remembering before chasing any quick win.
In Tom Sawyer, Tom asks Huck not to weaken, promising he won't either. Holding each other to a shared commitment helps people keep going when they are frightened.

In Tom Sawyer, Tom talks Becky out of her doubts by saying her mother would not mind. Twain shows how a persuasive friend can argue us out of our own good judgement, and how a sure pleasure now can outweigh a bigger cost later.
In Tom Sawyer, McDougal's cave is so vast that no one knows all of it, and even the most confident guides keep to the parts they know. Admitting the limits of what you know keeps you safe.
In Tom Sawyer, Huck is terrified, yet he thinks first of the Widow Douglas, who was kind to him, and runs to warn others. Concern for someone who has been good to us can outweigh our own fear.

In Tom Sawyer, the old Welshman takes in the frightened Huck and welcomes him warmly, a greeting Huck has rarely received. A plain welcome can mean a great deal to someone who has seldom been given one.
In Tom Sawyer, Huck asks that no one credit him for helping catch the men, because he fears their revenge. Quiet courage often prefers safety and anonymity to praise.
In Tom Sawyer, the Widow Douglas takes in the feverish Huck because she is sure there is good in him, whoever else has written him off. Looking for the good in people can change what they become.
In Tom Sawyer, Tom owns his mistake of not marking the way, and Becky chooses to hope again rather than pile on. Honest blame, shared and then set aside, helps frightened people find their courage.

In Tom Sawyer, lost in the cave, Tom snuffs out Becky's candle to save the last light, and she understands without words. In hard times, careful sharing of what little remains is a quiet form of care.
In Tom Sawyer, a single drop of water falls in the cave with clock-like regularity, and has done so for ages. Twain's image reminds us that slow, steady things can outlast any single moment of hurry.

In Tom Sawyer, Twain mocks a town that rallies behind a petition to pardon a killer because the feelings are loud. Strong sentiment is no guide to what is right, and it is worth asking what the facts say first.

PREFACE

Most of the adventures recorded in this book really occurred; one or two
were experiences of my own, the rest those of boys who were schoolmates
of mine. Huck Finn is drawn from life; Tom Sawyer also, but not from an
individual—he is a combination of the characteristics of three boys whom
I knew, and therefore belongs to the composite order of architecture.

The odd superstitions touched upon were all prevalent among children and
slaves in the West at the period of this story—that is to say, thirty or
forty years ago.

Although my book is intended mainly for the entertainment of boys and
girls, I hope it will not be shunned by men and women on that account,
for part of my plan has been to try to pleasantly remind adults of what
they once were themselves, and of how they felt and thought and talked,
and what queer enterprises they sometimes engaged in.

THE AUTHOR.

HARTFORD, 1876.

CHAPTER I

“Tom!”

No answer.

“TOM!”

No answer.

“What’s gone with that boy, I wonder? You TOM!”

No answer.

books.title: The War of the Worlds
books.author: H. G. Wells
books.subject: adventure
