notes.text: In The War of the Worlds, H. G. Wells shows how easily people go about their daily affairs, confident in their power, while a larger danger gathers unnoticed around them.
H. G. Wells reminds the reader that humans have wiped out animals and whole peoples, so we should be slow to call others cruel for doing the same.
In The War of the Worlds, Ogilvy waves away the strange signals from Mars with confident reasoning, and the story shows how certainty can blind a person to evidence in front of them.
In The War of the Worlds, Ogilvy goes to look at the fallen object himself while others assume it is an ordinary meteorite, which shows the value of checking for yourself.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator's first instinct is to go to the aid of whatever is trapped inside the cylinder, even though the heat stops him from doing so.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator feels a sudden impulse to help a man trapped in the pit, but fear overrules it, and he is honest about that failure.
In The War of the Worlds, two frightened strangers find some comfort in simply standing side by side in silence, a small kindness at a frightening moment.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator comforts himself with reasoning that leaves out key factors, a reminder that confident conclusions drawn from partial knowledge can be dangerously wrong.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator's excited imagination casts the invaders as easy to beat, a reminder that enthusiasm can make a hard problem look simpler than it really is.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator admits he failed to act on what he had seen because exhaustion and confusion clouded his judgment, a candid look at how fatigue weakens good decisions.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator starts to ask how our own machines would look to a far more advanced mind, a useful habit of seeing ourselves from the outside.
In The War of the Worlds, an experienced soldier insists on a few minutes of preparation before the narrator runs, a reminder that calm, practical steps often beat rushing in a panic.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator tries to warn people who are absorbed in their possessions, and the scene shows how hard it is to make people take a danger seriously before it arrives.
In The War of the Worlds, the Martians learn from their first defeat and change their tactics, a reminder that whoever adapts fastest to experience often gains the advantage.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator steadies a shaken man by reminding him that people have come through disaster before and that hope remains, while staying clear-eyed about the danger.
In The War of the Worlds, Wells notes that people become so used to alarming news in the papers that they read about a catastrophe without feeling any personal alarm, a trap worth watching for today.
In The War of the Worlds, Wells shows how fear spreads through a crowd until a whole city rushes to flee, a reminder to slow down and check the facts before a panic takes hold.
In The War of the Worlds, the disciplined gunners lay their guns calmly while the untrained volunteers bolt, a reminder that steady training and good leadership count for more than bravado.

In The War of the Worlds, the narrator's brother turns back to help two women against robbers, and the frightened woman then returns to help him, a reminder that courage often means going back for someone else.
In The War of the Worlds, H. G. Wells shows a stranger choosing to stay with two frightened women after a fight, offering protection before he knows what lies ahead.
H. G. Wells shows strangers in a crisis sharing what they have. One woman's hesitation ends when she decides to trust the narrator's brother enough to pool their money.
In The War of the Worlds, Wells shows how fear travels through a crowd, so that one quarrel or rumour can drive a whole multitude forward without any of them knowing why.
In The War of the Worlds, Wells shows a narrator's brother setting aside his own fear to lift a crying child and speak gently to her, even in the middle of a disaster.
In The War of the Worlds, Wells shows a man so fixed on grabbing his scattered money that he is cut down in the crush, a picture of how panic pulls people toward the wrong things.
In The War of the Worlds, Wells shows courage as a choice made after fear. The narrator's brother turns back, then, resolved, leads on, and the woman beside him proves her quality.

In The War of the Worlds, Wells describes invaders who aim at demoralisation, cutting telegraphs and railways so a people cannot coordinate its own defence. Communication is what lets a community act together.

In The War of the Worlds, Wells shows a self-appointed Committee of Public Supply seizing a family's pony for a promise in return. Emergency authority is often improvised, and its promises are not always kept.
In The War of the Worlds, Wells shows a frightened woman longing to return to the place that once felt safe. Fear can make the familiar look like safety even when it is not.
In The War of the Worlds, Wells shows the Thunder Child firing no gun as it closes in, and that holding back let it get near enough to strike. Restraint can sometimes be the stronger move.
In The War of the Worlds, Wells shows the Thunder Child steaming straight at a far stronger enemy to shield the fleeing ships. Its sacrifice makes courage plain to everyone watching.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator realises that in a crisis what is needed is not bravery but circumspection. Anxiety left to brood makes a person irritable and cut off from useful action.
In The War of the Worlds, Wells shows a companion who keeps saying they are safe, even after the danger has changed. The comfort of staying put can hide the fact that the way out has opened.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator takes careful stock of every loaf, tin and bottle in the pantry. Knowing exactly what you have is a quiet kind of safety when a long wait lies ahead.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator warns that a hasty secondhand picture can mislead more than it informs. Firsthand observation, slowly made, is the better guide to what is really happening.

In The War of the Worlds, the narrator and the curate fight over a turn at a peephole even while starving and in mortal danger. Wells shows how small privileges can grow fierce when people feel their chances slipping away.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator forces himself to face the facts in the dark, and finds that despair is not yet justified. Clear thinking can reveal a chance that panic hides.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator sets a strict ration to last ten days when no help is coming. Discipline about what is shared matters more than appetite in a long wait.

In The War of the Worlds, the narrator, driven by fear, turns the blade of his chopper back and strikes with the blunt end. It is a small act of restraint, showing that people can keep some humanity even at their worst.

In The War of the Worlds, Wells has his narrator feel the humbling thought that people are no longer masters of their world, only animals among animals. Mastery is never guaranteed, and that can be a useful humility.
In The War of the Worlds, the narrator judges his own violent act honestly, with no excuses and no self-pity. He admits he should have foreseen the harm, and accepts that the reader must judge him.

In The War of the Worlds, the narrator comes to feel what it is like to be hunted and made small. Wells suggests that knowing the fear of the powerless can teach a person pity for those they have dominated.
In The War of the Worlds, the artilleryman argues that in a crisis the person who keeps thinking, rather than squealing or rushing with the crowd, is the one who comes through.

In The War of the Worlds, the artilleryman argues that when the facts change, a person should fit their plans to what the facts point to, not to what they wish were true. Wells puts that discipline at the heart of survival.
In The War of the Worlds, the artilleryman argues that bare survival is not enough. What a people must save is its knowledge, its books and its science, and keep adding to them.

In The War of the Worlds, the narrator sees the gulf between a grand plan and the real work it takes. Wells suggests that big dreams should be tested against the hours and hands they will actually need.
In The War of the Worlds, Wells notes that even at the edge of ruin people play cards and take delight in small pleasures. Ordinary enjoyments can be a way of keeping hold of yourself.

In The War of the Worlds, the narrator's sense of wonder and proportion returns as he looks out over the dark city from a roof. Stepping back to see the whole picture can restore perspective after a run of foolish days.

In The War of the Worlds, the narrator looks out over London and sees the work of countless lives, and realises it can live again. Wells makes the point that what many people have built together is worth grieving for and protecting.

In The War of the Worlds, Wells shows strangers who have their own losses still taking in a grieving man, sheltering him and protecting him from himself. Kindness is often given quietly by people who have little to spare.
In The War of the Worlds, Wells's narrator suggests that the invasion, though terrible, has shaken people out of a false sense of safety and helped them see that they share one common fate.

preview.text:
No one would have believed in the last years of the nineteenth century
that this world was being watched keenly and closely by intelligences
greater than man’s and yet as mortal as his own; that as men busied
themselves about their various concerns they were scrutinised and
studied, perhaps almost as narrowly as a man with a microscope might
scrutinise the transient creatures that swarm and multiply in a drop of
water. With infinite complacency men went to and fro over this globe
about their little affairs, serene in their assurance of their empire
over matter. It is possible that the infusoria under the microscope do
the same. No one gave a thought to the older worlds of space as sources
of human danger, or thought of them only to dismiss the idea of life
upon them as impossible or improbable. It is curious to recall some of
the mental habits of those departed days. At most terrestrial men
fancied there might be other men upon Mars, perhaps inferior to
themselves and ready to welcome a missionary enterprise. Yet across the
gulf of space, minds that are to our minds as ours are to those of the
beasts that perish, intellects vast and cool and unsympathetic,
regarded this earth with envious eyes, and slowly and surely drew their
plans against us. And early in the twentieth century came the great
disillusionment.

notes.text: In The Purloined Letter, Poe shows a Prefect who calls whatever he cannot comprehend 'odd', and so never looks closely at the plain facts in front of him.
In The Purloined Letter, Poe shows that a secret's power lies in holding it, not using it, since the power departs once the document is employed.
In The Purloined Letter, Dupin reasons that a clever rival will have already anticipated the obvious searches, so the hiding place is somewhere nobody thought to look.
In The Purloined Letter, the Prefect repeats the same search with more labour and finds nothing, because the method was wrong rather than the effort.
In The Purloined Letter, the schoolboy wins at guessing by picturing himself in his opponent's place and reading that opponent's mind, a skill any good reasoner needs.
In The Purloined Letter, Dupin says the Prefect searches only by his own notions of cleverness, so he fails whenever the person he is chasing thinks differently.
In The Purloined Letter, Dupin warns against treating rules that hold for numbers as universal truths, because in human matters the parts often do not add up to the whole.
In The Purloined Letter, Dupin fits his method to the particular man, his capacity and his circumstances, rather than applying one standard procedure to everyone.
In The Purloined Letter, Dupin argues that the most obvious things escape notice, like the largest words on a map, so something may be hidden in plain view.
In The Purloined Letter, Dupin notes that odd signs only strengthen suspicion in someone who came intending to suspect, so it pays to test your own expectations.
In The Purloined Letter, Dupin notices a small wear on the edges of a letter, a detail that only a patient observer catches when he keeps his attention steady.
In The Thousand-and-Second Tale of Scheherazade, Poe's heroine wins the king's attention by stopping each night at a moment of suspense, showing how a good story keeps people wanting more.
In The Thousand-and-Second Tale of Scheherazade, Poe notes that a pleasant ending is not always a true one, and that a wrong record is worth correcting.
In The Thousand-and-Second Tale of Scheherazade, Sinbad regrets his folly once he is captured, then turns to making the best of his condition and winning over his captor.
In The Thousand-and-Second Tale of Scheherazade, Sinbad is ashamed of his contempt for his companion once he learns the man's own homeland, a reminder to withhold judgement until we know people.
In A Descent into the Maelstrom, the old fisherman tells the terrified narrator to get over his fancies, so he can look at the real facts of the danger in front of him.
In A Descent into the Maelstrom, the narrator finds that written accounts cannot convey what a thing is like to see with your own eyes, a reminder to test reports against direct experience.
In A Descent into the Maelstrom, the fisherman survives by instinct, lying flat and holding a solid fixture when he is too flurried to think, which is often the wisest move under pressure.
In A Descent into the Maelstrom, the narrator learns that his watch stopped hours earlier, so he had been acting on the wrong time, a sharp warning to check that your instruments are still running.
In A Descent into the Maelstrom, the narrator grows steadier once he stops hoping for rescue and faces the situation as it is, since fear often feeds on the hope itself.
In A Descent into the Maelstrom, the narrator saves himself by noticing which floating things survive the whirl, reasoning from careful observation of the evidence rather than from fear.
In Von Kempelen and His Discovery, Poe doubts a claimed invention partly because its teller took no quick action on it, a sensible test of whether a story holds together.

In Von Kempelen and His Discovery, Poe describes Davy as too careful to speak out until he had everything ready for a practical demonstration, a good model for claiming results only once they are proven.
In Von Kempelen and His Discovery, the police haul away a heavy trunk they dismiss as brass, never imagining its value, a reminder that we often overlook what we did not expect to find.
In Mesmeric Revelation, the narrator finds that abstract argument may amuse and exercise the mind but takes little hold on belief, which tends to come from lived experience.
In The Facts in the Case of M. Valdemar, Poe notes that when facts are kept back from the public, a garbled account fills the gap and breeds disbelief, so it pays to tell the true story early.
In The Black Cat, the narrator hopes a calmer, more logical mind will see his terrible events as ordinary causes and effects, a reminder that fear can make the everyday seem unnatural.
In The Black Cat, the narrator's drinking slowly turns a gentle man cruel, showing how unchecked habits wear down character one day at a time.
In The Black Cat, Poe describes the spirit of perverseness, the urge to do a thing only because we know we should not, and asks the reader to notice it in themselves.
In The Black Cat, the narrator's dread grows from a faint mark he slowly comes to read as a gallows, showing how an anxious mind can turn a vague stain into a certainty.
In The Black Cat, Poe shows a man who takes his own relief as proof he is innocent, and how easily a guilty mind talks itself into calm.
In The Black Cat, Poe shows how a guilty man's pride in his own cleverness can betray him, pushing him to speak when silence would have saved him.
In The Fall of the House of Usher, the narrator admits he cannot fully explain why a scene weighs on him, and sees that a simple arrangement of ordinary things can change how it feels.
In The Fall of the House of Usher, the narrator answers an old friend's distressed letter because of the heart behind it, showing that loyalty often matters more than strangeness.
In The Fall of the House of Usher, the narrator notices that dwelling on his own dread makes it grow, an observation about how fear feeds on attention.
In The Fall of the House of Usher, Roderick Usher dreads the results of events more than the events themselves, and shows how fear of fear can wear a person down.
In The Fall of the House of Usher, a painter's plain, stripped-down designs hold attention more firmly than detail does, because simplicity leaves nothing to hide behind.
In The Fall of the House of Usher, the narrator says a frightened friend's terror infected him too, a reminder that anxiety spreads between people who sit close together.
In The Fall of the House of Usher, the narrator reads aloud to calm a distressed friend, a small act of care that matters even when the book chosen is a poor fit.
In The Fall of the House of Usher, the narrator hides his own alarm so as not to agitate a fragile friend, a quiet form of kindness that costs him something.
In The Fall of the House of Usher, Usher's dread of speaking up torments him for days, showing how a truth we keep avoiding can weigh more heavily than the thing itself.
In the fable Silence, Poe suggests that a man who wants the world made still ends up facing a stillness that frightens him more than the noise ever did.
In The Masque of the Red Death, Prince Prospero walls himself off from the suffering outside and assumes it can take care of itself, a lesson in how shutting out trouble does not stop it.
In The Masque of the Red Death, Prince Prospero's rage and shame drive him to chase the intruder alone, and that pride leads straight to his death.
In The Cask of Amontillado, Poe shows that Fortunato's pride in his own expertise is the weak point a clever rival can use, since people often let vanity lead them.
In The Cask of Amontillado, Montresor wraps his plans in a show of concern for Fortunato's health, a reminder that a smooth tone of care can hide a cold purpose.
In The Imp of the Perverse, Poe notes that a passing thought of provoking someone can grow into a craving we indulge even against our own better judgment.
In The Imp of the Perverse, Poe describes how a task we must finish today becomes harder to start as the deadline nears, because the urge to delay grows with every hour we wait.
In The Imp of the Perverse, Poe describes the pull we feel toward a precipice, where the very warning of reason makes us lean closer, a sign that fear and temptation can grow together.
In The Imp of the Perverse, a reassurance the narrator repeats to himself turns into a haunting worry, a reminder that comfort we rehearse too often can wear thin.
In The Island of the Fay, Poe argues that some pleasures, such as music and the quiet beauty of nature, are felt most fully when we are alone with them.
In The Island of the Fay, the narrator watches a fairy's shadow fall away with each circuit of the sun, a reminder that every day, lived or wasted, carries us a little nearer the end.
In The Assignation, the narrator grieves a gifted friend and refuses to judge his visionary hours as wasted, a generous way of seeing someone whose dreams never fit the world.
In The Assignation, the Marchesa's grief leaves her staring at distant things rather than what is close at hand, a sharp observation of how sorrow can make us look away from the people who need us.
In The Assignation, a stranger leaps into the canal after the search has given up, showing courage that acts when everyone else has stopped trying.

In The Assignation, the host recalls the old idea that a sculptor finds the statue already inside the marble, a useful reminder that making something well is often a matter of cutting away what is not needed.
In The Pit and the Pendulum, the prisoner tears a strip from his robe to mark where he began, a sound method for finding his way that fails only because he underestimates the task.
In The Pit and the Pendulum, the prisoner miscounts the size of his cell because his fear has clouded his thinking, a reminder to slow down and check our reckoning whenever panic takes hold.
In The Pit and the Pendulum, the prisoner holds back terror by fixing his mind on small, trivial details, a coping habit that can steady a frightened person for a while.
In The Pit and the Pendulum, the prisoner finds that hope keeps him flinching and struggling even when reason says there is none, showing how hope can outlast the reasons we have for it.

preview.text:
“That is another of your odd notions,” said the Prefect, who had
      a fashion of calling every thing “odd” that was beyond his
      comprehension, and thus lived amid an absolute legion of
      “oddities.”

“Very true,” said Dupin, as he supplied his visitor with a pipe,
      and rolled towards him a comfortable chair.

“And what is the difficulty now?” I asked. “Nothing more in the
      assassination way, I hope?”

“Oh no; nothing of that nature. The fact is, the business is very
      simple indeed, and I make no doubt that we can manage it
      sufficiently well ourselves; but then I thought Dupin would like
      to hear the details of it, because it is so excessively odd.”

“Simple and odd,” said Dupin.

“Why, yes; and not exactly that, either. The fact is, we have all
      been a good deal puzzled because the affair is so simple, and yet
      baffles us altogether.”

“Perhaps it is the very simplicity of the thing which puts you at
      fault,” said my friend.

“What nonsense you do talk!” replied the Prefect, laughing
      heartily.

“Perhaps the mystery is a little too plain,” said Dupin.

“Oh, good heavens! who ever heard of such an idea?”

“A little too self-evident.”

“Ha! ha! ha—ha! ha! ha!—ho! ho! ho!” roared our visitor,
      profoundly amused, “oh, Dupin, you will be the death of me yet!”

“And what, after all, is the matter on hand?” I asked.

“Why, I will tell you,” replied the Prefect, as he gave a long,
      steady and contemplative puff, and settled himself in his chair.
      “I will tell you in a few words; but, before I begin, let me
      caution you that this is an affair demanding the greatest
      secrecy, and that I should most probably lose the position I now
      hold, were it known that I confided it to any one.”

notes.text: In The Twelve Dancing Princesses, Michael leaves home with his bundle while the village laughs at him, showing that a bold choice often starts with ignoring the mockery.
In The Twelve Dancing Princesses, Michael feels a strong longing to try his luck but holds back for fear of being jeered at, a familiar pull for anyone who has stayed quiet about a chance.
In The Twelve Dancing Princesses, Michael turns down Lina's purse of gold for his silence, saying he does not sell his silence. Integrity often means refusing a tempting reward.
In The Twelve Dancing Princesses, Michael stays clear-headed under flattery and fine food, refusing to be turned by praise even when everyone is trying to flatter him.

In The Princess Mayblossom, the Queen brushes aside the ugly stranger without a second thought, and the cost of that contempt follows her, showing that how we treat people we dismiss can come back to us.
In The Princess Mayblossom, the last fairy cannot undo Carabosse's curse but offers a long, happy life afterwards, showing that a kind hope can soften harm even when it cannot cancel it.
In The Princess Mayblossom, the Princess settles on her husband in a moment, dazzled by a splendid procession, a reminder that first impressions of show are a poor guide to character.
In The Princess Mayblossom, the Princess eases the tongue-tied ambassador with a light, kind remark, showing how graciousness can rescue someone from their own awkwardness.

In The Princess Mayblossom, the Princess tells Fanfaronade plainly how she feels and says she will love him though he is no prince, showing that honesty about the heart clears the way to a true match.
In The Princess Mayblossom, Fanfaronade grumbles about hunger and wishes her back in the tower once hardship arrives, showing how easily affection sours when it has no patience for hard days.

In The Princess Mayblossom, the Princess offers Fanfaronade a honeycomb she could have kept, and he takes it without thanks, a reminder that generosity is still worth giving even when it is not returned.
In The Princess Mayblossom, Fanfaronade's push over the cliff fails and he is lost to the sea, showing how a plot to harm someone can end by undoing the one who plots it.
In Soria Moria Castle, Halvor, who never stays at any task at home, comes into his own when he sets out to see the world, showing that a restless youngster can grow into a brave one.
In Soria Moria Castle, Halvor refuses to run from the Troll because he has done no wrong, showing how a clear conscience can give a person courage when others would flee.
In Soria Moria Castle, Halvor finds that comfort is not enough to hold him when he longs for his parents, showing that the pull of home can outweigh even a very pleasant life.
In Soria Moria Castle, the farm girls who once looked down on Halvor are left ashamed when he returns changed, a reminder that people who sneer at others may one day be humbled.
In Soria Moria Castle, the Princess asks who is truly worthy, and the one who freed her wins out over the one dressed in fine clothes, showing that deeds count for more than appearances.
In The Death of Koshchei the Deathless, Prince Ivan lets each sister choose her own husband and does not keep them by him, showing a generous kind of love that wants others to be free and happy.
In The Death of Koshchei the Deathless, Ivan cannot resist opening the forbidden closet, and his curiosity sets the enemy free, showing how one broken rule can carry large consequences.
In The Death of Koshchei the Deathless, Ivan goes back for Marya Morevna again and again, saying he cannot live without her, showing a devotion that will not give up even after great loss.

In The Death of Koshchei the Deathless, Ivan spares the lioness, the bees and the outlandish bird, and each later repays him, showing that small kindnesses to others can return when they are needed most.
In The Black Thief and Knight of the Glen, the dying Queen asks her husband to educate their sons so they can stand on their own feet, a plain plea that good parents have always made.
In The Black Thief and Knight of the Glen, the second Queen's jealousy of her stepsons turns into a plot against them, showing how envy of another's affection can lead a person to cruelty.
In The Black Thief and Knight of the Glen, the youngest prince chooses to go with his brothers into danger, showing a loyalty that will not leave others to face a hard road alone.
In The Black Thief and Knight of the Glen, the Thief of Sloan offers to guide the princes and share their risk, showing how someone who takes on danger alongside others earns real trust.

In The Black Thief and Knight of the Glen, the Thief of Sloan saves a child from a giant by quick thinking and a clever substitute, showing that ingenuity used for someone else's good can turn danger aside.
In The Black Thief and Knight of the Glen, the Knight pardons the thieves once he hears how the Thief once saved a child's life, showing that a known act of kindness can earn mercy from a hard man.
In The Black Thief and Knight of the Glen, the Knight gives up his prized steed rather than see a brave man die, showing that generosity can be the answer to a plea for mercy.

In The Master Thief, the youngest son wins a place among the robbers by taking the farmer's oxen through clever tricks and without harming him, showing that quick wit can achieve a lot without cruelty.
In The Master Thief, the Priest is talked out of his gold with a false promise of heaven, showing how greed and a wish for a shortcut to reward can make a person easy to fool.

In The Master Thief, the Governor keeps putting off his promise to give his daughter in marriage and sets ever harder tests, showing how a powerful person who will not keep his word teaches others to distrust him.

In Brother and Sister, the sister promises her transformed brother that she will never forsake him and keeps that promise through hardship, showing a loyalty that holds even when the other person has changed.
In Brother and Sister, the King looks kindly on the lonely maiden and promises that her Roe will be cared for too, showing that real kindness extends to the people and creatures someone loves.
In Brother and Sister, the Queen returns in secret to tend her child and her Roe, and a long, quiet love shows itself in small, faithful acts.
In Princess Rosette, the Queen covers her worry with small excuses, and the King sees through them until she tells him the truth, showing that honesty settles more between a couple than evasion does.
In Princess Rosette, the trusted nurse plots to drown the Princess for a bag of gold, a reminder that betrayal can come from the people meant to guard us most.
In Princess Rosette, the old man who finds the Princess drifting at sea wades in at risk to his own life and asks nothing in return, a quiet picture of kindness from a stranger.
In Princess Rosette, the Princess chooses not to reveal where she is, since the King tried to drown her, showing that a wronged person can be wise to keep their own counsel.
In Princess Rosette, the King and Princess freely forgive the nurse, the boatman and the false bride, and the story closes on mercy given without conditions.
In The Enchanted Pig, the sisters talk each other into breaking their father's rule by calling it harmless, showing how a group can coax one another into a small wrong.
In The Enchanted Pig, the youngest Princess is worn down by fear and guilt over her disobedience until she loses her colour and her joy, showing how a secret can slowly eat away at a person.
In The Enchanted Pig, the Princess keeps faith with her strange husband and comes to love him for his gentle kindness, showing that patient loyalty can bring out the good in someone.
In The Enchanted Pig, after her husband vanishes, the Princess weeps for a while and then sets out on the long road, showing how grief can be met with action and perseverance.
In The Enchanted Pig, the Princess keeps a brave heart through fire-flint mountains, ice and snow, showing that steady perseverance can carry a person further than strength alone.
In The Enchanted Pig, the Princess gives up part of her own finger to finish the ladder that reaches her husband, showing a readiness to pay a personal price to reach what she loves.
In the Romanian tale of the Pig, the Prince is freed less by cleverness than by the love and pity he feels on seeing his wife's suffering, which turns him back into a man.
In The Norka, the two elder brothers fail by spending the night drinking, while the youngest, mocked as simple, succeeds by planning ahead so his weapons would wake him.
In The Norka, the youngest brother is the only one willing to go down into the other world, and the story shows that courage often comes from the least expected person.
In The Norka, the Prince's kindness to a storm-soaked brood of young birds is repaid when their mother carries him to the other world, showing that small mercies come back.
In The Norka, the Prince takes humble work as a tailor's servant and quietly solves the King's problem without announcing who he is, showing that real skill does not need a crown to prove it.
In The Norka, a bride recognises her rescuer by the ring she once gave him, and the truth comes out once the brothers' lies are no longer able to hold.
In The Wonderful Birch, the girl keeps her mother's last instruction and refuses the soup, and from the buried bones grows the tree that later helps her.
In The Wonderful Birch, the narrator asks us to feel sorry for the witch's daughter, because it was not her fault that her mother was a witch.
In The Wonderful Birch, the deceitful bride is left stranded as a bridge over the river, while the true bride is only recognised once she speaks up for herself.
In The Wonderful Birch, the Prince listens to a wise widow and stands firm against the witch's objections, and it is patience and care that find the way back to his true wife.
In The Wonderful Birch, the husband holds steady through every shape his wife takes to escape him, and that steadiness is what brings her back to herself.
In Jack and the Beanstalk, Jack's foolishness costs his family their cow, but he is up at daybreak to try again, and that willingness to keep going is what opens a new path.
In Jack and the Beanstalk, Jack rests when he is tired but refuses to turn back, because he knows the way to succeed is not to give up.
In Jack and the Beanstalk, the old nurse persuades the grieving lady to stay alive for her child, showing that duty to the living can carry us through grief.
In Jack and the Beanstalk, Jack holds that courage comes from doing what is right, and he sets himself to be brave even while he is frightened.

The farmer began to scold him furiously, but he answered quietly, ‘I am
going away,’ made his clothes into a bundle, said good-bye to all his
friends, and boldly set out to seek his fortunes.

There was great excitement through all the village, and on the top of
the hill the people stood holding their sides with laughing, as they
watched the Star Gazer trudging bravely along the valley with his
bundle at the end of his stick.

It was enough to make anyone laugh, certainly.

III

It was well known for full twenty miles round that there lived in the
castle of Beloeil twelve princesses of wonderful beauty, and as proud
as they were beautiful, and who were besides so very sensitive and of
such truly royal blood, that they would have felt at once the presence
of a pea in their beds, even if the mattresses had been laid over it.

It was whispered about that they led exactly the lives that princesses
ought to lead, sleeping far into the morning, and never getting up till
mid-day. They had twelve beds all in the same room, but what was very
extraordinary was the fact that though they were locked in by triple
bolts, every morning their satin shoes were found worn into holes.

When they were asked what they had been doing all night, they always
answered that they had been asleep; and, indeed, no noise was ever
heard in the room, yet the shoes could not wear themselves out alone!

At last the Duke of Beloeil ordered the trumpet to be sounded, and a
proclamation to be made that whoever could discover how his daughters
wore out their shoes should choose one of them for his wife.

books.title: The Analects
books.author: Confucius
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 479 BCE, translator died 1897. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Analects, Confucius's disciple Zengzi checked himself each day on three points: was he faithful in business for others, sincere with friends, and did he practise what he had been taught.
In The Analects, Confucius held faithfulness and sincerity as first principles, and told people not to fear abandoning their faults.
In The Analects, Confucius says a person aiming for virtue does not chase comfort, is earnest in his work, careful in speech, and keeps company with people of principle.
In The Analects, Confucius says he will not mind people failing to know him, but he will mind that he does not know other people.
In The Analects, Confucius argues that people led by laws and punishment avoid the penalty without shame, while people led by virtue and propriety become good.
In The Analects, Confucius traces his own growth, from setting his mind on learning at fifteen to following his heart without going against what is right at seventy.
In The Analects, Confucius warns that learning without thought is wasted effort, and thought without learning is dangerous.
In The Analects, Confucius says a superior man acts first and speaks afterwards, so that his words follow from what he has done.
In The Analects, Confucius says a leader who presides with gravity, treats people with kindness, and advances the good while teaching the less capable wins loyalty and effort.
In The Analects, Confucius defines knowledge simply: to know what you know, and to admit what you do not know.
In The Analects, Confucius says a person without truthfulness cannot get on, just as a carriage cannot move without the yoke that joins it to the animals.
In The Analects, Confucius says that at festive ceremonies it is better to be sparing than extravagant, and at mourning to feel real sorrow rather than fuss over details.
In The Analects, Confucius says a person of virtue has no need for quarrels, and even in a contest bows to his rivals and stays a gentleman.
In The Analects, Confucius shows humility in learning: on entering the grand temple he asked about everything, and he treated that questioning as proper conduct.
In The Analects, Confucius says that what is already done need not be talked over, what has run its course need not be argued, and what is past need not be blamed.
In The Analects, Confucius says that ritual without reverence and high position without generosity are empty, and he could not bear to look on such ways.
In The Analects, Confucius says that riches and honours obtained by improper means should not be kept, and that a person of virtue does not act against virtue even for the length of a meal.
In The Analects, Confucius says that a superior person thinks of virtue and what is right, while a small person thinks of comfort and easy favours.
In The Analects, Confucius says a person should worry less about having no position than about fitting himself for one, and less about not being known than about being worthy to be known.
In The Analects, Confucius warns that someone who always acts for his own advantage will be much complained against.
In The Analects, Confucius says the ancients were slow to speak because they feared their actions would fall short of their words.
In The Analects, Confucius says that people with a ready tongue often make enemies, and that smooth talk is no proof of virtue.
In The Analects, Confucius changed how he judged people: once he took their words on trust, and later he watched what they actually did.
In The Analects, Confucius admires a man who was active, fond of learning, and not ashamed to ask those beneath him, which earned him a title of honour.
In The Analects, Confucius praises Zichan as humble in conduct, respectful to superiors, kind in caring for the people, and just in ordering them.
In The Analects, Confucius praises Yan Ping for keeping the same respect in a friendship however long it lasted.
In The Analects, Po-i and Shu-ch'i are praised for not keeping old wrongs in mind, so the resentment they drew was small.
In The Analects, Confucius despairs of anyone who cannot see his own faults and inwardly accuse himself.
In The Analects, Confucius's wish is to give rest to the aged, sincerity to friends, and tenderness to the young.
In The Analects, Confucius names Yan Hui as the disciple who loved learning, who did not vent his anger on others and did not repeat a mistake.
In The Analects, Confucius says a person of high character helps those in distress rather than adding to the wealth of those who already have plenty.
In The Analects, Confucius admires Yan Hui for staying cheerful on very little in a poor lane, because his joy did not depend on his circumstances.
In The Analects, Confucius ranks learning in three steps: those who know the truth are below those who love it, and those who love it are below those who delight in it.
In The Analects, Confucius says that where substance outruns polish we get rusticity, where polish outruns substance we get the manners of a clerk, and balance makes a person of virtue.
In The Analects, Confucius says a superior person can be led to the edge of a well but not into it, and can be imposed upon but not fooled.
In The Analects, Confucius says that helping others to stand is part of standing oneself, and that the art of virtue is to judge others by what is near in oneself.
In The Analects, Confucius lists four things to hold to: set the will on the path of duty, grasp every good attainment firmly, live by perfect virtue, and find relaxation in the arts.
In The Analects, Confucius says he does not open up a subject to someone who is not eager to learn, and if a person cannot take the other three corners from one, he does not repeat the lesson.
In The Analects, Confucius says that riches and honours obtained by unrighteousness are to him like a floating cloud, and that he still finds joy in very simple living.
In The Analects, Confucius says that when he walks with two others, one of them may serve as his teacher, and he takes their good qualities and avoids their bad.
In The Analects, Confucius describes the second kind of knowledge as hearing much, choosing what is good and following it, and keeping much in memory.
In The Analects, Confucius says that to pretend to have what one lacks, and to appear full while empty, makes it hard to keep constant to anything.
In The Analects, Confucius says the hardest thing for him is to carry out in conduct what he professes, more than skill in letters.
In The Analects, Confucius says the superior person is satisfied and composed, while the small person is always full of distress.
In The Analects, Zengzi recalls a friend who was gifted yet asked those less gifted, was full yet counted himself empty, and did not answer insults with argument.

In The Analects, Confucius says a person in high position should keep away from violence and carelessness in conduct, stay close to sincerity in expression, and avoid vulgarity and impropriety in speech.
In The Analects, Zengzi says a leader's load is heavy and his course long, because perfect virtue is the burden he carries, and it ends only with death.
In The Analects, Confucius says people can be led along a path of action, but cannot always be made to understand it.
In The Analects, Confucius says a learner should study as if they could never reach their goal, and always fear losing hold of it.
In The Analects, Confucius praises Yu for simple food and clothes, yet for pouring all his strength into the work of channels and ditches.
In The Analects, Confucius says a person can be free of fixed conclusions, arbitrary predeterminations, obstinacy and self-centredness.
In The Analects, Confucius does not claim to have knowledge, but when even a humble person asks him something, he explains it fully from one end to the other.
In The Analects, Confucius compares learning to raising a mound: stopping before the last basket is one's own choice, and each basket added is one's own going forward.
In The Analects, Confucius says that strict admonition is valuable only if it leads to a change in conduct, and gentle advice is valuable only if it draws out a person's aims.
In The Analects, Confucius says the wise are free from perplexity, the virtuous from anxiety, and the bold from fear.
In The Analects, when the stable burned Confucius first asked whether anyone was hurt, and did not ask about the horses.
In The Analects, Confucius takes responsibility for the burial of any friend who has no relatives able to see to it, saying he will bury them.
In The Analects, Confucius praises Min Ziqian as a man who speaks seldom, but when he does, always hits the point.
In The Analects, Confucius asks whether a person whose speech seems solid and sincere is truly a superior person, or whether his gravity is only in appearance.
In The Analects, Confucius says a great minister serves his ruler according to what is right, and retires when he cannot do so.
