books.title: Frankenstein
books.author: Mary Shelley
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1851. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Frankenstein, Mary Shelley has Walton say that a steady purpose calms the mind more than anything, because it gives the soul one point to fix on.
In Frankenstein, Walton spends years toughening his body and studying at night before his voyage, showing that a big goal is built from many small, hard habits.
In Frankenstein, Walton admits he needs a friend who will sympathise with him and tell him honestly where his plans are weak. Honest counsel is worth seeking out.
In Frankenstein, Walton describes a ship's master who gives up his farm and savings so a rival can marry the woman he loves. Real generosity often costs something.
In Frankenstein, Walton admits his dreams are wild but calls himself practically industrious, a workman who sticks at things with patience. Big dreams still need that plodding.
In Frankenstein, Walton sees a broken stranger's whole face light up at a small kindness, showing that even deep grief responds to ordinary care.
In Frankenstein, Walton tells of his drive to give up everything for his ambition, and the stranger he rescued is moved to tears. Others can see the cost of a goal before we do.
In Frankenstein, the stranger says a wiser, better friend helps refine our weak and faulty natures, so none of us is fully made up on our own.
In Frankenstein, the stranger warns Walton that the knowledge he chases may become a serpent that stings him. The price of a goal is not always visible at the start.

In Frankenstein, Victor's father grieves that his friend's false pride drove him into poverty and hiding, when a few honest words could have brought help. Pride can cut people off from help they need.
In Frankenstein, Caroline Beaufort keeps herself and her dying father going by plaiting straw and taking any work she can find. Courage often looks like plain daily perseverance.
In Frankenstein, Victor's father values tried worth above showy promise, and loves most those he has seen prove themselves. Judge people by what they have done.
In Frankenstein, Victor says his parents' care taught him patience, charity and self-control, guiding him as with a silken cord rather than force.
In Frankenstein, Victor's mother feels helping the poor is a duty and a passion, because she remembers how she was once helped. Kindness tends to be passed on.
In Frankenstein, Victor and Elizabeth are very different, and their contrast draws them closer. Good partnerships often rest on different strengths rather than sameness.
In Frankenstein, Victor says his parents were kind and indulgent, and that seeing other families made him grateful for his lot. Noticing how well off you are is a start to gratitude.
In Frankenstein, Elizabeth softens Clerval's love of heroic deeds until doing good becomes the aim of his ambition. The people around us can steer our ambition toward kindness.
In Frankenstein, Victor's father brushes off a book without explaining why. Victor reads on alone and is led astray, so a dismissed question can leave a young mind to find its own way.
In Frankenstein, Victor follows his authors and takes their word for everything. Learning from others goes wrong when you stop checking what they tell you.
In Frankenstein, Victor throws out all his old studies after one dazzling lecture. A single exciting idea is a poor reason to abandon a path you have chosen with care.
In Frankenstein, Victor says grief becomes an indulgence rather than a necessity once time passes, and the living still have duties to perform. Keep going while honouring what you have lost.
In Frankenstein, Elizabeth hides her own grief to comfort the whole family. Courage often looks like steady service to people who are hurting.
In Frankenstein, Professor Waldman says the labours of earlier thinkers, even when misdirected, usually end up helping people. Respecting those who came before you is a useful habit.

In Frankenstein, Professor Waldman advises a young student not to master one narrow field alone, since a person who studies only one branch makes a poor practitioner of it too. Breadth sharpens your own specialty.
In Frankenstein, Waldman teaches frankly and with good nature, free of pedantry, and makes hard ideas easy to take in. Good teachers clear the path rather than show off.
In Frankenstein, Victor says a mind of only moderate capacity will grow very skilled if it pursues one object closely. Steady focus can matter more than raw talent.

In Frankenstein, the narrator warns that the man who aspires to be greater than his nature allows comes to ruin, and asks his listener to learn from his example. Ambition needs a clear view of its cost.
In Frankenstein, Victor concludes that no pursuit should weaken your affection for the people and simple pleasures you love. A goal that costs you your home life has gone wrong somewhere.
In Frankenstein, Victor finds the dream he chased for two years looks very different once it is finished. Check that the goal you want still matches how you will feel when you reach it.
In Frankenstein, Clerval nurses his friend through months of illness and hides how bad it was so the family will not worry. Steady loyalty often looks quiet and unshowy.
In Frankenstein, Elizabeth says Justine's frank, cheerful manner could lift anyone's bad mood. Warmth is a real gift to the people around you.
In Frankenstein, Clerval sees his friend's pain and never pries, quietly steering the talk elsewhere. Respecting what someone will not yet say can be a form of care.
In Frankenstein, Victor says a narrow, single-minded pursuit had cramped him until a friend's gentleness opened him up again. Too much focus can shrink a person, and good company can widen them.
In Frankenstein, Victor's father urges him to come home in peace rather than brood on revenge, because hatred festers wounds that kindness can heal.
In Frankenstein, Victor dreads what may have changed at home and says the calm of the lake restores him. Fears of unnamed evils often loom larger than the facts.
In Frankenstein, Victor faces what his own creation has done and admits he let a wretch loose on the world. Owning the results of your work is where responsibility starts.
In Frankenstein, Victor keeps silent about the truth because he fears no one will believe him, and that silence lets harm grow. Hiding a problem seldom makes it smaller.
In Frankenstein, a servant's find and an accused girl's flustered manner turn her into the presumed culprit. Nervousness under pressure can look like guilt, so check the evidence before you judge.
In Frankenstein, the crowd at Justine's trial withdraws all its kindness once it imagines the worst of her. Public judgement often runs ahead of the facts.
In Frankenstein, Justine does not ask to be believed because she is good. She rests her case on a plain account of the facts, which is the honest way to answer a serious charge.

In Frankenstein, Elizabeth speaks up for a frightened friend when others go quiet, because she knows her character from years of living together. Standing up for someone when it costs you is a real test of friendship.

In Frankenstein, Justine confesses to a crime she did not commit after a confessor's threats and with no one to support her. Pressure and isolation can push people into saying things that are not true.
In Frankenstein, Victor's father says grief should not overwhelm the people who depend on you, since excessive sorrow stops a person being useful. Keep doing your daily duties while you mourn.
In Frankenstein, Victor is held back from despair by remembering the people who would be left unprotected without him. Responsibility to others can be an anchor when you feel lost.
In Frankenstein, Victor finds that standing before huge mountains and glaciers puts his sorrow in proportion. Grief eases a little when your attention is pulled outward toward something larger.
In Frankenstein, the creature says he was once benevolent, and that being shunned by everyone made him bitter. Rejection and loneliness can turn good intentions sour.
In Frankenstein, Victor finally sees that a creator owes his creation care before he can blame it for its faults. Whoever brings something into being carries a duty to look after it.

In Frankenstein, the creature learns to keep a fire going by watching what happens, testing wet and dry wood, and guarding the flame each night. Patient observation turns a lucky accident into a skill.
In Frankenstein, the creature is driven off with stones for entering a cottage, and learns that people judge by appearance first. Fear of the unfamiliar can turn quickly into cruelty.
In Frankenstein, the creature learns about kindness by quietly watching a family share work and food. People can learn good conduct just by seeing it practised together.

In Frankenstein, the creature stops stealing from a poor family once he sees it hurts them, and quietly does their chores instead. Noticing who bears the cost of your actions is the start of doing right by them.

In Frankenstein, Felix shows love in small daily acts, clearing snow from his sister's path and fetching water before she wakes, even when they have little. Ordinary kindness often holds a family together.
In Frankenstein, the creature hopes to win people over with gentle manners and kind deeds before they ever see his appearance. Good conduct over time can earn trust that looks alone cannot.
In Frankenstein, the creature says a gentle being with kind intentions deserves better than blows, even if its manners are clumsy. Judge people by their intentions as well as their manner.
In Frankenstein, Shelley has the creature learn language and history by close attention to a family's lessons, showing how patient listening can build a mind.
In Frankenstein, Mary Shelley has the creature see humanity as both noble and base, and only understand why laws exist once he hears of vice.
In Frankenstein, Shelley shows the creature learning that people are valued for wealth and birth, then realising he has neither and is judged worthless by that measure.
In Frankenstein, Shelley shows that watching a kind community from outside can deepen loneliness, because admiring their goodness only sharpens the sense of being shut out.
In Frankenstein, Shelley shows Safie's mother teaching her daughter to refuse bondage and seek freedom of mind, a lesson that outlives her.
In Frankenstein, Felix gives himself up to the law to try to free his father and sister, showing loyalty that costs him everything he has.

preview.text:
These reflections have dispelled the agitation with which I began my
letter, and I feel my heart glow with an enthusiasm which elevates me
to heaven, for nothing contributes so much to tranquillise the mind as
a steady purpose—a point on which the soul may fix its intellectual
eye. This expedition has been the favourite dream of my early years. I
have read with ardour the accounts of the various voyages which have
been made in the prospect of arriving at the North Pacific Ocean
through the seas which surround the pole. You may remember that a
history of all the voyages made for purposes of discovery composed the
whole of our good Uncle Thomas’ library. My education was neglected,
yet I was passionately fond of reading. These volumes were my study
day and night, and my familiarity with them increased that regret which
I had felt, as a child, on learning that my father’s dying injunction
had forbidden my uncle to allow me to embark in a seafaring life.

These visions faded when I perused, for the first time, those poets
whose effusions entranced my soul and lifted it to heaven. I also
became a poet and for one year lived in a paradise of my own creation;
I imagined that I also might obtain a niche in the temple where the
names of Homer and Shakespeare are consecrated. You are well
acquainted with my failure and how heavily I bore the disappointment.
But just at that time I inherited the fortune of my cousin, and my
thoughts were turned into the channel of their earlier bent.

books.title: The Count of Monte Cristo
books.author: Alexandre Dumas
books.subject: adventure
books.licence_note: Author died 1870, nineteenth century translation. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dumas shows how a leader treats people below him. Danglars is obsequious to superiors and insolent to his crew, and the crew dislike him, while Dantès is loved by them.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dumas shows envy at work in Danglars, who hints at a secret to Morrel and then, when pressed, says he may have been mistaken.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès judges Danglars fairly as an officer, even though he dislikes him personally. He keeps his grudge apart from his judgement of the man's work.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, old Dantès goes without rather than ask his son for help. Dumas shows a father's pride and love working together.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès says we are never quits with those who have helped us, because gratitude remains after a debt is repaid.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès notices the greedy look in Caderousse's eyes and quietly hides the money. Dumas shows a young man who reads people well.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Danglars and Caderousse feed each other's resentment, turning a friend's good fortune into a story against him. Dumas shows how gossip grows out of envy.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Mercédès turns Fernand down kindly but plainly, and tells him where her heart stands. Dumas shows that an honest no is kinder than false hope.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Mercédès will not let kindness pass for something it is not. She names the help she has been given honestly, and Dumas gives her quiet dignity because of it.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Mercédès warns that picking a fight with a rival does not win the person you want. Dumas shows jealousy defeating its own purpose.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès says that after a long time of suffering, people find good fortune hard to believe. Dumas shows the wariness that hardship leaves behind.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Danglars writes an anonymous accusation with his left hand so the handwriting cannot be traced. Dumas shows a schemer keeping his own name out of the harm he causes.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Caderousse, drunk as he is, understands the misery the accusation will bring and tries to take it back. Dumas gives even a weak man a moment of conscience.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès says that joy can weigh on us almost as heavily as sorrow. Dumas notices that great happiness can feel strangely like fear.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès compares happiness to an enchanted palace guarded by dragons that must be fought for. Dumas suggests that good things rarely come without a struggle.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Danglars says no one is responsible for the arrows they loose into the air. Dumas lets the reader see that whoever starts a harm owns what it does.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Caderousse's conscience gives way to caution as soon as he sees the cost. Dumas shows how easily a bystander drops his decency to protect himself.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Villefort drops his father's name to advance his career. Dumas shows how ambition can make a man disown where he came from.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Villefort takes pride in seeing the accused break down under his eloquence. Dumas shows a man who has lost sight of the human cost of his own work.

In The Count of Monte Cristo, Villefort has been taught to distrust first impressions, so he ignores the good one he has of Dantès. Dumas shows how a habit of suspicion can blind a judge to the truth.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès answers his suspicious judge with plain honesty, and leaves nothing to be guessed at. Dumas shows that candour can disarm suspicion better than cleverness.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès treats his dying captain's last request as sacred and carries it out, even though it brings him trouble. Dumas shows duty kept faithfully at a cost.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Villefort burns the letter that would clear Dantès, then tells him to deny all knowledge of it. Dumas shows a man who puts his own career ahead of the truth.

In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès trusted a kind official's soft words, and then finds those words were not kept. Dumas shows how a promise from a powerful person can be worth less than the person's actions.

In The Count of Monte Cristo, a jailer warns Dantès not to brood over what is impossible, because a mind that keeps returning to it can break. Dumas shows how fixation on the unreachable wears a person down.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Villefort realises that by ruining an innocent man he has become the executioner, not the judge. Dumas shows remorse arriving after the harm is done.

In The Count of Monte Cristo, Danglars treats people as numbers, so he feels nothing when his scheme ruins another man. Dumas shows how a person who counts others as worth less can justify almost anything.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, a minister of police says his desks are full of denunciations from people hoping for a reward. Dumas shows how the wish to be rewarded can fuel false accusations.

In The Count of Monte Cristo, Noirtier speaks of people as obstacles to be removed, so that harm can be described in cold words. Dumas shows how language that turns people into things can hide what is really being done.

In The Count of Monte Cristo, Villefort keeps an old friend waiting to show his power, reasoning that eagerness looks like weakness. Dumas shows how someone who values status over courtesy grows cold.

In The Count of Monte Cristo, Villefort writes a petition that would free Dantès, then keeps it in reserve in case it serves his own ambition. Dumas shows how a helpful-looking act can be a trap held back for later.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Morrel quietly pays for a dying man's funeral and debts, and Dumas notes that this took courage as well as kindness. Real decency often costs something.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, an inspector treats the prisoners' pleas as a formality to get through. Dumas shows how routine can make officials blind to the suffering in front of them.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès asks for no pardon, only a trial, because an accused man deserves to know his charge and be heard. Dumas makes a plain point about the basic right to a hearing.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, a prison file marks Dantès as dangerous on the strength of a note added later in another hand. Dumas shows how one unchecked line in a record can decide a person's fate.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès's pride in his innocence slowly wears away under long suspense, and he begins to doubt himself. Dumas shows how uncertainty can wear down even a clear conscience.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès sees that the hours he spent in hope and despair could have gone into steady work. Small daily effort adds up faster than waiting.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès gets nowhere until he sees he has been attacking the hardest stone. Working on the softer material around it is what opens the way.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès finds that a shared captivity is half a captivity. Having a companion gives him a reason to keep going.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Faria makes his tools from a bedframe clamp and digs fifty feet with them. Real resourcefulness is shown by making good use of whatever you have.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Faria puts years of strength into one plan with no margin, so one wrong angle wipes it all out. Leave room for error in any long undertaking.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès never even considers escape, because it looks impossible before anyone has tested it. Some ideas get dismissed in the mind before they are ever tried.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès takes heart from seeing an older man do what he thought impossible. If someone else has done a thing, it can be done again.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Faria finds that a man who knows a few good books well has nearly all he needs. Knowing a small set deeply can serve better than owning a big shelf.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Faria says that while he retraces history he forgets his cell. Absorbing work can steady a mind through hard times.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Faria makes a lamp from kitchen fat and a light from flint and sulphur. He says human intelligence can get around the limits of one's conditions.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Faria argues that hardship focused his mind, which in freedom might have scattered into idle pursuits. Limits can sharpen effort when they are met with purpose.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Faria teaches that when looking for the author of a wrong, you first ask who would gain from it. Working through the facts one question at a time leads to the truth.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Faria says that learning is not the same as knowing. Memory makes a learner, and understanding of principles makes the learned.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès keeps his word not to kill the sentry, even when it costs him the quickest route out. A promise kept is part of who a person is.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Faria asks whether a year of learning was really wasted. Time spent building yourself is not lost, even when it does not look like progress.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès gives up his own escape and swears to stay with his failing friend. Loyalty that holds when the cost is real is what makes a friend.

In The Count of Monte Cristo, Faria admits that thoughts of vengeance once comforted him in his dungeon, but he has let them go for the sake of a younger friend. Resentment can be set down when something better takes its place.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès says his real treasure is what he has learned from his friend and their company. Knowledge and friendship lift despair in a way that gold cannot.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Faria warns Dantès against sitting idle, because a body and mind not kept in use will not be ready when the chance comes. Keep your strength in shape before you need it.

In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès wins a crew's trust by showing his skill at the helm, and offers to pay for his keep from his wages. Proving your worth in practice tends to earn more than promises.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès sails past the island that holds his hope and decides to wait. Having learned patience through fourteen years in prison, he can wait longer for what he wants.
In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès teaches the sailor Jacopo navigation, saying he may one day be a captain himself. Passing on what you know can open doors for someone else.

In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès sees that the same wealth can seem worthless in one mood and precious in the next. Hope and desire bend our judgement, so it pays to be wary of what we want most in a rush.

In The Count of Monte Cristo, Dantès cannot see how a heavy rock was moved until he reasons that it was lowered, not lifted. Turning a problem around and asking how it was done the other way can clear up what looked impossible.

preview.text:
“Why, you see, Edmond,” replied the owner, who appeared more comforted
at every moment, “we are all mortal, and the old must make way for the
young. If not, why, there would be no promotion; and since you assure
me that the cargo——”

“Is all safe and sound, M. Morrel, take my word for it; and I advise
you not to take 25,000 francs for the profits of the voyage.”

Then, as they were just passing the Round Tower, the young man shouted:
“Stand by there to lower the topsails and jib; brail up the spanker!”

The order was executed as promptly as it would have been on board a
man-of-war.

“Let go—and clue up!” At this last command all the sails were lowered,
and the vessel moved almost imperceptibly onwards.

“Now, if you will come on board, M. Morrel,” said Dantès, observing the
owner’s impatience, “here is your supercargo, M. Danglars, coming out
of his cabin, who will furnish you with every particular. As for me, I
must look after the anchoring, and dress the ship in mourning.”

The owner did not wait for a second invitation. He seized a rope which
Dantès flung to him, and with an activity that would have done credit
to a sailor, climbed up the side of the ship, while the young man,
going to his task, left the conversation to Danglars, who now came
towards the owner. He was a man of twenty-five or twenty-six years of
age, of unprepossessing countenance, obsequious to his superiors,
insolent to his subordinates; and this, in addition to his position as
responsible agent on board, which is always obnoxious to the sailors,
made him as much disliked by the crew as Edmond Dantès was beloved by
them.

“Well, M. Morrel,” said Danglars, “you have heard of the misfortune
that has befallen us?”

“Yes—yes: poor Captain Leclere! He was a brave and an honest man.”

books.title: The Moonstone
books.author: Wilkie Collins
books.subject: detective
books.licence_note: Author died 1889. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Moonstone, Wilkie Collins follows three priests who keep their watch across generations, faithful to a sacred duty long after everyone else has forgotten its purpose.
In The Moonstone, Collins shows how a man's temper and boastful pride can turn a foolish argument into a wager he cannot back down from.
In The Moonstone, the narrator refuses to accuse his cousin on moral evidence alone, admitting he has no proof and did not see the deed himself.
In The Moonstone, Franklin Blake proposes that each person tell only what they personally witnessed, so the record rests on firsthand knowledge rather than rumour.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge rises from page-boy to house-steward by doing each job well, and keeps his place because his mistress trusts his work.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge notices his own life crowding out his subject, and learns that the way forward with a hard piece of work is simply to begin again.
In The Moonstone, Penelope suggests fixing each memory to a date in a diary, because a dated record lets recollection come back far more reliably than trying to remember at random.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge works out the plain, ordinary explanation for a strange scene, a juggler hoping for easy money, before he reaches for anything supernatural.
In The Moonstone, Lady Verinder gives a former thief a real chance in her service, and Rosanna repays it by working carefully and well, even while she struggles to fit in.
In The Moonstone, Collins shows how a quiet, capable woman can be resented by her coworkers for her solitary ways, and how easily a workplace turns difference into gossip.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge comforts a crying girl by sitting down beside her and asking what is wrong, rather than scolding her. Listening first does more good than a lecture.
In The Moonstone, Rosanna notes that a stain can be lifted from a coat while the mark it leaves still shows, a fair picture of how a forgiven past can still be seen.
In The Moonstone, Collins shows how a man who will not admit a mistake, even when everyone turns away from him, only digs his own isolation deeper.
In The Moonstone, Franklin Blake lays out a tangled problem by naming its separate questions one at a time, a habit that can calm a worry that feels like one big fog.
In The Moonstone, Franklin argues that people judge what is probable by their own everyday experience, so a strange claim needs evidence before anyone believes it.
In The Moonstone, Franklin tests a theory against the facts. A plot aimed at gain would have made the Diamond easier to steal, so greed alone cannot explain what happened.
In The Moonstone, Franklin reminds Betteredge that the same facts can support two very different explanations, so a sensible person weighs both before settling on one.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge's answer to a crisis is to wait, set a clear window of about four weeks, and move the valuable to safe keeping in the meantime.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge laughs at his daughter's sincere feelings, then sees her gentle rebuke has landed and admits he was unkind.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge and Franklin hold back their suspicions, because showing their hand too soon would only warn the people they are watching.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge observes that idle people often drift into spoiling things, and that having real work for the mind and hands is what keeps a person steady.
In The Moonstone, Lady Verinder says her daughter's best friend and worst enemy are one and the same: Rachel herself. Independence helps a person, but judgement can also undo them.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge admires Rachel for never breaking her word or telling a lie, even when her stubborn honesty earns her punishment and she will not explain herself.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge regrets advising a delay when the warning signs were already plain, and admits he should have acted on what he knew at the time.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge keeps to the plain facts and the duty in front of him, and does not let a restless mind that changes its view every few minutes pull him off course.
In The Moonstone, Rachel turns down a suitor firmly, then offers him a way back as a cousin, so the refusal can be made without causing a scandal.
In The Moonstone, Collins shows that cleverness without tact can do harm: Franklin says the wrong thing to the wrong person at the wrong time and leaves a whole table offended.
In The Moonstone, Murthwaite judges a risk by going through the details one step at a time, asking exactly how each trip was made, and so the real danger becomes clearer.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge finds comfort in Crusoe's point that dread of a danger can weigh more heavily than the danger itself, and that a steady mind lightens the load.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge admits that a small, unexpected sight shakes his confidence in his own judgment, and he is honest enough to let the evidence unsettle him.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge notes that trouble tests the metal of a person, and that some who seemed steady in easy times prove weaker under pressure, himself included.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge refuses to point suspicion at a girl whose honesty has been proven, holding that suspicion needs a real reason before anyone speaks it aloud.
In The Moonstone, Lady Verinder refuses to have her trusted servants searched like thieves, saying she owes them her trust and will not repay it with suspicion.
In The Moonstone, Wilkie Collins has old Betteredge observe that when you cannot see your way clearly, it is wise to hold your tongue.
In The Moonstone, Wilkie Collins shows that people in a crisis often take the gloomy view, because it gives them a kind of importance in their own eyes.
In The Moonstone, Franklin Blake asks his servant to watch closely and fairly, without anything degrading or cruel. Careful observation does not need to hurt anyone.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge judges Sergeant Cuff by his gloomy appearance and doubts his reputation, a reminder that looks are a poor guide to ability.
In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff says he has never met a trifle in an inquiry. Small details can decide the whole matter, so check them before dismissing them.
In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff tests a theory by counting back the hours from the known times. A confident conclusion can fall apart under simple arithmetic.
In The Moonstone, Franklin Blake sees that the narrower the question of time, the narrower the field of inquiry. A precise question makes a hard problem smaller.
In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff separates what is known from what is assumed. He has no evidence yet that the Diamond was stolen, only that it is lost, and he says so plainly.
In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff breaks a hard problem into three plain questions: what, whose, and how can they account for it. Each question has a clear answer that can be checked.
In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff wins cooperation by applying the same search to everyone, from the mistress down. People accept a hard request more readily when it is fair to all.
In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff wants every item accounted for, so that a missing piece becomes a clue. A thorough record of what should be there is the start of finding what is not.
In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff takes a delicate talk out into the open air, because doors and listeners have a knack of getting together. Discretion matters when a matter is sensitive.
In The Moonstone, the servants' reports after their interviews show how each one takes being questioned. The one who says almost nothing is the one worth noticing.
In The Moonstone, Franklin Blake builds a confident theory from a few scraps of gossip within minutes. Quick certainty often runs ahead of the facts, and it is worth slowing down to check them.
In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff names the footprints as a working assumption, to be held only until evidence to the contrary turns up. Good detectives keep their theories open to correction.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge admits he was ready to be convinced by an explanation that flattered his hopes for Rosanna. Wanting an answer can make a weak argument feel strong.

In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff reaches a sensitive subject by way of small talk about the price of fish and the Royal Family. Patience and an easy manner often open people up more than direct questions do.

In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff admits plainly that he has been puzzled, and he judges that moving in the dark is the bigger risk. Saying where your knowledge runs out is better than guessing your way forward.

In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff answers an angry accusation with good humour and says that anyone quick to take offence would not last long in his line of work. Patience with a hot temper makes a hard conversation easier.

In The Moonstone, Betteredge holds to his trust in Miss Rachel against a stranger's clever theory, because he knows her character. Long acquaintance is real evidence, though it can also blind a person to faults.
In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff points out that a man proved wrong about one conclusion may be wrong about others too. Each judgement should be tested on its own evidence, not carried over on trust.

In The Moonstone, Franklin Blake realises he has been a little hard on Rosanna in his own thoughts, and asks for an apology to be passed on. Owning an unfair private judgement is part of treating people decently.

In The Moonstone, Penelope sees that a careless hurt can wound someone who is already struggling, and her father comes round to her view. Gentle attention to how others are coping is often more useful than a quick reassurance.
In The Moonstone, Betteredge offers Rosanna friendship even if she has done wrong. Loyalty and honest judgement can sit together, and kindness does not require excusing the wrong.
In The Moonstone, Sergeant Cuff decides to drop speculation and get to business, checking the people and places that can actually be checked. Talk is cheap when a practical step is available.
In The Moonstone, Lady Verinder apologises plainly for her hasty words, without asking for an excuse. A simple, gracious admission of having been wrong goes a long way in a tense room.
In The Moonstone, Lady Verinder says she will speak boldly first so the hard talk is less painful for everyone. Going first with candour can lower the temperature of a difficult conversation.

preview.text:
Powerless to recover their lost treasure by open force, the three
guardian priests followed and watched it in disguise. The generations
succeeded each other; the warrior who had committed the sacrilege
perished miserably; the Moonstone passed (carrying its curse with it)
from one lawless Mohammedan hand to another; and still, through all
chances and changes, the successors of the three guardian priests kept
their watch, waiting the day when the will of Vishnu the Preserver
should restore to them their sacred gem. Time rolled on from the first
to the last years of the eighteenth Christian century. The Diamond fell
into the possession of Tippoo, Sultan of Seringapatam, who caused it to
be placed as an ornament in the handle of a dagger, and who commanded
it to be kept among the choicest treasures of his armoury. Even then—in
the palace of the Sultan himself—the three guardian priests still kept
their watch in secret. There were three officers of Tippoo’s household,
strangers to the rest, who had won their master’s confidence by
conforming, or appearing to conform, to the Mussulman faith; and to
those three men report pointed as the three priests in disguise.

III

books.title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland
books.author: Lewis Carroll
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Author died 1898. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Carroll shows Alice finding that after enough strange events, very few things seem truly impossible. A mind that has seen the rules broken can become more open to new answers.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Carroll has Alice read the label before she drinks, because she remembers the simple rules she was taught. Checking the label first is a good habit whenever something tempting is offered.
In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Carroll shows Alice giving herself very good advice, though she seldom follows it. Many of us know exactly what we should do and still do something else.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Carroll has Alice test herself by reciting lessons to check whether she is still the same person. Honestly checking what we still know is one way to notice how much we have changed.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Alice keeps stopping to apologise whenever she hurts the Mouse's feelings, even while she is struggling herself. Noticing how others feel and making amends quickly is a kind habit.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the Dodo's Caucus-race has no clear start or finish, yet everyone is declared a winner. Carroll pokes fun at prizes handed out for effort that nobody could actually measure.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Alice drinks from a bottle reasoning that something interesting is sure to happen. Carroll shows how curiosity can overrule caution, and how wishing afterwards does not undo the choice.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Alice works out a plan by ruling out what cannot help, then sets her goals in order. Breaking a problem into steps is useful even before you know how to take the first one.
In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Alice swallows her irritation to hear out the Caterpillar, and it turns out to have something worth saying. Staying patient long enough to listen can be rewarded.
In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Alice keeps to the truth even when the Pigeon has already decided what she is. Carroll suggests that honesty matters most when others are sure they know better.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Alice refuses to leave a helpless baby behind in the Duchess's kitchen, reasoning that it would be wrong to abandon it. Taking responsibility for someone who cannot protect themselves is a choice Carroll wants us to notice.
In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the Cheshire Cat points out that the right road depends on where you want to get to. Without a destination any path will do, which is a fair test for any plan.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the Cheshire Cat builds an argument that sounds neat, but it rests on a claim nobody has checked. Carroll reminds readers to test each step of an argument, not just how it sounds.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the Hatter shows that words which look alike can mean different things. Saying exactly what you mean, and checking that others hear the same meaning, matters more than it seems.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Alice finds her nerve against the Queen once she sees that the court is only a pack of cards. Carroll shows that much of what looks frightening loses its power when you look at it plainly.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Alice hides the frightened gardeners in a flower-pot and refuses to let the soldiers take them. Carroll shows courage most clearly in standing up for people who cannot protect themselves.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the Duchess finds a moral in everything she says, and most of her morals are nonsense. Carroll teases people who love a neat saying, and reminds readers not to take every pat lesson as wisdom.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the snail in the Mock Turtle's song quietly refuses to join a dance it sees as going too far, even though it is politely invited. Carroll lets a calm no stand on its own merits, without needing a reason the crowd will accept.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, the King runs the trial by striking out whatever he dislikes and threatening execution. Carroll satirises a court where the judge has settled the outcome before the evidence is heard, a reminder to question whoever is making the rules.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Alice challenges a rule the King has just invented and points out that it is not a real rule at all. Carroll shows that it takes some courage to ask where a rule came from before you obey it.

In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, Carroll closes with Alice's sister imagining Alice grown up and still keeping the loving, curious heart of her childhood. He suggests that the best parts of being young can be carried into adult life.

preview.text:
Suddenly she came upon a little three-legged table, all made of solid
glass; there was nothing on it except a tiny golden key, and Alice’s
first thought was that it might belong to one of the doors of the hall;
but, alas! either the locks were too large, or the key was too small,
but at any rate it would not open any of them. However, on the second
time round, she came upon a low curtain she had not noticed before, and
behind it was a little door about fifteen inches high: she tried the
little golden key in the lock, and to her great delight it fitted!

Alice opened the door and found that it led into a small passage, not
much larger than a rat-hole: she knelt down and looked along the
passage into the loveliest garden you ever saw. How she longed to get
out of that dark hall, and wander about among those beds of bright
flowers and those cool fountains, but she could not even get her head
through the doorway; “and even if my head would go through,” thought
poor Alice, “it would be of very little use without my shoulders. Oh,
how I wish I could shut up like a telescope! I think I could, if I only
knew how to begin.” For, you see, so many out-of-the-way things had
happened lately, that Alice had begun to think that very few things
indeed were really impossible.

There seemed to be no use in waiting by the little door, so she went
back to the table, half hoping she might find another key on it, or at
any rate a book of rules for shutting people up like telescopes: this
time she found a little bottle on it, (“which certainly was not here
before,” said Alice,) and round the neck of the bottle was a paper
label, with the words “DRINK ME,” beautifully printed on it in large
letters.

books.title: Tao Teh King
books.author: Laozi
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Ancient author, translator died 1897. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Laozi held that the Tao that can be named is not the enduring Tao, and that the deepest things cannot be pinned down by words.
Laozi observed that the best work gets done without a claim to ownership or a wait for reward, and that this quiet kind of effort lasts.
Laozi noticed that heaven and earth endure because they do not live for themselves, and that a person who puts his own ends last often finds they are still met.
Laozi warned that a full vessel is hard to carry, a sharp edge soon dulls, and success that turns into pride brings its own harm.
Laozi taught that usefulness lives in empty space: a wheel turns on its hollow hub, a pot holds because of its hollow, and a room works because of its open space.
Laozi observed that favour brings the fear of losing it, so being honoured can weigh on a person as heavily as being disgraced.
Laozi noticed that muddy water clears when it is left still, and that a person who is not full of himself can afford to seem unfinished.
Laozi held that the best leaders are hardly noticed, and that when their work is done the people say they did it themselves.
Laozi argued that setting aside cleverness and scheming for gain, and choosing plain and honest ways, would remove much of the trouble in a society.
Laozi noticed that a person who wants few things gets them, while one who wants many goes astray, and that the humble are the ones no one can out-strive.
Laozi observed that wind and rain never last long, so force cannot be sustained, and that steady, natural effort outlasts sudden fierce bursts.
Laozi taught that stillness rules movement, and that a wise leader who travels far still keeps close to his base, since losing steadiness costs him everything.
Laozi said that real skill leaves little trace: the best work gives no grounds for blame and needs no tallies or locks to hold it together.
Laozi held that some things cannot be seized by force, and that whoever grips too hard, whether for power or success, loses what he was after.
Laozi held that victory won by force should be met with sorrow rather than pride, since delighting in it means delighting in the killing.
Laozi drew a line between knowing others and knowing yourself, and said that the person who overcomes himself is mightier than the one who overcomes others.
Laozi said the Tao does nothing for the sake of doing it, so nothing is left undone, and that a leader without desire lets things go right of their own accord.
Laozi noticed that people with the most virtue do not display it, while those who work to keep up a show of it end up with less of it.
Laozi sorted people by how they meet the Tao: the best take it up in earnest, the middle keep it and then lose it, and the lowest laugh at it.
Laozi observed that some things gain by being reduced, and that the violent and strong do not die a natural death.
Laozi said that whoever is content has no reason to fear shame, and whoever knows when to stop meets no blame.
Laozi said that learning adds something each day, while the Way takes away effort each day until a person acts without strain and still gets everything done.
Laozi said that a wise leader has no fixed mind of his own and takes the mind of the people as his own, listening rather than imposing.
Laozi said the great way is level and easy, yet people love the byways, and he warned that a rule of show, with polished courts and empty granaries, runs against the way.
Laozi said that those who truly know do not talk much about it, while those eager to talk about it often do not know it.
Laozi observed that the more rules and prohibitions a state piles up, the poorer its people become, and that too much meddling breeds the trouble it means to prevent.
Laozi described the wise person as a square that cuts no one, straightforward without taking liberties, and bright without dazzling anybody.
Laozi said that stillness often overcomes force, and that a big power gains more by stooping to the small than by pushing them around.
Laozi said that hard things grow from easy beginnings, so the wise deal with a problem while it is still small, and that rash, easy promises usually breed difficulty.
Laozi noticed that people often ruin things just as they near success, and that care at the end should match the care taken at the beginning.
Laozi said that the sea is king of the streams because it sits lower than they do, and that a leader who puts himself behind others is followed without resentment.
Laozi named three treasures: gentleness, economy, and not pushing ahead of others, and he said gentleness can win even in battle.
Laozi counselled that there is no greater calamity than making war lightly, and that the one who grieves over conflict is the one who prevails.
Laozi said that knowing what you do not know is the highest attainment, and that thinking you know what you do not is the real flaw of the mind.
Laozi noticed that a stiff tree invites the axe while supple things keep going, and that leaning only on hardness and force is a risky habit.
Laozi contrasted the way of Heaven, which takes from excess to supply what is lacking, with the way of people, who take from those with little to add to their own surplus.
Laozi observed that everyone knows softness overcomes hardness, yet few put it into practice, and that words which are strictly true often sound like paradox.
Laozi said that sincere words are seldom fine, fine words are seldom sincere, and that the one who truly knows does not need to argue.
Laozi advised that after a bitter quarrel, a person of virtue does not insist on the other side keeping a deal to the letter, since insisting keeps the grudge alive.
Laozi observed that the wise person does not hoard, and that the more he gives to others, the more he finds he has himself.

4. All things spring up, and there is not one which declines to show
itself; they grow, and there is no claim made for their ownership;
they go through their processes, and there is no expectation (of a
reward for the results).  The work is accomplished, and there is no
resting in it (as an achievement).

The work is done, but how no one can see;
  'Tis this that makes the power not cease to be.

3. 1. Not to value and employ men of superior ability is the way to
keep the people from rivalry among themselves; not to prize articles
which are difficult to procure is the way to keep them from becoming
thieves; not to show them what is likely to excite their desires is
the way to keep their minds from disorder.

2. Therefore the sage, in the exercise of his government, empties
their minds, fills their bellies, weakens their wills, and strengthens
their bones.

3. He constantly (tries to) keep them without knowledge and without
desire, and where there are those who have knowledge, to keep them
from presuming to act (on it).  When there is this abstinence from
action, good order is universal.

4. 1. The Tao is (like) the emptiness of a vessel; and in our
employment of it we must be on our guard against all fulness.  How
deep and unfathomable it is, as if it were the Honoured Ancestor of
all things!

2. We should blunt our sharp points, and unravel the complications of
things; we should attemper our brightness, and bring ourselves into
agreement with the obscurity of others.  How pure and still the Tao
is, as if it would ever so continue!

3. I do not know whose son it is.  It might appear to have been before
God.

books.title: Dracula
books.author: Bram Stoker
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1912. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Dracula, Stoker tells the story only through records written as events happened, so the reader has to weigh the evidence rather than trust one narrator's memory.
In Dracula, Jonathan Harker researches the region before he meets its nobleman, showing that preparation matters most when you are about to deal with someone you do not yet know.
In Dracula, the Count's warm letter of welcome makes Harker feel expected and at ease, showing how a little courtesy can disarm even a careful person.
In Dracula, Harker brushes aside the frightened innkeeper's warnings and presses on, a reminder that ignoring an honest warning from someone who knows the place can be costly.
In Dracula, Harker accepts a crucifix from the old woman out of courtesy, even against what he was taught, showing how kindness can open a person to things they would normally refuse.
In Dracula, Harker is touched by the crowd that fears for him, showing that people who look strange to us are often acting out of care.
In Dracula, Harker does not dare to question the driver because he feels he has no power to change anything, showing how a person who feels helpless often stays silent when they most need to ask.
In Dracula, Harker notes that only a person who faces a danger directly can understand what it really means, a reminder that some knowledge can only come from experience.
In Dracula, the warmth and courtesy of the host dissolve Harker's doubts, showing how comfort can quiet the fears that good sense would otherwise raise.
In Dracula, Harker's body recoils from the Count before his mind can say why, a reminder that instinct often notices something that reason has not yet named.

In Dracula, the Count learns English from books but knows he has to hear and speak it among people to truly master it, a reminder that real skill comes from living the thing, not only reading about it.
In Dracula, Harker steadies himself by writing down only the facts and refusing to let imagination run wild, a useful habit when a situation feels frightening and unclear.
In Dracula, Harker panics at first, then forces himself to sit quietly once he accepts he is helpless, and only then starts to think clearly about what to do.

In Dracula, Harker knows his letters will be read, so he writes only harmless notes and sends the truth by a route the Count cannot see, a sound lesson in protecting what matters when you know you are being watched.
In Dracula, Harker finds that a door he took for locked only resisted because its hinges had sagged, a reminder to test an assumption before accepting that the way out is closed.
In Dracula, Harker admits to a sweet, dangerous longing for the three women, showing how temptation often feels pleasant right up until its cost becomes clear.
In Dracula, Harker refuses to trust either his fears or his reassurances until he has looked for proof, a habit worth keeping whenever a strong feeling tries to settle a question for you.
In Dracula, Harker chooses not to quarrel openly with the Count while he is powerless, and keeps watching for a chance to escape, a lesson in picking your moment when you hold the weaker hand.
In Dracula, Harker tells Mina only part of his situation so that he does not frighten her to death, showing how care can shape what we choose to reveal.
In Dracula, after a night of despair Harker notices how the morning restores his courage, and he resolves to act while that courage lasts rather than wait for things to improve.

In Dracula, Harker reasons that if the Count can leave by his window, the same route might work for him, a useful habit of studying what works for the person blocking you when the normal door is shut.
In Dracula, Mina keeps a journal as an exercise rather than for an audience, a way of sharpening memory and noticing what happens during the day.
In Dracula, Dr Seward turns down a proposal with honesty and gentleness, asking plainly, taking both hands and offering friendship, which shows that a kind no can still respect the other person.
In Dracula, Quincey Morris tells Lucy that her honesty has made him a friend, and says that friendship earned through straight dealing is rarer than a lover.
In Dracula, Mr Swales wins arguments by bullying and then takes other people's silence as agreement, a warning about how loud certainty can pass for being right.
In Dracula, Mina finds that a good and unselfish cause is what gives her the will to keep working through disappointment, a thought worth keeping for anyone who feels stuck.

In Dracula, the captain of the Demeter calms a frightened crew by searching the whole ship with them in plain view, a lesson that a leader can ease fear more by checking the facts together than by dismissing it.
In Dracula, the captain of the Demeter, facing a horror he cannot explain, refuses to leave his post and keeps to his duty to the end, a picture of steadiness that people in charge can learn from.
In Dracula, Mina wakes Lucy gently and covers her warmly so she is not startled, a small model of how to help someone who is frightened without making them feel worse.
In Dracula, Mina keeps Lucy's secret, weighing how gossip could distort a story and how much it could hurt someone already fragile.
In Dracula, Mina observes that sympathy cannot change the facts, but it can make them easier to bear.
In Dracula, Jonathan Harker offers to pay for his own hospital care so that others who need help are not left without it.
In Dracula, Mina chooses not to pry into Jonathan's fears, trusting that he will share what he can when he is ready.
In Dracula, Mina seals Jonathan's journal unread as a sign of their trust, keeping that promise even when the temptation is strong.
In Dracula, Seward finds his carefully made plan fails, and responds by adjusting it rather than clinging to it.
In Dracula, Seward admits that friendship makes it hard to judge someone clearly, and says so openly so Arthur can weigh his view.
In Dracula, Seward describes Van Helsing as a man with an open mind and real expertise, worth trusting even when his manner is brusque.
In Dracula, Van Helsing puts Lucy at ease by chatting about anything but her illness, so she relaxes before he asks his questions.
In Dracula, Van Helsing insists there is always a cause for everything, and refuses to dismiss a puzzling problem as nothing.
In Dracula, Van Helsing compares good work to a farmer who waits for the crop to grow rather than digging up the seed to check on it.
In Dracula, Van Helsing urges Seward to record even small details and doubts, because we learn from failure as much as from success.
In Dracula, Seward suggests we pause before condemning someone for selfishness, since it may have deeper roots than we can see.
In Dracula, Seward keeps a simple promise to watch over Lucy, and that trust is what finally lets her rest.
In Dracula, Lucy insists on keeping watch over the tired doctor who has watched over her, a small reminder that care should go both ways.
In Dracula, Van Helsing tells Seward not to fear thinking through even the improbable, a useful habit when a puzzle has no obvious answer.
In Dracula, Mrs Westenra tidies Lucy's room out of kindness, and the well-meant act undoes the care others had taken. Good intentions still need the full picture.
In Dracula, Van Helsing lets himself grieve for a moment, then stands up and acts anyway, insisting they fight on whatever the odds.
In Dracula, the zookeeper argues that a wolf is far less fearsome than the tales told about it, a reminder to judge a threat by evidence rather than legend.
In Dracula, the keeper and his wife grow so used to the wolf that it becomes an ordinary pet, showing how familiarity can shrink what once seemed frightening.
In Dracula, when every door is locked, Van Helsing and Seward look for another way in rather than wait, because when time matters a blocked path is no reason to stop.
In Dracula, Quincey Morris arrives unasked and simply says to count him in and do whatever is needed, the kind of loyalty that steadies a team in trouble.
In Dracula, Quincey Morris says nothing of his plan but walks the grounds all night, showing that steady, unannounced service is its own kind of care.
In Dracula, Mina helps Jonathan rebuild his confidence by believing in him first, showing that steady encouragement can restore someone's belief in themselves.
In Dracula, Van Helsing takes exhausted Arthur in hand and says no one should face their fears alone, offering simple company as a comfort.
In Dracula, Van Helsing searches Lucy's papers himself so that her private thoughts do not fall into strangers' hands, a quiet respect for privacy even after death.
In Dracula, Van Helsing asks Seward for faith rather than proof, arguing that a partnership works best when both trust the other's reasons.
In Dracula, a solicitor delights in a result that suits his side of a tragedy, showing how professional interest can crowd out real sympathy.
In Dracula, Van Helsing tells grieving friends they must pass through bitter times before the sweet, and that steady courage and unselfish duty will carry them through.
In Dracula, Mina holds back from questioning a distressed Jonathan, judging that pushing for answers could do more harm than good.
In Dracula, Van Helsing says grief and laughter can arrive together, and that a moment of lightness can ease the strain enough to keep going.

preview.text:
How these papers have been placed in sequence will be made manifest in
the reading of them. All needless matters have been eliminated, so that
a history almost at variance with the possibilities of later-day belief
may stand forth as simple fact. There is throughout no statement of
past things wherein memory may err, for all the records chosen are
exactly contemporary, given from the standpoints and within the range
of knowledge of those who made them.

DRACULA

CHAPTER I

JONATHAN HARKER’S JOURNAL

(_Kept in shorthand._)

_3 May. Bistritz._--Left Munich at 8:35 P. M., on 1st May, arriving at
Vienna early next morning; should have arrived at 6:46, but train was an
hour late. Buda-Pesth seems a wonderful place, from the glimpse which I
got of it from the train and the little I could walk through the
streets. I feared to go very far from the station, as we had arrived
late and would start as near the correct time as possible. The
impression I had was that we were leaving the West and entering the
East; the most western of splendid bridges over the Danube, which is
here of noble width and depth, took us among the traditions of Turkish
rule.

We left in pretty good time, and came after nightfall to Klausenburgh.
Here I stopped for the night at the Hotel Royale. I had for dinner, or
rather supper, a chicken done up some way with red pepper, which was
very good but thirsty. (_Mem._, get recipe for Mina.) I asked the
waiter, and he said it was called “paprika hendl,” and that, as it was a
national dish, I should be able to get it anywhere along the
Carpathians. I found my smattering of German very useful here; indeed, I
don’t know how I should be able to get on without it.

books.title: The Thirty-Nine Steps
books.author: John Buchan
books.subject: adventure
books.licence_note: Author died 1940. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Richard Hannay recognises that his restlessness is a signal to change course, and decides to act on it rather than drift.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Buchan shows that Hannay's boredom comes from having no real friend to share his days with, more than from a lack of money or sights.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay gives himself a clear deadline of one more day before he leaves. A set limit turns drifting into a decision.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay decides to judge the man rather than the story, and reasons that a liar would have told a milder yarn.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Scudder keeps his nerve by marking each day off towards the deadline and working steadily through his plan, even while he is afraid.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Scudder decides to share what he knows so that someone else can carry on if he dies. Passing on the work keeps it alive.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay turns down the easy safe road and carries on a dead man's work, because he feels bound to see it through.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay wakes doubting his plan, searches for a reason to drop it, finds none, and keeps going. A decision made with a clear head is worth holding to when the mood turns.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay reasons that a careful man would not hide a secret behind an easy code, so he looks harder for the real answer.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay's spirits lift in the open hill country. Buchan shows how a change of place can clear a weary mind.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, a herd's family takes Hannay in without asking questions. Buchan shows that plain hospitality from people who ask nothing is a kind of trust.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay reasons that his pursuers will expect him to keep going farther away, so he doubles back. Thinking about how others will read your moves helps you choose your own.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay tells a young innkeeper that adventure may already be on his doorstep. Buchan suggests that good material often sits in an ordinary, quiet place.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay cracks Scudder's cipher by trying a name Scudder had mentioned. The clue you already hold is often the key.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay is let down by Scudder's stories but trusts the notebook, because its account rings true. Buchan shows weighing the evidence rather than the charm of the teller.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay sees that no one will believe a bare tale, so he resolves to find some proof. A claim without evidence is easy to dismiss.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay realises that stealing the car makes him easy to trace. A shortcut can leave a trail that undoes you.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay finds that telling the whole truth to a stranger clears his own mind, as much as it helps the listener.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Sir Harry backs Hannay on his manner alone. Buchan shows a sound judge of character sometimes sees the truth before the proof arrives.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay takes a drunk roadman's work so the man can sleep it off and keep his place. Helping someone out of trouble can also open a door for you.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay recalls an old scout's advice that to play a part you must think yourself into it. Full commitment is what makes a role believable.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay nearly gives himself away with a tempting story, then catches the danger and says less. Knowing when to say nothing can be the wiser move.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay draws his pursuers onto a false scent by showing himself, then doubling back. Misdirection can buy a hunted man precious time.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay feels the pull of a dangerous man's cold charm and recognises it as a weakness. Being drawn in by a strong personality is not the same as being right.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay finds the nerve to act by remembering the man who trusted him, and by setting his fear aside long enough to move.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, the roadman Turnbull nurses Hannay through his fever without fuss. Buchan shows that real friendship often comes from ordinary people, when it is needed most.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Sir Walter Bullivant tests a stranger with a blunt rebuke, then gives him a meal and a way in. Buchan shows a shrewd judge of people can help without showing his hand.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay refuses to accept a respectable man's hospitality on false pretences, and tells him the truth first. Honesty comes before comfort.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Sir Walter describes Scudder as brave because he was always frightened and still would not stop. Buchan suggests courage is often simply acting while afraid.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay loses his temper and throws a punch, which makes his trouble worse. A flash of anger at a small provocation can cost you the chance to be believed.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, a butler faces down a noisy crowd with a calm, unmoved face and gives them nothing to grip. Steady composure can defeat a mob.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay points out that the officials were lulled because the visitor looked like someone they expected. People stop checking what they take for granted.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay faces hundreds of tide tables and narrows the search by asking what a clue really means. A sharper question shrinks an impossible list.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay reasons by putting himself in his enemy's shoes, asking where a man in a hurry would choose to leave. Thinking like your opponent narrows the field.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay keeps one list for what is fairly certain and another for what is guessed. Keeping facts apart from guesses keeps your reasoning honest.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay watches two innocent-looking men at tennis and wonders if he is the fool. Appearances can mislead, so it pays to test a suspicion before acting on it.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay recalls a scout's view that a fool tries to look different, while a clever man blends in with his surroundings and is different inside.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay remembers a buck that escaped by standing still against grey rock. Sometimes the safest move is to blend in rather than run.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Hannay is nearly lulled by three respectable faces until a small, unguarded gesture gives them away. Noticing small details can break a convincing performance.
In The Thirty-Nine Steps, Buchan shows that a villain can believe his cause is noble, which makes him more dangerous than a mere spy. Sincere conviction can be a strong force for harm.

preview.text:
I returned from the City about three o’clock on that May afternoon
pretty well disgusted with life. I had been three months in the Old
Country, and was fed up with it. If anyone had told me a year ago that
I would have been feeling like that I should have laughed at him; but
there was the fact. The weather made me liverish, the talk of the
ordinary Englishman made me sick. I couldn’t get enough exercise, and
the amusements of London seemed as flat as soda-water that has been
standing in the sun. “Richard Hannay,” I kept telling myself, “you have
got into the wrong ditch, my friend, and you had better climb out.”

It made me bite my lips to think of the plans I had been building up
those last years in Buluwayo. I had got my pile—not one of the big
ones, but good enough for me; and I had figured out all kinds of ways
of enjoying myself. My father had brought me out from Scotland at the
age of six, and I had never been home since; so England was a sort of
Arabian Nights to me, and I counted on stopping there for the rest of
my days.

books.title: Through the Looking-Glass
books.author: Lewis Carroll
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Author died 1898. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Through the Looking-Glass, Lewis Carroll shows Alice turning everyday play into make-believe, pretending to be a queen or a hungry hyaena. Imagination is a way of seeing a situation from another side.
In Through the Looking-Glass, Lewis Carroll shows Alice helping the flustered White Queen and King without being asked, and dusting the King off with care. Kindness is often practical and immediate.
In Through the Looking-Glass, the Queen warns the King that he will forget a painful moment unless he writes it down. A written note can be more reliable than memory.
Carroll has Alice solve a puzzle by changing her point of view, holding the text up to a mirror. When a problem stays stubborn, looking at it from the other side can make it readable.
In Through the Looking-Glass, Alice will not admit even to herself that she cannot make sense of the poem. Carroll shows how hard it can be to say plainly what we do not yet know.
Carroll has Alice find that the usual route keeps leading back to the house, and that walking the opposite way at last works. Sometimes the fix is a different direction, not more of the same effort.
In Through the Looking-Glass, Alice will not call a hill a valley just because the Red Queen insists. She holds to what she can plainly see, even against someone in authority.

In Through the Looking-Glass, the Red Queen tells Alice that in her country it takes all the running you can do just to stay in the same place. It is a fair picture of any business that must keep moving just to hold its ground.
In Through the Looking-Glass, Alice fears losing her name in a wood where nothing has one. Carroll quietly makes the point that knowing who you are is worth guarding.
In Through the Looking-Glass, Alice takes both of the twins' hands at once so that neither brother's feelings are hurt. It is a small piece of tact that is easy to overlook.
Carroll's poem about the Walrus and the Carpenter shows a pleasant invitation hiding a bad purpose. Before accepting kind words, it is worth asking what the speaker actually wants.
When Tweedledum flies into a rage over a broken toy, Alice answers him in a calm, soothing voice. Carroll shows how a steady tone can settle a heated argument.
In Through the Looking-Glass, the White Queen offers jam to-morrow and yesterday but never today. Carroll makes a wry point about rewards that are always promised for later.
Alice tells the Queen that a punishment is only fair when you really did the thing you were punished for. It is a sound instinct about accountability, and the Queen's logic falls apart on it.

In Through the Looking-Glass, Alice keeps reaching for the prettiest rush just out of her grasp while the ones already in her arms fade. Carroll shows how chasing the next shiny thing can cost the good things you already hold.

In Through the Looking-Glass, Humpty Dumpty insists that words mean whatever he chooses, and Alice asks whether anyone can stretch a word that far. Carroll makes the point that people only agree when they share what their words mean.
In Through the Looking-Glass, Alice is more worried for the Red Knight when he falls than for herself. Carroll gives her an easy, unselfish sympathy for people who have just been knocked over.

In Through the Looking-Glass, the White Knight insists he has had plenty of practice while he keeps tumbling off his horse. Carroll's joke is that experience shows in results, not in how often you claim it.

In Through the Looking-Glass, Alice remembers the gentle, slightly foolish White Knight for years afterwards. Carroll suggests that kindness, even from someone a little ridiculous, is what stays with us.
In Through the Looking-Glass, the Red Queen gives sound advice: speak the truth, think before you speak, and write it down afterwards. Carroll lets a poor model of manners say something wise.
In Through the Looking-Glass, the Red Queen says that once you have said a thing, it is fixed, and you must take the consequences. Words are hard to take back, so it pays to choose them with care.
Carroll ends Through the Looking-Glass by asking the reader which of the dreamers was real, and leaves the answer open. The book shows that a story can finish without tying up every question.

preview.text:
“Do you hear the snow against the window-panes, Kitty? How nice and
soft it sounds! Just as if some one was kissing the window all over
outside. I wonder if the snow _loves_ the trees and fields, that it
kisses them so gently? And then it covers them up snug, you know, with
a white quilt; and perhaps it says, ‘Go to sleep, darlings, till the
summer comes again.’ And when they wake up in the summer, Kitty, they
dress themselves all in green, and dance about—whenever the wind
blows—oh, that’s very pretty!” cried Alice, dropping the ball of
worsted to clap her hands. “And I do so _wish_ it was true! I’m sure
the woods look sleepy in the autumn, when the leaves are getting brown.

“Kitty, can you play chess? Now, don’t smile, my dear, I’m asking it
seriously. Because, when we were playing just now, you watched just as
if you understood it: and when I said ‘Check!’ you purred! Well, it
_was_ a nice check, Kitty, and really I might have won, if it hadn’t
been for that nasty Knight, that came wiggling down among my pieces.
Kitty, dear, let’s pretend—” And here I wish I could tell you half the
things Alice used to say, beginning with her favourite phrase “Let’s
pretend.” She had had quite a long argument with her sister only the
day before—all because Alice had begun with “Let’s pretend we’re kings
and queens;” and her sister, who liked being very exact, had argued
that they couldn’t, because there were only two of them, and Alice had
been reduced at last to say, “Well, _you_ can be one of them then, and
_I’ll_ be all the rest.” And once she had really frightened her old
nurse by shouting suddenly in her ear, “Nurse! Do let’s pretend that
I’m a hungry hyaena, and you’re a bone.”

books.title: Essays, First Series
books.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 1882. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Ralph Waldo Emerson held that all people share one universal mind, so any thinker's insight is open to anyone who reads with attention and reason.
Ralph Waldo Emerson argued that the thought always comes before the fact, so what a person later does is first pictured in their own mind.
Ralph Waldo Emerson observed that every reform was once a private opinion in one person's mind, so today's private ideas can become the solutions of the age.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that a sense of the worth of human life lies beneath all education, justice, charity and friendship.
Ralph Waldo Emerson urged readers to treat their own life as the main text and books as the commentary, reading history actively rather than passively.
Ralph Waldo Emerson urged people to sit solidly within themselves and judge the case for themselves, not be bullied into deference by the powers of the day.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that each mind must work through a lesson for itself, since a rule handed down unlived gives none of the understanding that comes from doing the work.
Ralph Waldo Emerson suggested understanding any great work by putting yourself in the maker's place and asking what needs and forces could have produced it, until it makes sense.
Ralph Waldo Emerson said clearer thinking looks past surface differences of colour and size to the underlying causes, which is where real understanding of a problem sits.
Ralph Waldo Emerson observed that nature casts one thought into many forms, as a poet makes twenty fables with one moral, so the same lesson can appear in very different situations.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that beneath endless variety on the surface lies a simple cause, so the many different acts of one person reveal one consistent character.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that ordinary people are known by what they do, while a deeply good person moves others simply by who they are.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that the whole of chivalry lies in courtesy, since a person of fine manners honours others with more grace than any title could add.
Ralph Waldo Emerson argued that the grand forms of architecture grew out of the plain needs and dwellings of earlier peoples, so humble beginnings often shape what comes later.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that public events are best understood through the people who lived them, and private experiences through the wider patterns they reveal.

Ralph Waldo Emerson contrasted restless curiosity with contented home-keeping, warning that scattering attention over too many things drains the mind, while staying at home risks monotony without fresh input.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that what we see around us corresponds to our own state of mind, and things become intelligible as our thinking grows deeper.
Ralph Waldo Emerson pointed to Xenophon rising in the snow to split wood, and others following, as a plain example of leading by doing the work first.
Ralph Waldo Emerson said we admire the old works not for their age but for their naturalness, made by people who spoke simply before reflection took over.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that a student reads the past through his own experience, so an old truth that echoes something from our youth is easy to recognise.
Ralph Waldo Emerson observed that each reformer repeats the steps of earlier reformers and meets new dangers, and that moral courage is needed to put something better in place of an old superstition.
