Ralph Waldo Emerson said great literature is a confession true for one reader and true for all, so a person finds his own story in very old fables.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that people who obey facts literally lose their inner light, while a person who stays true to their better instincts finds the facts falling into place.
Ralph Waldo Emerson noted that Plato said poets often utter great and wise things they do not fully understand, so good work can carry more truth than its maker sees.
In The Bride of Lammermoor and similar tales, Emerson saw faithfulness presented as always beautiful and always open to misfortune in this world, a truth that holds in everyday life too.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that a person's power lies in the many links between themselves and other people and the wider world, and that no one can truly live without a world to act upon.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that nobody can know in advance what a new experience will unlock in them, and that self-knowledge comes through meeting people and events.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that our actual knowledge is worth less than we think, and it is better to admit what we do not know than to pretend to a certainty we lack.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that genius is trusting your own thought, because what is true in your private heart is often what many people feel too, and we should not drop it just because it is ours.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that envy comes from ignorance and copying others drains your own power, so each person must work the ground they have been given and discover what they alone can do.
Ralph Waldo Emerson urged people to trust themselves and accept the place their own time has given them, acting as guides and benefactors rather than hiding in a protected corner.
Ralph Waldo Emerson warned that the pressure to conform works against the independent self, because society loves names and customs more than the realities behind them.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that the integrity of your own mind is the one thing finally sacred, and that goodness has to be tested rather than accepted just because it carries a respected name.
Ralph Waldo Emerson said a person of real strength keeps their independence in a crowd, and does what is right by their own judgement rather than by what others think.
Ralph Waldo Emerson said that doing your own work reinforces you, while keeping up customs that have gone dead scatters your force and blurs the character others can see.
Ralph Waldo Emerson said the displeasure of others is usually shallow and shifts like the wind, so a firm person who knows their own mind can treat it as a small thing.
Ralph Waldo Emerson called a foolish consistency the bugbear of small minds, and said a great mind may change its view as it learns, even if that contradicts what it said before.
Ralph Waldo Emerson said a true character reads the same whichever way you look at it, and that it shows itself in every moment, not just in the actions we consciously perform.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that the force of character builds up from all the honest days before it, so acting rightly today rests on what you have already done.
Ralph Waldo Emerson observed that an institution is the lengthened shadow of one person, and that a true person works as a cause, a country and an age.
Ralph Waldo Emerson urged people to know their own worth, and said we are often like a drunk who wakes up to find himself a true prince, forgetting our real standing until we pay attention.
Ralph Waldo Emerson said the stake in a private act done today is as great as the famous public deeds of kings, so the choices of ordinary people matter just as much.
Ralph Waldo Emerson observed that people fret over the past or stretch toward the future and miss the present, while a rose simply is what it is in every moment, and so should we be.
Ralph Waldo Emerson said that if we live truthfully we will see truly, and that repeating the borrowed phrases of others is less useful than trusting our own fresh perception.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that power lies in the moment of change and movement toward an aim, not in having lived or resting on what was done, so a person is always becoming.
Ralph Waldo Emerson saw self-reliance throughout nature: anything that lasts must be able to help itself, as a bent tree recovers from a strong wind.
Ralph Waldo Emerson advised that independence means not being pulled into every demand on your time, since others can only annoy us through our own weak curiosity.
Ralph Waldo Emerson said we should not sell our liberty and power to protect other people's feelings, and that living honestly, even at some cost, serves everyone in the end.
Ralph Waldo Emerson described people who were afraid of truth, fortune, death and each other as parlour soldiers, who shun the rugged battle where real strength is built.
Ralph Waldo Emerson admired people who try many things and live in the present rather than postponing life until a perfect career appears, since they have a hundred chances instead of one.

Ralph Waldo Emerson said discontent is a lack of self-reliance, and that when we cannot help someone who is suffering, the best thing is to attend to our own work, where the harm begins to be repaired.
Ralph Waldo Emerson warned that followers can mistake a teacher's system for the truth itself, and that a good teacher's gift is to help the student think for themselves.
Ralph Waldo Emerson said travel cannot cure a restless heart, because the same unsettled self comes along, so a wise person does the work where they stand.
Ralph Waldo Emerson urged people to design and make things from their own climate, soil, needs and circumstances, rather than copying models from far away.
Ralph Waldo Emerson insisted that each person should insist on themselves and never imitate, because a gift that is your own can be drawn on fully, while a borrowed talent is only half possessed.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that new tools and conveniences can weaken the very skills they replace, so that a person may gain gadgets and lose the ability to know the hour by the sun.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that new machinery and inventions are only the costume of an age and do not make people greater, and that the great ideas return to essential human qualities.
Ralph Waldo Emerson likened society to a wave: its form moves onward while the people who make it up keep changing, so its unity is only on the surface.
Ralph Waldo Emerson said that measuring people by what they own rather than by what they are shows a lack of self-reliance, and that a cultivated person grows ashamed of accidental wealth.
Ralph Waldo Emerson urged people to stop gambling on fortune and instead work and act, since steady effort brings a freedom from chance, while good luck alone brings no lasting peace.

preview.text:
Of the works of this mind history is the record. Its genius is
illustrated by the entire series of days. Man is explicable by nothing
less than all his history. Without hurry, without rest, the human
spirit goes forth from the beginning to embody every faculty, every
thought, every emotion, which belongs to it, in appropriate events. But
the thought is always prior to the fact; all the facts of history
preexist in the mind as laws. Each law in turn is made by circumstances
predominant, and the limits of nature give power to but one at a time.
A man is the whole encyclopaedia of facts. The creation of a thousand
forests is in one acorn, and Egypt, Greece, Rome, Gaul, Britain,
America, lie folded already in the first man. Epoch after epoch, camp,
kingdom, empire, republic, democracy, are merely the application of his
manifold spirit to the manifold world.

books.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
books.author: Oscar Wilde
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1900. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Wilde shows Basil refusing to show his finest work because he has put too much of himself into it. Creative work can expose its maker.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Basil argues that a portrait painted with feeling shows the painter more than the sitter. Good work reveals its maker.
Basil tells Harry he fears that a fascinating person could absorb his whole nature and his art. Wilde shows how an intense new influence can unsettle a person who has always been their own master.
Basil insists an artist should put nothing of his own life into the work, and that his age treats art as autobiography. Wilde lets the reader weigh how much of ourselves belongs in what we make.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Basil feels he has given his whole soul to someone who treats it like a flower for his coat. Wilde shows how easy it is to give yourself away to someone who does not value you.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Harry argues that the aim of life is self-development, and that people who live by borrowed thoughts become echoes of someone else. Wilde gives the idea to a character who is not to be trusted with it.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, a few offhand words from Harry stir Dorian deeply. Wilde shows how much weight a careless remark can carry when it lands on someone who is open to it.
Harry's speech on youth and pleasure is the temptation that Wilde sets in front of Dorian. It shows how a persuasive argument can push a person to waste the very thing they value most.
Wilde notes that people often fix their attention on trivial things when something frightening or important presses on them. Attention drifts to small details as a way of avoiding a larger thought.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian would give his soul to keep his youth, and the portrait would age in his place. Wilde shows how envy of what cannot last can turn into a bargain a person would regret.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Harry enjoys the power of shaping another person and plans to dominate Dorian. Wilde shows how the pleasure of influence can blind a person to the harm they do.
Mr. Erskine suggests that paradox can be a route to truth, because we test reality best when it is pushed to the edge. Wilde shows a clever idea being used to test what people believe.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Harry jokes that the problem of poverty is solved by amusing the poor. Wilde's barb still fits any help that makes the helper feel good without addressing the suffering itself.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Harry remarks that people now know the price of everything and the value of nothing. That gap between price and worth is still worth checking in any business.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian falls in love with the roles Sibyl Vane plays rather than with the woman herself. Wilde shows how we can idealise a person through the version of them we see on stage, and how that can blind us.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Harry decides that no sensation is too costly to pay for. Wilde lets the rest of the novel test that idea, asking what a life lived only for pleasure ends up costing.
Harry thinks experience is only the name people give their mistakes, and that we repeat them. Wilde leaves the reader to test that claim against what Dorian actually does next.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Harry notes that when we think we are testing other people, we are often testing ourselves. Wilde's point is that the motives we deceive ourselves about are the ones that govern us most.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Wilde observes that children begin by loving their parents, then judge them, and sometimes forgive them. Most people will recognise that path in their own family.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Harry claims that no life is spoiled except one whose growth has stopped. Wilde leaves room for the idea that a good life keeps changing rather than being fixed in place.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian says that being trusted by someone he loves makes him faithful and good. Wilde shows how another person's belief in us can steady our better selves.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Sibyl's voice is exquisite but false in tone, and the verse loses its life. Wilde shows that technique without real feeling leaves the audience cold, however lovely it sounds.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian turns on Sibyl once she stops dazzling him, saying he loved her only for what she gave him. Wilde shows how loving someone for their performance, and dropping them when it slips, does harm.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian blames Sibyl for his cruelty and waves away the evidence in his portrait as an illusion. Wilde shows how easily we excuse our own harm and dismiss the signs that we have caused it.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Wilde notes that there is a comfort in self-reproach, since blaming ourselves can feel like being forgiven. He shows that remorse alone does not repair what was done.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Harry says good resolutions are cheques drawn on a bank where we have no account. A promise with no real means behind it is worth little, and it can make us feel better without changing anything.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Basil tells Dorian he has lost his warmth and that a friend's influence is to blame. Wilde shows how a good friend can notice a change in us before we do, even when we do not want to hear it.

In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian asks his old friend to stay close even though he has changed, admitting that his friend is better than Harry, if not stronger. Wilde reminds us that asking to be loved after we change is a very human request.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Basil admits that an idol can consume the one who worships it, because losing what we adore is as real a peril as keeping it.
Oscar Wilde, through the painter Basil, suggests that art conceals its maker more completely than it reveals him, so a work is best judged on its own terms.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian realises that regret can settle the past, but the passions we feed now will shape what comes next.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian hides the portrait so he need not face his own decline, and the hiding only lets the damage grow out of sight.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian reads of a death he helped cause and tells himself he did not kill her, showing how easily we excuse ourselves.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian tells Harry that a book fascinated him without being liked, a useful distinction between what holds our attention and what we actually value.
Wilde warns through Dorian that appetite grows as it is fed, so every indulgence leaves the next one hungrier.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, the narrator notes that intellectual speculation is barren when it is separated from action and experiment, a check worth applying to our own big ideas.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian collects rare instruments with delight, then grows weary of them, showing how a hunger for novelty tends to fade once it is satisfied.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian fills his house with beautiful things to forget his troubles, a reminder that possessions can distract us from a conscience but cannot quiet it.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, society excuses a rich and charming man's conduct while quietly shunning him, a reminder that status often blinds us to what we are really seeing.
Wilde lets Dorian see himself as a complex creature with many lives, a view the novel later tests against its cost.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian treats evil as a material for beauty, a habit that slowly dulls the moral sense it depends on.
Basil insists that vice always shows on a man's face, yet the novel is built on the opposite, a secret hidden in a portrait, which is a reminder not to judge people only by appearances.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Basil says a person should be judged by the effect they have on their friends, a fair test of what kind of influence someone really has.
Basil admits he cannot truly say he knows a friend until he has seen that friend's soul, a sobering reminder of how little we see of other people.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Basil says both men are punished, one for worshipping another too much and one for worshipping himself too much, a sober note on what excessive devotion costs.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian believes the secret is never to face what he has done, showing how avoidance can pass itself off as a plan.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian asks a friend to look at a grim task purely as science, a reminder that a clean technical framing can hide an unclean purpose.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian appears perfectly at ease in company while carrying a hidden secret, a reminder that polish tells us little about what a person is carrying.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian hopes forgetting can stand in for forgiveness, a shortcut the novel shows to be hollow, since a wrong left unfaced keeps its hold.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Adrian Singleton says his habit has left him with no friends, a sad sign of how a craving can quietly crowd out the people who care about us.
Dorian tells himself that each man pays his own price for his life, yet the novel keeps showing how his choices land on other people.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, James Vane nearly kills the wrong man after one chance word, a warning about acting on a hunch before checking the facts.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian admits he chased pleasure rather than happiness and found it too often, a candid line on how pleasure alone rarely settles a restless person.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian plans to flee to a yacht to be safe and forget, a reminder that moving away from a problem rarely leaves the problem behind.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Lord Henry points out that one good act, even a sincere one, is a poor start, a reminder that a changed life is built from many acts rather than one gesture.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian insists that every person has a real soul that can be poisoned or made perfect, a conviction the novel then tests through its portrait.
Lord Henry observes that a scent, a colour or a half-forgotten tune can bring back whole moods, so our feelings are often set off by things we barely notice.
Dorian wishes each wrong had brought its penalty straight away, a wish that shows how hard it is to learn from consequences that arrive late or are hidden.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian resolves to be good while still blaming Basil and others for his ruin, a sign that a promise made without owning one's part is easily broken.
In The Picture of Dorian Gray, Dorian admits his good deed came from vanity and a wish to look good, a sharp reminder to check our motives before we praise ourselves.

preview.text:
“It is your best work, Basil, the best thing you have ever done,” said
Lord Henry languidly. “You must certainly send it next year to the
Grosvenor. The Academy is too large and too vulgar. Whenever I have
gone there, there have been either so many people that I have not been
able to see the pictures, which was dreadful, or so many pictures that
I have not been able to see the people, which was worse. The Grosvenor
is really the only place.”

“I don’t think I shall send it anywhere,” he answered, tossing his head
back in that odd way that used to make his friends laugh at him at
Oxford. “No, I won’t send it anywhere.”

Lord Henry elevated his eyebrows and looked at him in amazement through
the thin blue wreaths of smoke that curled up in such fanciful whorls
from his heavy, opium-tainted cigarette. “Not send it anywhere? My dear
fellow, why? Have you any reason? What odd chaps you painters are! You
do anything in the world to gain a reputation. As soon as you have one,
you seem to want to throw it away. It is silly of you, for there is
only one thing in the world worse than being talked about, and that is
not being talked about. A portrait like this would set you far above
all the young men in England, and make the old men quite jealous, if
old men are ever capable of any emotion.”

“I know you will laugh at me,” he replied, “but I really can’t exhibit
it. I have put too much of myself into it.”

Lord Henry stretched himself out on the divan and laughed.

“Yes, I knew you would; but it is quite true, all the same.”

books.title: Robinson Crusoe
books.author: Daniel Defoe
books.subject: adventure
books.licence_note: Author died 1731. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe has a father warn that a middle station in life brings fewer disasters than either great ambition or hard poverty, and that the choice to leave it is a risk worth weighing first.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe has the father say that a hard life is either fate or one's own fault, so a person should look honestly at which of the two is at work.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe shows a resolution made in a heated moment wearing off within days, so a promise needs a plan behind it to hold.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe describes a conscience that hardens each time it is ignored, so later warnings are heard less and less.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe has Crusoe value his father's counsel only while he is afraid, which shows how hard it is to value safety once the danger has passed.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe shows how the calm after a scare can wash away the promises made during it, as Crusoe drinks away his vows once the storm passes.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe has Crusoe admit he could have gone home safely and let the chance pass, a reminder that a clear chance to change course is easy to waste.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe has Crusoe feel pushed forward against his own calm reasoning, showing how an ingrained pattern can override what a person already knows is wise.

In Robinson Crusoe, the old shipmaster reads a near disaster as a plain sign to change course, yet keeps sailing because it is his calling, which shows that duty and wisdom do not always point the same way.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe observes that people are often more ashamed of turning back than of the mistake that made turning back necessary, and that the shame grows as the regret fades.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe has Crusoe go to sea dressed as a gentleman rather than working as a sailor, so he learns none of the trade. Skill comes from doing the ordinary work.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe's honest captain teaches him navigation because Crusoe delights in learning, which shows how a good teacher and an eager learner feed each other.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe shows a man keeping a wish for freedom alive for two years with no real plan, a reminder that a dream stays a dream until it has a way and people to carry it out.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe refuses to send his young companion ashore alone and says they will face the danger together, a good example of standing by the people who depend on you.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe admits he cannot find the islands without instruments and so follows the coast instead, a sound lesson that a plan should match the tools you actually have.
In Robinson Crusoe, the boy Xury spots the danger before Crusoe does, a reminder that the people around us can often see what we miss.
In Robinson Crusoe, the Portuguese captain refuses to take Crusoe's goods after rescuing him, reasoning that taking them would only undo the rescue. Real generosity leaves a person able to recover.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe realises too late that giving up his loyal companion left him short of help once the work grew, a cost that only shows itself later.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe has Crusoe see that the solitude he once complained of was the life he had earlier been unable to appreciate, a reminder that people often undervalue what they already have.
In Robinson Crusoe, the Portuguese captain advises Crusoe to risk only half of his capital first and keep the rest in reserve, so that one failed venture does not finish him.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe warns that success can breed restless ambition, and a head full of projects beyond one's reach often undoes the best of builders.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe takes great care over his property but never asks whether the voyage is wise for himself, showing how caution in small things can hide a blind spot in the large.
In Robinson Crusoe, the sailors in their worst moment cling to the small comfort that the ship has not yet broken, a habit that helps in any crisis.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe notes that sudden joy can overwhelm a person almost as much as grief, which is why good news sometimes needs to be handled gently.
In Robinson Crusoe, after the wreck Crusoe takes stock of what he still has before he gives in to panic. Taking stock is where recovery starts.
In Robinson Crusoe, finding fresh water lets Crusoe rest, showing how one small need solved can steady a person in a crisis.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe has Crusoe learn that sitting still and wishing gets nothing done, and that real need is what turns him to work, building a raft from spare spars.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe saves what he most needs, such as tools, before what merely looks valuable. In a crisis, usefulness matters more than appearance.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe holds his cargo steady on a shoal for half an hour until the rising tide frees him, a picture of patient persistence through a bad spot.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe waits for the tide to rise before landing his raft. Working with the natural timing of things can save what forcing it would lose.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe reasons that the next storm will break the wreck, so he salvages what he can first. When something is about to be lost, act while there is still time.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe shows Crusoe still unsatisfied with a store bigger than he can use, a reminder that piling up more does not by itself bring contentment.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe sees that coins are worth nothing on a desert island while a good knife is worth far more. What something is worth depends on what it does for you in your situation.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe weighs health, fresh water, shelter and a view of the sea before choosing where to settle, and he moves away from a low, damp spot to a better one.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe splits his gunpowder into about a hundred small parcels so one spark cannot destroy it all. Spreading a critical resource is a sensible way to limit risk.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe's own reason pulls him out of despair by asking where the other ten drowned men are. Setting a hard situation beside a worse one steadies the mind.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe plans for accidents and for the time when his strength fails, not only for the next day. Good preparation looks ahead.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe keeps a calendar by notching a post every day. A simple, steady record helps a person hold on to order when everything else is lost.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe finds slow work only troubles him when he is in a hurry. With time enough, the tedium of a task matters much less.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe writes his troubles on one side of a page and his comforts on the other, and finds that setting the good against the bad steadies his mind.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe concludes that even the most miserable condition holds something to be thankful for, and that training yourself to look for it is a comfort in its own right.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe learns to make most of what he needs without ever having handled a tool before, through labour, application and contrivance. Skill is built by patient practice.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe starts a daily journal only once his panic settles, and finds that a plain record of each day's work steadies him in hard times.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe strains his eyes after a distant sail that then vanishes, and finds that chasing such hopes only deepens his misery.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe sets his days into fixed times for work, walks, rest and leisure, a rhythm that keeps a lonely man steady.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe improvises a shovel from hard wood when the right tool is missing, and keeps the work moving. Making do with what is at hand is its own kind of skill.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe's cave collapses because he dug it too large, so he props up the roof before going on. Secure the base before you expand it.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe spends weeks failing to make a cask, then gives it up and turns to what works. Knowing when to drop a fruitless task is a skill too.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe comes to see that a handful of barley and rice growing unexpectedly moves a man who had earlier taken all his luck for chance. Small gifts deserve notice.

In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe's gratitude fades once he finds the ordinary cause of a gift, though he admits he should have been as thankful as if it were a miracle. Gratitude should not depend on how strange a gift is.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe runs for the wall in sudden fright at a collapse before he understands the danger. Sudden fear can make us act before we know what is really happening.
In Robinson Crusoe, after an earthquake Crusoe reasons that the storm following it is only a consequence and the danger has passed, and calm reasoning brings his courage back.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe refuses to abandon his shelter until a new one is ready, so a safe move builds the replacement before the old one is given up.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe spends a full week building a machine to keep his tools sharp, reckoning the time well spent. Looking after your tools first is an investment in all the work after.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe says he has learned not to despair of anything, and so takes the wreck apart piece by piece for whatever use it might still have.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe admits years among hardened companions wore away the good teaching of his father, a reminder that the company we keep shapes what we keep of what we were taught.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe admits his joy at surviving was a passing rush that he never turned into real thankfulness. Relief fades quickly unless we stop to reflect on it.
In Robinson Crusoe, Defoe shows that even a near-death fright fades once the danger passes, unless it is turned into a settled change in how a person lives.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe, sick and alone, admits he had turned down a secure life that could have made him happy, and owns the consequences of his own choices rather than blaming fate.
In Robinson Crusoe, Crusoe's own conscience answers his complaint by asking him to look at his whole past before blaming anyone else. Honest self-examination comes before blame.

preview.text:
My father, a wise and grave man, gave me serious and excellent counsel
against what he foresaw was my design. He called me one morning into
his chamber, where he was confined by the gout, and expostulated very
warmly with me upon this subject. He asked me what reasons, more than a
mere wandering inclination, I had for leaving father’s house and my
native country, where I might be well introduced, and had a prospect of
raising my fortune by application and industry, with a life of ease and
pleasure. He told me it was men of desperate fortunes on one hand, or
of aspiring, superior fortunes on the other, who went abroad upon
adventures, to rise by enterprise, and make themselves famous in
undertakings of a nature out of the common road; that these things were
all either too far above me or too far below me; that mine was the
middle state, or what might be called the upper station of low life,
which he had found, by long experience, was the best state in the
world, the most suited to human happiness, not exposed to the miseries
and hardships, the labour and sufferings of the mechanic part of
mankind, and not embarrassed with the pride, luxury, ambition, and envy
of the upper part of mankind. He told me I might judge of the happiness
of this state by this one thing—viz. that this was the state of life
which all other people envied; that kings have frequently lamented the
miserable consequence of being born to great things, and wished they
had been placed in the middle of the two extremes, between the mean and
the great; that the wise man gave his testimony to this, as the
standard of felicity, when he prayed to have neither poverty nor
riches.

books.title: Peter Pan
books.author: J. M. Barrie
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Author died 1937. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Peter Pan, J. M. Barrie suggests children grow up the moment they realise they will, and Wendy learns it from one look at her mother.
In Peter Pan, Barrie makes Nana, a dog who works as a nurse, the one who takes the children most seriously, showing that real care is shown through attention rather than status.

In Peter Pan, Barrie pictures a mother tidying her children's minds each night, folding the day's naughtiness away and setting out the prettier thoughts for morning. It reads like a fair description of an evening review.
Barrie notes that Mrs. Darling believed in Peter as a child, but grown-up good sense made her doubt him. The story quietly warns that sensible adults can lose their wonder without noticing.
In Peter Pan, the Darlings sit for years replaying every "if only", and Barrie shows how dwelling on what went wrong can keep a family stuck instead of moving on.
In Peter Pan, Mrs. Darling stays calm when her husband rages over a tie and simply offers to help. Barrie shows that a steady, kind response can defuse a storm faster than an argument.

In Peter Pan, Mr. Darling knows he is behaving badly but cannot back down, because his pride will not let him admit a mistake. Barrie shows how wounded pride can keep a person pushing on when they already know better.
In Peter Pan, Wendy meets a crying stranger with courtesy and curiosity rather than alarm. A polite, open question is how a friendship begins.
In Peter Pan, Peter says a fairy dies every time a child stops believing in fairies. Barrie uses it to show that wonder survives only while someone keeps believing in it.
In Peter Pan, Peter wins Wendy over with praise and promises that she would be respected and needed. Barrie shows how flattery can talk a person into leaving the safety of home.
In Peter Pan, Peter rescues Michael mostly to show off his cleverness, and the story notes that this is not the same as caring. Kindness done for applause is a thin kind of kindness.
In Peter Pan, Peter forgets people quickly, so Wendy has to keep saying her own name to be remembered. Barrie shows that being known often takes patient, repeated reminders.

In Peter Pan, Barrie observes that a jealous heart has room for only one feeling at a time, so Tink can't be kind to Wendy while she is envious. It is a sharp way of showing how envy crowds out goodwill.
In Peter Pan, Barrie says Tootles's bad luck gave him a gentle sadness, but it sweetened his nature rather than souring it. Hard knocks do not have to make a person bitter.
In Peter Pan, Barrie says Captain Hook is never more sinister than when he is most polite. Good manners can hide cruelty, so a polished surface is no proof of a good character.

In Peter Pan, Peter raises the arrow to strike Tootles twice and cannot bring it down, because he sees Wendy is alive. Barrie shows how a moment's pause, and a fact checked, can stop a hasty judgment.

In Peter Pan, Barrie notes that Peter treats make-believe and truth as the same thing, while the other boys know the difference. The story suggests that taking play seriously is a kind of imagination worth keeping.
In Peter Pan, Wendy worries her brothers are forgetting their parents, so she sets them quizzes about home. Barrie shows that keeping loved ones in mind takes deliberate effort, not just time.

In Peter Pan, Wendy keeps the boys on a cold rock because of her own bedtime rule, and it nearly costs them. Barrie shows that a rule followed too rigidly can work against the very people it is meant to protect.
In Peter Pan, Barrie notes that Hook needed his own belief in himself more than his men's belief in him. Once the inner confidence goes, outside respect tends to follow.

In Peter Pan, Peter could have finished Hook when he had the higher ground, but judges that unfair and gives his enemy a hand up. Barrie shows that fairness is a choice a person makes, even in a fight.

In Peter Pan, Barrie says every child is shaken the first time they are treated unfairly, and is never quite the same boy again. It is a reminder that people carry the first sting of unfairness for a long time.
In Peter Pan, the Never bird gives up her nest to rescue Peter, though the two cannot understand each other's words. Barrie shows that generosity needs no shared language.
In Peter Pan, the children enjoy one last glad hour without knowing what is coming. Barrie makes the reader feel how precious an ordinary evening is while it lasts.

In Peter Pan, Barrie observes that children can be careless with the people who love them because they trust that love will always be there. It is a gentle warning that taking care for granted is its own kind of blindness.
In Peter Pan, Tootles, usually overlooked, rises to the trust Wendy places in him and speaks with dignity. Barrie shows that people often grow to match the faith others put in them.

In Peter Pan, Peter has thought his mother out and remembers only her bad points, so he no longer misses her. Barrie shows how holding on to a grievance can quietly reshape what we remember about the people we have lost.

In Peter Pan, Barrie suggests Hook's hatred of Peter comes from Peter's easy confidence, which unsettles him like a sparrow in a lion's cage. Resentment of someone else's ease can grow into an obsession.
In Peter Pan, Peter pretends not to care that Wendy has gone, playing his pipes and sleeping in a huff. Barrie shows that bravado is often how hurt hides itself.
In Peter Pan, Barrie says Hook is moved by the peaceful sight of his sleeping enemy, but Peter's smug look steels his heart. Irritation can drown out a person's better nature.
In Peter Pan, Tinker Bell, who has been unkind to Peter's friends, drinks the poison meant for him. Barrie shows that someone who has behaved badly can still act selflessly when it matters most.
In Peter Pan, Hook cannot understand why the children love the plain-hearted Smee and not himself. Barrie hints that kindness which seeks no admiration is the kind people trust most.
In Peter Pan, John and Michael refuse to swear an oath they do not believe, even knowing the plank waits. Barrie shows that courage can be quiet, just a refusal to betray what you hold to be true.

In Peter Pan, Barrie notes that Peter turns the crocodile's misfortune to his own use without a thought for how it feels. The passage is a quiet prompt to ask who a situation is costing before you profit from it.

In Peter Pan, Hook dies clinging to outward appearances, his tie and socks all right, even as his inner life falls apart. Barrie shows how a person can guard a reputation so hard that they lose sight of what matters.

In Peter Pan, Mr. Darling answers his mistake by sleeping in a kennel and courteously lifting his hat to passers-by. Barrie suggests that owning a failure openly, without hiding behind it, can win a quiet kind of respect.
In Peter Pan, Wendy wonders whether she and her brothers remember the old life as well as they thought. Barrie reminds us that memories of home can be less reliable than we assume.

In Peter Pan, Mrs. Darling has dreamed of her children so often that she cannot believe they are really there. Barrie shows how longing can make the real thing hard to recognise when it finally arrives.
In Peter Pan, Mr. Darling is hurt to feel treated as a cypher in his own home, and the boys reassure him. Barrie suggests that everyone wants to be consulted about the place they live.

In Peter Pan, the boys lose the power to fly after they start school. Barrie says they called it lack of practice, but it really meant they had stopped believing, which is a sharp observation about how wonder fades.
In Peter Pan, Barrie ends with Wendy, now grown, watching her daughter fly off with Peter through wet-eyed smiles. Letting children go can itself be a loving act.

preview.text:
Mrs. Darling loved to have everything just so, and Mr. Darling had a
passion for being exactly like his neighbours; so, of course, they had
a nurse. As they were poor, owing to the amount of milk the children
drank, this nurse was a prim Newfoundland dog, called Nana, who had
belonged to no one in particular until the Darlings engaged her. She
had always thought children important, however, and the Darlings had
become acquainted with her in Kensington Gardens, where she spent most
of her spare time peeping into perambulators, and was much hated by
careless nursemaids, whom she followed to their homes and complained of
to their mistresses. She proved to be quite a treasure of a nurse. How
thorough she was at bath-time, and up at any moment of the night if one
of her charges made the slightest cry. Of course her kennel was in the
nursery. She had a genius for knowing when a cough is a thing to have
no patience with and when it needs stocking around your throat. She
believed to her last day in old-fashioned remedies like rhubarb leaf,
and made sounds of contempt over all this new-fangled talk about germs,
and so on. It was a lesson in propriety to see her escorting the
children to school, walking sedately by their side when they were well
behaved, and butting them back into line if they strayed. On John’s
footer days she never once forgot his sweater, and she usually carried
an umbrella in her mouth in case of rain. There is a room in the
basement of Miss Fulsom’s school where the nurses wait. They sat on
forms, while Nana lay on the floor, but that was the only difference.
They affected to ignore her as of an inferior social status to
themselves, and she despised their light talk. She resented visits to
the nursery from Mrs. Darling’s friends, but if they did come she first
whipped off Michael’s pinafore and put him into the one with blue
braiding, and smoothed out Wendy and made a dash at John’s hair.

books.title: Walden
books.author: Henry David Thoreau
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 1862. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Thoreau holds that a writer owes readers a plain and honest account of his own life, because a book that hides the writer's experience is hard to trust.
Thoreau asks whether the hard conditions people put up with at work and at home have to be as bad as they are, and whether they could be made better.
Thoreau warns that inherited farms and possessions can weigh a person down, since they are much easier to acquire than to get rid of.
Thoreau argues that people worn out by toil lose the leisure to live with integrity, and that the finest qualities of a person need gentle handling to survive.
Thoreau describes people stuck in debt who keep promising to pay tomorrow, and sees a life spent getting out of debt as one that buries the person who lives it.
Thoreau says the hardest master is the one a person becomes to himself, and that what a man thinks of himself shapes his fate more than public opinion does.
Thoreau says most people live lives of quiet desperation, and that a wise person avoids doing desperate things, including the amusements that come after work.
Thoreau urges us to question inherited prejudices, since no way of thinking can be trusted without proof, and what the old say cannot be done is often found to be possible.
Thoreau notes that what counts as a necessity differs from one circle to another, and that human capacities have never been fully tested by anyone.
Thoreau suggests that we might learn a great deal by seeing life through another person's eyes, and that much of what our neighbours call good is worth doubting.
Thoreau observes that we can trust life a good deal more than we do, and that constant anxiety is a kind of sickness that we bring on ourselves.
Thoreau suggests that the basic needs of life have changed little over the ages, so a person should ask honestly what they truly need before adding anything else.
Thoreau separates the true necessaries of life from habits that have simply become customs, and says we must secure the basics before we can take on life's real problems with freedom.
Thoreau mocks people who spend decades trading in distant lands only to live comfortably and return home at last, and asks whether that is how a life should be spent.
Thoreau argues that many luxuries and comforts hinder people rather than help them, and that a true philosopher lives by wisdom, not merely by teaching it.
Thoreau suggests that once basic needs are met, a person should turn to living more fully, instead of wanting more and more of the same comforts.
Thoreau speaks mainly to discontented people who complain about their lot when they could improve it, and warns that some people hoard possessions they cannot use.
Thoreau describes getting up early to meet each day, and says the present moment is where the past and future meet, so it is the one place we truly have to act.
Thoreau admits that much of his work of watching and listening brought no reward from others, and says that his effort was its own reward.
Thoreau tells of a basket seller who failed because he made goods without asking what buyers wanted, and says the life praised as successful is only one kind among many.
Thoreau mocks the sprawling duties of a merchant who must oversee every detail himself, and shows how a business that demands universal knowledge can wear down the person who runs it.
Thoreau argues that our love of novelty and our concern for what others think drive much of what we buy to wear, more than real usefulness does.
Thoreau points out that people worry more about being respected than about being truly respectable, and says a patch in one's clothes matters far less than a sound conscience.
Thoreau says a person who has found real work does not need new clothes for it, and that any new enterprise should begin with a new wearer rather than a new wardrobe.
Thoreau suggests that a person should live simply enough to lay hands on everything they own in the dark, so that losing possessions would cause no great anxiety.
Thoreau jokes that people are measured by their clothes instead of their character, and says that most of us worship Fashion rather than honesty.
Thoreau notes that every generation laughs at the old fashions while following the new ones religiously, and says only a sincere life gives any costume its dignity.
Thoreau doubts that the factory system clothes people well, since its real aim seems to be enriching the companies that run it, and reminds us that people only hit what they aim at.
Thoreau sees a home as one of the first human needs, and notes that people who build houses for comfort also crave warmth in their affections.
Thoreau observes that children love to play house and stay outdoors, and wonders whether we have covered ourselves so thoroughly that we rarely live under the open sky.
Thoreau warns that a house built without care can become a prison or a tomb, and urges us first to ask how slight a shelter is truly necessary.
Thoreau argues that the real cost of anything is the life we must exchange for it, so a person who spends most of their working years paying for a house may be poorer than one with a simple shelter.
Thoreau suggests that civilised life could be arranged so that we keep its advantages without paying the heavy sacrifices it often demands from us.
Thoreau notes that many farmers spend decades toiling to own land they inherited or borrowed for, and that few have truly paid for their homes, so the homestead itself can become the burden.
Thoreau says a farmer may try to solve the problem of making a living by a formula more complicated than the problem itself, and that the trap set for comfort often catches the one who set it.
Thoreau points out that civilisation has built finer houses faster than it has built finer people, and asks whether a better dwelling is earned by a life spent on mere necessities.
Thoreau notes that the comforts enjoyed by some are often paid for by the hardship of others, and that the people who build palaces may return each night to a poor hut.
Thoreau urges us to ask what a house truly is, since many people stay poor all their lives trying to match the homes of their neighbours, and suggests we might sometimes be content with less.
Thoreau laments that people have become the tools of their tools, settling down and forgetting to look up, and says the best art tries to free us from that condition.
Thoreau argues that our houses should first be lined with beauty where they meet our lives, and that beautiful living must come before beautiful ornament.
Thoreau says it is generous to borrow tools for a new venture, since it lets others share in the enterprise, and that a borrowed axe often comes back sharper.
Thoreau points out that for all our arts, sciences and appliances, we may know little more than the wind that blows, and he urges humility about what we claim to know.
Thoreau says people in almost every climate have dug into the earth for steady comfort, and that even grand houses are often little more than a porch at the entrance to a burrow.
Thoreau found that building with neighbours turned the work into an occasion for neighbourliness, and that a mind with time to spare can find real entertainment in the smallest scraps.
Thoreau argues that building a dwelling with your own hands has a fitness like a bird building its own nest, and asks where the division of labour will end and what it finally serves.
Thoreau says architectural beauty grows outward from the character of the person who lives within, and that ornament added to the surface is a poor stand-in for honest living.
Thoreau notes that the most interesting dwellings are often the humblest, because the life lived inside gives them character, while ornaments added from outside fall away like borrowed plumes.
Thoreau argues that wiser management of student life would cut the cost of education, since the comforts students pay for often cost others far more than they are worth.
Thoreau urges students to do more than study life from a safe distance, and to actually live it, since the best way to learn how to live is to try the experiment of living.
Thoreau says a boy learns more by making his own knife from ore he has dug than by attending lectures, and suggests that real education is the art of living, not only the professions.
Thoreau warns that many modern improvements are illusions, since they are improved means to an unimproved end, and that we rush to build fast connections before deciding what is worth saying.
Thoreau argues that the swiftest traveller is often the one who goes on foot, since the person who must work to pay the fare may end up working the whole journey.
Thoreau warns that a life spent earning money to enjoy a questionable freedom at the end of it is a poor trade, and that a crowd rushing for progress often leaves many people behind.
Thoreau argues that a person who lives simply, eats only what they grow and avoids trading for luxuries needs very little land, and gains independence by not being tied down to property.
Thoreau suggests that relying on animals to do our work makes us serve the animal within us and the animals around us, and that such luxury can leave the strongest in charge of everyone else.
Thoreau argues that nations try to memorialise themselves with hammered stone, yet one piece of good sense or honest manners would be more memorable than any monument.
Thoreau says the love of art behind many grand buildings is often mere vanity, and wonders who in those days was above such trifling and did not help build them.
Thoreau argues that the leisure and independence he secured were worth more to him than the modest way he chose to live, since a plain home was all he really needed.
Thoreau argues that obtaining what we truly need takes far less trouble than we think, and that people often suffer for want of luxuries rather than of necessities.
Thoreau's list of his own few belongings shows how little a person truly needs, and he remarks that the more things we own, the poorer we often are.

preview.text:
I should not obtrude my affairs so much on the notice of my readers if
very particular inquiries had not been made by my townsmen concerning
my mode of life, which some would call impertinent, though they do not
appear to me at all impertinent, but, considering the circumstances,
very natural and pertinent. Some have asked what I got to eat; if I did
not feel lonesome; if I was not afraid; and the like. Others have been
curious to learn what portion of my income I devoted to charitable
purposes; and some, who have large families, how many poor children I
maintained. I will therefore ask those of my readers who feel no
particular interest in me to pardon me if I undertake to answer some of
these questions in this book. In most books, the _I_, or first person,
is omitted; in this it will be retained; that, in respect to egotism,
is the main difference. We commonly do not remember that it is, after
all, always the first person that is speaking. I should not talk so
much about myself if there were anybody else whom I knew as well.
Unfortunately, I am confined to this theme by the narrowness of my
experience. Moreover, I, on my side, require of every writer, first or
last, a simple and sincere account of his own life, and not merely what
he has heard of other men’s lives; some such account as he would send
to his kindred from a distant land; for if he has lived sincerely, it
must have been in a distant land to me. Perhaps these pages are more
particularly addressed to poor students. As for the rest of my readers,
they will accept such portions as apply to them. I trust that none will
stretch the seams in putting on the coat, for it may do good service to
him whom it fits.

books.title: Moby Dick
books.author: Herman Melville
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1891. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Moby-Dick, Ishmael deals with a grim, low mood by changing his surroundings and going out into the world, calling it his substitute for a pistol and ball.
In Moby-Dick, Melville shows office and shop workers crowding down to the waterfront on a Sunday, a sign of how much people long for open space after a week penned indoors.
In Moby-Dick, Ishmael says that moving from a schoolmaster's authority to a sailor's humble work stings at first, but the sting wears off in time, and Stoic calm helps you get through it.
Ishmael notes there is all the difference in the world between paying and being paid, and that the act of paying is the uncomfortable side.
Melville's Ishmael observes that the commander on the quarter-deck breathes air the crew on the forecastle has already given him, and does not realise it.
Ishmael admits his choice to go to sea only felt like his own free judgement, while deeper curiosity about the unknown had quietly steered him there.
Melville quotes an old writer that the same storm looks very different from a warm window than from a cold one, so how a hardship feels depends on where you stand.
Ishmael stares at a puzzling painting until he finds the one portentous thing at its centre, and then everything else falls into place. Often one central fact makes the rest plain.
Ishmael catches himself nursing prejudices against a stranger he has never met, and decides to wait and judge the man in person before he settles his mind.
Ishmael refuses to be fobbed off with vague, muddled answers. He asks the landlord to speak plainly and say whether he will be safe before he commits to anything.
Ishmael admits that he was afraid of the stranger mainly because he did not understand him. Not knowing a person is often what makes them frightening.
Once Ishmael sees the tattooed harpooneer as a person, just as anxious as he is, he realises the stranger has as much reason to fear him, and he sleeps well.
Ishmael holds that a good laugh is a precious thing, and that someone willing to be the butt of a joke with good humour often has more in them than people think.
Ishmael notices that hardened whalemen who fear no whale go quiet and sheepish at a social breakfast. Skill in one setting does not automatically carry into another.
Ishmael reads Father Mapple pulling his ladder up into the pulpit as a sign of stepping back from worldly ties to draw strength from within, a self-contained stronghold.
Father Mapple preaches that the right course is hard because doing it means overruling our own wishes, so we must disobey ourselves to obey what we know is right.
Melville's Father Mapple notes that a wrongdoer with money can pass every border freely, while a poor person's virtue is turned away. Judgement often follows the purse.
Father Mapple praises Jonah's repentance as accepting the fair weight of his punishment rather than clamouring for pardon. Owning a mistake without excuses is a model for anyone.
Father Mapple closes his sermon with the duty to speak truth to the face of falsehood, even when the message is unwelcome to those who hear it.
Ishmael finds that the very things that put him off Queequeg, his strangeness and wildness, are what draw him in. Sincere, unpretentious people are often the friends worth making.
Ishmael settles his scruples about a stranger's customs with the golden rule: treat your fellow man as you would want to be treated, and let the rest be his own business.
Ishmael observes that nothing exists in itself, only by contrast. A little cold makes the warmth of the bed feel warmer, and comfort is best felt against its opposite.
In Moby-Dick, Queequeg is refused a berth on a ship, so he paddles out to meet it and clings to a ring-bolt, refusing to let go. Determination can open doors that a polite request cannot.

When a loose boom sweeps the deck and everyone freezes, Queequeg drops calmly to his knees, lassos it, then dives in to save the very man he had just frightened. Calm action in a panic is worth a lot.
Ishmael describes Nantucket fishermen working up step by step, from crabs in the sand to mackerel nets, then boats, then great ships. Mastery is built from small beginnings, one stage at a time.
Ishmael observes that a rare old craft, scarred by long service, has a melancholy air about it. Melville's view is that all noble things are touched with that kind of sadness.
When Ishmael says he wants to go to sea to see the world, Captain Peleg asks why he must go so far, since he can see the world right where he stands. Much of what we seek is closer than we think.
Captain Peleg tells Ishmael it is better to sail with a moody good captain than a laughing bad one, and not to judge a man by an unfortunate name. Character matters more than manner.
Ishmael argues that people should be charitable toward other people's beliefs and quirks, since everyone is somewhat cracked in the head and in need of mending.
Ishmael suggests that people of every faith share a common ground beneath their quirks and differences, and that this shared belief is what should hold them together.
In a storm that wrecks the masts, Captain Peleg says there was no time to brood on death. He and his captain thought only of how to save all hands, which is the practical focus a crisis demands.
Ishmael sees that it is the easiest thing in the world for a man to look as if he had a great secret in him. Mystique is not the same as substance.

Melville points out that a whaling voyage is a long housekeeping far from any shop, and that the ship carries spare boats, spars and lines because accidents are sure to come. Plan for what will go wrong.
Ishmael admits that a man who senses something wrong, and is already committed, will quietly try to hide his suspicions even from himself. Name the doubt early, while it is still easy to act on.
Melville suggests that deep, earnest thinking takes an intrepid effort, a willingness to stay in open water rather than crawl back to the safety of the shore. Comfort can be its own kind of trap.
Herman Melville has his narrator in Moby Dick argue that a trade's grubby look says little about its worth. Judge the work by what it does for people, not by how it looks.
In Moby Dick, Melville has Ishmael credit the unglamorous whaling ships with opening up distant coasts. The people who do the groundwork are often the ones nobody writes down.
Ishmael in Moby Dick says whatever worth he has comes from the whaling ship that taught him, which he calls his Yale and Harvard. A humble place can still be a real education.
In Moby Dick, Starbuck treats courage as a practical tool, not a show. He would not take a man into his boat who was not afraid of a whale, since fear that is weighed honestly keeps you alive.
Melville has his narrator find dignity in the arm that wields a pick or drives a spike, not in robes or rank. Honest work carries its own worth, whatever the job looks like from outside.
In Moby Dick, Stubb meets the deadliest moment of a whale hunt with an easy, good-humoured calm. Steadiness in a crisis can come from knowing the work well enough that it no longer rattles you.

In Moby Dick, Melville shows Ahab's unbending will as both a strength and a warning. Fixed resolve can make a leader fearless, and it can also keep him from seeing what he is pointing his crew towards.
In Moby Dick, Stubb notices that an insult from a living person stings far more than the same thing from an object. Who says a hard word can matter as much as what it says.
In Moby Dick, Ishmael promises nothing complete, because anything called complete is bound to be faulty. He is happy to sketch the plan and leave the building to others.
In Moby Dick, Ishmael admits his task is far too big for anyone, then tries it anyway because he is in earnest. Being honest about how hard a job is does not stop you from starting it.
In Moby Dick, Melville notes that sorting things by one striking feature fails, because the same feature turns up in unrelated kinds. Look at the whole thing before you sort it.

Melville ends his whale classification unfinished, saying small structures can be finished by their builders while grand, true ones leave the top stone to others. Work worth doing is often finished by someone who comes after.

In Moby Dick, officers who will argue with the captain on deck go quiet and deferential at his table. Power changes how people behave around the person holding it, and a good leader notices that and does not mistake it for agreement.
In Moby Dick, Flask finds that promotion brings more pressure than peace, and that the rank he wanted costs him simple comforts. Gains in status often come with a hidden price.
In Moby Dick, Ahab keeps himself so apart from his crew that no companionship reaches him, and his gloom feeds on itself. A leader who shuts people out ends up alone with his worst thoughts.
In Moby Dick, a young lookout drifts so far into idle daydreams that he forgets the job he was there to do. Even a beautiful view is no excuse for losing your watch.
In Moby Dick, Ahab nails a gold coin to the mast to rally the crew to his hunt. A bright reward can fire people up, but it can also pull them into a goal that is really someone else's obsession.

In Moby Dick, Starbuck tells Ahab he came to hunt whales, not to serve his commander's revenge, and asks what that vengeance will actually bring in. A good colleague says plainly what the work is for, even when the boss will not like it.
In Moby Dick, Ahab pours his hatred into a single target, and he says he will wreak it on the whale. Anger fixed on one thing can drown out reason and pull a whole crew along with it.
In Moby Dick, Ahab is so consumed by his purpose that even a lovely sunset feels like anguish. Obsession can take the enjoyment out of the good things right in front of you.

In Moby Dick, Starbuck is caught between obeying his captain and his own conscience, and he feels his duty turning into something he resents. Staying loyal to a leader who has gone too far is a hard, lonely place.
In Moby Dick, Stubb decides that whatever is coming, he will go to it laughing. He cannot control the future, but he can choose the spirit he meets it with.
In Moby Dick, Ishmael admits he shouted his oath loudest because of the dread in him, and took on another man's feud. Fear and group excitement can pull us into commitments we would never make alone.

In Moby Dick, rumours about the white whale grow and turn monstrous because news travels slowly across the empty sea. When people have few plain facts, fear fills the gap and swells into something bigger than the truth.

In Moby Dick, Melville says a grudge can seem to fade while it quietly sinks deeper, and an obsession can take a sharp mind and aim all its strength at one target. Watch for a fixation that looks calm on the surface.

preview.text:
“Oh, the rare old Whale, mid storm and gale In his ocean home will be
  A giant in might, where might is right, And King of the boundless
  sea.” —_Whale Song_.

CHAPTER 1. Loomings.

Call me Ishmael. Some years ago—never mind how long precisely—having
little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me
on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part
of the world. It is a way I have of driving off the spleen and
regulating the circulation. Whenever I find myself growing grim about
the mouth; whenever it is a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever
I find myself involuntarily pausing before coffin warehouses, and
bringing up the rear of every funeral I meet; and especially whenever
my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral
principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and
methodically knocking people’s hats off—then, I account it high time to
get to sea as soon as I can. This is my substitute for pistol and ball.
With a philosophical flourish Cato throws himself upon his sword; I
quietly take to the ship. There is nothing surprising in this. If they
but knew it, almost all men in their degree, some time or other,
cherish very nearly the same feelings towards the ocean with me.

There now is your insular city of the Manhattoes, belted round by
wharves as Indian isles by coral reefs—commerce surrounds it with her
surf. Right and left, the streets take you waterward. Its extreme
downtown is the battery, where that noble mole is washed by waves, and
cooled by breezes, which a few hours previous were out of sight of
land. Look at the crowds of water-gazers there.

books.title: The Wonderful Wizard of Oz
books.author: L. Frank Baum
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Author died 1919. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: L. Frank Baum wrote The Wonderful Wizard of Oz for children today, keeping the wonder and joy of fairy tales and leaving out their heartaches and nightmares.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Dorothy stays calm in the middle of the cyclone, waits and sees what happens. That steadiness carries her through.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Munchkins weep along with Dorothy when she cries, and the Witch of the North gives her a kiss and real help. Kindness starts with noticing someone's tears.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Dorothy hears the road will be dangerous, but she bravely resolves not to turn back. She keeps her eyes on the goal that matters most.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Dorothy tells the Scarecrow that if Oz cannot help him, he will be no worse off than he is now. Taking a chance on a hope costs little.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Dorothy tells the Scarecrow that however dreary home is, people would rather live there than anywhere else. Loyalty to home runs through the story.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Tin Woodman has groaned for more than a year and nobody came. Dorothy stops to listen and asks what she can do. Noticing a cry for help is a choice.

In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Tin Woodman rusted in the forest for a year after one forgotten bit of upkeep. His real loss was the heart that let him love. Small neglected habits can undo careful people.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Cowardly Lion roars to make others run, yet he knows he is a coward and it makes him unhappy. Bluster can hide fear but does not cure it.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Tin Woodman weeps after he steps on a beetle, then takes great care to step over even the ants. Care for small things is a habit worth building.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, when the Kalidahs are nearly across the fallen tree, the Scarecrow stops to think and has the far end cut away. Calm thinking under pressure can turn a lost fight.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Stork lifts the stuffed Scarecrow out of the river and says she always likes to help anyone in trouble. Help offered freely is what the story rewards.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Tin Woodman, who says he has no heart, saves a field mouse from a Wildcat because he helps anyone who needs a friend. Kindness is something you choose to do.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, thousands of small field mice, each with a piece of string, pull the sleeping Lion out of the poppies. Many small helpers working together can move a heavy load.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Guardian of the Gates makes everyone wear green spectacles, because the glare would blind them. What we see often depends on what we choose to look through.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Dorothy weeps rather than kill, even when the Wizard says it is the price of going home. She will not do harm to get what she wants.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Cowardly Lion sets out to face the Witch even though he believes he is a coward. Courage shows up in the doing, not in waiting to feel brave.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Scarecrow stands up to the crows and tells his friends to lie down beside him. He takes the danger on himself so that the others are safe.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Dorothy carries food to the caged Lion each night and they talk over their troubles together. Quiet, unseen kindness keeps hope alive.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the freed Winkies gladly help Dorothy rescue her friends, glad to repay the girl who set them free. Kindness given freely often comes back around.

In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, when the friends despair, Dorothy suggests asking the field mice for help, and the Scarecrow wonders why they did not think of it sooner. Asking for help is often the quickest way out of being stuck.

In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Monkey King says Quelala was not spoiled by his good fortune, and Quelala pleads for mercy for the pranksters. A kind word can turn a punishment into a fairer answer.

In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Wizard confesses he has fooled everyone so long he dreads being found out, and that he hid away from his own people. A great front can cost a person their peace of mind.

In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Wizard tells the Scarecrow that experience is the only thing that brings knowledge, so the longer you live, the more you learn. Wisdom grows from what you go through.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Wizard tells the Lion that true courage is facing danger while you are afraid. Everyone feels fear, and courage is acting anyway.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Scarecrow says his good luck is due to Dorothy, who lifted him from his pole, so he will stay with her until she is safely home. Loyalty and gratitude go together.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Dorothy forgives Oz for breaking his promise because he did his best. Forgiveness comes easily when someone has tried in good faith.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, the Tin Woodman warns the friends to take great care not to hurt the fragile china people. Strength carries a duty to be gentle with those who are easily broken.
In The Wonderful Wizard of Oz, Glinda reveals that Dorothy's Silver Shoes could have taken her home from the first day. The help you need is sometimes already with you, unnoticed.

preview.text:
Yet the old time fairy tale, having served for generations, may now be
classed as “historical” in the children’s library; for the time has
come for a series of newer “wonder tales” in which the stereotyped
genie, dwarf and fairy are eliminated, together with all the horrible
and blood-curdling incidents devised by their authors to point a
fearsome moral to each tale. Modern education includes morality;
therefore the modern child seeks only entertainment in its wonder tales
and gladly dispenses with all disagreeable incident.

Having this thought in mind, the story of “The Wonderful Wizard of Oz”
was written solely to please children of today. It aspires to being a
modernized fairy tale, in which the wonderment and joy are retained and
the heartaches and nightmares are left out.

L. Frank Baum
Chicago, April, 1900.

The Wonderful Wizard of Oz

Chapter I
The Cyclone

Dorothy lived in the midst of the great Kansas prairies, with Uncle
Henry, who was a farmer, and Aunt Em, who was the farmer’s wife. Their
house was small, for the lumber to build it had to be carried by wagon
many miles. There were four walls, a floor and a roof, which made one
room; and this room contained a rusty looking cookstove, a cupboard for
the dishes, a table, three or four chairs, and the beds. Uncle Henry
and Aunt Em had a big bed in one corner, and Dorothy a little bed in
another corner. There was no garret at all, and no cellar—except a
small hole dug in the ground, called a cyclone cellar, where the family
could go in case one of those great whirlwinds arose, mighty enough to
crush any building in its path. It was reached by a trap door in the
middle of the floor, from which a ladder led down into the small, dark
hole.

books.title: Thus Spake Zarathustra
books.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 1900, translator died 1919. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Nietzsche argued that a new set of values could reshape a people, as Christianity once did to the ancient world, so the Superman was an ideal to work toward now, not a distant species.
Nietzsche wrote that a new goal needs new means, a sturdier way of living than before, and that you cannot keep gaining it without also spending some of it.
Nietzsche found that being forsaken by friends is very different from choosing solitude on purpose, a distinction worth keeping when a hard path leaves you feeling alone.
Nietzsche found that even clear writing can go unheard: many readers misunderstood Zarathustra because nobody was yet ripe for his thoughts.
Nietzsche nearly stopped writing in Rome, but once back in the mountain air his creative energy returned, a reminder that a low stretch need not be the end.
Nietzsche described inspiration as ideas that arrive suddenly and unbidden, so that one hears them rather than seeks them.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, truthfulness is held up as the highest virtue, the opposite of the idealist who flees from reality.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, an old hermit advises that the best help is to carry part of people's load alongside them, rather than hand out alms.
Nietzsche has Zarathustra urge people to stay true to the earth and wary of those who promise hopes beyond it, since such promises can drain the life out of living.
Nietzsche warns that self-satisfaction, more than sin, leaves people stuck, and asks whether their own virtues and reason ever make them truly passionate.
Nietzsche has Zarathustra say that what is great in people is that they are a bridge and not a goal, living for what comes after them.
Nietzsche warns of the last man, who wants comfort above all, makes everything small, and can no longer despise himself or aim beyond himself.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, the hero decides he needs living companions who follow because they want to follow themselves, not a crowd or a dead weight to carry.
Nietzsche sets out three changes of the spirit: the camel that carries heavy loads, the lion that wins its own freedom, and the child who starts afresh.
Nietzsche contrasts the camel's obedience to 'Thou shalt' with the lion's 'I will', the courage to create your own values rather than simply inherit them.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, a useful evening question is what you overcame, reconciled and learned during the day, a daily review worth keeping.
Nietzsche suggests that the more honestly we speak about ourselves, the more we find worth in the body and the earth, instead of looking for escape beyond them.
Nietzsche suggests many strong passions can grow into virtues when aimed at a high purpose, though too many competing virtues can wear a person down.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, the answer to 'life is hard to bear' is not to act delicate about it, but to meet it with courage and some laughter.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, a tree on a hill shows that the higher we reach, the more our roots must struggle downward, so ambition always comes with its own inner pull.
Zarathustra tells a discouraged youth that whoever creates something new will stand in the way of those who want things kept as they are, so hold on to your highest hope.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, the advice is to respect your opponents rather than despise them, because a worthy rival can push you to grow and your own success can come from theirs.
Nietzsche observes that the devisers of new values usually work away from the market-place and fame, and that deep ideas take time to show what has fallen into them.
Nietzsche suggests a good friend is one who will stand against you when needed, since real closeness can survive honest disagreement.
Nietzsche holds that people create their own values rather than receiving them from heaven, so the values we live by are ours to examine and remake.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, freedom is asked about by what it is for, not only what it escapes from, since many who cast off a yoke lose their worth along with it.
Nietzsche observes that those who rise above others draw envy and misunderstanding, and must still shine for them regardless of how they are received.
Nietzsche wrote that to become new you must first be willing to burn away the old self, since nothing new grows without letting go of what was.
Nietzsche has Zarathustra say it is nobler to admit you are in the wrong than to press your right, though only someone secure enough can afford to do so.
Nietzsche has Zarathustra say that to be long loved, one should step back while still at one's best, knowing when to leave a stage.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, the highest virtue is a giving one: like gold, it is uncommon and always bestows itself rather than hoarding.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, the teacher urges his followers to stop leaning on him and find themselves, since believers who only follow a leader have not yet sought their own way.
Nietzsche observes that the hardest part of giving is keeping an open hand while staying modest, not letting generosity turn into pride.
Nietzsche says creating is a great relief from suffering, though the creator must be willing to endure the pangs of birth, much like a new beginning in one's own life.
Nietzsche observes that great favours can breed resentment rather than gratitude, so help is best given in a way that does not shame the person receiving it.
Nietzsche asks why we should expect a mother to be paid for her love, and suggests that good deeds are best done for their own sake, the way a parent loves a child.
Nietzsche suggests that letting go of revenge is a bridge to a higher hope, since a strong urge to punish often hides envy or resentment.
