Nietzsche describes the spirit as life cutting into itself, so that knowledge grows through its own struggle rather than comfort.
Nietzsche notes that someone who gives constantly can grow weary and hard-handed, so generosity needs its own care and renewal to stay alive.
After many losses and blows, Zarathustra finds something that persists through the years, which he calls his will: a quiet, unchanged resolve that keeps carrying him forward.
Nietzsche observes that commanding is harder than obeying, since the leader carries the burden of everyone who follows and must answer to their own law.
Nietzsche suggests that building something good often means breaking old values first, and that keeping hard truths unspoken is worse than saying them.
Nietzsche suggests real strength shows as relaxed grace rather than strain, and that the hardest thing for a determined person is to stand at ease.
Nietzsche holds that the purest will is the one that seeks to create beyond itself, so love of the world shows itself in making something new rather than only admiring it.
Nietzsche warns against people who sit in the cool shade and only comment on other people's thoughts, never risking their own. Be a thinker, not just a spectator.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, Nietzsche suggests that belief does not make anyone wise, not even belief in oneself. Check the reasons behind what you hold to be true.
Nietzsche observes that some writers muddy their water so it looks deep. Real depth can be seen through, so clarity is a good test of a thinker.
Nietzsche observes that the greatest events are not the noisiest but the stillest hours, and that the world turns on those who create new values rather than new noise.
Nietzsche suggests that what has been knocked down can rise again in a finer form, so a setback can be the start of a renewed life for an idea or a thing.
Nietzsche warns against people who are all one thing, a big eye or a big mouth, and lack everything else. A full life needs more than one strength.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, Nietzsche calls redemption the turning of every "it was" into "thus would I have it". We cannot rewrite the past, but we can choose what it means for what we do next.
Nietzsche warns that wishing the past undone breeds resentment, and a spirit of revenge that turns on everyone nearby. Accepting what has happened is the way out.
Nietzsche notes that when pride is wounded, something better than pride can grow up in its place.
Nietzsche observes that the stillest words can bring the storm, and that thoughts arriving on doves' feet often guide the world. Quiet ideas can carry more force than loud ones.
In Thus Spake Zarathustra, Nietzsche admits his fruit is ripe but he is not yet ripe for it. Some work has to wait until the maker has matured enough to carry it.
Nietzsche has Zarathustra learn to look away from himself in order to see many things. Stepping outside your own view is what lets you see the wider ground of a situation.
Nietzsche writes that the highest mountains come out of the sea, so the greatest heights grow from the deepest places. Hard low points can be where a higher life starts.
Nietzsche calls courage the best slayer of dread, especially the courage that attacks. Facing a fear head on, rather than waiting it out, is what lets you move forward.
Nietzsche shows courage as the will to say of every hard life, "Once more!", so that even suffering is met with a willingness to live it again.
Nietzsche asks us to imagine this very moment returning again and again, and to ask whether we could say yes to that. It is a test for living so each moment is one you would choose again.

This type must not be regarded as a fanciful figure: it is not a
nebulous hope which is to be realised at some indefinitely remote
period, thousands of years hence; nor is it a new species (in the
Darwinian sense) of which we can know nothing, and which it would
therefore be somewhat absurd to strive after. But it is meant to be
a possibility which men of the present could realise with all their
spiritual and physical energies, provided they adopted the new values.

The author of “Zarathustra” never lost sight of that egregious example
of a transvaluation of all values through Christianity, whereby the
whole of the deified mode of life and thought of the Greeks, as well as
strong Romedom, was almost annihilated or transvalued in a comparatively
short time. Could not a rejuvenated Graeco-Roman system of valuing (once
it had been refined and made more profound by the schooling which
two thousand years of Christianity had provided) effect another such
revolution within a calculable period of time, until that glorious type
of manhood shall finally appear which is to be our new faith and hope,
and in the creation of which Zarathustra exhorts us to participate?

In his private notes on the subject the author uses the expression
“Superman” (always in the singular, by-the-bye), as signifying “the most
thoroughly well-constituted type,” as opposed to “modern man”; above
all, however, he designates Zarathustra himself as an example of the
Superman. In “Ecco Homo” he is careful to enlighten us concerning the
precursors and prerequisites to the advent of this highest type, in
referring to a certain passage in the “Gay Science”:—

books.title: Little Women
books.author: Louisa May Alcott
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1888. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Little Women, Louisa May Alcott shows the March girls finding Christmas cheer in what they still have, with Beth reminding them they have each other.
In Little Women, Alcott introduces each sister through a few vivid habits and details, so the reader knows the people before knowing their characters.
In Little Women, Beth suggests each sister give their mother a gift and keep nothing for herself, showing that generosity can be simple and shared.
In Little Women, Mr March's letter asks his daughters to use the long wait for work and self-improvement, so the hard days are not wasted.
In Little Women, Mrs March says we are never too old for the pilgrim's game, because our burdens are real and the longing for goodness guides us through our mistakes.
In Little Women, Meg decides to read a little every morning because it will help her through the day, and her quiet habit inspires her sisters to follow.
In Little Women, the March girls give their own Christmas breakfast to a poor family without hesitating, showing that generosity is easiest when it is personal and immediate.
In Little Women, Meg says giving away your own breakfast is loving your neighbour better than yourself, and the girls leave the poor family comforted and the sisters feeling merrier for it.
In Little Women, the sisters make costumes from pickle-factory tin and preserve-lid scraps, showing how limited means can sharpen ingenuity and turn idle hours into useful practice.
In Little Women, old Mr Laurence answers the girls' small kindness with a feast, showing how generosity travels and often comes back around.
In Little Women, Mrs March notices the lonely boy next door looking wistful at their merriment, and she sees the need behind his shyness.
In Little Women, Jo and Meg work out how to share one good pair of gloves between them, showing that sisters can turn scarcity into cooperation.
In Little Women, Amy and Beth comfort Meg after her hair mishap, showing how kind words can make a small disaster bearable.
In Little Women, Laurie admits he feels strange among the crowd too, and Jo's ease returns once they both own up to being shy.
In Little Women, Jo's eager questions set Laurie talking about his travels, showing that curious questions are one of the quickest ways to make a new friend.
In Little Women, Laurie does not laugh at Jo's embarrassment but gently offers a way forward, showing that real kindness eases someone's shame.
In Little Women, Jo decides fine young ladies enjoy themselves no more than her family does, suggesting that contentment depends on how we see our lives, not on wealth.
In Little Women, Jo says a burden carried without complaint grows lighter, a reminder that our attitude shapes how heavy our duties feel.
In Little Women, Jo's parents let their daughters work early because they believe energy, industry and independence are best cultivated young.
In Little Women, Meg feels poor until she learns to see how rich she is in the blessings that alone make life happy, a lesson in gratitude.
In Little Women, Jo finds real happiness in doing useful work to support herself, even when daily chores keep interrupting what she loves.
In Little Women, Beth lovingly mends the battered dolls nobody else wants, showing that real care is measured by how we treat the overlooked.
Alcott notes that many quiet people live for others so cheerfully that no one sees their sacrifices until they are gone, a reminder to notice the unseen givers around us.
In Little Women, Jo observes that rich people have about as many worries as poor ones, a reminder that wealth does not remove the troubles of life.
In Little Women, Mr Laurence quietly hands a hungry woman a fish when a shopkeeper refuses her, showing that a small unasked-for kindness can mean a great deal.
In Little Women, Mrs March's fable says that when we feel discontented we should count our blessings and be grateful, because contentment grows from gratitude.
In Little Women, Jo sees the grand Laurence house as lonely, showing that comfort and luxury do not bring company or real connection.
In Little Women, Jo shares her family's warmth with the lonely Laurie, showing that inviting someone in is one of the simplest ways to be kind.
In Little Women, Jo tells the shy Laurie that bashfulness will not last if he keeps going out, a practical reminder that courage grows by showing up.
In Little Women, Laurie says a fellow cannot live on books alone, a reminder that fine possessions cannot replace human warmth and friends.
In Little Women, Mr Laurence tells Jo that the true worth of a man lies in being brave and honest, which matters more than how handsome he is.
In Little Women, Jo argues that a boy should be free to follow his own music rather than be pushed into a life he hates, a point about respecting another's true gifts.
In Little Women, Beth compares the girls' struggles to Pilgrim's Progress, where we get past the Slough by resolving to be good and up the hill by trying, so effort and intention matter.
In Little Women, once pride is set aside the two families trade kindnesses without keeping score, since neither feels it is only the giver.
In Little Women, Mr Laurence draws the frightened Beth out by talking about music, showing that patience and a gentle approach can soften shyness.
In Little Women, Beth's kindnesses come from people who work unseen, and her gratitude for one blessing brings a greater one, a lesson in thankfulness.
In Little Women, Alcott notes that love casts out fear and gratitude can conquer pride, as a simple hug from Beth softens the old man's crustiness.
In Little Women, Jenny Snow's spiteful plan to get back at Amy turns on herself, a reminder that pride goes before a fall and petty revenge rarely pays.
In Little Women, Mrs March tells Amy that conceit spoils the finest talent, and that modesty is the great charm of any power.
In Little Women, Jo's temper is her bosom enemy, and Alcott shows that mastering it takes years of patient effort and honest apology rather than a single resolution.
In Little Women, Mrs March urges her daughters not to let the sun go down on their anger, but to forgive, help each other and begin again tomorrow.
Alcott warns that anger nursed in the heart grows strong and takes possession unless it is cast out at once, a useful warning about holding on to resentment.
In Little Women, Mrs March tells Jo that conquering a fault takes watchfulness and perseverance, and that it should never be thought impossible.
Mrs March admits she has fought her own temper for forty years, showing that character grows through lifelong effort rather than instant perfection.
Mrs March's method for holding back hasty words is simple: she steps away for a minute before she speaks, a practical habit of pausing before reacting.
In Little Women, Mrs March says it was easier to become good for her daughters' sake than her own, showing that love can be a steadier motive for growth.
In Little Women, Meg notices that the more one gets the more one wants, a trap that makes contentment hard to reach however much we have.
Alcott warns that imitating fashionable people and envying their things leaves a person feeling poorer, even when surrounded by luxury.
In Little Women, a few loving words in a note cure Meg's envy and false pride better than fine clothes, showing that affection outweighs appearance.
Alcott shows how careless gossip can wound a sensitive person and shake trust in those she loves, a reminder to guard what we say about others.
Alcott's jackdaw in borrowed plumes is a timeless image: pleasure in borrowed finery brings only a fleeting sense of worth.
Alcott observes that fine clothes win respect at once, a sharp reminder that people often judge us by appearance rather than character.
Meg finds home restful once she stops performing for others, though it is not splendid, a reminder that being true to yourself is more comfortable than pretending.
In Little Women, Meg owns up to her silly mistakes with her mother instead of hiding them, which makes it easier to put things right.
Mrs March advises Meg to value the praise that is worth having, and to win admiration from good people by being modest as well as pretty.
Mrs March tells her daughters she would rather they were happy, contented wives of poor men than queens without self-respect or peace, since love and character matter more than wealth.
Alcott shows that each sister's garden reflects her character, a gentle reminder that our everyday tastes and choices reveal who we are.
Snodgrass argues the girls should welcome Laurie because they can do so little for him while he does so much for them, a generous case for inclusion.
In Little Women, Beth speaks up for the new member even though she is frightened, showing that quiet courage can sway a whole group.
Mrs March sees that all play and no work is as bad as all work and no play, a sensible reminder that balance keeps life healthy.

preview.text:
“Christmas won’t be Christmas without any presents,” grumbled Jo, lying
on the rug.

“It’s so dreadful to be poor!” sighed Meg, looking down at her old
dress.

“I don’t think it’s fair for some girls to have plenty of pretty
things, and other girls nothing at all,” added little Amy, with an
injured sniff.

“We’ve got Father and Mother, and each other,” said Beth contentedly
from her corner.

The four young faces on which the firelight shone brightened at the
cheerful words, but darkened again as Jo said sadly, “We haven’t got
Father, and shall not have him for a long time.” She didn’t say
“perhaps never,” but each silently added it, thinking of Father far
away, where the fighting was.

Nobody spoke for a minute; then Meg said in an altered tone, “You know
the reason Mother proposed not having any presents this Christmas was
because it is going to be a hard winter for everyone; and she thinks we
ought not to spend money for pleasure, when our men are suffering so in
the army. We can’t do much, but we can make our little sacrifices, and
ought to do it gladly. But I am afraid I don’t,” and Meg shook her
head, as she thought regretfully of all the pretty things she wanted.

“But I don’t think the little we should spend would do any good. We’ve
each got a dollar, and the army wouldn’t be much helped by our giving
that. I agree not to expect anything from Mother or you, but I do want
to buy _Undine and Sintran_ for myself. I’ve wanted it so long,” said
Jo, who was a bookworm.

“I planned to spend mine in new music,” said Beth, with a little sigh,
which no one heard but the hearth brush and kettle-holder.

“I shall get a nice box of Faber’s drawing pencils; I really need
them,” said Amy decidedly.

books.title: The Jungle Book
books.author: Rudyard Kipling
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Author died 1936. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Jungle Book, Kipling shows Mother Wolf standing up to a tiger she fears, to protect a child that is not hers, so courage often means defending someone weaker.
In The Jungle Book, Baloo speaks up for the cub with no gift of words, showing that a plain truth from an ordinary voice can change the outcome in a room.
In The Jungle Book, Bagheera offers a fresh bull to settle the dispute, showing that a generous offer can end a quarrel that anger would only prolong.
In The Jungle Book, Mowgli learns by paying close attention, so that every rustle, breath and bird call means something to him, which is how any craft is learned.
In The Jungle Book, Bagheera admits he was once caged by men and found his own strength, showing that an old hurt can become the source of a wise and loyal friend.
In The Jungle Book, Akela, an aging leader, offers his own life in place of the cub and shames the Pack for forgetting its honour, showing that a leader sometimes gives up what they hold.
In The Jungle Book, Mowgli spares the Pack after they betray him, choosing mercy over revenge, which shows that restraint can be a stronger thing than anger.
In The Jungle Book, Baloo's maxims warn the proud young not to mistreat strangers and to stay humble, since the jungle is far larger than any one creature.
In The Jungle Book, Baloo teaches with firm, loving patience, arguing that a little discomfort now is better than harm later through ignorance.

In The Jungle Book, the Bandar-log flatter Mowgli with nuts and promises of leadership, showing how easy praise from those with no lasting loyalty can lure a person away from the friends who truly care.
In The Jungle Book, when Mowgli is captured he stops struggling and starts to think, sending word to his friends, which shows that a steady head is the first tool in a bad spot.
In The Jungle Book, Bagheera tells the panicking Baloo to sit still and make a plan, since chasing in a rush would only tire them out and cost them the trail.
In The Jungle Book, the monkeys copy the ways of men in a ruined city without understanding what anything is for, showing that imitating the look of a thing is not the same as knowing it.
In The Jungle Book, Mowgli thanks Kaa courteously and promises to repay the debt one day, showing that gratitude is a debt a good person remembers and honours.
In The Jungle Book, Kaa's hypnotic dance leaves the monkeys unable to move by their own will, a warning that a smooth, clever voice can take away the judgement of even bold creatures.
In The Jungle Book, Mowgli accepts his punishment without argument once he owns his mistake, and sleeps soundly afterwards, showing that admitting a wrong and paying for it clears the air.
In The Jungle Book, Mowgli sees that to live among people he must learn their speech, so he copies every word he hears, showing that belonging begins with understanding.
In The Jungle Book, Mowgli keeps his temper when children tease him, because the jungle taught him that losing control is costly, showing that self-restraint is a skill learned through hard lessons.
In The Jungle Book, Mowgli challenges the village elders' tall tales, asking why anyone should trust ghost stories from a man who knows so little of the jungle at his own door.
In The Jungle Book, Mowgli stops to think through his plan before acting, then asks for help when he cannot do it alone, showing that a clear head and honest asking beat rushing in.
In The Jungle Book, Mowgli leaves the village without harming it because one woman had been kind to him, showing that a single act of kindness can hold back a person from revenge.
In The Jungle Book, Mowgli's song admits he belongs to two worlds and feels both pulls at once, showing that it is honest to hold mixed feelings rather than force them into one.
In The Jungle Book, the seal Sea Catch fights hard but never chases a beaten rival, because the Rules of the Beach forbid it, showing that a fair code keeps strength honourable.
In The White Seal, Kipling shows the young seal Kotick learning to swim through many small failures and retries, until he finds he truly belongs to the water, a picture of learning by doing.

In The White Seal, Kotick's friends tell him to accept the killing as part of the day's work, but he keeps asking questions, showing that refusing to accept what is simply normal is where change starts.

In The White Seal, a dying old seal tells Kotick to try once more, and Kotick keeps searching through years of disappointment, showing how a hope handed on can carry someone past their own discouragement.

In The White Seal, Kipling notes that the herd changes its ways only slowly, because creatures need a long time to turn things over in their minds, a useful thought for anyone trying to change a habit.
In Rikki-tikki-tavi, Kipling shows the cobra Nag making a grand speech about his marks while secretly afraid, a reminder that a loud threat often hides fear.
In Rikki-tikki-tavi, Rikki waits an hour, moving muscle by muscle, before choosing where to strike, showing that patient timing often counts for more than speed.
In Rikki-tikki-tavi, Darzee keeps singing his song of triumph while the real danger is still close, showing how easy it is to celebrate before the job is finished.
In Rikki-tikki-tavi, Rikki is proud of his victory but does not grow too proud, and keeps watch over his garden, showing that a real win is kept by steady vigilance rather than boasting.

In Toomai of the Elephants, Petersen Sahib notices the courage of a small boy who joined a wild elephant drive, and says he may grow into a hunter, showing that a good leader sees effort even when others do not.
In Toomai of the Elephants, a driver warns that a man who lives in one hut knows only its four walls, a reminder that a narrow life can leave us blind to the wider world.
In Toomai of the Elephants, Little Toomai, alone in the dark among hundreds of elephants, sets his teeth and stays still, showing that steady nerve in a frightening moment is a quiet form of courage.

In Toomai of the Elephants, Petersen Sahib and Machua Appa follow the tracks to check the child's strange story, and only believe him once the evidence is in, showing that good judgement tests a claim before accepting or dismissing it.
In Her Majesty's Servants, an old troop-horse says it is forgivable to be scared of things one does not understand, and that getting cross with others for their fear is the worse fault.
In Her Majesty's Servants, the elephant Two Tails admits he knows just enough to be uncomfortable and not enough to carry on regardless, a candid picture of how foresight can make fear heavier.

In Her Majesty's Servants, a young mule asks why they must fight at all and is told to obey and ask no questions, and the scene leaves the question hanging, a reminder that asking why is still worth doing.

preview.text:
Shere Khan had jumped at a woodcutter’s campfire, as Father Wolf had
said, and was furious from the pain of his burned feet. But Father Wolf
knew that the mouth of the cave was too narrow for a tiger to come in
by. Even where he was, Shere Khan’s shoulders and forepaws were cramped
for want of room, as a man’s would be if he tried to fight in a barrel.

“The Wolves are a free people,” said Father Wolf. “They take orders from
the Head of the Pack, and not from any striped cattle-killer. The man’s
cub is ours--to kill if we choose.”

“Ye choose and ye do not choose! What talk is this of choosing? By the
bull that I killed, am I to stand nosing into your dog’s den for my fair
dues? It is I, Shere Khan, who speak!”

The tiger’s roar filled the cave with thunder. Mother Wolf shook herself
clear of the cubs and sprang forward, her eyes, like two green moons in
the darkness, facing the blazing eyes of Shere Khan.

“And it is I, Raksha [The Demon], who answers. The man’s cub is mine,
Lungri--mine to me! He shall not be killed. He shall live to run with
the Pack and to hunt with the Pack; and in the end, look you, hunter of
little naked cubs--frog-eater--fish-killer--he shall hunt thee! Now get
hence, or by the Sambhur that I killed (I eat no starved cattle), back
thou goest to thy mother, burned beast of the jungle, lamer than ever
thou camest into the world! Go!”

books.title: Beyond Good and Evil
books.author: Friedrich Nietzsche
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 1900, translator died 1934. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Nietzsche asks why we should value truth above untruth at all, and suggests that asking this question ourselves is where real thinking begins.
Nietzsche warns that thinkers often build on unexamined opposites, such as truth against error. He suggests we test our own sharp black and white judgements before trusting them.
Nietzsche suggests that much of our careful reasoning is secretly driven by instinct and by the values we need in order to live. Even clever thinking carries hidden preferences.
Nietzsche notes that thinkers often present their heart's desire as the cold result of pure reason, then find arguments for it afterwards. He values the honesty to admit one's own leanings.
Nietzsche proposes that every great philosophy is a kind of confession by its author. To understand a thinker's bold claims, first ask what morality they are aiming at.
Nietzsche mocks answers that just repeat the question in grand language, like saying opium makes people sleep by its sleep-giving power. Ask whether an answer really explains anything.
Nietzsche suggests a better question than 'how is this possible?' is 'why do we need to believe this?' Asking what a belief does for us can teach more than asking if it is true.
Nietzsche warns against piling up unnecessary principles, and says good method is an economy of principles. Keep the assumptions you need and drop the rest.
Nietzsche points out that even a simple claim like 'I think' carries many hidden assumptions, so nothing feels as certain as it seems. He asks why a belief should be true just because it feels sure.
Nietzsche observes that we often feel simply deciding is enough to make things happen, when acting involves many steps. Good intentions still need follow-through.
Nietzsche suggests thinkers often reach similar conclusions because their language and inherited habits shape how they think. Noticing the shape of your own assumptions is a useful check.
Nietzsche argues that debates about free will often reveal what people want to claim or avoid. In ordinary life, he says, the real question is how strong or weak a person's will is.
Nietzsche observes that we simplify the world to make life feel easy, and that even good knowledge can keep us in a tidy picture of things. Be wary of simple stories you enjoy.
Nietzsche warns thinkers against making their ideas a cause to suffer for, since that turns them rigid and combative. He prefers a free, quiet solitude that keeps questioning.
Nietzsche argues that a thinker who avoids ordinary people and their everyday struggles never learns much about human nature. Staying close to real life, even when it is tiring, is part of wisdom.
Nietzsche suggests that talk about people without outrage is often more instructive than moral indignation, which can distort what we see. Listen closely to plain speech about human nature.
Nietzsche notes that Plato, for all his solemn ideals, kept a comic playwright's book by his bed. Even serious thinkers need humour and lightness.
Nietzsche says independent thinking is a privilege of the strong, and that striking out alone brings isolation and risks others may not see. Count that cost before you go your own way.
Nietzsche recalls that young people judge in absolute yes and no, and that nuance comes with experience. Look back at old convictions with some humour and kindness.
Nietzsche notes that people once judged actions by their consequences, and later by the intention behind them. He suggests intention is only a sign that needs interpreting.
Nietzsche asks us to examine even warm feelings of self-sacrifice, since an idea that pleases us has not thereby been proven. Pleasant beliefs deserve a second look.

Nietzsche questions the habit of assuming truth is always worth more than appearance, and suggests some useful seeming may be needed for life. Be wary of the story that you alone see things as they are.
Nietzsche points out that a belief is not made true by making us happy or good, nor false merely because it hurts. Judge ideas by the evidence, not by how comforting they are.
Nietzsche observes that deep people often wear a mask, and that others misread their words and steps. Be slow to judge someone by the surface of what they say.
Nietzsche says true independence means not clinging to any one person, cause or even your own virtues, since each can become a prison. Keep enough distance to think for yourself.
Nietzsche describes free thinkers as restless, curious investigators who love their own solitude and distrust comfortable dependencies. He invites the reader to be one.

Nietzsche admits that the inquiry into the human soul is too large for one person, and that helpers often lose their keen eye just when the real danger begins. Serious inquiry usually means doing much of the work yourself.
Nietzsche suggests we once believed in a thinking 'self' because grammar seems to demand a subject for every action. He asks whether the 'I' is something thinking creates, rather than its cause.
Nietzsche suggests that as our insight grows our world becomes larger, and some convictions we took most seriously may later look like a child's game. Hold big beliefs with some humility.
Nietzsche observes that great people are made less by sudden bursts of strength than by how long their deepest feelings last. Staying power matters more than intensity.
Nietzsche warns that a truth salted so heavily it no longer quenches thirst defeats itself. Make hard ideas plain enough that people can actually take them in.
Nietzsche suggests that maturity means recovering the seriousness we had as children at play. Grown-up work can still carry that spirit of play.
Nietzsche notes that a strong resolve can make us deaf even to the best objections. A good thinker stays willing to hear counter-arguments after deciding.
Nietzsche suggests that the more abstract a truth, the more you must bring it to the senses. Use concrete examples when you teach a hard idea.
Nietzsche says a good conversation begins when one person helps another bring their own thoughts to birth. Listening to draw out someone's ideas makes talk worth having.
Nietzsche warns that whoever fights monsters risks becoming one, and that a long gaze into an abyss gazes back. Notice how a long fight changes your own character.
Nietzsche observes that a deceit wounds less than the loss of being able to believe someone at all. Trust is the thing to protect.
Nietzsche suggests that before grand moral theories, we should first gather and compare the many forms moral feeling takes. Careful description comes before theory.
Nietzsche argues that many moral systems quietly assume the very morality they claim to examine. Test your starting assumptions, not just the conclusions you like.
Nietzsche asks whether a person who calls the world hopeless but still lives by everyday kindness is really a pessimist. Notice the gap between what someone says and how they live.
Nietzsche suggests a moral system can reveal what its author wants, whether to be admired, to feel calm or to take revenge. Ask what a principle says about the person who holds it.
Nietzsche observes that artists work most freely within strict rules, since discipline gives freedom its shape. Constraint is often what makes good work possible.

Nietzsche observes that lasting achievements grow from long discipline in one direction, not from doing whatever you feel like. Steady practice, even when it constrains you, builds what makes life worth living.
Nietzsche suggests Socrates tried to set instincts right with reasons, and admits much moral judgement is less rational than it looks. Check whether your reasons really cause your choices.
Nietzsche notes that our senses often see what they already expect, filling the gaps with the familiar. In conversation we often supply the expression we want to see on someone's face.
Nietzsche doubts that rules promising one recipe for happiness can suit everyone. He calls such advice mostly expediency, and warns against anything that speaks unconditionally about all people.
Nietzsche warns that a thinker who stops learning, or specialises too narrowly, loses the wide view that real judgement needs. Keep learning across fields, and keep asking what your work is for.
Nietzsche warns that someone who stays neutral and agreeable, reflecting everything and never deciding what they want, ends up unable to help themselves when trouble comes.
Nietzsche argues that endless doubt, dressed up as caution or wisdom, often hides a weak will rather than real open-mindedness.
Nietzsche says that doubting and criticising is not enough on its own: serious thinkers need clear standards, a consistent method and the courage to stand by their own judgments.
Nietzsche warns against judging an idea by how uplifting it feels, and suggests asking whether it is true, even when the truth is harsh.
Nietzsche separates the careful scholars who sort and organise what has been valued from the thinker who decides what is worth valuing and creates new values.
Nietzsche suggests that the most useful thinkers often challenge the ideals of their own age, asking what hypocrisy or comfort hides behind respected habits.
Nietzsche argues that real greatness includes strength of will and a readiness to take responsibility, qualities an easy-going age tends to undervalue.
Nietzsche suggests that for a practised mind, rigorous thinking can feel light and even joyful, while those who see it only as a grind miss what deep thought is.
Nietzsche warns that feeling sure of our own goodness can be an inherited habit rather than a judgement we have actually tested.
Nietzsche observes that people today are pulled by several moralities at once, so their actions are often mixed rather than clearly good or bad.
Nietzsche notes that people who badly need to be seen as morally subtle tend to hold a grudge against anyone who saw them make a mistake.
Nietzsche observes that even self-sacrifice usually brings something back, such as a sense of being more, and that honesty about this is worth more than a pleasing story.
Nietzsche argues that judging things only by pleasure and pain is too simple, since many of the deepest human achievements come through discipline and hard effort.

preview.text:
Sils Maria Upper Engadine, JUNE, 1885.

CHAPTER I. PREJUDICES OF PHILOSOPHERS

1. The Will to Truth, which is to tempt us to many a hazardous
enterprise, the famous Truthfulness of which all philosophers have
hitherto spoken with respect, what questions has this Will to Truth not
laid before us! What strange, perplexing, questionable questions! It is
already a long story; yet it seems as if it were hardly commenced. Is
it any wonder if we at last grow distrustful, lose patience, and turn
impatiently away? That this Sphinx teaches us at last to ask questions
ourselves? WHO is it really that puts questions to us here? WHAT really
is this "Will to Truth" in us? In fact we made a long halt at the
question as to the origin of this Will--until at last we came to an
absolute standstill before a yet more fundamental question. We inquired
about the VALUE of this Will. Granted that we want the truth: WHY NOT
RATHER untruth? And uncertainty? Even ignorance? The problem of the
value of truth presented itself before us--or was it we who presented
ourselves before the problem? Which of us is the Oedipus here? Which
the Sphinx? It would seem to be a rendezvous of questions and notes of
interrogation. And could it be believed that it at last seems to us as
if the problem had never been propounded before, as if we were the first
to discern it, get a sight of it, and RISK RAISING it? For there is risk
in raising it, perhaps there is no greater risk.

books.title: Jane Eyre
books.author: Charlotte Bronte
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1855. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Charlotte Bronte argued that conventionality is not morality and self-righteousness is not religion, and that exposing hypocrisy is a good act, not an assault on faith.
Charlotte Bronte shows how a child with no one to appeal to learns fear, and how adults who look away let a bully grow.
Charlotte Bronte shows a child punished for calling out cruelty, and Jane's first taste of courage is refusing to pretend that what was done to her did not happen.
In Jane Eyre, Bronte shows how favouritism works: the cruel are indulged and the blameless are punished, and a child who is always blamed starts to doubt herself.
Bronte has Jane look back and see clearly what she could not understand as a child, a reminder that hard years often only make sense later.
Bronte shows how one kind visitor with no stake in the household can make a frightened child feel safe, even when the people who should care for her do not.
Bronte notes that children can feel deeply without being able to analyse their feelings, so their hurt often comes out as a clumsy answer that still holds the truth.
Bronte shows how contempt spreads through a household: a child is judged unlovable because nobody bothers to look past her, and the judgment is repeated until it sounds like fact.
In Jane Eyre, Jane begins to refuse the cruel judgments placed on her, a first sign of the self-respect that carries her through the rest of the story.
Charlotte Bronte observes that human beings must love something, and a lonely child will pour her affection into even a shabby doll rather than go without.
Bronte shows how unjust punishment breeds fear so deep that a child hesitates at the door of a room she has every right to enter.
Charlotte Bronte shows Mr. Brocklehurst preaching humility to others while displaying his own pride, a gap between appearance and truth.
Jane speaks the plain truth to Mrs Reed in Jane Eyre and feels a sudden freedom in saying what was done to her, even though it costs her dearly.
Bronte notes that revenge tastes warm at first but leaves a corroding aftertaste, and that a burst of anger is always followed by a chill of regret.
Bronte shows that hardship is easier to bear when it is shared, and that a common grumble among people in the same bad position can be a small comfort.
In Jane Eyre, Miss Temple quietly overrules a harsh routine to feed hungry girls and takes the responsibility herself, a good model of leadership that puts people first.
Bronte shows Helen Burns bearing a public beating with calm dignity while still feeling the hurt privately, a picture of endurance that does not need to pretend it does not hurt.
Helen Burns tells Jane not to judge by appearances, a reminder that the people who look most ordinary or flawed may have the deepest character.
Helen Burns argues that violence does not best overcome hate and that patience and forgiveness heal injury more surely than vengeance, a view Jane finds hard to accept.
Helen Burns argues that life is too short to spend nursing grudges, and that you can forgive the wrongdoer while still condemning the wrong, which keeps revenge from wearing down your heart.
Bronte lets Mr. Brocklehurst lecture girls on plainness while his own wife and daughters arrive in silks and furs, so his hypocrisy is plain to the reader without her needing to say so.
Bronte observes that people who only see small faults are blind to the fuller character of others, a useful check on our own judgments.
Helen Burns helps Jane see that the scorn of a small circle is not the whole world, and that most people may quietly sympathise even when they dare not show it.
Miss Temple gives Jane a fair hearing, asking her to tell the truth plainly, add nothing and exaggerate nothing, and Bronte shows that a calm, honest account is what wins belief.
Once cleared of blame, Jane throws herself into her studies and her progress matches her effort, a clear lesson that a fresh start rewards steady, proportionate work.
Bronte shows that a friend who offers steady, patient affection, never soured by bad moods, is worth more than company that only amuses, and Jane knows it even when she strays.
Bronte shows a failing school turned into a useful one only after its faults were brought into the open and inquired into, a reminder that scrutiny is often what makes an institution better.
When her mentor leaves, Jane finds her calm was partly borrowed, and that steadiness has to rest on reasons she holds herself, not on the person who was steadying her.
With no friends to ask, Jane works out her own plan by stating what she wants, asking how others get it, and acting on the first clear step, which is self-reliance worth copying.
Jane leaves Lowood the proper way: she asks the committee's leave, gets a written testimonial, and only then takes up her new post, showing that doing things in good order protects your reputation.
Facing a new and uncertain start, Jane tells herself she can always try again if the worst comes, a steadying thought that makes a risk feel survivable.
After a hard day, Jane gives thanks and asks for the power to deserve kindness before it is earned, a humble and grateful habit worth keeping.
Jane finds that real equality, not condescension, makes the relationship easier, and notes that a dependent employee can be treated as a friend when respect is genuine.
Jane gained her French through a little practice every day, learning passages by heart and copying her teacher's accent, a reminder that steady small effort builds real skill over time.
Jane refuses to gush about her pupil, saying she is only telling the truth and will not flatter or prop up cant, a plain and honest standard that suits any good account of people.
Charlotte Bronte argues that people need purpose and a field for their abilities or they will find restlessness, and that women feel and need that exercise just as men do.
Jane finds quiet satisfaction in a small act of help that was needed and asked for, a reminder that being useful to someone, however small, lifts the spirit.
In Jane Eyre, Charlotte Bronte shows that a life of safe, unchanging comfort can slowly dull a person, and that a restless wish to be stirred is natural.
In Jane Eyre, Jane meets a moody, rude host with calm self-respect rather than fawning, and finds that composure gives her the upper hand.
In Jane Eyre, Jane says her sketches are pale copies of the vivid pictures in her mind, a gap every maker knows between the idea and the hand that makes it.
In Jane Eyre, Mrs. Fairfax asks for allowance for a difficult person, reminding us that nobody can fully help their nature and that old hurts can unsettle anyone's spirits.
In Jane Eyre, Rochester says hard knocks have left him tough, yet with one tender point still in him, a useful thought about how setbacks can harden us without wholly closing us off.
In Jane Eyre, Jane will not chatter just to show off for a rude man, but when he apologises she accepts it with dignity and offers to answer his questions honestly.
In Jane Eyre, Jane says a person's claim to be superior, whether by age or experience, depends on the use they have made of that time and experience.
In Jane Eyre, Rochester sees that regret alone does not cure a wrong, since only real reform does, though he finds it hard to act on what he knows.

In Jane Eyre, Jane tells Rochester that a stained memory can be replaced over time, since a person who resolves to correct their thoughts and actions builds a new store of recollections to be proud of.
In Jane Eyre, Jane points out that fallible people should not claim the right to excuse an unusual action just by declaring it right, since that power belongs to the perfect alone.

In Jane Eyre, Rochester warns that a smooth stretch of life often ends at a craggy pass where things break into turmoil, and that people come through it either dashed down or carried into calmer water.
In Jane Eyre, Rochester resolves to break the obstacles to his own goodness and to be a better man than he has been, a clear way to frame personal change.
In Jane Eyre, Jane chooses to cling closer to a lonely child rather than a spoilt one, showing that real kindness looks to whoever needs it most.
In Jane Eyre, Jane sees Rochester's faults clearly yet still believes there are good materials in him, a fair and generous way to judge someone whose flaws are plain to see.
In Jane Eyre, Jane keeps her head in a fire, using whatever water is at hand and acting at once rather than waiting for others, which is how calm action in a crisis works.
In Jane Eyre, Grace Poole argues that trusting to luck is no substitute for sensible precautions, since a drawn bolt guards against trouble, a saying worth remembering in business too.
In Jane Eyre, Jane checks her hopes against the plain facts she has, bringing her wandering imagination back to common sense after it has run ahead of the evidence.
In Jane Eyre, Jane steadies a runaway hope by facing her own plain situation, and finds the discipline lets her stay calm when hard news arrives.
In Jane Eyre, the servants note that Grace Poole quietly saves each quarter, a reminder that steady saving over time is what builds independence.
In Jane Eyre, Jane is drawn to quiet, gentle grace over showy rank, a reminder that real dignity is not measured by display.
In Jane Eyre, Jane sees that Blanche Ingram's cleverness is used to belittle a kinder woman, and concludes that talent without good nature is a poor gift.
In Jane Eyre, Jane is drawn to real force of character over polished charm, judging people by their substance rather than by rank or manner.
In Jane Eyre, Jane observes that warmth which comes naturally, with no pretence, draws people in far better than calculated charm, which can only glance off them.

preview.text:
Conventionality is not morality. Self-righteousness is not religion. To
attack the first is not to assail the last. To pluck the mask from the
face of the Pharisee, is not to lift an impious hand to the Crown of
Thorns.

These things and deeds are diametrically opposed: they are as distinct
as is vice from virtue. Men too often confound them: they should not be
confounded: appearance should not be mistaken for truth; narrow human
doctrines, that only tend to elate and magnify a few, should not be
substituted for the world-redeeming creed of Christ. There is—I repeat
it—a difference; and it is a good, and not a bad action to mark broadly
and clearly the line of separation between them.

The world may not like to see these ideas dissevered, for it has been
accustomed to blend them; finding it convenient to make external show
pass for sterling worth—to let white-washed walls vouch for clean
shrines. It may hate him who dares to scrutinise and expose—to rase the
gilding, and show base metal under it—to penetrate the sepulchre, and
reveal charnel relics: but hate as it will, it is indebted to him.

Ahab did not like Micaiah, because he never prophesied good concerning
him, but evil; probably he liked the sycophant son of Chenaanah
better; yet might Ahab have escaped a bloody death, had he but stopped
his ears to flattery, and opened them to faithful counsel.

books.title: English Fairy Tales
books.author: Joseph Jacobs (editor)
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Editor died 1916. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Joseph Jacobs, collecting English fairy tales, took what was good wherever he could find it, from Scotland, America and an English Gipsy alike.
In Tom Tit Tot, a clever girl escapes a cruel bargain by quietly listening to the impet's secret, then turning what she overheard into her own victory.
In The Three Sillies, a family weeps over a harm that has not happened yet, and the traveller's lesson is that fretting over imagined troubles is its own kind of foolishness.
In How Jack Went to Seek His Fortune, a boy's ordinary animal companions scare off robbers by all raising their voices together, showing that a small team working as one can beat a bigger threat.

In Mr. Vinegar, a man keeps trading what he has for the next thing that he is sure will make him happiest, until a parrot shows him he has gained nothing. Chasing the next shiny thing can cost you what you already had.
In Nix Nought Nothing, a giant's daughter helps the young man through impossible tasks, even giving up her own fingers and toes to make steps for him, showing how loyal courage can cost a great deal.
In Binnorie, a jealous sister's crime comes to light when a harp made from her victim's bones sings out the truth, showing how jealousy can hide a wrong only for a while.
In Cap o' Rushes, a father who rewards flattery drives out the daughter who speaks plainly, yet her honest worth shows through in hard, humble work.
In Jack and the Beanstalk, Jack takes a gamble on strange beans that his mother calls foolish, and that bold step opens a road to the sky that no sensible bargain could have reached.
In The Three Little Pigs, the pig who took the slow, solid route with bricks is the one who stays safe, and his early preparation lets his wits beat the wolf's tricks.
In The Master and His Pupil, a foolish lad summons a power he cannot control because he never learned how to send it away. Know how to stop a thing before you start it.
In Jack and His Golden Snuff-box, Jack is handed a helper with the rule to use it only when it truly matters, and when the hard moment comes it turns a deadline he could not meet into a win.
In Jack and His Golden Snuff-box, a little mouse that Jack spared says it may do him good someday without him knowing, and it does. Small kindnesses have a way of coming back.
In Jack and His Golden Snuff-box, the travelling companions drop the treasure when they quarrel over who deserves the credit, a neat lesson that squabbling over the win can lose the win itself.
In The Three Bears, the intruder tries each porridge, chair and bed until one is just right. Finding what fits often means testing a few options patiently, until the right one shows itself.
In Jack the Giant-Killer, a captive keeps his nerve, studies the room and finds the rope that turns the tables on his captors. Staying calm and paying attention is often the way out.
In Jack the Giant-Killer, a prince gives away everything he has to the people his father's town owes, and the story shows generosity as a quiet kind of strength that others will follow.
In Jack the Giant-Killer, Jack rides ahead to clear the way for his master, handling the danger first so the prince can arrive safely. Good support often means going first to deal with the hard part.
In Henny-Penny, a flock of barnyard birds follows a fox who offers a shortcut, and none of them asks whether he really knows the way. Check who you are trusting before you follow them somewhere.

In Childe Rowland, the two elder brothers set off without learning the rules and are lost, while the youngest is taught the rules, repeats them until he knows them by heart, and comes back. Prepare properly before you go.
In Childe Rowland, the hero is tempted by a bowl of food when he is hungry, but he remembers his purpose and refuses it, a neat picture of holding to your commitments when comfort tempts you away.
In Molly Whuppie, the youngest of three sisters outwits a giant by swapping the rope and gold charms while he sleeps, showing that quick thinking can save the people you love in a bad spot.
In Molly Whuppie, the clever girl goes back into the giant's house twice more for the sword and the purse, each time bold enough to try again after a near miss.
In Molly Whuppie, a small and clever girl beats a giant by her wits, turning his own threats back on him rather than meeting force with force.
In The Red Ettin, the younger brother patches his leaking can with clay and then chooses his mother's blessing over a bigger cake with her curse. Good sense and good character go together.
In The Red Ettin, the younger brother shares his johnny-cake with an old woman, and her gift of a magic wand later saves him. Kindness comes back round.
In The Red Ettin, the young man survives because he took the good fairy's advice and listened to it. Preparation and humility beat bravado.
In The Golden Arm, a man loves his dead wife's gold arm more than her, and his greed is undone when her ghost asks him the one question he cannot dodge.
In Tom Thumb, the boy's cunning turns to thieving, and each clever trick lands him in worse trouble. Being clever is not the same as being good.
In Tom Thumb, a court favourite's rise is fragile, and one spiteful word from the queen brings the little knight to ruin. Favour can vanish overnight.
In Mr. Fox, Lady Mary exposes a murderer by telling her dream calmly to his face, with the proof hidden in her dress. Courage can be quiet and clever.
In Lazy Jack, the boy does exactly what he is told and never what is meant, always promising to do better another time. Understanding what is actually wanted is a skill.
In The Johnny-Cake, the boastful cake outruns everyone who chases it, then trusts a fox's flattery and is eaten. Pride tends to go before a fall.
In Earl Mar's Daughter, the girl does not panic at a stranger in her locked room. She asks him plainly who he is and how he got in, and her courage opens the story.
In Earl Mar's Daughter, the girl keeps faith with her secret husband through seven years and holds to her own choice when her father demands another.
In Mr. Miacca, Tommy Grimes is saved by his quick wit when the ogre has him. Cleverness can get you out of a bind, but it is better not to need it.
In Dick Whittington, a poor orphan finds the courage to ask the waggoner for a ride towards London. That small brave step starts his whole story.
In Dick Whittington, Alice tells the cruel cook she will be turned away unless she treats the boy kindly. A word from someone with standing can stop cruelty.
In Dick Whittington, the boy gives up his only possession, a cat, to the captain's venture with tears in his eyes. Giving what you have, however little, is how a chance begins.
In Dick Whittington, the boy turns back from giving up when he hears the bells urge him to return. Staying with the work, instead of running from it, is what changes his luck.
In Dick Whittington, the merchant Mr. Fitzwarren insists the treasure belongs wholly to Dick and refuses to take a penny of it. Honesty about what is rightly someone else's marks a good man.
In Dick Whittington, the boy shares his good fortune with the captain, the servants and even the cruel old cook. Generosity after success is the mark of a kind heart.
In The Strange Visitor, a woman who keeps wishing aloud for company gets a visitor far from what she pictured. Be careful what you wish for.
In The Laidly Worm of Spindleston Heugh, Childe Wynd does not turn away from the monster. Three kisses from a loving brother break the spell and bring his sister back.
In The Fish and the Ring, a band of robbers reads a murderous letter, thinks it a shame, and rewrites it so the girl is saved. A small act of conscience can turn a cruel plan around.
In The Fish and the Ring, a cruel baron tries to escape a fate he feared, and his own plots bring it about. Forcing the future through cruelty tends to backfire.
In The Magpie's Nest, the birds leave the teacher before the lesson is finished, so each one learns only a piece. Staying for the whole lesson is how you really learn.
In Kate Crackernuts, Kate is brave enough to sit up alone with a mysterious sick prince, and her quiet watchfulness reveals what is really happening.
In The Ass, the Table, and the Stick, Jack's magic rewards are swapped for worthless copies while he is not looking. Check what you have been given before you rely on it.
In The Ass, the Table, and the Stick, Jack's new power turns him cruel, and he strikes the poor sweetheart who had nothing to give him. Power without kindness goes sour.
In Fairy Ointment, Dame Goody's curiosity costs her the sight of one eye when she lets the pixy see she can see him. Some things are best left unremarked.
In The Well of the World's End, the girl keeps her promise to the frog who helped her, even though it costs her. Keeping your word to those who help you is a good habit.
In The Three Heads of the Well, a princess tends three golden heads with patient care, and they reward her with beauty, a sweet voice and a royal marriage.
In The Three Heads of the Well, the stepsister who refuses to share her bread and wine with the old man earns his curse. Being mean with what you have costs you.
In The Three Heads of the Well, a poor cobbler helps a cursed stranger purely out of charity, and that plain kindness is what changes her life.

preview.text:
The first adjective of our title also needs a similar extension of its
meaning. I have acted on Molière's principle, and have taken what was
good wherever I could find it. Thus, a couple of these stories have been
found among descendants of English immigrants in America; a couple of
others I tell as I heard them myself in my youth in Australia. One of
the best was taken down from the mouth of an English Gipsy. I have also
included some stories that have only been found in Lowland Scotch.
I have felt justified in doing this, as of the twenty-one folk-tales
contained in Chambers' “Popular Rhymes of Scotland,” no less than
sixteen are also to be found in an English form. With the Folk-tale as
with the Ballad, Lowland Scotch may be regarded as simply a dialect
of English, and it is a mere chance whether a tale is extant in one or
other, or both.

I have also rescued and re-told a few Fairy Tales that only exist
now-a-days in the form of ballads. There are certain indications that
the “common form” of the English Fairy Tale was the _cante-fable_, a
mixture of narrative and verse of which the most illustrious example in
literature is “Aucassin et Nicolette.” In one case I have endeavoured to
retain this form, as the tale in which it occurs, “Childe Rowland,”
 is mentioned by Shakespeare in _King Lear_, and is probably, as I have
shown, the source of Milton's _Comus_. Late as they have been collected,
some dozen of the tales can be traced back to the sixteenth century, two
of them being quoted by Shakespeare himself.

books.title: Utilitarianism
books.author: John Stuart Mill
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 1873. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: John Stuart Mill argued that a practical art needs a clear idea of the end being aimed at first, because the rules for acting take their shape from that end.
John Stuart Mill said a set of principles needs one fundamental principle or a clear order of precedence, so that when two principles clash you know which one wins.
John Stuart Mill observed that even people who reject a principle are still shaped by it, since concern for what adds to or takes from happiness quietly guides many of their judgments.
John Stuart Mill held that some ends cannot be proved directly, but reasons can still be weighed, so a thoughtful person can accept or reject a principle on good grounds.
John Stuart Mill believed many people rejected his idea of happiness only because they misunderstood it, so a principle should be explained clearly before anyone judges it.
John Stuart Mill suggested that the better of two pleasures is the one that people who have tried both prefer, even when it brings some discontent with it.
John Stuart Mill argued that being content is not the same as being happy, and that a person with richer abilities may feel less settled yet still have the fuller happiness.
John Stuart Mill noted that people often drift to lesser pleasures not by choice but because their higher capacities wither without use, so keeping them in practice matters.
John Stuart Mill argued that a noble character matters not only to the person who has it but because it makes others happier, so the good of the whole is the real test.
John Stuart Mill described happiness not as constant rapture but as a life with few pains, many varied pleasures, and the sense of not expecting more than life can give.
John Stuart Mill saw a satisfied life as mostly calm and excitement, and felt that caring for others keeps life interesting, even as its end draws near.
John Stuart Mill believed real care for others and an interest in the common good are within reach of most people, and that the main work is reducing the big sources of suffering.
John Stuart Mill asked whether self-sacrifice is good in itself, and concluded that it matters only when it serves others, so the purpose behind a sacrifice is what counts.
John Stuart Mill suggested that being able to do without happiness can free a person from anxiety about life's blows, so they can calmly enjoy what is still within reach.
John Stuart Mill saw the golden rule as the spirit of utilitarian ethics, and suggested that good laws and education should link each person's own happiness with the good of the whole.
John Stuart Mill separated the rule of right action from the motive behind it, noting that most of what we do comes from other motives, and that this is fine if the rule is kept.
John Stuart Mill held that most of our moral duty concerns the particular people our actions affect, and that the wider public good only needs weighing when our actions reach far.
John Stuart Mill argued that the best proof of a good character is good actions over time, and that a disposition which mostly produces bad conduct should not be called good.
John Stuart Mill admitted that some in his own school judged too narrowly by the rightness of actions and neglected sympathy, a warning for anyone who measures everything by a single test.
John Stuart Mill warned that a short-term gain can undermine a rule worth far more, such as truthfulness, since trust in each other's word is what holds society together.
John Stuart Mill pointed out that people do not need to calculate every consequence before acting, because humanity's long experience has already taught which actions help or harm others.
John Stuart Mill compared general moral rules to signposts on a journey: knowing your destination does not mean ignoring the roads that get you there.
John Stuart Mill noted that every moral system faces hard cases, and that self-deception creeps in wherever a creed allows exceptions, so honesty with yourself is needed under any philosophy.
John Stuart Mill argued that one ultimate standard lets you settle conflicts between duties, which is better than none, even if applying it is hard.
John Stuart Mill held that an act's rightness depends on what the agent intends to do, while motive shapes how we judge the person and their habits of character.
John Stuart Mill noted that every moral standard faces the question of why we should obey it, and that familiar customs feel binding in a way that a new principle has to earn.
John Stuart Mill hoped education could make a feeling of unity with our fellow creatures as natural to people as their horror of crime, so doing good feels like part of who they are.
John Stuart Mill described conscience as the felt pain that follows breaking a duty, which can harden into remorse afterwards and gives a moral rule its binding force.
John Stuart Mill observed that people feel moral pressure through their own inner feeling, and that conscience is easily silenced whatever one believes about where it comes from.
John Stuart Mill pointed out that intuitive moralists already treat concern for others' interests as a core duty, so the two schools agree more than they argue.
John Stuart Mill argued that moral feelings are learned rather than innate, yet still natural, and that upbringing can shape them for good or for harm.
John Stuart Mill located the strength of a shared morality in the human desire to be united with fellow creatures, since living in society requires regard for everyone's interests.
John Stuart Mill observed that working together makes a person's ends blend with others', so the good of others comes to feel like a natural concern.
John Stuart Mill said a person with social feeling cannot bring themselves to see others as rivals for happiness, and feels that harmony with others is a natural need.
John Stuart Mill argued that the only proof something is worth wanting is that people actually want it, in the same way that the only proof something is visible is that people see it.
John Stuart Mill held that a good person loves virtue for its own sake, and that this becomes part of their happiness rather than a rival to it.
John Stuart Mill observed that what we first pursue as a means, such as money or fame, can become desired for its own sake, which shows how habits and associations shape what we want.

John Stuart Mill held that a person who loves virtue for its own sake is a real blessing to others, and that other acquired desires are only good up to the point where they stop serving the common good.
John Stuart Mill noted that habit can turn a purpose we once chose into something we act on without fresh desire, so the habits we build deserve careful choosing.
John Stuart Mill argued that a feeble will to do right is awakened by linking right action with pleasure and wrong with discomfort, and that habit later carries it on without effort.
John Stuart Mill pointed out that a natural feeling, such as a sense of justice, does not prove itself right, and that our instincts need to be checked and enlightened by reason.
John Stuart Mill noted that law is not the final test of justice, since a law can be bad, and that a wrong against a moral right is real even where no law is broken.
John Stuart Mill observed that people generally think justice means getting what one deserves, and that generosity such as returning good for evil goes beyond what justice requires.
John Stuart Mill described impartiality as being moved only by the considerations that properly apply to the case in hand, and resisting pressure from other motives.
John Stuart Mill noticed that people's ideas of fair treatment shift with what they think is useful, so many claims about justice are really claims about what works.
John Stuart Mill traced the idea of justice back to law and custom, noting that the sense of injustice later attached to laws that ought to exist, not only to the laws in force.
John Stuart Mill suggested that to call an act wrong is to say the person ought to answer for it, whether through law, public opinion or their own conscience.

John Stuart Mill separated duties that give someone a claim, such as keeping faith, from acts of charity that we must practise but not towards any particular person, and placed justice in the first group.

John Stuart Mill noted that people differ from other animals in extending sympathy beyond their own young to all human and even all sentient beings, and in seeing their safety bound up with their community's.
John Stuart Mill held that a natural urge to resent harm becomes moral only when guided by concern for the common good, so we resent what society has a shared interest in stopping.
John Stuart Mill noted that a person whose resentment is truly moral asks whether an act is blameable before reacting, and so considers the good of others as well as their own.
John Stuart Mill explained that a right is something society ought to protect for us, so a person has a right to what they can fairly earn, but not to an income society has no duty to provide.

John Stuart Mill argued that security is the most vital of all interests, since every other good depends on being safe from whoever is stronger, which is why our sense of right and wrong feels so absolute.
John Stuart Mill pointed out that people who call justice a clear, self-evident standard still disagree sharply about what is just, so the claim alone does not settle hard questions.
John Stuart Mill observed that competing claims about justice can each look sound on their own, and that they only get settled when we look to the deeper principles beneath justice.
John Stuart Mill noted that clever devices such as the social contract often sidestep hard questions of justice rather than answer them, so it is better to face the conflict openly.
John Stuart Mill argued that when two fair principles of justice conflict, as with rewarding skill or sharing equally, social usefulness is what can finally decide between them.
John Stuart Mill concluded that when people's ideas of justice contradict each other, the only way out is to ask what serves the general happiness.
John Stuart Mill argued that the rules forbidding people to harm one another matter most, because they keep the peace and are what everyone needs others to observe.
John Stuart Mill noted that refusing to return a kindness when it is needed hurts a person by breaking a reasonable expectation, which is why fairness in repaying kindness belongs to justice.

preview.text:
It is true that similar confusion and uncertainty, and in some cases
similar discordance, exist respecting the first principles of all the
sciences, not excepting that which is deemed the most certain of them,
mathematics; without much impairing, generally indeed without impairing
at all, the trustworthiness of the conclusions of those sciences. An
apparent anomaly, the explanation of which is, that the detailed
doctrines of a science are not usually deduced from, nor depend for
their evidence upon, what are called its first principles. Were it not
so, there would be no science more precarious, or whose conclusions were
more insufficiently made out, than algebra; which derives none of its
certainty from what are commonly taught to learners as its elements,
since these, as laid down by some of its most eminent teachers, are as
full of fictions as English law, and of mysteries as theology. The
truths which are ultimately accepted as the first principles of a
science, are really the last results of metaphysical analysis, practised
on the elementary notions with which the science is conversant; and
their relation to the science is not that of foundations to an edifice,
but of roots to a tree, which may perform their office equally well
though they be never dug down to and exposed to light. But though in
science the particular truths precede the general theory, the contrary
might be expected to be the case with a practical art, such as morals or
legislation. All action is for the sake of some end, and rules of
action, it seems natural to suppose, must take their whole character
and colour from the end to which they are subservient. When we engage in
a pursuit, a clear and precise conception of what we are pursuing would
seem to be the first thing we need, instead of the last we are to look
forward to. A test of right and wrong must be the means, one would
think, of ascertaining what is right or wrong, and not a consequence of
having already ascertained it.

books.title: Don Quixote
books.author: Miguel de Cervantes
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1616, translator died 1895. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In his preface to Don Quixote, translator John Ormsby argues that plain everyday language usually comes closest to the original, and that affectation should be avoided.

Translator John Ormsby, writing about Cervantes, sets out to separate what is known as fact from what is only conjecture, then lets the reader judge. Good advice for anyone, and for Tali, when the evidence is thin.
Before the sea battle at Lepanto, Cervantes was ill with fever but got up and insisted on taking his post. Whatever you think of the cause, showing up when it counts is a quality worth respecting.
When his companions were caught in a failed escape from Algiers, Cervantes insisted the whole plot was his alone, even under threat of torture. Loyalty that protects the people around you.
With his army career closed off by a crippled hand, Cervantes turned to writing in his thirties and published his first book. When one road shuts, a new one can still be built.

Ormsby says Cervantes's plays were not booed off the stage, but were not good enough to hold their place on it. Cervantes could not make a living as a playwright for long. Honest feedback like that is worth more than applause.

Cervantes wrote down the everyday life he saw while travelling for work, the barbers, travellers and inn-keepers, and that observation became the raw material for Don Quixote. Good ideas often come from paying attention to ordinary days.

Ormsby describes Cervantes as a sanguine man who kept trying as a playwright despite repeated failure, sure his plays would be recognised if only they got a fair hearing. Persistence is a strength, provided you also check whether the audience agrees.
Ormsby observes that Cervantes was proud of Don Quixote's popularity but longed for success as a dramatist, and so was chasing the wrong kind of success. Know which win you are actually after.
Ormsby argues that Cervantes met poverty and disappointment with a strong spirit, and even treated poverty as something to laugh about. Fortitude is a choice you can practise.
Ormsby says Don Quixote is one of the most widely read books in the world and also one of the most intensely Spanish. Being specific and true to your own place is what lets a story reach everyone.

Ormsby reads the moral of Don Quixote as this: enthusiasm that is pursued for its own sake, acts on impulse and ignores circumstances does harm to its owner and to everyone around them. Passion needs a sensible plan behind it.

Ormsby says Sancho Panza grounds Don Quixote in plain reality, so that every flight of fancy is brought back to earth by a steady, unpretentious partner. A good business needs someone who keeps the big dreams honest.
Ormsby notes that once Don Quixote found its readers, they wanted more of the characters they loved and not new digressions. Listen to what your audience is actually asking for.

Ormsby praises the plain, grave narration of Cervantes, which never nudges the reader to notice how clever it is. Good writing lets the people and the story do the work, and does not keep looking over its own shoulder.
Ormsby says every character in Don Quixote feels alive, even minor ones, and that Cervantes gives them a kind of humanity. Treat even small roles with real care.
In the preface to Don Quixote, Cervantes says he will not dress his book up with borrowed quotes and grand endorsements to look learned. He presents it plain and lets it stand on its own.

In the preface to Don Quixote, a friend advises Cervantes to write plainly and clearly, so that the simple are not wearied, the wise admire it, and the grave do not despise it. Clear writing serves every reader at once.
The verses in front of Don Quixote warn that if your own roof is made of glass, it is foolish to throw stones at the people passing by. Check your own house before you criticise others.

At the opening of Don Quixote, Cervantes shows a gentleman so absorbed in his reading that he neglects his land and sells off the fields to buy more books. A passion that quietly starves the real work is a warning worth heeding.

In Don Quixote, reading romances night and day leaves the hero convinced that the tales are literally true, and he loses touch with the world as it is. Test your big ideas against the facts before you act on them.

Don Quixote sets off on his grand mission before the basics are sorted, promising to fix the gaps on the road. Sorting out the basics first, before the big launch, is usually cheaper than fixing them along the way.

In Don Quixote, the innkeeper warns the hero never to travel without money and the basic supplies, because you rarely know when you will need them. A small reserve for the unexpected is plain common sense.
In Don Quixote, the hero forces a farmer to settle the wages he owes a young worker before he can ride on. Paying people what you owe them, on time, is not optional.
When a youth argues that a rich farmer is no knight, Don Quixote answers that everyone is the son of his works. Cervantes judges people by what they do, not by their titles.

In Don Quixote, the hero demands that travellers swear to a lady they have never seen, and when they ask to see proof he charges at them. Insisting that people accept your word without evidence only starts fights.

In Don Quixote, the niece blames herself for not raising her uncle's strange habits earlier, when the friends who could help might have stepped in. Speak up about warning signs while they are still small.
In Don Quixote, the curate refuses to burn a whole shelf in one go, and judges each book on its own merits, pardoning the good ones. Judge the thing in front of you, not the family it belongs to.

In Don Quixote, the niece and curate decide to take the nearest temptation out of their friend's way, the books that have led him astray. If you want to change a habit, start by removing the trigger from your path.
In Don Quixote, the hero insists the windmills are giants and charges them, ignoring his squire who can plainly see what they are. Being sure of your story does not change the facts in front of you.
In Don Quixote, Sancho tells his master he would rather he complained when something hurt than hide the pain. An honest team surfaces problems early, and a good leader wants to hear them.
In Don Quixote, Cervantes shows a man who reads ordinary travellers as sorcerers because his head is full of old stories, while his squire Sancho keeps pointing at the plain facts.
In Don Quixote, Cervantes shows how a man who is certain of his story will charge at people who calmly tell him the truth, and never stop to listen.
In Don Quixote, Cervantes has his narrator insist that a historian must stay exact and free from passion, interest, fear, hatred and love, because true history is the witness of the past.
In Don Quixote, Cervantes shows the squire Sancho often right about the danger, yet he still follows his master, so loyalty can run ahead of good sense.
In Don Quixote, Sancho asks whether a rash oath still makes sense when keeping it costs everyone comfort for no gain, a good test for any promise made in the heat of the moment.
In Don Quixote, Sancho would rather eat plain bread alone in his own freedom than sit at a grand table with honours he cannot enjoy, so comfort and liberty can outweigh status.
In Don Quixote, Cervantes has the knight long for an age when justice was not bent by favour or self-interest, a complaint that still fits any setting where connections decide outcomes.
In Don Quixote, Chrysostom gives up his fortune and his scholar's gown to chase a love that will not return, a warning about how a single passion can strip a person of their own life.
In Don Quixote, Marcela turns down every suitor and chooses her own life, and the story treats her independence as her right rather than a fault.
In Don Quixote, the knight argues that the soldier who carries out an order does as much as the one who gave it, a fair point about the worth of doing the work.
In Don Quixote, Vivaldo argues that a plainly unreasonable last wish should not be obeyed to the letter, and that the papers are better kept as a warning to others.
