In Don Quixote, Marcela argues that love cannot be compelled, and that being admired or beautiful does not oblige anyone to love in return.
In Don Quixote, Marcela holds that being honest about what you can offer is not cruelty, and that someone who ignores a clear answer cannot blame the one who gave it.
In Don Quixote, Sancho chooses to walk away from a pointless fight because he has a family to provide for, a sober reminder that a careless quarrel can cost those who depend on you.
In Don Quixote, the knight holds that fortune always leaves a door open in adversity, a steadying thought for a bad day, though Cervantes shows his eyes often see what he wishes.
In Don Quixote, Sancho calls the inn an inn while his master insists it is a castle, a neat picture of how a strong wish can argue against plain facts.
In Don Quixote, Sancho remarks that when one thing is looked for, another is often found, a fair note on how plans rarely go the way they were drawn up.
In Don Quixote, the knight explains a night of blows as enchantment rather than a plain mix-up, a good example of how a story we want to believe can explain away what actually happened.
In Don Quixote, the innkeeper cuts through a fine speech about chivalry with a plain demand for the bill, a reminder that noble principles still have to settle what is owed.
In Don Quixote, Sancho notices the men who tossed him had names and were flesh and bone, and reasons that the plain explanation is usually the right one, even when a grander story is on offer.
In Don Quixote, the knight says fear can warp the senses so that things look other than they are, though the joke is that he is the one charging at a flock of sheep he has taken for armies.
In Don Quixote, the knight tells his discouraged squire that one man is no more than another unless he does more, and that bad times cannot last for ever, a steadying thought for a hard stretch.
In Don Quixote, Sancho begs his master not to go hunting for danger that serves no purpose, a sensible friend asking whether the risk is worth taking at all.
In Don Quixote, Sancho's endless tale of counting goats is a comic lesson in story-telling: it hangs on a tiny detail that the listener cannot let go, so the whole thing stalls.
In Don Quixote, a whole night of dread turns out to be six fulling hammers, a good reminder that many fears shrink once you walk over and look at the real cause.
In Don Quixote, the knight takes heart from the old saying that where one door shuts another opens, a handy thought after a failed plan, though he reads every sign the way he wishes.
In Don Quixote, Sancho points out that a deed nobody sees is soon forgotten, so it is wiser to serve someone with real work to do, where your merit can be recognised.
Cervantes has Don Quixote split families into those who were great and have faded, and those who rise step by step from the common ranks. Both paths are real, and the second is open to anyone.
In Don Quixote, Cervantes has the knight ask each chained prisoner for his own account instead of judging the whole group by the chain. Listen to each person before you decide what they are.

preview.text:
My purpose here is not to dogmatise on the rules of translation, but to
indicate those I have followed, or at least tried to the best of my
ability to follow, in the present instance. One which, it seems to me,
cannot be too rigidly followed in translating “Don Quixote,” is to
avoid everything that savours of affectation. The book itself is,
indeed, in one sense a protest against it, and no man abhorred it more
than Cervantes. For this reason, I think, any temptation to use
antiquated or obsolete language should be resisted. It is after all an
affectation, and one for which there is no warrant or excuse. Spanish
has probably undergone less change since the seventeenth century than
any language in Europe, and by far the greater and certainly the best
part of “Don Quixote” differs but little in language from the
colloquial Spanish of the present day. Except in the tales and Don
Quixote’s speeches, the translator who uses the simplest and plainest
everyday language will almost always be the one who approaches nearest
to the original.

Seeing that the story of “Don Quixote” and all its characters and
incidents have now been for more than two centuries and a half familiar
as household words in English mouths, it seems to me that the old
familiar names and phrases should not be changed without good reason.
Of course a translator who holds that “Don Quixote” should receive the
treatment a great classic deserves, will feel himself bound by the
injunction laid upon the Morisco in Chap. IX not to omit or add
anything.

CERVANTES

books.title: Celtic Fairy Tales
books.author: Joseph Jacobs (editor)
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Editor died 1916. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Joseph Jacobs held that a good story collection needs a due mix of the comic and the romantic, since neither alone keeps a listener engaged.
In Connla and the Fairy Maiden, the tale shows how a longing for somewhere else can pull a person away from the folk they love, and how hard that pull is to resist.
In Guleesh, a rough farm boy with a soft heart refuses to abandon a frightened girl who has lost her voice, and his kindness matters more than his cleverness.
In Guleesh, when no safe way forward is clear, the boy and the priest agree to keep quiet and wait for a better chance rather than act rashly.
In The Field of Boliauns, Tom Fitzpatrick rushes off for a spade to chase a quick fortune and returns with nothing, a sharp lesson about greed and haste.
In The Horned Women, a frightened woman is saved by plain resourcefulness: she binds a leaking sieve with clay and moss so it holds water, and the trick works.
In Conall Yellowclaw, Conall is caught stealing the king's horse, but he tells the plain truth about why he came, and that honesty earns the king's mercy.
In Conall Yellowclaw, trapped in a giant's cave, Conall keeps his head, works calmly and waits out the night, showing how patience can turn a hopeless spot.
In Hudden and Dudden and Donald O'Neary, two rich farmers scheme against a poor neighbour because the more they have the more they want, and their envy makes them fools.
In Donald O'Neary, a poor man turns the death of his cow into a shrewd plan, showing that a setback can still be made to pay if you think hard about it.
In The Shepherd of Myddvai, the lake-maiden leaves her husband after he strikes her three times without cause, showing how small careless wrongs add up until a bond breaks.
In The Sprightly Tailor, the tailor keeps stitching calmly while a giant rises through the church floor, a picture of steady work held to a task under real fear.
In The Story of Deirdre, the young woman trusts her own sense of compassion over her guardian's caution and lets a cold, hungry stranger in from the storm.
In The Story of Deirdre, Naois brushes aside Deirdre's warning dream as a woman's fear, and the story shows what it costs when a sincere warning is not taken seriously.
In The Story of Deirdre, Ferchar's sons refuse the king's offer of free bridges for their family, preferring to go home with their honour than to buy safety by betraying their friends.
In Munachar and Manachar, one grudge sets off a comic chain where each helper demands something first, a fine reminder of how a good story builds momentum by piling up small steps.
In Gold-tree and Silver-tree, a queen's jealousy of her stepdaughter's beauty drives her to murder again and again, and in the end her own envy is what brings her down.
In King O'Toole and his Goose, the king gives his last acre for a bargain he has made, and the saint tells him that a kept word is what made the whole deal work.
In The Wooing of Olwen, Kilhuch answers each impossible task with the same calm reply, that it will be easy for him, and his steady confidence is what carries the quest forward.
In Jack and His Comrades, Jack pulls a stranded ass out of the bog without a second thought, and that small kindness brings the animals back to help him on his road.
In Jack and His Comrades, after winning back the stolen gold, Jack and his friends carry it straight back to its owner rather than keep it, and their honesty is what finally earns them a home.

In The Shee an Gannon, the young cowboy finds fresh strength in a fight with a giant when he thinks of his parents and of what he is working towards, a reminder that a clear purpose can steady the nerve.
In The Story-Teller at Fault, a dice game with a stranger starts small and keeps raising the stakes until the storyteller has lost everything, a warning that chasing a loss only deepens it.
In The Story-Teller at Fault, the stranger tells the storyteller that a wrong done under a spell was not really his wife's doing, and urges him to forgive and forget.
In a Celtic tale retold by Joseph Jacobs, a young herd shares a kill fairly among a dog, an otter and a falcon, and each one later comes to his aid. Generosity comes back around.
In a Celtic tale retold by Joseph Jacobs, the one who fled the beast later claims the victory, and only the true hero can prove it by his deeds. Truth shows itself in the end.
In a Celtic tale retold by Joseph Jacobs, a wife wins back her husband by playing her harp and stopping at each step, so the sea-maiden has to keep bargaining. Patient cleverness can undo a loss.

In the Fin M'Coul legend Joseph Jacobs retells, Fin hides his real reason for choosing a windy hilltop, a clear view of a rival coming, and laughs off his neighbours' doubts. Foresight is often quietly practical.
In the Fin M'Coul legend Joseph Jacobs retells, Oonagh meets a frightening rival calmly and turns his own strength against him with a clever trick. Calm wits can outmatch brute force.
In Fair, Brown, and Trembling, retold by Joseph Jacobs, two sisters spend their days envying a stranger's finery and copying it. Envy keeps people busy with the wrong things.
In Fair, Brown, and Trembling, the youngest sister is kept hidden and scorned, but she finally speaks up and is believed once she shows the proof. Quiet people often have the most to say.

In Jack and His Master, retold by Joseph Jacobs, a servant turns his master's vague orders into the letter of the law, and the master learns that loose instructions get literal results. Say exactly what you mean.

In Beth Gellert, retold by Joseph Jacobs, Llewelyn kills his faithful hound in a rage after jumping to conclusions, and only then finds his child safe beside a dead wolf. Check the facts before acting in anger.
In The Tale of Ivan, a servant who keeps to the old road escapes robbers that catch his companions on the new one. Tried and familiar paths are often the safer choice.
In The Tale of Ivan, a lodger refuses to hang for a murder he did not commit and insists that the real culprits be found. Standing up for the truth matters most when you are the one under suspicion.
In Andrew Coffey, a story from Joseph Jacobs, a man is so busy puzzling over strange goings-on that he neglects the fire he is minding and is rebuked for it. Attend to the task in front of you.

In The Battle of the Birds, a prince rashly promises his firstborn to a giant to win back a bundle, and the promise returns years later. Think hard before promising something you may not be able to keep.

In The Battle of the Birds, Auburn Mary tells the prince exactly how to climb the giant's tree and warns that one missed step leaves a part of her behind. Careful attention to small details can matter more than strength.
In The Battle of the Birds, the prince recognises his true helper when a golden pigeon reminds him of the help it gave him. Keeping a record of what others have done for you is worth the effort.
In The Lad with the Goat-skin, retold by Joseph Jacobs, Tom beats every challenger in the palace yard but takes care not to kill any of them. Real strength shows in restraint.
In The Lad with the Goat-skin, Tom heals the envious Redhead who tried to steal his flail, and it is Redhead who is left ashamed and grateful. Showing mercy to a rival costs far less than it seems.
In King O'Toole and His Goose, Samuel Lover makes a point about keeping your word through humour, so the moral slips in without a lecture. Stories teach best when they entertain.

preview.text:
In making my selection I have chiefly tried to make the stories
characteristic. It would have been easy, especially from Kennedy, to
have made up a volume entirely filled with "Grimm's Goblins" _a la
Celtique_. But one can have too much even of that very good thing, and
I have therefore avoided as far as possible the more familiar
"formulae" of folk-tale literature. To do this I had to withdraw from
the English-speaking Pale both in Scotland and Ireland, and I laid down
the rule to include only tales that have been taken down from Celtic
peasants ignorant of English.

Having laid down the rule, I immediately proceeded to break it. The
success of a fairy book, I am convinced, depends on the due admixture
of the comic and the romantic: Grimm and Asbjoernsen knew this secret,
and they alone. But the Celtic peasant who speaks Gaelic takes the
pleasure of telling tales somewhat sadly: so far as he has been printed
and translated, I found him, to my surprise, conspicuously lacking in
humour. For the comic relief of this volume I have therefore had to
turn mainly to the Irish peasant of the Pale; and what richer source
could I draw from?

For the more romantic tales I have depended on the Gaelic, and, as I
know about as much of Gaelic as an Irish Nationalist M. P., I have had
to depend on translators. But I have felt myself more at liberty than
the translators themselves, who have generally been over-literal, in
changing, excising, or modifying the original. I have even gone
further. In order that the tales should be characteristically Celtic, I
have paid more particular attention to tales that are to be found on
both sides of the North Channel.

books.title: On Liberty
books.author: John Stuart Mill
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 1873. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: W. L. Courtney observes that a thinker of abstract ideas gains a great deal from a partner who brings concrete examples, and the concrete examples gain their foundation from the abstract reasoning.
W. L. Courtney warns that a society which crushes individual initiative ends in a dead level of uniformity, so the variety individuals bring is needed for progress.
Mill opens On Liberty by asking how much power society may legitimately hold over the individual, a question he says shapes most practical arguments of his age.
Mill traces liberty as the early fight to limit rulers, first through guaranteed rights and later through checks that required the consent of the governed.
Mill notes that a government answerable to the majority still needs limits, since the majority may wish to oppress part of its own number.
Mill warns that social pressure can enslave the soul as surely as the state can, so protection is needed against the tyranny of prevailing opinion too.
Mill observes that custom so often passes for nature that people rarely question the rules of their own age.
Mill argues that an opinion without reasons is only one person's preference, however firmly it is held, so it is worth asking why you believe what you do.
Mill notes that most people accept others' dissent only up to the edge of what they themselves believe, so toleration is usually granted with tacit reserves.
Mill observes that people judge government interference by personal preference rather than principle, so they are often wrong in both directions.
Mill's one principle is that the only reason to force someone against their will is to prevent harm to others. Their own good is not enough, though persuasion is always fair.
Mill says that where outside control cannot reach, a person's own conscience should guard the interests of others, and judge itself all the more strictly.
Mill's list of liberty covers conscience, the freedom to shape your life to suit your own character, and the freedom to join with others for any purpose that harms no one.
Mill holds that the only freedom worth the name is pursuing your own good in your own way, so long as you do not stop others pursuing theirs.
Mill notes that societies put as much effort into forcing conformity in private life as in public life, and that the urge to impose opinions on others is held back mainly by lack of power.
Mill argues that silencing an opinion robs everyone, dissenters most of all, of the chance to swap error for truth, or to see truth sharpened by argument.
Mill argues that stopping an opinion from being heard assumes you are infallible, since you cannot be sure it is false and even a sure opinion gains from being tested.
Mill notes that people feel very sure of their opinions and rarely guard against their own fallibility, treating the views of their own circle as if they were the whole world's.
Mill concedes that we must act on our best opinions even though we may be wrong, but says presuming a view true is different from refusing to let it be tested.
Mill holds that human judgment is valuable because errors can be corrected, and it stays reliable only while the means of correction, discussion and experience, are kept at hand.
Mill says a wise person builds judgment by hearing every side, seeking out objections rather than avoiding them, and only then has a right to trust their own view.
Mill argues that the beliefs we have most reason to trust are the ones that keep an open invitation to the world to prove them wrong.
Mill says that to call a view certain while silencing anyone who would deny it is to judge certainty without hearing the other side.
Mill notes that restricting opinions because they seem useless or harmful still assumes infallibility, since usefulness is itself a matter of opinion that needs testing.
Mill's test is not how sure we feel but whether we decide a question for others without letting them hear what can be said on the other side.
Mill reminds us that Socrates was condemned by his own city, and that the people a generation silences are often the ones later honoured most.
Mill argues that the people who once condemned great reformers were usually as sincere and respectable as people today, so we should doubt the certainties of our own era.
Mill notes that even a wise and gentle ruler can wrongly suppress new ideas, so being the most enlightened person around is no guarantee of being right.
Mill says that someone who reveals a truth the world had got wrong performs a great service, and treating them harshly shows how little the world values that service.
Mill warns that truth does not win on its own strength, since suppression often works, but a true idea tends to be rediscovered until one rediscovery finally survives.
Mill says social stigma, more than the law, is what really silences unpopular views, and that it works just as well.
Mill warns that when people keep their real convictions private and say only what the public wants, a society loses its moral courage and its thinkers grow timid.
Mill argues that truth gains more from the errors of someone who thinks for themselves than from the right opinions of people who never think at all.
Mill notes that a people only becomes intellectually alive when the big questions are open to debate, as Europe did after the Reformation and in the eighteenth century.
Mill says a true opinion that is never openly discussed becomes a dead dogma rather than a living truth, and so it needs fearless testing.
Mill warns that a truth held without knowing its grounds is just one more superstition, clinging to the words that state it.
Mill points out that mathematics has arguments on one side only, while most real questions need a balance between two sets of reasons, so you must learn both sides to know your view.
Mill, citing Cicero, says that if you know only your own side of a question you have no real ground to prefer it, so you must study the opposing case as hard as your own.
Mill says you only truly know your view once you can state the strongest case against it, so imagine the sharpest opponent and give them their best arguments.
Mill warns that without open argument the words of a belief lose their meaning, leaving phrases learned by rote instead of a living understanding.
Mill notes that a belief loses its living power once people inherit it rather than choose it, and that it is most vivid while it is still fighting for its place.
Mill warns that a belief handed down and accepted passively goes dead, and can end up guarding the mind against any fresh conviction.
Mill notes that many people profess high principles but guide their conduct by the customs of their group, so the principles never shape what they actually do.
Mill observes that teachers and learners go to sleep at their post once there is no opponent, so a belief stays most alive while it is actively defended.
Mill observes that proverbs we hear all our lives only come alive once experience teaches us their meaning, and that open argument would bring that understanding sooner.
Mill notes that when a truth is universally accepted we lose the benefit of defending it against opponents, so teachers should look for a way to keep its difficulties alive for learners.
Mill praises Socratic questioning, which shows people that they do not yet understand the beliefs they have simply adopted, so they can build a firm belief of their own.
Mill says criticism that exposes weak points is a route to real knowledge, so when someone challenges your view, listen and be grateful they have done the hard work for you.
Mill observes that popular opinions are usually part of the truth but rarely the whole of it, so a dissenter's view often holds the missing piece and is worth hearing.
Mill argues that on the great questions of practical life, truth lies in reconciling opposites, so the side in the minority deserves a fair hearing as the voice of what is neglected.
Mill argues that no single body of moral teaching holds the whole truth, so a part of the truth should not be mistaken for the whole, and good moral thinking draws on several sources.
Mill argues that the real evil is not the clash between parts of the truth but the quiet suppression of one side, so truth only has a chance when every side is argued and listened to.
Mill sums up four reasons for free opinion: a silenced view may be true, even an error may hold part of the truth, a view not contested becomes a prejudice, and its meaning fades.
Mill notes that a telling attack always feels intemperate to the person it lands on, so calls for temperate debate are hard to police fairly.
Mill argues that name-calling by people who hold the prevailing view deters others from speaking, so restraint matters most on that side.
Mill's rule for public debate is to judge people by their candour rather than by the side they take, and to credit opponents for stating the other view fairly.
In On Liberty, Mill warned that true toleration means freedom for everyone who holds their beliefs in good faith, not only for those who share one creed.
John Stuart Mill held that people should be free to act on their own opinions in their own lives, so long as they do not harm others. Only conduct that hurts others can rightly be controlled.
John Stuart Mill argued that since no one is infallible and most truths are only half-truths, different ways of living are worth trying, so each can be proved in practice.
Mill held that the free development of individuality is a necessary part of well-being and progress, though people rarely value it for its own sake.

preview.text:
Every one will judge for himself of this romantic episode in Mill's
career, according to such experience as he may possess of the
philosophic mind and of the value of these curious but not infrequent
relationships. It may have been a piece of infatuation, or, if we prefer
to say so, it may have been the most gracious and the most human page in
Mill's career. Mrs. Mill may have flattered her husband's vanity by
echoing his opinions, or she may have indeed been an Egeria, full of
inspiration and intellectual helpfulness. What usually happens in these
cases,--although the philosopher himself, through his belief in the
equality of the sexes, was debarred from thinking so,--is the extremely
valuable action and reaction of two different classes and orders of
mind. To any one whose thoughts have been occupied with the sphere of
abstract speculation, the lively and vivid presentment of concrete fact
comes as a delightful and agreeable shock. The instinct of the woman
often enables her not only to apprehend but to illustrate a truth for
which she would be totally unable to give the adequate philosophic
reasoning. On the other hand, the man, with the more careful logical
methods and the slow processes of formal reasoning, is apt to suppose
that the happy intuition which leaps to the conclusion is really based
on the intellectual processes of which he is conscious in his own case.
Thus both parties to the happy contract are equally pleased. The
abstract truth gets the concrete illustration; the concrete illustration
finds its proper foundation in a series of abstract inquiries. Perhaps
Carlyle's epithets of "iridescent" and "vivid" refer incidentally to
Mrs. Mill's quick perceptiveness, and thus throw a useful light on the
mutual advantages of the common work of husband and wife. But it savours
almost of impertinence even to attempt to lift the veil on a mystery
like this. It is enough to say, perhaps, that however much we may
deplore the exaggeration of Mill's references to his wife, we recognise
that, for whatever reason, the pair lived an ideally happy life.

books.title: The Odyssey
books.author: Homer
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Ancient author, translators died 1910 and 1912. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Butcher and Lang argue that each age wants different qualities from a translation, so there can be no final version of a great work, only versions suited to their own time.
In The Odyssey, Odysseus's reckless boast to the Cyclops sets off ten years of wandering, showing how one rash choice can shape everything that follows.
In The Odyssey, the crew eat the Sun's sacred cattle out of hunger, despite a clear warning, and lose the ship. Stories show that a known warning, ignored for a short-term need, often costs far more.
Butcher and Lang note that the Odyssey weaves many older folk tales into one plot through a single master craftsman, which is how a strong story usually gets its unity.
In The Odyssey, Zeus points out that people blame the gods for troubles their own reckless choices bring on. It is an old observation that still holds for most of us.

In The Odyssey, Athene tells Telemachus not to wait for his absent father to rescue the household, but to call the assembly himself and go and find out what he can. Waiting for a rescuer rarely fixes a problem.

In The Odyssey, young Telemachus stands up to the suitors in plain words and claims his place as master of his own house. Courage often starts with simply saying clearly what you will and won't accept.
In The Odyssey, Penelope holds off her suitors for years by weaving a shroud by day and unpicking it by night. It shows how patient, clever tactics can buy time when you cannot win by force.
In The Odyssey, Mentor scolds the people of Ithaca for sitting silent while a few men plunder a household they outnumber. Wrongs last when the many who could speak up say nothing.

In The Odyssey, Telemachus stops putting up with the losses at home once he is grown and sees the facts for himself, and he decides to act. Growing up often means seeing clearly what you have been putting up with.
In The Odyssey, Nestor recalls how the Greek army split after a hasty night assembly, held in drink and anger, and a quarrel of pride. Decisions made in heat often leave everyone worse off.
In The Odyssey, Athene reminds Telemachus that death comes to everyone, even those the gods love. It is a plain fact that makes the time we have worth using well.
In The Odyssey, Nestor will not let his guests sleep on a ship when they could have a proper bed in his house. Generous hospitality, offered freely to a stranger, is a mark of a good household.

In The Odyssey, Menelaus admits he grieves for his lost comrades for a while, then turns back to living, because even sorrow wears thin. Letting grief have its time, then getting on with the day, is a sensible way to carry loss.
In The Odyssey, Helen looks back and admits that her choice long ago brought all the grief. Owning a past mistake honestly, without excuses, is where any change of direction starts.

In The Odyssey, Menelaus recalls how Odysseus, hidden inside the horse, held his impatient comrades back from answering a call that would have betrayed them all. Self-control in a tight moment can save the whole group.

In The Odyssey, Ajax is drowned after boasting that he escaped the sea in spite of the gods. Pride that mocks a power greater than yourself so often ends in a fall, and the story makes that point without any lecture.

In The Odyssey, Penelope points out that Odysseus never wronged anyone, and that the suitors have repaid his household's kindness with cruelty. Fair dealing is what people remember long after, and it is the mark of a good name.

In The Odyssey, the old nurse Eurycleia steadies the grieving Penelope by asking her to wash, dress and pray, rather than sink further into fear. A small practical step can steady a mind that is swamped with worry.
In The Odyssey, Calypso loves Odysseus and could keep him, yet she helps him build a raft and sends him home. Letting go with generosity, rather than holding on, is its own kind of love.

In The Odyssey, Odysseus turns down an offer of endless life with Calypso because he would rather have a short mortal life with his own people. Knowing what matters most to you is the best test for any tempting offer.
In The Odyssey, Odysseus clings to his raft while its timbers hold and only swims once it truly breaks apart. Keep using what still works, and change course when it has really failed, not before.
Homer shows Odysseus, stripped of everything, pray to the river as a humble suppliant. Asking for help plainly, with nothing to offer but his need, is its own kind of courage.
In The Odyssey, Homer has Odysseus, cold and half drowned, weigh each option aloud before he acts, and choose the safer path rather than the first one that comes to mind.
In The Odyssey, Homer has the battered Odysseus weigh a bold approach against a gentle one, and choose smooth words over force, so the strangers he needs do not turn against him.
In The Odyssey, Nausicaa takes in a shipwrecked stranger because strangers in need come from Zeus, and a little kindness is dear. Homer makes hospitality a duty as well as a virtue.
Nausicaa plans ahead so gossip cannot harm her reputation or the stranger's. She arranges for Odysseus to follow at a distance into town, which shows how careful thought protects both people.
In The Odyssey, Athene tells Odysseus that the bold man does best in every adventure, even a stranger in a strange land. Walking in with steady nerve matters more than knowing everyone first.
In The Odyssey, Odysseus will not pass himself off as a god. He says plainly that he is only a mortal man weighed down by sorrow, which is a good model for honesty about who you are.
Homer has Odysseus cling to the keel of his wrecked ship for nine days while his crew is lost. Endurance, held on through long odds, is what keeps him alive.
Odysseus steps in to spare Nausicaa her father's rebuke and takes the fault onto himself. Loyalty to the person who helped you is shown in what you say when they are blamed.
In The Odyssey, King Alcinous says due measure in all things is best, and will not keep a guest against his will. Generosity, for Homer, respects the freedom of the person being helped.
In The Odyssey, Odysseus hides his tears under his cloak while the court celebrates, and only the king notices. Homer shows that grief can be carried quietly without spoiling other people's pleasure.
Odysseus answers an insult without losing his temper, pointing out that the gods share out looks, speech and wisdom unevenly. Then he accepts the challenge and proves himself with action.
Odysseus tells the Phaeacians that anyone who challenges the man who has welcomed him is a fool, because he only harms his own standing. Gratitude to a host is a matter of honour in The Odyssey.
In The Odyssey, Euryalus repairs an insult with soft words and a gift of his own. Homer shows a fair apology has both the words and the cost behind it.
Odysseus honours the minstrel Demodocus with the best cut of meat, even while he is sorrowful himself. Recognising other people's craft generously, even when you are hurting, is a mark of character.

In The Odyssey, Odysseus says there is no more gracious delight than a whole company feasting together and listening to a singer. He also holds that a person's own home and family are worth more than any comfortable life elsewhere.
In The Odyssey, after a successful raid Odysseus's men ignore his order to leave and linger over wine and sheep, and pay for it. A win that tempts you to stay too long can cost you dearly.
Homer's lotus-eaters show how a sweet, easy comfort can make people forget the way home. Keep your goal in view, even when the present feels pleasant.

Trapped in the Cyclops's cave, Odysseus holds back from a rash attack because he sees his crew could not then move the great stone. Homer shows that thinking through the consequences first can save everyone.

In The Odyssey, Odysseus, facing death, searches for every option and settles on the plan that looks best, tying the rams together to slip out. Calm, careful planning under pressure is what gives a team its chance.

In The Odyssey, Odysseus cannot resist taunting the blinded Cyclops from the sea, and his crew begs him to stop. The urge to have the last word nearly sinks the whole ship. Homer shows how pride can cost more than the victory is worth.
In The Odyssey, Odysseus's crew, jealous of the gifts he is carrying, open the bag of winds and throw the voyage away. Envy and suspicion inside a team can wreck a journey that was almost done.

In The Odyssey, Eurylochus holds back from Circe's hall because he senses a trap, while the others walk in without a second thought. A quiet instinct for danger is worth heeding, even when the rest of the group is keen.
Odysseus will not lie down with Circe until she swears a mighty oath not to harm him. He is willing to trust, but only once a clear promise is made binding, a sound habit in any deal.

In The Odyssey, Odysseus will not taste food in Circe's hall until his companions are freed and he can see them. He puts the people who depend on him before his own comfort, which is what good leadership looks like.

In The Odyssey, a whole year of feasting in Circe's hall passes before Odysseus's companions gently remind him it is time to go home. Good friends are the ones who keep you true to what you actually came for.
In The Odyssey, Odysseus promises the ghost of Elpenor, a companion who fell from a roof, that he will bury him properly. Keeping faith with someone who can no longer repay you is a mark of decency.

The seer Teiresias tells Odysseus he can still get home if he restrains his own spirit and that of his men. Homer treats self-control, more than strength, as what carries a crew through a long voyage.

In The Odyssey, when a crowd of spirits rushes the blood, Odysseus lets them come forward one at a time so each can be heard properly. Taking people in turn, rather than all at once, is how you get a real answer from each of them.

In The Odyssey, the dead Achilles tells Odysseus he would rather work as a hired hand in the light of day than rule over the dead. Homer's shades long for life, a good reminder to value the living days you have.
In The Odyssey, Odysseus tries to soothe the old anger of Ajax even among the dead, urging him to master his wrath and proud spirit. A grudge outlives its use, and letting it go is the wiser course.
In the Odyssey, Homer has Odysseus recall that even Heracles, a son of Zeus, endured hard tasks set by a lesser man. Hardship alone does not show a person's worth.
In the Odyssey, Odysseus stops to bury his fallen crewman Elpenor properly and weeps as he does it. He does not rush past the people he has lost.

In the Odyssey, Circe tells Odysseus to have his crew plug their ears with wax and bind him to the mast, so he can hear the Sirens without being steered onto the rocks. Wise people plan ahead for their own weak moments.
In the Odyssey, Circe tells Odysseus that against Scylla there is no defence and that flight is the bravest course. Knowing when a fight cannot be won, and choosing to move on, is a kind of courage.
In the Odyssey, Circe's warning is simple: leave the sacred cattle alone and you may still get home. Heeding clear warnings keeps a hard journey survivable.
In the Odyssey, Odysseus tells his crew the full danger ahead so they can face it with foreknowledge. Sharing the real risks in advance helps a team act well.
In the Odyssey, Odysseus steadies his frightened crew by reminding them they have survived worse before and will look back on this too. Recalling past courage helps people face fear.

preview.text:
There would have been less controversy about the proper method of
Homeric translation, if critics had recognised that the question is a
purely relative one, that of Homer there can be no final translation.
The taste and the literary habits of each age demand different
qualities in poetry, and therefore a different sort of rendering of
Homer. To the men of the time of Elizabeth, Homer would have appeared
bald, it seems, and lacking in ingenuity, if he had been presented in
his antique simplicity. For the Elizabethan age, Chapman supplied what
was then necessary, and the mannerisms that were then deemed of the
essence of poetry, namely, daring and luxurious conceits. Thus in
Chapman’s verse Troy must “shed her towers for tears of overthrow,” and
when the winds toss Odysseus about, their sport must be called “the
horrid tennis.”

books.title: The Happy Prince and Other Tales
books.author: Oscar Wilde
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Author died 1900. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Happy Prince, Wilde mocks a statue that is admired for its looks but judged as if its only worth were usefulness, a reminder that people are worth more than how they look or what they produce.
In The Happy Prince, the Swallow drops the Reed once autumn comes and she no longer suits him, a sharp look at loyalty that only lasts while it is convenient.
In The Happy Prince, the Swallow calls the rain the Reed's selfishness and only stops to care once he looks up and sees the Prince weeping. Attention to others changes how we judge things.
In The Happy Prince, Wilde shows that the Prince only sees the misery of his city once he is dead and set up high above it. A comfortable life can keep us from seeing other people's suffering.
In The Happy Prince, the Swallow feels warm after doing a good action, and the Prince tells him that is the reason. Generosity tends to reward the giver as well as the receiver.
In The Happy Prince, the Prince gives away his own eyes to help a match-girl, and the Swallow gives up Egypt to stay with him. Wilde shows that real love is measured by what we are willing to give.
In The Happy Prince, the Prince asks the Swallow to report what he sees in the city, calling human suffering the greatest mystery. Looking honestly at hardship comes before we can help.
In The Happy Prince, the Swallow dies out of loyalty and the Prince strips off his gold for the poor. Wilde suggests that generosity can cost everything and still be worth it.

In The Happy Prince, the Mayor and Councillors tear the statue down as soon as it looks shabby, while God values the leaden heart and dead bird most. Wilde shows that public praise follows appearance, but true worth lies in self-giving.
In The Nightingale and the Rose, the Student's whole misery rests on one red rose, showing how easily we make a small thing the centre of our happiness.

In The Nightingale and the Rose, Wilde has the Nightingale say that love cannot be bought in the marketplace or weighed for gold. It is worth remembering when we are tempted to treat relationships as transactions.

In The Nightingale and the Rose, the Nightingale gives her life so the Student can have his rose, judging love to be worth more than life itself. Wilde asks what we would really give up for the things we want most.

In The Nightingale and the Rose, the Student dismisses the Nightingale as all style and no sincerity because she does not serve any practical purpose. Wilde warns us that judging by usefulness alone can make us miss real feeling.

In The Selfish Giant, the Giant builds a high wall around his garden and shuts out the children who loved to play there. Wilde shows how keeping good things to ourselves can cost us the joy we could share.
In The Selfish Giant, the Giant realises how selfish he has been and tears down his wall, and the Spring returns. Wilde shows that a change of heart can bring joy back, even after a long winter.
In The Selfish Giant, the old Giant says the children are the most beautiful flowers of all, showing that we find the most joy in the people we make room for.
In The Devoted Friend, the Miller talks grandly about unselfish friendship while only ever taking from Hans. Wilde shows the gap between what people say about loyalty and what they actually do.

In The Devoted Friend, the Miller keeps away when Hans is in hardship and calls it respect for his troubles. Wilde suggests a friend is judged by how they show up when times are hard, not by their fine words.
In The Devoted Friend, the Miller claims to protect Hans from temptation while keeping him at a distance. Wilde shows how easily we excuse our own selfishness with fine reasons.
In The Devoted Friend, the Miller's gifts always come with a bill attached, so every favour becomes a debt. Wilde shows that generosity which expects a return is really a trade.
In The Devoted Friend, the Miller hides behind 'honest' criticism to pressure Hans into giving more. A real friend respects your time and your needs as well as your words.

In The Devoted Friend, the Miller's funeral speech is all about himself, and his real regret is the wheelbarrow he no longer has to give. Wilde shows how to watch what people actually mourn when they say they care.

In The Remarkable Rocket, a little Squib boasts that travel has cured all his prejudices, and a wiser Roman Candle reminds him the world is far bigger than the King's garden. Wilde mocks the big talk of those who have seen very little.

In The Remarkable Rocket, the vain Rocket insists he is the most sensitive creature alive, yet he thinks only of himself. Wilde shows that people who talk most about their feelings are often the least attentive to others.
In The Remarkable Rocket, self-pity leaves the Rocket too damp to go off at all, while his relations shine. Wilde shows how self-absorption can stop us doing the very thing we were made for.

In The Remarkable Rocket, the Rocket looks down on useful work and says only the idle labour, yet the plain usefulness of the Duck is worth more. Wilde reminds us that a life of contribution beats a life of display.

In The Remarkable Rocket, the Rocket ends by boasting that he created a great sensation, though nobody even saw him go off. Wilde warns against mistaking noise and self-importance for real achievement.

preview.text:
“I am glad there is some one in the world who is quite happy,” muttered a
disappointed man as he gazed at the wonderful statue.

“He looks just like an angel,” said the Charity Children as they came out
of the cathedral in their bright scarlet cloaks and their clean white
pinafores.

“How do you know?” said the Mathematical Master, “you have never seen
one.”

“Ah! but we have, in our dreams,” answered the children; and the
Mathematical Master frowned and looked very severe, for he did not
approve of children dreaming.

One night there flew over the city a little Swallow.  His friends had
gone away to Egypt six weeks before, but he had stayed behind, for he was
in love with the most beautiful Reed.  He had met her early in the spring
as he was flying down the river after a big yellow moth, and had been so
attracted by her slender waist that he had stopped to talk to her.

“Shall I love you?” said the Swallow, who liked to come to the point at
once, and the Reed made him a low bow.  So he flew round and round her,
touching the water with his wings, and making silver ripples.  This was
his courtship, and it lasted all through the summer.

“It is a ridiculous attachment,” twittered the other Swallows; “she has
no money, and far too many relations”; and indeed the river was quite
full of Reeds.  Then, when the autumn came they all flew away.

After they had gone he felt lonely, and began to tire of his lady-love.
“She has no conversation,” he said, “and I am afraid that she is a
coquette, for she is always flirting with the wind.”  And certainly,
whenever the wind blew, the Reed made the most graceful curtseys.  “I
admit that she is domestic,” he continued, “but I love travelling, and my
wife, consequently, should love travelling also.”

books.title: Essays
books.author: Francis Bacon
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 1626. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Francis Bacon noticed that people can come to love a lie for its own sake, even when the truth would serve them better.
Francis Bacon held that knowing the truth, and believing it, is the highest good of human nature, a kind of standing on high ground above the mists below.
Francis Bacon held that clear and straight dealing is the honour of human nature, and that mixing in falsehood debases a person as alloy debases gold.
Francis Bacon observed that the fear of death is often fed by the show around it, the groans, the black clothes and the mourning, more than by death itself.
Francis Bacon noted that a mind fixed on something worthwhile scarcely feels the hurt of death, much as a man wounded in the heat of a good pursuit barely feels the blow.
Francis Bacon argued that open division among people who share a cause does more harm than bad habits, because a wound is worse than a corrupt humour.
Francis Bacon warned against two extremes: those who scorn all talk of peace, and those who settle every dispute with a lukewarm middle way. The real line runs between fundamentals and mere opinion.
Francis Bacon separated unity from uniformity: a varied garment is fine, a torn one is not. He warned against quarrels over trifles, and over matters so subtle that the words hide the agreement.
Francis Bacon held that people should not force belief by the sword, since that forgets they are men before they are members of a faith.
Francis Bacon called revenge a wild justice that law should weed out. He held that a man who broods on a wrong keeps his own wounds green, while passing over an offence shows true superiority.
Francis Bacon held that prosperity shows up vice while adversity shows up virtue, much as precious oils are most fragrant when crushed.
Francis Bacon judged that dissimulation is a weak kind of wisdom, since it takes a strong wit and a strong heart to know when to tell the truth and to do it.
Francis Bacon noticed that the ablest people usually earn a name for openness, and that this good name lets their occasional discretion pass almost unseen.
Francis Bacon held that secrecy is a virtue, because people confide in a discreet listener, and that a face should not give away what the tongue keeps to itself.
Francis Bacon thought that keeping a secret often forces a little pretence, but that deliberately feigning to be what one is not is a vice, except in great and rare matters.
Francis Bacon weighed concealment honestly: it can catch opponents off guard and keep a way out open, but it costs trust, which he called a key instrument for action.
Francis Bacon observed that people who build a family's name often care most for their children, seeing them as the continuance of their work as well as their kind.
Francis Bacon warned that parents who favour one child, or stir up rivalry between brothers in childhood, plant a discord that can split a family later in life.
Francis Bacon noticed that a person with no virtue of their own tends to envy virtue in others, since anyone who has no hope of reaching another's worth will try to pull that person down.
Francis Bacon observed that people who rise by degrees are envied less than those raised suddenly, and that people of merit are envied most when their good fortune lasts a long time.
Francis Bacon advised that honour won through real labour and risk draws less envy, since people pity a hard-earned position, while showing off greatness draws the most.
Francis Bacon saw public envy as a bridle that keeps the great within bounds, and warned that showy gestures to prove one is not afraid of envy only invite more of it.
Francis Bacon noted that when envy falls on every minister of a state at once, the true target is often the state itself, even if it is hidden.
Francis Bacon held that great and busy minds are rarely undone by love, but that love slips in when the watch is not kept, so a wise person guards the heart as well as the gate.
Francis Bacon warned that whoever prizes passion too highly gives up both riches and wisdom, and that love is best kept apart from serious affairs, lest it spoil a person's own ends.
Francis Bacon observed that people in high office are servants three times over, to the state, to fame and to business, so they lose much of their freedom along with their power.
Francis Bacon said that good examples are a globe of precepts, and that a leader should examine their own conduct strictly, asking whether they did best at the start.
Francis Bacon named four vices of authority: delay, corruption, roughness and facility. He advised leaders to explain plainly when they change course, since unexplained changes breed suspicion.
Francis Bacon advised leaders to treat their predecessors and colleagues fairly, and to call colleagues in before they expect it, since a debt of that kind is always paid in the end.
Francis Bacon observed that boldness is blind to danger, so it does well in carrying out a plan but poorly in giving counsel, and bold people are best as seconds rather than leaders.
Francis Bacon noticed that boldness impresses shallow judges and timid hearts far more than real skill does, and that the bold often shrug off broken promises as if they never mattered.
Francis Bacon called goodness, the wish for the good of others, the greatest of the mind's virtues, though he warned that it needs judgment, or it can leave a good person open to being used.

Francis Bacon advised seeking the good of others without becoming a prisoner of their moods, since mere softness takes an honest mind captive. Common benefits suit everyone, but special ones should be chosen with care.
Francis Bacon judged goodness by its signs: courtesy to strangers, compassion for others' troubles, a readiness to pardon, and gratitude for small kindnesses.
Francis Bacon noted that rumours and false news running against an authority are early signs of trouble, and that despising them often checks them better than heavy-handed suppression.
Francis Bacon warned that a leader who acts as one party among many loses the trust a common parent of the people needs, and that authority is weakened when it becomes a side in a quarrel.
Francis Bacon held that the most dangerous discontent is where the fear is greater than the actual feeling, so worries should be taken seriously before they grow into real trouble.
Francis Bacon held that the surest cure for unrest is to remove its causes, such as want and poverty, rather than only to manage its symptoms.
Francis Bacon said money is like muck, not good unless it is spread about, and that a community can hold great stock and still starve if wealth gathers in too few hands.
Francis Bacon held that letting grievances be voiced in moderation lets them evaporate safely, while turning them back inward only makes the wound fester.
Francis Bacon praised the keeping of hope alive. A wise leader holds people's hearts by hope when satisfaction is not possible, and leaves some outlet of hope in every hard matter.
Francis Bacon noted that a sharp remark can do lasting harm, since short sayings fly abroad like darts and are taken to reveal a person's real intent, so words should be weighed in tense times.
Francis Bacon held that a little learning can turn the mind away from the whole, while deeper study, seeing how the parts link together, carries it back toward the whole.
Francis Bacon warned that good forms and orders corrupt into a swarm of petty observances, and that a reform driven by the crowd often throws out the good along with the bad.
Francis Bacon thought travel is education for the young and experience for the elder, and that a traveller who has not yet got some of the language is at school rather than travelling.
Francis Bacon advised travellers to keep a diary, change lodgings within a town, and seek out people of standing, so that a short trip gathers much.

Francis Bacon advised a returning traveller to keep up letters with the best acquaintances, and to show what was learned in conversation rather than in dress, speaking less of stories and more of wisdom.
Francis Bacon observed that people with few things to desire and many things to fear grow languid and unclear in mind, and that one clear, predominant aim is what puts all the rest in order.
Francis Bacon noted that authority is ruined by power swung too far one way and then too far the other, and that a wise leader prevents the spark rather than relying on putting out fires.
Francis Bacon warned that a leader who depresses the great may become more absolute but less safe, since nobles who are crushed stop working alongside him, and he is left to do everything himself.
Francis Bacon held that the greatest trust between people is the trust of giving counsel, because a counsellor is entrusted with the whole of a matter, so the duty of faithfulness is greatest.
Francis Bacon read the old fable of Jupiter and Metis as a lesson: take matters to your advisers to be shaped, then bring the final decision forth as your own.
Francis Bacon warned that one idle person who loves to tell secrets does more harm than many who know how to keep quiet, so a leader should share matters carefully with advisers.
Francis Bacon held that the best safeguard against biased advice is for a leader to know their advisers as well as the advisers know them.

Francis Bacon advised that good counsel depends on choosing the right people, since the greatest errors are made in choosing individuals, and that advisers should be heard both privately and together.

Francis Bacon thought weighty matters should be raised one day and debated the next, since a night's sleep ripens a decision, and that a leader who reveals their own inclination too early gets only flattery.

Francis Bacon held that there is no greater wisdom than timing the beginnings of things well. Watch the start closely, then act swiftly, since secrecy in planning and speed in execution are what keep a plan out of sight.
Francis Bacon separated cunning from wisdom: a person can read other people well and still lack understanding of the matter itself, and such people are good only within their own familiar ground.
Francis Bacon warned that nothing does more harm in a community than cunning people passing for wise, and that tricks built on using others are no substitute for soundness in one's own dealings.
Francis Bacon warned that a servant who bends every matter to their own ends can do great harm, even to a master who trusts them, and advised balancing self-love with real care for others.

preview.text:
WHAT is truth? said jesting Pilate, and would not stay for an answer.
Certainly there be, that delight in giddiness, and count it a bondage to
fix a belief; affecting free-will in thinking, as well as in acting. And
though the sects of philosophers of that kind be gone, yet there remain
certain discoursing wits, which are of the same veins, though there be
not so much blood in them, as was in those of the ancients. But it is
not only the difficulty and labor, which men take in finding out
of truth, nor again, that when it is found, it imposeth upon men's
thoughts, that doth bring lies in favor; but a natural, though corrupt
love, of the lie itself. One of the later school of the Grecians,
examineth the matter, and is at a stand, to think what should be in it,
that men should love lies; where neither they make for pleasure, as with
poets, nor for advantage, as with the merchant; but for the lie's sake.
But I cannot tell; this same truth, is a naked, and open day-light, that
doth not show the masks, and mummeries, and triumphs, of the world, half
so stately and daintily as candle-lights. Truth may perhaps come to the
price of a pearl, that showeth best by day; but it will not rise to the
price of a diamond, or carbuncle, that showeth best in varied lights.
A mixture of a lie doth ever add pleasure. Doth any man doubt, that if
there were taken out of men's minds, vain opinions, flattering hopes,
false valuations, imaginations as one would, and the like, but it would
leave the minds, of a number of men, poor shrunken things, full of
melancholy and indisposition, and unpleasing to themselves?

books.title: The Iliad
books.author: Homer
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Ancient author, translator died 1902. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Iliad, Agamemnon refuses to give back a priest's daughter, and the whole army pays for his pride with plague. One person's stubborn pride can cost everyone around them.
In The Iliad, Calchas will only speak the truth once Achilles promises to protect him from a powerful king. Honest counsel needs a safe place to be heard.
In The Iliad, Achilles nearly draws his sword in rage, but a calm word from the goddess stops him. Pausing before acting on fury can keep a bad moment from becoming a disaster.
In The Iliad, old Nestor calms two proud rivals by reminding them that their quarrel only pleases the enemy. A trusted elder can end a fight by pointing to what both sides stand to lose.
In The Iliad, Achilles brings his hurt to his mother, who asks him to say what grieves him. Naming a wound to someone who cares is often the first step to bearing it.

In The Iliad, Vulcan steps in to calm his quarrelling parents with a cup of nectar and some cheerful jokes. A peacemaker who lightens the mood can stop a family fight from spoiling everyone's evening.
In The Iliad, Agamemnon tests his army by pretending they should all sail home, and the damage nearly becomes a rout. A leader who tests morale with a bluff risks losing the very people he needs.
In The Iliad, Ulysses calms a panicking army by going to each leader in turn and speaking fairly to them. Steady, one-to-one conversation can turn a stampede back into a team.

In The Iliad, Ulysses acknowledges that a weary army has every reason to be restless, then asks them to hold on a little longer. Naming people's frustration before asking for patience is more persuasive than scolding.
In The Iliad, Nestor advises splitting the army into tribes and clans so they can stand by one another and compete. Small teams that look out for each other show who is truly committed.
In The Iliad, Agamemnon admits he was the first to give offence in his quarrel with Achilles, a rare confession from a proud king. Owning your part of a dispute is what makes mending it possible.
In The Iliad, Nestor urges that talk should give way to action once the decision is made. Sound counsel knows when to stop deliberating and get on with the work.
In The Iliad, the Muses strip the boastful singer Thamyris of his gift after he claims he can outdo them. Pride in one's own talent can cost the very skill one is proud of.
In The Iliad, Achilles sulks at his ships and his men drift about with nothing to do, having no one to lead them. When a team's leader withdraws, the whole group can lose its purpose.

In The Iliad, Hector shames his brother Paris for fleeing a duel he started, pointing out that fine looks and sweet words are no substitute for courage. Charm means little when someone won't stand behind their choices.
In The Iliad, Antenor notices that Ulysses looks awkward and silent at first, yet his speech wins the room once he starts. First impressions can miss what a quiet person is really worth.

In The Iliad, Helen refuses the goddess's flattery and says plainly that a man who brags and then runs from a fight is no true partner. Honest self-respect can turn down comfort that would only diminish you.
In The Iliad, Juno and Jove settle their dispute by agreeing to give and take, each yielding on some points. Lasting partnerships rest on taking turns to give way.
In The Iliad, Pandarus is talked into breaking a sworn truce by promises of glory. Flattery that dangles honour for a bad act is a trap, and a sensible person learns to see through it.
In The Iliad, Nestor accepts that his body has slowed, and stays useful by offering the counsel that age is good for. Knowing which role suits your season of life is a mark of wisdom.
In The Iliad, Agamemnon takes back his harsh words to Ulysses once he sees real anger, and offers amends. A leader who makes a rash remark right keeps trusted people close.
In The Iliad, Diomed hushes a friend who boasts about their fathers' deeds and gets on with his own duty. Living up to your own work counts for more than trading on past glory.
In The Iliad, Pandarus blames his bow and the gods for failing him, yet he admits he chose to leave his chariots at home. Owning the choices you made is where improvement starts.
In The Iliad, Dione comforts her wounded daughter by reminding her that even the gods suffer hurts and simply bear them. Setbacks are part of every life, and making the best of them is a skill.
In The Iliad, Sarpedon shames Hector for boasting while his allies bear the brunt of the fight. Leaders who ask others to take risks should be seen taking their share too.

In The Iliad, Glaucus compares the generations of people to the leaves of a forest, with new ones coming as the old fall. It is a steadying thought for anyone who feels the weight of their own short season.

In The Iliad, Diomed and Glaucus discover an old family friendship in the middle of battle and agree to spare each other. Finding a shared bond with someone you were ready to fight can change the whole encounter.

In The Iliad, Hector knows his duty keeps him at the front even though he dreads what will become of his family. Sometimes doing what is right means leaving the people you love most, and still feeling the weight of it.

In The Iliad, Hector offers a challenge with fair terms: whoever wins will return the other's body with honour. Setting the terms of a contest in the open, so both sides know what is at stake, keeps a fight honest.

In The Iliad, Agamemnon urges his hot-headed brother to be patient in spite of his passion and weigh a risk before taking it on. Pausing to think a dangerous step through is not the same as backing down.

In The Iliad, Nestor shames the leaders into action by recalling how, as the youngest man, he stepped up when none of the others would. One willing person can lift a hesitant group, and courage can spread.
In The Iliad, Homer shows Hector and Ajax ending their duel by trading gifts and respect. Rivals can fight hard and still part with honour.
In The Iliad, Homer shows Antenor urging an end to a costly war by giving up what caused it, while Paris's pride refuses. Pride often overrules good counsel.
In The Iliad, Homer shows both armies mourning their dead in the same silent, grieving way. Shared loss reminds enemies how alike they are.
In The Iliad, Homer shows Jove threatening the gods with his power, then smiling and saying he was not really in earnest. Even the most powerful can choose kindness.
In The Iliad, Homer shows Diomed stepping alone into danger to shield old Nestor when others have fled. Real courage often means standing up for someone who cannot defend themselves.

In The Iliad, Homer shows Agamemnon rallying a losing army by owning his part in the trouble and shaming them with their own boasts. Honest words that call people back to their promises can steady a failing side.
In The Iliad, Homer shows Teucer shooting from behind Ajax's shield, each protecting the other so both can do their work. Good partnership is one person covering another.
In The Iliad, Homer shows Ajax standing over his fallen brother Teucer with his shield and carrying him to safety. Loyalty means staying with the person who has been hurt.
In The Iliad, Homer shows Minerva nursing a grudge over favours she felt were forgotten. Resentment can cloud even a wise person's judgement.
In The Iliad, Homer shows Agamemnon, in despair, proposing the whole army simply sail home. A leader's fear can spread quickly through everyone who follows.
In The Iliad, Homer shows Diomed telling Agamemnon that rank is not the same as courage. A title gives authority, but the nerve to lead has to be shown.
In The Iliad, Homer has Nestor tell Agamemnon that a king must listen as well as speak, and that his pride caused the quarrel. A leader who will not hear wise counsel harms everyone under him.
In The Iliad, Homer shows Agamemnon admitting plainly that he was wrong, then offering amends. Owning a mistake openly is the first step to repairing it.
In The Iliad, Homer shows Achilles, a great warrior, cooking and serving his guests himself. Real hospitality is a personal act, not just a gesture from a host.
In The Iliad, Homer has Peleus advise his son Achilles to check his temper, because goodwill is worth more than winning every quarrel. Restraint earns more respect than anger.

In The Iliad, Homer shows Achilles bitter that the brave and the idle are treated alike and that his hard work has earned him nothing. Feeling unrecognised can harden a person against the very people who need them.
In The Iliad, Achilles says his life cannot be bought back once lost, so no wealth can truly repay what has been taken. Some losses can't be settled with gifts.
In The Iliad, Achilles weighs a long, quiet life against a short, famous one and sees clearly what he values most. Knowing your own values makes hard choices simpler.
In The Iliad, Phoenix tells Achilles that a proud anger should be beaten, and that a humble, timely apology can still heal what was harmed.
In The Iliad, Phoenix observes that even a wise person can be carried away by anger, and that anger nursed in private can ruin them. Wisdom has to guard against its own temper.
In The Iliad, Ajax points out that even a killer can make amends and be restored among his people. Forgiveness is always open to someone who chooses it.
In The Iliad, Diomed advises against flattering a proud man, since giving in to his pride only makes it grow. Kindness that feeds someone's ego is not the same as help.
In The Iliad, Homer shows Agamemnon, facing ruin, humbly asking for shrewd counsel and sending others to help. Good leaders know when to call in people they trust.
In The Iliad, Agamemnon defends his brother as someone who waits for a lead rather than being lazy. Good leaders look for the reason behind what seems like slackness before they judge.
In The Iliad, Diomed says two people together see more than one alone, because one may notice what the other misses. A team is usually sharper than a lone hero.
In The Iliad, Agamemnon tells Diomed to pick the best man for the job, not the one with the highest rank. Choosing people on merit is sound leadership.

In The Iliad, Dolon accepts a dangerous mission for the promise of a prize, and admits the flattering promises led him from his better judgement. Be wary of rewards that pull you away from your own good sense.
In The Iliad, Diomed lingers over the chance of more spoils until a warning tells him to leave. Knowing when to stop is a discipline of its own.
In The Iliad, Homer notes that Antimachus was bribed to block peace, so one private gift corrupted the counsel of a whole city. Watch who is quietly paying for the advice you hear.
