“Sons of Atreus,” he cried, “and all other Achaeans, may the gods
      who dwell in Olympus grant you to sack the city of Priam, and to
      reach your homes in safety; but free my daughter, and accept a
      ransom for her, in reverence to Apollo, son of Jove.”

On this the rest of the Achaeans with one voice were for
      respecting the priest and taking the ransom that he offered; but
      not so Agamemnon, who spoke fiercely to him and sent him roughly
      away. “Old man,” said he, “let me not find you tarrying about our
      ships, nor yet coming hereafter. Your sceptre of the god and your
      wreath shall profit you nothing. I will not free her. She shall
      grow old in my house at Argos far from her own home, busying
      herself with her loom and visiting my couch; so go, and do not
      provoke me or it shall be the worse for you.”

The old man feared him and obeyed. Not a word he spoke, but went
      by the shore of the sounding sea and prayed apart to King Apollo
      whom lovely Leto had borne. “Hear me,” he cried, “O god of the
      silver bow, that protectest Chryse and holy Cilla and rulest
      Tenedos with thy might, hear me oh thou of Sminthe. If I have
      ever decked your temple with garlands, or burned your thigh-bones
      in fat of bulls or goats, grant my prayer, and let your arrows
      avenge these my tears upon the Danaans.”

books.title: The Wind in the Willows
books.author: Kenneth Grahame
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Author died 1932. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Kenneth Grahame has Mole discover that the best part of a holiday is watching everyone else busy at work, a reminder to be glad of other people's effort even on your own time off.

In The Wind in the Willows, Grahame shows the Water Rat finding real joy in simply messing about in boats, with no fixed destination. It is a gentle reminder not to measure every hour by what it produces.

In The Wind in the Willows, Grahame has the Rat describe Toad, who drops each new craze as soon as it stops being fresh. Enthusiasm that never settles leaves a person with plenty of starts and little to show.
When Mole begs to row, the Water Rat tells him to wait for a few lessons because it is not as easy as it looks. Grahame makes a quiet case for learning the craft before you take the oars.

After Mole upends the boat through his own pride, he apologises plainly without excuses. The Rat forgives him at once and offers to teach him, a good model for repair: an honest apology and a generous second chance.

In The Wind in the Willows, Toad paints the trip so brightly that the plan is settled before anyone has really agreed. Grahame is a useful warning about a glowing pitch that runs ahead of good judgement.
Grahame's Rat admits he thinks about his river all the time, yet stays by Toad because a friend needs him. Keeping faith with someone, even at a cost to yourself, is its own quiet kind of courage.

When the cart is wrecked, the Water Rat does not panic. He lays out the next practical steps one at a time: report it, get it mended, and rest until everyone's nerves settle. That is a steady way to handle a setback.

On a bare winter afternoon, Grahame has Mole find the stripped country honest and strong, the bones of things showing plainly. Sometimes the plain, unpainted view of a situation is the most useful one.
Entering the Wild Wood alone, Mole's fear grows as he imagines a face in every hole, until ordinary shadows seem hostile. Grahame shows how imagined threats can grow faster than the real ones.

In The Wind in the Willows, the Rat tells Mole that unfamiliar ground is best entered with local knowledge and in company. Grahame suggests that going into new territory alone, without learning its ways, is how trouble finds you.

Grahame has Rat reason from a clean cut to a door-scraper, then a door-mat, and then the hidden door, following each clue rather than guessing. Careful, step-by-step reasoning from the evidence finds what a quick dismissal would miss.

After a cold, frightening night, Grahame's Badger takes in his wet guests, feeds them and never once says I told you so. Generous hospitality without judgement is a kind of welcome many people still remember.

In The Wind in the Willows, the Otter finds a frightened rabbit who could have helped but only asks, what, us? Grahame shows that many willing hands achieve nothing until somebody steps up and asks them to act.
The Badger tells Mole that a great city once stood where the Wild Wood now grows, and that ruin and regrowth come slowly. Grahame's point is that patience and endurance outlast even grand plans.

Walking home, Mole sees that he is an animal of the tilled field and hedgerow, not of rough nature. Grahame has him choose the pleasant places where his life is laid out, which is a good lesson in knowing your own nature.
Even while pulled toward his old home, Mole keeps faith with the Rat and does not abandon him. Grahame shows loyalty holding firm under a strong temptation to leave.
Seeing that his silent friend is worn out, the Rat stops, sits him down and asks kindly, tell me your trouble. Grahame suggests that noticing someone's quiet distress is often where real help begins.

Hearing Mole's grief, the Rat owns that he has been unkind and calls himself a plain pig, then turns straight to making things right. Grahame shows that a fair admission of fault works best when it leads to action.

Meeting Mole's low mood with brisk praise, a blazing fire and a job to do, the Rat lifts his friend out of the blues. Grahame shows that practical encouragement can turn a dismal room into a cheerful one.

Mole shows off the things he has bought by careful saving and going without, and takes real pleasure in them. Grahame suggests that a home or a business built slowly, with care, is worth more to its owner.

With no supper in the house, the Rat puts everyone to work, sends a field-mouse for supplies and makes sure each guest is fed while Mole has nothing to worry about. Grahame shows a good host taking the load so the others can enjoy the evening.

Mole sees that his small home is a real anchor, a place of his own that welcomes him back without rancour, even though the wider world still calls. Grahame suggests a secure base is what makes adventure possible.

Toad admits he would have said anything while the Badger was lecturing him, and that a promise made only to end the sermon is not a real change of heart. Grahame shows that lasting commitment has to come from the person making it.

Toad feigns a serious illness, and the Rat, moved by kindness, nearly falls for it. Grahame reminds us that generosity is still good, but a kind heart should keep noticing when its goodwill is being used.

After escaping his friends, Toad is so pleased with his own cleverness that he cannot see his folly. Grahame shows how unchecked conceit can lead a clever person into the very mistakes they think they have outgrown.

Toad tells himself that just looking at the motor-car cannot do any harm, and then the old passion takes him over completely. Grahame shows how a small first step, taken with a reassuring excuse, can carry a person straight back into an old habit.

Otter keeps watch by the old ford every night, on the chance that his lost young son might come back. Grahame honours a patient, steady hope that keeps showing up, and the Mole refuses to sit idle while a friend is in trouble.

Kenneth Grahame shows in The Wind in the Willows that real help is often given quietly. The Mole and Rat are granted the gift of forgetting the vision they saw, so they can return to ordinary life without it weighing on them.

Kenneth Grahame shows Toad's despair lifting not through a grand rescue but through small comforts. The smell of a warm meal and memories of home turn his mind back to hope, friends and what he can still do.

Kenneth Grahame has Toad admit he was wrong and thank the girl who was trying to help him. Owning a mistake plainly, and taking good advice from someone who has your interests at heart, is what lets help work.

In The Wind in the Willows, the engine-driver says plainly that Toad has behaved wickedly, yet will not abandon him in his distress. Grahame shows that you can judge what someone has done and still help them when they are in trouble.

In The Wind in the Willows, the field-mice rush to prepare for winter so hard they cannot enjoy the fine day they are in. Grahame gently shows how fretting over what is coming can crowd out the present.

In The Wind in the Willows, a swallow who tries to stay behind when the season turns finds the long cold nights unbearable. Grahame suggests that fighting a natural change only makes its cost harder to bear.

In The Wind in the Willows, the Water Rat's contented world suddenly feels small once he imagines what lies beyond the hills. Grahame shows how a settled life can start to feel narrow, and that this restlessness is worth looking at honestly.

Grahame shows how a gifted talker can hold a listener spellbound and make his own settled life feel dull by comparison. It is a useful reminder to ask whether a bright story describes something real before you let it change your plans.

In The Wind in the Willows, Mole does not argue with his shaken friend. He turns to the warm, ordinary pleasures of the season, then gently offers Rat a pencil and some paper. Grahame shows that patient, practical kindness can do more than reasoning with someone in a low mood.

Kenneth Grahame shows Toad boasting about skills he does not have, and being found out within the half hour. Talking yourself up is risky when the work will show the truth, so it is wiser to let your results speak for themselves.

Kenneth Grahame shows Toad selling his horse while hungry, frightened and short of money, so a small sum looks like a fortune. Desperation distorts judgement, so it is worth pausing before a big decision made under pressure.

In The Wind in the Willows, Toad's run of lucky escapes makes him so proud that he starts showing off and is caught again. Grahame shows how a streak of good fortune can breed carelessness, and how overconfidence undoes many a clever plan.

In The Wind in the Willows, the Water Rat tells Toad plainly that his boasting has been foolish, while making clear he does not want to hurt him. Grahame shows that a true friend says the uncomfortable thing straight and with care.

In The Wind in the Willows, Mole and Badger stay loyal to Toad through thick and thin, guarding his home for his return even when he has been a trial to them. Grahame shows that loyalty is judged by steady action done quietly, over time.

In The Wind in the Willows, the Water Rat warns that friends who have quietly worked for us are easy to take for granted until they are gone. Grahame's point is to value the loyal people in our lives while we still have them.

In The Wind in the Willows, the Badger holds back a secret passage until Toad is truly in trouble, because Toad cannot keep a secret. Grahame shows that wise friends match what they share to how much someone can be trusted with it.

In The Wind in the Willows, Toad is eaten up with jealousy when the Badger praises Mole's cleverness. Grahame shows how envy of a friend's small win makes a person sour, when a generous word of admiration would have served them better.

In The Wind in the Willows, Mole sees his defeated foes properly cared for and lets them go with a roll instead of a beating. Grahame shows that someone you can trust to finish a job well, and to show mercy once the fight is won, is worth more than any show of strength.

Once things settle, Toad makes amends to everyone who helped him, from the gaoler's daughter to the engine-driver, and pays back the barge-woman for her horse. Grahame shows that gratitude is best proven by sincere thanks and honest repayment, not by fine words alone.

preview.text:
“This is fine!” he said to himself. “This is better than whitewashing!”
The sunshine struck hot on his fur, soft breezes caressed his heated
brow, and after the seclusion of the cellarage he had lived in so long
the carol of happy birds fell on his dulled hearing almost like a
shout. Jumping off all his four legs at once, in the joy of living and
the delight of spring without its cleaning, he pursued his way across
the meadow till he reached the hedge on the further side.

“Hold up!” said an elderly rabbit at the gap. “Sixpence for the
privilege of passing by the private road!” He was bowled over in an
instant by the impatient and contemptuous Mole, who trotted along the
side of the hedge chaffing the other rabbits as they peeped hurriedly
from their holes to see what the row was about. “Onion-sauce!
Onion-sauce!” he remarked jeeringly, and was gone before they could
think of a thoroughly satisfactory reply. Then they all started
grumbling at each other. “How _stupid_ you are! Why didn’t you tell
him——” “Well, why didn’t _you_ say——” “You might have reminded him——”
and so on, in the usual way; but, of course, it was then much too late,
as is always the case.

It all seemed too good to be true. Hither and thither through the
meadows he rambled busily, along the hedgerows, across the copses,
finding everywhere birds building, flowers budding, leaves
thrusting—everything happy, and progressive, and occupied. And instead
of having an uneasy conscience pricking him and whispering “whitewash!”
he somehow could only feel how jolly it was to be the only idle dog
among all these busy citizens. After all, the best part of a holiday is
perhaps not so much to be resting yourself, as to see all the other
fellows busy working.

books.title: The Consolation of Philosophy
books.author: Boethius
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died about 525, translator died 1931. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Boethius, through Philosophy, warns that soothing words which only feed a sad mood are sweet poison, and that a troubled mind needs real remedies, not more indulgence.
In The Consolation of Philosophy, Boethius shows that when someone is overwhelmed, the time calls for healing rather than more lamenting.

In The Consolation of Philosophy, Philosophy reminds Boethius that wise people have always been attacked, and that a crowd can only grab at outward possessions while the wise stay safe on higher ground.
Boethius, in his Song on virtue, holds that a calm and steady person cannot be subdued by fate, while anyone who lets hope or fear rule them forges their own chains.
Boethius explains that he took his duties in public life from his study of philosophy and acted for the common good, even when this cost him the goodwill of the powerful.
Boethius holds that a good conscience gives its own quiet reward, and that seeking public praise for good deeds takes some of that reward away.
Boethius notes that people judge outcomes rather than merit, so a person who falls on hard times often loses their reputation first, even when they did nothing wrong.
Philosophy tells Boethius that no one can truly be banished from a life of reason, and that anyone who stops wanting to live by reason has effectively exiled themselves.
Boethius sings that everything has its appointed time, so planting or harvesting out of season leaves a person short, and the wise wait for the right moment.
Philosophy asks Boethius to remember that he is a reasoning, mortal being, and notes that grief can shake a person without uprooting them from their own nature.
Boethius holds that a person who forgets their own nature and purpose will feel bewildered and see wicked people as happy, and that recovery starts by remembering who we are.
Philosophy argues that wealth and status were never truly ours to keep, so losing them cannot take away anything of real worth.
Philosophy says that if you chose to trust changeable fortune, you cannot demand it stay still, just as a sailor who hands over the sails goes where the wind takes them.
In Boethius, Lady Fortune argues that wealth and status were only ever lent, so we should be grateful for their use rather than resent their loss.
Boethius's Fortune says that anyone who rises should accept the fall that comes with the rise, because life runs on a turning wheel that no one can keep still.
Boethius observes that a greedy heart is never satisfied, since each new gift only feeds a deeper craving for more.
Philosophy urges Boethius to count the blessings he has had, because someone who dwells only on what is lost overlooks what still remains.
Philosophy points out that nobody's lot is perfectly satisfying, and that something is only wretched if we think it so, so any lot borne with equanimity can feel good.
In The Consolation of Philosophy, Philosophy says true happiness lies within, in mastery of oneself, because what chance can take away cannot be the highest good.
Philosophy argues that wealth is only really ours while we give it away, because what passes to someone else is no longer ours to keep.
Philosophy warns that people who gather many possessions end up needing more to protect them, while those who measure abundance by real need are the ones who lack least.
Boethius argues that honour comes to a position from virtue, not the other way round, so a title alone never makes a person worthy of respect.
Philosophy calls the love of glory a last weakness, and reminds Boethius that the whole inhabited earth is tiny against the heavens, so reputation has little room to spread.
Boethius says that people who chase popular applause abandon conscience and virtue, and that real worth is measured by inner integrity rather than the praise of others.
Philosophy argues that hard times can serve us well, because misfortune shows who our true friends are, and loyal friends are a richer gain than the wealth that was lost.

Philosophy observes that everyone is really seeking the same thing, happiness, but many chase false versions of it such as wealth, status or pleasure, and the error lies in the path rather than the goal.
Philosophy shows that wealth brings its own need for protection and creates new wants, so it cannot make a person free from want, only soothe it for a while.
Philosophy argues that power does not guarantee safety, since rulers live in fear, and that friends won by fortune rather than virtue will turn away once fortune changes.
Song V of The Consolation of Philosophy says whoever wants power must first master their own spirit, since a ruler who cannot drive out haunting fear is powerless however wide their reach.
Boethius says that noble birth is only the fame of one's ancestors, so its real value is the duty not to fall below their virtue.
Philosophy sums up that wealth, office, power, glory and pleasure each carry hidden costs, and none of them can make a person fully happy on its own.
Philosophy warns that chasing one part of the good alone, such as money to escape want, often loses the whole, because you give up the other goods that would have made the prize worth having.
Philosophy points out that we rarely want a thing for its own sake: we ride a horse for the health it brings. So it pays to ask what a thing is really for before chasing it.
Boethius notes that plants thrive in the soil that suits them and wither when moved elsewhere, so every thing does best where its nature fits its surroundings.
In Boethius's retelling of Orpheus, the hero loses his prize by looking back just as he nears the light, a reminder to keep your eyes on the way ahead.
Philosophy says every action needs both will and power, and that a person's real strength is what they can actually bring about, not what they merely wish for.
Philosophy argues that someone working through their natural strengths will outdo someone forcing an unnatural route, like walking on hands, so good results come from the way that suits you.
Boethius's song on passion says that a powerful ruler who cannot master his own appetites is in fact bound by hidden chains, so real power starts with self-control.
Philosophy argues that doing right carries its own reward, because goodness cannot be separated from the good person, whereas a prize handed out by someone else can be taken away.
In Boethius's tale of Circe's cup, wrongdoing changes the inner person far more than the outward one, so the deepest damage from vice is to the soul.
Philosophy holds that we raise or lower ourselves by our own choices, so good character needs no outside judge to reward it and bad character carries its own consequences.
Philosophy compares wrongdoers to the sick, who deserve treatment rather than hatred, and suggests that the wise have no room for hatred at all.
Boethius's song on wonder says that weak minds magnify whatever is rare or strange, while a mind freed from ignorance meets unexpected change with calm understanding.
Philosophy suggests that adversity tests the true self and builds patience, and that a hard lot is often matched to the strength of the person who must bear it.

Philosophy says a wise person should not take hard times badly, just as a soldier does not resent the trumpet call, because adversity is the chance to show courage and perfect wisdom, and it is best to hold the middle way.
Following Aristotle, Philosophy describes chance as an unplanned result of separate causes meeting, like finding gold while digging a field, so surprises usually have traceable causes behind them.
Philosophy holds that free choice comes with reason, and that people who give in to vice become captive to their own habits, so good choices are what keep us free.
Boethius points out that seeing something in advance does not cause it to happen, a useful distinction for anyone who forecasts the future and mistakes a prediction for a decision.
Boethius explains that we understand things through the faculty of the knower, so the same roundness is grasped by sight as a whole and by touch piece by piece, and our viewpoint shapes what we see.
Boethius's song on the upward look notes that a bent head dulls the soul, and asks us to lift our minds as well as our eyes, so that our thoughts do not stay stuck in the dirt.
Boethius closes his argument by urging us to resist vice, practise virtue, and lift our hopes to what is right, since our choices are made in full view of a judge who sees all.

preview.text:
While I was thus mutely pondering within myself, and recording my
sorrowful complainings with my pen, it seemed to me that there appeared
above my head a woman of a countenance exceeding venerable. Her eyes
were bright as fire, and of a more than human keenness; her complexion
was lively, her vigour showed no trace of enfeeblement; and yet her
years were right full, and she plainly seemed not of our age and time.
Her stature was difficult to judge. At one moment it exceeded not the
common height, at another her forehead seemed to strike the sky; and
whenever she raised her head higher, she began to pierce within the very
heavens, and to baffle the eyes of them that looked upon her. Her
garments were of an imperishable fabric, wrought with the finest threads
and of the most delicate workmanship; and these, as her own lips
afterwards assured me, she had herself woven with her own hands. The
beauty of this vesture had been somewhat tarnished by age and neglect,
and wore that dingy look which marble contracts from exposure. On the
lower-most edge was inwoven the Greek letter [Greek: P], on the topmost
the letter [Greek: Th],[A] and between the two were to be seen steps,
like a staircase, from the lower to the upper letter. This robe,
moreover, had been torn by the hands of violent persons, who had each
snatched away what he could clutch.[B] Her right hand held a note-book;
in her left she bore a staff. And when she saw the Muses of Poesie
standing by my bedside, dictating the words of my lamentations, she was
moved awhile to wrath, and her eyes flashed sternly. 'Who,' said she,
'has allowed yon play-acting wantons to approach this sick man--these
who, so far from giving medicine to heal his malady, even feed it with
sweet poison? These it is who kill the rich crop of reason with the
barren thorns of passion, who accustom men's minds to disease, instead
of setting them free. Now, were it some common man whom your allurements
were seducing, as is usually your way, I should be less indignant. On
such a one I should not have spent my pains for naught. But this is one
nurtured in the Eleatic and Academic philosophies. Nay, get ye gone, ye
sirens, whose sweetness lasteth not; leave him for my muses to tend and
heal!' At these words of upbraiding, the whole band, in deepened
sadness, with downcast eyes, and blushes that confessed their shame,
dolefully left the chamber.

books.title: War and Peace
books.author: Leo Tolstoy
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1910, translators died 1938 and 1939. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Leo Tolstoy shows Anna Pavlovna becoming enthusiastic so she does not disappoint people who expect it of her, and how a social role can outlive the feeling behind it.
Leo Tolstoy shows guests performing a polite greeting to an aunt none of them know or care about, then leaving relieved. It is a reminder to notice which rituals we keep up only out of habit.
Leo Tolstoy shows a lively, full-of-life person lifting a whole room, so dull and dispirited guests leave feeling more alive too. Energy spreads, and so does gloom.
Leo Tolstoy likens Anna Pavlovna to a mill foreman who keeps the machines running, nudging quiet groups and loud ones until the talk keeps moving. A good host keeps a room in steady motion.
Leo Tolstoy describes Prince Hippolyte speaking with such confidence that listeners cannot tell whether he is clever or foolish. Confidence alone is not the same as substance.
Leo Tolstoy notes that influence is a capital to be spent carefully. A man who grants every plea soon has none left for himself, so goodwill needs the same thought as any other resource.
Leo Tolstoy shows Pierre, awkward and blunt, still won over a room because his kind, modest face says more than his manners. Warmth often counts for more than polish.
In War and Peace, Pierre spends months drifting without choosing a career, and his friend Andrew tells him he must decide. Waiting to feel certain can quietly become a choice of its own.
Tolstoy observes that even in close friendships, praise and encouragement are needed to keep things running smoothly, the way grease keeps wheels turning.
Leo Tolstoy shows Pierre talking himself out of a promise he has just made, calling such words of honour meaningless. Notice when you are explaining away a commitment you made.
In the window scene, Tolstoy shows a crowd egging on a drunk young man until he wants to outdo the stunt. Be wary of applause that pushes you towards a risk you would never take sober.

Leo Tolstoy shows Count Rostov greeting every guest with the same warmth, whatever their rank, and fussing over the small details that make a gathering work. Treating everyone equally is a good way to run a house or a business.

Leo Tolstoy contrasts Boris, who settles into a room and tells a story quietly and with humour, with the flustered Nicholas, who blushes and cannot find his words. Calm composure is what people remember.
Leo Tolstoy shows Vera saying things that are true and proper, yet leaving the room awkward because of her cold manner. How you say a true thing can matter as much as the thing itself.

Leo Tolstoy has Anna Mikhaylovna win favours by calling on important people again and again until she gets what she wants, and not minding what they think. Persistence with a thick skin opens doors that a polite once-off request will not.
Leo Tolstoy shows Boris answering a curt, dismissive great man quietly and respectfully, giving nothing away. Keeping your composure under rudeness says a lot about you.
Leo Tolstoy shows Boris clearing up a misunderstanding head on, calmly and quickly, so both men can move on. Saying plainly what you suspect, rather than letting it sit, can save a relationship.
Leo Tolstoy describes Marya Dmitrievna, a woman known for common sense and blunt speech. People laughed at her, yet all respected her. Plain, sensible honesty tends to earn respect over time.

Tolstoy shows Berg talking only about his own prospects, yet doing it so cheerfully and sincerely that he disarms his listeners. Openness about your ambitions can win people over where hidden ones would not.

Leo Tolstoy has Marya Dmitrievna, with four sons at war, answer her own worry with plain calm: she cannot control the outcome, so she does not fret. Accepting what you cannot control frees your energy for what you can.
In the dance scene, Leo Tolstoy notes that Marya Dmitrievna impresses the room with the smallest movements, while the count's showy leaps draw the eye. Restraint can carry more weight than display.

In this scene Tolstoy has Prince Vasili insist he only wants to help, while pressing hard for a document that serves his own interest. When someone says they only have your interests at heart, look closely at what they are asking you to do.
Leo Tolstoy shows an old grudge hardening into hatred, so that one person becomes the explanation for everything that has gone wrong. Old resentment can warp how we read people and what they did.
Leo Tolstoy shows a dying man giving a wry smile at his own helplessness, which moves his son to tears. Gentleness with your own weakness can reach people more deeply than strength does.

Leo Tolstoy has old Prince Bolkonsky hold that idleness and superstition are the two sources of vice, and activity and intelligence the two chief virtues. He keeps his days fixed and busy to match that belief.
Tolstoy shows a frightened pupil unable to take in a lesson at all, because fear fills her mind. Fear, more than difficulty, is often what stops learning.

Leo Tolstoy shows Princess Mary never seeing the warm, luminous look her eyes have when she is not thinking of herself, because she tightens up the moment she looks in a glass. We often hide our best selves by watching ourselves too closely.
In a letter, Princess Mary says a good heart is the quality she values most in people, and worries that riches bring their own temptations. Character matters more than what someone owns.
In War and Peace, Tolstoy shows Princess Mary accepting marriage as a duty to be carried out faithfully, without dwelling on her own feelings about it.
In War and Peace, Prince Andrew sees his father's foibles clearly yet still loves and honours him. Tolstoy shows that you can respect people fully and still see their weak spots.

In War and Peace, Princess Mary recalls Sterne's observation that we often love people more for the good we have done them than for the good they have done us. It is a useful thing to notice in your own team and customers.

In War and Peace, Prince Andrew says he will not blame his wife and can see no fault in how he treats her, even while admitting the marriage is unhappy. Tolstoy shows integrity that refuses to pass blame on.

In War and Peace, a regiment spends a whole night polishing for an inspection because nobody checks an unclear order. Tolstoy shows how a vague instruction that is guessed at, not clarified, wastes effort and sleep.
In War and Peace, the officer Dolokhov, reduced to the ranks, does not sulk. He asks for a real chance to make up for his fault, which is the attitude that earns trust back.

In War and Peace, Kutuzov turns down a plan with polished courtesy and gives the other general no grounds to argue. Tolstoy shows that a calm, courteous manner can close a debate that would otherwise go on for ever.
In War and Peace, Prince Andrew loses his old languor once he has serious work he cares about. Tolstoy shows that purposeful work changes a person's bearing more than any polish does.

In War and Peace, Prince Andrew says a good officer shares in the cause, grieving its setbacks and rejoicing in its wins, rather than treating it as a joke. Tolstoy shows that people who care about the shared mission act differently from those who only care about themselves.

In War and Peace, Rostov confronts a fellow officer who has stolen money privately, not in front of others, and once the truth is out he feels pity rather than triumph. Tolstoy shows that a hard truth is best raised quietly, with the dignity of the person still in mind.

In War and Peace, an older officer tells a proud young man that personal pride can hurt the whole group. Tolstoy shows that people who will stay with a team long term tend to value its honour above their own offence.

In War and Peace, Tolstoy notes that facing an unknown challenge brings both fear and a pull to find out what lies beyond. The point of the line is that you cross it, with the people beside you, rather than hang back forever.

In War and Peace, young Rostov is so absorbed in his grudge against the colonel that he stands idle on the bridge while the real danger unfolds. Tolstoy shows how personal feuds can blind a person to what the moment actually requires.

In War and Peace, Prince Andrew stops his carriage to give money to a convoy of wounded soldiers and encourages them, though no one asked. Tolstoy shows that small, unprompted kindness often means more than the grand gesture.

In War and Peace, the diplomat Bilibin is valued not for avoiding mistakes but because he likes the work and does it well, even at night. Tolstoy describes him as caring more about how a thing is done than about what it is for.

In War and Peace, Bilibin tells Prince Andrew that a real victory can still land badly, because the listeners judge news by what it means for them. Tolstoy shows that a good report starts with the audience's needs, not with your own achievement.

In War and Peace, a sergeant who warns his commander that the enemy is at hand is arrested for speaking out of turn. Tolstoy shows how a team that punishes the person bringing bad news ends up losing the warnings it most needs.

In War and Peace, Prince Andrew speaks up for a frightened woman against a bullying officer, even though it risks ridicule and he is uneasy about it. Tolstoy shows courage as standing up for someone weaker, whatever it costs your pride.

In War and Peace, Kutuzov sets out each of his bad options in full, from holding still to retreating, before choosing the least damaging one. Tolstoy shows that laying out every path and its cost makes a hard decision clearer, even when none is good.

In War and Peace, the polished staff officer scolds a rumpled, kindly artillery officer, yet Prince Andrew finds the scruffy man the more attractive of the two. Tolstoy suggests that warmth and real care count for more than polish and rank.

In War and Peace, Prince Andrew sketches the ground and works through the likely moves in plain if-then steps, such as if the enemy attacks here, then we hold there. Tolstoy shows that a short plan of the real possibilities is worth more than a long list of everything that could go wrong.

In War and Peace, a calm artillery officer says plainly that everyone fears the unknown, and the talk carries on as normal. Tolstoy shows that admitting fear without drama is a steady way to keep doing the job.

In War and Peace, Bagration's calm presence steadies anxious officers and men, even though much of what happens is down to chance. Tolstoy suggests that a leader's steadiness can matter as much as the orders they give.

In War and Peace, two commanders spend the crucial hour squabbling over rank and who is offended by whom, while their men go unprepared. Tolstoy shows how wounded pride can cost a team the very thing it is there to do.
In War and Peace, Tolstoy shows two proud officers each hunting for signs of cowardice in the other, so busy testing one another that they lose sight of the real danger.

In War and Peace, Tolstoy shows a general so afraid of being blamed that he gallops into the gunfire, a reminder that fear of blame can push people to protect their reputation rather than solve the problem.

In War and Peace, Tolstoy shows a small company that kept its order in the wood and struck with desperate resolve, turning a panic back into a fight. Steady people acting together can change how a whole day goes.

In War and Peace, Tolstoy shows the artillery officer Tushin so absorbed in doing his job well that fear never enters his mind, a reminder that deep focus on the task in front of you can steady the nerves.

In War and Peace, Prince Andrew refuses to let the thought of fear take hold, then stays under fire to help move the guns. Courage can be a choice you make again and again, not a feeling you wait for.

In War and Peace, Tolstoy shows officers praising a battle that some of them never saw, and a commander unable to tell what really happened. In the confusion of a hard day, the loudest account is often not the accurate one.
In War and Peace, Prince Andrew speaks up in front of the generals to give Tushin the credit he has earned. Honest praise for a quiet, capable person can matter more than rank.

In War and Peace, Tolstoy shows Prince Vasili working every useful connection without ever admitting to himself that he is scheming. A habit of looking out for yourself can quietly replace honest dealing.

Prince Vasíli always spoke languidly, like an actor repeating a stale
part. Anna Pávlovna Schérer on the contrary, despite her forty years,
overflowed with animation and impulsiveness. To be an enthusiast had
become her social vocation and, sometimes even when she did not
feel like it, she became enthusiastic in order not to disappoint the
expectations of those who knew her. The subdued smile which, though it
did not suit her faded features, always played round her lips expressed,
as in a spoiled child, a continual consciousness of her charming defect,
which she neither wished, nor could, nor considered it necessary, to

books.title: Japanese Fairy Tales
books.author: Yei Theodora Ozaki
books.subject: fairytales
books.licence_note: Author died 1932. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Japanese Fairy Tales, Ozaki shows that the Dragon King chose Hidesato because he was the only traveller who could look at a frightening creature without running. Calm courage is what makes a person worth asking for help.
In Japanese Fairy Tales, Hidesato keeps his nerve and makes his last arrow count. Steady nerve under pressure, and trying the one option left, is what wins.
In The Tongue-Cut Sparrow, the bird owns her mistake and asks forgiveness politely, but the old woman refuses. Quick anger and refusing to forgive turn a small wrong into a cruel harm.
In The Tongue-Cut Sparrow, the bird bears no grudge for her cruel treatment and feels sorry for the old man instead. Letting go of a grudge leaves a person free and at peace.

In The Tongue-Cut Sparrow, greed blinds the old woman to her own cruelty, and her own wickedness is what finally brings her undone. Her husband's kind words and her later change of heart show that people can still learn to do better.
In Urashima Taro, the fisher lad does not fight the boys who are tormenting the tortoise. He wins them over with a kind smile and a fair offer, and the animal is saved.

In Urashima Taro, the fisher lad meets a grand and unfamiliar world calmly and without shame, and so he is able to enjoy it fully. Meeting new things with an open, steady heart lets a person make the most of them.
In Urashima Taro, Urashima is so absorbed in the joy of the palace that he forgets home for days. Pleasure can quietly crowd out the things and people we meant to return to.

In Urashima Taro, sadness pushes Urashima to talk himself into breaking his promise, persuading himself it is the right thing to do. A tempting excuse can feel reasonable in a weak moment, so it pays to check it against the promise you made.

In The Farmer and the Badger, the old woman's good nature is turned against her by a cunning creature who promises not to run. Kindness is a good thing, but it helps to notice when a promise does not match what someone really intends.

In The Farmer and the Badger, the grieving farmer is steadied when a kind neighbour comes up the mountain to sit with him. Being there for someone in their distress is one of the simplest and most useful kindnesses.

In The South Pointing Carriage, Emperor Kotei does not give up after his army is fooled by fog, and he thinks hard until he invents a way through. A setback is often the thing that pushes a person toward a better tool.

In The South Pointing Carriage, Kotei is stuck on a river until he watches a spider ride a leaf across a pond and builds the first boat. Good ideas often come from paying close attention to ordinary things.
In The Adventures of Kintaro, the monkey asks for a rematch and then wins by pulling the hare's ear. Asking for a second chance is fair, but a win gained by trickery is not really a win.
In The Adventures of Kintaro, the Golden Boy uses his great strength to build a bridge so his friends can get home. Strength is worth most when it is used to help the people around you.

In The Adventures of Kintaro, Kintaro's mother hides her grief so her son can leave for a better life, and she does not discourage him as he sets out. Loving someone well sometimes means letting them go.
In The Story of Princess Hase, the dying mother asks her daughter to be kind to everyone beneath her in station. Kindness that does not depend on rank is a value worth carrying through life.
In The Story of Princess Hase, the girl meets her stepmother's unkindness with patience and good conduct and never gives trouble. Steady, patient goodness is a quiet kind of strength.
In The Story of Princess Hase, the stepmother's jealousy grows into a wish to harm the girl, and her own child is the one who dies. Unchecked envy can hurt the people we love most.
In The Man Who Did Not Wish to Die, the Chinese Emperor who has everything is still miserable because he cannot stop fearing death. Wealth and comfort alone do not bring peace of mind.
In The Man Who Did Not Wish to Die, the hermit's god doubts Sentaro has the patience and endurance a hard goal needs. Wanting a result is not the same as being willing to do the work it takes.

In The Man Who Did Not Wish to Die, Sentaro finds that a life with no end grows wearisome, and he longs to go home. Meaning comes from the people and purpose in our lives, not simply from having more time.
In The Man Who Did Not Wish to Die, the teaching is to stop chasing what no person can have and to live a good, industrious life. Selfish wishes, even when granted, do not bring happiness.

In The Bamboo-Cutter and the Moon-Child, the First Knight is too daunted by the long journey and buys a temple bowl instead. A shortcut dressed up as a quest may fool others, but it does not fool the person who took it.

In The Bamboo-Cutter and the Moon-Child, the Fourth Knight blames the Princess for his failed quest instead of looking at his own choices. Blaming someone else for our setbacks stops us learning anything from them.
In The Bamboo-Cutter and the Moon-Child, the Princess grieves most that she cannot repay the love and care she was given. Gratitude to the people who raised us is worth keeping alive.

In The Bamboo-Cutter and the Moon-Child, the Princess keeps the impatient messengers waiting so she can write a proper goodbye to the Emperor. Taking the time to say goodbye well is a kindness, even when others are in a hurry.
In The Mirror of Matsuyama, the wife is told that a mirror shows your own face and, in the old saying, the state of your heart. Looking honestly at yourself is worth treating with care.

In The Mirror of Matsuyama, the grieving girl looks into her mother's mirror each morning for strength and each evening for comfort, and grows into her mother's gentle ways. Keeping a loved one's good qualities close can steady us through grief.

In The Mirror of Matsuyama, the stepmother admits her jealousy caused her to misjudge the girl, and asks for forgiveness. Owning a mistake openly and choosing to change can repair what suspicion has damaged.

In The Goblin of Adachigahara, the pilgrim promises not to look into the back room, then gives in to curiosity and peeks. Breaking a small promise for a moment's curiosity can lead straight into trouble.

In The Sagacious Monkey and the Boar, the monkey, facing the butcher, seeks wise counsel rather than giving up, then acts on the plan. Asking for good advice when we are cornered is a sensible first step.

In The Happy Hunter and the Skillful Fisher, the Happy Hunter takes the blame and offers hundreds of replacement hooks, but his brother wants only the one that was lost. Sometimes an apology is only complete when we return what was actually lost.

In The Happy Hunter and the Skillful Fisher, the Sea King's daughters are wary of the stranger until he speaks with dignity and courtesy. The way we ask for help can open doors that suspicion had closed.

In The Happy Hunter, the hunter admits the mistake was his own clumsiness and asks the Sea King to forgive the fish who swallowed the hook. Owning your share of a mistake makes it easier for others to be shown mercy.
In The Happy Hunter, when he has the power to drown his brother, the Happy Hunter pulls the tide back and saves him. Restraint matters most when we hold the power to hurt someone.
In The Happy Hunter, the brother who tried to kill him is forgiven only once he promises to throw away his evil ways. Forgiveness holds best when it comes with a real change in behaviour.

In The Old Man Who Made Withered Trees to Flower, the greedy neighbour blames the dog for his own disappointment rather than his greed. It is easy to blame the messenger when a result we chased for the wrong reasons lets us down.

In The Old Man Who Made Withered Trees to Flower, the envious neighbour copies the old man's visible steps, assuming the method is simple. Copying what people do without the skill and care behind it rarely gives the same result.

In The Jelly Fish and the Monkey, the monkey hides his fear when he learns the danger and calms himself to think of a way out. Staying composed under threat gives a clever mind room to find a way through.

In The Quarrel of the Monkey and the Crab, the young crab's first rage gives way to second thoughts, and he sees he cannot win alone. Knowing when you need friends to help you is a sensible kind of strength.

In The Quarrel of the Monkey and the Crab, the monkey tells himself nothing can be done about his wrong, yet he cannot rest while he hides his guilt. Telling yourself a wrong is over does not make it stop weighing on you.
In The White Hare of Inaba, a spiteful man pretends kindness and sends the hare off with harmful advice. Advice that sounds kind is not always kind, so it is worth checking who is giving it and why.
In The White Hare of Inaba, the hare admits his deceit and promises never to use it again, and then is helped by a kind man anyway. Owning a wrong openly is the first step towards putting it right.

In The Story of Prince Yamato Take, the young prince sees that a head-on attack will fail in rough country and chooses a cunning plan instead. Knowing when the direct approach will not work is a part of wisdom, at any age.

In The Story of Prince Yamato Take, when a grass fire closes in, the prince does not freeze. He uses what is at hand and acts rather than waiting for the end, and that calm action is often the way out of a trap.
In The Story of Prince Yamato Take, the prince scoffs at the sea as if it were only a brook, and a storm soon humbles him. Mocking what we do not respect can be a dangerous mistake.

In The Story of Prince Yamato Take, the wife he had scorned gives her life to save him, and he understands her worth only afterwards. Taking loyal people for granted is a mistake that can cost the most.

In Momotaro, the old man says raising a child is simply what a parent does, and that there is no profit or loss between them. Care given freely, without keeping a tally, is one of the most generous ways to love someone.

In Momotaro, the young leader tells his quarrelling companions that harmony comes first, and that unity among themselves is worth more than any gain. A team that cannot get along will struggle against any outside challenge.

In The Ogre of Rashomon, Watanabe rides into a storm because he cannot bear to look afraid in front of his companions. Pride can push a person into danger for the wrong reason, so ask whether a challenge is about the truth or about appearances.

In The Ogre of Rashomon, Watanabe holds firm against his old nurse's emotional pleading to see the box, because he understands the risk. A sensible boundary is not unkind, even when someone you trust asks hard.
In How an Old Man Lost His Wen, the old man's love of dancing overcomes his fear, and his skill wins over a crowd of demons. Doing what you love well can open doors, even in a frightening moment.

In The Stones of Five Colors, two rival generals nearly fight over who should lead, and the Empress settles it by giving each a share of command. Rivalry between capable people can often be turned into shared responsibility rather than a fight.

In The Stones of Five Colors, the Fire King finds out the secret of the wizard's power and prepares against it, and he wins without needing brute force. Understanding what makes a rival strong is often more useful than matching them blow for blow.

preview.text:
“I have lived now for many years in this lake and I have a large family
of children and grand-children. For some time past we have lived in
terror, for a monster centipede has discovered our home, and night
after night it comes and carries off one of my family. I am powerless
to save them. If it goes on much longer like this, not only shall I
lose all my children, but I myself must fall a victim to the monster. I
am, therefore, very unhappy, and in my extremity I determined to ask
the help of a human being. For many days with this intention I have
waited on the bridge in the shape of the horrible serpent-dragon that
you saw, in the hope that some strong brave man would come along. But
all who came this way, as soon as they saw me were terrified and ran
away as fast as they could. You are the first man I have found able to
look at me without fear, so I knew at once that you were a man of great
courage. I beg you to have pity upon me. Will you not help me and kill
my enemy the centipede?”

books.title: Pragmatism
books.author: William James
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 1910. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: William James held that everyone has a philosophy, a half-spoken sense of what life honestly means, and that it quietly shapes how each person sees their world.
William James said philosophy does not bake bread, yet it can give people courage and light up the wider view of the world.
William James noticed that every philosopher's temperament quietly biases their conclusions, so honesty means naming that bias rather than hiding it behind neutral reasons.
William James observed that tender-minded and tough-minded people tend to look down on each other, each judging the other as lacking in some way.
William James warned that a good intellectual conscience cannot survive mixing incompatible beliefs, even though most of us like a bit of both sides.
William James argued that a philosophy so abstract it never touches concrete life is sterile, because it could fit almost any world and so tells us nothing about this one.
William James described abstract philosophy as a clean marble temple that can become an escape from messy real life rather than an honest account of it.
William James held that the actual world is wide open, while tidy systems must close themselves off, so a neat system can miss what is really happening.
William James argued that the thoughtful amateur, who asks philosophy for a way to live, is a fair judge of it, and any theory that leaves actual things blank will fail that test.
William James suggested that every theory is in part a place of escape from raw reality, and that abstract ideas can still give the mind a worthwhile home if they stay tied to facts.

William James's pragmatic method settles a dispute by asking what practical difference each side would make. If no difference can be traced, the argument is idle, and a serious dispute should always show one.
Charles Peirce held that the meaning of a thought is the practical conduct it could produce, so a vague idea becomes clear once you ask what it would actually do.
William James argued that any difference in abstract truth should show up as a difference in real life, and that philosophy is worth doing only if it shows what difference an idea makes to you.
William James warned that a grand word such as God, Reason or the Absolute can feel like the end of a search, but under the pragmatic test it should become a plan for work that changes things.
William James likened pragmatism to a corridor in a hotel. It has no dogmas of its own, only a method, and every kind of thinker must pass through it to get in or out of their room.
William James noted that scientific laws are a man-made shorthand for summarising facts and leading to new ones. They are useful tools rather than perfect copies of reality.

William James described how people change their minds. They keep as much of their old beliefs as they can, changing one thing at a time until a new idea fits the existing stock with the least disturbance.
William James noticed that when people meet surprising facts they usually either ignore them or attack the people who report them, because loyalty to older truths comes first for most of us.
William James argued that concreteness is a real virtue. A thinker who prefers a pale, pure outline to the rich thicket of everyday reality is often mistaking thinness for nobility.
William James held that a view which is noble but unfit for humble, everyday service should count against it, because real life is mostly sweat and dirt.

William James judged an idea of the Absolute by what it does for people, such as letting them take a moral holiday from anxiety and trust that the world is in good hands, and not by its abstract grandeur alone.
William James saw truth as one kind of good: a belief counts as true when it proves good to hold, for definite and traceable reasons, such as helping us live well.
William James observed that the greatest threat to any one of our beliefs is often our other beliefs, which clash with it and cost us something we value.
William James held that a good test of an idea is how well it fits every part of life, and that a method this open should count even the humblest and most personal experience.
William James praised Berkeley for testing an idea by its practical difference. Matter means the sensations it brings us, so if a notion makes no difference to experience, it adds nothing.
William James noted that Locke grounded personal identity in memory and conscious continuity, and that fairness depends on this, since no one should answer for what they cannot remember.

William James pointed out that many arguments between spirit and matter are really just taste, with one side calling matter gross and the other calling spirit pure, and that such preferences are not evidence.
William James argued that a philosophical debate with no traceable future consequences is idle, and that every genuine debate should involve some practical issue, however distant or uncertain.
William James held that the real objection to materialism is not that matter is crude, but that it offers no lasting guarantee for our highest hopes and ideals.
William James observed that many people deeply need to believe their ideals will not be finally lost, and he saw that this need can shape how a whole philosophy feels.
William James said an abstract word like design is a blank cartridge: it carries no consequences until you ask what sort of design and what sort of designer, and answer that from the facts.
William James held that the only possibility we can rationally claim is that things may become better, so a hopeful stance toward the future is a reasonable one.
William James argued that the vital question is what this world is going to become, and that philosophy should turn its attention from lofty first principles towards the facts and the future.
William James compared abstract ideas to air above water: not enough to live on alone, but able to redirect how we swim through experience, so something not sufficient for life can still shape it.

William James held that our minds aim at totality, which needs both the variety of things and their unity. Curiosity about particular details runs alongside the urge to systematise, and both are part of a good mind.
William James noticed that the vague feeling that everything is one can dazzle a thinker into losing interest in the details, whereas a more empirical mind keeps its curiosity about specific facts.

William James saw oneness and manyness as equally real and co-ordinate. Sometimes we need conductors that join things, sometimes non-conductors that separate them, and wisdom lies in knowing which the moment calls for.
William James pointed out that learning from the past depends on things coming in kinds. If every fact were unique, we could not reason from past experience to future experience at all.
William James observed that people start with vague goals such as being great or good, and that each step reveals new chances and closes others, so purposes must be reshaped as we go.
William James held that it is rash to call the world one story or one purpose dogmatically. Unity is a legitimate hypothesis, but it needs better evidence than we have before we treat it as settled.
William James treats the idea of one all-knowing Absolute as a hypothesis to test, not a truth to accept just because it sounds grand.
William James's test for any grand idea is what practical difference it would make to live by it. That keeps you grounded instead of carried away by excitement.
William James notices that a strong feeling can shield a weak argument from criticism, so it is worth checking the feeling behind a conclusion you are sure of.
William James suggests the unity of the world may grow over time through human effort, rather than being fixed from the start.
William James says pragmatism loosens rigid theories, so a belief held with fierce certainty can be tested again and softened by reasonable discussion.
William James's working question for any idea is how far experience verifies it, so a good pragmatist turns towards the facts rather than abstract certainty.
William James observes that our knowledge grows in spots, so new learning changes older beliefs gradually, as we line up old opinions with new ones.
William James says we tend to patch our beliefs rather than renew them, so new facts usually soak in and are tinged by what we already think.
William James argues that our most basic ways of thinking are very old and survive every later change of opinion, so it is worth examining them.
William James says all our concepts are tools for handling facts by thinking about them, and experience does not come labelled until we work out what it is.
James compares raw experience to Boston weather: chaotic until we place each event within a larger pattern, and that placing is what makes it understood.
James quotes Santayana saying that understanding the order of events makes each moment meaningful, so calm times fill with power and hard times with resources.
William James says kinds and sameness of kind are the instruments of logic, and without them our experience would have no order to find our way by.
James suggests our search for causes began with asking who or what is to blame for a problem, a habit worth noticing when we look for reasons behind trouble.
William James notes that everyday concepts work well for practical purposes but blur at the edges when we speculate, so it pays to know where they stop applying.
William James observes that ideas which look purely theoretical often pay off in practical results nobody could have foreseen at the start.
James warns that being established or fashionable is not proof of truth. Common sense is entrenched mainly because it came first.
James reports that scientists treat their theoretical entities as useful short-cuts, like logarithms, and advises not to be fooled into taking them literally.
James holds that different ways of thinking suit different parts of life, so judge them by their use rather than by a claim to absolute truth.
William James argues our theories are instruments for adapting to reality, not final revelations, which is why each can be useful for some purposes and none settles the matter for all.

preview.text:
I think with Mr. Chesterton in this matter. I know that you, ladies and
gentlemen, have a philosophy, each and all of you, and that the most
interesting and important thing about you is the way in which it
determines the perspective in your several worlds. You know the same
of me. And yet I confess to a certain tremor at the audacity of the
enterprise which I am about to begin. For the philosophy which is so
important in each of us is not a technical matter; it is our more or
less dumb sense of what life honestly and deeply means. It is only
partly got from books; it is our individual way of just seeing and
feeling the total push and pressure of the cosmos. I have no right to
assume that many of you are students of the cosmos in the class-room
sense, yet here I stand desirous of interesting you in a philosophy
which to no small extent has to be technically treated. I wish to fill
you with sympathy with a contemporaneous tendency in which I profoundly
believe, and yet I have to talk like a professor to you who are not
students. Whatever universe a professor believes in must at any rate be
a universe that lends itself to lengthy discourse. A universe definable
in two sentences is something for which the professorial intellect has
no use. No faith in anything of that cheap kind! I have heard friends
and colleagues try to popularize philosophy in this very hall, but they
soon grew dry, and then technical, and the results were only partially
encouraging. So my enterprise is a bold one. The founder of pragmatism
himself recently gave a course of lectures at the Lowell Institute with
that very word in its title-flashes of brilliant light relieved
against Cimmerian darkness! None of us, I fancy, understood ALL that he
said--yet here I stand, making a very similar venture.

books.title: Crime and Punishment
books.author: Fyodor Dostoyevsky
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1881, translator died 1946. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Dostoevsky is remembered for a wisdom of the heart, won through his own suffering, that readers say teaches them how to live.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov fears taking a new step more than anything, and talks so much about a bold idea that he never acts on it.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov finds that a small, overlooked detail can spoil a whole plan, so the trivial things need as much care as the big ones.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov asks himself what he would do if he is this frightened before a bold act, a fair test that Dostoevsky uses to show how fear grows as an idea gets closer.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov is horrified by his own dark thoughts and runs off to a tavern to escape them, a reminder that we often flee an uncomfortable thought rather than look at it.
In Crime and Punishment, Dostoevsky notes that some strangers draw us in from the first moment, before a word is spoken, and that we often read meaning into those first impressions.
In Crime and Punishment, the drunken clerk Marmeladov says every person needs at least one place where people feel for him, a simple truth about why belonging matters.
In Crime and Punishment, Sonia gives what she has to a family in need without a word and without looking at anyone, showing that the deepest kindness is often silent.

In Crime and Punishment, Marmeladov's family lifts him with trust after he finds work, and he says that treatment changes how he feels about himself, showing how much a man can rise when people expect good of him.
In Crime and Punishment, Marmeladov says being forgiven without blame can hurt more than blame, because it asks more of the one who was forgiven.

In Crime and Punishment, Marmeladov argues that mercy goes most readily to those who never thought they deserved it, a reminder that humility and a clear view of our own faults can open the door to kindness.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov decides that people are likely to be scoundrels, a bleak theory that sounds clever to him but hollows out how he treats everyone around him.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov pulls away from everyone like a tortoise in its shell, showing how isolation can feel comfortable while it quietly deepens a person's troubles.
In Crime and Punishment, Marfa Petrovna, who wronged Dounia, publicly clears her name and begs forgiveness, showing that owning a mistake openly is a real way to put it right.
In Crime and Punishment, a mother warns her son not to judge a man too hastily, since first impressions and prejudices are hard to correct once they set in.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov reads every kind word from his family as a trick, showing how resentment can make even love look like deception.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov judges a match by its tone rather than its numbers, noticing that how people treat each other early on tends to become the pattern later.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov notes that people with generous hearts often refuse to see the truth until it forces itself on them, turning a plain goose into a swan to avoid it.
In Crime and Punishment, Dostoevsky shows how someone who sacrifices for a loved one can talk themselves into calling it duty, and how a good cause can hide a bad bargain.
In Crime and Punishment, an idea that starts as a daydream slowly takes a menacing shape, a reminder to notice when a fantasy is quietly becoming a plan.

In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov steps in to protect a girl, then in an instant turns his back on her, showing how quickly feelings swing and how a good impulse can be dropped as fast as it was taken up.

In Crime and Punishment, Dostoevsky shows how a comforting phrase like "percentage" lets people stop feeling responsible for real harm to real people, so watch for the words that make a hard thing easy to ignore.
In Crime and Punishment, Razumihin keeps his good humour through poverty and setbacks, showing that steady warmth can be the most useful kind of friend.

In Crime and Punishment, a child's dream shows a crowd laughing as a helpless horse is beaten, and only the child sees clearly what is wrong, a lesson on how a group can make cruelty feel like a joke.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov finds his reasoning "true as arithmetic", yet his own heart refuses to act on it, a reminder that a clever argument can still fail the test of conscience.

In Crime and Punishment, a student argues that one wicked act could pay for many good deeds, until his friend asks whether he would do it himself, a sharp test for any argument that makes harm sound like simple arithmetic.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov ends up hunting for arguments as if something outside him were pushing him on, and the doubt he keeps hiding is the real signal.

In Crime and Punishment, Dostoevsky suggests that a clear view of the consequences would have stopped Raskolnikov, since the horror he feels is his own conscience speaking, a reminder to listen to that voice before acting.

In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov's torment begins inside him, with a mind that cannot rest, long before any outside authority catches up, a picture of how guilt punishes the person who carries it.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov, weighed down by fear, feels a sudden urge to confess everything, a sign that the truth keeps pressing for an exit even when we are busy hiding from it.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov trembles with relief when his summons turns out to be about a small debt, not his crime, a sign of how fear can attach itself to the wrong thing.
In Crime and Punishment, Dostoyevsky shows a desperate man pouring his private troubles out to officials who have no interest in them, and feeling more exposed for it.
In Crime and Punishment, Dostoyevsky shows how shame and vanity can drop away in an instant, leaving a man feeling completely alone.
In Crime and Punishment, Dostoyevsky shows a plan settled on in a fever losing its certainty in daylight, so that a man who once felt sure ends up wandering and unable to act.
In Crime and Punishment, Dostoyevsky shows a man blaming his illness for doubts he would rather not face, when the real question is why he acted at all.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov turns away the one friend who could help him, insisting he needs nothing from anyone. Dostoyevsky shows how guilt and pride can cut a person off from help.
In Crime and Punishment, a beaten and ragged man is pressed for coins by a poor mother and daughter who only see that he is hurt. Dostoyevsky shows kindness coming from unexpected people.
In Crime and Punishment, Razumihin looks after his sick friend with plain, unfussy care, simply turning up with soup and tea and staying close, which is often what real help looks like.
In Crime and Punishment, Razumihin quietly takes on his friend's debt and simply hands back the proof. Dostoyevsky shows that real help can be hard to accept when pride is involved.
In Crime and Punishment, a man who has hidden something keeps going back to the hiding place, unable to settle. Dostoyevsky shows guilt as a restless loop that gives no peace.
In Crime and Punishment, Razumihin argues that facts are not everything, since much of the work lies in how you interpret them. It is a useful reminder for anyone weighing evidence.
In Crime and Punishment, a pawnbroker's shrewd maxim is that the further you hide a thing, the quicker it will be found. Dostoyevsky shows how concealment so often gives itself away.

In Crime and Punishment, a doctor warns his friend that a story which fits too neatly, with every detail falling into place, should make you suspicious. Dostoyevsky shows how a tidy explanation can be a trap.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov suspects a visitor of reciting fashionable opinions he has learnt by heart to look clever. Dostoyevsky shows how borrowed ideas can pass for wisdom.
In Crime and Punishment, Razumihin cuts through a man's fine phrases about progress to see what sort of man he really is. Dostoyevsky shows that fluent talk can hide a shallow character.

In Crime and Punishment, Razumihin suggests that a society which has grown used to having everything handed over is left floundering when the hard hour comes. It is a useful thought about dependence and character.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov feels a sudden calm once he has fixed on a desperate course. Dostoyevsky shows that such calm comes from a settled purpose, not from being right.
In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov recalls a condemned man's thought that even a narrow ledge is better than dying. Dostoyevsky shows how fiercely people cling to life, however bleak it gets.

In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov points out that a scheme relying on many untrustworthy partners tends to fall apart through one careless slip. It is a fair warning for any business that depends on people who cannot be relied on.

In Crime and Punishment, Zametov warns that even a practised, desperate man cannot always rely on his own nerve when it comes to the test. Dostoyevsky shows how hard it is to know yourself under pressure.

In Crime and Punishment, Razumihin tells his friend, who has just pushed him away, that people who quarrel with those who care for them often come back. Dostoyevsky shows loyalty that keeps knocking even when it is turned away.

In Crime and Punishment, a policeman throws off his coat and boots and jumps into a canal to pull a drowning woman out, without any fuss. Dostoyevsky shows courage in ordinary people doing their duty.

In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov, lost in his own torment, still insists that an injured stranger be carried home at once and offers to pay for it. Dostoyevsky shows that compassion can break through even the most troubled heart.
In Crime and Punishment, Katerina Ivanovna would rather wear herself out washing linen at night than let dirt into her home, even while poor and ill. Dostoyevsky shows dignity kept up under hardship.

In Crime and Punishment, Dostoyevsky notes that a crowd gathers round a sudden accident partly out of a strange satisfaction, even among those close to the victim. It is a sharp observation of how people watch misfortune.
In Crime and Punishment, a dying man, ashamed of his failings, reaches out to his daughter for forgiveness and falls as he tries. Dostoyevsky shows love and shame arriving together, often too late.

In Crime and Punishment, a grieving little girl who has just lost her father promises to pray for a stranger all her life. Dostoyevsky shows that simple, unguarded kindness can reach someone at their lowest.

In Crime and Punishment, Raskolnikov refuses to let his sister marry for his sake, saying he will not accept the sacrifice. Dostoyevsky shows a love that is proud and unwilling to be repaid with someone else's sacrifice.

In Crime and Punishment, Dostoyevsky observes that a person's true nature shows through whatever their mood, so people soon see what sort of man they are dealing with. Character tends to reveal itself under pressure.

In Crime and Punishment, Razumihin argues that it is better to go wrong in your own way than to go right in someone else's, because a life lived on borrowed ideas is cramped. It is a good reminder to think for yourself.

preview.text:
A few months later Dostoevsky died. He was followed to the grave by a
vast multitude of mourners, who “gave the hapless man the funeral of a
king.” He is still probably the most widely read writer in Russia.

In the words of a Russian critic, who seeks to explain the feeling
inspired by Dostoevsky: “He was one of ourselves, a man of our blood
and our bone, but one who has suffered and has seen so much more
deeply than we have his insight impresses us as wisdom... that wisdom
of the heart which we seek that we may learn from it how to live. All
his other gifts came to him from nature, this he won for himself and
through it he became great.”

CRIME AND PUNISHMENT

PART I

CHAPTER I

On an exceptionally hot evening early in July a young man came out of
the garret in which he lodged in S. Place and walked slowly, as though
in hesitation, towards K. bridge.

He had successfully avoided meeting his landlady on the staircase.
His garret was under the roof of a high, five-storied house and was
more like a cupboard than a room. The landlady who provided him with
garret, dinners, and attendance, lived on the floor below, and every
time he went out he was obliged to pass her kitchen, the door of which
invariably stood open. And each time he passed, the young man had a
sick, frightened feeling, which made him scowl and feel ashamed. He was
hopelessly in debt to his landlady, and was afraid of meeting her.

books.title: The Wisdom of Life
books.author: Arthur Schopenhauer
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 1860, translator died 1928. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Schopenhauer holds that what a person is, their inner make-up, shapes their happiness more than their surroundings, because we only ever experience the world through our own ideas and feelings.
Schopenhauer observes that a thoughtful person can find good company in their own thoughts, while a dull person stays bored even amid parties and amusements.
Schopenhauer notes that time wears away health, beauty and mental gifts, but moral character is untouched by it, so character is the part of us worth building.
Schopenhauer advises us to make the most of the qualities we have, choosing work and a way of life that calls them into play rather than leaving them idle.
Schopenhauer argues that beyond meeting real needs, wealth adds little to happiness, while mental culture gives a rich inner life that money cannot buy.
Schopenhauer holds that the pleasure we take in anything depends largely on who we are, since to a sour person even good things taste bitter.
Schopenhauer notes that misfortune from outside is easier to bear than trouble we bring on ourselves, because fortune can change but character cannot.
Schopenhauer calls good spirits the coin of happiness, a direct gain that lifts us in the present moment, so cheerfulness should be welcomed rather than held at arm's length.
Schopenhauer, quoting Epictetus, reminds us that people are shaped not by things themselves but by their thoughts about things, so one event can delight one person and trouble another.
Schopenhauer, following Plato, notes that the anxious person expects the worst and so meets fewer real disappointments, while the easy-going person finds more reasons to rejoice.
Schopenhauer sees pain and boredom as the two foes of happiness, and says inner wealth of mind is the best protection, since the richer the mind, the less room is left for boredom.
Schopenhauer observes that the more a person has within themselves, the less they need from other people, so a rich inner life brings a measure of independence.
Seneca observes that folly is its own burden, since a fool cannot escape their own company, while a person of talent fills even solitude with thought.
Schopenhauer distinguishes ordinary people, who only think how to spend their time, from thoughtful people, who try to use it, since idle leisure so often breeds boredom.
Schopenhauer holds that what one person can be to another is limited, so we must find our own contentment within, since in the end every person stands alone.
Schopenhauer, quoting Aristotle, says happiness means self-sufficiency, because pleasures from outside are uncertain and fade, while what we have within lasts longest.
Schopenhauer warns against sacrificing the inner life for the outer, trading quiet, leisure and independence for rank and show, since the wise guard the springs of happiness they carry within.
Schopenhauer, following Aristotle, holds that every pleasure needs some activity of our powers, so unused gifts become a burden and people chase distractions to escape boredom.
Schopenhauer ranks the pleasures of thought, learning and culture above those of bodily appetite, because the nobler the power we use, the greater and more lasting the pleasure it gives.
Schopenhauer says a life of the mind deepens over time like a work of art, whereas a life devoted only to comfort can broaden but never deepen.
Schopenhauer, quoting Seneca, says leisure without learning is a kind of living tomb, and that a life of the mind guards us against boredom and the costly company boredom invites.
Schopenhauer uses the image of a centre of gravity: if our happiness rests on things outside us, it keeps shifting with every wish, but a person whose centre lies within stays steady.
Schopenhauer, quoting Aristotle, says the free exercise of any power is happiness, and Goethe agrees that we find our greatest happiness in using the talent we were meant to use.
