Schopenhauer admits the other side too: a great mind feels pain more keenly and may find ordinary company shallow, so every gift carries its own cost.
Epicurus, as Schopenhauer retells him, divides our needs into the necessary, the natural but less pressing, and the endless needs of luxury and show, which are the hardest to satisfy.
Schopenhauer notes that happiness depends on the gap between what we want and what we expect, so riches, like sea water, leave us thirstier, while a person with modest hopes can be content.
Schopenhauer observes that discontent springs from raising our claims faster than we can satisfy them, so contentment often means adjusting our demands to what we can reach.
Schopenhauer values independence as the freedom to say that this day is one's own, but warns that a person with means who does nothing with their time will find boredom a misery of its own.
Schopenhauer warns that being a slave to others' opinions, whether flattering or hurtful, undermines our peace of mind and independence, so we should temper our craving for praise.
Schopenhauer suggests that what others think of us lives in their minds, not ours, and that treating their opinions as too precious is paying them too much honour.
Schopenhauer insists that our real existence is in our own skin, not in other people's opinions, so our temperament, relationships and daily life matter far more than applause.

Schopenhauer says many people reverse the natural order, treating others' opinions as real and their own inner life as shadowy, which he calls vanity, like a miser who forgets the end in chasing the means.
Schopenhauer argues that many of life's worries come from anxiety about what others will say, and that much of our show and pride rests on this same fear.
Schopenhauer's remedy is to recognise that most opinions in people's heads are unreliable and that honour has only an indirect value, so a quieter, more private life brings real peace of mind.

Schopenhauer separates pride, a conviction of our own worth that works from within, from vanity, which seeks that conviction from others, and notes that quiet confidence often earns more respect than constant talk.

Schopenhauer defines honour as other people's opinion of our worth on one side, and the respect we give that opinion on the other, and notes that a person alone can accomplish little, like a castaway.
Schopenhauer notes that nothing gives a person more courage than knowing others regard them with goodwill, since that regard brings help and protection against life's troubles.
Schopenhauer holds that honour rests on the belief that character is unalterable, so once trust is broken it is hard to win back, unless the loss came from a mistake or from slander.
Schopenhauer notes that honour is something we keep by what we do and leave undone, unlike fame, which must be won, so honour lies largely within our own power.
Schopenhauer shows the folly of a code of honour in which any insult defines a person, handing a good person's worth to the most careless tongue, so judge yourself by your own conduct instead.
Schopenhauer recalls Socrates meeting a kick with calm, asking whether he should resent a donkey's kick, and treating an abuser's words as not really aimed at him.
Seneca advises that when a wise person is insulted, they should simply let it pass rather than flare up or seek revenge, since the insult says more about the one who gives it.
Schopenhauer observes that a person who knows they have done nothing wrong can meet a baseless accusation with contempt, since a real fault stings far more than a false charge.
Schopenhauer holds that a true sense of our own worth makes us largely indifferent to insult, since real worth cannot be lost through a rude word.
Schopenhauer distinguishes honour, which anyone can earn by doing what is expected of them, from fame, which comes only through extraordinary achievement.
Schopenhauer notes that actions are fleeting, while a lasting work of thought or art keeps speaking to people across the ages, so he values the work of the head over the deed alone.
Seneca, quoted by Schopenhauer, says fame follows merit as surely as a body casts a shadow, sometimes in front and sometimes behind, though envious silence may delay it.

Schopenhauer, with Goethe, notes that our finest thoughts can fall flat before minds that cannot take them in, so we should not be discouraged, since even a stone thrown into a marsh can make no rings.
Schopenhauer observes that those who work from love of their subject, rather than from ambition for fame, are the ones who leave lasting work behind.
Schopenhauer says fame is only a measure of what a person is compared with others, so it is worth less than the great heart or great head that deserves it.

Schopenhauer reminds us that every person lives mainly in and for themselves, so what they are matters more than the ideas other people form of them, and other people's heads are a poor home for true happiness.
Schopenhauer holds that a person is made happy not by fame but by the merit that brings it, so someone who deserves fame without receiving it still has the more important part of happiness.
Schopenhauer says the value of lasting recognition lies in deserving it, and that this is its own reward, since praise from a crowd is often no more than the echo of a few voices.
Schopenhauer finds great consolation in age in having put the full force of one's youth into work that still remains alive, like a plant that is green in winter.

Schopenhauer encourages people who lack the highest powers but have sound judgment to take up laborious study, since patient work lifts a person above the crowd who see the facts without ever examining them.

Schopenhauer advises a person of great mental powers to look broadly at nature and human life rather than lose themselves in narrow specialties, since everyday life supplies material for serious and true thought.

preview.text:
The differences which come under the first head are those which Nature
herself has set between man and man; and from this fact alone we may
at once infer that they influence the happiness or unhappiness of
mankind in a much more vital and radical way than those contained
under the two following heads, which are merely the effect of human
arrangements. Compared with _genuine personal advantages_, such as a
great mind or a great heart, all the privileges of rank or birth, even
of royal birth, are but as kings on the stage, to kings in real life.
The same thing was said long ago by Metrodorus, the earliest disciple
of Epicurus, who wrote as the title of one of his chapters, _The
happiness we receive from ourselves is greater than that which we
obtain from our surroundings_[1] And it is an obvious fact, which
cannot be called in question, that the principal element in a man's
well-being,--indeed, in the whole tenor of his existence,--is what he
is made of, his inner constitution. For this is the immediate source
of that inward satisfaction or dissatisfaction resulting from the
sum total of his sensations, desires and thoughts; whilst his
surroundings, on the other hand, exert only a mediate or indirect
influence upon him. This is why the same external events or
circumstances affect no two people alike; even with perfectly similar
surroundings every one lives in a world of his own. For a man has
immediate apprehension only of his own ideas, feelings and volitions;
the outer world can influence him only in so far as it brings these to
life. The world in which a man lives shapes itself chiefly by the way
in which he looks at it, and so it proves different to different
men; to one it is barren, dull, and superficial; to another rich,
interesting, and full of meaning. On hearing of the interesting events
which have happened in the course of a man's experience, many people
will wish that similar things had happened in their lives too,
completely forgetting that they should be envious rather of the mental
aptitude which lent those events the significance they possess when he
describes them; to a man of genius they were interesting adventures;
but to the dull perceptions of an ordinary individual they would have
been stale, everyday occurrences. This is in the highest degree the
case with many of Goethe's and Byron's poems, which are obviously
founded upon actual facts; where it is open to a foolish reader to
envy the poet because so many delightful things happened to him,
instead of envying that mighty power of phantasy which was capable
of turning a fairly common experience into something so great and
beautiful.

books.title: Les Miserables
books.author: Victor Hugo
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1885, translator died 1928. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Victor Hugo argued that a book about injustice stays useful for as long as poverty, ignorance and hunger remain unsolved in the world.
Victor Hugo notes that what people say about a man, true or false, can shape his life and destiny as much as what he actually does.
In Les Miserables, Hugo has Bishop Myriel answer Napoleon with the thought that a good man and a great man can each learn from the other. Respect runs both ways.
In Les Miserables, Bishop Myriel gives up his own palace so that thirty-six sick people have room. Hugo shows kindness that is practical and asks for no credit.
In Les Miserables, Hugo shows Bishop Myriel deciding in advance, once and for all, where every part of his income will go, and then keeping to that plan.
Hugo says there is always more hardship below than brotherhood above, so Bishop Myriel gave his money away almost as soon as it came in. Generosity that is planned tends to last.
In Les Miserables, the poor of the district choose the name Welcome for their bishop from the part of his name that meant most to them. Kindness is often named by the people it helps.
When a mayor sneers at Bishop Myriel for riding a donkey, he says he does it from necessity, not vanity. Plain honesty answers a sneer best.
Hugo shows Myriel teaching by pointing to communities that care for their poor and sick, rather than preaching in the abstract. A good example persuades.
Hugo says Myriel taught through parables and vivid images rather than long argument, and was persuasive because he was convinced himself.
Hugo shows Myriel answering a rich man's show of charity with a joke that hides a serious point. Giving a little for appearances is not the same as generosity.
In a sermon, Myriel asks his listeners to look at the suffering around them, from cramped housing to hunger, and to have pity. Seeing clearly is the first step to caring.
Bishop Myriel tells people to examine the road a fault has travelled before they condemn it, and to aim to be upright rather than perfect.
Hugo has Myriel argue that society is responsible for the ignorance it allows, so the guilty party is often the one who let the shadow form.
Hugo shows Myriel questioning a prosecutor who tricked a woman into betraying her lover. Being clever at winning is not the same as being just, and someone must answer for the trick.
Hugo shows Myriel staying all day with a condemned man, giving him truth and comfort when everyone else had stepped away. Showing up for someone at their lowest is a real choice.
After an execution, Hugo shows Bishop Myriel asking by what right people take a life. Compassion can lead a person to question what the law allows.

Myriel comforts the bereaved by turning grief from the grave towards hope, so sorrow is made larger and more dignified rather than erased. Knowing when to be silent matters as much as knowing when to speak.
Hugo has Myriel give his charity first to the needy, sick and afflicted, then spend his remaining time working. He called all his work gardening: the mind is a garden to be tended.
In Les Miserables, Myriel writes in a margin that Solomon calls God Compassion, the most beautiful of all his names. For Hugo's bishop, kindness is the highest way to know the divine.
Bishop Myriel gave to the poor the money friends raised for a new altar, saying the finest altar is a troubled soul that has been comforted. Put value where it does real good.
Myriel allowed himself one luxury, cleanliness, because it took nothing from the poor. Choose comforts that do not come at someone else's expense.
Myriel tells his housekeeper that the beautiful is as useful as the useful, and perhaps more so. Hugo's bishop respects the learned and the unlearned alike, and the ignorant most of all.
Myriel wrote that a person who is embarrassed by his name is often the one who most needs shelter, so do not ask him for it first. His door was never locked.
Myriel says there is a bravery of the priest as well as the bravery of a soldier, but the priest's should be a calm courage.
Myriel says he is not in the world to guard his own life but to guard souls. Purpose should come before self-protection, though he also judges fear carefully.
Myriel tells his sister that outside dangers are small, and that prejudices are the real robbers and vices the real murderers. The greatest dangers lie within ourselves.
Hugo has Myriel point out that a philosophy saying nothing matters can conveniently excuse taking whatever one wants. Test your beliefs by what they allow you to do.
In Les Miserables, Baptistine's letter describes a household that shares what it has with the sick and needy and finds joy in that, even when money is tight.
Baptistine learns to stop fighting her brother's courage and to pray and trust instead. Fear eases when you rest on something larger than yourself.
Hugo observes that the people who love a man best learn his nature rather than just his words, and sometimes step back to let him be who he is. Good loyalty understands.
Bishop Myriel sees a lonely man everyone avoids and says he owes him a visit, even though he feels a pull of reluctance. Duty can come before comfort, and sheep scabs do not make a shepherd recoil.
Hugo admits that even a kind bishop feels a petty flash of pride at being addressed as citizen. Being honest about our own small contradictions makes us more trustworthy.
In Les Miserables, the old conventionary calls ignorance the real tyrant. Learning frees people from the tyrannies that grow in the dark.
In Les Miserables, the old conventionary says that tearing down abuses is not enough, because the customs behind them must change too. Pulling out the old system is only half the job.
Hugo has the old man insist that pity be even-handed, weeping for the children of the powerful and the children of the people alike. Fairness means not picking favourites in who deserves sympathy.
Hugo shows the conventionary apologising for using his own advantages to win an argument. Not using your power to beat someone in debate is good taste and good character.
Hugo's dying old man says he did his duty as far as his powers allowed, was hated for it, and carried that isolation without hating anyone himself. Doing right does not depend on being loved for it.
After the old man's death, Bishop Myriel grows even more tender towards children and the suffering. A hard encounter can deepen compassion rather than harden it.
Myriel says he embarrassed a room of powerful churchmen, and that outside air came in through him like an open door. Plain honesty can change the atmosphere of any room.
Hugo says that anyone who serves the poor should carry a little of their hardship, like a workman near a furnace. Living close to need changes how a person lives.
Hugo says a good man is better served by keeping his eyes on truth, justice and charity than by getting caught in party quarrels. Partisanship can dim the things that matter most.
Hugo judges Myriel flawed in some political views, yet says he was just, humble and kind, and more tolerant than the narrator. A person can be wrong in part and still be good.
Hugo satirises careerists who flatter the powerful and then dress their ambition up as a vocation. Self-deception is easiest when it sounds noble.
Hugo warns that success is easily mistaken for merit, and prosperity does not prove ability. Look past the gilding to what has really been done.
Hugo describes Myriel's kindness as wide enough to include even the spiders and ants in his garden. Real goodwill extends to the humblest of things.
Hugo says character is worn like rock by drops of water: a gentle conviction, thought by thought, leaves hollows that do not wash away. Daily habits shape who we become.
Hugo notes that a pleasant manner makes a man seem good on first meeting, but real depth only shows after a few hours of his company. Give people time before you judge them.
Hugo says Myriel took the short path of the Gospel instead of grand speculation, and that a humble soul who loves is enough. Keep your faith practical.
Hugo says Myriel did not try to solve the mystery of suffering, but set about dressing its wounds. Let compassion guide your action more than abstract theory.
Myriel's whole teaching was simply to love one another. When a senator calls that nonsense, he replies that the soul should shut itself up in it, as a pearl in its oyster.
Hugo shows a traveller turned away from an inn because of his worn appearance, even though he has money to pay. Appearances are a poor guide to a person's worth.
In Les Miserables, a town's gossip runs ahead of a stranger, and one innkeeper after another turns him away before anyone asks what he has done. Rumour can shut doors long before facts are known.
Hugo has a woman tell a man, turned away from every other door, to knock at the one he has not tried yet. Sometimes the help you need is at the door you have not thought of.
When rumours of danger run through the house, Bishop Myriel listens calmly and asks plainly whether they are really in danger, rather than being swept along by fear.
Hugo shows a man turned away at every door until he feels the world has no place for him. Being shut out again and again breeds despair, and it is a warning for anyone who sees a stranger.
Myriel tells a stranger that a good door asks whether a person is suffering, not what his name is. Hospitality is about need, not reputation.
Myriel tells a released convict that if he leaves his past with goodwill rather than hatred, he is more worthy than many of those who judge him. Judge people by the direction they choose.
Baptistine notices that her brother never raises a guest's past and treats him as an ordinary person. Hugo suggests the truest pity is not to touch a sore point at all.
When a guest hints that he could be dangerous, Myriel answers that judging him is God's concern, then blesses him anyway. Trust can be a choice made in the face of risk.

preview.text:
So long as there shall exist, by virtue of law and custom, decrees of
damnation pronounced by society, artificially creating hells amid the
civilization of earth, and adding the element of human fate to divine
destiny; so long as the three great problems of the century—the
degradation of man through pauperism, the corruption of woman through
hunger, the crippling of children through lack of light—are unsolved;
so long as social asphyxia is possible in any part of the world;—in
other words, and with a still wider significance, so long as ignorance
and poverty exist on earth, books of the nature of Les Misérables
cannot fail to be of use.

HAUTEVILLE HOUSE, 1862.

VOLUME I
FANTINE

BOOK FIRST—A JUST MAN

CHAPTER I—M. MYRIEL

In 1815, M. Charles-François-Bienvenu Myriel was Bishop of D—— He was
an old man of about seventy-five years of age; he had occupied the see
of D—— since 1806.

books.title: The Conduct of Life
books.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 1882. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Ralph Waldo Emerson asks how shall I live. He says the great questions of the age are too large to solve, so the practical task is to conduct your own life well.
Emerson suggests that when two truths seem to clash, such as fate and freedom, you take each one seriously in turn, and a reasonable balance can appear over time.
Emerson observes that every spirit builds its house, but afterwards the house confines the spirit. Our habits and surroundings can end up limiting us.
Emerson argues that our own power is only half of what shapes us, with circumstance the other half. Knowing the limits you cannot change is part of living well.
Emerson says that whatever limits us, we call Fate, and that the limits grow finer as we refine ourselves. He suggests we learn the shape of our limits by pushing against them.
Emerson holds that what is useful lasts and what is hurtful sinks over time, so wrongdoing tends to meet its consequences sooner or later.
Emerson insists that power matters as much as limitation. We should respect the natural limits of life, but a person is more than nature and holds both within.
Emerson argues that thinking and choosing keep a person free even inside fate. Dwelling too much on destiny, he warns, breeds meanness and invites the evils we fear.
Emerson says the right use of fate is to lift our conduct to the scale of nature, meeting danger with steady courage for the sake of duty.
Emerson says real insight, seeing the unity and law in things, lifts a person out of servitude. When truth comes to us, we expand to its size.
Emerson says a person who sees the larger truth grows less egotistical and cares more for principle than for personal pride.
Emerson holds that thought and will cannot be separated. Of two people each following their own thought, the one with the deeper thought will be stronger.
Emerson argues that a strong will rests on a unity of purpose and a belief in something true. A will that rests only on self-interest can be bought or bent.
Emerson says insight is not yet will. Goodness dies in wishes unless perception is joined to energy, and no one truly grasps a truth until they are ready to act on it.
Emerson sees limits as the measure of a growing person. Like a child's height marks on a wall, we outgrow them, and the next wall is always bigger.
Emerson says that what threatens us can become strength once we understand it. Learn to swim and trim your boat, and the wave that drowned others can carry you.
Emerson says life is self-direction from the first moment. A person is not contained in their skin, but reaches outward and makes their own surroundings.
Emerson argues that events fit a person like a skin, shaped by their own thoughts and character, so we are less at the mercy of chance than we think.
Emerson says a person's fortunes are the fruit of their character, so the surest way to better circumstances is often to become a better person.
Emerson says the power to shape hard material to a purpose is a measure of the mind. A weak person is shaped by the earth, while a strong one shapes it.
Emerson says a person's character shows in everything they do, so a fault of temper will turn up in speech, work and kindness. Seeing that pattern helps us see our own.
Emerson notes that what we seek we tend to find, so it is wise to ask only for high things, since we may well get them.
Emerson says a good intention clothes itself with sudden power, and that what lames or paralyses us can draw out a hidden strength in return.
Emerson says life is a search after power. A person should value events and possessions for the power they add to the self, not for their own sake.
Emerson says successful people believe things go by law rather than luck, and that nothing is got for nothing. They adjust their efforts to the obstacles in front of them.
Emerson says a person who is in step with how things work can read what is coming and stands ready for whatever happens to them.
Emerson says an enterprising person brings life into a stagnant place, and that a good leader often gathers others who build on their work.
Emerson says a person of force sees the possible farms and houses where a feeble person sees only what is already built. Presence of mind often decides who leads.
Emerson observes that resilient people meet setbacks with fresh interest, and that a hurt can leave them tougher rather than discouraged.
Emerson says strong natures with great impulses have great resources and return from far, while timid conservatism disgusts the young and drives them to extremes.
Emerson says energy is good when it is put in the right place, but excess turns it against its owner, like an axe that chops off one's own fingers. Learn to direct power well.

Emerson recounts Michelangelo mixing his own paints to learn fresco, and a painter's advice that a failure usually means someone dreamed instead of working. Success comes from showing up and doing the work.
Emerson says concentration is the one prudence in life and dissipation the one evil. Choose your work, take what you can carry, and drop the rest, because only then does knowing turn into doing.
Emerson recalls that Newton, asked how he made his discoveries, said he kept his mind always intending on the matter. Steady attention is the secret of strength in most affairs.
Emerson says in fast-moving affairs any decision is better than none. A person who brings all they know to bear on the instant is worth a dozen who know as much but think slowly.
Emerson quotes Democritus that more people are made good by practice than by nature, and says mastery comes from thousands of repetitions, not one bright spark.
Emerson says every achievement is paid for with spent energy. A person is only efficient as a vessel of that force, so it is worth husbanding carefully and not wasting.
Emerson says success is not an accident. If the laws of effort can be read, then success is within reach of anyone willing to learn them.
Emerson says a person is not whole until they can earn a blameless living, and that a good citizen pays their debt and adds something to the common wealth.
Emerson says wealth comes from applying the mind to nature. Getting ahead depends less on hard labour or saving than on good order, timing and being in the right place.
Emerson says the merchant's craft is bringing a thing from where it abounds to where it is needed. Real wealth extends our powers, like tools that give us hands and eyes.
Emerson says the richest person is the one who can draw on the faculties and labour of many people, in distant places and past times, not just the one who has most.
Emerson says the world is a tool-chest, and a person succeeds in proportion to how well their faculties are married to nature and to the things they can take into themselves.
Emerson says a well-done piece of work gives its doer a quiet dignity. A craftsperson at the bench can deal on even terms with anyone, because good work answers for them.
Emerson says the true use of wealth is power to give form to one's thoughts, not to chase show and pleasure. He calls the fine candy of luxury a poor aim.
Emerson notes that rival ambitions check one another, as trees in a forest stop any one of them taking all the sap, so the wider world is kept in balance.
Emerson says to be truly rich is to have a ticket of admission to the best works of every culture. The curious traveller takes the whole world into their life.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that wealth belongs with those who can administer it well, since a rich person is one whose work opens a path for others.
Ralph Waldo Emerson saw property as an intellectual production, built from the accumulated skill of many people over many years.
Ralph Waldo Emerson saw good luck as another name for tenacity of purpose, and held that a sound trader sticks to facts and takes small, sure gains.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that money is a representative of value, so its worth grows with the honesty, skill and care of the community that uses it.
Ralph Waldo Emerson observed that cheap-looking conveniences often hide costs somewhere else, and that money and power are never really cheap.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that real waste is effort spent off the line of one's career, so a person should do the work that fits their own talent.
Ralph Waldo Emerson advised spending on the work that is truly yours and cutting false expenses, since vanity costs far more than a good pride does.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that lasting wealth comes from the relation of income to spending, since bigger incomes do not help when spending grows faster.
Ralph Waldo Emerson warned that no property stays sound without constant watching, because things change in your hands and leak away if left alone.
Ralph Waldo Emerson praised the engineer who followed the natural valley rather than forcing a straight line, and found the result safer and cheaper.
Ralph Waldo Emerson observed that people who buy a dream property often ignore practical needs, and that those who know the ground are worth listening to.
Ralph Waldo Emerson held that in economy, as in friendship or justice, you get back the same kind of thing you put in.
Ralph Waldo Emerson urged people to spend their energy on power rather than pleasure, and to keep reinvesting what they gain so it grows into lasting capital.

preview.text:
It chanced during one winter, a few years ago, that our cities were bent
on discussing the theory of the Age.  By an odd coincidence, four or
five noted men were each reading a discourse to the citizens of Boston
or New York, on the Spirit of the Times.  It so happened that the
subject had the same prominence in some remarkable pamphlets and
journals issued in London in the same season.  To me, however, the
question of the times resolved itself into a practical question of the
conduct of life.  How shall I live?  We are incompetent to solve the
times.  Our geometry cannot span the huge orbits of the prevailing
ideas, behold their return, and reconcile their opposition. We can only
obey our own polarity.  'Tis fine for us to speculate and elect our
course, if we must accept an irresistible dictation.

In our first steps to gain our wishes, we come upon immovable
limitations.  We are fired with the hope to reform men.  After many
experiments, we find that we must begin earlier,--at school.  But the
boys and girls are not docile; we can make nothing of them.  We decide
that they are not of good stock.  We must begin our reform earlier
still,--at generation: that is to say, there is Fate, or laws of the
world.

books.title: Gulliver's Travels
books.author: Jonathan Swift
books.subject: classics
books.licence_note: Author died 1745. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Jonathan Swift has Gulliver grumble that his book changed nothing it was meant to change. A useful reminder that one piece of writing rarely fixes what its author hoped, so expect to keep working after the first attempt.
Gulliver says he wrote for the amendment of his readers, not for their applause. Write to make something better, and the praise matters less than the change.

Swift's Gulliver, a surgeon, turns down the bad practices that other doctors use to get business because his conscience will not let him copy them. Doing the work honestly can cost you, but it keeps you clear with yourself.

In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver could crush the Lilliputians who have tied him down, but he holds back because they have treated him generously. Power is more honourable when it is used with restraint and gratitude.

In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver holds six captured rioters in his hand, then sets them free one by one. His mercy earns more goodwill than force could have, and it goes on to shape how the court treats him.

In Gulliver's Travels, Swift shows Lilliput's courtiers risking broken limbs and necks in rope-dancing contests to win the emperor's favour. It is a sharp picture of how chasing status can make people reckless with their own safety.

Swift mocks two factions in Gulliver's Travels that fight a long war over which end of an egg to crack. Petty quarrels can cost far more than the thing they are about, so ask what a dispute is really worth before you join it.

In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver refuses to help his emperor enslave a free people, even after saving the fleet for him. He is right to hold the line, though it costs him favour and sets his rivals against him.

In Gulliver's Travels, the Lilliputians punish a false accuser with death and repay the innocent accused generously. A fair system makes people think hard before they lay a charge against someone else.

Swift's Lilliputians treat fraud as worse than theft, because honest dealers cannot protect themselves against clever cheats. For a small business, trust in suppliers and customers only holds when cheating has a real cost.
Swift has Gulliver note that Lilliput rewards good conduct with honours and money, not only punishing bad conduct. Recognising people who do the right thing keeps a community's rules working.

In Gulliver's Travels, the Lilliputians choose people for their character before their brilliance. A clever person with weak morals can do far more harm than an honest person of ordinary ability, so hire for integrity first.

In Gulliver's Travels, a jealous minister spreads a rumour about his wife and Gulliver, and the lie costs Gulliver his standing at court. Gossip can do real damage, so check the facts before you pass on or believe a story about someone.

In Gulliver's Travels, the admiral wants Gulliver condemned because he is supposedly a traitor at heart, though he has done nothing wrong. Judging people by what you suspect they think, rather than by what they have done, is one of the oldest injustices.

Swift notes in Gulliver's Travels that the Lilliputian court praises its own mercy loudest just before its cruellest sentences. Be wary of leaders whose fine words grow more elaborate as their actions grow harsher.

Stranded among giants in Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver reflects that nothing is great or small except by comparison. Our sense of how big our problems are depends on what we measure them against, so check the comparison before you panic.
In Gulliver's Travels, Swift says he cut passages of less moment from his first draft for fear of being tedious. Trimming for the reader is a form of respect.
In Gulliver's Travels, the young Glumdalclitch shows steady kindness, sewing, washing and teaching Gulliver her language. Quiet, repeated care is often what keeps a person safe.
In Gulliver's Travels, a miserly farmer wants to profit from a stranger on display. Greed turns a person into an exhibit, and the one exhibited bears the cost.
In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver keeps his dignity and hope while others plan to exploit him. He reasons that a misfortune imposed by others is not a disgrace to him.
In Gulliver's Travels, exaggerated reports draw crowds ready to break down the doors. Hype can make a crowd dangerous to the one on show.
In Gulliver's Travels, Glumdalclitch teaches Gulliver to read in her spare hours, a small lesson at a time. Steady, patient teaching builds real skill.
In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver asks that Glumdalclitch, who cared for him, be kept on at court with him. He values loyalty above his own comfort.
In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver tells the queen plainly how his master drove him hard for profit, but he speaks with courtesy and sticks to the facts.
In Gulliver's Travels, the queen lets Gulliver give his own account rather than judging him by his appearance. Let the person being judged speak for themselves.
In Gulliver's Travels, the king first suspects a rehearsed story, then tests it with more questions and weighs the answers. Good thinking checks the claim before it dismisses it.
Swift mocks scholars in Gulliver's Travels who reason from theory, dismiss what they have not seen, and hide their ignorance behind a grand label. Look closer before you name something.
In Gulliver's Travels, the king dismisses his experts and checks the facts himself, questioning the farmer privately before confronting everyone together. Let evidence settle the matter.
Gulliver's Travels shows careful planning for the fragile: Gulliver's room is quilted against jolts and carelessness, and he asks for a lock against rats. Plan for the accidents that will happen.
In Gulliver's Travels, ordinary things look terrifying from a different scale. Perspective depends on where you stand.
Swift gives the king in Gulliver's Travels a view of human pride that sees nests, cities and titles as the work of tiny insects. It is a useful check on self-importance.
In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver's horror fades as he grows used to his surroundings, and he sees how a comparison can make anything look absurd. Familiarity changes what seems strange.
Swift shows, in Gulliver's Travels, a petty and spiteful dwarf who picks on someone he sees as beneath him. Bullying of the smaller is a sign of insecurity, not strength.

In Gulliver's Travels, Swift has Gulliver admit that his standing at court owed more to the king and queen's favour than to any merit of his own, a useful honesty about where success really comes from.
In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver makes a clever jab at a dwarf and is repaid with a shower of apples, a reminder that a cheap joke at someone else's expense can come back on you.

In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver hides his small mishaps from his minder so she will keep trusting him to be alone, a quiet warning that hidden small problems tend to surface later, often at a worse moment.
In Gulliver's Travels, the queen notices Gulliver is low and gives him a boat and a trough to row in, a reminder that a useful skill and a little kindness can lift someone out of homesickness.
In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver boasts of his courage to the king and gets only laughter, which leads him to see how vain it is to seek honour from people far above or beyond your own standing.
In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver tells the king that reason does not grow with the size of the body, so judge people by their mind rather than their stature.
In Gulliver's Travels, the king quizzes Gulliver on whether honours go to merit or to favour, bribes and party interest, a sharp test to put to any institution: who really earns its rank and power?
In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver admits he painted his own country in a kinder light than the strict truth allowed, a loyalty that is worth noticing whenever we tell our own story.

In Gulliver's Travels, Swift warns that a ruler who knows little of other nations will hold narrow prejudices, and that one people's notions of virtue should not be offered as the standard for all mankind.

In Gulliver's Travels, the king judges that whoever makes two blades of grass grow where one grew before does more good than all the politicians put together, a useful test of where real value is made.

In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver notes how readily people lecture on human weakness, and how that often turns into discontent with our lot, when our quarrels with nature are usually less well founded than we think.
In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver is kindly treated and admired at court, yet he longs for freedom, because being well looked after is not the same as being treated as an equal.

In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver grieves for the nurse who cared for him even while he is in mortal danger at sea, a sign of how good people keep thinking of others when they are in trouble themselves.
In Gulliver's Travels, a ship's captain sees a shaken stranger about to faint and gives him a drink and a bed before asking any questions, a small, practical kindness that steadies someone in crisis.

In Gulliver's Travels, the captain comes to believe an astonishing story once Gulliver tells it plainly and shows his evidence, a reminder that a calm, honest account backed by proof can persuade even a sceptic.
Gulliver says many travel writers chase wonder, vanity or profit over the truth, so he resolves to tell only plain events, a fair test for any story we tell about ourselves.
In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver behaves oddly at home because he has grown used to a very different world, a sharp reminder of how habit and prejudice shape what we take to be normal.

In Gulliver's Travels, the Laputians are so absorbed in abstract speculation that they need servants to flap them back into the conversation and stop them walking into posts, Swift's satire of thinkers cut off from ordinary life.
In Gulliver's Travels, Gulliver learns a language by writing words in columns, practising short sentences and sorting them into order. Structured notes build understanding quickly.
In Gulliver's Travels, one wrong figure in the tailor's calculation ruins six days of work. Check the early numbers in any careful process, because small errors compound.
Swift mocks, in Gulliver's Travels, a people who scorn practical work, so their houses have no right angles. Theory that never meets the workshop gives crooked results.
Swift observes in Gulliver's Travels that people are most opinionated about matters they know least about. Modesty about the limits of your own competence is a useful check.
In Gulliver's Travels, the people fret endlessly over distant, unlikely dangers and never enjoy peace of mind. Worry about what you cannot affect steals the present.

Swift notes in Gulliver's Travels that people who dwell on dreaded news pass it around like terrible stories, and the fear grows with each telling. Notice when conversation feeds worry rather than action.
In Gulliver's Travels, the king ignores what the traveller knows of other lands and asks only about his own narrow field. Curiosity that stays narrow misses most of what is useful.
In Gulliver's Travels, a tyrant's ministers hold back from the worst cruelty because it would cost them their own standing. Power rests on the willingness of those who serve it.
In Gulliver's Travels, a town that has suffered long oppression builds its own towers and plans to bring the ruler down. Pressure pushed far enough invites organised resistance.

preview.text:
I do, in the next place, complain of my own great want of judgment, in
being prevailed upon by the entreaties and false reasoning of you and
some others, very much against my own opinion, to suffer my travels to
be published. Pray bring to your mind how often I desired you to
consider, when you insisted on the motive of public good, that the
_Yahoos_ were a species of animals utterly incapable of amendment by
precept or example: and so it has proved; for, instead of seeing a full
stop put to all abuses and corruptions, at least in this little island,
as I had reason to expect; behold, after above six months warning, I
cannot learn that my book has produced one single effect according to
my intentions. I desired you would let me know, by a letter, when party
and faction were extinguished; judges learned and upright; pleaders
honest and modest, with some tincture of common sense, and Smithfield
blazing with pyramids of law books; the young nobility’s education
entirely changed; the physicians banished; the female _Yahoos_
abounding in virtue, honour, truth, and good sense; courts and levees
of great ministers thoroughly weeded and swept; wit, merit, and
learning rewarded; all disgracers of the press in prose and verse
condemned to eat nothing but their own cotton, and quench their thirst
with their own ink. These, and a thousand other reformations, I firmly
counted upon by your encouragement; as indeed they were plainly
deducible from the precepts delivered in my book. And it must be owned,
that seven months were a sufficient time to correct every vice and
folly to which _Yahoos_ are subject, if their natures had been capable
of the least disposition to virtue or wisdom. Yet, so far have you been
from answering my expectation in any of your letters; that on the
contrary you are loading our carrier every week with libels, and keys,
and reflections, and memoirs, and second parts; wherein I see myself
accused of reflecting upon great state folk; of degrading human nature
(for so they have still the confidence to style it), and of abusing the
female sex. I find likewise that the writers of those bundles are not
agreed among themselves; for some of them will not allow me to be the
author of my own travels; and others make me author of books to which I
am wholly a stranger.

books.title: The Pleasures of Life
books.author: John Lubbock
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: Author died 1913. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: John Lubbock argues that happiness is a duty, but our own pleasures must not be allowed to rule us, or they soon hand us over to sorrow.
John Lubbock says a cheerful person brightens everyone around them, and that keeping ourselves happy takes effort, an art we must manage as if we were somebody else.
John Lubbock says life is meant to be lived well, not merely lived. Not magnifying small troubles and using the blessings around us makes life a glorious inheritance.
John Lubbock notes that few of us realise the privilege of living, and that we hold more power to secure peace and triumph over pain than we think.
John Lubbock, quoting Ruskin, urges us to turn the voices of nature into a song of rejoicing, and to practise the duty of delight as well as self denial.
Marcus Aurelius reasoned that what does not make a person worse cannot make their life worse, a useful test for everyday setbacks.
John Lubbock warns that walling ourselves off to avoid pain also shuts us out of sympathy and happiness, so we lose more than we gain.
John Lubbock, quoting Helps, suggests that suffering can bring knowledge, so what we go through may be good for us even when it looks like evil.
John Lubbock, quoting Seneca, says misfortune boldly faced can often turn to our advantage, and that great ruins can make way for greater things.
John Lubbock, drawing on Epictetus, argues that whether our life is happy depends greatly on us, since few are ever made utterly miserable except by themselves.
John Lubbock observes that most of our suffering comes from small daily worries and from dreading misfortunes that never happen, so we should do our best and wait calmly.
John Lubbock, citing Epicurus, says a person who is not content with little is content with nothing, and that possessions beyond our needs are only a burden to carry.
Marcus Aurelius advised that bearing a trouble nobly is itself good fortune, since our own anger often does more harm than the event that provoked it.
John Lubbock says that if we cannot be happy, the fault generally lies in ourselves, and that we should notice the everyday blessings we tend to take for granted.
John Lubbock, quoting Ruskin, lists watching things grow, reading, thinking, loving and praying as what makes people happy, and notes that contentment comes from having few wants.
John Lubbock, quoting Greg, marvels that the world offers more beauty and delight than we could ask for, and that our senses and minds are made to take it in.
Marcus Aurelius held that philosophy keeps the inner self unharmed and above both pain and pleasure, so we act with purpose and accept what happens.
John Lubbock warns that giving way to self-indulgence is no true freedom, because repetition turns pleasure into a craving that becomes a tyranny.
John Lubbock says self-control grows easier with practice, and that ruling oneself is a greater triumph than any rank or power over others.
John Lubbock says each of us must conquer ourselves, which is a truer monarchy than any inherited power, and that conscience is our best guide.
John Lubbock held that a life is noble or ignoble by the spirit it is lived in, not by the work chosen, so trade can be as dignified as any calling.
Lubbock wrote that cheerfulness comes from employment, and that modest merit and patient industry are more sure of reward than people think.
Lubbock observed that battles are won before they are fought, so self-control is built through daily habits and the small details of everyday life.
Lubbock describes breaking a bad temper by counting the days without anger and cutting the habit back a little at a time, rather than all at once.
Marcus Aurelius, quoted by Lubbock, said we can always retire into our own soul for quiet, so peace of mind is something we can secure for ourselves.
Lubbock argues that the mind is shaped by what it dwells on, so we should fill it with pure and peaceful thoughts and keep it free of constant dwelling on wrongdoing.
Lubbock, recounting Socrates, holds that the real penalty of injustice is becoming more and more unjust, so wrongdoing harms the person who does it first.
Lubbock quotes Marcus Aurelius on Antoninus, who examined things carefully before judging them, bore unjust blame without blaming in return, and never did anything in a hurry.
Richard de Bury, quoted by Lubbock, said books teach without anger or ridicule, are never asleep when we need them, and so are the best of teachers.
Petrarch, quoted by Lubbock, described books as friends who are always at hand, who can be dismissed at will, and who teach us how to live, how to die and how to restrain our desires.
Lubbock, quoting Aikin, notes that a well-stocked library lets us question the wisest and most able minds of every age, drawing on their choicest thoughts at our own pace.
Carlyle, quoted by Lubbock, said a collection of books is a real university, one that is open to us for as long as we like.
Lubbock says reading is not necessarily study, and that the poetic and emotional side of literature is what we most need for everyday life.
Lubbock, recalling Macaulay, says books were a main source of his happiness, and warns that we must not let our love of reading crowd out other duties.
Lubbock notes that switching between several books on different subjects keeps reading fresh, so we come back to each with renewed interest rather than tiring of one.
Lubbock advises reading widely but starting with the best books in each field, reading most books quickly, and learning something of everything and everything of something.
Lubbock says a library is open to rich and poor alike, because wealth gives no advantage there, and that it brings us the company of the greatest thinkers.
Lubbock warns that in an age of plenty the problem is choosing what to read, and that we should not waste precious reading time on trash.
Lubbock recalls Darwin advising him to study whatever interested him most, and holds that choosing work we are drawn to applies to life generally.
Lubbock, quoting Herschel, says owning a library is quite different from using it wisely, and that people often read almost by hazard, so choosing books with care matters.
Lubbock suggests that a book which has lasted is a fair sign of its worth, while the most recent history and science give the most accurate information, so we should read both old and new.
Lubbock places the Enchiridion of Epictetus at the head of the moral writers outside Christianity, with Marcus Aurelius beside it, as among the noblest books in all literature.
Lubbock says we should be grateful to Aristotle, whose method taught us how to advance, and that the dialogues of Socrates stay as instructive now as ever.
Lubbock observes that history is increasingly about the development of human thought, art, science and law rather than the doings of kings, and that this makes it more interesting.
Lubbock, quoting Cicero, notes that we take great care choosing a horse or a dog, yet leave the choice of friends, which shapes our whole life, almost to chance.
Sir Thomas Browne observed that people who cannot bear their own company are a prison to themselves, while those with rich thoughts sometimes need company to escape their own crowd.
Lubbock says that with well-chosen friends, conversation can be made instructive and delightful, and that we can learn something from almost anyone who will take the trouble to talk with us.
Lubbock warns that friendships built only on living nearby, sharing a trade or travelling the same route are mere images of friendship, so real friends need to be chosen with care.
Marcus Aurelius advised that when we want cheering up we should think of the virtues of the people around us, since good examples in those we live with keep virtue in front of us.
Cicero held that true friends stay with us even when absent or dead, and Lubbock adds that we should choose friends for what they are, not for what they have.
Lubbock argues that most people can find time for what they really choose to do, so the real lack is will, and that what matters is how we use our hours, not how many we have.
Lubbock, quoting Pater, holds that life is measured by depth of thought and action rather than by length, and that habit dulls the finest moments we could be living.
Lubbock suggests that idleness lets the mind grind on against itself, and that it is care and worry, more than honest work, that wears people down.
Lubbock notes that time is not so much what flies as we who waste it, and, quoting Jeremy Taylor, that people careful with their time are also careful with their company and their actions.
Sir Arthur Helps, quoted by Lubbock, argues that there is no excuse for dullness, since nature invites us to learn, understand and do something with every part of the world around us.
Lubbock says the world belongs to whoever has seen it, and that anyone who wants a delightful journey must first make himself delightful company on the way.
Lubbock, following Bacon, says the wise traveller observes whatever is memorable in each place, while the fool merely wanders, and that the time we have decides how deeply we can look.
Lubbock tells of a holy man who realised late in life that he had preached about heaven while seeing almost nothing of the world he lived in, and so went to see it.
Tyndall, quoted by Lubbock, describes nature as a patient sculptor shaping mountains and valleys over ages, a reminder of how much slow work lies behind the scenes we see.
Lubbock argues that loving travel does not mean loving home less, since we enjoy home more when we sometimes wander away, and one of the great pleasures of travel is the return.

preview.text:
PART I

"All places that the eye of Heaven visits
    Are to the wise man ports and happy havens."

SHAKESPEARE.

"Some murmur, when their sky is clear
      And wholly bright to view,
    If one small speck of dark appear
      In their great heaven of blue.
    And some with thankful love are fill'd
      If but one streak of light,
    One ray of God's good mercy gild
      The darkness of their night.

"In palaces are hearts that ask,
      In discontent and pride,
    Why life is such a dreary task,
      And all good things denied.
    And hearts in poorest huts admire
      How love has in their aid
    (Love that not ever seems to tire)
      Such rich provision made."

TRENCH.

CHAPTER I.

THE DUTY OF HAPPINESS.

"If a man is unhappy, this must be his own fault; for
    God made all men to be happy."--EPICTETUS.

Life is a great gift, and as we reach years of discretion, we most of us
naturally ask ourselves what should be the main object of our existence.
Even those who do not accept "the greatest good of the greatest number" as
an absolute rule, will yet admit that we should all endeavor to contribute
as far as we may to the happiness of our fellow-creatures. There are many,
however, who seem to doubt whether it is right that we should try to be
happy ourselves. Our own happiness ought not, of course, to be our main
object, nor indeed will it ever be secured if selfishly sought. We may
have many pleasures in life, but must not let them have rule over us, or
they will soon hand us over to sorrow; and "into what dangerous and
miserable servitude doth he fall who suffereth pleasures and sorrows (two
unfaithful and cruel commanders) to possess him successively?" [1]

books.title: The Way to Wealth
books.author: Benjamin Franklin
books.subject: business
books.licence_note: Author died 1790. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Benjamin Franklin, through Father Abraham, says we are taxed far more by our idleness, pride and folly than by any government, and that these taxes cannot be lifted by an abatement.
Benjamin Franklin argues that time is the stuff life is made of, so wasting it is the greatest extravagance, since lost time is never found again.
Benjamin Franklin holds that wishing for better times achieves nothing, since industry must make them better, and that work done today is worth two lots of work put off until tomorrow.
Benjamin Franklin says leisure belongs to those who use their time well, and that an owner must oversee his own affairs, since leaving workers unwatched is like leaving one's purse open.
Benjamin Franklin warns that trusting too much to others is the ruin of many, since a little neglect can breed great mischief, and that a person's own careful attention is what pays.
Benjamin Franklin warns that many small expenses add up to ruin, and that buying what we do not need is a poor bargain however cheap it looks.
Benjamin Franklin says it is easier to suppress the first desire than to satisfy all the ones that follow, and that pride in appearances only brings envy and misfortune.
Benjamin Franklin warns that debt gives another person power over your freedom, and that the shame of unpaid debts can slide a person into evasion and, eventually, into lying.
Benjamin Franklin says gain may be temporary and uncertain while expense is constant, so it is better to go to bed supperless than to rise in debt.
Benjamin Franklin notes that his listeners approved his advice and then bought extravagantly anyway, so good sense has to be practised as well as admired.

preview.text:
I. 'It would be thought a hard government that should tax its people
one-tenth part of their time to be employed in its service: but
idleness taxes many of us much more; sloth, by bringing on diseases,
absolutely shortens life.

[Illustration: Published by W. Darton, Junr. Octr. 1, 1805.]

"Sloth, like rust, consumes faster than labour wears, while the used
key is always bright," as Poor Richard says.--"But, dost thou love
life? then do not squander time, for that is the stuff life is made
of," as Poor Richard says.--How much more than is necessary do we spend
in sleep! forgetting that, "the sleeping fox catches no poultry, and
that there will be sleeping enough in the grave," as Poor Richard says.

[Illustration]

"If time be of all things the most precious, wasting time must be" as
Poor Richard says, "the greatest prodigality;" since, as he elsewhere
tells us, "Lost time is never found again; and what we call time
enough, always proves little enough." Let us then up and be doing,
and doing to the purpose: so by diligence shall we do more with less
perplexity. "Sloth makes all things difficult, but industry all easy;
and he that riseth late, must trot all day, and shall scarce overtake
his business at night; while laziness travels so slowly, that poverty
soon overtakes him. Drive thy business, let not that drive thee; and
early to bed, and early to rise, makes a man healthy, wealthy, and
wise," as Poor Richard says.

[Illustration: The Sun shone yesterday, and I would not work, to-day it
rains and I cannot work.]

books.title: Acres of Diamonds
books.author: Russell H. Conwell
books.subject: business
books.licence_note: Author died 1925. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Russell H. Conwell held that every town fails to do something, and that the chance to make more of yourself usually lies in your own surroundings, with your own skill, energy and friends.
In Acres of Diamonds, Ali Hafed grows poor not from losing anything but from discontent, fearing he is poor and so wanting more.
In Acres of Diamonds, Ali Hafed sells his farm to chase a fortune far away and ends in ruin, a warning against overlooking what is already yours.
Conwell's old guide held that Ali Hafed could have found his acres of diamonds by digging on land he already owned, since the treasure lay in the ground under his own feet.
Conwell warns that leaving one job before you have another is a foolish move, so secure the next step before you let go of the current one.
In Acres of Diamonds, the farmer learns oil from its origins to its refining, so that he can honestly say he understands the business before he asks for work in it.
In Acres of Diamonds, a young mining engineer turns down a raise he thinks too small and runs off after riches, while his mother reminds him that being happy matters as much as being rich.
Conwell tells of a mineralogy professor who sold his family homestead while a block of silver sat in its stone wall, because he never looked at what was in front of him.
Conwell admits that we all overlook what is near us, so we have little right to laugh at the man who sold the silver without looking.
Conwell notes that young people are the most open to opportunity, because they have not yet grown into prejudices or customs they cannot break.
Conwell holds that getting rich honestly is a worthy aim, and that ordinary people with little capital can find real chances to build wealth where they already live.
Conwell argues that money is a kind of power, and that a person can do more good with it than without it, as long as the spirit using it is right.
Conwell points out that the Bible warns about the love of money, not money itself, and that quoting a source carefully matters more than quoting it quickly.
Conwell says the real danger with money is idolising it, hoarding it instead of asking what it is for, and he counts that miserly habit as the root of evil.
Drawing on his father's country store, Conwell admits that turning customers away with a shrug is poor business, and that a shop should meet what its neighbours actually need.
Conwell argues that a fair profit is honest, but each sale should leave the buyer as well served as the seller, so both can prosper.
Conwell holds that treating others fairly and sharing the gains gives a clear conscience and is the surest road to lasting wealth, while urging people to enjoy life along the way.
Conwell says a business succeeds when its owner takes a real interest in the neighbours who buy from them, learning their needs, rather than shrugging off their affairs.
Conwell argues that capital is not what makes a person rich, and that inherited money can be a burden to someone who has not yet grown through their own experience.
Conwell says the deepest satisfaction comes from a home you have earned yourself, saved for step by step, rather than one handed to you.
Conwell says a rich man's son gains the discipline of hard work only by starting at the bottom, as the elder Vanderbilt did, rather than by being handed everything.
Conwell tells how A. T. Stewart, after a costly early loss on goods nobody wanted, learnt that success comes from first finding out what people need and then supplying it.
Conwell argues that who you are matters more than where you are, and that a person who cannot get rich in one city is unlikely to find it in a bigger one.
John Jacob Astor saved a failing millinery shop by watching what customers liked and having the stock made only to match it, rather than pouring in more money.
Conwell says that knowing what people need is worth more than any amount of capital, because it tells you where a fortune is before you spend a dollar.
Conwell tells of a Hingham carpenter who learnt what to make by asking his own children, judging what others want by what his own household wanted.
Conwell notes that a person who quietly makes up their mind to act, and says nothing about it, usually does it, as the woman who improved the collar button did.
Conwell says wealth is often too near to see, and that people look straight over the opportunity sitting right under their own chin.
Conwell says greatness is usually plain, practical and easy to overlook in the neighbours we see every day, so the great people around us are often unrecognised.
Conwell confesses he was more afraid walking into the President's office than under shellfire, and says courage is simply going in anyway, even when you feel afraid.
Conwell says Abraham Lincoln's rule for greatness was to put his whole mind into whatever he had to do, and hold it there until the task was finished.

Conwell tells of an injured factory worker who put a rubber on the end of a stick to erase faster, and whose daughter saw that the idea was worth protecting, so useful ideas often come out of ordinary work.
Conwell argues that communities fall behind when their own people talk their city down, and that people should talk up and back what they already have.
Conwell says that if you are not great before you get an office, you will not be great when you hold it, so greatness has to come first.
Conwell argues that a humble person who does their full duty deserves as much honour as the leader in front, and that history too often credits only one name.
Conwell tells of a man who won a speaking role through his office but had never practised speaking, and says a title does not make a speaker, which takes practice from the start.
Conwell says the real honour belongs to the ordinary soldiers doing their duty, who are often forgotten when all the praise goes to one leader at the front.
Conwell concludes that greatness comes from doing great deeds from ordinary life, and that anyone who wants to be great must begin where they are, by making their own town better.
Robert Shackleton says Conwell's power lay in making his church and talks interesting, so attention came first and inspiration followed, as Howells had noticed of the Lexington congregation.
Robert Shackleton describes Conwell as a dreamer whose dreams became facts, because he paired his vision with practical effort, patience and earnestness.
Conwell admits he once mocked his devout young servant for reading the Bible, and that the servant's steady faithfulness outlasted the mockery, showing how much patience and kindness can teach.
Shackleton relates that after a young friend died for him, Conwell vowed to live his own life and the friend's too, a vow that shaped everything he did afterwards.
Shackleton argues that Conwell's real force in the world came from who he was, not from his office as a minister, since his character did the work.
Shackleton notes that as a lawyer Conwell would take only cases he believed were right, and would not fight on the wrong side, however good the fee.
Shackleton recounts that Conwell defended a wrongly accused young man, who later confessed and lived honestly, suggesting that a fair hearing can turn a person toward honesty.
Shackleton recounts that Lincoln, after a clumsy start, set aside his written speech and spoke freely with conviction, a lesson in trusting your own voice when it counts.
Shackleton tells of Conwell asking a dwindling Lexington congregation why not start over, showing how one leader's question can turn a sense of ending into a new beginning.
Shackleton tells how Conwell began tearing down a rundown church before anyone else arrived, and how his visible commitment drew a donor, showing that effort often attracts the help it needs.
Conwell kept quietly at the work while doubters said the money would never come, and his steady effort won the doubters over, a lesson in showing commitment rather than arguing for it.
Shackleton says Conwell's triumphs came from putting his enthusiasm into others, so that each step forward was shared with the people around him rather than carried alone.
Conwell tells of a little girl who saved pennies for a church building she would not live to see, showing how small, steady gifts can build something that lasts.
Shackleton describes how Conwell's church inscribed the name of every helper, even those who gave a single dollar, into its walls, to show that the house belongs to the people who built it.
Conwell argues that aiming big can be the safer course, since a modest building would have left his church weighed down by debt for years.
Conwell wrote that enthusiasm invites enthusiasm, and that a speaker must have a large-hearted regard for the audience, which he treated as the heart of good oratory.
Conwell's advice to speakers is to be truthful and scrupulously clear, and to use illustrations that really illustrate the point, not decorate it.
Conwell wrote that a man has no right to use words carelessly, and that a speaker should be intensely in earnest, a principle he lived by in both pulpit and conversation.
Shackleton describes Conwell aiming to preach so simply that listeners felt they were hearing a friend, and holding that everything should be put so that all can understand it.
Conwell turned a dry line of scripture into a living picture by naming the little church on the hill, showing that a concrete image makes an idea come alive for listeners.
Shackleton notes that people who do big things also keep hold of small details, such as the exact street number a funeral needed, and that attention to detail earns trust.
Conwell's favourite maxim, trust in God and do the next thing, is a plain way to keep moving through difficulty without waiting to see the whole path ahead.

preview.text:
As a student, schoolmaster, lawyer, preacher, organizer, thinker and
writer, lecturer, educator, diplomat, and leader of men, he has made his
mark on his city and state and the times in which he has lived. A man
dies, but his good work lives.

His ideas, ideals, and enthusiasms have inspired tens of thousands of
lives. A book full of the energetics of a master workman is just what
every young man cares for.

1915. {signature}

ACRES OF DIAMONDS

_Friends_.--This lecture has been delivered under these circumstances:
I visit a town or city, and try to arrive there early enough to see the
postmaster, the barber, the keeper of the hotel, the principal of the
schools, and the ministers of some of the churches, and then go into
some of the factories and stores, and talk with the people, and get into
sympathy with the local conditions of that town or city and see what
has been their history, what opportunities they had, and what they had
failed to do--and every town fails to do something--and then go to the
lecture and talk to those people about the subjects which applied to
their locality. “Acres of Diamonds”--the idea--has continuously been
precisely the same. The idea is that in this country of ours every man
has the opportunity to make more of himself than he does in his own
environment, with his own skill, with his own energy, and with his own
friends.                    RUSSELL H. CONWELL.

ACRES OF DIAMONDS
[1]

books.title: As a Man Thinketh
books.author: James Allen
books.subject: habits
books.licence_note: Author died 1912. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: James Allen argues that people are makers of themselves, since the mind weaves both their character and the circumstances they meet, so they can choose to weave with more understanding.
James Allen holds that every act grows from a seed of thought, so character is the lasting result of the thoughts a person keeps returning to and acting on.
James Allen urges readers to watch and alter their thoughts, tracing the effects on themselves and their circumstances, as a patient practice of self-understanding that grows wisdom over time.
James Allen compares the mind to a garden that will bring forth whether cultivated or neglected, so the sensible course is to weed out wrong thoughts and grow useful ones on purpose.
James Allen says good thoughts bear good fruit and bad thoughts bear bad, so the habits of mind a person nurtures shape the life they receive over time.
James Allen holds that circumstance does not make a person but reveals them to themselves, since the inner thoughts a person has long nurtured are what the hour of opportunity brings out.
James Allen says people attract not what they want but what they are, and that fighting circumstances is often fighting an effect while still feeding its cause.
James Allen notes that a worker who shirks and deceives his employer while hoping for better pay is working against the very prosperity he wants, because his habits undo his aims.
James Allen warns against judging a person's inner life from outward circumstances, since an honest person may suffer and a dishonest one may prosper, and a shallow view misses this.
James Allen says a person begins to grow when they stop blaming others and look for what their circumstances can teach them, using hard situations as aids to progress.
James Allen holds that as a person changes how they think about things and people, those things and people tend to change in response, so the work starts inside.
James Allen shows how thoughts crystallise into habits, and habits solidify into circumstances, so changing a habit is the practical way to change one's situation.
James Allen says a person cannot choose their circumstances directly but can choose their thoughts, and so shape their circumstances indirectly but surely over time.
James Allen argues that until thought is linked with a central purpose there is no intelligent accomplishment, since thinking that drifts without aim leads only to worry and loss.
James Allen says a person should set a purpose and steadily focus their thoughts on it, and that even repeated failure builds the strength of character that becomes the start of later success.
James Allen says doubt and fear break up the straight line of effort, and that the will to act springs from knowing one can act, so doubt is the enemy to be dismissed.
James Allen holds that a strong person cannot lift a weaker one unless the weaker is willing, and that each person must develop by their own effort the strength they admire in others.
James Allen says progress requires giving up some lower impulses, since a mind given over to indulgence cannot plan clearly or stand on its own, and each person can lift their thoughts.

James Allen says the size of an achievement follows the size of the sacrifice made, and that business, learning and spiritual goals all rest on the same directed thought, differing only in their object.
James Allen holds that a person who cherishes a lofty vision and stays true to it will one day build it, citing Columbus and Copernicus as dreamers whose visions came to pass.
James Allen says dreams are the seedlings of realities, and that a person who holds a clear ideal and strives for it can outgrow even a hard workshop.
James Allen holds that a person becomes as small as their controlling desire and as great as their dominant aspiration, so the aims a person chooses shape how far they go.
James Allen says people who call others lucky see only the result and not the effort behind it, and that the strength of effort is the true measure of what a person achieves.
James Allen argues that calm self-control makes a person more trusted, and that people prefer to deal with someone whose manner is steady, which helps any business.
James Allen concludes that self-control is strength, right thought is mastery and calm is power, the qualities that let a person steer their own life.

preview.text:
As the plant springs from, and could not be without, the seed, so
every act of a man springs from the hidden seeds of thought, and
could not have appeared without them. This applies equally to those
acts called "spontaneous" and "unpremeditated" as to those, which
are deliberately executed.

Act is the blossom of thought, and joy and suffering are its fruits;
thus does a man garner in the sweet and bitter fruitage of his own
husbandry.

"Thought in the mind hath made us, What we are
  By thought was wrought and built. If a man's mind
  Hath evil thoughts, pain comes on him as comes
  The wheel the ox behind....

..If one endure
  In purity of thought, joy follows him
  As his own shadow--sure."

Man is a growth by law, and not a creation by artifice, and cause
and effect is as absolute and undeviating in the hidden realm of
thought as in the world of visible and material things. A noble and
Godlike character is not a thing of favour or chance, but is the
natural result of continued effort in right thinking, the effect of
long-cherished association with Godlike thoughts. An ignoble and
bestial character, by the same process, is the result of the
continued harbouring of grovelling thoughts.

Man is made or unmade by himself; in the armoury of thought he
forges the weapons by which he destroys himself; he also fashions
the tools with which he builds for himself heavenly mansions of joy
and strength and peace. By the right choice and true application of
thought, man ascends to the Divine Perfection; by the abuse and
wrong application of thought, he descends below the level of the
beast. Between these two extremes are all the grades of character,
and man is their maker and master.

books.title: Character
books.author: Samuel Smiles
books.subject: habits
books.licence_note: Author died 1904. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Samuel Smiles held that character outlasts genius in the long run, because the heart rules in life more than the brain does.
Samuel Smiles held that you can judge a person's character by how they treat those closest to them and how they handle ordinary daily duties.
Samuel Smiles held that learning must be allied to goodness, because a clever person can still lack honesty and a sense of duty.
Samuel Smiles held that character is a kind of property, an estate of goodwill and respect that pays off for those who invest in it.
Samuel Smiles held that a steady purpose, built on sound principles, holds a person straight, and that without principles a person drifts like a ship without a rudder.
Epictetus taught that a person with firm principles and few wants is richer than one who depends on status and possessions.
Samuel Smiles held that truthfulness is the foundation of personal excellence, because people trust someone who does what they say.
Samuel Smiles observed that people of pure and noble aims exert quiet influence beyond their intellect, and that true character cannot be hidden for long.
Samuel Smiles held that character is formed by small everyday choices, so a person should never give way to what seems little.
Samuel Smiles held that good character needs constant self-watchfulness and self-control, and that aiming higher improves us even when we fall short.
Samuel Smiles described character as conduct guided by principle and practical wisdom, which chooses its way carefully and keeps to it, even when that is unpopular.
Samuel Smiles held that energy without integrity can be destructive, while energy governed by duty is just, honest and generous even to opponents.
Samuel Smiles held that the man of character puts his conscience into his work, his words and every action.
Samuel Smiles held that reverence for high aims and good people is essential to trust, faith and social progress, because it binds people together.
Samuel Smiles held that energy of will, a self-originating force, is the soul of great character, and that a strong person carves a path and carries others with them.
Samuel Smiles quotes Gladstone on Palmerston, whose force of will and sense of duty kept the weight of age at bay, and whose freedom from anger came naturally rather than through effort.
Samuel Smiles held that a leader of courtesy, courage and disinterestedness draws out the admiration and best effort of the people who follow them.
Samuel Smiles held that a person of upright character in a position of trust lifts up everyone who serves under them, and they feel their own power grow.
Samuel Smiles held that the thoughts and acts of great people outlive them and help shape the character of later generations, like lights set on a hill.
Samuel Smiles held that a great thinker's ideas can outlive them by centuries, slowly working their way into everyday life and practice.
