Samuel Smiles held that a leader's greatness lies more in honour, integrity, truthfulness and a sense of duty than in intellect or skill.
In Samuel Smiles's account, Walter Scott judged a nation's character by its ordinary working people rather than its fine folk, since they form the real backbone of a country.
Samuel Smiles held that a nation's character rests on the moral qualities of its ordinary people, because a corrupt people will in the end be ruled by rogues.
Samuel Smiles held that personal character is the real safeguard of liberty, since political rights alone will not lift a people whose individuals are debased.
Samuel Smiles held that a nation's character is built through trial and suffering nobly borne, and that noisy nationalism is no substitute for honest work.
Samuel Smiles recounts Colbert telling Louis XIV that a country's greatness depends on the character of its people, not the size of its territory.
Samuel Smiles held that the stability of institutions depends on the integrity of individual character, and that a people living only for pleasure is doomed.
Samuel Smiles held that the home is the first and most important school of character, where the habits and principles that last a lifetime are formed.
Samuel Smiles held that a child's first great instructor is example, since children learn by imitation almost without effort, long before any formal lessons.
Samuel Smiles held that the bias given to a person's character in early life is of immense importance, because the young are so easily shaped by their surroundings.
Samuel Smiles held that if we want fine characters, we must present them with fine models, because people copy what they see every day.
Samuel Smiles likened small daily acts to snowflakes: each one seems trivial, but repeated acts harden into habit and build up into character, like an avalanche.
Samuel Smiles held that people follow example far more than precept, and that saying one thing while doing another teaches hypocrisy, which children see through.
Samuel Smiles recounts how Augustine's mother Monica prayed and counselled her wayward son for years, and her steady example eventually shaped his character.
Samuel Smiles held that lessons absorbed in childhood can lie dormant for decades and then spring up as good conduct, so sincere effort in raising children is never wasted.
Samuel Smiles held that a good home is the best school, in youth and in age, where people learn cheerfulness, patience, self-control and a sense of service.
Samuel Smiles held that quiet, patient effort in ordinary duty shapes character in ways that are rarely recorded, but whose influence goes on for generations.
Samuel Smiles recounts how Washington's mother raised five children alone after her husband died, through good sense, industry, vigilance and tenderness.
Samuel Smiles recounts Wesley's mother urging her son to organise his work by method and to act on principle, so that every precious moment is used well.
Samuel Smiles recounts Ary Scheffer's mother advising him to stay modest and to measure his best work against his own ideal, not against others, to guard against pride.
Samuel Smiles quotes Ary Scheffer saying that the moments he valued most were those in which he made sacrifices or denied himself enjoyments.
Samuel Smiles held that method is the soul of business, since work only gets done when it is organised, and that punctuality is part of method.
Samuel Smiles held that prudence is practical wisdom that grows from cultivated judgment and experience, and that it means weighing the right means, order and timing before acting.
Samuel Smiles argued that the education which fills a man's mind is equally good for a woman, because intelligence gives strength, foresight and better methods in every part of life.
Owen Feltham advised that we should copy the best examples and never rest until we equal or excel them, as a painter copies the finest work.
Samuel Smiles held that custom and example slowly consolidate into habit, and that habit can take hold of us so quietly that we give up our freedom before we notice.
Samuel Smiles recounts Plato telling a boy that custom is not a little thing, since bad habits become a tyranny that people cling to even while they curse them.
Samuel Smiles held that the young need not simply copy those around them, because each person has the will to choose their own friends and conduct.
Samuel Smiles held that people are known by the company they keep, and that living among good people lifts us up while bad company drags us down.
Samuel Smiles held that time with wiser and more experienced people enlarges our view of life, while living alone can leave us blind to the needs of others.
Samuel Smiles recounts how Henry Martyn, a nervous boy, was steadied for life by an older friend who guarded him, guided him and kept him on the right path.
Samuel Smiles recounts how a friend's honest, caring warning woke Paley from idleness, and he became one of the most industrious students of his year.
Samuel Smiles describes Dr Arnold trusting pupils with a share of responsibility for their school, which gave them strength and self-respect and lifted the whole place.
Samuel Smiles held that a great teacher's example teaches young people to respect themselves, and that self-respect is the root from which the manly virtues grow.
Samuel Smiles held that a person of good character sets the tone for everyone in a workshop, just as a person of bad character drags the others down.
Samuel Smiles quotes George Herbert saying that people need good examples more than precepts, because a good life persuades more powerfully than any words.
Samuel Smiles held that the portrait of a good person hung on a wall is a kind of companionship, linking us to a better nature and steadying us when we might otherwise do wrong.
Samuel Smiles recounts Tyndall on Faraday, whose strength was joined to modesty, tenderness and sweetness, and whose contact warmed and elevated those around him.
Samuel Smiles recounts Marshall Hall telling young men to take up a subject and pursue it well, since a new idea is worth chasing if you pursue it with energy.
Samuel Smiles held that energy in one person awakens energy in others through sympathy, so an earnest person carries those around them along without trying.

preview.text:
When Dr. Abbot, afterwards Archbishop of Canterbury, drew the character
of his deceased friend Thomas Sackville, [101] he did not dwell upon his
merits as a statesman, or his genius as a poet, but upon his virtues as
a man in relation to the ordinary duties of life. "How many rare things
were in him!" said he. "Who more loving unto his wife? Who more kind
unto his children?--Who more fast unto his friend?--Who more moderate
unto his enemy?--Who more true to his word?" Indeed, we can always
better understand and appreciate a man's real character by the manner in
which he conducts himself towards those who are the most nearly related
to him, and by his transaction of the seemingly commonplace details of
daily duty, than by his public exhibition of himself as an author, an
orator, or a statesman.

At the same time, while Duty, for the most part, applies to the conduct
of affairs in common life by the average of common men, it is also a
sustaining power to men of the very highest standard of character. They
may not have either money, or property, or learning, or power; and
yet they may be strong in heart and rich in spirit--honest, truthful,
dutiful. And whoever strives to do his duty faithfully is fulfilling
the purpose for which he was created, and building up in himself the
principles of a manly character. There are many persons of whom it
may be said that they have no other possession in the world but their
character, and yet they stand as firmly upon it as any crowned king.

books.title: Plutarch's Lives
books.author: Plutarch
books.subject: history
books.licence_note: Author died about 120, editor died 1861. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Plutarch says that where legend resists probable fact, he lets reason refine it as far as it can, and asks readers to weigh old stories fairly.
Plutarch says that great founders can still carry serious faults, noting that Theseus and Romulus both faced jealousy and domestic trouble despite their greatness.
Plutarch shows how a vague oracle can be bent to suit whoever wants a certain answer, as Pittheus did when he persuaded Aegeus.
Plutarch has Theseus take the dangerous road to Athens rather than the safe sea route, wanting to prove himself by his own deeds.
Plutarch shows Theseus shamed by the thought of fleeing the dangers Hercules faced, so he chooses to meet them and make his name by action.
Plutarch weighs rival accounts of Sciron by asking which version fits the character of the men involved, a habit of judging old stories by probability.
Plutarch describes Theseus punishing each robber with the same cruelty that robber used on others, so the punishment fits the crime.
Plutarch has Theseus let his father recognise him through the sword token rather than announce himself, so the truth comes out at the right moment.
Plutarch shows Theseus defeating a conspiracy because a crier passed on the enemy's plans, a reminder that good information can beat brute strength.
Plutarch notes that Hecale's hospitality to Theseus was honoured for generations, showing that small kindnesses can outlast great deeds.
Plutarch notes that the Athenian stage painted Minos as a villain, though he was in fact a king and lawgiver, a reminder that storytellers shape how people are remembered.
Plutarch has Theseus offer himself for the tribute without waiting for the lot, choosing to share his people's suffering rather than stand apart from it.
Plutarch shows Theseus preparing his fleet in secret, in quiet places far from common roads, so he arrives before his enemies know he is coming.
Plutarch shows how one forgotten signal, a black sail left up instead of the white, costs Aegeus his life, as joy over success made Theseus neglect a small detail.
Plutarch notes that the Athenians kept replacing the planks of Theseus's ship, which led philosophers to ask whether a thing with all its parts replaced is still the same thing.
Plutarch describes Theseus uniting scattered towns by going from township to township and persuading them, then giving up kingly power to earn their trust.
Plutarch says Theseus welcomed strangers as equals while still giving the growing city clear order and roles, so that openness did not turn into confusion.
Plutarch admits that history from such ancient times is in disorder, so he weighs each surviving trace of the past and trusts it only as far as the evidence goes.
Plutarch sorts old stories by testing them, dismissing a poem's tale as invention while accepting another that the historians do not contradict.
Plutarch tells how Theseus, instead of punishing Pirithous for seizing his oxen, forgave him and made him a lifelong friend, turning a rival into a companion.
Plutarch describes Menestheus winning the crowd by stirring old grudges and promising a dream of liberty, a warning about how easily resentment can be turned against a leader.
Plutarch shows Theseus returning to find the people expecting flattery rather than obedience, and losing ground to factions, a lesson about leading those who have grown used to being pleased.
Plutarch notes that Athenians made Theseus's tomb a refuge for the weak and afflicted, honouring a man who never turned away those who came to him for help.
Plutarch notes that the old authors disagree even about how Rome got its name, a reminder that the origins of great things are often contested.
Plutarch says Romulus and Remus spent their youth on hunting, running and defending the wronged rather than idleness, and that Romulus acted by counsel, which marked him as a leader.
Plutarch has Remus praise a ruler who hears the case before punishing, against one who condemns before the cause is heard, a principle of fair process.
Plutarch observes that people who act out of fear or passion tend to make hasty mistakes, as the tyrant Amulius did when he sent for news of the twins.
Plutarch describes Romulus founding a refuge that welcomed fugitives, servants and debtors, which helped the young city grow quickly, a lesson that openness draws people in.
Plutarch recounts how Remus mocked the work on the city wall and was killed in the quarrel that followed, a warning about scorning the efforts of people building something together.
Plutarch describes the old patron and client bond, where the powerful owed protection and the less powerful gave loyalty, so that each side kept faith with the other.
Plutarch credits much of Rome's growth to its habit of incorporating the peoples it conquered as citizens rather than leaving them outside, a point about how inclusion builds strength.
Plutarch observes that those who profit from a traitor's help tend to despise the traitor once the work is done, a reminder that someone who betrays for a reward will betray again.
Plutarch describes Romulus, wounded and with his army in flight, turning to face them and calling them back, so that shame and respect for their leader stopped the retreat.
Plutarch tells how the women who had been carried off stepped between the armies and begged for peace, ending the battle by appealing to the love both sides had for them.
Plutarch shows how a leader who delays punishing a crime lets the quarrel grow, as Tatius's failure to act on a murder led to his own killing.
Plutarch says Romulus, raised by great success, grew haughty and dropped the popular manner that had won him support, as many who rise by good fortune do.
Plutarch shows how a leader who makes decisions without the council meant to advise him breeds suspicion, so that when Romulus vanished the senate fell under blame.
Plutarch shows Romans readily accepting a sworn tale of Romulus's ascent while they were grieving, a reminder that people in grief tend to believe comforting accounts.
Plutarch recounts the servant Philotis, who, rather than let the Romans either fight or hand over their women, set a false signal that let them ambush the enemy, a lesson in finding a third way.
Plutarch contrasts a man who takes on hard things by free choice with one who grows brave only from necessity, suggesting the braver act is the one chosen when you need not act.
Plutarch says a leader who is too lax or too harsh loses respect, one through easiness and the other through pride, so a good leader must avoid both extremes.
Plutarch admits the historians disagree so much about Lycurgus that little is certain, so he follows the accounts least contradicted, a sound method for any uncertain history.
Plutarch says that when Eurypon loosened the strict monarchy to win popularity, later kings were pushed into force or weakness, and disorder followed, showing how small concessions compound.
Plutarch has Lycurgus refuse a wicked offer from the queen and hold power only as guardian for the child, earning a trust that his rivals could not match.
Plutarch says Lycurgus went abroad to avoid envy at home, studying other peoples' laws and keeping only the parts that would serve his own country.
Plutarch says Lycurgus valued Homer for its serious lessons on conduct and gathered them, judging that the good outweighed the poor lines.
Plutarch notes that the Spartans wanted a leader whose character itself earned obedience, not one who only held the titles of royalty.
Plutarch has Lycurgus argue that a few patched laws cannot cure a sick state, which needs a full change of its basic arrangements, much as a physician treats a complicated illness.
Plutarch praises Lycurgus's senate as ballast in a ship, keeping the state steady between the pull of monarchy on one side and mob rule on the other.
Plutarch tells how king Theopompus, asked whether he left his heirs less power, replied that he left them greater, since it would last longer, showing that yielding a little can keep the whole.
Plutarch notes that when the trade in luxuries was cut off, Spartan craftsmen turned their skill to plain, useful things and made them well, a lesson that good work can come from simplicity.
Plutarch tells how Lycurgus, struck and blinded by a hot-tempered young man, answered with calm and then kept him close, and the young man became one of the city's most steady citizens.
Plutarch says the shared meals taught young men temperance and listening to older statesmen, and kept a rule that no words went out of the room, a lesson in discretion.
Plutarch says Lycurgus would not write his laws down, trusting that good education would form the habits the law exists to protect, and keeping minor rules open to change.
Plutarch says Lycurgus warned against fighting the same enemy too often, since that trains them to be better soldiers, a lesson that rivals grow sharper from every contest with you.
Plutarch says the Spartan boys were trained to judge people and things quickly and to give a reason in as few words as possible, a skill any leader still needs.
Plutarch notes that people who talk loosely seldom say many sensible things, and admires the Spartan habit of saying much in few words, a good test for anyone who speaks for a living.
Plutarch records the Spartan saying that whoever knows how to speak also knows when to, so timing matters as much as the words themselves.
Plutarch describes Spartan soldiers marching calmly in step, moved by steady hope rather than fury, and stopping the chase once the enemy gave up, which he calls both noble and wise.
Plutarch credits Lycurgus with helping to set up the sacred truce for the Olympic games, which he takes as a sign of a man who loved peace and quiet.

preview.text:
As geographers, Sosius, crowd into the edges of their maps parts of the
world which they do not know about, adding notes in the margin to the
effect, that beyond this lies nothing but sandy deserts full of wild
beasts, unapproachable bogs, Scythian ice, or a frozen sea, so, in this
work of mine, in which I have compared the lives of the greatest men
with one another, after passing through those periods which probable
reasoning can reach to and real history find a footing in, I might very
well say of those that are farther off, Beyond this there is nothing but
prodigies and fictions, the only inhabitants are the poets and inventors
of fables; there is no credit, or certainty any farther.  Yet, after
publishing an account of Lycurgus the lawgiver and Numa the king, I
thought I might, not without reason, ascend as high as to Romulus, being
brought by my history so near to his time.
Considering therefore with myself

Whom shall I set so great a man to face?
Or whom oppose?  who's equal to the place?

(as Aeschylus expresses it), I found none so fit as him that peopled the
beautiful and far-famed city of Athens, to be set in opposition with the
father of the invincible and renowned city of Rome.  Let us hope that
Fable may, in what shall follow, so submit to the purifying processes of
Reason as to take the character of exact history.  In any case, however,
where it shall be found contumaciously slighting credibility, and
refusing to be reduced to anything like probable fact, we shall beg
that we may meet with candid readers, and such as will receive with
indulgence the stories of antiquity.

Theseus seemed to me to resemble Romulus in many particulars.  Both of
them, born out of wedlock and of uncertain parentage, had the repute of
being sprung from the gods.

books.title: Up from Slavery
books.author: Booker T. Washington
books.subject: habits
books.licence_note: Author died 1915. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In Up From Slavery, Washington declines a clergyman's title he has not earned and judges his work by its practical results. Be accurate about what you actually do.
The introduction to Up From Slavery describes skilled, responsible work as a form of education and character. Real skills change the economic life of a person and a people.
The introduction to Up From Slavery says a plan is easy to work out on paper. The real test is carrying it out with rough material, in hard conditions, and with the people around you against you.
The introduction to Up From Slavery describes students studying real families and building a plan from the resources those families already have. Learning from real life beats the textbook.
In the introduction to Up From Slavery, Walter Page notes that Washington won Southern support by working with local opinion, since no plan could succeed if it ran against it.
In Up From Slavery, Washington recalls that a schoolroom looked like paradise to a boy who was denied one. Being kept from something can teach you to value it for the rest of your life.
In Up From Slavery, Washington's older brother wears a painful new shirt in his place until it is worn soft. A small act of sacrifice like that is worth noticing and returning.
In Up From Slavery, a freed man walks back to Virginia to pay off his last debt, because he gave his word. A promise kept at real cost is worth keeping.
Washington argues that slavery made manual work look degrading, so owners' children learned no trade and lost self-reliance. How people regard work shapes what they can do.
In Up From Slavery, the sudden weight of responsibility after freedom turns joy into gloom. Big change brings its own load, and people need time and planning to carry it.
In Up From Slavery, Washington teaches himself the alphabet from an old spelling book with no teacher. A steady, stubborn wish to learn can make up for having nobody to help.
In Up From Slavery, Washington describes a whole community of old and young crowding into schools after freedom. A hunger to learn, held in common, can lift everyone.
When Washington is kept from day school, he arranges night lessons and learns a great deal from them. When one route is blocked, look for another that still gets you there.
In Up From Slavery, Washington's mother refuses to buy a store hat on credit and sews a cap from cloth instead. Living within what you can pay for is a source of pride.
Washington notes that inherited name and fortune can tempt a person to lean on ancestry instead of effort. He resolved to build his own record so his children would have one to be proud of.

In Up From Slavery, Washington measures success by the obstacles a person has overcome rather than the position they reach. The hard struggle gives a strength and confidence that an easy path does not.
Washington says that real merit, whatever its background, is in the long run recognised and rewarded. Borrowed rank without personal worth will not carry anyone far.
In Up From Slavery, Washington hears of a school and fixes on it day and night, even without knowing where it is. A clear goal held steadily can pull you forward through hardship.
Under Mrs Ruffner, Washington learns that cleanliness, promptness, system and absolute honesty matter. He comes to notice every loose board and grease spot, and good order becomes a habit.
In Up From Slavery, Washington starts his first library in a dry-goods box with a few shelves. Start with what you have, and build it up book by book.

In Up From Slavery, Washington passes his entrance test by sweeping and dusting a room over and over, because he knows a strict inspector will check every corner. Do the plain job as if someone will look closely.
In Up From Slavery, Washington says that daily contact with a great person teaches more than books and costly equipment. He wishes schools would study people and things, not only books.
Washington describes General Armstrong, even while paralysed, losing sight of himself and working for others. Real leadership shows in how little a person thinks of their own interests.
In Up From Slavery, students volunteer to live in cold tents because it pleases the teacher they respect and makes room for others. A shared purpose makes hardship bearable.
In Up From Slavery, Washington says he never had patience for people who always explain why success is impossible. He also found that the happiest people are those who do the most for others.
Washington recalls starting a debating society in about twenty minutes that young men had been spending in idle talk. Small pockets of unused time add up to a great deal.
In Up From Slavery, Miss Mackie, from a cultured family, cleans windows beside her students before term begins. Washington later says a school should teach students the dignity of labour.
In Up From Slavery, Washington learns at Hampton that labour is no disgrace. Being able to do something the world needs done brings a real independence and self-reliance.
Washington uses his teaching pay to help his brother through Hampton, and then the two of them help a third young man there too. Helping one person up can start a chain that carries on.
Washington warns that believing a little schooling frees a person from manual work is a mistaken idea. Learning is worth most when it is joined to honest labour.
In Up From Slavery, Washington resists the pull of politics because he believes building skill, mind and character lasts longer. Be wary of the exciting shortcut and back the slower work that holds.
In Up From Slavery, Washington finds that students who earn their own way build self-reliance that students with paid-for needs lack. Effort you make yourself is part of the building.

Washington notes that Hampton kept adapting to the real needs of its people instead of copying what was done elsewhere. Find out what the situation actually needs before you borrow someone else's model.

In Up From Slavery, Washington wins the trust of the Indian students by kindness, noting that people of every kind respond to kind treatment and resent cruelty. Patience and respect earn more than force.
Washington says he has come to see that a person lifts themselves by helping to lift others, and that the more disadvantaged the people, the more the helper grows.
Washington recalls Frederick Douglass saying that no one can degrade the soul within him. Mistreatment says more about the one who inflicts it than about the one who suffers it.

In Up From Slavery, Armstrong's night school lets earnest students work by day and study by night, saving part of their earnings to pay for their later schooling. You can earn your start while you learn.
Washington names his hardest-working night students the Plucky Class and gives them a simple certificate. Recognising effort with a plain honour encourages more of it.
Washington's chance to lead a school came when a trusted mentor put his name forward. Being willing to try, when the chance comes, opens doors you cannot knock on yourself.
When Washington reaches Tuskegee, he finds no building ready, only hungry, earnest people who want knowledge. Willing people matter more than costly buildings when you start something.
Before teaching, Washington spends his first month travelling and eating and sleeping in people's homes to see their everyday life. Learn how people really live before you design anything for them.
After a month of seeing real village life, Washington concludes that copying a book-only education would waste time. Lifting people up needs training that fits the life they actually lead.

Washington says his school's success rests on two trusted advisers, a merchant and a craftsman, who never refused help when it mattered. Find a few steady, honest people whose judgment you can rely on.
Washington argues that the craftsman Lewis Adams gained his strength of mind from mastering three trades by hand. Practical skill can train the mind as well as the hands.
Washington finds his students can recite complicated rules but cannot apply them to daily life, so he insists on mastering the basics first. Knowledge you cannot use is not yet knowledge.
Olivia Davidson refuses to hide her background to make life easier in a new school, and later gives Tuskegee years of unselfish service. Integrity under pressure tends to show its worth over time.
Washington and Olivia Davidson decide that books alone leave students unprepared. They also teach self-care, a trade, thrift and how to earn a living, so learning connects to real life.
When Washington needs a loan to buy the school's farm, he writes frankly to a friend and asks directly. Stating your situation honestly often gets you a real answer.
Washington sees his students unwilling to clear land, so he goes first each afternoon with his own axe. Leading by doing the work you ask of others wins people over.
An old woman with no money gives six eggs she has saved, because she understands what the school is trying to do. Small gifts given with real belief can mean the most.
Washington makes the school part of the community by asking local people to contribute, so they feel it belongs to them. People support what they have helped to build.
In Up From Slavery, a poor old man brings a hog to a building fund and others offer days of labour. Everyone can give something, even without money to spare.
Miss Davidson wins her first Northern gift by talking with a stranger on a boat, then keeps working tirelessly for the cause. Good support often starts with an ordinary conversation.
George Campbell tells Washington that credit is capital. Keeping your word and your reputation high is an asset you can draw on when money runs short.
Washington has his students build their own school buildings, arguing that self-help and self-reliance matter more than polished finish. Mistakes made along the way teach lessons for the future.
Washington's students build most of Tuskegee's buildings, and the skill is handed down from one group to the next. Skills that are taught and passed on keep a place running.
Washington's brickmaking fails three times before it succeeds. A task that looks simple often needs real skill, and persistence through failure is part of learning it.
Washington says the visible, tangible result of good work softens prejudice more than pages of argument. A person who supplies what the community needs will make their way.

When Washington goes north to raise funds, he is told he will never get more than his travel costs. He goes anyway and finds more welcome than he expected. Do not let discouraging advice decide for you before you have tested it.
Washington describes trustee Robert Bedford, who asks for the most disagreeable service and never seeks credit. Quiet service that others avoid earns a deep and lasting trust.

preview.text:
In turn, Samuel Armstrong, the founder of Hampton Institute, took up
his work as a trainer of youth. He had very raw material, and doubtless
most of his pupils failed to get the greatest lessons from him; but, as
he had been a peculiarly receptive pupil of Dr. Hopkins, so Booker
Washington became a peculiarly receptive pupil of his. To the formation
of Mr. Washington’s character, then, went the missionary zeal of New
England, influenced by one of the strongest personalities in modern
education, and the wide-reaching moral earnestness of General Armstrong
himself. These influences are easily recognizable in Mr. Washington
to-day by men who knew Dr. Hopkins and General Armstrong.

I got the cue to Mr. Washington’s character from a very simple incident
many years ago. I had never seen him, and I knew little about him,
except that he was the head of a school at Tuskegee, Alabama. I had
occasion to write to him, and I addressed him as “The Rev. Booker T.
Washington.” In his reply there was no mention of my addressing him as
a clergyman. But when I had occasion to write to him again, and
persisted in making him a preacher, his second letter brought a
postscript: “I have no claim to ‘Rev.’” I knew most of the coloured men
who at that time had become prominent as leaders of their race, but I
had not then known one who was neither a politician nor a preacher; and
I had not heard of the head of an important coloured school who was not
a preacher. “A new kind of man in the coloured world,” I said to
myself—“a new kind of man surely if he looks upon his task as an
economic one instead of a theological one.” I wrote him an apology for
mistaking him for a preacher.

books.title: Discourses on Livy
books.author: Niccolo Machiavelli
books.subject: strategy
books.licence_note: Author died 1527, translator died 1921. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Machiavelli notes that people judge other men's new methods more harshly than they praise them, yet a new path is still worth taking if it offers a common benefit.
Machiavelli wonders why people treasure old statues and yet never copy the ancients in government, war and leadership, even though doctors and lawyers still rely on them.
Machiavelli says most readers enjoy history for its stories and never think to imitate it, because they assume the world has changed too much. He writes to show what can still be learned from it.
Machiavelli argues that a rich land can make people soft, so the rules must impose the hardship the land does not. Good strategy balances comfort with discipline.
Machiavelli tells how Dinocrates offered Alexander a striking city design, but had not thought about how its people would live. Alexander chose a site where people could actually make a living.
Machiavelli says reforming the institutions of a state is risky, because people accept change only once the need is clear, and by then it may be too late.
Machiavelli notes that every good form of rule slides easily into its corrupt twin, monarchy into tyranny and democracy into anarchy, so no founder can make one last by design alone.
Machiavelli sees leadership move from choosing the strongest man to choosing the most prudent and just, once people learn that wrongs done to others can be done to themselves.
Machiavelli warns that good government decays when heirs, never taught by hardship, chase pleasure and privilege. Those who have never known adversity tend to lose what their elders built.
Machiavelli holds that power lasts best when its parts check each other, as Sparta's kings, nobles and people did. A single pure form of rule tends to fail quickly.
Machiavelli says people behave well mainly when compelled, so rules are needed when good habits are missing. Anyone who builds a system should start from that realism.
Machiavelli argues that open conflict between groups in a city can produce good laws, so the noise of disagreement is not always a sign of disorder.
Machiavelli says that when people's fears are groundless, an honest person speaking openly can show them they are mistaken, because people are readily persuaded by someone they trust.
Machiavelli observes that people who already hold something often fight as hard as those who want more, because they never feel secure in what they have.
Machiavelli says that in human affairs no remedy comes free of cost, so the wise choice is the course with the least inconvenience. No path avoids every disadvantage.
Machiavelli says a well-defended, non-ambitious state is seldom attacked, yet circumstances never stand still, so plans should allow for growth and for keeping what is gained.
Machiavelli argues that people need a lawful outlet for their complaints. Unless grievances are channelled through the rules, they spill out in more dangerous ways.
Machiavelli warns that when people have no lawful way to challenge a powerful figure, they turn to violence or even foreign help. Fair channels for complaint protect everyone.
Machiavelli shows how Manlius, unable to bear a rival's renown, spread rumours to stir up trouble. Envy of another person's reputation can quietly do real damage.

Machiavelli says whispered calumny needs no evidence and spreads in the streets, while proper impeachment is open and needs trustworthy proof. A fair process for accusing people is the best protection against rumour.
Machiavelli holds that a good system is usually shaped by one capable person, but lasts longer when many people share the job of keeping it.
Machiavelli warns that a founder's absolute power should not pass to an heir, since men tend toward evil more than good and the heir may use that power for selfish ends.

Machiavelli says many capable people choose the glory of domination over lasting building, forgetting how much they lose in reputation, security and peace of mind. Reading history well should steer people to the better path.
Machiavelli notes that the Roman emperors who ruled within the law needed no bodyguards, protected by good conduct and goodwill, while cruel rulers were undone by their own behaviour.

Machiavelli urges leaders to compare good reigns, which brought security, fair dealing and trust, with cruel ones that bred fear and informers. He says a leader should choose the path that leaves people safe.
Machiavelli says the surest route to lasting honour is to restore a broken institution rather than wreck it. A leader who can rebuild without giving up power has no good excuse not to.
Machiavelli says a state is safe not because its leader rules well while alive, but because things are arranged to keep working after he is gone. Good systems outlast the people who build them.
Machiavelli says people long used to being governed by others struggle to act for themselves once freed, and can quickly be brought back under a yoke. Freedom needs people who can stand on their own.
Machiavelli observes that people rarely thank those who merely leave them unharmed, and that the benefits of security are easily taken for granted until they are lost.
Machiavelli says most people ask little more than to live securely. A leader who keeps to the laws and avoids arbitrary acts will win their contentment.
Machiavelli notes that a city already corrupted is hard to free, and that one virtuous leader can keep freedom only for his own lifetime. Lasting good needs a system, not one person.
Machiavelli says good customs need good laws to support them, and good laws need good customs to be respected. Rules and habits have to be kept in step with each other.
Machiavelli points out that new rules will not hold if the underlying structures stay the same, because those structures keep pulling things back to the old way.
Machiavelli shows how a fair process can decay slowly. When office goes to those with influence rather than merit, good people stop putting themselves forward. Watch for that drift in any group.
Machiavelli notes that an open process for proposing laws works well among good citizens. When the powerful dominate it and fear silences critics, the same openness can be turned against the people.
Machiavelli says gradual reform needs someone who spots trouble early and can persuade others, and such people are rare. Men used to one way of living are slow to change.
Machiavelli concludes that a weak leader can follow a strong one, but two weak leaders in a row will ruin a state. A leader with foresight and readiness, like Romulus, holds on to what he has.
Machiavelli says a well-ordered community should plan for a steady succession of capable leaders rather than leave it to chance.
Machiavelli argues that when a group lacks capable people, the fault usually lies with its leader, who has not trained them. He points to Tullus turning an unpractised people into fine soldiers.
Machiavelli warns against staking everything on one narrow point. If you cannot bring your whole strength to a place, defending it can be the very thing that loses the fight.
Machiavelli says a fair system judges each act on its own, so past service should not excuse wrongdoing, and a reward should not make anyone think they are above the rules.
Machiavelli holds that even a small reward for real service is prized, so a group should recognise good work even when its means are limited.
Machiavelli advises anyone reforming an organisation to keep familiar names and forms, because people accept what looks familiar and are unsettled by novelty.
Machiavelli argues that a people who have just recovered their freedom punish hard, since they remember old wrongs and suspect everyone. Fear of past harm can make a group quick to judge.
Machiavelli says ingratitude comes from greed or suspicion, and that failing to reward someone who has served you well is inexcusable and brings lasting shame.
Machiavelli notes that leaders often grow suspicious of a capable subordinate and belittle that person's success. Credit given freely builds loyalty, while jealousy wears it away.
Machiavelli warns that a free city errs in two ways, by wronging citizens who deserve reward and by suspecting those who deserve trust. Both are costly, even if they keep people careful.
Machiavelli says that when many capable people share a task, no single person becomes a threat, and jealousy has less room to grow. Spreading responsibility widely keeps a team healthy.
Machiavelli observes that harsh punishment for every failure makes leaders timid. Honest mistakes made in good faith deserve a different response from deliberate misconduct.
Machiavelli notes that Rome distinguished deliberate wrong from honest error, honouring a commander whose mistake came without bad intent. Judge the intention behind a mistake.
Machiavelli warns that kindness shown only when trouble arrives earns little thanks, because people see it as forced. Look after the people you depend on before you need them.
Machiavelli advises that when a problem has grown, it is often wiser to manage it patiently than to crush it by force, since heavy-handed moves can add fuel to the flame.
Machiavelli describes how attempts to crush Cosimo de' Medici only made him stronger. Heavy-handed moves against a popular rival often backfire.

Machiavelli advises a leader to study a problem's symptoms and act only if confident of the cure. Otherwise, waiting lets the trouble fade, while clumsy intervention can drown the plant it means to water.

Machiavelli argues that power is dangerous mainly when it is kept too long or taken outside proper process, not when it is given for a set term to meet a clear emergency. Time limits keep authority safe.
Machiavelli says a group needs a fast, time-limited way to act in a real emergency, because ordinary processes are slow. Any such power should be defined in advance by the rules.
Machiavelli warns that unchecked authority corrupts quickly, even among a good people. Any power given to a leader needs limits, a set term and checks from others.

Machiavelli praises Rome's willingness to serve under someone they had once commanded. He argues that a person who has held high office should not disdain a lesser role, since people trust those who step down with grace.
Machiavelli says a sudden law with retrospective effect, meant to fix a long-standing abuse, does more harm than good. Gradual change often lets an abuse fade on its own.
Machiavelli says a sound leadership group decides clearly and picks the least harmful course, since people forced into disobedience by necessity may later disobey by choice.

preview.text:
Make the most, therefore, of this good or this evil, as you may esteem
it, which you have brought upon yourselves; and should you persist in
the mistake of thinking my opinions worthy your attention, I shall not
fail to proceed with the rest of the History in the manner promised in
my Preface. _Farewell_.

DISCOURSES

ON THE FIRST DECADE OF

TITUS LIVIUS.

BOOK I.

PREFACE.

Albeit the jealous temper of mankind, ever more disposed to censure
than to praise the work of others, has constantly made the pursuit of
new methods and systems no less perilous than the search after unknown
lands and seas; nevertheless, prompted by that desire which nature has
implanted in me, fearlessly to undertake whatsoever I think offers a
common benefit to all, I enter on a path which, being hitherto
untrodden by any, though it involve me in trouble and fatigue, may yet
win me thanks from those who judge my efforts in a friendly spirit. And
although my feeble discernment, my slender experience of current
affairs, and imperfect knowledge of ancient events, render these
efforts of mine defective and of no great utility, they may at least
open the way to some other, who, with better parts and sounder
reasoning and judgment, shall carry out my design; whereby, if I gain
no credit, at all events I ought to incur no blame.

books.title: The Art of Money Getting
books.author: P. T. Barnum
books.subject: business
books.licence_note: Author died 1891. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Barnum held that wealth comes from spending less than you earn, and warned that many people think they understand economy when they do not.
Barnum warned that economy is not meanness. Someone who scrimps on small things while wasting in other directions is not really being economical.
Barnum suggested tracking spending in two columns, necessities and luxuries, to see where money really goes. He found the luxuries column usually far outweighed what people believed they spent.
Barnum observed that trying to keep up appearances with money you do not have wears down families and deceives nobody. Being as good as someone else means behaving well, not spending like them.
Barnum urged people to regulate what they spend by what they earn and lay something by for a rainy day. Living right up to one's means leaves no room for a setback.
Barnum warned that prosperity is a harder ordeal than adversity, and that pride which spends to make a sensation can swallow income as fast as it arrives.
Barnum observed that people have different aptitudes, and someone pushed into work that does not suit their gifts will spend a whole career working uphill, seizing every excuse to idle.
Barnum warned that even the right skill fails in the wrong place. A business should not open where competitors already meet demand, and it should be located where customers actually pass by.
Barnum advised young people to avoid borrowing for everyday food, drink and clothes, since debt that buys things that do not grow can keep a person poor for life.
Barnum said money is a fine servant but a terrible master. Let it work for you through careful investment, and never let interest pile up against you.
Barnum held that perseverance is a form of self-reliance. Someone blown about by every piece of advice cannot succeed until they can trust their own judgement and keep going.
Barnum warned against waiting for something to turn up. Fortune favours those who do their own part, and only then trust to luck for what remains.
Barnum held that no one can fully understand their business without learning its details personally, and that mistakes become useful lessons when a person pays attention to them.
Barnum read the Rothschild maxim 'be cautious and bold' as caution in planning and boldness in carrying plans out. He held that luck is not a plan, and that results follow from sound methods.
Barnum advised keeping good staff, since their experience grows more valuable each year, and noted that an employee who thinks himself indispensable has stopped being worth much.
Barnum observed that money earned through effort is valued, while capital handed to someone who has not earned it is often lost quickly. Self-denial and patience teach what money is worth.
Barnum urged people to study the rules of business and above all human nature, observing that heirs who never earned money often lose it, while experience is what steadily builds wealth.
Barnum argued that no honest trade is beneath respect, and that whoever excels in their own line, with good habits and integrity, will find plenty of customers and does not need to fear competition.
Barnum advised every parent to give their children a useful trade or profession, so they have something to fall back on if fortune turns against them.
Barnum recommended working by a system, doing one thing at a time and keeping appointments, while warning that too much system becomes its own red tape. Aim for the sensible middle.
Barnum advised reading a trustworthy newspaper to stay informed about the world and one's trade, since someone who ignores what is changing can be left out in the cold.
Barnum warned that people who succeed in their own field often lose it by chasing speculations they do not understand, lured by flattery. Stay with the business you know well.

Barnum cautioned against guaranteeing other people's debts without good security, and observed that money obtained too easily tempts people into risky speculation that can ruin both lender and borrower.
Barnum held that a good product nobody knows about earns nothing, so a business should advertise what it genuinely offers. Like a farmer, sow to the public first and reap afterwards.
Barnum observed that advertising pays only when it is kept up long enough for people to know what you sell, and that a spurious product brings customers once before they walk away.
Barnum said that politeness and civility are among the best capital a business can invest in, since abrupt treatment undoes even the most lavish store or sign.
Barnum advised keeping business profits, hopes and plans to yourself, since telling others how you made money gains nothing, and losses shared too freely can cost you your reputation.
Barnum held that the best charity quietly helps people who are struggling to help themselves, rather than handing out alms without asking who deserves them.
Barnum argued that strict honesty underpins lasting success, because people will not deal with anyone whose integrity is doubted, while a known honest person can borrow on trust alone.
Barnum distinguished getting rich from being successful, and held that money is worth having when it is used to enlarge the happiness and influence of others.
Barnum held that trade has long funded learning, art and the institutions a society values. Making money honestly is nothing to be ashamed of, and the wealth it brings should be used well.

preview.text:
Those who really desire to attain an independence, have only to set
their minds upon it, and adopt the proper means, as they do in regard to
any other object which they wish to accomplish, and the thing is easily
done. But however easy it may be found to make money, I have no doubt
many of my hearers will agree it is the most difficult thing in the
world to keep it. The road to wealth is, as Dr. Franklin truly says,
"as plain as the road to the mill." It consists simply in expending less
than we earn; that seems to be a very simple problem. Mr. Micawber,
one of those happy creations of the genial Dickens, puts the case in a
strong light when he says that to have annual income of twenty pounds
per annum, and spend twenty pounds and sixpence, is to be the most
miserable of men; whereas, to have an income of only twenty pounds, and
spend but nineteen pounds and sixpence is to be the happiest of mortals.
Many of my readers may say, "we understand this: this is economy, and we
know economy is wealth; we know we can't eat our cake and keep it also."
Yet I beg to say that perhaps more cases of failure arise from mistakes
on this point than almost any other. The fact is, many people think they
understand economy when they really do not.

books.title: The Human Machine
books.author: Arnold Bennett
books.subject: habits
books.licence_note: Author died 1931. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Arnold Bennett notes that the inventors who lose their evenings to a machine are happier for it, because a pursuit that keeps absorbing you stops life from dragging.
Arnold Bennett argues that the most fascinating machine you will ever own is yourself, and that people do themselves less than justice by taking that machine for granted.
Arnold Bennett points out that we often wish our habits would practise themselves, yet give no attention to the machine we already have.
Arnold Bennett observes that most of us give our schooling and early working years to preparation, and very little deliberate attention to the art of living itself.
Arnold Bennett warns that much self-improvement is really self-indulgence, polishing one part of the machine while the more important parts go neglected.
Arnold Bennett suggests planning in advance what you will do at the moments you can foresee, so that you already know your response when pressure arrives.
Arnold Bennett notes that clever people can still muddle their own lives, so the real task is keeping the brain in order rather than hoping for more of it.
Arnold Bennett compares the wandering brain to a well-meaning volunteer who drifts off just when pressure is highest, and says we should not sit back and accept it.
Arnold Bennett argues that the brain is a servant outside the central self, and that when it runs out of control it is because its discipline was neglected. It can be trained.
Arnold Bennett describes the brain as a diplomat whose job is to give the instincts the most freedom with the least friction, and to stop them making fools of themselves.
Arnold Bennett holds that the brain must be trained to obey, through the will, so that it acts on the good intentions it already holds.
Arnold Bennett suggests giving your mind one chosen topic for half an hour and bringing it back each time it wanders. It is hard at first, and it is the foundation of an efficient life.
Arnold Bennett says that regular practice of concentration builds the habit of obedience, so the mind becomes less forgetful and less easily taken by surprise by its instincts.
Arnold Bennett argues that character is the total result of our habits of thought, and that reason can guide how it is built, rather than leaving it to chance.
Arnold Bennett points out that inherited tendencies are not destiny. A single shock, or contact with a stronger character, can reshape a whole life.
Arnold Bennett observes that most of our habits form without a plan, and that a habit we choose on purpose shapes character in exactly the same way.
Arnold Bennett asks why, if most of our character is shaped without thought, we should not give far more of that shaping to conscious choice.
Arnold Bennett shows that a bad habit is not cured by one good intention, but by fixing the better idea in mind each day until the brain remembers it at the critical moment.
Arnold Bennett holds that when life creates friction, the fault lies in the machine, meaning ourselves, and not in the facts of the universe.
Arnold Bennett reminds us that we can control nothing but our own mind, and that worrying over other people's minds is effort spent in the wrong place.
Arnold Bennett notes that we do not live in a universe of oughts. Losing sleep over a rejected application only costs us our own health and dignity.
Arnold Bennett separates the hardships we accept calmly, like a shower of rain, from those we protest against like a child denied the moon. Accepting what cannot be changed is the sensible course.
Arnold Bennett notes how easily we accept the faults of strangers in theory, then fume when the same fault turns up in someone close to us.
Arnold Bennett argues that, in the end, no one can really harm us except ourselves. Feeling wronged is a choice of how we respond, much like sitting in the rain with an umbrella beside us.
Arnold Bennett says the art of living is tested in our daily dealings with other people, and that good ideas should be able to hold up on an ordinary day.
Arnold Bennett concludes that calm cheerfulness rests on kindliness, and that the inmost secret of smooth living is to stop blaming and judging the people around us.
Arnold Bennett admits that he explains his own failings kindly, yet secretly blames others whenever they block his path, and that this hidden blame makes kindness harder.
Arnold Bennett suggests that the people we deal with are as shaped by circumstance as we are. Reflecting on each of them each morning builds the self-possession that good conduct needs.
Arnold Bennett describes the ordinary day, with its small frictions, as worth close attention, because the wear from friction builds up unnoticed.
Arnold Bennett argues that most daily friction comes from tone of voice rather than the words themselves, since every speaker conveys an attitude as well as a thought.
Arnold Bennett notes that adopting a pleasant tone on purpose can soften real resentment, because tone and attitude feed each other.
Arnold Bennett asks why we would not always use a gentle, persuasive tone, since small avoidable frictions in daily dealings add up to a great deal of unhappiness.
Arnold Bennett advises us to watch for small signs of a wrong attitude, such as a frown at a necktie, because those small moments reveal how the day is really going.
Arnold Bennett compares a person in a rage to a house on fire, where a warning only makes the owner fan the flames. Calm is the better response.
Arnold Bennett describes losing your temper as being burnt out, a brief collapse of dignity and common sense that most of us have suffered to some degree.
Arnold Bennett insists that a bad temper is curable rather than a misfortune to be endured, and that a person can stay master of his own mind by will or by cleverness.
Arnold Bennett argues that reasoning alone will not break a bad temper, but the near universal dislike of looking ridiculous can. A loss of temper only makes us look a fool.
Arnold Bennett advises rehearsing, in calm hours, a clear picture of ourselves at our angriest, so that it comes to mind first when the temper starts to rise.
Arnold Bennett suggests that truth is patient and needs no custodian, so we do not have to spend our energy winning every small point in an argument.
Arnold Bennett warns against trying to rearrange other people's minds. He calls it dangerous and generally futile, when our own mind is hard enough to manage.
Arnold Bennett holds that one central secret of efficient daily living is to leave our companions alone more often, and to be in charge of ourselves rather than the universe.
Arnold Bennett suggests treating other people as part of our environment, to be used without blame, while recognising that the responsibility for their own lives is theirs.
Arnold Bennett insists that human nature does change, slowly and through the efforts of individuals on themselves. We miss it because we rarely look closely, like grass growing.
Arnold Bennett points out that believing we cannot change is a quiet form of fatalism, one that releases us from responsibility for ourselves and for others.
Arnold Bennett suspects that claims of being unchangeable are often plain idleness dressed up as fate, and that most of us can alter ourselves at least a little.
Arnold Bennett argues that most failures to change come from forgetting, at the critical moment, what our reason would have us do. Remembering is a skill, and skills are built by practice.
Arnold Bennett argues that any habit can be replaced by a better one, formed by daily concentration on the new response until it becomes an instinct that beats the old one.
Arnold Bennett suggests that once we see how much our own thinking can prevent unhappiness, the working of the mind becomes a richer interest in life than any garden.
Arnold Bennett describes the common habit of waiting for worries to clear before we begin to live, and offers instead a daily resolve to weave a good life from today's material.
Arnold Bennett recommends foreseeing each day in the morning and adjusting our point of view, so that small annoyances look like material to work with rather than worries.
Arnold Bennett points out that preparing for the dangers we can see also arms us, to some degree, against the ones we did not expect.
Arnold Bennett says we should treat even our own failures as material for learning, and that a healthy measure of self-interest is essential to living well.
Arnold Bennett warns that mastering the mind is simple in principle but slow in practice, and that early surprises and setbacks should not persuade us to give up.
Arnold Bennett argues that the feeling of great effort with no progress is usually mistaken, often just fatigue, and that feeling overwhelmed can be a sign we are succeeding.
Arnold Bennett notes that most people drop self-discipline from plain lack of interest, and that this interest has to be fed from outside, through a little reading each day.
Arnold Bennett recommends a daily page of Epictetus, who stays close to ordinary life, followed by Marcus Aurelius, whose private notes are a deep confession of the inner life.
Arnold Bennett warns that self-discipline should not become an excuse to endure a bad situation. Sometimes the wiser effort is to climb out of the canal and change the setting.
Arnold Bennett says a well-kept mind lets us judge whether our unhappiness comes from a disordered self or from surroundings that do not suit us, so we can change the right thing.
Arnold Bennett notes that most friction between people is avoidable, but where it runs deep, a clear mind can calmly decide whether separation is the only cure.
Arnold Bennett warns that we often sacrifice the present to ambitions that are rarely realised. If an ambition still thrives alongside daily care for the present, it is probably a genuine one.

preview.text:
There are men who are capable of loving a machine more deeply than they
can love a woman. They are among the happiest men on earth. This is not
a sneer meanly shot from cover at women. It is simply a statement of
notorious fact. Men who worry themselves to distraction over the
perfecting of a machine are indubitably blessed beyond their kind. Most
of us have known such men. Yesterday they were constructing motorcars.
But to-day aeroplanes are in the air--or, at any rate, they ought to be,
according to the inventors. Watch the inventors. Invention is not
usually their principal business. They must invent in their spare time.
They must invent before breakfast, invent in the Strand between Lyons's
and the office, invent after dinner, invent on Sundays. See with what
ardour they rush home of a night! See how they seize a half-holiday,
like hungry dogs a bone! They don't want golf, bridge, limericks,
novels, illustrated magazines, clubs, whisky, starting-prices, hints
about neckties, political meetings, yarns, comic songs, anturic salts,
nor the smiles that are situate between a gay corsage and a picture hat.
They never wonder, at a loss, what they will do next. Their evenings
never drag--are always too short. You may, indeed, catch them at twelve
o'clock at night on the flat of their backs; but not in bed! No, in a
shed, under a machine, holding a candle (whose paths drop fatness) up to
the connecting-rod that is strained, or the wheel that is out of centre.
They are continually interested, nay, enthralled. They have a machine,
and they are perfecting it. They get one part right, and then another
goes wrong; and they get that right, and then another goes wrong, and so
on. When they are quite sure they have reached perfection, forth issues
the machine out of the shed--and in five minutes is smashed up, together
with a limb or so of the inventors, just because they had been quite
sure too soon. Then the whole business starts again. They do not give
up--that particular wreck was, of course, due to a mere oversight; the
whole business starts again. For they have glimpsed perfection; they
have the gleam of perfection in their souls. Thus their lives run away.
'They will never fly!' you remark, cynically. Well, if they don't?
Besides, what about Wright? With all your cynicism, have you never
envied them their machine and their passionate interest in it?

books.title: Self and Self-Management
books.author: Arnold Bennett
books.subject: habits
books.licence_note: Author died 1931. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Arnold Bennett argues that many people confuse happiness with distraction, and so chase excitement that leaves them hollow. Happiness is a different thing from pleasure.
In Running Away from Life, Arnold Bennett shows a woman who makes peace with what she cannot control, and finds her pleasure in literature and in cheerful, dutiful living.
Arnold Bennett suggests that the restless and the content may both be running away from life itself, and that refusing to listen to the voice within costs everyone equally.
Arnold Bennett holds that the supreme offence against life is taking refuge from it, whether in good works or bad, because only full engagement with life brings real happiness.
In Running Away from Life, Arnold Bennett sets out the price of following an instinct, such as a gift for writing, against a safe and respected path, and asks us to weigh that price honestly.
In Running Away from Life, Arnold Bennett shows a dutiful man who succeeds in every outward way, yet carries a poisonous regret because he never followed the path his own instinct pointed to.
Arnold Bennett defines happiness as satisfaction after full, honest effort. Someone who has failed to take up life's challenge in a major affair cannot truly be happy, however respectable they are.
Arnold Bennett says an ordinary unhappiness is easier to bear than the inner verdict of having run away from a call to act. Avoiding a task leaves its own lasting sting.
Arnold Bennett points out that good work seldom comes knocking at the door, so those who want to contribute must go and find it, and that searching for the work is part of the work.
Arnold Bennett warns that the work we actually find is rarely the ideal we pictured. Accepting dull, unsuitable work without complaint is part of doing any real service.
Arnold Bennett notes that everyone fills every hour, so taking on something new means something must go. Giving up idle sociability is harder than giving up study, and we should expect that.
Arnold Bennett insists that real service requires sacrifice, since it cannot be fitted around everything else. As he puts it, a full cup must be emptied before anything more can go in.
Arnold Bennett suggests that an impossible colleague is still part of the work. A good worker who quits in disgust leaves the table to the very people they objected to.
Arnold Bennett says the most valuable service is often working with difficult people, and warns that becoming official-minded is the gravest danger for anyone who rises to a position of authority.
Arnold Bennett says the reward for service comes slowly, and that proving our decency lies in sticking to the work long after we are weary of it, rather than chasing something more pleasant.
Arnold Bennett argues that writing down something we are ashamed of, honestly and in black and white, shows how much we fear our own truth. Most of us find an excuse not to.
Arnold Bennett describes how hard it is to be fully honest even on a private page. Most of us soften the truth without noticing, and then feel relief when the page burns.
Arnold Bennett warns that a diary is rarely fully true, since two honest people recounting the same quarrel will each leave something out. Truth is the hardest thing on earth to attain.
Arnold Bennett argues that a life is worth recording when it interests the person living it. He notes that Pepys wrote mostly of ordinary daily happenings, and that these became the great book.
Arnold Bennett holds that the only good reason to keep a diary is the pleasure of writing it. The act should be its own reward, and posterity should not be the motive.
Arnold Bennett advises that a diary should be written as we think and speak. Worrying about literary style gets in the way of plain, honest writing, and writing well comes from clear thinking.

Arnold Bennett says a good diary still takes effort: honest recall, care not to leave out the interesting part, and resisting the temptation to be slack and casual. Negligence cannot be repaired afterwards.
Arnold Bennett argues that real desire is definite and concrete, the sort that keeps working on us. A vague wish taken up only in idle moments is a pastime, not a sign of energy.
In Running Away from Life, Arnold Bennett suggests that a man with many interests, who never became lopsided, may have succeeded more than the friends who called him a waster.
Arnold Bennett suggests that a world of people all ruthlessly set on succeeding would be a grim place. He also says we should question our conscience fairly, not only in the dark hour before dawn.
Arnold Bennett notes that envy of the successful, wanting their rewards without their costs, is not the same as a genuine drive to get on in life.
Arnold Bennett describes a person who has talked themselves into needing one particular thing to function. The need grew from habit and imagination, and it had no real power beyond what they gave it.
Arnold Bennett describes the complete fusser, who gives fatal importance to ten thousand small things and so loses the ease of living. Most people carry a little of this microbe.

Arnold Bennett suggests that most of what we fuss over matters only slightly. Fussing about trifles is a delusion that the world may end over a small provocation, and changing a few of our habits would help.
Arnold Bennett warns that the instinct to fuss grows steadily unless it is firmly checked, and that pride pushes it from one small obsession on to the next.
Arnold Bennett observes that the complete fusser cannot be cured, mostly because he does not know he is fussy. The useful warning is to pull up early, before the habit hardens.
Arnold Bennett says fussiness can be cured in its early stages, when we suspect our own quirks, if we act at once and choke the 'but' that excuses them.

Arnold Bennett suggests that human motives are usually mixed, and that because they are so human they are forgivable. Our choices often serve several desires at once, from the wish to attract to the sense of beauty.
Arnold Bennett argues that common sense is relative, and that human progress is too complex for a slogan. We should be slow to scorn the habits of the past, or to assume our own sense is final.

preview.text:
You observe how sarcastic I am about the social butterfly. It is
necessary to be so. The social butterfly never has since the earliest
times been mentioned in print without sarcasm or pity, and she never
will be. She is greatly to be pitied. What is her aim? Her aim, like
the aim of most people except the very poor (whose aim is simply to
keep alive), is happiness. But the unfortunate creature, as you and
I can so clearly see, has confused happiness with pleasure. She runs
day and night after pleasure--that is to say, after distraction:
eating, drinking, posing, seeing, being seen, laughing, jostling, and
the singular delight of continual imitation. She is only alive in
public, and the whole of her days and nights are spent in being in
public, or in preparing to be in public, or in recovering from the
effects of being in public. Habit drives her on from one excitement to
another. She flies eternally from something mysterious and sinister
which is eternally overtaking her. You and I know that she is never
happy--she is only intoxicated or narcotised by a drug that she calls
pleasure. And her youth is going; her figure is going; her complexion
is practically gone. She is laying up naught for the future save
disappointment, dissatisfaction, disillusion, and no doubt rheumatism.
And all this inordinate, incredible folly springs from a wrong and
childish interpretation of the true significance of happiness.

II

books.title: Pushing to the Front
books.author: Orison Swett Marden
books.subject: habits
books.licence_note: Author died 1924. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Marden argues that people usually get what they expect, so someone who half expects to stay stuck will work against their own progress.
Marden holds that before a person can lift themselves they must lift their thoughts, so mastering thought habits comes first.
Marden contrasts commanders who had the supplies but lacked grit with Napoleon, who did not shrink from difficulties and made his own opportunity.
Marden tells of Grace Darling, who rowed out with her father to rescue shipwrecked sailors, showing how courage can find strength nobody knew was there.
Marden holds that weak people wait for opportunities while strong people make them.
Marden holds that every ordinary task, conversation and responsibility is an opportunity, and that the idle person is the one who complains of having none.
Marden tells how Elizabeth Fry saw her chance in the English prisons and, by treating the women with respect, turned a wild crowd into a school.
Marden says open eyes, ears, hearts and hands will always find something worth doing, so attention is the first step to opportunity.
Marden notes that Galileo saw a useful principle in a swinging lamp, showing that close attention to ordinary things can reveal what others walk past.
Marden observes that Newton and Franklin were not favoured by chance, only quicker to see and use common facts and occasions.
Marden says the feeble and the purposeless see no meaning in good occasions until it is too late, because they never trained themselves to act on the present.
Marden argues that accidental circumstances only count for those who have been trained to take advantage of them, so the preparation comes before the moment.
Marden urges readers to make their own opportunities rather than wait for them, since industry makes the commonest chances golden.
Marden says the world wants people who keep their individuality, have the courage to say no, and see their work as more than a way to earn a living.
Marden wants people who are well rounded rather than one-sided, with common sense alongside their theories and their education.
Marden quotes Rousseau that a person should first learn to be a man, since a well-rounded character will find its place whatever fortune brings.
Marden says a young person who keeps every promise and guards their reputation as a priceless treasure will earn the lasting trust of others.
Marden holds that to be a man is to do no one a wrong and to stay within the unseen law of rectitude when desire tempts you.
Marden tells of the deaf boy Kitto, thought fit only for pauper shoemaking, who became a great Biblical scholar through steady study.
In the story of Creon and his sister Cleone, Marden shows devotion and courage, as Creon steps forward to confess and save the sister who protected his work.
Marden says Henry Wilson seized spare moments as though they were gold, reading widely and turning every circumstance of his life into material for success.
Marden tells of Horace Greeley, young and poor, who gave most of his earnings to help his father, then set out on foot to seek his fortune in New York.
Marden tells how James Gordon Bennett, after repeated failures, built the New York Herald from a cellar with a plank desk, steadily working toward his ideal.
Marden tells of George Childs, a poor boy whose motto, nothing without labour, carried him from bookshop clerk to owner of a great newspaper.
Marden quotes William Cobbett, who learned grammar as a private soldier with his knapsack for a bookcase, which shows a determined mind can learn almost anywhere.
Marden tells how Theodore Parker, with little schooling, saved his odd moments for reading and earned his way to Harvard, showing that steady effort can make up for a lost start.
Marden tells of Elihu Burritt, a blacksmith's apprentice who studied languages between heats at the forge, showing that a hard trade need not block learning.
Marden quotes Talmage that a poor young man is already equipped with a body and mind of wonderful make, and that reading is a free place to start.
Marden shows two unknown young men, Lundy and Garrison, taking on a powerful institution because they were fired by a lofty purpose and were in earnest.
Marden says Garrison, with no money, friends or influence, started his paper in a small upstairs room and vowed not to retreat a single inch.
Marden tells of Richard Cobden, who learned French by rising early while his companions slept, a reminder that the quiet hours can do the most for a person.
Marden tells how Michael Faraday, a bookbinder's apprentice, wrote to Humphry Davy with his lecture notes and was brought into the great chemist's laboratory.
Marden quotes Disraeli's belief that what has been done can be done again, and shows a determined will carrying a man from scorn to the top of politics.
Marden says Kepler worked calmly for seventeen years on his laws of planetary motion despite poverty, exile and burned books, a model of patient work.
Marden says Galileo, pushed into medical study, still built his own telescope and found the moons of Jupiter, showing that a real calling can outlast the path others choose.
Marden tells how George Stephenson, who could not read, learned from the engine itself by taking machines apart in the holidays while others idled.
Marden says Vanderbilt started again after losing his first boat in a wreck, working through the night to build the busiest trade in the harbor.
Marden tells how Frederick Douglass learned the alphabet from scraps of paper and almanacs, showing that no limits should be placed on someone who keeps reaching for learning.
Marden says Abraham Lincoln inherited no opportunities and gained nothing by luck, and that his good fortune came from untiring perseverance and a right heart.
Marden tells how James Garfield worked his way through school by sweeping floors, ringing the academy bell and planing boards, and says such an example is worth more than wealth.
Marden says a boy's start in life matters less than a resolute purpose, and that anyone who holds to one clear aim can rise from any beginning.
Marden suggests that too many advantages can be a disadvantage, since the hunger to learn often grows out of having little to start with.
Marden quotes Disraeli that the secret of success is to be ready for your opportunity when it comes.
Marden says many people who think they are poor are rich in opportunities, if only they could see the possibilities around them.
Marden tells of Ali Hafed, who left a good farm in search of diamonds and came to ruin, while the man who stayed found diamonds in his own garden.
Marden says the more opportunities people use, the more new ones appear, and that each person should find their own place and fill it.
Marden advises finding out what the world needs first and then supplying that want, since a clever idea is useless if nobody needs it.
Marden tells how Michelangelo saw a David in a spoiled block of marble, a reminder that a discarded or damaged thing may still hold real value.
Marden tells how Faraday, offered only bottle-washing at the Royal Institution, treated that humble job as an opportunity and went on to a professorship.
Marden says a person who studies their own wants will find that millions share them, and that supplying a great human need is the safest kind of work.
Marden tells how Franklin would not haggle over a book, because he would rather keep his time for his work than sell it cheaply, a lesson in what time is worth.
Marden says successful people gather the leftover fragments of time, the odd minutes and gaps between tasks, and turn them into real results.
Marden notes that days come like friends in disguise, and that lost time is gone for good, while lost knowledge or wealth can be won back.
Marden says an hour a day given to useful study can turn an ordinary person into a well-informed one within ten years.
Marden tells of Charles Frost, a shoemaker who gave one hour a day to study and became a noted mathematician.
Marden notes that Goethe stepped out in the middle of an interview to write down a passing thought, so that it would not be lost.
Marden says the present is the raw material we make everything from, so a person should get their lesson from the hour they are in.
