Marden says the worst of a lost hour is the wasted power it leaves behind, since work has a system and laziness has none.
Marden says the way a young person spends evenings and idle time reveals their character, and each evening is a turning point in a career.
Marden says a student who starts from almost nothing and builds his life on self-reliance and integrity can still rise to great success in his field.

preview.text:
Crowned heads, presidents of republics, distinguished members of the
British and other parliaments, members of the United States Supreme
Court, noted authors, scholars, and eminent people in many parts of the
world, have eulogized this book and have thanked the author for giving
it to the world.

This volume is full of the most fascinating romances of achievement
under difficulties, of obscure beginnings and triumphant endings, of
stirring stories of struggles and triumphs.  It gives inspiring stories
of men and women who have brought great things to pass.  It gives
numerous examples of the triumph of mediocrity, showing how those of
ordinary ability have succeeded by the use of ordinary means.  It shows
how invalids and cripples even have triumphed by perseverance and will
over seemingly insuperable difficulties.

The book tells how men and women have seized common occasions and made
them great; it tells of those of average ability who have succeeded by
the use of ordinary means, by dint of indomitable will and inflexible
purpose.  It tells how poverty and hardship have rocked the cradle of
the giants of the race.  The book points out that most people do not
utilize a large part of their effort because their mental attitude does
not correspond with their endeavor, so that although working for one
thing, they are really expecting something else; and it is what we
expect that we tend to get.

No man can become prosperous while he really expects or half expects to
remain poor, for holding the poverty thought, keeping in touch with
poverty-producing conditions, discourages prosperity.

books.title: Poetics
books.author: Aristotle
books.subject: writing
books.licence_note: Author died 322 BCE, translator died 1910. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Aristotle held that the arts of poetry are all forms of imitation, and that they differ in their medium, their objects and their manner.
Aristotle argued that a writer is a poet for imitating well, not merely for writing in verse, so a medical treatise in verse does not make its author a poet.
Aristotle held that a work may show people as better than they are, as they are, or as worse, and that tragedy aims at the better while comedy aims at the worse.
Aristotle held that the instinct to imitate runs deep in people, and that we enjoy a faithful likeness because we learn from it and recognise what it shows.
Aristotle held that tragedy began as improvisation and grew by slow degrees, each new element developed in turn until it found its natural form.
Aristotle held that comedy shows a defect or ugliness that is not painful or destructive, which is why a comic mask can be distorted without implying pain.
Aristotle held that action springs from character and thought, so the plot, the arrangement of incidents, is the imitation of action on which success or failure depends.
Aristotle held that plot is the soul of a story and character comes second, since people are judged by what they do, and a well-built plot moves an audience more than fine speeches.
Aristotle held that the most beautiful colours laid on confusedly give less pleasure than a plain outline, so clear structure matters more than ornament.
Aristotle held that a well-made plot needs a beginning, a middle and an end, each following from what came before, so that it never starts or stops at haphazard.
Aristotle held that a story must be long enough to carry a change of fortune yet short enough to be held in the memory as one whole.
Aristotle held that a story's unity comes from one action rather than one hero, and that any part whose removal changes nothing does not belong to the whole.
Aristotle held that poetry is higher than history because it shows what may happen as a certain kind of person would act, so the writer is a maker of plots more than of verses.
Aristotle held that the worst plots are episodic, with events following one another without probable or necessary sequence, and that surprises work best when they also follow as cause and effect.
Aristotle held that the strongest moments come when a situation turns to its opposite, and when a character passes from ignorance to knowledge, most powerfully when both happen together.

Aristotle held that the most moving downfall belongs to a person who is not wholly good but falls through some error or frailty, since we pity unmerited misfortune and fear what could befall someone like us.
Aristotle held that a well-made story should turn on one change of fortune, from good to bad, caused by a great error rather than by vice.
Aristotle held that a plot should move its audience even when only heard, since relying on spectacle is a less artistic method that depends on outside aids.
Aristotle held that the most moving conflicts happen between people who are close, and that a writer should keep the familiar story but show invention in how it is handled.
Aristotle held that a harm nearly done and then averted through recognition makes the strongest scene, while a shocking act with no consequence is not truly tragic.
Aristotle held that a character should be good, fitting to their type, true to life and consistent, even when the model being portrayed is inconsistent.
Aristotle held that a story's resolution must grow out of the plot itself rather than from a convenient outside intervention, and that a flawed character's type should be kept but ennobled.
Aristotle ranked the ways of recognition, placing tokens and scars near the bottom and recognition that grows naturally from the incidents at the top.
Aristotle advises a writer to see the scene as if a spectator, since a vivid picture helps them catch what fits and any inconsistencies they would otherwise overlook.
Aristotle advises a writer to sketch the general outline of a story first, then fill in the episodes and detail.
Aristotle holds that the essence of a plot can be told briefly, and that every episode must be relevant to the action.
Aristotle advises a writer to combine as many poetic elements as possible, noting that many poets tie a knot well but unravel it poorly.
Aristotle held that a story suited to a long epic will fail on stage if squeezed into a play, and that the chorus should share in the action rather than sit as mere interlude.
Aristotle held that dramatic incidents should speak for themselves without verbal explanation, while speeches are used to prove points and stir feelings.
Aristotle explains metaphor as carrying a name across by analogy, and a good one reveals a likeness, such as calling evening the old age of the day.
Aristotle holds that good style is clear without being mean: plain words give clarity but can sink into the commonplace, while a touch of the unusual lifts language above it.
Aristotle holds that the greatest thing in writing is a command of metaphor, which cannot be taught by another and implies an eye for resemblances.
Aristotle holds that a narrative should have a single whole action with a beginning, middle and end, unlike a chronicle that lists events tending to no single result.
Aristotle observes that a narrative can carry many simultaneous events that add dignity, while a play must stay with one stage action, since sameness soon wearies an audience.
Aristotle admires a writer who speaks as little as possible in their own voice, bringing in characters who each have a character of their own.
Aristotle observes that audiences enjoy the wonderful, and that an absurdity which would look ridiculous on stage can pass unnoticed when it is told as a story.
Aristotle advises a writer to prefer a probable impossibility to an improbable possibility, and to keep irrational parts out of the action where possible.
Aristotle holds that a writer imitates things as they are, as people say they are, or as they ought to be, and that a flaw touching the essence of the craft matters more than a minor fact.
Aristotle warns that critics often judge a text against their own fancies, and advises weighing how many senses a word may bear before finding fault.
Aristotle holds that the impossible in a story is justified by the needs of the art, and that an ideal type may rightly surpass reality.
Aristotle argues that a concentrated work, achieving its effect within narrow limits, gives more pleasure than one spread out and diluted over a long time.

preview.text:
I propose to treat of Poetry in itself and of its various kinds, noting
the essential quality of each; to inquire into the structure of the plot
as requisite to a good poem; into the number and nature of the parts of
which a poem is composed; and similarly into whatever else falls within
the same inquiry. Following, then, the order of nature, let us begin
with the principles which come first.

Epic poetry and Tragedy, Comedy also and Dithyrambic: poetry, and the
music of the flute and of the lyre in most of their forms, are all in
their general conception modes of imitation. They differ, however, from
one: another in three respects,--the medium, the objects, the manner or
mode of imitation, being in each case distinct.

For as there are persons who, by conscious art or mere habit, imitate
and represent various objects through the medium of colour and form, or
again by the voice; so in the arts above mentioned, taken as a whole,
the imitation is produced by rhythm, language, or 'harmony,' either
singly or combined.

Thus in the music of the flute and of the lyre, 'harmony' and rhythm
alone are employed; also in other arts, such as that of the shepherd's
pipe, which are essentially similar to these. In dancing, rhythm alone
is used without 'harmony'; for even dancing imitates character, emotion,
and action, by rhythmical movement.

books.title: The Theory of the Leisure Class
books.author: Thorstein Veblen
books.subject: economics
books.licence_note: Author died 1929. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Thorstein Veblen argued that the work a group treats as honourable is often set by status, not by how useful the work is to everyone else.
Thorstein Veblen noted that what seems important about a set of facts depends on the interest we bring to them, so the same facts can be sorted in different ways.
Thorstein Veblen describes an instinct of workmanship: people take real satisfaction in effective work and dislike futile effort, and that pride can be seen in what they make.
Thorstein Veblen argued that much of the drive to accumulate wealth comes from wanting the respect that wealth brings, not only from what the goods themselves can do.
Thorstein Veblen observed that once wealth became the easiest visible sign of success, people felt they had to acquire it just to keep a good name.
Thorstein Veblen noted that most people's self-respect rests on the respect of their neighbours, so falling behind the group's standard can hurt how we see ourselves.
Thorstein Veblen observed that a new standard of comfort soon stops feeling like enough, because people keep measuring themselves against those around them.
Thorstein Veblen argued that wealth or power only earns esteem when others can see it, and that outward signs of it also steady a person's own sense of self-respect.
Thorstein Veblen suggested that good manners usually begin as a real wish to show goodwill and ease, though they can later become a display of rank.
Thorstein Veblen observed that customs which begin as a symbol of something often outlast that meaning and come to be valued for their own sake.
Thorstein Veblen observed that a practice which first made sense comes to feel right in itself, and it only lasts while it still fits the habits that support it.
Thorstein Veblen noted that the more elaborate a household's possessions become to keep up appearances, the more time and help they demand, so display creates its own burdens.
Thorstein Veblen pointed out that a lavish gathering can have warm, sociable reasons and still serve a display purpose, and both motives can be true at once.
Thorstein Veblen observed that each social layer tends to take the way of life of the layer just above as its ideal of decency, so keeping up appearances spreads down through a whole society.
Thorstein Veblen noted that in large, mobile communities, where strangers only know us by what they see, visible signs count for far more than reputation built slowly among people who know us.
Thorstein Veblen argued that almost everyone has a built-in urge to accomplish something and shape things that are useful, and that this urge shows more clearly when work is free rather than forced.
Thorstein Veblen warned that we often judge taste or intelligence as if they were refinement, when the gap between people is really a gap in money.
Thorstein Veblen pointed out that most goods are both useful and showy, and the fair test is whether they add to a person's life as a whole, not whether they have come to feel necessary.
Thorstein Veblen observed that spending habits stretch easily as income grows but are hard to scale back, so a higher income can quietly become a higher floor.

Thorstein Veblen observed that gains in efficiency often get swallowed by rising expectations of what a good life looks like, so people work just as hard for a higher standard instead of gaining time.

Thorstein Veblen noted that most people spend to fit in with what seems normal rather than to show off on purpose, and that this quiet habit of conforming can drive spending as much as any deliberate display.
Thorstein Veblen argued that much of the pleasure we take in a costly product is really pleasure in its price, dressed up as a sense of beauty. Useful for any business thinking about perceived value.
Thorstein Veblen argued that differences in taste between social groups come from different ideas of what is proper to enjoy, not from any built-in difference in how people see beauty.
Thorstein Veblen noted that the most satisfying everyday things are often simple designs that plainly show what they are for, and that this kind of beauty does not need to cost much.
Thorstein Veblen observed that people can come to look down on anything inexpensive even when it works just as well, and then insist on paying for an extra margin of show.
Thorstein Veblen observed that buyers often judge goods by their finish and presentation more than by how well they perform, which is worth remembering when a business presents what it sells.
Thorstein Veblen argued that social norms rarely invent new ways of doing things; they act as a filter, and whatever new idea survives is the one that fits the norm.
Thorstein Veblen observed that people will often go short on comfort to keep up a respectable appearance, so much of what we spend on clothes is for how we look to others rather than for protection.
Thorstein Veblen suggested that fashions keep changing because each new style only pretends to have a real purpose, and people eventually tire of the pretence and move on.

Thorstein Veblen noted that as audiences grow more discerning, cruder signals of status give way to subtler ones that only an informed circle can read. Worth remembering when deciding how loudly to market a brand.
Thorstein Veblen argued that habits of thought outlast the conditions that created them, so people usually change only when circumstances force them to.
Thorstein Veblen noted that people tend to adjust their views reluctantly, usually under outside pressure, and that those shielded from everyday pressure adapt most slowly.
Thorstein Veblen observed that a way of working that suited earlier conditions may still function under new ones, but it is usually not the best fit, and it could do better if it were adapted.
Thorstein Veblen noted that the people who have to change their way of life are the ones most ready to accept new standards, because the need is felt in their own pay packets.
Thorstein Veblen argued that changing habits takes mental energy, so people who are stretched thin and people who are comfortable both tend to stick with what they know, for different reasons.
Thorstein Veblen contrasted the comfortable motto "whatever is, is right" with the view that every institution is somewhat out of date, and that the second is the more useful habit to keep.

Thorstein Veblen separated business, which aims at pecuniary gain, from industry, which aims at making things that serve human needs. Keeping those two aims apart helps a founder see what the work is really for.

Thorstein Veblen warned that a person driven only by self-interest would be of little use to modern industry, because the work depends on steadiness, care and cooperation as well as on looking after one's own gain.
Thorstein Veblen argued that good work depends on a genuine interest in the work itself, not only on getting ahead of others, and that this interest is what keeps complex work going.
Thorstein Veblen observed that people find purposeless effort tedious and want their activity to point at a real end, which is why a visible purpose matters in any routine.
Thorstein Veblen held that the instinct of workmanship is older and deeper than the urge to compete for standing, so a life lived only for contests falls short of it.
Thorstein Veblen argued that cunning and ferocity serve a person's own rise in a contest for standing, but do little for the common life of a community.
Thorstein Veblen observed that modern work runs on cause and effect, so the intelligence it asks for is a quick grasp of how one thing leads to the next.
Thorstein Veblen held that the impulses of charity, sociability and a sense of belonging to the common life pull against the habit of showing off through waste.
Thorstein Veblen noticed that many people who run work take real pride in seeing it done well, even apart from the profit it brings.
Thorstein Veblen noted that even good works done partly for standing show that a non-competitive interest in helping others is a real, accepted motive in modern life.
Thorstein Veblen warned that organisations can drift from their first purpose toward looking respectable, until the stated aim is only a front and the real work fades.
Thorstein Veblen observed that a vanity motive often hides behind good-sounding labels, quietly steering well-meant effort away from the work that actually helps, often without the person noticing.
Thorstein Veblen held that habits of thought formed in an earlier economy lose their hold once they stop fitting the way people now earn a living.
Thorstein Veblen observed that established institutions tended to accept new knowledge only after it had become commonplace outside them, so new ideas often met a cool welcome.
Thorstein Veblen argued that much of modern science grew out of practical work with real materials, and that many of its builders worked outside the schools.
Thorstein Veblen observed that people often judge the worth of goods, and of learning, by decorative finish rather than by what the thing actually does.
Thorstein Veblen pointed out that cumbersome, old-fashioned language is often used to look respectable, while plain and direct speech carries more force.

preview.text:
The work of the men in the lower barbarian culture is no less
indispensable to the life of the group than the work done by the women.
It may even be that the men's work contributes as much to the food
supply and the other necessary consumption of the group. Indeed, so
obvious is this "productive" character of the men's work that in the
conventional economic writings the hunter's work is taken as the type of
primitive industry. But such is not the barbarian's sense of the matter.
In his own eyes he is not a labourer, and he is not to be classed with
the women in this respect; nor is his effort to be classed with the
women's drudgery, as labour or industry, in such a sense as to admit
of its being confounded with the latter. There is in all barbarian
communities a profound sense of the disparity between man's and woman's
work. His work may conduce to the maintenance of the group, but it is
felt that it does so through an excellence and an efficacy of a kind
that cannot without derogation be compared with the uneventful diligence
of the women.

books.title: The History of the Peloponnesian War
books.author: Thucydides
books.subject: history
books.licence_note: Author died about 400 BCE, translator died 1893. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Thucydides judged his own account by the evidence he could check, and admitted that the distant past could not be known clearly.
Thucydides observed that fertile land invited invasion and let a few individuals grow powerful, and that this rivalry was a steady source of ruin.
Thucydides saw that the love of gain would reconcile the weaker to the rule of the stronger, and that accumulated capital let the powerful bring smaller towns under their rule.
Thucydides warned that appearances mislead, since a city built of villages can look weaker than it is, so judge power by what it actually did.
Thucydides noticed that the great expedition failed more from a shortage of money and supplies than of men, and that scattering into plunder and farming undid the siege.
Thucydides observed that rulers who look only to their own comfort and family standing make safety their whole aim, and so achieve nothing great.
Thucydides argued that the long wars gave both sides hard practice, because experience learnt in the school of danger is the kind that peace cannot teach.
Thucydides warned that most people accept tradition as it is handed down, applying no critical test, so it is worth checking what you hear before you repeat it.
Thucydides tested each account against several witnesses and wrote for readers who want an exact knowledge of the past to help them read the future.
Thucydides held that the real cause of the war was the one least openly admitted: Athens's growing power and the fear it caused in Sparta.
In Thucydides, the Corcyraean envoys say anyone asking for help must first show that granting it is sensible for the other side, and that they will remember the kindness.
In Thucydides, the Corinthian speakers argue that a claim to honesty is only proved by conduct, by giving and taking what is just, and that isolation can hide wrongdoing.
In Thucydides, the Corinthians advise that avoiding injustice towards powerful neighbours is a greater strength than a quick gain bought at the cost of lasting peace.
Thucydides noticed that after the sea battle at Sybota both sides claimed the victory, each reading the same events in its own favour.
Thucydides has a Corinthian speaker argue that responsibility for harm lies not only with the one who acts but with the one who could prevent it and does not.
Thucydides has a Corinthian speaker argue that improvement prevails in statecraft as in art, because constant necessity demands constant improvement of methods.
Thucydides notes that people feel a wrong done under cover of law more sharply than open force, because it feels like being cheated by an equal.
Thucydides warns that going to war is a common mistake of acting first and waiting for disaster before discussing it, when chance plays a large part and the outcome is risked in the dark.
In Thucydides, the Spartan king Archidamus counts the ships, money and supplies before any war, warning that hope of a quick victory is a fatal trap against a richer rival.
Thucydides has Archidamus argue that war is decided less by arms than by money, so a careful leader secures resources before being carried along by the urging of allies.
Thucydides has Archidamus say that a decision touching many lives should be made calmly rather than in a day, and that wise moderation is not the same as cowardice.
Thucydides notes the Spartans voted for war less because the allies argued well than because they feared Athens's growing power, which is how fear often decides what reasons only dress up.
Thucydides has Themistocles warn that rumours deceive, so send trusted people to inspect the facts for themselves instead of believing what they hear.
In Thucydides, Pausanias loses his allies by acting like a despot, and they turn to Athens, which shows how quickly a leader's arrogance can cost the trust that holds a coalition together.
Thucydides observed that allies who paid money instead of providing their own ships were left without resources or experience when revolt came, so the power that kept the skills kept the control.
Thucydides shows how an unspoken suspicion can turn a partner into an enemy: Sparta dismissed its Athenian allies without saying why, and they went over to Argos.
Thucydides records the great Athenian expedition to Egypt ending in ruin after six years, a sober warning about how a campaign stretched far from home can outrun its supplies and support.
In Thucydides, a Corinthian speaker notes that plans look safe on paper and that fear causes failure once action begins, so test a plan against what it will take to carry it out.
In Thucydides, a Corinthian speaker says war follows no fixed rules, so the side that keeps its temper and meets each emergency calmly fares best.
Thucydides has a Corinthian speaker say that what was won through hardship should not be lost in comfort, so a little extra wealth is no reason to drop the habits that built the success.
Thucydides notes that Pausanias betrayed his ambition in small things, through his pride, his unapproachability and his temper, and that people judge a leader by trifles long before any grand act.
Thucydides describes Spartan ephors who would not act against a citizen on suspicion alone, and wanted indisputable proof before a decisive step, even when the case against Pausanias looked strong.
Pericles argues in Thucydides that giving way on a small demand invites a larger one, so a firm refusal on a minor point shows others how they must treat you.
Pericles observes in Thucydides that a common cause quietly decays when each member assumes someone else will look after it, and that capital sustains a long effort better than forced contributions.
Pericles tells the Athenians in Thucydides that houses and land do not gain men, but men gain them, so the real loss to grieve is of lives, not property.
Pericles tells the Athenians in Thucydides that he fears their own blunders more than the enemy's schemes, so the biggest threat is often how you yourself act under pressure.
Thucydides observed that zeal is always at its height at the start of an undertaking, so the early enthusiasm of a project is no measure of how it will go in the long middle.
Archidamus tells his army in Thucydides that confidence suits an invader only when paired with precaution, since overconfidence that despises preparation is how larger forces get beaten.

Pericles, in Thucydides, declares in advance that he would hand over his own estate to the state if it were spared, so no one could suspect him of favour. Declaring a conflict early keeps trust intact.
In Thucydides, Pericles refuses to call an assembly while anger runs high, because a debate driven by passion rather than prudence is dangerous. Sometimes the wise move is to let the heat pass first.
Pericles tells the Athenians in Thucydides that men can bear hearing others praised only while they believe they could match the deeds; past that point envy and disbelief set in.
Pericles says in Thucydides that freedom in ordinary life is safe only when citizens also keep the laws and the unwritten code, because easy private habits do not excuse lawlessness in public.
Pericles, in Thucydides, says the real disgrace of poverty lies in declining the struggle against it, not in admitting it, and that a generous person wins friends by giving rather than receiving.

In Thucydides' funeral speech, Pericles calls discussion an indispensable step before any wise action, not an obstacle to it, and says a citizen who takes no part in public judgment is useless, not modest.
Thucydides shows that in a crisis people who think tomorrow is uncertain drop long-standing standards and chase present enjoyment, a warning to keep your principles when times are hardest.
When Athens turned on Pericles after its losses, Thucydides shows him calling an assembly to calm the anger and restore confidence, rather than simply defending himself.
Pericles tells the Athenians in Thucydides that they backed his plan in good times and then blamed it under misfortune, and that a resolution made in comfort often gives way to a sudden reverse.
Pericles argues in Thucydides that confidence grounded in a clear view of your own resources is sounder than hope, which is the prop of the desperate.
Thucydides says Athens dropped Pericles's advice to wait quietly, guard its navy and avoid new conquests, and let private ambitions lead it into projects that ruined it.
Thucydides says Pericles led the people rather than being led by them, because he never flattered them and so could afford to contradict them when they were wrong.
Thucydides shows that when Athens's leaders each grasped for supremacy, their private rivalries paralysed the work in hand and did more damage than any honest miscalculation of the enemy.
In Thucydides, the Plataeans remind Sparta that a promise made by its fathers still binds it, and that breaking the oath dishonours the men who made it.
Thucydides describes the Plataeans building a second wall behind the first, so that if the outer defence fell, the attackers would face the whole job again. Plan a fallback before you need it.
In Thucydides, the Chaonians rush ahead alone, keen to take the glory for themselves, and are routed by an ambush because they would not wait for the rest of the army.

Thucydides shows Phormio beating a larger fleet by circling it, waiting for the wind to throw its formation into confusion, then striking at the moment of advantage. Patience and timing can beat size.
In Thucydides, Cnemus tells his crews that fear steals presence of mind, so skill counts for little without the courage to use it.
Phormio tells his men in Thucydides that a rival who leans on numbers trusts strength more than resolution, and that choosing to face long odds calls on deep inner reserves.
Phormio refuses to fight in the cramped strait, where crowded ships turn the contest into one decided by numbers. Choose the ground that suits your strengths before the contest begins.

Thucydides shows Sitalces giving up a campaign that had achieved none of its aims once his army ran short of supplies. Knowing when to cut losses on a venture that is not working is a discipline in itself.
Thucydides notes that the Athenians first refused to believe a warning about Lesbos because they wished it were not true. Wishful thinking delays the response to bad news.

preview.text:
Thucydides, an Athenian, wrote the history of the war between the
Peloponnesians and the Athenians, beginning at the moment that it broke
out, and believing that it would be a great war and more worthy of
relation than any that had preceded it. This belief was not without its
grounds. The preparations of both the combatants were in every
department in the last state of perfection; and he could see the rest
of the Hellenic race taking sides in the quarrel; those who delayed
doing so at once having it in contemplation. Indeed this was the
greatest movement yet known in history, not only of the Hellenes, but
of a large part of the barbarian world—I had almost said of mankind.
For though the events of remote antiquity, and even those that more
immediately preceded the war, could not from lapse of time be clearly
ascertained, yet the evidences which an inquiry carried as far back as
was practicable leads me to trust, all point to the conclusion that
there was nothing on a great scale, either in war or in other matters.

books.author: Julius Caesar
books.subject: history
books.licence_note: Author died 44 BCE, nineteenth century translation. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Thomas de Quincey argues that Caesar was a sober, measured statesman rather than a wild destroyer, and that judging anyone by a single hostile trait misses their whole character.
Thomas de Quincey suggests that Caesar's early independence came partly from losing his father young, and that hardship can sometimes build a strong mind.
Thomas de Quincey notes that Caesar stood almost alone in refusing a powerful dictator's order, and that even his enemy Sylla admired that boldness.
Thomas de Quincey admires how Caesar met disaster head on instead of softening it, and turned a bad omen into a purpose through quick presence of mind.
Thomas de Quincey notes that Caesar's soldiers went without pay and rations to stay with him, a loyalty that his generosity had earned.
Thomas de Quincey argues that Caesar's debts were the cost of his political work rather than its cause, a useful distinction when judging why a person takes a risk.
Thomas de Quincey notes that Caesar often walked beside his soldiers on the march, and that sharing their hardship won their loyalty more than rank would have.
Thomas de Quincey says Caesar's courtesy was so constant that many took it for weakness, though his mercy to enemies showed more magnanimity than most people could understand.
Thomas de Quincey says Caesar's projects were patriotic in purpose and colossal in scale, and that a worthwhile plan needs both a clear purpose and real ambition.
Thomas de Quincey notes that Caesar wrote his campaigns as plain, simple records, and their clarity was so strong that later writers did not dare to rewrite them.
Thomas de Quincey defines greatness in action as widening what is possible, opening closed doors and making once-vast obstacles seem trivial.
Julius Caesar records that the Helvetii burned their own towns so there was no return, a reminder that people often commit harder once retreat is cut off.
Julius Caesar shows a leader buying time: he told the envoys he would deliberate while gathering soldiers, so that his eventual reply would be backed by force.
Julius Caesar blocked the Helvetii with a wall, a trench and guarded posts, showing how preparation can keep a difficult route closed without open fighting.
Julius Caesar answers a threat by moving fast, marching his existing legions hard and raising new ones along the way rather than waiting for better numbers.
Julius Caesar decided he could not wait while the Helvetii ravaged his allies, a reminder that letting harm spread often costs more than acting early.
Julius Caesar attacked while only part of the Helvetii had crossed a river, showing the value of watching for the moment an opponent is divided.
Julius Caesar built a bridge in a day, crossing faster than the enemy had managed in twenty, a sign that quick practical work can change the balance.
Julius Caesar held his cavalry back from a full battle, judging it enough to stop the enemy raiding for food, a lesson in choosing the fight that actually matters.
Julius Caesar tested a troubling report by quietly speaking with several people one at a time, and only acted once the accounts matched.
Julius Caesar spoke with Divitiacus privately before judging his brother, so the matter could be handled without public humiliation.
Julius Caesar forgave the past at his ally's request but still warned the man and kept watch over him, showing that mercy and vigilance can go together.
Julius Caesar sent scouts to check the ground before committing his men, so his plan rested on what was seen rather than what was hoped.
Julius Caesar found that a scout had reported enemy forces he had never actually seen, and learned to check frightened reports against other sources.
Julius Caesar sent his own horses out of sight so that every man faced the same danger, which removed the hope of escape and steadied his army.
Julius Caesar had the burnt towns rebuilt and the displaced people fed, so that the land would not be left empty for others to take.
Julius Caesar noticed that the Sequani, who dared not even complain in private, suffered most, showing how fear that silences people can hide the worst trouble.
Julius Caesar set out clear, specific terms for peace, stating exactly what he required and what would follow if they were not met.
Julius Caesar hurried to act before two threats could join together, reasoning that one problem is easier to face than two combined.
Julius Caesar saw that panic spread through the camp from officers with little experience, and that fear is contagious when people in charge show it openly.
Julius Caesar rebuked his officers for guessing at his plans, reminding them that their own resolve counted for more than rumours of the enemy's strength.
Julius Caesar acted at once on a move he had planned to delay, using the crisis to see whether duty or fear would move his men, a reminder that hard moments reveal who will follow.
Julius Caesar refused to return fire during a parley, because he would not let anyone say he had set a trap under cover of a meeting, and so protected his good name.
Julius Caesar built his camp behind three lines, so some men held off the attack while others did the building, a sound way to get important work done under pressure.
Julius Caesar attacked where the enemy was weakest and appointed officers to witness the valour of each legion, so that courage was seen and recorded.
Julius Caesar relied on neighbours of the enemy to report what was happening, and moved only once their reports were consistent.
Julius Caesar asked an ally to raid the enemy's land, so that a large opposing army would be split and pressed at its edges rather than all at once.
Julius Caesar sent relief at midnight to a besieged town, and the arrival of help restored its defenders' hope while draining the attackers' resolve.
Julius Caesar tested his men in small daily skirmishes before deciding on a full battle, learning what they could really do rather than guessing.
Julius Caesar kept his men inside camp when the enemy seemed to flee, fearing an ambush, and pursued only once his scouts had confirmed what was happening.
Julius Caesar's visible siege works amazed the defenders of one town so much that they surrendered, showing how thorough preparation can persuade people to stop resisting.
Julius Caesar's army was caught out because enemy observers had learned its marching routine, a reminder that predictable habits can be studied and used against you.

Julius Caesar found that in a sudden attack, soldiers trained through experience could act sensibly without waiting for orders, a strong case for training people until good judgement becomes second nature.
Julius Caesar moved from one part of the line to another, encouraging his men with only a few words, a reminder that a leader's presence in a crisis matters more than long speeches.
Julius Caesar's army fought in scattered pieces because no one could issue orders across the whole line, a lesson in keeping communication working when pressure is highest.
Julius Caesar's rearguard panicked and spread word of defeat, showing how one wrong report can travel faster than the facts.
Julius Caesar took a shield from a soldier and went to the front, calling the centurions by name, and his presence restored hope where it had almost failed.
Julius Caesar spared the broken survivors of the Nervii who surrendered and ordered their neighbours not to harm them, showing mercy once resistance has ended.
Julius Caesar's men were caught by a night attack after a surrender, because the defenders had hidden weapons and expected the guard to relax, a reminder that an agreement does not replace vigilance.
Julius Caesar's enemies underestimated the small force in their midst, and that contempt led them to attack, a warning against underrating a smaller rival.
Galba had not stocked food or finished his defences, because a surrender had led him to think the danger was over, and the enemy soon proved him wrong.
When a defence is failing, the people closest to the fight can see that a bold move is needed, and a leader who listens to them can still act in time.
Galba, having won, chose not to tempt fortune again and withdrew once his aim was met, a sound instinct for knowing when a win is enough.
Julius Caesar, facing an enemy strong on the sea, had ships built and sailors found before he arrived, preparing for ground he did not yet know well.
Julius Caesar judged that an insult left unanswered would encourage other states to do the same, so he acted early to stop the spread.
Julius Caesar split his forces so that neighbouring states could not unite, dividing a growing threat before it became one large danger.
The Veneti built ships suited to their own stormy coast, flatter in the keel and high in the bow, a reminder that good tools are the ones fitted to the conditions you actually face.
Julius Caesar's men cut the enemy's sail rigging with hooks, taking away the one thing their ships depended on, a reminder to find an opponent's dependency and target it.
Q. Titurius Sabinus refused to fight on ground that favoured the enemy, even when it made him look timid, a reminder that sound strategy can look weak from outside.
Sabinus's enemies walked into a trap because they were eager to believe what they wanted to hear, a reminder that wishful thinking is one of the most dangerous mistakes a leader can make.

preview.text:
The character of the First Caesar has perhaps never been worse
appreciated than by him who in one sense described it best; that is,
with most force and eloquence wherever he really _did_ comprehend it.
This was Lucan, who has nowhere exhibited more brilliant rhetoric, nor
wandered more from the truth, than in the contrasted portraits of Caesar
and Pompey. The famous line, _"Nil actum reputans si quid superesset
agendum,"_ is a fine feature of the real character, finely expressed.
But, if it had been Lucan's purpose (as possibly, with a view to
Pompey's benefit, in some respects it was) utterly and extravagantly to
falsify the character of the great Dictator, by no single trait could he
more effectually have fulfilled that purpose, nor in fewer words, than
by this expressive passage, _"Gaudensque viam fecisse ruina."_ Such a
trait would be almost extravagant applied even to Marius, who (though in
many respects a perfect model of Roman grandeur, massy, columnar,
imperturbable, and more perhaps than any one man recorded in History
capable of justifying the bold illustration of that character in Horace,
"_Si fractus illabatur orbis, impavidum ferient ruinae_") had, however,
a ferocity in his character, and a touch of the devil in him, very
rarely united with the same tranquil intrepidity. But, for Caesar, the
all-accomplished statesman, the splendid orator, the man of elegant
habits and polished taste, the patron of the fine arts in a degree
transcending all example of his own or the previous age, and as a man of
general literature so much beyond his contemporaries, except Cicero,
that he looked down even upon the brilliant Sylla as an illiterate
person--to class such a man with the race of furious destroyers exulting
in the desolations they spread is to err not by an individual trait, but
by the whole genus. The Attilas and the Tamerlanes, who rejoice in
avowing themselves the scourges of God, and the special instruments of
his wrath, have no one feature of affinity to the polished and humane
Caesar, and would as little have comprehended his character as he could
have respected theirs. Even Cato, the unworthy hero of Lucan, might have
suggested to him a little more truth in this instance, by a celebrated
remark which he made on the characteristic distinction of Caesar, in
comparison with other revolutionary disturbers; for, said he, whereas
others had attempted the overthrow of the state in a continued paroxysm
of fury, and in a state of mind resembling the lunacy of intoxication,
Caesar, on the contrary, among that whole class of civil disturbers, was
the only one who had come to the task in a temper of sobriety and
moderation _(unum accessisse sobrium ad rempublicam delendam)_....

books.title: The Voyage of the Beagle
books.author: Charles Darwin
books.subject: big ideas
books.licence_note: Author died 1882. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Charles Darwin saw that clearing the trees around Porto Praya had left the land almost barren, and that the same had happened on other islands. Cutting down what holds the soil in place can take a long time to undo.

Charles Darwin read the lava flows on St. Jago as a timeline, judging the age of each stream by how high its cliffs stood. Patient reading of ordinary evidence can reveal the order in which things happened.

Charles Darwin found that the first life on St. Paul's rocks was dirt-feeding insects and spiders, not the grand palms of the popular story. He kept to what he saw, even when it spoiled a pretty tale.
Charles Darwin looked at the granite coast of Brazil and wondered how slow forces could have worn away so much rock. Big changes in the land can take far longer than a human life makes us expect.

Charles Darwin openly admitted where his explanations ran out, saying he could not see where the countless tiny organisms came from. Naming the gap plainly in your own thinking is a habit worth copying.

Charles Darwin wrote that good people can be blind to harm when their interest and habit are at stake. He saw a man he thought kind still ready to split up families for money, so decency has to be checked against what people actually do.
Charles Darwin cut flatworms in two and watched the missing parts grow back over several weeks. He learned by testing a thing directly and watching it change, rather than only reading about it.
Charles Darwin watched a column of ants refuse to go around a small stone, though a short detour would have worked. Sticking to a blocked route can cost far more than a small change of course.

Charles Darwin found small piles of stones on a hilltop as almost the only trace of the people who had once lived there. People everywhere feel the urge to mark that they were there, even though most lives leave few lasting records.

Charles Darwin tested a neat explanation for where trees grow against the counterexamples he could find. When Australia broke the pattern, he said another cause must be at work. A tidy theory has to survive the cases that don't fit.

Charles Darwin first doubted that two similar-looking birds were the same, because their habits differed slightly. Watching how things behave, not only how they look, can reveal what a quick look misses.

Charles Darwin found a small living world inside salt lakes, with worms in the mud feeding flamingoes. Life turns up in harsher places than most people expect, so a hard-looking place may still hold more than it first seems.

Charles Darwin noticed an animal that an old sailor's account had called numerous had vanished from those shores, and asked what could have changed. Asking what caused a change, rather than assuming things stay put, is a useful habit.

On a long dry road, Charles Darwin found that tiny dips and rises in the ground were the only reason any water pooled at all. Small differences in the terrain can decide whether a journey succeeds, though we seldom notice them.

On the Patagonian plain, Charles Darwin's companion was ready to flee from three riders he was sure were a threat, until they turned out to be women looking for eggs. It is worth gathering the facts before acting on a fright.

Charles Darwin noticed that salt lakes in Siberia and Patagonia matched in many small details, and reasoned that such matches on distant continents point to a shared cause. When unrelated places show the same pattern, look for the common thread that produced it.

Charles Darwin challenged an assumption that had passed from book to book, that big animals need lush plants, by checking it against what travellers had actually seen. An idea repeated often enough can still be wrong, so trace where it came from before relying on it.

Charles Darwin argued that frozen Siberian animals did not need a sudden catastrophe to explain them, because the food they required was never as scarce as people assumed. Removing one false assumption can make a dramatic story unnecessary.

Charles Darwin found that animals woke from their winter torpor according to the climate they were used to, not by the absolute heat. What counts as the trigger for change depends on what is normal for the setting, so judge it against that.

Charles Darwin recorded how the men carrying out a massacre called it the most just war. Giving a cruelty a respectable name does not make it right, and a group's own story about itself needs testing against what is actually done.

Charles Darwin gave up climbing the two highest peaks because the extra height added little and the risk was not worth it. Knowing when you have learned enough, and stopping there, is a skill of its own.

Charles Darwin saw a European thistle, the cardoon, spread across hundreds of square miles of Banda Oriental until nothing else could grow there. Something introduced into a place can reshape the whole landscape, far more than anyone planned.

Charles Darwin told of boatmen puzzled by giant bones in a cliff. Needing an answer, they settled on a theory that the animal must have been a burrower. A gap that demands an answer tempts us to invent a story, so test it before you believe it.

Charles Darwin called his conclusion about the birds' feeding a suspicion, and judged a single report of another habit too improbable to be general. Keep track of how far your evidence actually reaches, and say so when it stops.

Charles Darwin found that a land he had first called level looked like hills once he had crossed the flat plains. Our sense of what is ordinary depends on what we have compared it with, so recheck a judgement when your frame of reference changes.

Charles Darwin noticed that an animal's everyday habits reveal little about the rare, long-spaced hardships, such as a great drought, that can decide whether a species survives. Ordinary good days can hide the risks that matter most, so plan for the rare bad year.

Charles Darwin rode with a landowner who could not grasp why he would not spur an exhausted horse for the animal's own sake, since the horse was his to use. Kindness can slip away when a creature's welfare is not tied to our own gain.

Charles Darwin tested a claim by a leading authority, Ehrenberg, against his own observations, and reported plainly where they differed. A respected expert is no substitute for checking a claim yourself, and it is worth saying clearly when your results disagree.

Charles Darwin wrote down trifling details, such as where guanacos tended to lie down to die, because he thought they might one day explain a puzzle in the fossil record. Small, unremarkable observations can matter later, so it pays to write them down.

Charles Darwin reminded readers how little we know of what keeps any species in check. Every population meets some limit, and the cause is often too small to see, so admit how much of any system you do not yet understand.

Charles Darwin argued that species usually grow rare before they vanish, so extinction needs no sudden culprit. He compared it to illness before death. Look for the slow, gradual cause before reaching for a dramatic one.

Charles Darwin tested whether condors found carrion by smell, by wrapping meat in paper and watching their response. He set his result beside other experiments that disagreed and called the evidence finely balanced. A simple test can settle what stories cannot.

Charles Darwin's river expedition disappointed nearly everyone who went, yet he judged it by what it taught him, a clear section of the rock layers. What you count as a good outing depends on what you went looking for.

Charles Darwin noted that a rabbit the French had named as a separate species seemed to breed freely with the common kind, and he warned naturalists to be cautious before splitting things into new categories. Test a distinction before treating it as a fixed boundary.
Charles Darwin admitted that some puzzles of nature had no answer yet, and trusted that the growth of knowledge would one day give a simple explanation.
Charles Darwin warned that it is a common mistake to assume a species is plentiful just because it breeds quickly. Count what you actually see before you judge.
Charles Darwin noticed that guanacos keep to the same tracks, and that a beaten path makes hard going much easier. Use the paths others have already worn.
Charles Darwin saw rocks moved on a beach many times before he understood the cause. Sometimes you need to see the mechanism at work before a pattern makes sense.
Charles Darwin noticed that beds of kelp, flexible and only slightly thick, softened the biggest waves before they reached the harbour. Light, loose defences can outlast rigid ones.
Charles Darwin warned that a clue as striking as a bed of tropical shells can mislead. Test your first conclusion against the wider evidence before you act on it.
Charles Darwin reasoned that the height of the snow line depends more on the hottest season than on the yearly average. An average can hide the peak that actually matters.
Charles Darwin looked closer at what seemed to be ordinary soil and found it was really sea mud, full of tiny remains. Check what a thing is made of before you file it away.

Charles Darwin doubted his own theory that earthquakes had shattered a mountain top, so he checked a similar peak in a place with no earthquakes. Test a favourite explanation where its cause is missing.
Charles Darwin describes Chilean miners who threw away copper ore as worthless, and Cornish visitors who bought it cheaply and profited. What you dismiss as waste may hold the value you are missing.
Charles Darwin saw that mountains wear away while the heavy, durable metals sink and are left behind. What lasts through hard times is often what remains after everything else has been washed out.
Charles Darwin noticed that a careful naturalist, Molina, left out a bird species that was everywhere and very striking. The most familiar things are the easiest to leave out of a record.

Charles Darwin found granite fascinating because it is the deepest rock people have reached, and he saw the limit of human knowledge as the most interesting place to stand. Know where your own knowledge stops.
Charles Darwin argued that a small, rare creature may look insignificant today yet be essential in another place or time. Judge things by the setting they belong to, not only by how they seem here.

When distant volcanoes erupted on the same night, Charles Darwin admitted he could not tell whether it was chance or a hidden link. Say so plainly when the evidence cannot yet separate coincidence from cause.

Charles Darwin saw helpers ordered about without being told whether they would be paid, and blamed that treatment for their discontent. Tell the people who work for you what is expected and what they will get.
Charles Darwin described a Valdivia man who made cider, wine, spirit and syrup from one crop of apples. Get several useful products out of the one thing you already have.

Charles Darwin wrote that people in Concepcion survived the earthquake because they ran outside at the first tremor. Settle the response to the first warning in advance, so it happens without thinking.
Charles Darwin argued that great mountain ranges rise through many small upheavals over long ages, not one violent blow. Steady small steps can build what a single sudden push never would.
Charles Darwin noted that the mind struggles to grasp what a small cause can do when it is repeated over and over. Repetition is hard to picture, so trust the arithmetic over your gut.

Charles Darwin noticed that many rich Chilean mines were found by ordinary people who spent time on the hills and knew what ore looked like. Those closest to the ground often spot what the experts miss.
On a high mountain pass, Charles Darwin's companions blamed a new pot for potatoes that would not cook, when thin air was the real cause. Look for the real cause before you blame the nearest object.

Charles Darwin noticed that two sides of the Andes had nearly the same climate yet almost entirely different animals, because the mountains had long kept them apart. History and barriers can explain differences that conditions alone never will.
Charles Darwin found the Andean passes were far less dangerous than the stories about them. Check a risk with your own eyes before other people's tales set your fear.

Charles Darwin saw English mining companies waste their money on showy extras, such as machinery that could not be used and libraries nobody needed. He thought one practical manager who knew the work would have done far better.
Charles Darwin marvelled at how much hard work habit lets a person endure. Steady, repeated effort can build a capacity that looks impossible to someone who has never done it.

preview.text:
The neighbourhood of Porto Praya, viewed from the sea, wears a desolate
aspect.  The volcanic fires of a past age, and the scorching heat of a
tropical sun, have in most places rendered the soil unfit for
vegetation.  The country rises in successive steps of table-land,
interspersed with some truncate conical hills, and the horizon is
bounded by an irregular chain of more lofty mountains.  The scene, as
beheld through the hazy atmosphere of this climate, is one of great
interest; if, indeed, a person, fresh from sea, and who has just
walked, for the first time, in a grove of cocoa-nut trees, can be a
judge of anything but his own happiness.  The island would generally be
considered as very uninteresting, but to anyone accustomed only to an
English landscape, the novel aspect of an utterly sterile land
possesses a grandeur which more vegetation might spoil.  A single green
leaf can scarcely be discovered over wide tracts of the lava plains;
yet flocks of goats, together with a few cows, contrive to exist.  It
rains very seldom, but during a short portion of the year heavy
torrents fall, and immediately afterwards a light vegetation springs
out of every crevice.  This soon withers; and upon such naturally
formed hay the animals live.  It had not now rained for an entire year.
When the island was discovered, the immediate neighbourhood of Porto
Praya was clothed with trees, [1] the reckless destruction of which has
caused here, as at St. Helena, and at some of the Canary islands,
almost entire sterility.  The broad, flat-bottomed valleys, many of
which serve during a few days only in the season as water-courses, are
clothed with thickets of leafless bushes.  Few living creatures inhabit
these valleys.  The commonest bird is a kingfisher (Dacelo Iagoensis),
which tamely sits on the branches of the castor-oil plant, and thence
darts on grasshoppers and lizards.  It is brightly coloured, but not so
beautiful as the European species: in its flight, manners, and place of
habitation, which is generally in the driest valley, there is also a
wide difference.

books.title: Flatland
books.author: Edwin A. Abbott
books.subject: maths
books.licence_note: Author died 1926. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Edwin Abbott shows in Flatland that a penny looks round from above but like a straight line from the table's edge, so what we perceive depends on where we stand.
Edwin Abbott satirises a rigid class order that calls its own privilege natural and divine, showing how a hierarchy can dress itself up as the way things must be.
In Flatland, Abbott's narrator works out a shape from how faintly its edges fade, a reminder that patient attention to small differences can reveal what a quick glance misses.
In Flatland, Abbott has his narrator argue that everyday life depends on trust that people are what they appear to be, and that without it even simple arrangements become impossible.
In Flatland, Abbott's narrator finds life dull without colour, a reminder that small pleasures in how things look can make ordinary days feel rich.
In Flatland, Abbott shows a skilled speaker calming a crowd by working through each group's self-interest in turn, a reminder that fair-sounding persuasion can hide its real aim.
Abbott's narrator notices that people who say conduct is fixed by nature still scold their children as if choices really matter, a sharp reminder that we all act on the belief that choices count.
In Flatland, Abbott's Lineland monarch is sure his one straight line is the whole of space, a reminder that what we have never experienced can be quietly mistaken for all there is.

In Flatland, Abbott shows each new dimension forming when a shape sweeps through the one before it: a point makes a line, a line makes a square, and a square makes a cube. Simple steps can build something new.
In Flatland, the Stranger from Spaceland sees the insides of things that Flatlanders can only see as edges, a reminder that a higher vantage point can show what is hidden from below.

In Flatland, Abbott's Sphere argues that what a lower world sees of a higher thing is only a slice, so a Circle in Flatland is really a Sphere passing through, a reminder that a partial view can mislead.
In Flatland, the Sphere teaches by Analogy: a point, line, square and cube have 1, 2, 4 and 8 corners, so a clear pattern can reveal what cannot yet be seen directly.

In Flatland, the narrator finds that the household he had only inferred in his head is far richer when he sees it directly, a reminder that reasoning about people and things is no substitute for looking at them.
In Flatland, the Sphere points out that seeing everything does not make anyone more just, merciful or loving, so being able to see more is not the same as being better.
In Flatland, the Council answers a new idea by ordering its messenger silenced, a warning about how established powers can resist ideas that unsettle them.
In Flatland, a pattern can suggest a new truth, but only evidence can settle it, as the narrator reasons by analogy toward a fourth dimension while the Sphere asks for the facts.
In Flatland, the Sphere finds that lecturing a self-satisfied mind rarely shifts it, a humbling reminder that telling people they are wrong seldom changes what they believe.

In Flatland, the narrator struggles to get an idea across because his readers lack the tools to picture it, a useful reminder to check whether others share the frame you are working in before you explain.
In Flatland, a claim that cannot be pointed to or measured is hard to test, so Abbott's narrator is silenced by the challenge to show what he means. Ask what would show an idea is true.
Abbott's Square warns that every mind, whatever its dimension, is prone to the same error of locking up the idea it cannot yet picture. Blind spots are a common human habit.
Abbott closes by hoping readers will neither say "this can never be" nor claim to know all about what lies beyond experience, a humble stance towards anything not yet tested.

preview.text:
In such a country, you will perceive at once that it is impossible that
there should be anything of what you call a “solid” kind; but I dare
say you will suppose that we could at least distinguish by sight the
Triangles, Squares, and other figures, moving about as I have described
them. On the contrary, we could see nothing of the kind, not at least
so as to distinguish one figure from another. Nothing was visible, nor
could be visible, to us, except Straight Lines; and the necessity of
this I will speedily demonstrate.

Place a penny on the middle of one of your tables in Space; and leaning
over it, look down upon it. It will appear a circle.

But now, drawing back to the edge of the table, gradually lower your
eye (thus bringing yourself more and more into the condition of the
inhabitants of Flatland), and you will find the penny becoming more and
more oval to your view, and at last when you have placed your eye
exactly on the edge of the table (so that you are, as it were, actually
a Flatlander) the penny will then have ceased to appear oval at all,
and will have become, so far as you can see, a straight line.

books.title: Passages from the Life of a Philosopher
books.author: Charles Babbage
books.subject: computing
books.licence_note: Author died 1871. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Charles Babbage said he would rather spend his strength on better work than on writing the story of his own life.
Charles Babbage observed that a famous name is an empty basket until you fill it with your own work.
Charles Babbage said he would keep any fact, even an unflattering one, because it might prove useful one day.
Charles Babbage said truth was the only object of his search, and he never turned aside from fear of where it might lead.
As a boy, Charles Babbage settled a doubt with a simple test, deciding in advance he would accept whatever result it gave.
Charles Babbage held that every school room should have a library, since his own school's books gave him so much.
Charles Babbage noticed a learner can solve the same problem in any notation, so the idea behind the symbols matters more than the symbols.
Charles Babbage saw that even small duties can absorb the time needed for the work that matters most, so guard your focus.
Charles Babbage re-marked his exam papers with new numbers and reached the same answer, a good way to test a judgement before acting on it.
Charles Babbage won over reluctant teachers by giving them ready-made examples, so the new method spread because it saved them effort.
Charles Babbage judged a calculating machine by one test: could it finish its work once set, with no person steering it along the way?
When his finished wheels failed, Charles Babbage traced the fault to a small mismatch at the workshop, not to his own reasoning.
Charles Babbage guarded against errors by building a check into the parts themselves, so a wrong piece would jam the test wire.
Charles Babbage showed that stepwise working is fast but lets one slip spread through everything after it, so a direct check at the end catches errors.
Charles Babbage held that a learner who knows what he does not know has overcome one of the greatest obstacles to learning, and has the courage to say so.
Charles Babbage tested a guessed rule against a case he already knew, found it three times too big, and corrected it before trusting it.
Charles Babbage saw that a slow job can be sped up by doing the easy parts all at once and dealing with the carries as a separate step.
Charles Babbage tried to teach his machine to foresee the carries it would need and then act on that foresight, an early picture of planning ahead.
Charles Babbage's funding talks went wrong because no minute was taken and the terms were never made clear, so write down agreements at the time they are made.
Charles Babbage's funders had each supplier bill checked by independent engineers before paying it, a simple control any business can copy.
While his work was stalled, Charles Babbage used the pause to think about first principles, and found an idea he had not reached while busy.
When an idea is too uncertain to put in writing, Charles Babbage asked for a face-to-face talk, since a conversation can show what a letter cannot.
Charles Babbage found that his plans had been misunderstood because he had not stated clearly what he was asking for, so say the ask plainly.
Charles Babbage pressed for a final decision because an open-ended job with no end date kept him from planning anything else.
Charles Babbage would not give opinions on costs outside his expertise, having learned not to trust his own judgment in areas he had not mastered.
Lord Rosse set out a practical order for a big decision: first ask whether it can be estimated, then whether anyone can build it, and only then whether it is worth the cost.
Charles Babbage's machine was slow to build because it needed new tools first, and those tools later proved useful for other work, so early effort can pay off elsewhere.
Charles Babbage warned that inventions with no precedent always take longer than planned, and each change made along the way brings hard choices.
Charles Babbage held that a clear system of signs is a thinking tool, and said he could not have invented the Analytical Engine without his own notation.
Charles Babbage set himself a rule: except in rare cases, never do a task himself if he could afford to hire someone who could do it well.
Charles Babbage found that tweaking a stuck design got him nowhere, so he went back to the principle itself, and that is what finally broke the problem open.
Charles Babbage found that explaining his plan to an assistant exposed flaws in it, and each question he was asked showed him another gap to fix.
Charles Babbage separated the instructions a machine follows from the material it works on, so one design could handle many different jobs.
Charles Babbage designed his engine to check each input against the number it had asked for and refuse any mismatch, so a wrong input could not pass unnoticed.
Charles Babbage showed that a limited machine can do unlimited work if it is given enough time, trading the infinity of space for the infinity of time.
Charles Babbage noted that the hard part of a process was rarely the steps themselves, but knowing when to change course, which is the judgment that no fixed list can supply.
Charles Babbage held that whenever a result is sought, the question should be which course of working reaches it in the shortest time.
Charles Babbage showed that errors in hand-copied tables bred further errors in every correction, so accurate records need checking at the source.
Charles Babbage labelled his drawings by a consistent rule, so fixed parts and moving parts could be told apart at a glance, which made complex machines much easier to understand.
Charles Babbage wanted his finished engine placed where the most people could see it daily, because work hidden away is hard for anyone to learn from or champion.
Charles Babbage saw crowds gather when his machine ran with someone explaining it, but a cramped spot with no one to talk people through it wasted the interest.
Charles Babbage argued that cost-cutting is only respectable when judgment guides it, not favouritism, since cutting the cheap, useful expense while favouring insiders is a false economy.
Charles Babbage said that before choosing a design, you should ask several strong firms for proposals and open the plans to public criticism, which guards against a poor choice.
Charles Babbage found that a capable friend's clear explanations reached far more people than he could alone, so he trusted that friend with access.
Charles Babbage kept no notes of his private talks with the Duke of Wellington, believing that writing down a friend's words breaks faith and wears away trust.
Charles Babbage found that a hard problem in his own field, too many combinations to check, was the same problem a great commander faces, showing how ideas carry across fields.
Charles Babbage recalled the Duke of Wellington as an economist of time, who changed his dress in his carriage on the way so he arrived on time without rushing.
Charles Babbage said the Duke of Wellington kept backup plans ready: once he had weighed the alternatives, he could quickly build a new plan when the first one broke.
Charles Babbage faulted the good men on a council for lacking the moral courage to oppose a president's dictation, or to set it aside later when it was irregular.
Charles Babbage offered to retract a public remark once the papers proved him wrong, and wanted the correction made in a suitable manner.
Charles Babbage thought his friend, the poet Samuel Rogers, had a genuine kindness that was not appreciated enough, and kept walking him home as his strength failed.
Charles Babbage described two ways to write: draft the whole plan roughly and polish later, or finish each sentence before moving on, which he thought the poet Samuel Rogers did.
Charles Babbage recorded that the older Biot found new inquiry slow and painful, but could still advance the studies of his youth with help from younger friends.
Charles Babbage saw that Alexander Humboldt took real pleasure in helping any inquirer, however humble, with his information and advice.
Charles Babbage remembered that Alexander Humboldt's sharp remarks about colleagues were caustic at times but never ill-natured, a fair standard for wit.
Charles Babbage recorded a princess who set out alone to nurse her ailing uncle and father-in-law, and he admired her devotion to family duty.
Charles Babbage tested a bold idea in the water and found it both risky and workable, and he concluded that a real trial is the only way to learn which is true.
Charles Babbage admired the younger Brunel, who met a sudden breach in the Thames Tunnel by calmly getting workmen to form a line and pass tools to the spot.
Charles Babbage understood a large effect by building a small model of it and tracing its motion with smoke, a sound way to learn how something really works.
Charles Babbage checked a difficult field measurement by repeating it and finding it agreed to within about a foot, which is the habit of verifying before trusting a number.

preview.text:
Others write their personal history, lest some kind friend should
survive them, and, in showing off his own talent, unwittingly show them
up.

Others, again, write their own life from a different motive—from fear
that the vampires of literature might make it their prey.

I have frequently had applications to write my life, both from my
countrymen and from foreigners. Some caterers for the public offered
to pay me for it. Others required that I should pay them for its
insertion; others offered to insert it without charge. One proposed to
give me a quarter of a column gratis, and as many additional lines of
eloge as I chose to write and pay for at ten-pence per line. To many of
these I sent a list of my works, with the remark that they formed the
best life of an author; but nobody cared to insert them.

I have no desire to write my own biography, as long as I have strength
and means to do better work.

The remarkable circumstances attending those Calculating Machines,
on which I have spent so large a portion of my life, make me wish
to place on record some account of their past history. As, however,
such a work would be utterly uninteresting to the greater part of my
countrymen, I thought it might be rendered less unpalatable by relating
some of my experience amongst various classes of society, widely
differing from each other, in which I have occasionally mixed.

This volume does not aspire to the name of an autobiography. It relates
a variety of isolated circumstances in which I have taken part—some
of them arranged in the order of time, and others grouped together in
separate chapters, from similarity of subject.

books.title: The Ten Books on Architecture
books.author: Vitruvius
books.subject: design
books.licence_note: Ancient author, translator died 1910. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Vitruvius held that a builder needs both practice and theory. Practice is skilled hands-on work, and theory is the ability to explain why the work succeeds.
Vitruvius held that honesty and not grasping for perks are what make a professional trustworthy, because no work can be done rightly without integrity.
Vitruvius advised that a well drafted contract protects both client and builder, so disputes get settled before the work starts rather than after it is finished.
Vitruvius held that a professional does not need to master every field, only to know enough of the core principles to judge the work of specialists.
Vitruvius held that good design comes from two things: reflection, meaning careful and laborious thought about the plan, and invention, meaning solving hard problems with fresh ideas.
Vitruvius defined economy as managing materials and site well and balancing cost against common sense, so a builder uses local alternatives rather than chasing what is costly to find.
Vitruvius said every good building must be durable, convenient and beautiful. Durability starts with sound foundations, and convenience means a layout that never gets in the way of use.
Vitruvius tells how Marcus Hostilius, when a town kept suffering, investigated thoroughly before acting, then moved the whole town to a better site.
In Vitruvius, Alexander turned down a showy design for a city on Mount Athos because the site could not feed it. A plan has to work in the real world, not just look good on paper.
Vitruvius described how early builders improved their shelters by watching what others made and adding their own new details, so their skill grew step by step.
Vitruvius warned that bricks used before they had properly dried would shrink and pull the finish away from the wall, so rushing materials causes failures that show up later.

Vitruvius advised letting quarried stone lie open to the weather for two years, then using the pieces that weathered badly in the foundations and only the sound ones above ground. Test before you commit.
Vitruvius criticised builders who rushed to finish the visible faces of a wall and packed the middle with loose rubble, because the hidden part is what fails. Do not skimp on the work nobody sees.
Vitruvius argued it is better to spend properly on sound construction than to save time and money with cheap methods that put people at risk later.
Vitruvius complained that good work often goes unnoticed while charm and flattery win praise, so he chose to let his knowledge speak through a written treatise.
Vitruvius praised Hermogenes for dropping inner rows of columns that added nothing, which saved cost and labour without weakening the effect. Cut what is not needed.
Vitruvius noticed that tall parts of a building look as if they lean back, so he tilted them slightly forward to appear upright. Good work is judged from where the viewer stands.
Vitruvius complained that many writers left only scattered fragments on architecture, so he set out to present the whole subject in one ordered plan.

Vitruvius tells how the Corinthian capital came from Callimachus noticing an acanthus growing around a basket on a grave. A good designer looks closely at ordinary things and finds a new idea in them.
Vitruvius held that a building's form must be justified by the truth of its structure. An element copied from a source where it could not exist has no valid reason to be in the copy.
Vitruvius held that the ideal arrangement applies only when nothing stands in the way. When the site forbids it, the principle should bend to suit the place.
Vitruvius noted that timbers laid tight against each other trap moisture and begin to rot. Leaving a small gap for air keeps a structure sound.
Vitruvius wrote briefly for readers with little leisure, explaining hard terms in short plain sentences so they could be remembered. Clear and concise beats sheer volume.
Vitruvius held that what bears the load should be stronger than what sits above it, taking his lesson from trees that are thick at the root and taper toward the top.
Vitruvius showed that dropping ornament saves labour and cost, while carrying columns unbroken to the roof lends a building dignity. Simplifying always trades something away.
