Vitruvius held that a rule of proportion should bend where use demands it. When materials run short, a good builder makes sensible adjustments through practical experience, not rigid formula.
Vitruvius held that the same kind of work calls for different standards depending on its purpose. A temple needs dignity, while a public colonnade needs elegance and usefulness.
Theophrastus, quoted by Vitruvius, held that learning goes with a person anywhere, while trust in luck leaves a person unsteady. Learning is the surer support.
Vitruvius concluded that surplus is of no real use and that feeling no want is the true riches. He valued learning above money.
Vitruvius preferred a good reputation to wealth, and held that a professional should wait to be asked for work rather than chase it.
Vitruvius held that a house must be designed for its climate, and that good building can amend by art what nature would otherwise spoil.
Vitruvius observed that a building looks different close up than from a height, and that the eye can mislead, so a designer must judge what the viewer actually sees.
Vitruvius held that a small room cannot simply borrow the proportions of a large one. Scale has to be fitted to size or the room will not be usable.

Vitruvius held that a house should fit its owner's standing and daily use. Rooms open to visitors should be arranged differently from private ones, and people of ordinary means need not build grand entrances.
Vitruvius gave a simple test for daylight. Draw a line from the top of the obstructing wall to the point needing light, and if plenty of open sky shows above it, the room will be bright enough.
Vitruvius describes guest rooms with their own front doors, so visitors need not be shown into the family's rooms. Good design protects privacy while still welcoming people.
Vitruvius held that weight must sit directly over solid support, because a load resting in the middle of a span will sag and wear a building down over time.
Vitruvius advised building so that worn timbers can be replaced without propping up the whole structure. A sound design makes repairs easy.
Vitruvius judged a work under three heads: the craftsman's delicacy, the owner's generosity in spending, and the architect's design of proportion. Each earns its own credit.

Aristophanes, the librarian, exposed plagiarists by checking the recited poems against the original books on the shelves. Careful reading and checking sources is the way to see through a borrowed work.

Vitruvius said he drew on earlier writers as from springs, put no false name on their work, and aimed to go somewhat further. Building honestly on what came before is the honest way to add something new.
Vitruvius noticed that materials move as they dry and settle, so a rigid wall running into a floor will crack it. Leave room for movement rather than locking everything solid.
Vitruvius tested lime by how it clung to a hoe. Lime that sticks like glue was ready, and weak lime showed itself. Check your materials before you rely on them.
Vitruvius compared thin plaster to a thin silver plate: it cracks and fades, while a solid base takes a lasting finish. Put the strength underneath before the polish.
Vitruvius found that layering two sets of reeds at right angles stops a surface from cracking. Crossing the grain of a layer below is a simple way to hold a finish together.
Vitruvius argued that skill alone does not make a picture right. A work that shows what cannot exist should not be praised for its craft, and good work should rest on what is real.
Vitruvius observed that costly colours can hide a lack of craft, so people stop noticing refinement. Do not mistake showy materials for skill.
Vitruvius recorded that a finish which looks right indoors can fade in open sunlight. Test a finish in the conditions it will actually face.

Vitruvius held that a searcher should study the nature of each piece of ground before digging, since different soils hold their resources in different ways. Learn the terrain before you commit to the work.
Vitruvius trusted a long straightedge with plumblines over sighting tools, which he called deceptive. When wind spoils one method, he checked with a second, such as a water groove.
Vitruvius split a city's water into tanks by use, so private taking could not drain the public supply, and asked the users to help pay to keep the system running.
Vitruvius advised lowering a lit lamp into a well before anyone climbs down. If the flame goes out, the air is unsafe, so ventilate first. Test for danger before you enter.
Vitruvius argued that writers whose books sharpen the minds of many deserve honour as much as athletes, whose gains end with themselves.
Vitruvius tells how Archimedes checked a crown's gold by the water it pushed aside. Sometimes a stuck problem gives way to a fresh way of measuring it.
Vitruvius admired Democritus for setting down only the principles he had himself put to the test. Share what you have actually proven, not just what sounds right.
Aristarchus of Samos, as Vitruvius reports him, held that the moon has no light of her own and shines only by reflecting the sun, so her phases follow her position relative to it.
Vitruvius credits Thales, Anaxagoras, Pythagoras and others with working out nature's laws by patient study, with each generation building on the last.
Vitruvius says a sundial has to be laid out for its own place, because the equinox shadow of the same upright pin differs from town to town.
Vitruvius tells how Ctesibius, a barber's son, tinkered with a hidden cord to lift a shop mirror, and that play with a small problem led him to the principles of compressed air.
Vitruvius describes an old law in Ephesus where an architect who names a price for public work must cover any overrun from his own property, and he wishes Rome had the same rule.

preview.text:
3. Owing to this favour I need have no fear of want to the end of my
life, and being thus laid under obligation I began to write this work
for you, because I saw that you have built and are now building
extensively, and that in future also you will take care that our public
and private buildings shall be worthy to go down to posterity by the
side of your other splendid achievements. I have drawn up definite rules
to enable you, by observing them, to have personal knowledge of the
quality both of existing buildings and of those which are yet to be
constructed. For in the following books I have disclosed all the
principles of the art.

CHAPTER I

THE EDUCATION OF THE ARCHITECT

1. The architect should be equipped with knowledge of many branches of
study and varied kinds of learning, for it is by his judgement that all
work done by the other arts is put to test. This knowledge is the child
of practice and theory. Practice is the continuous and regular exercise
of employment where manual work is done with any necessary material
according to the design of a drawing. Theory, on the other hand, is the
ability to demonstrate and explain the productions of dexterity on the
principles of proportion.

2. It follows, therefore, that architects who have aimed at acquiring
manual skill without scholarship have never been able to reach a
position of authority to correspond to their pains, while those who
relied only upon theories and scholarship were obviously hunting the
shadow, not the substance. But those who have a thorough knowledge of
both, like men armed at all points, have the sooner attained their
object and carried authority with them.

books.title: The Elements of Drawing
books.author: John Ruskin
books.subject: art
books.licence_note: Author died 1900. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: John Ruskin held that children should be praised for effort and hard work, not for cleverness, because praise for cleverness teaches them to work for vanity.
John Ruskin argued that owning fewer things sharpens attention and makes the pleasure in them deeper.
John Ruskin warned against letting the demands of manufacture interfere with training the artist. Build the best skill first, then decide how to produce it at scale.
John Ruskin held that an artist's excellence rests on refined perception, which a good teacher can develop, while invention is a personal gift.
John Ruskin held that learning to see truly matters more than the drawing itself, and that seeing carefully is what lets us appreciate other people's work.
John Ruskin argued that a great skill is worth some tedious toil, and that nobody gains it while refusing to pay any price for it.
John Ruskin said the simple rules of perspective are too few and crude for subtle forms, so the eye must do the hard work and rules serve only as a rough aid.
John Ruskin said learning to draw is worth the effort when it has a real purpose, such as seeing beauty more clearly or understanding great work, rather than just looking accomplished.
John Ruskin believed almost anyone willing to pay the price of steady practice can learn to draw, because talent changes the speed of learning, not whether it is possible.
John Ruskin taught that the first thing to see in any subject is its broad patch of colour, before any texture or detail.
John Ruskin advised that doing two or three things perfectly teaches faster than doing many things badly.
John Ruskin advised learners to test each attempt against the original, find the faults and correct them patiently, rather than rushing on.
John Ruskin said the real difficulty of drawing is keeping the hand under full control at every part of a line, not making a sweep that only looks free.
John Ruskin urged students to look closely at ordinary things, such as the sky through a window or a white cup, to notice how light changes gradually across them.
John Ruskin argued that good work is usually done slowly, and that boldness meant as carelessness or show is a poor guide. He thought Nature itself is never bold at her work.
John Ruskin said the main point is that what we intend is right. If we see rightly and mean rightly we will get on, even if the hand staggers, so do not torment yourself over imperfect lines.
John Ruskin said the temptation in any work is to be slovenly, and that a deliberate check, like an outline, forces idle habits into precision.
John Ruskin said the jagged edges left in a practice exercise are an exact measure of your unskillfulness, so use them to see where to improve.
John Ruskin noted that even the best artists do not always get their work quite to their mind, and that they go back to touch it up.
John Ruskin said that if you can draw a simple stone well, with its roundness, you can draw most things, since nearly everything in nature is rounded.
John Ruskin held that true boldness comes from care and that ease in any skill rests on early precision. He said Nature will show you nothing if you set yourself up as her master.
John Ruskin said that when your work disappoints you, it is usually too coarse or too uneven rather than wrong. Make it more tender and true, and it will become more powerful.
John Ruskin said the best observer sees how a thing looks without needing reasons, and that a rule explained badly makes people caricature a third of nature and miss two-thirds.
John Ruskin mocked the painter who follows a rule like shadow is always darker, instead of painting what is really there, and the critic who then wonders why the hand looks so light.
John Ruskin said it is always dangerous to treat anything in art as a rule, and that the only way to find the truth is to look for it.
John Ruskin advised that a little bit finished well is worth more than many scrawls, and that when you feel yourself scrawling, you should stop and come back the next day.
John Ruskin said the greatest masters took pains over humble patterns, because learning to draw simple manufactured forms prepares you for the living world.
John Ruskin advised finishing a small area with full care rather than a large one carelessly, working steadily up to a marked limit so you always see what is done and what is not.
John Ruskin held that we must be right at whatever cost of pains, and that only then can we be right with freedom.
John Ruskin said that when work goes wrong it is usually refinement that is missing, not force. Fix errors slowly rather than rushing at them or rubbing out in despair.
John Ruskin said to keep the broad masses distinct before any detail, because we see the big shapes first, and that it is better to leave some detail unfinished than to lose the overall relations.
John Ruskin urged drawing whatever is actually there, background included, ugly or not, because only a complete and honest study shows whether you got it right.
John Ruskin urged a steady habit of careful study, several times a week, and looking at a subject from more than one side, since each view shows a different structure.
John Ruskin said to draw nothing more than you really see. Once you understand that, the difference between a careful drawing and a mere miniature comes down to honesty about what the eye sees.
John Ruskin held that technique is useless until you truly know the form. If you cannot draw a branch perfectly you will not draw a tree, so gain decisive form first and add method after.
John Ruskin said a beginner learns best by thinking long over a few good things, and that people who seem to know everything rarely know anything rightly. Beware of handbook knowledge.
John Ruskin said copying fine work reveals the real labour and skill behind it, and helps you understand how people must work when they have to do anything in this world.
John Ruskin advised that for an amateur it is better to err on the side of precision than vagueness, and to learn from more than one master.
John Ruskin said shorthand methods are only a way of recording an object in the time you have, not a display of your own cleverness, so keep trying to draw things rightly.
John Ruskin warned that you will not make a great drawing by copying a master's rough handling, because great work is economical, not hurried. Learn what he knew and felt first.
John Ruskin held that a good artist sees masses rather than edges, and can say more with rapid shade than with outline alone.
John Ruskin said that if you have no time to draw carefully, do not draw at all, because hasty marks waste your work and spoil your taste.
John Ruskin said that keeping order amid mystery is harder than creating mystery, so early practice should lean always to the definite side, keeping the eye true enough to find its way.
John Ruskin said we see only flat colours and learn to read them as light and shade. A good artist recovers the innocence of the eye and sees colours as they are.
John Ruskin said the aim is not a free hand but a right one, since a great master's swiftest touch is still under perfect control. There is no merit in doing wrong easily.
John Ruskin said that when a whole scene is too full to copy, judgment must choose what is principal or fleeting, and effort should go into concise methods that catch the characteristic points.
John Ruskin said the wise observer sees which way things are going, while the dunce draws everything as if it stood still. Great people in life and in art share this habit.
John Ruskin said there is no recipe for any subject. Look at the thing as it is, and do not draw from what someone told you to do with grass or stone.
John Ruskin said a quarter hour of true zeal and patience beats a whole day of sulky, inattentive labour, and that you should never work when you are tired.
John Ruskin said speed for its own sake, or dash for show, is harmful, but a quick and decisive hand can work alongside accuracy. Occasional practice at speed guards against slow, servile habits.
John Ruskin noted that at a distance the shadow is often more important than the thing casting it, and that a great painter reduces distant objects to their essential shadows.
John Ruskin warned that anxiety for a piece of work to look nice is fatal to progress. Care only that it is right and that you learn something while making it.
John Ruskin advised beginners to choose rough, worn and clumsy subjects over neat, polished ones, since the ugly things that look wrong at first often teach the most.

John Ruskin held that a pattern which is too uniform must be false, because individual variety is as true to nature as the unity of the whole. Any rule that makes every part alike has missed something.
John Ruskin argued that inferior work shows order only by giving up individuality, while great work keeps both order and difference. He thought the difference is what gives work its life.
John Ruskin warned that once the hand falls into a habit it runs on by itself, and that a good worker must stop and decide each mark, or the fingers become the master.
John Ruskin said we see nature only in fragments, so we should be humble about how well we understand the people around us. Much that seems clear turns out to be full of mystery on closer watching.
John Ruskin said the shortcuts commonly used for water are vain. Calm water holds a true picture of what is above it, and only patient drawing of the reflections gives a true effect.
John Ruskin said some things have no rule at all. For the true curve of a shore, only the instinct of an eye trained by long looking can judge what is right.
John Ruskin told students not to be frightened by complexity, nor to hope to render it in a hurry. Look well first and separate each part of the effect before drawing.

preview.text:
i. It may perhaps be thought, that in prefacing a manual of drawing, I
ought to expatiate on the reasons why drawing should be learned; but
those reasons appear to me so many and so weighty, that I cannot quickly
state or enforce them. With the reader's permission, as this volume is
too large already, I will waive all discussion respecting the importance
of the subject, and touch only on those points which may appear
questionable in the method of its treatment.

ii. In the first place, the book is not calculated for the use of
children under the age of twelve or fourteen. I do not think it
advisable to engage a child in any but the most voluntary practice of
art. If it has talent for drawing, it will be continually scrawling on
what paper it can get; and should be allowed to scrawl at its own free
will, due praise being given for every appearance of care, or truth, in
its efforts. It should be allowed to amuse itself with cheap colors
almost as soon as it has sense enough to wish for them. If it merely
daubs the paper with shapeless stains, the color-box may be taken away
till it knows better: but as soon as it begins painting red coats on
soldiers, striped flags to ships, etc., it should have colors at
command; and, without restraining its choice of subject in that
imaginative and historical art, of a military tendency, which children
delight in, (generally quite as valuable, by the way, as any historical
art delighted in by their elders,) it should be gently led by the
parents to try to draw, in such childish fashion as may be, the things
it can see and likes,--birds, or butterflies, or flowers, or fruit.

books.title: How to Listen to Music
books.author: Henry Edward Krehbiel
books.subject: music
books.licence_note: Author died 1923. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Henry Edward Krehbiel argued that the ability to listen attentively to music is better proof of musical talent than playing an instrument or singing, and is far rarer.
Henry Edward Krehbiel observed that music is the art people practise most and think about least, and that a frank diagnosis has to come before any cure.
Krehbiel argued that the greatest need is not more teachers of playing and singing, but people who can teach others how to listen to music.
Henry Edward Krehbiel warned that the most harmful writers on music are foolish rhapsodists who sound sensitive instead of pointing listeners to the music itself.
Krehbiel held that music has a material side grasped by the intellect and a spiritual side reached through the imagination, and that real appreciation needs intelligent hearing.
Krehbiel observed that music exists only while it sounds, so the listener must rebuild it in memory at every hearing, and that memory is what makes deeper listening possible.
Henry Edward Krehbiel held that repetition is the basic principle of building anything in music, and that this is what makes memory easy to use while listening.
Krehbiel advised listeners to follow a work's main themes, because that reveals the unity that makes a symphony one whole rather than a set of loose pieces.
Henry Edward Krehbiel held that intelligent listening does not require knowing what music means beyond itself, and that each listener works that out for himself.
Krehbiel said composers listen for beauty and the overall design, while many listeners get lost hunting for pictures and stories in the details.
Moritz Hauptmann held that music says the same thing to everyone, and that any confusion comes from people trying to put their own feelings into words.
Krehbiel credited Beethoven as the first great democrat among musicians, one who made the aristocracy of genius outrank the aristocracy of birth.
Krehbiel said that chamber music depends on sympathy between performers and listeners, and that the musical life of a community shows in whether it flourishes.
Krehbiel held that a title or motto can help a listener, but a piece must be judged by its music itself, not by how clever its commentary is.
Krehbiel observed that music cannot copy water, but it can do what water does and so suggest water, which he saw as the better way to describe things in sound.
Krehbiel noted that true composers avoid musical cartooning, and that music which only copies external things loses artistic value.
Beethoven titled his Pastoral symphony as more expression of feeling than painting, which Krehbiel saw as an admonition that should always guide listeners.
Krehbiel argued that the Classic and Romantic principles are two forces whose opposition keeps art alive, and that what is Romantic today tends to become Classic tomorrow.

Krehbiel said that learning to tell the instruments of an orchestra apart adds an intellectual pleasure to listening without spoiling the sensuous enjoyment, and opens the ear to beauties never noticed before.
Krehbiel noted that Bach understood the possibilities of instruments far ahead of his time, when most composers still used them only to support the voices.
Krehbiel recounted how a critic mocked Berlioz's delicate violin effect at its Paris premiere, a reminder that a listener can mistake a clever intention for a fault.
Krehbiel held that a melody must suit the instrument it is given to, since a bold fanfare turned into a weak-voiced wind part can become absurd. The fit between idea and medium matters.
Krehbiel recalled Mendelssohn's view that the trombones are too sacred to use often, a reminder that the most powerful voices keep their impact through restraint.
Krehbiel argued that no composer can write down signs for everything he means, so a performer's taste and judgment are needed to give the music life for an audience.
Krehbiel warned that a symphony is one unified work, not a string of unrelated pieces, and that a listener who hears only the parts misses the whole.
Krehbiel said the movements of a symphony are held together by a key relationship and by an emotional bond, and that the emotional bond is the more elusive one yet essential to any truly great work.
Krehbiel described the first movement of a symphony as a three-part shape: present the themes, develop them, then return to them. Knowing that shape lets a listener follow the whole.
Krehbiel observed that in the hands of great composers like Beethoven and Schumann, playfulness can invite thoughtfulness rather than merriment, blending deep melancholy with wild humour.
Krehbiel explained that a work can express many moods and still hold together when its main idea is presented in many transformations. Unity comes from that one idea reappearing, not from sameness.
Krehbiel noted that Ysaye thought a performer had little to add after Beethoven, since composers are usually more eloquent with their own ideas than the performers who play them.
Krehbiel recorded Gluck's aim that an opening should prepare the audience for what follows, serving as a kind of argument for the piece.

Krehbiel held that technical mechanics are a low plane of art, and that real emotional power comes from the player's touch, which is why the most skilled mechanician can still be outshone by a player with more soul.

Krehbiel noted that Bach changed his hand technique, bringing in the thumb and loosening his fingers, because his polyphonic style demanded it. Technique should serve the music, not the other way round.
Krehbiel quoted Kullak and Dannreuther to show that Beethoven changed form only as his expression required, not for the sake of novelty. Change should come from need.

Krehbiel warned that music fitting an instrument well is not thereby good. Content matters more than how idiomatic a piece is, and praising a piece only for its fit with the instrument can hide weak content.
Krehbiel observed that Liszt, for all his showmanship, set aside his own vanity when he played Beethoven and became a peerless interpreter. The best performers serve the work in front of them.
Krehbiel observed that opera audiences often enjoy the music and ignore the words, even though the lyric drama has grown so that its words and drama now matter far more than they once did.
Krehbiel argued that opera is a reasonable art form, since it aims to charm the senses, stir the emotions and persuade the reason all at once, and that it is no absurdity when done well.

Krehbiel held that the best light opera, such as Gilbert and Sullivan, satirises a popular folly with a smile, the way good comedy corrects manners. When it sinks into vulgarity it loses that purpose.

Krehbiel argued that a true lyric drama should stay musical from beginning to end. Switching between speech and song keeps the audience pulled between the real and the ideal, so the drama never fully takes hold.
Krehbiel observed that music can turn an inner emotional struggle into the feel of a story full of incident, as in Tristan, where the outward action is barely more than a meeting of two lovers.
Krehbiel judged that singing exists to serve dramatic meaning, and that technical display without feeling is hollow, however dazzling it sounds.

Krehbiel explained Wagner's starting point: music had become the end when it was meant to be the means. Words, music, staging and action should work together, with music raising the drama to a higher power.

Krehbiel warned that memorising a catalogue of labels teaches little. A listener learns more by noting the attributes that give a passage its mood and fitness, because feeling the mood matters more than knowing the name.
Krehbiel held that taking part in music, especially singing in a choir, teaches more than listening alone, because it builds sympathy and gets to the heart of a piece faster than anything else.
Krehbiel held that size is no sign of merit in a singing group, and that a well-trained group of modest size can perform most choral music well.

Krehbiel argued that a strong group needs each member to give up some of their individuality for the blend, while still mastering their craft, because the collective effect depends on each person's precision.

Krehbiel criticised performances that sing every piece the same way, and held that each work should be sung according to its own character, which is how a familiar piece like Handel's Messiah can regain its freshness.

Krehbiel advised listeners to hear music in terms of the purpose it was written for. Palestrina's church music aims to exalt a mystery rather than voice personal feeling, so judging it as personal drama misses its point.
Krehbiel explained that a drama presents incident to the eye, while an oratorio relates, expounds and celebrates its story through the ear, so the listener has to build the scene in the imagination.
Krehbiel held that musicians, critics and public keep each other honest through friction, and that a world with no tension among them would bring stagnation rather than harmony.

Krehbiel argued that a critic who simply echoes the crowd, measuring praise by applause, is failing the audience. People enjoy being flattered, but the critic's real job is to guide judgment, even when it is unwelcome.
Krehbiel advised that before judging a work, you should go to the author to find his meaning, not your own, and only judge it afterward if you feel qualified.
Krehbiel noted that the public are neither bad judges nor good critics: their popular verdicts are quick and swayed by fashion, while a judgment built on principle and precedent lasts longer.
Krehbiel held that a judge of music need not be a composer, but must be able to feel with one. Discussing a work only through its technical side, as a pedant does, misses what music is for.
Krehbiel held that a critic's duty is to separate excellence from defect, and to look harder for beauty as the faults grow more apparent. Without sympathy, he said, judgment is also lacking.

preview.text:
The capacity properly to listen to music is better proof of musical
talent in the listener than skill to play upon an instrument or
ability to sing acceptably when unaccompanied by that capacity. It
makes more for that gentleness and refinement of emotion, thought, and
action which, in the highest sense of the term, it is the province of
music to promote. And it is a much rarer accomplishment. I cannot
conceive anything more pitiful than the spectacle of men and women
perched on a fair observation point exclaiming rapturously at the
loveliness of mead and valley, their eyes melting involuntarily in
tenderness at the sight of moss-carpeted slopes and rocks and peaceful
wood, or dilating in reverent wonder at mountain magnificence, and
then learning from their exclamations that, as a matter of fact, they
are unable to distinguish between rock and tree, field and forest,
earth and sky; between the dark-browns of the storm-scarred rock, the
greens of the foliage, and the blues of the sky.

[Sidenote: _Ill equipped listeners._]

books.title: The Book of War
books.author: Sun Tzu and Wu Qi
books.subject: strategy
books.licence_note: Ancient authors, translator died 1915. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: Sun Tzu and Wu Qi held that an enemy should never be completely surrounded, because a way out keeps him from fighting desperately and weakens his resolve.

Sun Tzu and Wu Qi treated the spirit of the troops as a decisive factor in war, and held that a general far from home is the best judge of events and that interference from the ruler causes delay and disaster.
Sun Tzu advised starting with discretion and letting the opponent make the first move, then striking only once he has tired or made a false step.
Wu Qi insisted that war should not begin until a careful comparison shows that victory is certain, since the army that wins plans first and then attacks.
Sun Tzu and Wu Qi held that good intelligence about the enemy is vital, and that managing the people who gather it is among the most delicate duties a leader has.
Sun Tzu and Wu Qi held that knowing the opponent, preparing well and training thoroughly give an army its strength, and that a deep sense of what is at stake can drive it to win.
Sun Tzu held that a leader must understand five matters, the Way, Heaven, Earth, the Leader and Law, and that any plan must bend as circumstances change.
Sun Tzu held that a strategist's real plans should stay hidden, and that the side with more of the key advantages tends to win before any fighting starts.
Sun Tzu warned that a long campaign drains morale, equipment and funds, and that no country has ever benefited from a prolonged war.
Sun Tzu taught that the supreme art is to subdue an opponent without fighting, and that a good leader is judged by how well he protects the lives and welfare of the people.
Sun Tzu warned that a siege should be avoided where possible, since rushing in before the time is ripe wastes people for no purpose.
Sun Tzu held that a leader who knows both himself and his opponent has nothing to fear, while one who knows only his own side will eventually be defeated.
Sun Tzu held that the best leader wins without a desperate struggle and attacks only once the opponent has made his own mistakes, so true success is not measured by applause.
Sun Tzu taught that steady, ordinary moves combined with unexpected ones keep an army from defeat, and that the unexpected move is often what breaks the opponent.
Sun Tzu held that a good leader builds the spirit of his people, waits patiently for the opportunity, and pushes hard the moment an opening appears.
Sun Tzu held that a leader who keeps the opponent guessing where the blow will land forces him to be weak everywhere, while the attacker keeps his strength.
Sun Tzu advised never repeating a stratagem that has already won, and likened a sound approach to water, which shapes itself to the ground it flows over.
Sun Tzu held that a leader who changes his tactics to suit his adversary keeps control of the outcome, since nothing in war stays fixed.
Sun Tzu held that a leader who does not know the terrain and the intentions of others cannot lead well, and that he should wait for a favourable moment and adjust as circumstances require.
Sun Tzu advised not to take the bait an opponent offers, not to press a desperate enemy, and to leave him a way out when surrounding him.
Sun Tzu named five faults of a leader that prove disastrous: reckless impetuosity, over-caution, quick temper, rigid propriety, and excessive concern for his troops.
Sun Tzu advised treating suspicious terrain such as narrow passages and thick woods as likely places for an ambush, and never assuming the opponent will simply not come.
Sun Tzu taught that a leader can read an opponent's intentions from small signs, such as a sudden offer of truce made without consultation, which he took as a mark of hidden design.
Sun Tzu held that obedience follows from humane but consistent treatment, and that orders are obeyed when the general and his soldiers are in sympathy.
Sun Tzu taught that most defeats come from the general's own incapacity, such as strong troops under weak officers or vague orders, rather than from bad ground or bad luck.
Sun Tzu held that a good general cares for his soldiers like children, yet warned that over-indulgence makes them unserviceable, so care has to be balanced with firm command.
Sun Tzu observed that speed sustains morale, and that a leader should strike before the opponent is ready and from a direction he does not expect.
Sun Tzu held that a general should be calm, fair and prudent, keep his plans from his own people, and vary his routes so that his intentions cannot be guessed.
Sun Tzu held that a leader must study the hearts of his people as carefully as the ground, and that people who cannot turn back tend to commit fully.
Sun Tzu held that plans should be shaped to the actual circumstances of the opponent rather than fixed rules, and that an army facing real danger fights hardest.
Sun Tzu warned that war should not be started because a ruler is angry or in a passion, and that a leader should move only where there is a real prospect of victory.
Sun Tzu held that knowledge of the opponent comes through people who bring it back, so good intelligence depends on watching the people who gather it closely.
Sun Tzu observed that passion passes but a lost state cannot be restored, so a wise leader is circumspect before acting.
Sun Tzu held that informants must be treated with benevolence and uprightness and watched closely, since the truth is not otherwise obtained from them.
Wu Qi told the Lord of Wei that weapons mean little without a competent leader, and that a ruler's conduct reveals his real mind more than his words do.
Wu Qi held that a leader must establish harmony among his people before a great undertaking, since discord in the state, the army or the camp rules out different courses of action.
Wu Qi observed that victory is easy in attack but hard in defence, and that those who gained power through many victories were rare, since repeated wars wear a people out.
Wu Qi named ambition, greed, hatred, internal disorder and hardship as the common causes of war, a list that still explains many conflicts.
Wu Qi held that when capable people are put in authority and the people feel secure and proud of their leader, the foundations of strength are already laid.
In the story of Lord Chuang of Chu, a ruler troubled to have no equal among his advisers is shown as wiser than one pleased to be the wisest, since good advisers are the foundation of a realm.
Wu Qi analysed each rival by its character, such as a proud and neglectful court or a disciplined but brittle army, and chose tactics to suit each one's weakness.
Wu Qi held that trained troops are of little use when their leaders are despised and they lack a spirit of sacrifice, so respect and purpose matter as much as training.

Wu Qi listed signs that a rival is weak and ripe to strike, such as a confused command and a shaken army, and also named signs of a strong rival that should be avoided, such as wide lands and capable officials.
Wu Qi advised advancing when a course looks good and retreating when it is known to be difficult, judging each undertaking honestly before committing to it.
Wu Qi held that the foundation of victory is good government, with clear laws and just rewards and punishments, since a large army is of no use without them.
Wu Qi held that procrastination is a leader's greatest enemy, since disasters to an army are born of indecision.
Wu Qi held that men are lost through lack of ability, so training is the first requirement of any army, and that skill spreads when those who know a thing teach others.
Wu Qi held that people and the animals they depend on must be well treated and in accord before either can be used well, and that work should be paced with discretion.
Wu Qi named five qualities of a leader: reason, preparation, determination, vigilance and simplicity, and held that courage alone is not enough.
Wu Qi taught that a leader's personality can decide the value of a whole force, and that dignity, virtue, benevolence and courage calm people and remove their doubts.
Wu Qi advised learning the character of an opposing leader, since a rival who is careless, greedy or proud can be enticed or set against his own people.
Wu Qi judged an opposing general by his discipline, since a wise general keeps his ranks in order and avoids reckless pursuit, while a disordered and eager army signals a fool.
Wu Qi held that the outcome of a hard contest depends on the schemes of a wise person rather than on might, and that the weaker side should choose narrow ground where its numbers matter less.
Wu Qi advised a leader not to pursue too far after a victory, and to send envoys first to learn an opponent's intentions before committing to battle.
Wu Qi taught that in hard country a leader should watch the enemy's ranks closely and strike the moment confusion appears.
Wu Qi advised a leader to climb high and see the whole ground before acting, and to wait for conditions to change before moving.
Wu Qi advised that a conquering army should spare homes and livelihoods and show the people there is no cruel intent, so that those who wish to surrender are received.
Wu Qi showed Lord Wen that rewards given openly by merit, with care for the families of the fallen, lead people to go to war gladly and without waiting for orders.
Wu Qi held that a small body of desperate men can strike fear into a far larger force, so encouragement and a clear sense of purpose can count for more than numbers.

preview.text:
Written in the fifth century B.C., Suntzu and Wutzu still remain the
most celebrated works on war in the literature of China. While the
chariot has gone, and weapons have changed, these ancient masters have
held their own, since they deal chiefly with the fundamental principles
of war, with the influence of politics and human nature on military
operations; and they show in a most striking way how unchanging these
principles are.

When these books were written, China was a conglomerate of
principalities in continual ferment. Personal ambition and intrigue,
and not the wishes of the people, were the main factors in these wars.
Patriotism, or a popular cause, could not, therefore, be relied on
to maintain the _moral_ of the levies. Instead of these, what may be
called the force of despair is pointed out as the most powerful agent
in giving cohesion and energy to an army. The general is urged to
take a vigorous offensive; and to act at a distance from his base,
where defeat means disaster, and where desertion is minimised owing to
the distance from home. He should, in fact, burn his boats before an
action, or, in Chinese phrase, act as one who removes the ladder from
under those mounted upon the roof.

On the other hand, every care must be taken not to render the enemy
desperate; and, as an instance of this, Sun observes that an opponent
should on no account be completely surrounded. A loop-hole of escape
weakens the resolution of the general and the energy of his troops.

books.title: The Prophet
books.author: Kahlil Gibran
books.subject: philosophy
books.licence_note: First published 1923, author died 1931. Public domain in the USA and Australia.

notes.text: In The Prophet, Gibran shows Almustafa feeling that staying too long in one place is to freeze and be bound in a mould, so leaving is a kind of growth.
Gibran has Almustafa ask whether the day of parting might be the day of gathering, suggesting that endings can also be a harvest.
Gibran observes through the people of Orphalese that love often does not know its own depth until the hour of separation.
In The Prophet, Gibran says that love tests and prunes a person so that they may come to know the secrets of their own heart.
Gibran writes that love gives nothing but itself and takes nothing but from itself, and that love is sufficient unto love.
In The Prophet, Gibran advises partners to share their lives while keeping their own selves, like the strings of a lute that quiver to the same music yet remain separate.
Gibran holds that the truest giving is of oneself rather than of possessions, and that those who give with joy are rewarded by the joy itself.
Gibran says that receiving with courage and grace is a gift in itself, and that a receiver should not carry a heavy debt of gratitude, which can become a yoke.
Gibran teaches that work keeps us in step with life, and that idleness makes us strangers to the seasons.
Gibran holds that work done with love is love made visible, while work done with indifference yields a bitter bread that feeds only half a person's hunger.
Gibran says that joy and sorrow are inseparable, since the well that fills our laughter is often the same well that was filled by our tears.
Gibran warns that comfort can enter a house as a guest, then become a host and finally a master, so that we end up serving the things we own.
Gibran notes that clothes can give privacy yet can also become a harness, and that much of our need to hide comes from shame rather than from nature.
Gibran holds that trade brings abundance only when it is conducted in love and kindly justice, since without them it breeds greed in some and hunger in others.
Gibran argues that wrongdoers are not strangers to the rest of us, since a wrong done in a community springs partly from a hidden will shared by all.
Gibran says that remorse is often a truer justice than any punishment, since it calls in the night so that people wake and look honestly at themselves.
Gibran likens human laws to sand-towers that children build and destroy, and warns that those who live only by the shadows cast by laws miss the sun that casts them.
Gibran argues that freedom is not won by burning law books or toppling tyrants, since the law and the tyrant are first built within ourselves.
Gibran says reason alone is confining and passion alone burns itself out, so the soul should lift reason to the height of passion and guide passion with reason.
Gibran advises treating reason and passion like two loved guests in one house, honouring neither above the other, so that the heart can rest in reason and move in passion.
Gibran says pain breaks the shell of our understanding, as the stone of a fruit must break so that its heart can stand in the sun.
Gibran says that the self is a boundless sea, so we should say we have found a truth rather than the truth, and meet the soul walking on our own path.
Gibran holds that a true teacher does not hand over his wisdom but leads students to the threshold of their own mind, since no one can give another their understanding.
Gibran holds that friendship exists for the deepening of the spirit, not for what can be gained from it, and that a friend meets our needs without filling our emptiness.
Gibran says that much talk half murders thought, since a thought caged in words may open its wings but cannot fly.
Gibran suggests that what we call evil is often good that has lost its way, hungry and thirsty, and that a divided self is not evil but only divided.
Gibran says time, like love, is undivided, so the seasons we measure should each embrace the others, and today should hold both remembrance and longing.
Gibran says prayer is the expansion of yourself into the living air, and should be offered in the fullness of joy as well as in distress.
Gibran says pleasure is a freedom-song but is not freedom itself, so we should sing it with a full heart without losing our hearts in the singing.
Gibran advises remembering past pleasures with gratitude, as one remembers a summer harvest, rather than with regret that clouds the mind.
Gibran uses the bee and the flower to show that giving and receiving pleasure can both be a need and an ecstasy, with each giving the other life.
Gibran says beauty is not a need but an ecstasy, a heart enflamed and a soul enchanted rather than a hand held out for something.
Gibran holds that faith cannot be separated from our daily work, since all our hours are wings that carry the soul from self to self.
Gibran says daily life is itself a temple, and that we should bring our whole selves, our work and our care for others into it, since neither revery nor adoration can rise above our deeds.
Gibran likens our fear of death to a shepherd trembling before a king who is about to honour him, and suggests that trust in our dreams opens the way to what lies beyond.
Gibran says that a farewell need not be an ending, since a truth well spoken returns in a clearer voice and finds its way into the understanding of others.
Gibran says that our needs change but our love does not, and that a day which does not fully satisfy us can still be a promise of another day.
Gibran says people should not be measured by their smallest deed or their failures, since judging an ocean by its foam is a poor way to reckon its power.
Gibran observes that the kind often give without knowing they give at all, and that a kindness which gazes at itself in a mirror turns to stone.
Gibran admits that he was both believer and doubter, and that he put his own finger in his wound to deepen his belief in others and his knowledge of them.
Gibran praises the patient captain who waits quietly while the sails and rudder grow restless, a picture of steady leadership that does not hurry the moment.
Gibran ends his farewell by saying that if people meet again in memory, they will speak together and sing a deeper song, so that a parting can deepen a bond rather than end it.

preview.text:
Then the gates of his heart were flung
open, and his joy flew far over the sea.
And he closed his eyes and prayed in the
silences of his soul.

*****

But as he descended the hill, a sadness
came upon him, and he thought in his
heart:

How shall I go in peace and without
sorrow? Nay, not without a wound in the
spirit shall I leave this city.

Long
were the days of pain I have spent
within its walls, and long were the
nights of aloneness; and who can depart
from his pain and his aloneness without
regret?

Too many fragments of the spirit have I
scattered in these streets, and too many
are the children of my longing that walk
naked among these hills, and I cannot
withdraw from them without a burden and
an ache.

It is not a garment I cast off this
day, but a skin that I tear with my own
hands.

Nor is it a thought I leave behind me,
but a heart made sweet with hunger and
with thirst.

*****

Yet I cannot tarry longer.

The sea that calls all things unto her
calls me, and I must embark.

For to stay, though the hours burn in
the night, is to freeze and crystallize
and be bound in a mould.

Fain would I take with me all that is
here. But how shall I?

A voice cannot carry the tongue and
the lips that gave it wings. Alone
must it seek the ether.

And alone and without his nest shall the
eagle fly across the sun.

*****

Now when he reached the foot of the
hill, he turned again towards the sea,
and he saw his ship approaching the
harbour, and upon her prow the mariners,
the men of his own land.

And his soul cried out to them, and he
said:

Sons of my ancient mother, you riders of
the tides,

How often have you sailed in my dreams.
And now you come in my awakening, which
is my deeper dream.

Ready am I to go, and my eagerness with
sails full set awaits the wind.
